imp_text: This application proposes to investigate the role and underlining mechanisms for XLF in NHEJ repair and to develop an XLF-targeted radio/chemosensitizer. The central hypothesis is that XLF and its binding partner, XRCC4 form a filament that binds the two ends of a DSB and promotes their juxtapositioning to facilitate end joining. Aim 1 will define the interaction of XLF with DNA and its role in end joining fidelity. Aim 2 will determine to what extent XLF/XRCC4 disruption by inhibitors is a viable strategy for chemo- and radiosensitization of cancer cells. Success of the proposed research will provide mechanistic details on the role of XLF in NHEJ and insights in both radio/chemosensitization as well as carcinogenesis. The strategies being used in Aim 1 are using cell-free extract system to explore XLF binding to DSB in, which could be powerful. However, solely in this way, it is not so clear how the PI will be able to obtain convincing and solid data to define the role and mechanism of XLF and XRCC4 in end joining. The application lacks direct approaches such as filament formation of XLF and XRCC4 with DSB using purified XLF & XRCC4 -/+ Ku complex.

imp_text: The project aims to uncover the structural mechanism for circadian rhythm regulation, specifically the molecule interactions with CLOCK:BMAL1 and its flexible C-TAD domain. This work would provide a structural perspective of key activation event, namely a conformational “switch” induced by a cis-trans proline isomerization. The overall methods to be used are appropriate for direct observation of this event on a micro- to millisecond timescale and for mapping minimalistic binding sites for other regulators to CLOCK:BMAL1. If successful, the proposal may elucidate a structural mechanism linking circadian misregulation and somatic cancer. However, the proposal lacks clear milestones and quantifiable criteria for success, does not sufficiently justify the impact of the work other than a general corollary with cancer, and does not justify the requested funds. Overall, the project will have a marked positive impact on the circadian regulation field.
sig_text_str: . Diseases affecting large groups within the population (e.g. diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer) are linked to circadian misregulation. . Currently the structural mechanism of a key regulator (CLOCK:BMAL1) is unknown. . The proposed work to elucidate the structural dynamics of CLOCK:BMAL1 regulation will begin to describe the structure-function relationship for circadian regulation. . The work will benefit from the PI’s previously determined crystal structure of CLOCK:BMAL1. . A better understanding of the structural interactions of CLOCK:BMAL1 with PER, CRY, and the PASD1 mimic may provide insight for new/complimentary therapies for the aforementioned complex diseases. . From end of Aim 2: “We expect that by doing do, we will highlight novel points for intervention by small molecules to modulate clock timing or reinforce oscillator robustness in human cancer.”
sig_text_wkn: . More detail about previous approaches to therapeutically target CLOCK:BMAL1 would provide better context on their strengths/weaknesses and how structure-based hypotheses may have improved their outcome. . If there have been no attempts, it is important to describe how one would attempt to create a therapeutic using the basic research in this proposal. Given what is currently known, what is the best target? . Assuming the proposed work is successful, it is difficult to ascertain the practicality of the results by other cancer researchers other than “it will be clear once a structural mechanism is known.” . Is it known whether re-establishing a circadian rhythm can have a therapeutic effect on cancer, etc. or is it known to only reduce long-term risks?

PI’s group can perform all gold-standard circadian assays in-house.

Although PI has applied NMR to this type of task, is it indeed the most cost-effective tool for solving the problem? Site-directed mutation perturbation coupled with their existing assays could achieve a similar result. Is NMR the best approach or just the one the PI favors? . Much effort is spent identifying minimal binding motifs, afterwards structural studies seemed focused on peptide interactions. While these motifs may be sufficient for binding, they are arguably too far removed from larger domain constructs or full-length proteins and can lead to a limited structural representation of the protein complexes under investigation. imp_text: The project aims to extend the computational capabilities of the BMRB by including emerging technologies to extract higher-level information from experimental NMR, incorporate experimental and simulated descriptions of structural dynamics, and to improve the process of standardizing and depositing highly-variable experimental NMR data from researchers and to access that detailed data for future use. This represents a special application where the main budget request is for day-to-day operations of the BMRB. Some new structural biology research is proposed to address the open issue of quantifying NMR-based structure quality; however, much of the proposal focuses on integrating existing gold standard NMR analysis software to provide a more holistic view of the deposited data. That being said, the letters of support clearly demonstrate that BMRB is a critical resource to the worldwide NMR community and its dissolution would result in a field-wide loss of productivity, hinder experimental reproducibility, and ultimately lead to wasted effort where the nature of the data becomes ephemeral as technology and techniques advance. The research team has abundant expertise and experience in NMR research and software development to carry out the project. Overall, the project will exert a significantly high impact on the field.
sig_text_str: . NMR has the ability to directly observe different types of structural dynamics. . Characterizing and understanding protein flexibility/plasticity/dynamics is a critical part of understanding the structure-function relationship for a biopolymer. . BMRB is already a valuable and indispensable resource for structural biologist, collecting and curating NMR spectral data, and has an existing global user base. . Many scientific software programs have been developed using or rely on BMRB-hosted data. . Loss of the services provided by BMRB will be detrimental to the structural biology community. . Structure quality metrics to describe the strengths and limitations of an NMR structure for the average biologist are sorely needed.

Automating basic validation inquiries so that depositions can be more quickly validated at the partner wwPDB website, which provides faster feedback about errors to depositors for correction. . More complete automatic annotation to characterize whether regions are well or ill-defined, and the extended ability to characterize whether ill-defined regions are due to disorder/flexibility or experimental error. . imp_text: The investigators propose to develop an amino-acid peptide based inhibitor of a serine protease called mesotrypsin as a therapy for metastatic prostate cancer. The investigators have worked together previously on developing understanding of the potential role of this protein in prostate cancer progression and are established in a research environment that is equipped to conduct the proposed investigation. Evidence that the institution is prepared to conduct research in prostate cancer includes a funded SPORE by the NIH, which provides support for an interdisciplinary team to conduct research in this area. Preliminary data support the hypothesis that (1) mesotrypsin represents a key protease in prostate cancer progression, and (2) that potent and selective inhibitors of mesotrypsin could be used to define the specific role of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer models, and (3) [these inhibitors] could also potentially offer novel therapeutics. Preliminary data are particularly in support of (1) and are suggestive that (2) and (3) are possible. These preliminary data strongly support the work that is proposed in Aim 1. However, concerns over the likely instability of the amino acid based inhibitors that are proposed dampen enthusiasm for Aims 2 and 3. Further, the dependency of Aim 3 on Aim 2 raises concerns that inability to complete Aim 2 could lead to failure to advance to Aim 3 research. It is suggested that at least an alternative strategy to screen small molecules that inhibit the activity of mesotrypsin could have a higher likelihood of advancing to a inhibitor that could advance to clinical use.

imp_text: Colorectal cancer one of the most diagnosed cancers in the United States and new therapies are needed for this difficult to treat disease, establishing the significance of the project. The investigators have established collaboration with Merck, GSK and this support for the project adds enthusiasm that the work can translate into routine use if successful. Integration of patient-derived tumor grafts into small animal studies is innovative. Pathways of resistance and inhibition are substantiated by literature evidence and some preliminary data, but inability to read specific figures in the proposal dampens enthusiasm. The investigators propose a substantial amount of work that includes clinical and preclinical research and the workload seems potentially too much to handle and may be more effectively handled in two proposals. The clinical trials could easily be substantiated independently of proposed tumorgraft research.
sig_text_str: Colorectal cancer is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers in the United States and resistance that develops quickly to current therapies leads to poor prognosis for colorectal cancer patients. The investigators have identified specific pathways that may lead to resistance and propose to develop a detailed understanding of the mechanisms of these resistance pathways and potentially to identify new targets that could lead to improved outcomes for these patients. The goal of developing an adaptive approach in which information gathered from tumor biopsies could be used to adapt the therapeutic strategy has potential if successful of identifying therapeutic strategies that are effective/ineffective and providing an avenue for treatment regimens to be modified based on clinical evidence. This has the potential to improve outcomes for patients. The investigators provide metrics that identify specific subpopulations of patients that might benefit from the information that is gathered through the adaptive approach.

study_section: Developmental Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: The investigators propose to develop a more detailed mechanistic understanding of the relationship between melanogenesis and drug resistance to BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib and tumor suppressor PTEN pathway related signaling/expression. Further study explores the potential for B-Catenin activation as a potential pathway that may be responsible for the development of melanoma and resistance to therapy. These studies lead to the potential for combination therapies for metastatic melanoma that target multiple pathways. The proposed study is innovative and given the prognosis for metastatic melanoma (and rapid increase in incidence of the disease), the potential impact is significant. The facilities and investigator are excellent and the investigator has intiated MTA’s with several companies to obtain drugs in the experimental stage from several pharmaceutical drug companies. The investigator has published several manuscripts on the science that leads to the hypothesis of the proposed investigation. The long-term, over­arching goal of the research is to contribute to the design of new melanoma therapies that increase the overall anti-tumor response of drugs; forestall the onset of drug resistance and; and mitigate the pro-tumorigenic side effects of BRAF inhibitors. Overall, the research proposed here has the potential to illuminate a deeper mechanistic understanding of how BRAF and PI3’-kinase signaling pathways cooperate in melanoma initiation and potentially in the development of resistance. Moreover, Aims 2 and 3 will inform development of new regimens of combined pathway-targeted therapy. The investigators suggest these pathway interdependencies may have broad applicability. Preliminary data in GEM models developed by the investigators support the hypothesis of that BRAF mutant cells depend on PTEN suppression for melanomagenesis. The investigators have assembled an appropriate panel of cells and established MTAs to gain access to experimental therapeutics from pharmaceutical companies. Minor technical issues with specific experimental plans for Aim 2 are noted. Overall, this is an excellent proposal and is regarded with high enthusiasm.
sig_text_str: Melanoma incidence is increasing faster than any other cancer and is the most diagnosed cancer in young adults under 30 in the US. The combination therapies are based on success of a BRAF inhibitor called vemurafenib, which targets the BRAF proliferative pathway that is constitutively active in melanoma cells with a V600E mutation (~50% of melanomas). While initial response to vemurafenib treatment of melanoma can be remarkable, only about 50% of melanoma patients possess the mutation and only about 80% of those patients respond. In addition, resistance to the drug develops rapidly in almost all patients. The investigators hypothesize that a simultaneous inhibition of the AKT pathway through PI3K has the potential to circumvent resistance and provide insight on the resistance mechanism that could lead to greater understanding of the potential for combination therapies and the underlying resistance mechanisms of melanoma cells in the in vivo setting. The potential for significant findings concerning the mechanistic understanding that could be illuminated through this research lies in evidence that suggests that the combination of mutated BRAFV600 and PTEN silencing is reported present in ~44% of human melanomas 4,22-25. However, the mechanism(s) by which mutationally activated BRAFV600E cooperates with PTEN and/or INK4A/ARF silencing to promote conversion of normal melanocytes to metastatic melanoma cells remains to be fully elucidated. Thus, the combination therapies explored can result in new treatments and in new mechanistic understanding of the disease.

imp_text: Meso-trypsin is shown to be a key component of the mechanism that drives progression and metastasis of human prostate cancer, the second leading cause of death in men. Based on a modified scaffold (e.g. BPTI), a polypeptide-based, non-hydrolyzable drug will be developed that has pico-molar specificity. Because the PRSS3 gene (which encodes meso-trypsin) is transcriptionally upregulated in lung, colon, and breast cancers, the proposed drug development may expand the therapeutic options for treating other metastatic cancers.

imp_text: Non-Homologous End Joining (NHEJ) is the primary double strand break repair pathway in mammalian cells that opposes the intended effects of chemotherapy and ionizing radiation on DNA for destroying tumor cells. Therefore, the central strategy is to inhibit NHEJ so as to enhance chemo- and radio-sensitivity. This proposal focuses on the binding and mapping of a protein XLF, a newly discovered component of the NHEJ apparatus.  XLF is a binding partner of XRCC4, a core NHEJ protein. XLF provides a preferred target because, unlike the other NHEJ components, the only proposed role for XLF is in the NHEJ process during which it is thought to form a filament with XRCC4. In Specific Aim 1, the PIs will investigate a model for the role of XLF in NHEJ. In Specific Aim 2, the synthesis (based on a X-ray crystal structure) and testing of a well-designed, highly diversified library of unique cell permeant peptides containing unnatural and cyclized amino acids will be used to identify those peptides that inhibit the XLF/XRCC4 interaction (and possibly filament formation), and thereby sensitize intact cells to ionizing radiation. Owing to earlier success with synthetic peptides that disrupt BRCA1 interactions with other DNA repair proteins, the proposed research has a high probability to impact strategies for overcoming chemotherapy and radio-resistance of tumors.

imp_text: Proposed studies of melanoma-genesis and progression will explore the cooperation of mutation-activated BRAFV600E.MEK and silencing of PTEN in a genetically-engineered mouse (GEM) model that recapitulates certain aspects of human melanoma pathophysiology. Melanoma generated in mice bearing BRAFV600E and PTENnull (already known to generate rapidly growing melanomas) will be compared with BRAFV600E and constitutively active PI3K. Mouse melanoma growth via BRAFV600E synergizes with constitutively-activated PI3’K and can be blocked by a PI3’K inhibitor.  Since the latter only generates slow-growing melanomas as compared with malignant melanomas generated by the PTENnull mutation, it would seem that PTEN has other sites of action contributing to the malignant phenotype.  A weakness is that most of the aims focus largely on the relationship of the canonical PI3K pathway and BRAFV600E to evaluate those PI3K pathway components that contribute to the development of melanomas that (at best) are slow-growing in a GEM model.  However, human melanoma cell lines do not have activated PI3K. Therefore, it seems questionable whether the central focus on constitutively-activated PI3K is the relevant strategy for human melanoma. Studies may reveal a combination of drugs used with the GEM models that inhibit genesis of melanoma having the BRAFV600E/PTENnull phenotype. Such findings could inform clinical diagnosis and therapeutic options for melanoma treatment.

These models will be used to evaluate the cooperation of BRAFV600E with PI3’K, and compared with PTEN silencing. . Use of GEM to evaluate combinations of clinically-relevant drugs for treating melanoma . Determination/identification of signaling components as potential diagnostic indicators and drug targets in melanoma cell lines. . Combined inhibition of PI3’K and MEK is highly effective for inhibiting protein synthesis in cell lines.  In the PI3’K pathway, studies will address the dependency on pAKT and other downstream targets in the context of PTEN silencing.

study_section: Basic Mechanisms of Cancer Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: This application proposes to define how mesotrypsin promotes prostate cancer progression in order to develop mesotrypsin inhibitors with improved selectiviey and stability toward mesotrypin digestion, as well as to evaluate mesotrypsin inhibitors for therapeutic efficacy in models of prostate cancer progression.  The Significance is considered a major strength of the proposal, as the project addresses a significant need for developing inhibitors for enzymes that may promote prostate cancer progression and/or invasiveness. It was unclear what percentage of primary prostate cancers might benefit from mesotrypsin inhibition. Unclear on the significance these inhibitors will have in preventing or halting bone metastases, the most common metastatic site for advanced prostate cancer. The investigator and environment are excellent, the PI was at the time an Assistant Professor with a 10 year research record on serine protease inhibition and substrate recognition.  One weakness was that the PI lacks publications and expertise in prostate cancer research, appearing to have focused mostly on breast cancer research previously. Investigator does not have phage display experience and this would be critical for aim 2. Innovation is considered to be moderate since the investigators already have isolated a prototype drug with relatively high affinity (nM range) and may not need new inhibitors if this prototype is effective in animal models. Mesotrypsin is a novel therapeutic target and this is a strength.   In Approach, experiments were generally well-designed and appropriate controls proposed. One major weakness is that too much is proposed for the scope of the grant, in particular in Aim 1. Preliminary data on the prototype in animal models is necessary to determine whether we need to generate the complex pM inhibitors or whether the prototype already is effective in inhibiting mesotrypsin.  Comparison of whether inhibiting mesotrypsin inhibition in culture is equally or more effective as inhibiting another type of enzyme with relevance to prostate cancer invasion would have been optimal (shRNA or pharmacological inhibition). The collaborator with expertise in phage display does not have effort on the grant and this is a concern with feasibility of aim 2b. Potential alternatives are identified and are adequate. A timeline was not given and this is considered inadequate.  Overall an excellent proposal considered to have moderate impact on the field of inhibition of prostate cancer invasion.

study_section: Developmental Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: This application proposes to enhance understanding of the mechanisms of colorectal cancer (CRC) resistance to treatment and to identify new targets for therapy, leading to clinical trials that can potentially used more effective combinations of agents to treat CRC. Also, biomarkers may be identified for selecting patients most likely to respond to new therapies.  The Significance is considered a major strength of the proposal, as CRC is the most commonly diagnosed cancers in the US and the second most common cause of cancer related deaths. Overcoming resistance to treatment could have major and immediate impact for CRC patients. Examining the effect of Kras mutations on the downstream mutations enhances significance.  The investigator and environment are outstanding, the PI is an MD/PhD with a strong record in CRC and in clinical trials. Innovation is considered to be moderate since the molecules and types of pathways targeted are not novel. However, major strengths are the novelty of using CRC tumorgrafts, which retain patient stroma until at least F3, and the ability to examine drug efficacy on these grafts from the same patients enrolled in the clinical study. Technology of assaying for RPPA and RNAseq on the tumorgrafts is also innovative.  In Approach, experiments were generally well-designed and appropriate controls proposed.  Potential alternatives are identified and are adequate.  A timeline was given and appears adequate. The clinical trial component is ambitious for the timeline but given the expertise, it seems appropriate.  Overall an excellent proposal considered to have high impact on the field of enhancing  therapies for CRC as it may lead to a greater understanding of the downstream events involved in PI3K and Kras signaling.The immediate and long term impact were well articulated.

imp_text: This application proposes to examine the necessity, sufficiency and elucidate the mechanisms of how BRAF and PI3K interact and cooperate in the genesis of melanoma. The  implications of the project are to increase overall response rate to antitumor therapy, forestall the onset of drug resistant disease, and reduce the pro tumorigenic side effect of BRAF inhibitors. The Significance is considered a major strength of the proposal, as the project addresses a significant need for understanding the mechanistic foundation for developing and implementing rational combination therapies for treating melanoma patients with mutated BRAF oncogene. The investigator and environment are outstanding, the PI has a strong record in BRAF and related signaling in melanoma and also a strong history of funding in the field. Collaborators are outstanding and the addition of physician scientist interactions are key to potentially rapid translation of the discoveries gained. Innovation is considered to be high since novel and relevant genetically engineered mouse models were proposed and also a panel of melanoma derived cell lines representing the key subtypes of the disease.  In Approach, experiments were generally well-designed and appropriate controls proposed. The letter of support section is extensive and many experts have lent their support to the approach. The GEM model is particularly robust and well suited for the experiments proposed. Potential alternatives are identified and are adequate. A timeline was given and appears adequate. Overall an outstanding proposal considered to have high impact on the field of melanoma combination therapy.

imp_text: Pre-mRNA splicing is an essential step in gene expression and mutation of the minor spliceosomal U4atac snRNA leads to severe genetic diseases such as MOPD 1.  This proposal seeks to understand the molecular basis of these genetic defects by analyzing:  1) how the mutations affect snRNA and snRNP stability, 2) how a mutation affects changes in the transcriptome, and 3) the expression patterns and functional defects associated with SNPs in the snRNA genes.  The overall impact is judged to be high considering the biomedical significance and potential for producing new insights into minor spliceosome function and its connections with gene expression.
sig_text_str: . Pre-mRNA splicing is an essential process in all eukaryotic cells and it is important to develop a better understanding of how splicing is affected by genetic polymorphisms. . The direct relationship to the human disease MOPD1 is a fascinating aspect of this proposal.
inv_text_str: . The investigator has a strong record of accomplishment in the pre-mRNA splicing field.  The investigator also maintains strong collaborations and it noted that a previous collaboration resulted in a high impact publication in Science.
inn_text_str: • The transcriptomic analysis of snRNA genes is a somewhat novel approach.  Currently there is little understanding of which snRNA genes are differentially expressed in the various tissues, and this is something that needs to be studied.  This aspect of the proposal has strong potential to produce innovative insights into gene expression, pre-mRNA splicing, and the role of SNPs in genetically inherited diseases. • The orthologous spliceosome system is an innovative approach for testing the effects of SNPs on snRNAs.

The induced pluripotent stem cells containing the MOPD 1 mutations will be a very valuable reagent and strengthens the approach. . The orthologous spliceosome assay is an excellent approach for testing the effects of SNPs in cells.

imp_text: DNA replication is critically important to living cells and mutations in the replication machinery are associated with genome instability and cancer.  This proposal is from a productive leader in the DNA replication field.  The proposal aims to answer fundamentally important questions, including the identity of the replicative polymerases responsible for leading and lagging strand synthesis, interaction partners with the CMG complex, and influence of mutations in Psf1 on replication.  The proposal contains a large amount of impressive preliminary data.  The feasibility and potential impact are judged to be very high.
sig_text_str: . DNA replication is a highly significant and fundamentally important problem in biology. Despite decades of research, there are still fundamental knowledge gaps in this field. Ribosome biogenesis is an important biological process for all living organisms and is not fully understood.  The proposal will test a model in which the methyltransferase Bud23 protein activates the helicase Ecm16 to displace the U3 snoRNA and Imp4 protein. imp_text: This is a well-conceived and carefully drafted proposal by an experienced investigator who has focused his career on drug discovery research, specifically new approaches to treating cancers driven by mutation-activated BRAF. Here, he proposes to study the role of combined inhibition of the BRAFV600E mutation and the PI3’-kinase-AKT pathway versus single agent inhibition on melanoma cell growth and metastasis progression both in genetically engineered mouse (GEM) models and melanoma cell lines.  The study is built around a series of three specific aims, the first to create GEM models that will test the necessity of PI3’-kinase-AKT signaling for the cooperation between oncogenic BRAFV600E and PTEN silencing in melanoma progression, the second that combined blockade of both BRAFV600E and PI3’-kinase signaling will elicit profound and durable regression of BRAFV600E/PTENNull melanomas compared to single agent therapy, and the third that combined blockade  of  BRAFV600E and  PI3’-kinase is synergistic for  inhibiting melanoma cell proliferation. He has assembled a strong team of collaborators and consultants who will provide reagents, mutant mouse strains, tumor cell lines, analytical methods, statistical support and pathology analysis. His study is based on a reasonable hypothesis that the variation in response, duration and outcome to BRAFV600E mutation therapy is modulated by the related PI3’-kinase-AKT signaling pathway, although he acknowledges that both other intrinsic and extrinsic factors may modulate this response. Surprisingly, the issue of whether PI3’-lipid signaling is not essential or a minor requirement for BRAFV600E/PTENNull melanomagenesis has not been addressed to date.  This is an important issue to resolve, but it may also prove to be a contingency for the subsequent work of the proposal; should it prove true, the necessity of performing the work of aims 2 and 3 is questionable. Although the PI has back-up plans for other pathways to study, doing so would represent a significant shift from the proposed studies.

imp_text: This is a well-written proposal that seeks to understand the function of newly discovered scaffold protein XLF in the repair of DNA double strand breaks by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), and identify peptide inhibitors that could inhibit DNA repair by preventing interaction of XLF with XRCC4. These inhibitors may be useful in sensitizing tumor cells to radiotherapy and chemotherapy. The investigator team is highly qualified to pursue the proposed research. The PIs of this multi-PI grant have complimentary expertise in the areas of DNA repair and the synthesis of peptide library. The focus on XLF as a therapeutic target is a relatively unexplored area. The aims of the proposal are reasonable and include elegant methodologies, such as unnatural mRNA display. The experimental design is well developed, and the preliminary data demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approaches.  There was, however, no data to demonstrate that targeting XLF could cause selective tumor cell killing. This is important since defect in XLF could be severe and was identified in severe combined immune deficiency patients. The studies aimed at investigating chemo/radiosensitization of tumor cells are somewhat descriptive. No in vivo studies have been proposed to determine the effectiveness of the peptide inhibitors.

imp_text: An understanding of the mechanisms by which PI3K/PDPK1/Akt and mutant KRAS contribute to resistance to PI3K/Akt inhibitors in colorectal cancer (CRC) will have significant impact on the development of more effective therapies for CRC and identifying patients that would benefit from such targeted therapies. It is, however, well established that monotherapy with PI3K/Akt inhibitors is not effective and there have been numerous attempts to target multiple signaling pathways. The PI is a physician scientist with significant expertise in CRC. Several co-investigators with expertise in various aspects of the project have been recruited. Although PI3K/Akt pathway has been studied extensively as a potential target for cancer therapy, the concept that a molecular switch between PI3K/Akt and PDPK1/mTORC, and different mutations in K-Ras activate distinct signaling pathways is novel. The aims of the proposal are reasonable and include mechanistic studies using cell culture, biomarker development from biopsy samples, animal studies using patient-derived xenografts and clinical trials with inhibitors of Akt, MEK or both. The experimental design is somewhat sketchy. It is not clear how data will be analyzed and interpreted.  The critical preliminary data presented in Figure 3 was illegible. In addition, the proposal was not assembled properly.

imp_text: Since mutation in BRAF at T1799A is detected in more than 50% of patients with melanoma, constitutively-active mutant BRAFV600E provides an important target for the treatment of melanoma. Unfortunately, a majority of patients recur. Since melanoma progression also requires silencing of tumor suppressor genes, such as PTEN and CDKN2A, an understanding of how these pathways contribute to melanoma, and if targeting these pathways improves therapeutic efficacy of BRAF inhibitors is important. The PI is highly qualified to pursue the proposed research and appropriate collaborators have been sought. Genetically-engineered mouse (GEM) model that mimics adult human melanoma will be useful to determine the contribution of these pathways in melanoma. In addition, several different human melanoma cell lines that are proficient or deficient in PTEN will be useful to interrogate the importance of the PI3K signaling pathway in melanoma progression/maintenance and as a potential target for combination therapy. The concept of targeting PI3K along with BRAF is, however, not novel. Although the observation that inhibition of PI3K but not Akt suppresses melanoma tumor growth is interesting, no studies have been proposed to discern the Akt-independent PI3K signaling responsible for melanoma growth. The mechanistic studies are underdeveloped. Even though several different pharmacological inhibitors with distinct mechanisms of action will be used, they are likely to have additional targets. Most importantly, it is not clear how the information gained from the proposed study would be applied to predict responses to targeted therapy.
sig_text_str: . Although BRAF oncogene is often mutated in melanoma, targeting BRAF with pharmacological inhibitors had limited clinical success due to the emergence of resistance to BRAF inhibitors. Combining BRAF inhibitors with additional pathway-targeted inhibitors could improve therapeutic potential of BRAF inhibitors.
sig_text_wkn: . It appears that loss of PTEN or CDKN2A tumor suppressor rather than activation of PI3K pathway is the primary cause for the development and progression of melanoma. Moreover, PTEN appears to contribute to melanoma independent of the PI3K pathway. Thus, it is not clear why the proposal focuses primarily on the PI3K pathway. . There was no consideration of how combined treatment with pathway-targeted inhibitors would cause toxicity to normal tissues. . The outcome of the proposed study is not clear. It is expected that combination of PI3K inhibitor with BRAF inhibitor will be more effective compared to BRAF inhibitor alone but how the proposed study would help develop rational combinatorial therapy or identify melanoma patients who would benefit from such therapy is not clear.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an established investigator who has significant expertise in oncogenic protein kinase signaling. He has published in high quality journals. . The proposal includes numerous collaborators who have agreed to provide reagents, cell lines and share their expertise.
inn_text_str: . The concept that PTEN loss contributes to melanoma independent of its ability to inhibit PI3K/Akt is somewhat novel. . Genetically-engineered mouse model that mimics adult melanoma has been developed.
inn_text_wkn: . It is now well established that targeting a single molecule is ineffective in curing cancer. Numerous studies have focused on targeting multiple pathways to improve cancer therapy, and PI3K pathway is considered a major target for combination therapy.
app_text_str: . Genetically-engineered mouse model (GEM) of BRAFV600E-mutated melanoma that recapitulates the key features of human melanoma has been developed. This model will be helpful to establish the contribution of PI3K versus PTEN in melanoma, and to determine if combined inhibition of both BRAF and PI3K is superior compared to inhibition of either pathway. . Preliminary results show that BRAFV600E-PTENNull melanomas were sensitive to PI3K inhibition, suggesting that loss of PTEN contributes to melanoma, at least, partly via activation of PI3K. . The reverse phase protein array (RPPA) will be useful to determine how the downstream signaling pathways are affected by activation of BRAF or PI3K pathway and following treatment with pathway-targeted inhibitors. . Since mutation in CDKN2A tumor suppressor gene can contribute to melanoma, the use of BRAFV600E/PTENNull/CDN2ANull mice will be helpful to determine how they respond to BRAF and PI3K inhibitors. . The genetically diverse panel of BRAF-mutated human cell lines and melanoma cells that are proficient or deficient in PTEN or carry amplification/mutation in different Akt isoforms will be useful to determine the importance of targeting the PI3/AKT pathway in combination with BRAF inhibitors.
app_text_wkn: . It is not clear why some of the proposed studies would utilize BRAF inhibitors and some studies would use MEK inhibitors rather than focusing on BRAF inhibitors that are used in the clinic. . Since there is cross-talk between PI3K/Akt and Raf/MEK/ERK signaling, the expectation that PLX-4032 will only inhibit MEK and MK-2206 will only inhibit Akt may not always be true.  . The mechanistic studies are underdeveloped. The effects of different inhibitors on different target pathways will be monitored using RPPA assay but it is not clear how this information will be utilized to develop more effective therapeutic strategies. . It is well established that mTOR/p70S6K acts downstream of MEK and PI3K signaling. Thus, it is expected that inhibition of these kinases will inhibit pS6 and p70S6K. Although it was mentioned that melanoma cells are highly sensitive to mTORC1/2 inhibitor PP242, it is not clear if targeting mTORC1/2 would be sufficient to inhibit melanoma growth, similar to combined inhibition of BRAF and PI3K. According to Figure 2, combined treatment with MEK inhibitor PD901 and mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin caused only a modest regression of BRAFV600E-PTENNull melanomas. . It is not clear why in A375 cells (Figure 8) both PI3K and Akt inhibitor had similar effects on p70S6K inhibition but only PI3K inhibitor but not Akt inhibitor inhibited phosphorylation of S6, a downstream target of p70S6K. It is important to determine the specificity of the pharmacological inhibitors since they lack absolute specificity and their effects may depend on the cellular context. . Some of the preliminary results are over-interpreted. It was mentioned that whereas MEK blockade inhibited the activity of p70S6K, PI3’K blockade had no effect on p70S6K. Based on Figure 8, PI3K inhibitor attenuated both T389S6K1 and S6 phosphorylation although less effectively than MEK inhibitor. In Figure 9, however, PI3K inhibitor was more effective than MEK inhibitor in inhibiting S6 phosphorylation. . The in vivo studies rely entirely on GEM model.

Although the idea of inhibiting mesotrypsin for the treatment of prostate cancer is novel, the significance of the proposal has been reduced because mesotrypsin expression has been observed in many tissues under normal physiological condition and therefore inhibition of mesotrypsin can result severe side effects. Inclusion of an investigator with expertise in prostate cancer research would be helpful. Research strategy is mostly well developed with some weaknesses. Overall impact of the proposal is therefore moderate.

study_section: Molecular Genetics A Study Section
imp_text: This proposal by a New Investigator/Early Stage Investigator focuses on the study of proteins involved in meiosis. Although much is known about meiosis, the molecular mechanisms by which proteins function within the segregation machinery is not well characterized. Using S. cerevisiae as a model system, the PI proposes to use biochemical and structural studies of individual chromosome-associated proteins to inform functional studies in the model system. Understanding how these proteins function in yeast is proposed to correlate to a better understanding of human diseases resulting from mistakes in chromosome recombination and segregation, including Down syndrome. The proposal is over-ambitious, and involves projects that are largely unconnected and independent of each other. It is unlikely that a new professor will be able to simultaneously progress forward on all three specific aims efficiently in a 5 year time frame, even with 4 staff members. It is telling that there is no timeframe attached to the experimental priorities – if they were included, it would be obvious that there is not enough time to accomplish all the sub-aims in a 5 year period. Although completion of any single aim will likely have impact in the field, partial completion of all three Aims would greatly lower that impact. It is unlikely even with multiple collaborators that a significant portion of all three Aims could be completed within the timeframe of the proposal, and this limits the enthusiasm for the proposal as written.

study_section: Molecular Genetics A Study Section
imp_text: The proposal addresses various questions concerning the function of mutant forms of the minor spliceosome snRNA U4atac. Recently the human dwarfism disease MOPD I was shown to be caused by mutations in U4atac. The PI proposes to study MPD I mutations in the 5’ stem loop of U4atac in vitro, to study MOPD I patient-derived cell lines for changes in minor spliceosome splicing, and to functionally screen for new snRNA SNPs that may compromise minor spliceosome function. In general, this is a very strong proposal, focused on a question that is both interesting in the broader sense (function of the minor spliceosome) and relevant to disease (albeit a very rare one). It is clear that many sub-aims within the proposal are inter-dependent, and the proposed cell model that will substitute for patient mutation data is not shown to recapitulate existing data on the patient mutant G>A. SA3 is a bit of a fishing expedition, looking for functional SNPs when it is likely that most are functionally silent, and the proposed expansion to study major spliceosome snRNAs might be over-ambitious. However the impact of the data, especially if splicing changes can be tied to validated MOPD I transcripts as proposed in SA2, would be highly significant.
sig_text_str: . There are several knowledge gaps that will be addressed by this proposal, from basic function of U4atac to study of disease-causing mutants. There is a dearth of information connecting mutant spliceosome to alterations in alternative splicing, and even less information connecting alterations in splicing patterns to specific transcriptional events. The intersection of simplified data analysis (less than 1% of splicing events are tied to minor spliceosome) and defined phenotype (growth defect signaling in MOPD I patients) is a powerful combination for the PI to exploit in this proposal.
sig_text_wkn: . SA3 is relatively weak in premise compared to SA1 and SA2; disease-causing snRNPS are relatively rare, and the idea that an extremely rare occurrence can be screened for in vitro and then ever actually observed in the human population is difficult to buy into.
inv_text_str: . The PI and senior persons are extremely well positioned to play their stated roles in the proposal.
inn_text_str: . The PI is working in a very appropriate system to address a complex and very important question – that of connecting mutations in the human spliceosome to phenotype through alterations in signaling pathways. Addressing this concept by using disease-causing mutants in minor spliceosome components, and targeting genes relevant to MOPD I disease, is compelling and a highly innovative use of existing biology.
inn_text_wkn: . We will have to wait and see the results to know what the greater significance of this approach will be – the power of this approach is its biological simplicity, but this is also its weakness in terms of the broader impact.
app_text_str: . SA1. 7 disease causing mutants have been identified in MOPD I patients, and 6 of them cluster to the 6’ stem loop region. This region is known to interact with the proteins 15.5L and hPRP31, which then incorporates into the U4atac/U6 atac di-snRNP. Previously U4/U4atac have been thought to mainly play a chaperone role in the tri-snRNP, but the prevalence of disease-causing mutations in 5’ stem-loop implies a more important functional role in splicing. The hypothesis that one of the effects of mutation of U4atac is to disrupt snRNA:protein interaction is supported and highly feasible to test. The experiments showing that patient-derived U4atac is less competent to form tri-snRNP are reasonable to follow up on. The idea to express suppressor snRNAs in cell lines to study hypotheses when patient cell lines are unavailable adds substantially to the feasibility of this Aim. . SA2. This Aim proposes to further characterize the 51G>A MOPD I mutation by finding candidate genes that may be responsible for disease pathology. This Aim is well-organized and reasonable, although preliminary data is somewhat lacking. As there are “only” 800 genes thought to be affected by minor spliceosome mutation, the data analysis of differences between patient and normal lines should be directed and therefore more efficient.  Indeed, the striking degree of intron retention of U12-dependent genes in disease patients compared to control is clear. It is extraordinarily challenging to tie defects in spliceosome to transcriptional changes, which are presumably indirect, and then to find a link between transcription changes and phenotype. The ability to focus on causative genes for dwarfism increases the chances that a link will be found, and is an important strength of this Aim. . SA3. The orthogonal spliceosome assay is pretty complicated, but appropriate for studying mutated minor spliceosome components. In Figure 8 lanes 3 and 4, with obvious splicing, are not explained – a minor point. Also, a splicing enhancer mutation (155% of WT) is called “modest”? That seems like an interesting finding, if not one relevant to the current study.
app_text_wkn: . SA1. Certainly the PI is well-suited to perform the mutant snRNA experiments outlined in SA1. However, the key proof-of-principle experiments, comparing the effect of expressing the 51G>A suppressor snRNA to the effects seen in the patient cell line, are not shown. Even preliminary data on stability or protein binding would build confidence in using this system for further experiments. This seems foundational for this Aim. . SA2. There are experiments where preliminary results are referenced but not shown, which makes it difficult to assess how successful the aim is likely to be. The final section, concerning development of iPS cells from patient lines, is a bit unclear in terms of significance. It’s not clear what the disease connection to MOPD I patient neurobiology is, and therefore the logic behind differentiation is murky. It is clear that many of the sub-aims are reliant upon each other for success, which is problematic given the lack of preliminary data. If the iPS are unsuitable for analysis, if the suppressor snRNA lines do not re-capitulate patient data, etc., then several aims in this grant will be compromised. . SA3. As noted elsewhere, the premise that a SNP isolated from presumably healthy individuals could be disease-causing under homozygous condition is really only reasonable if examples can be cited. It seems that since minor snRNAs are single copy, most mutations would be tolerated only if they are silent in the general population, so spending a lot of time trying to isolate, characterize them seems like a high-cost, low-return investment.

study_section: Molecular Genetics A Study Section
imp_text: This proposal focuses on the detailed interactions between proteins of the human replicative helicase (CMG) and replicative DNA polymerases. The PI is certainly is in excellent position to continue to impact the fields under study in the proposal. Preliminary data is present and reasonable for all three SAs. Overall, the proposal suffers from a lack of compelling significance. The connection between these experiments and impact on public health is lacking. Multiple times in the proposal it is mentioned that mutation of components in the CMG complex lead to developmental defects and cancers, yet a direct link to public health is only addressed in SA3. SA2 is rather bloated compared to SA1 and SA3, and most of the sub-Aims are highly inter-dependent. Both SA1 and SA3 are not well-fleshed out as a consequence, and there is relatively little cross-talk between the SAs. Categorizing protein:protein interactions is a valid enterprise, but enthusiasm for the project must be tempered when there is not a clear biological rationale for why the study of those protein:protein interactions are relevant. Modest changes in in vitro behavior that cannot explain observed phenotypes tempers enthusiasm for the proposed experiments.
sig_text_str: . The question, characterizing the human CMG complex and its role in targeting replicative polymerases to the replication fork, is intriguing. As mutation of components of the CMG complex lead to developmental defects and cancers, there is a compelling reason to understand the function of CMG components and associated proteins in humans.
sig_text_wkn: . Each of the SA within the proposal begins with a strong set of preliminary data. However, in no case is there a direct line drawn from the proposed experiments to the expected significance of the findings. Especially in SA2 and SA3, the observed biology in either model systems or in human patients does not seem to correlate to the modest in vitro effects measured, limiting the enthusiasm for funding these aims. Often the proposed experiments are given short shrift in favor of detailed explanations of the presented preliminary data. It is often unclear how the completion of the experiments proposed in each Aim will either inform experiments in other Aims, or clarify/disprove specific hypothesis about the biological roles of the CMG complex at the replication fork in humans.

inn_text_str: . It is powerful to be able to purify individual components of a complex machine and study them in isolation, and to be able to study activity and function outside of the context of crude cell extracts. Further characterization of the bio-UTP incorporation experiments is likely to have a significant impact on those labs working on replicative polymerases.
inn_text_wkn: . The central hypothesis, that the CMG complex is at the core of the replication fork, is not presented as a controversial one. The experiments described seem directed more towards characterization of biology in humans and comparison to work done in other labs on other model organisms, and is expected to contribute details rather than significantly shift paradigms.
app_text_str: . Preliminary data is solid on all three Aims, and experimental strategies are appropriate to the questions being asked.
app_text_wkn: . Each SA is written in a unique voice, and there seem to be very few connections between each aim’s goals and the overall mission of studying the role of the CMG complex at the replication fork, except for token lip service to the rolling circle replication experiment. . In SA1, after explaining the discovery and characterization of Pol epsilon inhibition by bio-dUTP, the SA devolves into a “look what I can do!” set of experiments. As further protocol development is needed before use in the rolling circle reaction, some proof-of-principle data would have been useful here. Also, the tangent into the stud of ChlR1 helicase detracts from the overall goal of the Aim, which is to study epsilon and delta. Finally, the EM system seems highly complementary to the goals for Aim1, and as this assay is already working, it seems that there are greater opportunities for cross-pollination and collaboration than have been explored here. . In SA2, Each sub-Aim is a very large set of complicated experimentals, and to evaluate their feasibility there would need to be some sort of preliminary data presented. It is also somewhat questionable what the biological significance is of the CTF4 interaction; it is non-lethal in yeast, and the effect on helicase activity is modest. The fact that it is essential in higher organisms doesn’t really correlate to the in vitro activity being measured, and no hypothesis is proposed that bridges these inconsistencies. The technical challenge of engineering a monomeric version of CTF4 is not balanced by a clear rationale for why this effort is even necessary. . SA3 is perhaps more appropriate for a separate proposal, as the story is somewhat unrelated to SA1 and SA2. As the limited patient data indicates that deletion of exon 1 is always present, the importance of studying Psf1 point mutants in forms of the protein without this deletion is questionable.

study_section: Basic Mechanisms of Cancer Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: This is an application from experience investigator that focuses on DNA damage and double-strand break repair in human cancers.  The ultimate goal is to determine if disruption of the double-strand break repair mechanism in tumor cells more sensitive to chemotherapy and radiation therapy.  This is a highly ambitious application with 2 specific aims from and investigative team with a long track record performing this type of work.  The main weakness of the proposal is the need for this team to develop an inhibitor of the XLF/XRCC4 interaction.  No known inhibitors of this interaction of yet been produced and it is possible that any such inhibitors would not be viable therapeutic agents because of problems with bioavailability, low in vivo potency, toxic side effects, and many other potential problems.  However, this remains an exciting proposal that could yield data that will have a large impact on how we treat human malignancies.
sig_text_str: . DNA damaging agents are widely used in the treatment of human cancers and if these investigators demonstrate that disruption of the double-strand break repair mechanism in tumor cells can lead to improved efficacy of chemotherapy and radiation therapy this could have a significant impact and how we approach the treatment of patients with many different types of cancer. . Investigative team has a long track record in the field of DNA damage and repair and they have proposed and ambitious yet straightforward set of experiments will likely yield important data.
sig_text_wkn: . The main weakness of this proposal is the speculative nature of Specific Aim 2.  This is a classic “fishing expedition,” though a very well designed one. . A second weakness of the application is that the investigators have yet to show that XLF targeting will give the desired result of chemo- and radio-sensitization.
inv_text_str: . The principal investigator is an experienced scientist with a long track record studying DNA damage and repair.  He has published some of the seminal papers on this subject and has the experience and expertise to complete the work proposed in this application. . Dr. Murray has assembled an excellent team of co-investigators, including a co-principal investigator who is an experience chemist and brings needed expertise to this project.

There is also a disconnect between the specific aims; the investigator proposes combinatorial approaches targeting the 2 pathways in later specific aims while proposing to examine if the 2 pathways collaborate in the first place in the first specific aim. imp_text: This is a very interesting application submitted by a strong team of investigators focused on elucidating the role of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer progression and metastasis, and on identifying and testing peptide inhibitors of this enzyme suitable for eventual clinical testing. The preliminary data provided are in general highly supportive of further studies on mesotrypsin as a major mediator of prostate cancer metastasis; studies in cultured cells and in vivo models suggest that mesotrypsin may have a major impact on invasion and metastasis. There are also interesting preliminary studies on mechanism, including protease targets and signaling pathways influenced by mesotrypsin action, although these studies are a bit too premature to fully support the proposed experiments expanding on them. In vivo experiments using orthotopic tumor models do support an important role for mesotrypsin in metastasis, but the effort involved in producing inhibitors in aim two and testing them in aim three could be better supported by reduction of mesotrypsin in extant tumors, vs solely a prophylactic reduction prior to cell injection. On the plus side, there is high confidence that if specific inhibitors of mesotrypsin can be produced, this group will identify them, but in the absence of such candidates, further studies of these compounds of course remains speculative. Finally, the experiments aimed at testing inhibitors of mesotrypsin in cell culture and in vivo are reasonable (with the exception of an apparent lack of study of cell proliferation and survival), but these would generate much more enthusiasm if preliminary data with an available prototype inhibitor were included. In summary, positives are the strength of the team and the intriguing initial studies that support mesotrypsin as an important contributor to prostate cancer spread and metastatic growth. In addition, the combination of appropriate cell culture and in vivo studies with strong chemistry approaches is compelling. Negatives somewhat offset this however, and include some prematurity or speculation that reduces the potential impact of many of the proposed studies, which are in some cases extensive. Overall, this is a very good application that could be outstanding with a few additional pieces of key preliminary data.

imp_text: This application is focused on a compelling subject: the mechanistic analysis of key driver pathways in CRC, namely PI3k, AKT, ras activation, and their role in response to targeted therapy. Both mechanistic/preclinical studies and a clinical trial are proposed. Strengths of the application include the detailed mechanistic studies of AKT activation and mutant ras subtypes, as well as the use of cell lines, the novel use of PDXs, and the incorporation of data from these to inform the clinical trial and vice versa. Overall, the research team and environment are very strong. Key weaknesses exist however, and rather than centered on the specifics of the investigation, are focused on the rather enormous amount of molecular work proposed in aims one and two, on top of a very complex (yet exciting) clinical trial in aim three, which will itself feed into further interesting studies, and generate numerous PDX mice. Taken separately, each aim is well thought out and exciting, but it would seem that each aim could almost stand alone as an R01. Given that the applicant, Dr. Walsh, is accomplished but at a rather early stage in terms of leading successful studies of the type described in aims one and two, this may be a rather risky undertaking for this PI. The participation of Dr. Polik is acknowledged, and indeed it would seem from the track record and writing in the plan of attack that this lab would lead the studies, but this is not clear from the budget justification description of investigator roles. Finally, the fact that the application was not ordered properly was rather distracting (e.g. specific aims at the end, references at the beginning). Thus, while these are very exciting studies, the ambitious nature of the overall study and the unclear division of labor cause considerable concern that the potential of described studies will not be realized as conceived.

imp_text: This is an outstanding application from a leader in the field of melanoma studies. The application focuses on the use of a novel mouse model of BRAF driven melanoma created by the investigator, and uses this model to maximum utility to study the roles of the PTEN and mutant PI3K enzymes in collaborating with mutant BRAF. Importantly, preliminary data strongly indicate that PI3K mutation and PTEN loss are different in terms of their impact on drug response and tumorigenesis, and provide some surprising evidence that AKT may not be key to PI3K function in some or most melanomas. The application proposes a very thorough set of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical experiments to test the overarching hypothesis that inhibition of Pi3k and downstream mediators may collaborate with BRAF inhibition to improve melanoma therapy. The studies are also highly mechanistic, and results are likely to not only provide a strong preclinical framework for clinical trials, but are likely to open up new avenues of fundamental understanding and therapeutic targets in melanoma. Thus, strengths are numerous and include the well-described rationale design of all three aims, strong preliminary data, outstanding PI, and key input from 21 collaborators who provide letters of support. Weaknesses are minor and include a rather large amount of work proposed overall, and a surprising lack of plans to study human melanoma cell line in vivo (e.g. in xenograft) in aim three, at least by the end of the requested funding period. Despite these minor concerns, the study as proposed is likely to be of very high impact and will be mechanistically and translationally transformative, so is judged to be of outstanding merit.

study_section: Basic Mechanisms of Cancer Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: The overall aim of this proposal is to develop an atypical trypsin isoform mesotrypsin (PRSS3) as a therapeutic target for advanced forms of prostate cancer. Strong preliminary data reveals that mesotrypsin expression correlates with prostate cancer progression, highest being in metastatic patients and aggressive human prostate cancer PC3 cells, and elevated levels are associated with early cancer recurrence. Strong preliminary data shows functionally that mesotrypsin promotes prostate cancer cell invasion and branching morphology in a COX-2 dependent manner in vitro. PRSS3 knockdown in PC3-M cells orthotopicaly implanted into the prostate only slightly reduced tumor load but had a more dramatic effect on limiting lung metastasis. Treatment of highly aggressive human prostate cancer cells with shRNAs to knockdown PRSS3/mesotrypsin expression blocks invasive behaviors. Therefore, targeting mesotrypsin could be a novel therapeutic target for aggressive prostate cancer, a conditional that is currently incurable and lethal – underscoring the significance of this work. The main goal of this proposal is to identify mesotrypsin inhibitors that will block progression of aggressive prostate cancer. The aims are: 1) Understand how mesotrypsin promotes prostate cancer progression on a molecular and biochemical level by identifying downstream mesotrypsin substrates and involvement of COX2 pathways in vitro and in vivo. 2) Identify potent and selective mesotrypsin inhibitors and study their kinetics and structure 3) Test efficacy of inhibitors in vitro and in vivo. A particular strength in this proposal is the amount of preliminary data generated for mesotrypsin activity, kinetics, and interaction with inhibitors. Major concern for this proposal is that it is not yet well established what role mesotrypsin plays in the progression to aggressive, metastatic prostate cancer – for example does it have functions outside of that as a protease inhibitor. Therefore, much work to identify inhibitors and elucidate crystal structures will be expended before understanding if mesotrypsin is a major player in this disease and if its targeted inhibition will suppress cancer progression. Furthermore, much time and resources will be expended to biochemically and structurally define mesotrypsin inhibitors before they are tested for their biological relevance in prostate cancer. A better plan of how to prioritize inhibitors that should be tested in vitro and in vivo should be described. Investigators should also include different types of prostate cell lines and animal models to determine how suppression of mesotrypsin activity modulates tumor load and metastasis – such as testing the agents in the context of hormone responsive versus castration resistant prostate disease. The investigators have the necessary background and expertise to complete the proposed experiments and have collaborative successfully in the past. The environment for this work is excellent and the key investigators are supported by the Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center Prostate CORE.

study_section: Basic Mechanisms of Cancer Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: This grant focuses on how XLF functions in a complex to mediate NHEJ (non-homologous end-joining) DNA repair and its use as a therapeutic target to sensitize cancer cells to chemotherapy and radiation therapy. XLF does not have catalytic activity and is hypothesized to associate with XRCC4 in a filament spanning the ends of double stranded breaks and allow additional protein enzymes to perform DNA repair. Preliminary data indicates that XLF is necessary to align broken DNA ends and plays an essential role in mediating gap filling and ligation of DSB. The proposal’s ultimate intent is to identify novel XLF-inhibitors that can be developed for clinical use to sensitize cancer cells for chemotherapy and radiation treatments. Aim 1 will determine what parameters during NHEJ are dependent on XLF. To identify XLF binding sites near the double stranded break, an established cell extract assay is proposed that employs oligonucleotide substrates with incorporated photo-crosslinkers for XLF mapping. Preliminary data to show feasibility of the XLF binding assay would help to assuage concerns that the assay will generate consistent and interpretable results. A 1-Sce1 vector system will also be used to study if XLF is involved in gap filling repair. Published reports indicate that XLF is not required for gap filling and this group’s own preliminary data suggests that the 1-SCE1 assays will not appropriately resolve the exact role of XLF in the gap-filling process. Preliminary data for this assay resulted in inaccurate DSB repair and end-joining as well as failure of reporter DsRed expression. Therefore, concerns remain that Aim 1 will not determine the fundamental importance of XLF in NHEJ. In Aim 2, novel and potent XLF drug peptide-inhibitors will be identified using unnatural mRNA display methods and candidate XLF inhibitors will be validated using stringent assays in various cancer cell lines, i.e. foci assays following irradiation, cell death assays, clonogenic survival assays. The fundamental flaw for this Aim is that preliminary data has not been conducted to knockdown XLF in cancer cells to show definitive roles in modulating DNA repair following irradiation, cell death, sensitization or radioresistance. XLF knockdown or deletion mutants could also serve as controls in these studies when evaluating the effects of the candidate XLF inhibitors. This proposal would be strengthened by a more direct role for Drs. Griffin and Vogler in the design and evaluation of the cancer cell assays cursorily described for Aim 2 and collaborative support is recommended to help translate these findings in animal models.

study_section: Developmental Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: Melanoma is a prevalent and deadly disease. One of the earliest and most common mutations noted in melanoma is the activating BRAF mutation T1799->A. However, this group previously showed that mice expressing activating BRAF mutations in melanocytes only develop benign melanomas and not metastatic disease. Preliminary work shows that only when combined with loss of PTEN or CDKN2A do animals develop aggressive melanoma. Therefore, cooperation between BRAF and PI3’K -> AKT signaling may be crucial in melanoma progression, indicating that combination therapies to inhibit BRAF and the PI3-kinase pathways will be more effective then single arm therapies. The overall goal of this study is to characterize synergistic pathways/molecular mechanisms involved in melanoma progression and ultimately develop an effective treatment course particularly for lethal metastatic disease. In Aim 1, use of the cre-inducible melanoma mouse models, in which activated BRAF and loss of PIK3CA and/or PTEN in melanocytes of adult mice will be compared for their combined ability to cause aggressive, metastatic disease. The GEM models are a particular strength of this proposal and will be used in Aim 1b to test the effectiveness of drugs blocking PI3K, AKT, and BRAF activity individually to treat arising melanomas. Aim 2 is similar to Aim 1, in that the detriment of melanoma progression caused by BRAF activation mutations will be explored in combination with loss of additional tumor suppressor genes that include PTEN and CDK2NA as well as activation of Beta-catenin. In this aim, combinations of drugs to inhibit BRAF and PI3-kinase pathways will be administered in mice of different mutant backgrounds to determine if multimodal therapy is more effective in cancer treatment and the molecular mechanisms involved in tumor regression will be carefully analyzed. However, toxicology or cross-reactivity issues are not addressed. In Aim 3, human melanoma cell lines will be employed to investigate cooperation of BRAF and PI3K signaling and compared to GEM mouse melanoma cell lines. Drug inhibitors and siRNA treatment against MEK, ERK, PI3K and AKT will be tested for synergy to induce anti-proliferative effects in human and mouse melanoma cell lines with activated BRAF and with/without PTEN loss. Further analysis of protein (phosphorylation) modification and regulation of protein translation (via ribosome profiling) will be performed to determine how these changes lead to synergistic BRAF/PI3K signaling in melanoma. It is expected that very important insights will be made in the proposed study – and a  considerable strength is the focus on animal models to elucidate the heterogeneity of cancer. A strong team of collaborators will provide the necessary experitise to perform these experiments. The main risk of this entire proposal is that BRAF activating mutations together with PI3K and/or AKT mutations may not act synergistically to induce aggressive melanoma. Preliminary data supports the notion this is correct, but all of the described experiments hinge on the fact that such interactions are pivotal in cancer progression of melanocytes. A weakness in this study is the failure to test if any of these treatment options will be effective long-term and will accelerate/suppress drug resistance and disease relapse in the GEM models. Furthermore, the complicated writing style and numerous variations of genetic backgrounds used in the GEM analysis make this proposal difficult to read. The large numbers of animals and phenotypic analysis involved in all these experiments will be very expensive and will require a more detailed plan to track and systematically score/evaluate the outcomes.

imp_text: Major focus of this application is to understand the function of XLF in non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and evaluate is as a target for in radio and chemotherapy. This investigation is based on the fact that therapies that target cellular growth control signaling, cytotoxic DNA damaging agents remain which kills tumor cells by double stranded break (DSBS) are compromised due to DSB repair. The primary mechanism for DSB repair in mammalian cells is non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), with homologous recombination repair (HRR) being the secondary pathway. XLF, also called Cernunnos, is a recently discovered core protein of the NHEJ pathway. The interaction of XLF and its binding partner XRCC4 is essential for efficient NHEJ, but exactly how this interaction promotes NHEJ remains to be determined. PI has proposed following aims to understand the function of XLF, and evaluate it as a target for sensitization in radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Aim-1 is developed to define the interactions of XLF with DNA in the vicinity of a DSB and its role in end joining fidelity; Aim-2 will determine to what extent XLF/XRCC4 disruption by inhibitors is a viable strategy for chemo- and radio-sensitization of cancer cells. Studies are well developed and supported by relevant preliminary data by suitable team of investigators. However, enthusiasm was dampened due to lack validation in preclinical model to justify clinical significance.

imp_text: Major focus this grant application is to conduct mechanistic studies on a novel molecular switch between PI3K/AKT and PDPK1/TORC that could lead to resistance to PI3K and AKT inhibitors; and of amino acid forms of mutant KRAS that activate different downstream signaling pathways and their role in resistance to specific therapies. PI has proposed two clinical trials with PI3K, AKT and MEK inhibitors, namely 1) an adaptively randomized multiarm-targeted Phase II clinical trial and 2) a post-treatment biopsy Phase II trial of the AKT inhibitor MK-2206 in PTEN negative and positive colorectal cancer (CRC). PI has proposed three specific aims to test proposed hypothesis. Aim 1) will determine the mechanisms of alternate pathways of PI3K signaling for sensitivity and resistance to targeted therapy for CRC; Aim 2) is developed to determine the mechanisms of alternate downstream signaling by different amino acid-substituted forms of mutant KRAS for sensitivity and resistance to targeted therapy for CRC; and Aim 3) will conduct clinical trials of inhibitors of AKT, PI3K, and mut-KRAS signaling in patients with advanced CRC using patient tumor biopsy results to identify potential biomarkers for selecting patients with CRC for therapy. Proposed studies are supported by relevant preliminary data. Strengths of application is well trained PI, suitable investigative team, Support of SGK and Merck as well as resources available for successful completion of work. PI has proposed to use PDX and it is unclear how tumor hetrogenecity will be normalized while taking a piece to develop PDX from resected tumor. In addition to this stroma of PDX get replaced with mouse stromal cells and PI has not addressed these issues which seems to be a limitation to take preclinical findings in clinical setting.

There are three innovative points in the proposal: novel signaling switch of PDPK1 and mutation-dependent kRas down-stream pathway, as well tumorgrafts derived from patient biopsy specimens. The study is significant since it will capitalize the patient specimens and treatment response from patient that will be integrated into molecular and signal pathway analysis.
