imp_text: This is an interesting, well-written proposal in which the applicants, building on new knowledge concerning the basic machinery of double stranded DNA repair, propose to further characterize, XLF, a newly discovered member of the (nonhomologous end joining) NHEJ complex, and find cyclic peptides containing unnatural amino acids that interfere with the interaction of XLF with its partner XRC44, potentially leading to a new therapy that would sensitize cancer tumor cells to agents that create double stranded DNA breaks, leading to improved responses to radiation/chemotherapeutics, and patient outcomes.  Although, the proposal contains innovative elements, and interesting synthetic methods, the overall significance, and the research plan have several critical flaws.  Consequently, despite some enthusiasm, it was neither sufficient nor sustained. It is also rather difficult to determine if the apparent fraud within the application is an artefact of the non-standard review of this application, for example this ‘review’ is actually a test of how a name may influence a reviewer’s opinion of an application or a test as to whether reviewers are skilled enough to detect fraudulent application, or is instead an example of actual fraud.  It is also not apparent if these detected flaws in application should be used in the scoring.
sig_text_str: The application addresses the fundamental mechanism of double stranded DNA repair mechanisms.  The applicants have uncovered a member of the nonhomologous end joining complex of proteins named XLF. XLF has homology to, as well as, binds XRCC4, and was identified as mutated in SCID patients with microencephaly.  Targeting the process of double stranded DNA repair mechanism would enhance the sensitivity of tumor cells to DNA damaging agents and might improve the therapeutic response of patients.  Revealing the activity of the essential components of double stranded DNA repair could lead to therapies targeting this essential mechanism.  Moreover, as proposed by the applicant’s, successful targeting of this mechanism though interfering with the XLS/XRCC4 interaction, might retard/prevent DNA repair, leading to cancer cell apoptosis and tumor regression.  In the first Aim of the research plan the applicants will attempt to determine the specific interaction of XLF with nonhomologus DNA joints using two different photoactivatable cross-linkers, XLF-deficient fibroblast lysates, and His6-tagged recombinant XLF.  This work could identify specific sights of XLF/DNA interaction, which would further enhance our understanding of XLF function.  In Aim 2, using a novel peptide display library, the applicant will attempt to find specific peptides which interfere with the XLF/XRCC4 interaction.  This work might lead to the identification of peptides that block this potentially essential interaction, which then could be used to help therapeutically target cancers. .
sig_text_wkn: Although the applicants have made a discovery that appears to help uncover an essential cell function, it is not at all apparent that the any new knowledge potentially uncovered through the proposed work would be anything more than an incremental increase.  The methods used in Aim 1 do not appear to be rigorous enough, such that even if the Aim were accomplished as described we would not know much more about XLF function (see below).  In addition, while Aim 2 has a laudable goal, there is a substantial chance that no peptide with sufficient specificity and activity will be developed. On the other hand, if interfering peptides are uncovered, the clinical utility of such a reagent is likely to be many years away, if at all.  Thus, Aim 2, if it yields no potentially clinically useful therapy, may not yield any useful new knowledge. Overall, this appears both high risk and low reward. .
inv_text_str: The PIs of the project are T. F. Murray, Professor of Pharmacology and Toxicology, and M.C.T. Hartford, Assistant Professor of Chemistry, Virginia Commonwealth University.  Dr. Murray has real expertise in double stranded DNA repair and has had continuous NIH support since 1985. Dr. Hartford is a well trained chemist with the expertise in the design, creation, and use of mRNA-displayed peptide libraries necessary to complete the project.  Together they are highly appropriate to lead this project.  The two PIs are assisted by co-Investigators D. Griffin and K. Vogler who will, assist in the studies to evaluate candidate radiosensitizing peptides in cancer cell lines, and in the genetic manipulation of human cell lines, including generation of cells containing NHEJ repair probes, lentiviral complementation of XLF-deficient cells, and transduction with adenovirus constructs, respectively.  Both co-investigators are established researchers and will be able to assist the PIs in this project.  Overall, the team has the necessary expertise to complete the described work. .
inv_text_wkn: Dr. Hartford is only devoting 1.5 summer months to the project and given the complexity and amount of the synthesis work involved, leaving the vast majority of the work to two graduate students seems inappropriate.  It is also apparent that neither Dr. Murray nor Dr. Hartford author the reports listed in the provided biosketchs.  According to PubMed Dr. Murray and Dr. Vogler are substituted for L.F. Povirk and K. Valerie, while Dr. Hartford is substituted for M. C. Hartman. . .
inn_text_str: The applicants have uncovered, XLF, a member of the NHEJ complex, a fundamental part of DNA repair, and its interaction with XRCC4.  Consequently, finding peptides that specifically interfere with this interaction, and lead to repressed double stranded DNA repair, would be an innovative method of enhancing cancer chemotherapeutics.  The applicants will also apply a novel method of mRNA display that can yield libraries of mRNA-peptide fusions, with 10 (13) sequences, containing 10 unnatural, and 10 natural amino acids, thereby, creating an enormous library of biostable cyclic peptides that may have drug-like properties.  Overall, there is a substantial amount of innovation in this proposal. .
inn_text_wkn: There is nothing novel about targeting DNA repair in cancer therapy, so, although, the specific aspects of the targeting approach are novel, the application of this sort of therapy in conjunction DNA damaging agents has long been considered.  In addition, although the use of the mRNA-peptide display library containing unnatural amino acids, with a high degree of cyclized peptides, is somewhat original, the applicants have used this strategy before in targeting BRAC1, and the applicants have several reports of using unnatural amino acid libraries.  Thus, this aspect of the proposal cannot, any longer, be considered novel. Consequently, the novelty of the both the goal and the method are somewhat diminished. .
app_text_str: The approach considered by the applicants is built on interesting new knowledge concerning the fundamental machinery of DNA repair.  In the first Aim the applicants will further characterize the interaction of XLF with nonhomologous DNA breaks, specifically, regarding the positioning of XLF proximal to the junction.  They will also further determine the absolute dependence of filling and ligation of double stranding junctions on XLF.  This is an important Aim, insofar as it will help determine the mechanism of double stranded DNA break repair, and confirm the critical role of XLF.  Certainly, if XLF is to be pursed as a therapeutic target these studies are both useful and necessary. In the second Aim, the applicants will search for peptide-based drugs to interfere with the XLF/XRC44 interaction and consequently, interfere with DNA repair.  This includes both testing in extracts and in cells. This investigation could potentially yield new therapies that might have application to cancer treatment.  There also appears to be several interesting and innovative methods of synthetic chemistry/biochemistry used in the proposal, e.g., the creation of the cyclic unnatural peptide library, that are positive features of the application. .
app_text_wkn: The approach has several flaws:  1) Aim 1 appears somewhat problematic, insofar, as its not apparent how the applicant will distinguish molecularly important, from spurious, trivial interactions.  Given the length of time that end joining requires and the ability of XLF to interact non-specifically with DNA, there seems a high likelihood of low affinity interactions to be detected and how these will be distinguished from significant interactions is not clear.  Overall, the research plan for the initial part of this Aim is not well described, e.g. time courses and amounts His6-tagget XLF are not indicated.  There is also some concern regarding the propagation of the XLF depleted fibroblasts---Are the applicants confident that during the propagation of these cells that other mutations in the NHEJ complex have not developed?  How this may effect the conclusions the authors draw is not clear.  The second part of this Aim in which the applicants will determine whether end joining is XLF dependent is very important, but really needs to be accomplished prior to the current proposal.  How will the research plan be affected if XLF isn’t as necessary in cells, as it is in cell lysate? Aim 2 is a really poor way to approach an Aim in a competitive proposal.  There are several concerns: 1) There really is no biological/biochemical hypothesis tested here; 2) A large fraction of the Aim involves tool making (in this case a library making and drug screening), while important to accomplish, it really is a poor way to construct an Aim because if the tool cannot be created no new knowledge can be generated; 3) Because of the possibility that no new candidate drugs will be developed here, the better way to construct this Aim would be to perform the initial screen and then use this award mechanism to propose hypothesis-based Aims using the potential drug candidates. 4) An additional concern that would be abrogated by performing the initial screen prior to submitting the proposal is the possibility of too many drug candidates. The binding affinity to XLF to XCR44 is of low affinity and in under assay conditions could easily be susceptible to disruption. This problem is further amplified by the lack of details concerning the binding assay i.e. temp, time, presence of detergents, divalent cations etc. are not indicated. .

study_section: Developmental Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a serious and fatal human disease in which chemotherapy has only moderate efficacy.  Mutations in critical signaling molecules and dysregulation of signaling pathways are central elements in the progression of CRC.  The applicants propose that chemotherapeutics, which target specific signaling components (Akt and Mek) have more or less efficacy depending on specific mutations in KRAS that change its substrate preference and the levels of PIP3, which alter the target preference of PDK1.  Consequently, if the molecular signature of of CRCs are determined, then specific therapies can be applied to patients with a favorable profile.  In addition, determining the subsequent mutations that are selected for as a response to therapeutics and permit resistance to chemotherapeutic regimens, would enable the tailoring of therapies to attack those elements, thus allowing for improved patient outcomes. Using cell lines, tissue cultures and xenografts generated from the biopsies of patients enrolled in clinical trails of drugs targeting Akt and Mek, the applicants will examine various signaling molecules and tumor responses to therapeutics.  There is a substantial chance that the proposed work will lead to new knowledge and potentially to improved patient therapeutics, including individualized therapies specifically tailored to the tumor’s molecular signature.  Although, somewhat innovative and quite significant, the application has some serious flaws in the research plan that damper enthusiasm. sig_text_str: The application addresses mechanisms of resistance in colorectal cancer (CRC) to drugs that target Akt and MEK.  The applicants propose that depending on the level of PIP3, the major target(s) of PDK1 is altered.  Since PDK1 has a pleckstrin homology domain (PH), it binds PIP3, and thus is targeted to the membrane where it phosphorylates Akt. Low levels of PIP3 allow PDK1 to remain mostly cytoplasmic, where its target preference includes the p70 ribosomal S6 kinase (S6K), SGK isoforms, and PKC. Furthermore, the applicants suggest that drugs that target Akt would be more or less effective depending of the PIP3 levels due to the effects that this has on Akt activation, i.e., drugs targeting Akt would not be as effective in the absence of elevated PIP3.  The authors also propose that KRAS mutants have different targets depending on the specific amino acid substations in the protein i.e. different mutated KRAS forms activate different downstream signaling pathways with mut-KRAS- G12D activating PI3K and MEK signaling and mut-KRAS- G12C activating RAL signaling but not PI3K or MEK.  The net effect of this is that patients receiving Akt and Mek inhibitors would do more of less well depending on the level of PIP3 and specific KRAS mutations found in patients’ tumors.  The applicants will test this hypothesis by deriving cell lines and tumor xenografts from patients enrolled in 2 clinical trails, one in which the patients will receive MK-2206, an Akt inhibitors and a second in which patients will receive various combinations of experimental agents including a MEK inhibitor, a PI3K inhibitor, and an AKT inhibitor.  Cell lines and/or tumors will be examined for levels of PIP3, activated signaling molecules, and sensitivity to the tested drugs.  Consequently, the applicants have developed a plan that may lead to new knowledge concerning the precise molecular changes in tumor cells that effect resistance/sensitivity to chemotherapeutic drugs.  This could ultimately lead to predictions about what drugs patients’ tumors may respond to after initial therapy fails.  The plan may also improve the assignment of patients to alternate treatment regimens depending on the specific molecular signature of the tumor.  In addition, valuable new knowledge concerning how specific mutations affect signaling will add to our knowledge of specific signaling pathways involved in the promotion/propagation of cancer cells.  Overall, there is a high level of clinical and biological significance to the proposed studies.

imp_text: This is an interesting, ambitious proposal in which the applicant proposes to examine the roles of mutational active BRAF (BRAFV600E) and signaling pathways directed by PI3K in the development/progression of melanoma, a serious human disease with much associated morbidity and mortality.  Using genetically engineered mouse models of melanoma, specific inhibitors of signaling molecules, and a panel of human melanoma cell lines, the applicant will test whether conditionally expressed, mutationally active PI3K cooperates with BRAFV600E, whether drugs that target The PI3K signaling pathway cooperate (synergize) with BRAF targeting to retard tumor/cell growth, whether, Akt, an important oncogenic mediator of PI3K signaling, is a potential therapeutic target for melanoma therapy, and, explore the potential mechanism through which BRAF and PI3K inhibitors cooperate to retard melanoma growth. The proposal addresses a lethal disease, proposes to develop new insights into the targeting of the disease with chemotherapeutics, has some innovative elements (although it does not develop novel targets or drugs, per se), and has a thorough research plan (perhaps a bit ambitious).  Consequently, there is some sustained enthusiasm for the proposal. It is also rather difficult to determine if the apparent fraud within the application is an artefact of the non-standard review of this application, for example, this ‘review’ is actually a test of how a name may influence a reviewer’s opinion of an application, or a test as to whether reviewers are skilled enough to detect a fraudulent application, or is instead, actual fraud.  It is also not apparent if these detected flaws in application should be used in the scoring.
sig_text_str: The application addresses how mutation of key signaling molecules cooperate to initiate and promote melanoma, a serious human disease with a high level of incidence and death (approximately 74,000 cases and 10,000 deaths in the US/annum) and test whether clinically useful drugs that target these pathways collaborate to retard tumor growth and inhibit cancer cell proliferation.  It is possible that through these investigations new drug combinations will be developed for the treatment of human disease, and perhaps, as importantly, drug combinations that may not be efficacious are avoided.  In addition, potentially important new basic knowledge concerning the mechanism of how drugs that target BRAF and other signaling elements work together (the applicant proposes effects on translation) to inhibit tumor progression may be developed through this work.  Overall, the application addresses a significant problem and investigates reasonable therapies to tackle human disease. .

There are no new drugs or therapies that are likely to emerge from the proposed work.  The new knowledge generated is incremental in nature and no new paradigms are tested here. .

imp_text: This is a MPI proposal from highly productive investigators who have complementary expertise required for this project.  The objectives of the proposal are to elucidate the mechanism by which the XLF protein regulates DNA repair of double strand breaks, and to target XLF with small peptide-based inhibitors to render cancer cells with greater radiosensitivity and chemosensitivity.  Two aims are proposed.  The first aim will address the hypothesis that XLF and XRCC4 form a filament that facilitates end joining of a DNA double-strand break. The second aim will prepare and screen a massive library of small peptides to identify inhibitors of XLF-XRCC4-based NHEJ, which would then be tested for their ability to make cancer cells more radiosensitive and chemosensitive.  This is a significant and innovative proposal that has high potential for clinical significance. The hypothesis is exciting and the proposed experiments are feasible and within the expertise of the PIs.  However, the second aim is largely exploratory, expeditious and risky.  The approach is entirely based upon in vitro experimentation, and it is not clear whether any identified peptide inhibitors will have in vivo applicability.  This lack of in vivo experimentation, combined with potential unaddressed concerns about the selectivity, bioavailability, pharmacokinetics, and immunogenicity of any identified peptide inhibitors have somewhat dampened enthusiasm.
sig_text_str: . Radiotherapy and chemotherapy have dismal response rates in the clinic. This application will explore the role of XLF protein in DNA DSB repair, which plays an important role in response to radiotherapy and chemotherapy. . The proposed work will elucidate the mechanism of XLF in DSB repair through NHEJ, which will significantly advance the field. . The work will potentially identify XLF inhibitor peptides that may enhance efficacy of radiotherapy and chemotherapy by interfering with XLF-mediated NHEJ-based DSB repair.  This may have significant application in clinical oncology.

inv_text_str: . This is a MPI application with two highly accomplished and well trained PIs with complementary expertise. . The two co-investigators will also lend important expertise to the project. . All investigators are at the same institution, so that the collaboration will be feasible with frequent interaction. . There is strong evidence of past collaboration among the PIs.
inn_text_str: . XLF as a therapeutic target is novel and innovative. . Selective inhibition of XLF-mediated NHEJ via small peptide is innovative. . Unnatural mRNA display is an innovative technology. . A novel cell-extract-based assay will be used to screen candidate peptides.
inn_text_wkn: . No weaknesses noted.
app_text_str: . The approach is well-designed, well-developed, and well-described. . The preliminary data are strong and support the rationale and hypothesis. . The proposed experimental outcome will likely be successful in identifying the role of XLF in DSB repair and as a potential therapeutic target. . Expected outcomes, interpretations, pitfalls, and alternative strategies are appropriately discussed. . The use of mRNA display, and a highly diversified and massive peptide library (10 trillion unique sequences) is exciting.
app_text_wkn: . Aim 2 seems largely a fishing expedition.  While the approach seems feasible, it is highly risky. imp_text: XRCC-Like Factor (XLF) is essential for efficient non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), but its precise role in the pathway is poorly understood. The goal of this study is to clarify the role of XLF and test the hypothesis that XLF and XRCC4 polymerize into a filament that aligns DNA ends. The PIs also predict that peptides that disrupt this interaction sensitize cells to DNA damaging agents. Their hypotheses will be tested in 2 aims. The goal of aim 1 is to define the interactions of XLF with DNA in the vicinity of a DSB and its role in end joining fidelity while the goal of aim 2 is to determine to what extent XLF/XRCC4 disruption by inhibitors is a viable strategy for chemo- and radiosensitization of cancer cells. Overall, the primary goals of this work are to elucidate in more detail the role of XLF in NHEJ and to develop an XLF-targeted radio/chemosensitizer. In the long term, these inhibitors, or derivatives thereof, may find clinical utility as sensitizers for cancer chemo/radiotherapy. imp_text: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in the US. The goal of this project is to better understand the mechanisms of resistance to therapy for CRC so that more effective therapies can be designed and biomarkers can be used to identify CRC patients most likely to have responses to specific therapies. The hypothesis to be tested is that the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and RAS signaling pathways play major roles in CRC development and when aberrantly regulated confer resistance to many new molecularly targeted therapies. Three specific aims are proposed to test this hypothesis, and include: 1) determine the mechanisms of alternate pathways of PI3K signaling for sensitivity and resistance to targeted therapy for CRC; 2) determine the mechanisms of alternate downstream signaling by different amino acid-substituted forms of mutant KRAS for sensitivity and resistance to targeted therapy for CRC; and 3) conduct clinical trials of inhibitors of AKT, PI3K, and mutant KRAS signaling in patients with advanced CRC using patient tumor biopsy results to identify potential biomarkers for selecting patients with CRC for therapy. A panel of CRC cell lines and isogenic mutant KRAS immortalized colonic epithelial cell lines will be used for mechanistic studies in aims 1 and 2. Patient-derived CRC tumorgrafts will be used to compare tumor responses to drug treatment in vivo with patient response to therapy in aim 3. The strengths of the study include the focus on CRC, the team of investigators, translation to the clinic, and the environment. Enthusiasm is dampened by a few weaknesses in the approach but overall successful completion of the aims is likely to advance the field and therefore impact is considered high.

imp_text: Melanoma is the most lethal form of skin cancer. Although targeted therapies are now FDA approved in this disease, both primary and secondary resistance have become significant clinical problems. The goal of this research is to design BRAF inhibitor-based combination therapies that enhance the overall response rate and the depth of each patient's primary anti-tumor response and extend indefinitely the duration of remission of patients with BRAF mutated melanoma. Three aims are proposed to accomplish this goal. In Aim 1, genetically engineered mouse (GEM) models will be used to evaluate the importance of PI3’-kinase/AKT signaling in cooperation with oncogenic BRAF-V600E in converting normal melanocytes to metastatic melanoma cells. In Aim 2 the superiority of combined versus single agent inhibition of BRAF-V600E or PI3’-kinase in promoting tumor regression will be evaluated using GEM models of BRAF-V600E-initiated melanoma. To complement analysis of mouse melanoma specimens in Aim 2, a panel of bona fide human BRAF-V600E expressing melanoma cell lines will be employed in Aim 3 to elucidate the molecular mechanism(s) by which BRAF-V600E cooperates with PI3’-kinase/AKT signaling in regulating the melanoma cell division cycle and/or apoptosis through effects on protein synthesis. This is a well-written proposal by an outstanding investigator. While there are some clearly worthwhile experiments described in this application, from an overall perspective it is overly ambitions and in some key situations it is not clear what the results will mean in the context of the type of infections that these investigators want to examine (e.g. early colonization and long term survival in the lungs of CF patients or in the context of a wound infection. Another issue that will not be clearly resolved from this study is whether strains that fail to make one of these polysaccharides (e.g. PA14 – Psl) show any specific defects in their pathogenicity in the context of biofilm formation. imp_text: The researchers are leaders in the area of molecular host-pathogen interactions in Ehrlichia. If all aims are successful, it is likely that the results will have a strong impact on our views in general of such interactions, and the examples they uncover will impact significantly the study of Ehrlichia and related pathogens, which could then lead to improved therapeutics. Enthusiasm is reduced significantly by a number of weaknesses in the approach, and the likelihood that results of some of the experiments as envisioned will not be interpretable in a meaningful way.
sig_text_str: . The critical issue being addressed is the regulation of host processes by proteins from obligate intracellular bacteria, and that these proteins may be modified by host post-translational modification mechanisms in order to perform their functions ("molecular host-pathogen interactions"). Such issues are complex and inherently interesting intellectually, and improved understanding of such interactions will lead to a better understanding in general of how different species can interact on a molecular level and specifically may prove to assist in efforts to combat bacterial pathogenesis and disease.

app_text_str: . Study 2.1 will mimic previous studies with TAL to identify amino acids important for DNA binding. Although there are no preliminary results, these methods are not particularly challenging, and most likely will give some interpretable results. . In study 2.2, transcription activation by TRP-120 (in vitro, and in vivo) will be measured. Again, although no preliminary results, these methods are straightforward, and should give interpretable results. .
app_text_wkn: . There are some significant inconsistencies in the preliminary results. First, during normal E. chaffeensis infections, TRP-120 translocates to the nucleus. However, ectopically expressed TRP-120 does not. Why?  There is something wrong here. Perhaps the GFP tag (ectopic) is problematic in some way (?). There may be many explanations. Furthermore, accepting this ("this model is optimal for studying nuclear localization since protein") ignores the issue. Second, TRP-120 ectopically expressed does not localize to the nucleus despite the fact that all the ubiquitination machinery is present. However, if the lysine-null ubiquitin is also co-expressed, then it does localize. Again, this is problematic. The results of Study 1.1 and 1.2 may not be interpretable (or perhaps it is more correct to say interpreted correctly) based on these problems. The researchers first need to determine what modifications are actually present on TRP-120 under normal conditions when it is localized to the nucleus. . Study 1.3 is probably feasible, but is not very exciting, given no preliminary results and the possibility that the hypothesis is not correct. At the very least, there should have been two 2D gels run (healthy versus infected) to demonstrate that there is a difference (if there is), and then the study should have been to identify the proteins that vary. . Study 2.3 will use truncations to identify TAD and ID domains. There are no guarantees that truncation mutants will maintain structural integrity necessary to bind (even if the binding entity is present, i.e. not part of the truncation). Because feasibility is not established, it is unsure if reliable results can be obtained. . The studies in Aim 3 will examine changes in gene expression levels (Affymetrix methods), epigenetic changes (DNA methylation, EpiTect Methyl II PCR), and immune and related responses (cytokine assays with kits, ROS production by chemiluminescence, apotopsis/necrosis with kit). This reads like an R21 with no preliminary results and the like, although none of the experiments are really very challenging. There is also the issue that in all cases a lysine-null Ub will be used, but this is certainly not typical of normal cells, so how all of this really relates to normal cell function and TRP-120 involvement isn't clear.

study_section: Bacterial Pathogenesis Study Section
imp_text: The research proposed is to characterize the means that Pseudomonas aeruginosa uses to detect and metabolize (degrade) the important host signaling molecule sphingosine-1-phosphate, its precursor (sphingosine) and related. S1P and sphingosine are important immune signaling molecules for the host, and modulating their presence may have relevance for infection and pathogenesis The overall impact is compromised by some weak subaims ('Approach'), one of which is by a number of measures untenable, and another is unlikely to provide the ability to discriminate between the possibilities stated, and thus may have no value. There is also a tendency, in some subaims worse than others, to avoid proposing reliable alternate methods and approaches (in 'alternate approaches' sections) in favor of simply deciding that the proposed experiments will work as described.
sig_text_str: . How bacteria sense and react to molecules in their environment, in general, is critical for understand their survival and pathogenesis, and, ultimately, for understanding how to control and prevent infections. . The observation that the important host immune signaling molecules sphingosine and sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) are recognized and degraded by pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) (and presumably by other serious bacterial pathogens as well), and that this process facilitates PA survival, is highly significant. . If successful, the research will advance our understanding of an important mechanism that bacteria use to survive, and may be useful in strategies for mitigating infections. .
sig_text_wkn: . There are many metabolic pathways in bacteria that may, or may not, prove to be useful for controlling infections. It is unclear if the ones in this proposal are any more or less significant in this regard.
inv_text_str: . The PI (Murphy) is both a new investigator and an early stage investigator (assistant professor). He has build a solid research program in the general areas of microbiology, infectious disease, lung biology/disease, immunology and related, and has significant expertise in the areas of investigation documented in this proposal. He has secured extramural funding from multiple sources, and he seems very well suited to lead the research efforts. . The co-investigator (Heyn) is also an assistant professor who has likewise built an active, productive research program at the interface between microbiology and analytical chemistry. The Co-I brings significant, valuable expertise to bear on the research proposed both intellectually and from an experimental perspective. . There are a lot of letters of support from various individuals who, collectively, bring quite a lot of expertise to bear on the research proposed (synthesis, NMR, mass spec, microarray analysis). This all is very positive.
inn_text_str: . The researchers describe the aspects of their proposal that represent innovation, including the realization that PA detection and metabolism of S1P and sphingosine represent a good avenue for potentially regulating PA virulence. . In addition, the lack of published research on sphingosine and related metabolism by bacteria makes the research not only more significant and likely to have a stronger impact, their . Although not hugely innovative, most of the proposal is built on a solid foundation of established procedures and builds on the strong research programs of the Pi and Co-I, and this is much more important than innovation.
inn_text_wkn: . Most of the 'innovation' simply stems from the fact that these particular systems have either not been well characterized or previously envisioned. This can be said of most all research.
app_text_str: . Aim 1, Subaim 1A, is strong. The goal (identify the SphR binding site) is clearly defined, and the proposed experiments based on established, solid methodologies. The protein constructs necessary for the EMSA have been produced and purified. The likelihood of success is very high, and based on preliminary results the expected results will probably be realized. . In Aim 1, Subaim 1B, it is proposed to examine the ability of sphingosine analogues to bind to SphR it order to determine the relevance of the chemical functionalities for binding to SphR, so that other molecules that might regulate SphR-regulated genes might be identified. This is a worthwhile goal. . Aim 1, Subaim 1C, is to attempt to determine how sphingosine and S1P activate sphR-dependent regulons. It is clear that sphingosine activates sphR, and if S1P does also, then the results will be important for identifying the specific regulons and for a comprehensive understanding of how these modulate virulence. . Aim 2, Subaim 2A (identify "the" PA S1P phosphatase) builds on strenghts of the researchers with genetic screens and reporter/functional screens of their PA library. if successful, this will be critical for understanding how S1P is metabolized and host immune signaling interrupted. . Aim 2, Subaim 2B is a mostly very strong aim designed to test if SphC and SphD are the enzymes that participate in catalytic conversion (degradation) of sphingosine. Multiple, complementary approaches are proposed. The preliminary results indicate that the proposals (Fig. 10) are sound. The experiments are likely to be successful and are integral to the ideas put forth by the researchers regarding S1P/sphingosine breakdown and its relationship to modulation of the host immune response by PA. . Aim 3 is also strong. In the first part, the proposal is simply to repeat successful competition experiments they've done (Fig. 6) using sphD and sphC mutants. These experiments are very likely to be successful and will likely demonstrate that the sphD and sphC genes have the hypothesized role. The second part of the aim is also strong, taking advantage of the researchers strengths and demonstrated experience in making measurements of airway and lung functions in mice. The prediction that "a mutant PA unable to metabolize sphingosine will cause less damage to the mouse lung during infection" is very reasonable and likely given preliminary results.
app_text_wkn: . For Aim 1, Subaim 1B, as envisioned (lacZ reporter, in vivo assay), it is unlikely that the results will reflect a true interaction with SphR. First, the solubilities of the compounds are very different (sphingosine is 'insoluble' in water, trimethylsphingosine is highly soluble in water, etc.). There is no mention of how to overcome this. Second, although the authors state that the compounds "have membrane permeabilities similar to sphingosine", there is no evidence to back this up, and the authors give only marginal assurance ("thus we 'predict' that all [compounds] will have access to SphR within the cytosol). It is difficult to see how water soluble trimethylsphingosine, which carries an obligate positive charge, would cross the membrane equally to sphingosine. Third, the authors have evidence that molecules such as S1P and sphingomyelin have to be metabolized (to sphingosine) to bind SphR. So, without evidence that the proposed compounds are not modifed in vivo, there is no way to decide what a positive or negative response might mean. For these three reasons, this subaim is not tenable. These experiments need to be performed in vitro using a direct binding assay (many to choose from). . Aim 1, Subaim 1B, no alternate approaches are proposed (even there is an 'alternate approaches' section). It is mentioned that if the molecules tested do not prove informative, others will be tried, but no specifics (other than "additional commercially available sphingosine analogues") are offered or justified. This isn't an alternate approach, but the same approach with different molecules. The authors should have proposed some type of direct binding measurements to alleviate problems noted above. . For Aim 1, Subaim 1C to be successful, S1P has to be able to enter PA and bind to SphR. However, the authors indicate in many ways that most likely S1P cannot enter the cells, and in fact they state that "We predict the decreased reporter activity in response to S1P is dependent upon dephosphorylation of S1P to sphingosine prior to detection by the transcription factor". Thus, if there are no S1P-specific regulons detected, the experiments will not be able to differentiate between the two possibilities (S1P doesn't get into the cells intact, S1P doesn't activate the SphR). . For Aim 2, Subaim 2B, the letter from Skura (Lipidomics Core Shared Resource Synthetic Facility, MUSC) is not terribly reassuring ("I am quite confident that.....we would be able to develop appropriate protocols for the synthesis of relevant sphingolipids, labeled with a stable isotope...". It would have been better to get a quote from a reliable custom organic synthesis company that would guarantee that the product could be synthesized (perhaps it already has). .

The core facilities, the PI and Co-I lab facilities, and other facilities appear to be quite adequate for all the proposed research.

imp_text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a pathogen that commonly causes infections in lungs of cystic fibrosis patients.  This organism elaborates a biofilm that interferes with chemotherapeutic and immunological efforts to eliminate it from the host.  Furthermore, the composition of these biofilms changes over the course of the protracted infection and these so-called mucoid cells are now even more difficult to treat.   A central hypothesis of this application is that a therapeutic window exists prior to appearance of mucoid cells as normal P. aeruginosa biofilms are non-mucoid and contain different constituents.  This is thought to serve as a sensitive condition during which these infections can be successfully treated.  Positive aspects of this work include the potential utility of a new avenue to treat a chronic and refractory disease, strong research team, clear experimental goals with convincing feasibility data for most approaches and investigations into the impact of biofilms on both host and pathogen side of the infection equation.  Minor weaknesses were no feasibility demonstration for characterization of the Psl exopolysaccharide that exists in a high molecular form and not entirely clear mutagenesis strategy for CdrA.  Given the prodigious experience of this PI, these concerns remain minor and the impact of this work seems likely to be very high.

imp_text: This application focuses on understanding the action of an effector protein released from Erllichia chaffeensis cells during infection of the host.  This protein, called TRP120, is transferred into the infected host cells where it is thought to regulate host defense gene expression profiles in order to facilitate productive infection of the bacterium.  The strongest aspects of this application include the focus on a pathogen effector protein that appears to a be a regulator of host gene expression, a logical research plan that is centered on the role of this transcription factor and a strong aim 3 that seem likely to provide important new information about the target gene suite of TRP120 across the genome.  Weaker features that ultimately reduced my enthusiasm include a real lack of feasibility data for a number of different experimental goals, unclear reasoning for selection of technical aspects employed here and lack of utilization of pre-existing data sets.  These reservations drove my less positive view of this proposal.
sig_text_str: . TRP120 represents a relatively understudied pathogen-encoded protein. . The reprogramming of host gene expression by TRP120 could be a high significance in the disease process.
sig_text_wkn: . A goal to confirm that TRP120 is required for pathogenesis seems like it should be a high priority.
inv_text_str: . An experienced and active investigator who is making important strides in Ehrlichia studies.
inn_text_str: . The notion that post-translational modification pathways are subverted by a pathogen to provide function for proteins involved in the disease process is innovative.
app_text_str: . Aim 3 seems an important early step. . The experiments are laid out in a logical order.
app_text_wkn: . Not made clear why TRP120 has no NLS.  This is crucial as the rationale for much of aim 1 relies on the need for post-translational modifications to permit nuclear localization. . Evidence for role of Ubiquitin in trafficking is not strong.  Micrographs are very small and hard to read.  Effect of ubiquitin ligase inhibitor could have many different mechanisms.  There are 27 lysine residues in TRP120-one plan is to mutant all to arginine.  If there is not a single lysine of critical importance, this may consume a tremendous effort with uncertain outcome.  Why not identify modified residues by sequencing the protein? . Plan to carry out mass spec analysis of host proteins associating with PML nuclear bodies lacks any feasibility data. . Why is in vitro transcription necessary?  Don’t even have strong evidence that TRP120 regulates expression in vivo.  No feasibility data here either. . Argument made that testing in vivo regulation by TRP120 using synthetic reporter system (not yet known to work properly) is better than authentic target genes.  How can one be sure that results from this artificial system will equate to behavior at bona fide regulatory targets?  Verification is essential at a minimum yet this is not proposed. . Extensive comparison is made of the potential overlap in binding sites of TRP120 and Sp1 but no mention is made of the ChIP-seq dataset available for Sp1.  This would help support the possible interaction between the host and bacterial factor discussed here.

imp_text: This application is directed towards understanding the role of degradation of host sphingosine/sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) during Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection.  The PI has identified a factor called SphR that is an AraC type protein required for induction of a P. aeruginosa operon required for S1P breakdown.  This application is focused on exploring the role of SphR in control of gene expression, identifying a presumptive phosphatase involved in S1P dephosphorylation and determing how S1P breakdown influences P. aeruginosa pathogenesis.  The strengths of this application include some solid preliminary data, well-trained PI, and a focused research plan that seems likely to succeed.  Weaker aspects are a lack of some important feasibility demonstrations and an unclear utility to certain experimental goals.  Even with these reservations, this application seems poised to provide new insight about an interesting and understudied interaction between an important pathogen and the host.

sig_text_wkn: . Lack of key feasibility demonstrations make impact difficult to assess.  Especially for phosphatase screening and enzymatic characterization of sphingosine cleavage in Aim 2. . Missing an opportunity to couple ChIP experiments of SphR with planned microarray experiments.

What is the benefit of finding other sphingosine analogues that could influence expression control by sphR?  This provides a tool for which a direct and/or necessary application seems to be missing. .

imp_text: Despite decades of study, Shigella species remain significant human pathogens.  A principal mechanism of pathogenesis relates to their type-III secretion complex, through which critical virulence factors are introduced into host cells.  Yet, considerable gaps in knowledge exist in the structure and function of type-III secretion complex proteins in Shigella spp. The application is well-crafted and clearly written.  It includes considerable preliminary data related to in vitro studies that support the overall goals as proposed. Aim 1 studies are likely to yield only incremental new knowledge; location of the complex is not a quantal advance, and the approach described is not innovative. Aim 2 studies appear to be straight forward; however, developing crystal structures of proteins in complex states (e.g. IpaB with IpgC) can be elusive, and create spurious structural artifacts.  Aim 3 appears to be a derivative of Aim 2, in which structural variants will tests hypotheses from Aim 2. All proposed studies appear to be performed entirely in vitro (e.g. in the absence of any host pressures that may influence the structure or function of IpaB or partner proteins.  This is a significant weakness, and may render results of limited relevance to health or pathogenesis. With no medical or healthcare implications mentioned in the application (e.g. IpaB protein as a vaccine immunogen, etc.) the translatability to benefit human health is very low.  In this regard the application may be best suited for NSF, rather than NIH.

imp_text: Beyond pathogenic capabilities in immune competent hosts, Pseudomonas species are difficult pathogens in immune compromised individuals, and particularly those with cystic fibrosis (CF).  A key virulence determinant in these organisms is the biofilm complex that forms in relevant contexts in vivo.  Compounding this concern, Pseudomonas biofilms are believed integral to antibiotic resistance.  Yet, much knowledge remains to be gained regarding the structure and function of Pseudomonas biofilms with respect to host defense and antimicrobial efficacy. The application is well-crafted and clearly written.  It includes considerable preliminary data related to in vitro studies that support the overall goals as proposed.  Hypotheses are clearly stated in each section. Aim 1 studies are straight forward and not particularly innovative as written.  It is unclear that the approach will examine structure-activity relationships in vivo; thus results of the studies may be limited to in vitro conditions.  Of greater concern, structural relationships in Aims 1 and 2 do not appear to integrate immune recognition systems, such as PRRs or Tc / Bc receptors that recognize epitopes in biofilm components such as CdrA.  Thus, studies in Aim 2 do not address structural-immune response relationships that would be innovative. The absence of deep immunology expertise (e.g. pattern recognition, adaptive immunity) and experimental infection models to bridge the gap between in vitro and human sera studies is a significant limitation.  This is particularly true given the difference between immune response that occurs in all humans facing CF, and protective immune response that occurs in few of these patients.  Thus, the translatability to benefit human health is low in this application as written.  Addressing this concern would significantly enhance the strength of this proposal.

imp_text: Ehrlichia species are obligate intracellular pathogens of human cells.  In this regard, they exhibit a highly-evolved strategy to engage, subvert and exploit human immune defenses.  Although not a priority CDC or NIH pathogen, the studies leverage highly innovative data regarding a type 1 secretion mechanism and host gene expression modification process to achieve intracellular parasitism.  Thus, studies have great potential to quantally advance understanding of pathogenesis regarding Erhlichia, Rickettsia, Coxiella and many other agents that are high priority pathogens. The application is logically sound, evidence based & clearly written.  It includes considerable preliminary data related to in vitro studies that support the overall goals as proposed. Ehrlichia species are not high priority human pathogens, which somewhat lessens the impact and significance of this proposal.  However, if studies lend new insights into generalizable mechanisms or strategies by which intracellular pathogens subvert immune defenses, these studies would represent significant advances. The proposed studies apply a leading-edge convergence of molecular & imaging techniques, small molecular inhibitors and a fundamental translational approach that will at the same time define the molecular mechanisms of the T1S system and identify potential inhibitors thereof.  Thus, the translatability to benefit human health is high regarding Ehrlichia and indeed perhaps other intracellular pathogens that rely upon homologous T1S systems.

imp_text: The goal of this project is to demonstrate that the tandem repeat protein Trp120 is a dual-function transcriptional factor that utilizes the host cell ubiquitin and SUMO pathways to mediate nuclear translocation and regulate host gene expression to enhance infection. While the proposal seeks to enhance our understanding of a unique bacterial virulence protein, the significance is diminished as the entire proposal focuses on Trp120. Moreover, while the area of investigation is significant, many of the proposed studies replicate data in the literature. Dr. O’Brian has an extensive background and record of success to execute the proposed project. The proposed experiments are thorough and should result in successful generation of data. However, the lack of study of additional Trp proteins and the potential of only incremental advances limit the overall impact of the proposal.
sig_text_str: . E. chaffeensis causes an emerging tick-borne infection through infection of mononuclear phagocytes. It remains unknown how the pathogen establishes infection and avoids host immune defenses. . Trp120 is an essential E. chaffeensis protein that can affect numerous eukaryotic proteins involved in transcription and cell signaling. It remains unknown how Trp120 can target several different proteins to enhance infection. . The application could help to enhance our understanding of survival of intracellular pathogens.
sig_text_wkn: . While the proposal is interesting, there are two publications in the literature analyzing TRP120 from 2011. As presented the proposal appears to replicate many of these findings (for example Trp120 binding to G+C-rich motifs) and is the next logical step in the continuation of these studies. In reading the proposal, it appears that many of these studies are already being conducted, so the question of the use of the funding needs to be considered. . imp_text: The goal of the proposal is to understand Pseudomonas aeruginosa sphingosine metabolism during lung infection, a new area of research for lung pathogens. The application is of significant clinical relevance and could lead to a greater understanding of P. aeruginosa host-pathogen interactions that may result in the development of novel therapeutics. Dr. Murphy is an early stage investigator with a strong background to conduct the proposed experiments. Overall, the approach is thorough and the experiments are expected to generate important data to enhance the understanding of P. aeruginosa degradation of sphingosine. Finally, the environment is well-equipped and the institution is supportive for Dr. Murphy’s research.
sig_text_str: . Strong clinical relevance for study given P. aeruginosa rate of infections in CF and COPD patients, need to address problems related to antibiotic resistance, and broad relevance to other lung pathogens. . Important to understand sphingosine as a host response mechanism to bacterial pathogens, and P. aeruginosa appears to degrade sphingosine to ensure survival during infection. Significant gap in literature warrants the investigation proposed in the application. . Understanding of the response to P. aeruginosa could provide a new therapeutic target.

Dr. Murphy is an early stage investigator with a strong training background, extensive experience with P. aeruginosa host-pathogen interaction research, several publications relevant to the proposal in addition to his successful publication history, and the experience in successfully obtaining and managing grants related to his research. Dr. Murphy has an established staff for execution of the research. . Dr. Heyn has a strong background and experience required for the successful implementation of the grant including experience in advanced mass spectrometry, HPLC, and applications with bacterial pathogens including P. aeruginosa. Her publication and funding history support the application.
inn_text_str: . A new therapeutic target could be developed based on the understanding of P. aeruginosa degradation of sphingosine, which may be applied to other pathogens if homologous gene targets are present. . Investigating how bacterial pathogens sense and respond to immune modulators like sphingosine is a new area of research that can have important implications in our understanding of host-pathogen interactions.

app_text_wkn: . Some of the preliminary data could be presented better. For example, the growth analysis of P. aeruginosa on sphingosine is missing details on the length time (e.g. overnight?). Providing full growth curve analysis should be considered. Moreover, the purification blot provided in Figure 8 does not have sizes and no information was provided regarding Western blot confirmation of purified SphR. . The authors should consider ChIP-Seq as an alternative to the EMSA analysis. . Given the homology of SphR to AraC-family regulators, the authors do not consider if additional genes, especially virulence factors, are also regulated by SphR. imp_text: This is a new RO1 application from an established investigator and collaborator to investigate the physical and molecular events that dictate the mechanisms by which IpaB control the steps that lead to induction of Shigella type III secretion. The aims of the proposal are: 1) determine the location IpaB within nascent and active needles; 2) investigate the crystal structure of IPaB bound to cytoplasmic chaperon IpgC and to TTSS needle tip protein, IpaD; 3) Target key sites that are involved in interaction of IPaB and its cognate partners. Strength of the application is evident in the importance of type II secretion system, which is a key virulence factor for several Gram negative bacterial pathogens such as Shigella and Salmonalla. In addition, Shigella-induced gastroenteritis in children is a major health problem owing to high virulence of shigella that cause inflammation and damage of colonic mucosa as well as ease of transmission via fecal-oral route. Immunization of mice with IpaD and IpaB provide protection against homologous and heterologous challenge with Shigella using murine lung infection model. The proposal will focus on understanding structure and function of IPaB as main translocator proteins that regulate steps initiated to facilitate induction of type II secretion.
sig_text_str: 1. Diarrheal diseases are the second leading cause of death in children in the developing world 2. Shigella is the most common cause of bloody diarrhea and it is responsible for 1.1 million deaths each year.  Thus, it is a serious public health threat 3. Difficulties posed by shigellosis are compounded by an increased incidence of antibiotic resistance 4.  The project will examine the mechanism used by Shigella to move IpaB from its chaperone-bound state in the cytoplasm to another macromolecular complex at the tip of the TTSA needle. This information will have global applications to all TTSSs. 5. The proposed investigation will exploit a novel pathogen system to provide the basis for future studies on preventing diseases caused by gram-negative pathogens that use TTSS.

imp_text: This is a new RO1 application from an established investigator addressing how Pseudomonas aeruginosa survive within biofilm in patients with cystic fibrosis. The focus of this application is on the role of two P. aeruginosa extracellular polysaccharides and a protein (CdrA) in the biofilm structural integrity and the tolerance of Pseudomonas to antimicrobial and host defense.   Chronic pulmonary infection due to P. aeruginosa in patients with cystic fibrosis or immunocompromised patients is significant problem. In specific aim 1, the structure-function relationship required for P. aeruginosa biofilm matrix integrity will be investigated. In particular, the role of Psl,  Pel, and CdrA proteins  expressed in clinical isolates in biofilm structure and development of mucoid phenotype of strains will be examined . In Specific aim 2, the role of biofilm matrix molecules in modulating interaction of P. aeruginosa with innate host defense (complement and phagocytic cells) as well as with antimicrobial will be examined. Strength of the application is evident in the importance of the research questions and the availability of well characterized clinical isolates. Additionally the innovative in vitro biofilm model is already well established in PI lab. However, several minor to moderate weaknesses exist (which are described below) regarding the authenticity of the biofilm model using mutants that are expected to be defective in formation of biofilm,  and how this in vitro system can be translated in vivo among other concerns. Enthusiasm for this application is dampened by these weaknesses which will somehow limit the impact on the field.
sig_text_str: 1. The project will focus on EPS and proteins that are integral parts of the polymeric matrix. Understanding the structure-function relationship of these molecules and composition of biofilm matrix will help in designing strategies that disrupt the biofilms and enhances immune mediated clearance 2.  The concept that early intervention targeting the non-mucoid species of P. aeruginosa that express these EPS and protein is important as intervention may be more likely effective compared to targeting mucoid strains that are already developed multiple mechanism of resistance to antimicrobial and host defense.
sig_text_wkn: 1. The proposal is all focused on in vitro studies, which may not accurately reflect in vivo biofilm formation and the temporal and spatial changes in the matrix formation in patients with chronic pulmonary infections 2- The proposal examines interaction of wild type bacteria and mutants with complement and neutrophils only. Although these are primary innate host defense mechanisms, there exist multiple complex arrays of other host defense mechanisms such as cytokines, chemokines, natural killer cells, and newly discovered innate immune T cells. Thus an in vivo model system would be important to validate the data from the in vitro studies.

The close proximity of their lab will facilitate the collaboration. 2. The inclusion of Dr. Petnick strengthens the application and increases the likelihood of successfully completing the proposed in vitro biofilms studies.

app_text_wkn: Specific aim 1: 1. In aim 1.2, the PI will utilize several clinical isolates to examine the role of Pel and Psl in Biofilms integrity. However, the fact that several clinical isolates express either Psl or Pel or do not express any, but yet they are able to form biofilms and isolated from patients with CF is not well addressed in the proposal.  Is Psl and Pel play redundant functions? Or their absence can be compensated by other molecules that are not defined or explored at all in the proposal? 2- The PI hypothesis is that expression of Psl, Pel by non-mucoid strains enables them to establish biofilm and mucoid phenotype, which further provide resistance to antimicrobials and host defense. However, the PI selected to analyze environmental isolates claiming that those are the source of P. auroginosa in patients. This is not true. P.aurigonsa is opportunistic infection, and so many clinical isolates could be derived from endogenous sources rather than environmental bacterial strains. Also, it would have been more informative if they compared the expression and role of these EPS and proteins between the non-mucoid and mucoid clinical isolates. Also, it could be important to correlate the expression of EPS or CdrA to virulence as marked by severity of clinical manifestation in the patients from whom these strains were isolated.   For example, 3. The PI mentioned that one of the reason that Pel and Psl is not detected in certain clinical isolates is the fact that antisera used is generated from two strains PAO1 and PA14, and that structural difference between these EPS may influence the specificity of the antisera and thus could lead to false negative with other clinical isolates. If there is a significant structural diversity between the EPS and the CdrA protein, then why the expression of these molecules in clinical isolates not established and confirmed by QPCR looking at mRNA expression. If mRNA expression is consistent with protein detection or lack thereof, then one would assume a true results rather than limitation of the screening method. 4. Specific aim 2 is dependent on construction of mutants in specific aim 1. This interdependency may pose a problem in successful completion of aim 2 if the mutants were defective in their ability to adhere and establish biofilms. 5. In the biofilm-neutrophils studies, the PI will use different WT and mutant strains that vary in their virulence and ability to form biofilm. Thjese mutants may not be defective in their ability to adhere and form biofilms but also may be defective in other virulence factors that are undefined in this proposal. Thus, comparison of WT and mutants interaction with neutrophils may not provide the required information about the role of EPS and CdrA in P. aeruginosa pathogenesis. 6- in aim 2.2, the PI propose that Pel, Psl, CdrA antagonize the complement -mediate opsonization and phagocytosis of Pseudomonas strains. But the PI did not exclude the possibility that incubation of complement with the bacteria could have bactericidal effect independent of phagocytosis. Experiment that block phagocytosis of bacteria by neutrophils or macrophages in presence or absence of complement could address this issue. 7-Although the focus of aim 2 on two essential host defense mechanisms; complement and neutrophils antimicrobial effector functions, the immune system is complex and include a cognate and non-cognate interactions between different innate and acquired immune cells. Thus, the in vitro analysis may not well represent in vivo situation, especially if mutants are used in the study where their adhesion, invasion, replication may be affected by many factors that are not examined in this proposal. This concern is a major one and dampens the enthusiasm to this proposal

A lack of potential problems and alternatives diminished some enthusiasm for the proposal, but given the track record of the PI and team it is felt that the work would be accomplished. A better description of future work and potential translation would have benefited this proposal.
sig_text_str: . Important pathogen that causes a human disease, but pathobiology is not well understood. This proposal seeks to understand how E. chaffeensis utilizes proteins containing tandem repeats in regulating host gene expression to evade host immune defenses. . Study is focused on a potentially important mechanism that involves post-translational modification of a prokaryotic protein TRP120 by ubiquination and sumolylation that conveys properties that allow it to regulate eukaryotic host cell gene expression. . Potential to identify novel targets for therapies to treat disease. . More thorough understanding of bacterial mechanisms involved in pathogenesis.
sig_text_wkn: . No evidence is provided that demonstrates that TRP120 modulates pathogenesis or virulence. It does bind to DNA and regulate expression of genes involved in the immune response. . Future work and explicit payoff of research not well described.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an expert in the field and has published a number of papers in the field relevant to the work. His accomplishment is well recognized by colleagues as indicated by appointment as Vice President of the American Society for Rickettsiology and numerous other awards.
inv_text_wkn: . It is not clear if the postdoc Dr. Dubose has adequate training to carry out the research indicated in the personnel justification section. Seems trained in pharmacology and small molecules rather than molecular biology that would be required for this proposal.
inn_text_str: . Research is innovative as it seeks to provide evidence for a new and different way of considering host-pathogen interactions. The studies provide the first investigation into how a bacterial pathogen transcription factor utilizes host post-translational modifications to hijack transcriptional regulation of host genes as part of its pathobiology. It potentially establishes a new paradigm (sumoylation of bacterial proteins) related to interkingdom relationships that could be relevant to other host-pathogen interactions.
inn_text_wkn: . Nothing significant.
app_text_str: . The preliminary data demonstrates that TRP120 undergoes both sumoylation and ubiquination. These PTMs affect nuclear localization. In Aim 1, the PI proposes a series of structure/function studies with lysine residue mutations and chemical inhibitors to identify the residues that are modified and which are important for localization. Preliminary studies indicate that this approach will succeed. . In Aim 2, similar approaches will be used to identify transcription factor binding domains and transcriptional activation domains and the importance of PTMs in these activities. Extensive preliminary data demonstrates the TRP120 binds to a DNA sequence that resembles that of host transcription factor SP1 (GC-box). . In Aim 3, the PI proposes to identify global changes in host gene transcription, epigenetic changes in the chromatin of the host and changes in host cellular functions that are caused by TRP120. Preliminary data supports success of this aim. . Approach is relatively straightforward and well-reasoned. Preliminary data indicates that proposed experiments should be successful and generate informative data.

While these are fairly straightforward experimental approaches and protocols that use technology that is familiar to the PI, a serious consideration of problems is warranted. . The preliminary data and other figures are far too small and in many cases of poor quality even with enlargement on the computer screen. This greatly diminished an appreciation for the work that was presented. . The rational for introducing recombinant TRP120 via Chariot reagent is not fully explained. What if this approach does not work, what alternative would be used?

imp_text: This is a new R01 application by a productive PI who has made significant advances in molecular basis for how Shigella flexneri uses its type III secretion systems (TTSS) to invade human colonic epithelial cells. This group is the first to prove that incubation of Shigella with bile salts promotes recruitment of the first translocator protein, IpaB, to the needle tip where it is stably maintained and is able to interact with host cell membrane components. The proposed study is a natural extension of their previous findings, but will further delve into the detail of structural-function relationship between IpaB and host surface molecules. They will try to determine the mechanism by which bile salts are able to promote maturation of the Shigella TTS needle tip complex as IpaB recruitment to the needle tip will facilitate the association with IpaD. Based on some critical preliminary data including the partial crystal structure of IpaB, they will mainly employ a diverse set of physical and molecular methods to investigate IpaB structural plasticity and molecular interactions that dictate how it controls the final induction of type III secretion in Shigella. Among the three Aims, Aim 2 is most intriguing and may result in novel information about IpaB structural requirement and alterations during interactions with host cytosolic components; however, Aim 3 is relatively less developed and identification of key sites for protein-protein interaction may have difficulty and unknown significance. This grant is innovative and feasible because of their excellent preliminary observations and experience. Their results derived from the proposed work may help to prevent disease caused by Shigella.
sig_text_str: . Shigella is the most common cause of bloody diarrhea and difficulty in controlling shigellosis is compounded by an increased incidence of antibiotic resistance. Understanding of the molecular mechanism of Shigella TTSS will provide a basis for future studies on preventing infection of gram-negative pathogens that use TTSS. . The applicants are the only group to elucidate the molecular structures and mechanisms that govern the stepwise mobilization of the first translocator protein in the onset of T3SS induction. . Translocator proteins are required for host cell contact and effector delivery in all TTSSs. The lack of structural information on TTSS translocator proteins greatly hampers developing a full understanding the onset of type III secretion.

inn_text_str: . The applicant along with the collaborators were the first to demonstrate that IpaD is the Shigella needle tip of the outer proteins of the TTSA. . The research team has taken the lead in applying a rigorous interdisciplinary approach to understanding an important problem in bacterial pathogenesis. . The group has elucidated the structure of a major portion of IpaB, the first high-resolution structural information on this or related TTS components. In this study, they will more fully characterize the structure of IpaB and its various protein-protein complexes, and thereby determining the unique structural forms that IpaB assumes as it is passed from one protein partner to the next, and also assess its location as it moves from the cytoplasm to the needle channel and to the needle tip.

Following strong preliminary data, the researchers will further understand the full mechanisms involving the structural basis and functional significance with IpaB and IpaD. . imp_text: This new R01 application was proposed to understand the organization and composition of the P. aeruginosa biofilm matrix (i.e., PsI, PeI, alginate, and CdrA) to facilitate the development of novel therapeutics. Biofilms are critical surface components that play critical roles in bacterial pathogenesis to attack human cells; however, the mechanisms of biofilm regulation and interaction with host cells are extremely poorly understood. The research is aimed at disrupting biofilms with mutant strains to enhance immune-mediated clearance targeted to phagocytosis, complement and antimicrobial molecules), which may help translate into effective treatments and a better quality of life for patients afflicted. This timely proposal is significant and seems highly innovative as the rationale for the aims was clear and supported by some preliminary data. The experimental approaches to exploring the structure-function relationship of biofilms and the interaction with host anti-microbial mechanisms are truly creative and logically laid-out. The applicant has also described in great detail the preliminary supporting evidence, the expected outcome and the alternatives. Because of a strong applicant with significant relevant experience as well as uniquely assembled multi-institutional team, it is highly likely to achieve the proposed objectives and provide a better understanding of the molecular basis for biofilm persistence. The significance is to help design therapies to control matrix synthesis in vivo, leading to an improved quality of life for patients colonized with biofilms of P. aeruginosa. However, there are some weaknesses including lack of details in some bacterial strains and introduction of the biofilm research, structural analysis without crystallography, and some deletion strains without complementation. Thus the enthusiasm for the outstanding proposal is very high.

imp_text: This is a new R01 application by a productive PI with solid experience regarding the pathogenesis of Ehrlichia chaffeensis.  Ehrlichia are excellent model organisms to study intracellular survival and investigate how microbes with small genomes effectively interact with complex eukaryotes. The applicant’s lab has focused on understanding the role of ehrlichial tandem repeat and Ankyrin effectors in the molecular basis of humoral immunity to Ehrlichia. The PI demonstrated that TRP120 is translocated into the host cell nucleus, binds to a GC-rich DNA motif with a novel TR DNA binding domain, and is a substrate of host Ub and SUMO post translational modification pathways. The applicant proposed that TRP120 is a dual-function transcription factor that has interplay with the Ub/SUMO pathways to mediate nuclear translocation, subnuclear associations and regulate host defense gene expression. With multiple approaches, the PI will carry out characterization of the host cell pathway modulated by ehrlichial TRP effectors and the molecular mechanisms through which these are mediated will expand the understanding of the cell biology of infection mechanisms through intracellular microbes. It is necessary to identify novel host targets for therapeutics based on mechanistically defined host-pathogen interactions potentially utilized by a wide variety of pathogens. However, the impact of the proposed molecule TR120 on host complex ubiquitylation and PTM is still unclear as the proposed approaches may not directly define such complex mechanism. This is a very good to excellent grant with some very interesting and well developed approaches.

imp_text: The investigators propose to use a combination of physical biochemistry, crystallography, and genetic manipulation to determine how the proteins which make up the type III secretion needle are organized and by extension how the generation of this structure occurs biologically.  While this is an interesting question and the Shigella system is important to study, the enthusiasm for this proposal was dampened by three concerns.  First, the investigators propose to study whether needles are filled with their target protein IpaB without sufficient justification for the importance for these studies.  Second, the crystallography is based upon partial structures.  While this can lead to important insights it can also result in misinterpretations.  The investigators do not discuss how they would distinguish these two possible interpretations.  Third, the genetic analyses in general are weak.  They speak of using mutants for analyses but do not explain how the mutants would be chosen.  This is truce in most parts of the proposal.
sig_text_str: . Shigella is an important human pathogen and a leading cause of death in young children.  The type III secretion machinery is an important contributor to the pathogenesis of this bacterium.  Understanding how the structure of type III secretion is generated may help to develop strategies to reduce infection.  The studies are designed to elucidate how the type III secretion needle is generated.
sig_text_wkn: . It is not clear why there is such an emphasis on whether the needle is empty or full at the earliest stages of the formation of the type III needle.  This seems like a minor technical point to this reviewer.  Similarly, in aim 3.A there is no good justification for the mutations to be tested.  Much of the proposed mutational analyses of this proposal appear to be a fishing expedition to look for interesting mutations.

inn_text_str: . The proposed structure for the interacting proteins may be considered innovative.
