imp_text: This is a very ambitious proposal from a group of PIs to characterize the elements of the P. Aeruginosa biofilm and its effects on the efficacy of certain antibiotics and the immune response.  Although this reviewer was enthusiastic for this proposal on initial review, upon rereading my enthusiasm decreased.  While there are elements that would be important to study, overall I believe that the proposal is really only incremental and very costly for what would be learned.  This reviewer is also concerned that important aspects of the methods are not sufficiently developed to determine whether the results will be meaningful.  For example, In aim 1 where the structure of the various biofilms will be determined, the strategy and methods are only described superficially.  There is no mention of how specific vs nonspecific interactions between proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates will be distinguished.
sig_text_str: . P aeruginosa is a significant human pathogen and its ability to form biofilms contributes to its pathogenicity.  Understanding how biofilms are generated and how they prevent antibiotics and cellular immunity to function is important for eventually treating these infections.
sig_text_wkn: . Some of the aims are incremental.  Aim 1.1 is diesigned to test whether published results on soluble matrix will have the same structure as cell bound matrix.  Moreover, it is unclear from the description how the PIs propose to distinguish specific interactions within the cellular matrix from nonspecific interactions based upon the rather crude purification procedure proposed.  Similarly, it is not clear what the significance would be to analyze various clinical strains unless there is a phenotype associated with the strains in aim 1.2.  The PIs indicate that this would help to develop therapies but do not explain how or why.  A similar criticism relates to the mutational studies.  They seem to be more fishing than actual hypothesis testing. . It is not clear why knowing the structure of the matrix will lead to the inhibition of its formation.  The PIs state this without giving any justification.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an established investigator with a number of relevant publications.  Dr. Terrizzi is a new investigator working on a K99/R00 grant.  While trained in the area of human alveolar microenvironment, Dr. Terrizzi has not yet established herself since her publication record is a little weak.  The other investigator, Dr. Petnick is also a established investigator in the area of biofilm biochemistry.  Together this group covers the major areas of the proposal.
inv_text_wkn: . The only weakness is the relative newness of Dr. Terrizzi who has not established an independent position yet.
inn_text_str: . The PIs propose that the matric plays a critical role during the establishment of an infection and that at this time it may be possible to inhibit the establishment by inhibiting the formation of the early biofilm.  This is an innovative approach if it actually works.  The studies in aim 2 correlating the extent of matrix with response to either antibiotics or immune response is also relatively innovative using the available mutant strategy.
inn_text_wkn: . Many of the studies appear to be incremental.  As noted above the PIs will look at the structure associated with the cells although they have already defined the structure of the soluble form of the matrix.
app_text_str: . The PIs are knowledgeable and productive.  The PIs have many of the reagents needed for the studies including some critical mutants.  The approaches tend to be standard and to have been used either by the PIs or others previously.  Finally, in general the approaches are appropriate for the proposed studies.
app_text_wkn: . The experimental procedures lack detail.  As indicated above it is not clear if aim 1 will yield useful results.  While the aim is to determine the structure of the biofilm associated with cells it is not clear exactly how the strategy used will do this.  There are questions about how specific interactions will be distinguished from nonspecific interactions.  Similarly it is not clear how results will interpreted from the generation of point and deletion mutations.

Second, the proposal is very ambitious and somewhat unfocused.  For example, aim 3 the analysis of epigenetic effects could be its own R01 proposal.  Finally, the PI does not seem to have sufficient understanding of the issues related to each of the aims.  Again, in aim 3 the PI does not discuss any of the relevant bioinformatics considerations. imp_text: This application focuses on the role of miR-30 in the de-regulation of ras induced senescence. More specifically the applicant has identified the transcriptional co-activator CHD7 and the RNA-binding protein TNRC6A as targets of miR-30.  They propose 3 aims, in aim 1, they will focus on CDH7 and test the hypothesis that CDH7 acts to prevent senescence by inhibiting the transcription of p16 or act as a co-regulator of IkB to regulate the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). In aim 2, they will focus of TNRC6A and test the hypothesis that it is involve in the regulation of miRNA processing. In aim 3, they will investigate the role of miR-30 on tumorigeneity by overexpressing or inhibiting its expression in cell lines in culture or in tumor formation in xenograft. The strengths of the application are strong preliminary data and a logical, well described experimental plan, the inclusion of alternative approaches in each aim, which ensure that even in the unlikely scenario that the primary hypothesis fails, important data will nevertheless be obtained. In addition, the three aims are interconnected  but independent on each other, the first two aims address mechanistic aspects and the third aim complement nicely the first two aims by addressing a more functional aspect on tumor formation. The weaknesses are counterbalanced by alternative approaches. Overall, this is a very well written application on an exciting topic based on strong and logical set of data. Therefore the enthusiasm is very high.
sig_text_str: . The significance of microRNA in cancer is undeniable and the function of miR-30 in blocking oncogene-induced senescence highly significant.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an associate professor at Scripps and has a solid publication record especially during his post-doc with David Beach at Cold Spring Harbor. Of note he has a paper on microRNA17-92 cluster in the regulation of senescence in 2010 in cancer Research.

inn_text_str: . The idea that a miRNA can promote the disruption of miRNA processing is very innovative. . The regulation of p16 by miR-30 target is also very novel.
app_text_str: . Aim 1 (experiments 1, 2, 3, 4) proposes a standard approach of inhibiting and overexpressing CDH7 and see if it affects levels of p16, affects p16 promoter activity and binding to p16 promoter. . Experiments 5, 6, 7, and 8 of aim 1 are also well described. . imp_text: This project plans to study how a non-coding RNA (ncRNA), in particular an orphan small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) called ACA11, is involved in resistance to chemotherapy (reduced ROS production) in multiple myeloma. At first, seems an innovative project for several reasons; ncRNA functions are been unraveled, and it is now clear that many contribute to cancer disease. However, very little is known about snoRNA and their contribution to chemoresistance. Many research efforts towards fighting chemoresistance have been made but still, chemoresistance is a common issue for many types of cancers, leading to sub-optimal treatments and inefficient therapies. Thus, tackling the role new players such as snoRNA’s may have in chemoresistance could represent a significant advance. Furthermore, the project aims are ambitious and preliminary data showing similar approaches supports the ability of the team to carry out successfully the aims and methodologies. Although it is not always clear which part of the aims have been already achieved and there is a certain uncertainty in the outcome of all the proposed experiments mainly by the complexity of the model, there is no doubt this is a challenging project with great potential to discover new players in chemoresistance. Even though the link between ACA11 overexpression and ROS-induced chemoresistance in MM is not altogether evident, and the translational value of the proposal for MM is not demonstrated, the project should yield useful and interesting information on the mechanisms underlying non-coding RNA function in general and non-coding nucleolar RNAs in particular. The proposal should generate a potential high impact.

imp_text: The proposal describes the identification of miRNA-30 as one of the overexpressed miRNAs upon ras-induced senescence in BJ primary human fibroblasts. The applicant designed shRNAs for 15 target genes for miRNA 30 and found that suppression of two of them, namely CHD7 and TNRC6A, abrogated ras-induced senescence in BJ cells. The proposal is well organized and the preliminary data support the proposed experiments. The three specific aims are built on specific hypotheses and there is a high degree of confidence that several objectives may be reached. The success in the proposal would yield interesting information on the function of micro RNAs in general and the function of miR30 in tumorigenesis by interfering with oncogene-induced senescence, an essentially unexplored area. The main weaknesses relates to the relatively modest scope of the proposal, fulfilling only one aspect of the connection between microRNA biology and cancer, as well as the predictable resulting incomplete picture, as senescence may not be the only relevant mechanism underlying miRNA malfunction in cancer pathogenesis. Despite these criticisms the proposal is view with a high level of enthusiasm.
sig_text_str: . The project explores novel mechanisms linking miRNAs and cancer through the abrogation of oncogene-induced senescence. . The study is well presented, the aims are clearly stated and the proposed experiments are sound to explore the main hypotheses: - that miRNA-30 inhibits ras-induced senescence by suppressing CHD7 (SA1) - that miRNA-30 inhibits senescence by suppressing TNRC6A, which in turn regulates other miRNAs (SA2) - that miRNA-30 overexpression contributes to cancer development/promotion through senescence-bypass mediated by CHD7 and TNRC6A (SA3)
sig_text_wkn: . As stated by the authors, the downstream targets of miR-30 are still unexplored. It is not clear what other genes, in addition to CHD7 and TNRC6A, are suppressed by miR-30 that also might play a role in the senescence-bypass phenotype. . Whether TNRC6A also controls miR-30 level, as a feed-back control mechanism, is not explained nor proposed. . Whether up-regulation of miR-30 leads to down-regulation of other miRNAS in human cancers, as expected if the TNRC6A is a mediator of miR-30, is not presented in the application, albeit data answering this question might had been accessible in public databases.

Amplification or over-expression of miR-30 family members had been reported in several human cancers. Several miR-30 targets contributing to metastasis and evasion of apoptosis had been previously identified. The applicants explored other possible targets using a computational approach (TargetScan) and constructed 3’UTR reporters for the best 40 hits. Of these, 15 were suppressed by cotransfection with miR-30. Suppression of two of them by shRNA, CHD7 and TNRC6A, abrogated ras-induced senescence in BJ cells. By site mutagenesis of the shRNA-target sites in these genes, the applicant verified that senescence disruption was due to specific inhibition of these two genes, rather than off-target effects of the shRNAs.

imp_text: This is an excellent proposal by an experienced investigator that focuses in the descriptive analysis of one class of long non-coding RNA (long intergenic non-coding RNA or lincRNA) in murine B-cell lymphomas induced by Myc. The strategy consists in three steps (specific aims) to identify lincRNAs down-regulated or overexpressed in the tumors (SA1), followed by a functional in vivo characterization of the promising candidates (SA2). The last specific aim is designed to further characterize the lincRNA genes with potential oncogenic or tumor suppressor activities presumably identified in the previous aims, by construction of transgenic or know-out mice and monitoring their consequences in phenotype. The main weakness irremediably arises from the uncertain outcome despite the reasonable main hypothesis as well as the encouraging preliminary results. There is no warranty that the approach may yield bona-fide oncogenes or tumor suppressor genes, but an uncertain number of promising candidates that would complicate the analysis in the first place and make difficult to apply sound criteria for deciding which ones may be the ones deserving further in depth characterization. The impact of the project is thus, unclear. Despite these weaknesses, the proposal should yield interesting results for understanding the role of lincRNA in mouse development and/or B cell lymphomagenesis and raises considerable enthusiasm.
sig_text_str: . The project focuses on some unexplored area of the non-coding RNAs and would shed new insights in this exciting field. . The proposal is logical and well organized and the underlying hypotheses reasonable. . The focus on one particular class of long non-coding RNAs is a plus and well rationalized.
sig_text_wkn: . Albeit the assumption that among the down-regulated or over-expressed lincRNAs in Myc-driven B-cell lymphomas there may be some ones with oncogenic and/or tumor suppressor functions is reasonable, the expected results are somewhat uncertain. The main problem originates by the ambiguity of the concepts. Are ‘true” oncogenes the potential lincRNAs that may be selected during Myc-driven tumorigenesis, and if so, what would be their specific roles in the process? Would not be expected that Myc itself is the main initiating oncogene, and the putative oncogenic role of the lincRNAs be more contributing and secondary? Reversely, the putative tumor suppressors, would be really suppressing or only indirectly contributing to tumor progression? . The attempt by the applicant to support the previous evidence of the tumorigenic role of long non-coding RNAs is not convincing. The publications cited are only suggestive but not demonstrative of the main tenant.

The technology to manipulate the mice model system is within the reach of the PI for his excellent training in Tyler Jacks’ group. . The application discusses the rationale for focusing in the lincRNAs as well as the goal to extrapolate to human lymphomas the studies with mice Myc-driven B-cell lymphomas despite the intrinsic difficulty to determine conserved function due to the little sequence conservation. . There is also an effort to provide some criteria for the selection of the candidate genes for further study. Moreover, the possible identification of a multitude of genes altered in the Myc-induced tumors in the mice is also addressed by proposing the use of pools in the interference RNA libraries.
app_text_wkn: . The hypothesis to be tested is very broad and open-ended. It is not clear what would be the definitive proof for any of the candidates over-expressed or down-regulated in the mice tumor system to conclude that indeed they are bona-fide oncogenes and tumor suppressors. For instance, a lincRNA may be overexpressed in the Myc-driven tumor system and its ectopic overexpression may have some impact in cell phenotype, but not able to transform cells. Then, would it be categorized as an oncogene and its characterization be considered a success in the project?  . The proposal also makes an effort to justify and rationalize the strategy and criteria for definition (SA3) in the genetically engineered mice, but again, the arguments are not altogether convincing. A result showing knock-out of a lincRNA been sufficient to induce tumors in wt. mice is not the same as similar results requiring the concomitant presence of another oncogene, such as Myc, which is the starting point of the studies. Perhaps the difficulty emanates from the broad and lax definition of “oncogene” and “tumor suppressor genes” and it would be more logical to call them “contributors to tumor progression”. . The proposal states that either class of putative cancer genes (oncogenes and tumor suppressors) predictably existent in the tumor system will be pursued. That is, lincRNAs that may be downstream effectors of Myc, or lincRNAs that may be altered as consequence of chromosomal alterations (deletions, translocations, amplifications, etc). The rationale for this is not clear. Besides, the proposal later on does not discuss the pursuit of the second class of lincRNAs. . The preliminary results presented in the application show that the approaches proposed are feasible despite their complicated and challenging nature, but only from the technical point of view, not from the functional one. . The application describes the intention of analyzing DNA copy alterations by CGH arrays but no further discussion is found later on in the proposal. . The possibility that many candidates will come up is discussed, but an alternative course of action in addition to the one proposed (pooling libraries of interference RNA) could be more logical, by increasing the stringency of the criterion for selection. A four-fold variation in expression levels is not very impressive, and to diminish the number of putative candidates by restricting those with larger variation may also increase the probabilities of hitting relevant genes. . In SA1, the number of mouse lymphomas to be studied is not clearly defined or justified. In this context, the application discusses the criteria that would be applied in the predictable situation whereby the number of candidate lincRNAs is too large. The criteria seem fair, but have a flaw because the information used to apply the criteria can be obtained only after the analysis is completed.

It is proposed to have a plethora of effects in altering splicing, binding other snRNAs, proteins, and regulating ROS levels and p53. The PI proposes to map all the interactions of ACA11 and then determine which portions of it are responsible for those interactions.  It would be better to interrogate the sequence first to determine which of the RNA parts are most important for MM cell survival.  Little evidence is presented to show that it is the specific sequence which is important versus the double stranded nature of it.  Thus this proposal would be better received as an R21. The approaches taken to investigate the function follow standard biochemical experiments but what will follow is not specified. Meanwhile the proposal is unfocused and attempts to cover all bases with a complicated set of hypotheses for what this molecule does.

imp_text: This project focuses on elucidating the underlying molecular mechanism(s) that govern Akt activation in various types of breast cancers. They hypothesize that aberrant activation of Cdk2/Cyclin A, Skp2 and Akt somatic mutations contribute to the hyperactivation of this pathway in breast cancers. A major strength is that the aims use both biochemical and cellular approaches; various animal models (both xenograft and engineered transgenic mouse models) will be tested. These studies may provide a rationale for designing novel therapeutic approaches to combat breast cancers by suppressing the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway.
sig_text_str: • The PI 3-K/Akt signaling axis is critical for both the initiation and progression of many cancers, including breast cancer, by promoting cancer cell survival and growth. Akt hyperactivation is observed in a large proportion of patients and is considered a hallmark of cancer. • The proposed studies will provide new molecular insights into the activation of Akt in breast tumors, that would be unresponsive to PI 3-K inhibitors. The studies may inform the use of Cdk2, Skp2 and Akt inhibitors for targeted therapy to achieve optimal treatment efficacy in the clinic.

imp_text: Multiple myeloma (MM) is an important problem for which a solution is needed. The investigators have made the very interesting and potentially important observation that the expression of aca11, a noncoding RNA, is associated with a subset of MM. They characterized this aca11 as a snoRNA and demonstrate that aca11 expression decreases cellular ROS. Based on their results they propose that aca11 decreases ROS by its action in promoting RPL13a splicing. These preliminary results are compelling. The proposed hypothesis is also reasonable and consistent with the data. The concerns with this grant proposal lie in the proposed experimental approaches in SA2 and SA3. The authors have concluded, based on indirect evidence (such as the presence in RPL13a of three interacting snoRNAs in RPL13a transcript), that aca11 interacts directly with the RPL13a transcript. In view of the evidence presented, which does not distinguish between a direct interaction between the two RNAs and one that that is mediated by a protein, this conclusion is premature. Although the investigators recognized need for more evidence of interaction and proposed to investigate this question in SA2, nothing is proposed in SA2 to validate the stated conclusion of a direct interaction. Therefore, the results in SA2 will not provide incisive information that could result in a mechanistic understanding of the action of aca11. In SA3 it is proposed to test the hypothesis that aca11 inhibits ROS accumulation by interfering with p53 promoted increase in ROS. In designing their experiments to test this hypothesis the investigators evidently made the basic assumption that the mechanism by which aca11 works can be revealed in cells that are not under stress and where p53 may not be actively promoting ROS accumulation. Consequently, all experiments are proposed to be performed with cells that are not under oxidative stress.  Different results might be obtained if the experiments were performed under the oxidative conditions in which the investigators have observed suppression of ROS by aca11. A second major concern for SA3 is the proposal to use a nucleolar stressor to examine the effect of aca11 on p53 expression and snoRNA function (3D). Here the choice of 5FU as stressor is unfortunate as it affects the very functions that the investigators propose to evaluate. This inhibitor is incorporated into RNA where it has the potential of altering RNA structure. Consequently, it might affect aca11 and snoRNA structures and alter their functions, perhaps even inactivating them, which will affect the interpretations of results from the proposed experiments.

However, these snRNPs have been shown to associate with many RNAs, any of which could form the structural foundation of the snRNP rather than aca11. . It is unclear what the in silico assessments in SA2B are intended to accomplish. The search strategy was not described and was not clarified by the cited website links, particularly as one is directed to searching for plant miRNAs. . The conclusion that the interaction between RPL13a and aca11 is direct seems premature because the described results do not discriminate between a direct interaction between two RNAs and indirect interaction mediated by a protein. Regardless of the frequently stated hypothesis that aca11 “interacts directly” with snoRNAs, nothing is proposed in SA2 to validate this hypothesis. Direct interaction between RNAs usually involves hybridization, which can be readily assessed in vitro. . This assumption seems risky in light of the limited knowledge of the aca11 mechanism of action. Different results might be obtained if the experiments were performed under the oxidative conditions in which the investigators have observed suppression of ROS by aca11. . In SA3D the investigators propose to use 5FU as a nucleolar stressor to examine the effect of aca11 on p53 expression and snoRNA function. Although 5FU interferes with nucleotide metabolism, it is also incorporated into RNA from where it has been shown to alter RNA processing and function. Thus, 5FU affects the very functions that the investigators propose to evaluate. . The leadership plan does not include Dr. Cao in the monthly meetings to discuss progress and problems. imp_text: This proposal describes an unbiased search, by way of biology-driven selection, for noncoding RNAs that alter tumor progression. Despite the title, in which lncRNAs are identified as the subject of the proposal, the majority of the proposal refers to lincRNAs as the focus of this proposal. Although, at its base, the proposed approach is a “fishing expedition”, it is well-planned and supported by clearly stated rationales for each proposed experimental section.  In addition, trial experiments are presented that demonstrate the feasibility of each segment of the proposal. The preliminary results suggest a high probability of the proposed studies identifying some lincRNAs that are either tumor suppressors or promoters. The output from this proposed project promises to have the effect of catapulting progress in this relatively new area of research on the impact of noncoding RNAs in tumor biology by identifying a group of noncoding RNA candidates as tumor suppressors and promoters that are available for further exploration by many tumor biology groups.
sig_text_str: . Long noncoding RNAs are an as-yet almost completely uncharacterized segment of the human transcriptome with the potential to alter transcription of protein encoding genes and thereby alter cell functions that contribute to the cancer phenotype. . The overall approach proposed here has the potential of being a powerful way of rapidly identifying new lincRNAs that might be involved in tumorigenesis. If successful, it might serve as a model for exploration of the role of lincRNAs in the etiology of other cancers.

The inclusion of “Loew” as a collaborator on this proposal would have provided a stronger statement as to the commitment of this investigator to the project. . The first aim will require computational capabilities that seem to be the domain of Leisey, who is also not listed as a collaborator. Although her letter is stronger than Loew’s, she is not a collaborator on this proposal. Thus, her continued commitment to progress on this project is unclear.

app_text_str: . The strategies to be taken are logical and clearly presented. . Preliminary data supports the feasibility of the approach. . The high-throughput approach uses biological selection as a means of identifying the lncRNAs worthy of further investigation. . The general strategy for honing down on the most likely lncRNAs for further study is well thought through. . The strategy of using Burkitt lymphoma as a test for the likely relevance of the identified mouse lncRNAs to human lymphomas is good.
app_text_wkn: . The investigator does not reveal the composition of the “full set of lymphomas” that will be used for identifying the pool of lincRNAs to be sorted through in this proposal. On what basis will the members of the set be chosen? The choice of members of this set is important as it will determine opportunities for later discovery. . The strategy for choosing the most likely lincRNAs for further study from the large number that are expected to be identified from the original “full lymphoma set” is presented in general but the actual approach (algorithms, etc.) is not discussed. This work and the identification of the human orthologues of the identified mouse genes is likely to involve the computational skills of Dr. Leisey, who is not a collaborator, but did provide a letter of support. . It was not identified what Burkitt lymphoma data will be used for comparison between mouse and human lymphomas and how much different BL lines or primary cell preparations differ in their lincRNA expression profiles. If a single BL cell line is used for this comparison, it may result in ineffective binning of the mouse dataset. . In SA2.2.2, the investigator proposes a 30 lincRNA cutoff before using the pooled approach. This seems too high as it would require an excessive number of animals. Even if fewer than 30 lincRNAs were found involved, initial prescreening of these candidates in pools as a first stage of selection should greatly reduce the number of animals sacrificed for this purpose and would also decrease the expense of performing these screens. . In SA3.1, it is proposed to insert a floxed transcriptional stop cassette immediately downstream from the start site to prevent lincRNA expression. However, it is not clear that the pol II complex that transcribes lincRNA uses the same transcriptional stop sequences as for pol II transcribed mRNA. Consequently, the choice of transcriptional stop site should be carefully considered and needs testing for efficacy in the case of lincRNAs. . SA3.4.1 proposes to evaluate the effect of lincRNAs on spontaneous B cell lymphogenesis. Twenty mice are proposed per group. But, there is no information that this choice of 20 is justified by the rate of spontaneous lymphogenesis in this mouse line. . The investigator proposes that he will be able to determine if the lymphomas are “addicted” to the overexpression of individual lincRNAs after suspension of doxycycline treatment. But, the mice will apparently be assessed for lymphogenesis at necropsy and no blood tests or other testing is proposed to track the development of the lymphomas. So, it is unclear how these experiments will be performed. In addition, the mice will be maintained until they are moribund. It would surely be unethical to remove the treatment at the endpoint of the assay and wait to determine if the tumor regresses. . A weakness of the proposed studies for overexpression of the lincRNAs is the possibility (already known for some lncRNAs) that the RNA acts in cis and must be transcribed from its endogenous promoter in order to be effective. Although, at some point early in the proposal, this problem is mentioned, the investigator does not consider this as a potential problem in SA3 in which overexpression studies are proposed.

imp_text: Effective treatments for breast cancer are needed, particularly for some of the more aggressive subsets. The investigators propose to test the hypothesis that Akt signaling is activated by PI-3-K-dependent and independent mechanisms in breast cancer. This statement is not a viable hypothesis but rather a general statement of the goal to establish the existence of a mechanism of PI-3-K independent regulation of Akts. First, it does not identify one or the other Akt although at the time of this submission, it was known that Akt1 and Akt2 had overlapping but different cellular roles. Second, it does not define a postulated mechanism. The general nature of this statement is reflected in the diffuse nature of the proposed research. The investigators focus sequentially on Cdk2, PIK3C2, and Skp2 as regulating Akt activity, but do not propose a unifying hypothesis and do not explain why they leave out some well-known regulatory events that are expected to impact on this system. For example, why is the effect of Skp2 on destabilizing p57Kip1 (thereby activating Cdk2) not discussed as a possible mechanism by which Skp2 increases Akt1 C-terminal domain phosphorylation?  Third, although it is proposed to explore the molecular nature of the mechanisms of regulation of Akt signaling, little use is made of the known structural features of this kinase to better design tests of the molecular mechanisms. Despite these concerns, the cell biology experiments are generally well-designed. However, the crux of this proposal seems to be focused on the goal of identifying a more effective drug cocktail for treating breast cancer. For this purpose the animal biology is important. But, it is not clear from the descriptions exactly what genetic components will be present in the proposed new animal lines, which makes unclear the extent to which these animals will provide good model system for hypothesis testing.  In this regard, the investigators would benefit by a collaborator with experience in creating transgenic animals.
sig_text_str: . Breast cancer is a prevalent disease and its eradication will benefit by a better understanding of the mechanisms that drive cell proliferation and metastasis and prevent apoptosis of aberrant cells.
inv_text_str: . These are strong investigators with a history of success in investigating cells signaling mechanisms and publishing their findings.
inv_text_wkn: . The proposed studies include a significant portion of time and funds to be committed to creating transgenic animals and using them for drug testing. The investigators would benefit by the addition to the project of an expert in this area.
inn_text_str: . The investigators proposed two innovations (a novel mechanism of Akt activation by Cdk2 and functional redundancy between PI 3-K and Skp2 in promoting Akt localization and activation) with both innovations being linked to clinical application of drug combinations based on their proposed signaling mechanisms.
inn_text_wkn: . The innovation proposed by the investigators that this work will provide a basis for using Cdk2 inhibitors combined with Akt inhibitors is not innovative as it was shown many years ago that this combination of inhibitors is highly effective against prostate cancer cells (Mohaptra et al. Int J Biochem Cell Biol. 2009 41(3):595-602) although the proposed mechanistic link was different than proposed here. . In general the proposed experimental approaches are not innovative.
app_text_str: . In SA1, the investigators will test the question of whether Akt is phosphorylated in its C-terminal domain by CDK2/cyclin A. These experiments are generally well-designed, with robust controls. In addition, the investigators will test the role if any of the Rxl cyclin A binding motifs in Akt1 for regulation of Akt activity by CDK2/cyclin. These studies are likely to determine if Cdk2-mediated phosphorylation of Akt1 regulates Akt1 cellular function. . SA2, which focuses on the role of PIK3C2 and regulation of Akt by Skp2 includes some good approaches to tease out a better understanding of how these enzymes might regulate Akt activity. . The proposal to follow up on the preliminary data, which showed that an inhibitor of class II PI-3 kinases was most effective in preventing Akt phosphorylation, is potentially important for improving chemotherapeutic strategies.
app_text_wkn: . In SA1.2 the anticipated results seem inconsistent with the proposed studies. For example the investigators anticipate observing that the Akt1-DE mutant responds more rapidly to insulin stimulation. However, none of the described experiments involve establishing a time course or any type of chronological study. . In SA1.4 it is stated that the Cdk2 inhibitors are expected to lead to reduced transformation, but it was not proposed to determine the effect of these inhibitors on transformation. . Some experimental approaches seem to have been only casually considered. For example it is stated “Since T479 is not present in Akt2 and Akt3, the T479A and T479D mutants on Akt2 and Akt3 will be generated”. But, if T479 is not present, how can a mutation of T479 be made? . As described in SA1.5, the approach to developing transgenic animals is flawed in several ways. The Akt1-DE mutants will be placed under a TET-off system, targeted to the collagen A1 locus by flp recombinase then the mice will be bred with Cre-recombinase mice. It is unclear how the marriage of the Cre-lox and FLP-FRT systems will be accomplished. In addition, the TET-off regulation is incorporated but not proposed to be used to regulate expression.  Adding to this, the number of proposed crosses with the necessary subsequent breeding will take many years to accomplish. With this commitment of time it is important for the investigators to be more incisive in their choice of mouse strains to create and in their technical approaches to obtaining these strains. . Rather than referring to available structural information for guidance, the investigators propose to make the seemingly uninformed mutation of inserting additional Ser/Thr residues in the Akt2 activation loop to compensate for pT309. . Although the complication for interpreting animal studies due to the presence of endogenous Atk is recognized for SA1 and SA2, the investigators propose to test the effect of the E17K mutants in a background of wild-type Atk. Perhaps the argument is that the tumor cells that have been found to have this mutation also have wild-type alleles? However, the lack of justification of this decision flags this experimental design as weak.

env_text_wkn: . There is no description of an available transgenic animal facility where the various proposed transgenic animals will be produced. More importantly, the available expertise in animal genetics and the technologies required for creating transgenic animals is not described.

imp_text: The proposal has the goal of identifying de-regulated functional lincRNAs in the pathogenesis of Myc-driven B cell lymphomas and studies their roles in tumor initiation and tumor progression. The approach consists a high-throughput screening of de-regulated lincRNAs, in vitro and in vivo functional screens assays, and generating loss-of-function and gain-of-function engineered mice, which is innovative and straightforward and should make an impact on the field. The primary concern is the screening, identification and verification of human homologues of lincRNAs deregulated in Myc-driven mouse B cell lymphomas in Aim 1. The investigator elucidates several problems and strategies related to Aim 1 including setting restricted criteria for screening. This application is a bit of overambitious. The investigator is well experienced to conduct the proposed studies, and has strong collaborators.
sig_text_str: . Potential roles of lincRNAs in the pathogenesis of human cancer. . This novel approach is likely to identify novel lincRNAs with oncogenic or tumor-suppressive potential in Myc-driven B cell lymphomas. . Preliminary data are encouraging that a subset of lincRNAs was de-regulated in Myc-driven B cell lymphomas and identified as Myc direct targets. . Cancer-associated lincRNAs will be tested by gain- and loss-of-function experiments in genetically engineered mice.

imp_text: The proposed project is to study novel upstream regulatory pathways of Akt, with focus on Cdk2 and Skp2 and somatic mutations of Akt genes, and design novel inhibitors and/or combination therapies in treating breast cancer. The pathway of Cdk2/Cyclin A-mediated activation of Akt (Aim 1) and Skp2-mediated activation of Akt (Aim 2) will be extensively studied on tumor progression. All two aims are strong with considerable rational and preliminary data, and are convinced to identify novel regulators in Akt pathway. The project is enhanced by strong collaborators for single cell dynamic imaging and mouse models.
sig_text_str: . Increased Akt activity is found in agreesive human breast cancer and is associated with poor prognosis and drug resistance. . Potent Akt inhibitor leads to extensive cell death in clinical studies. . Targeting cancer-specific Akt upstream signaling components will provide novel therapeutic strategy. . Aberrant activation of Cdk2/Cyclin A links Akt activity to cell cycle and tumorigenesis, and provides therapeutic targets for Akt signaling. . Aberrant activation of Skp2 mediates hyperactivation of Akt in a PI3K-independent manner, and serves as alternative therapeutic targets in treatment of breast cancer patients with PI3K resistance.

Dr. Weimin Wan is Associate Professor of Pathology at Harvard Medical School, and has identified Skp2 as novel regulator in Akt signaling pathway and evidenced with many high impact journals. . The proposed study begins with the considerable amount we already know about activation of Akt in human cancers, and extends this pathway in two novel areas: Cell cycle regulation (Aim1) and Skp2 signal without PI3K involved (Aim2). In aim 1, Dr. Robinson and his colleagues will emphasize studies of Cdk2/Cyclin A in S phase, and its regulation on activation of Akt. Phosphorylation sites as Akt C-terminal pS477 and pT479 will be examined in Akt activity and their role in breast cancer development. As novel phosphorylation sites in Akt tail, this project will determine whether loss of these phosphorylation in Akt will cause resistance in breast cancer developed by MMTV-Ras and MMTV-Her2. . Aim 2 is focused on the other regulator, Skp2 in Akt activation in cancer in PI3K-independent manner. The goal is to identify alternative pathway to evaluate Akt reactivation subsequent to PI3K inhibition in breast cancer. In this aim, it first studies reactivation of Akt isoforms, Akt2 or both Akt1 and Akt2  and Skp2 when inhibiting PI3K. Next it evaluates whether inhibition of PI3K with small molecule inhibitors phenocopies PI3K silencing and lastly they will perform xenograft models to provide physiological evidence for Akt reactivation. . Besides upstream regulator in Akt signals, the proposal will also determine the effects of activation of Akt E17K somatic mutations in breast cancer cells, which will provide a solid basis for this mutation in cancer patients. . The proposal is well written with strong preliminary data, and the rationale sounds reasonable.

The preliminary finding and specific proposal that ACA11 non-coding RNA overexpression reduces ROS-induced cell death in t(4;14) translocation positive MM, is poised to make a major impact on our understanding of this aggressive form of plasma cell cancer and will lead to potential new ways of therapeutics. sig_text_str: • The current proposal is based upon the finding that ACA11 which is a 125 bp orphan H/ACA class non-coding RNA (ncRNA), strongly up-regulated in cell lines and MM patient samples harboring t(4;14). In preliminary studies using RNA FISH in MM samples, they classified ACA11 as a small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) because ACA11 was predominately localized to nucleoli and was found to be part of snRNP complex comprising DHX9, ILF3 (NF90) and SF3B1 etc. Further, ACA11 expression significantly reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, and knock down of ACA11 increased oxidative stress in MM cells and slowed their growth.  Three major aims are proposed. In Aim 1, experiments are proposed to further characterize the members of ACA11-snRNP complex, and regions in ACA11 responsible for its biological activities. In Aim2, ACA11 interaction with ribosomal protein transcripts leading to changes in response to oxidative stress are proposed. And in Aim 3, experiments are proposed to examine the effects of ACA11 expression on nucleolar morphology and function; and p53 activation and its effect on ROS. • Overall, the proposed aim and experimental designs are novel and of potential high impact. Each Aim and sub-aim is clearly written and follows a nice logical pattern. • This proposed study will also have translational significance in the long term.

This proposal focuses on mechanistic studies of the novel function of microRNA (miR-30) in oncogene-induced senescence, an important fail-safe tumor suppressing defense response in mammals. In a genetic screen, author found that miR-30  disrupts a critical tumor suppressing mechanism called oncogene-induced Senescence by directly targeting CHD7, a transcriptional co-activator, and TNRC6A, an RNA-binding protein essential for miRNA functionality. In this grant application, they propose to investigate the mechanisms underlying the roles of CHD7 and TNRC6A in miR-30-mediated bypass of oncogenic ras-induced senescence, and examine the impact of the miR-30-CHD7/TNRC6A regulatory circuit on cancer development. imp_text: This proposal aims to investigate biological functions of ACA11, a small nucleolar RNA (snoRNA) encoded in the intron of WHSC1 gene and is overexpressed in the multiple myeloma (MM) with t(4;14) chromosomal translocation. The strength of the proposal is that ACA11 is a novel snoRNA whose biological functions are not yet characterized. The preliminary data supported the hypothesis that ACA11 may play a role in ROS regulation. The proposal studies may lead to identification of proteins interacting with ACA11, possible targets of ACA11, and mechanisms of ACA11 mediated ROS regulation. ACA11 may also play a role in the disease progression is subgroup of MM with t(4;14) translocation. The weakness of the proposal is that the hypothesis that ACA11 is critical in MM progression and/or resistance to the treatment is not sufficiently supported or documented in the preliminary study. There is no effort in proposed studies to demonstrate the role of ACA11 in MM progression and/or treatment resistance. There is no much novelty in the research strategies. The experimental models limited to a few cell lines, which is not sufficient to document the role of ACA11 in t(4;14) MM. The overall impact is likely low.

imp_text: This proposal aims to determine miR30 and its downstream targets in Ras-induced senescence and cancer development and possible underlying mechanisms. The applicants presented relatively strong preliminary data to support that miR30 prevented HRas induced senescence and that CHD7 and TNRC6A could be possible downstream targets in this proposes. The proposed studies will further investigate possible mechanisms of CHD7 and TNRC6A in Ras-induced senescence and tumorigenesis. The strength of the proposal is possible novel information might be generated in terms of miR30 mediated regulation of senescence. Ras-induced senescence is regarded as a barrier for oncogenesis and regulation of miR30 in this process is not yet characterized. The regulations of p16 by CHD7 and microRNA metabolism by TNRC6A could be potentially novel. The research strategies are feasible and can be completed in the PI’s. The weakness of the proposal is that most studies were performed or will be performed in fibroblasts with HRas, while most human cancers with Ras mutations were derived from epithelial cells with mutations in KRas and NRas. The proposed studies focused primarily on cultured cell lines. Whether miR30 and/or CHD7, TNRC6A are contributing to Ras-mediated tumorigenesis is not extensively investigated. The proposed studies will not provide a clear conclusion to this question. The overall impact is moderate.

imp_text: This proposal aims to characterize molecular mechanism of PIK3CA independent activation of AKT and its role in breast cancer development or resistance to treatment. The strength of proposal is the strong preliminary data to support that CDK2/CylcinA and SKP2 may be involved in AKT activation or reactivation after PI3K inhibition, which are relatively novel pathways regulating AKT activity, and possible role of AKT activation in resistance to breast cancer treatment. The approaches to further investigate the roles of CDK2/cyclinA and SKP2 in breast cancer cell lines and transgenic animal models are appropriate. The studies will further confirm the effects of the CDK2/cyclinA and SKP2 in regulating AKT activity in breast cancer cells. The PIs are established investigators with expertise in pathways for CKD2/cyclinA and SKP2. However, the investigations limited to cell lines and some transgenic models. Breast cancer patient specimens is not included. The proposed studies investigate different pathways or molecules that may activate AKT independent of PI3K, however, further strategies to explore those pathways for clinical implications (enhancing treatment efficacy or identifying responders etc), were either missing or only shallowly touched. The interaction between the two aims is weakness. It will remain unclear whether CDK2/CyclinA and/or SKP2 mediate AKT activation are involved in specific subsets of breast cancer patients/specimens, or whether there is any interactions between these two pathways. Overall, the proposed studies may lead to some novel information on AKT activations, but its relevance on breast cancer treatment is not rigorously investigated.

imp_text: This is a new proposal from a team of successful investigators. This proposal aims at deciphering the contribution of overexpression of the non-coding RNA ACA11 in the etiology of multiple myeloma and response to chemotherapy. The proposed experiments stem from the recent identification by the applicants of ACA11 as an overexpressed non-coding RNA in multiple myeloma cells harboring the t(4;14) translocation. In the previous study, the applicants have shown that ACA11 decrease sensitivity to oxidative stress in these cells, thus providing a potential molecular basis for the exquisite resistance of this multiple myeloma subtype to therapy. In this proposal, the PI will extend these findings to test the hypothesis that ACA11 overexpression reduces ROS-induced cell death through its ability to modulate splicing of snoRNAs and thus inhibit nucleolar stress.  The preliminary data are elegant and convincingly demonstrate that ACA11is overexpressed in t(4,;14) MM cells and is part of a specific RNP complex, which targets snoRNA. The significance of the proposed research could be high, as the identification of a molecular marker that underlines the exquisite resistance of t(4;14) MM to chemotherapy is very important. In addition, the experiments that are proposed, while exploratory in parts, are likely to reveal how ACA11 modulates snoRNA splicing. However, the molecular link between the snoRNAs targeted by ACA11 and the sensitivity to oxidative stress appears largely correlative at this point. In addition, the third aim seems disconnected and is currently not supported by strong preliminary data. Overall, the reservations regarding the rationale for the third aim and for the link between snoRNA and oxidative stress decreased the enthusiasm for this application. The impact of the proposed research is likely to be moderate to high.

imp_text: This is a new proposal from a mid-career investigator who has made important contributions in the field of oncogene-induced senescence. This proposal aims at deciphering the contribution of miR30 in the regulation of oncogene-induced senescence, the molecular mechanisms underlying such effect, and their implications for human tumorigenesis. The proposed experiments stem from the interesting observation, presented in the preliminary data section, that overexpression of miR30 prevents Ras-induced senescence, and that this effect is mediated at least in part through its ability to down-regulate CHD7 and TNRC6A expression. In this proposal, the applicant will decipher the mechanisms underlying the effect of CHD7 and TNRC6A on Ras induced senescence (aim 1 and 2), and test hypothesis that miR-30 levels are unregulated in cancer, thus providing a molecular basis for the the bypass of cellular senescence (aim 3). The significance is high, as the identification of novel regulators of cellular senescence may provide novel insight on this largely elusive process. In addition, the possibility that a global disruption of miRNA (through TNRC6A downregulation) is involved in cellular senescence could be a very exciting finding. The preliminary data are elegant and convincingly demonstrate that miR-30 and its two downstream targets regulate cellular senescence. In addition, the PI has a unique blend of expertise in cellular senescence and microRNA biology, placing her in an ideal position to perform the proposed experiments. The enthusiasm for the application was however strongly dampened by the weaknesses in the experimental approach, that include as a narrow scope and a slightly incremental aim 1. Aim 2 could be much more exciting, but the experiments that are proposed lack physiological relevance, as they are all performed via overexpression and not in senescent cells. Finally, the third aim, while important, lacks experimental details and controls. In balance, the weaknesses in the experimental approach drove the score for this application which is likely to have a moderate impact.

imp_text: This is a new proposal from a relatively new investigator who has made important contributions in the field of lncRNAs and cancer. This proposal aims at identifying novel lncRNAs that modulate myc-driven oncogenesis using expression analysis and elegant in vivo screens. The proposal is highly significant as the contribution of lncRNAs in cancer is just beginning to be investigated. The investigator is very well qualified to perform the proposed experiments, as evidenced by the impressive set of preliminary data. The experimental design is elegant and will undoubtedly provide novel insight in the identity of specific lncRNAs that are involved in cancer. Slight reservations regarding the experimental research design include the very broad and open ended nature of the experiments, and are somewhat balanced by the demonstration that the investigator has already identified potential candidates. The interdependence between the aims (especially aim 3), and the lack of validation of the results in other systems, including in human samples, slightly dampened the enthusiasm for an otherwise exciting proposal, which, if completed properly, could have a very high impact in the field.

sig_text_wkn: . The lack of crossvalidation using independent systems or human data decrease the potential relevance of the findings.

imp_text: The t(4;14) chromosomal translocation found in 20% of multiple myeloma (MM) patients is known to lead to a shorter survival rate.  Examination of a 2 MB region around the t(4;14) breakpoint, in the PIs laboratories, revealed the overexpression of a 125 bp orphan H/ACA class non-coding RNA, termed ACA11, which was confirmed to be up-regulated in t(4;14) MM cell lines and patient samples. Additional preliminary data  demonstrated that  ACA11 localizes to the nucleolus as part of a novel small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex, that other snoRNAs resident within introns of ribosomal protein (RP) genes, including snoRNAs in the RPL13a gene that were documented as mediators of oxidative stress. The PIs provide preliminary data that ACA11 overexpression reduces the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in response to oxidative stress and increases cell survival. Based on these findings the PIs hypothesize that the overexpression of ACA11 in t(4;14) MM reduces ROS-induced cell death leading to the development and/or progression of MM. Significance and innovation are high and the PIs are well qualified to conduct the proposed work. Overall the experimental design is hypothesis driven and adequately  designed. However, the role of the candidate oncogene overexpressed from the t(4;14)translocation, WHSC1 (MMSET), has not been rigorously ruled out. The PIs state that experiments conduced in their laboratories provided evidence that the  candidate oncogene overexpressed from the t(4;14)translocation, WHSC1 (MMSET), was unable to transform cells in culture or drive tumorigenesis in mice on its own, Yet, no preliminary data are provided to support this statement. Additionally Aim 3, to  test if overexpression of ACA11 leads to an inhibition of nucleolar stress-induced, p53-regulated ROS production, is largely descriptive and lacks preliminary data. These weaknesses reduce the overall impact. The PIs state that experiments conduced in their laboratories provided evidence that the  candidate oncogene overexpressed from the t(4;14)translocation, WHSC1 (MMSET), was unable to transform cells in culture or drive tumorigenesis in mice on its own (data not shown). However, examination of a 2 MB region around the t(4;14) breakpoint revealed the overexpression of a 125 bp orphan H/ACA class non-coding RNA, termed ACA11, which was confirmed to be up-regulated in t(4;14) MM cell lines and patient samples. Further preliminary studies demonstrated that  ACA11 localizes to the nucleolus as part of a novel small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) complex. Deep sequencing revealed that RNA targets of this snRNP are other snoRNAs resident within introns of ribosomal protein (RP) genes, including snoRNAs in the RPL13a gene that were documented as mediators of oxidative stress. The PIs provide preliminary data that ACA11 overexpression reduces the levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in response to oxidative stress and increases cell survival. Based on these findings the PIs hypothesize that the overexpression of ACA11 in t(4;14) MM reduces ROS-induced cell death leading to the development and/or progression of MM. To elucidate the mechanism by which ACA11 exerts its inhibitory effects on ROS-induced cell cycle inhibition and cell death in t(4;14) MM cell lines,   The PIs delineate 3 specific Aims. In Aim 1,  the PIs will test the hypothesis that ACA11 must interact with snRNP’s to exert its inhibition of oxidative stress induced cell death by determining: a) the members of the ACA11-snRNP complex; b) which bases of the ACA11 RNA are required for snRNP complex formation, and c) ability of the ACA11 mutant to alter oxidative stress, cell growth, and resistance to chemotherapy in MM cells. In Aim 2 the PIs will test the hypothesis that ACA11 regulates ROS levels through modulating splicing of snoRNAs from ribosomal protein transcripts. The will examine: a) interaction of ACA11 with ribosomal protein transcripts; b) effects of ACA11 levels on snoRNA levels; and c) effects of ACA11-targeted snoRNAs on MM cell line response to oxidative stress. Finally, in Aim 3 the PIs propose to  test the hypothesis that overexpression of ACA11 leads to an inhibition of nucleolar stress-induced, p53-regulated ROS production, given that  the cell death program activated by p53 was documented to be in part  mediated by increasing ROS levels. Thus, overall the experimental approach is hypothesis driven. In all of the  aims expected results and alternative approaches are adequately discusses. Also, Aims 1&2 are supported by adequate preliminary data.

Given that the significnace of overexpression of ACA11 in the development and/or progression of MM relies heavily on these observations, the PI should provide rigorous data to support this notion. . The PI do not include   primary MM samples obtained from patients in any of their experiments, and preliminary data show increased expression of ACA11 in only four t(4;14)-positive MM patient samples in comparison to twelve t(4;14)-negative MM patient samples. Additional t(4;14)-positive MM patient samples would strengthen the significance of the role ACA11 overexpression plays in he etiology of MM. .

imp_text: . the overall goal of the proposed research is to investigate the mechanisms underlying the roles of CHD7 and TNRC6A in miR-30-mediated bypass of oncogenic ras-induced senescence, and examine the impact of the miR-30-CHD7/TNRC6A regulatory circuit on cancer development. The PI and collaborators are are well qualified to conduct the proposed experiments. Overall the proposed research approach is hypothesis driven, well designed and feasible. It is likely to yield novel data  regarding  the roles CHD7 and TNRC6A play in miR-30-mediated bypass of oncogenic ras-induced senescence, and in cancer development/progression. Nevertheless, the overall hypothesis is not well integrated. On the one hand,  the PI provides preliminary data suggesting that mir-30 suppression of CHD7 plays a role in down regulation of p16INK4 and I.B. SASP, implicating that mir-30 bypass of ras induced senescence is mediated by blunting both p16INK4 and I.B./SASP.  On the other preliminary data suggest that mir-30 suppression of TNRC6A, results in global down-regulation of miRNAs functionality, which in turn leads to disruption of ras-induced senescence. app_text_str: . The long term goal of this multiple PI project is to design novel anti-breast cancer targeted therapies to suppress the oncogenic PI 3-K and Akt signaling pathway that is frequently deregulated in breast cancer, since available potent Akt inhibitors exhibit marked side effects that enhance apoptosis in both cancer and normal cells. It is known that the Class I lipid kinase PIK3CA, promotes conversion of PtdIns-4,5-P2  to PIP3. Both PtdIns-3,4-P2  and PIP3 recruit inactive Akt to the membrane for activation, where  PIP3 is converted back to PtdIns-4,5-P2  by PTEN, terminating PI3K/Akt signaling. Recruitment of  Akt to membranes, promotes phosphorylation of two critical residues responsible for maximal catalytic activity, i.e. T308 mediated by PDK1  &  S473 mediated by mTORC2. PI 3-K/Akt pathway is known to be hyperactivated in human tumors, as a result of amplifications or mutations in molecules that regulate PI 3-K &/or Akt. PI 3-K/Akt hyperactivation occurs as a result of loss of function mutations in PTEN, amplification/somatic mutations of the p110..subunit of PIK3CA, or Akt amplification or somatic mutations. The E17K somatic mutation was identified in both Akt1 & Akt2. The Akt1,E17K mutation results in a constitutively active kinase with modest oncogenic properties, whereas the effect of E17K on Akt2 activity has not been examined. The PIs provide novel preliminary data showing that during cell cycle progression, Cdk2/CyclinA triggers Akt activation by phosphorylating the C-terminus of Akt at S477/T479. Intriguingly, additional  preliminary data indicate that: a subset of TNBC lines display Akt reactivation upon PIK3CA inhibition; that Class II PI 3-K contributes to Akt reactivation, implicating PtdIns-3,4-P2 (made by PIK3C2) in reactivation of Akt independent of PIK3CA; that Skp2 E3 ligase contributes to Akt reactivation; & that Akt1 E17K & Akt2 E17K have different signaling properties in breast epithelial cells, where only Akt2 E17K promotes robust S473 phosphorylation & cell growth in serum-deprived media. Based on these findings the driving hypothesis is that in breast cancer, Akt signaling is activated by both PI 3- K-dependent & -independent mechanisms, where the PIs propose to define novel upstream regulatory pathways of Akt, including Cdk2, Skp2, and somatic mutations of Akt  that will guide the development of novel inhibitors to treat breast cancer. To this end, in Aim 1 the PIs will characterize molecular mechanisms by which Akt activation is modulated by Cdk2/Cyclin A during the cell cycle & in response to growth factor signaling, in vitro & in vivo using breast cancer cancer cell lines, as well as xenografts and transgenic mice models to determine if Cdk2/CyclinA inhibitors can suppress breast tumors displaying elevated Akt activity. On the other hand, in Aim 2 the PIs will determine the mechanism by which Skp2 contributes to Akt activation, and the functional significance of Akt1 and Akt2 E17K mutations, using cell culture models as well as Akt1 E17K and Akt2 E17K transgenic mice to evaluate tumorigenesis to guide the development of novel targeted therapies for blocking Akt signaling in breast cancers. Taken together this research approach is hypothesis driven, well designed, and interesting. It is likely to provide novel data that will be valuable for design of breast cancer targeted therapies to suppress oncogenic PI 3-K and Akt signaling. .

imp_text: This application seeks to study the role of a specific chromosomal translocation event in the progression of multiple myeloma, which is an incurable malignancy.  This particular translocation is apparent in 20% of patients and is associated with poor prognosis and survival. The candidate oncogene resulting from this translocation is a non-coding RNA, ACA11 that can transform cells in culture and cause tumorigenesis in mice. ACA11 localizes to the nucleolus and forms a complex as a small nuclear ribonucleoprotein (snRNP) that is overexpressed in patients with multiple myeloma.  As a result of nuclear translocation, the applicant proposes that snRNP inhibits the ability of reactive oxygen species (ROS) to kill B cells and acts as an important driver of multiple myeloma. While the proposed studies have the potential to result in a potential new drug target or diagnostic marker for multiple myeloma, the limited scope of the proposal to cultured cells limits the overall enthusiasm for the application.

imp_text: This is an overly ambitious proposal from a talented, promising new investigator to study specific structures that participate in various aspects of meiosis. This is highly relevant area of research that currently suffers from a lack of structural biology, and thus the proposed work has potential for highly impactful discoveries. The proposal is very clearly written and organized and beautifully illustrated. Most of the structural targets and approaches are worthwhile, while some are low-hanging fruit that seem to be proposed because they can be done, but might not have as much impact. The proposal suffers from two major flaws: it is overly ambitious in its design; there is simply too much work to be done in a single grant term. Secondly, there is a lack of preliminary data to demonstrate feasibility of the structural aims. This latter point would normally be a minor one given that the PI has a good track record and is also new, but coupled with the volume of experiments proposed and the lack of a reasonable timeline for their completion, I question whether the aims can be completed as written. The proposal would benefit greatly from inclusion of preliminary data, or paring down and focusing on fewer targets.

imp_text: This proposal addresses the molecular mechanisms of the human DNA replication, which is highly significant to human health. Recent breakthroughs in this field have set the stage for significant progress to be made. This proposal is focused on the CMG helicase complex, which is believed to constitute the core component of the replisome, and seeks to address 1) how interactions of the two replicative polymerases (epsilon, delta) with CMG affect leading and lagging strand synthesis, 2) how Ctf4 and other interacting partners affect CMG assembly in vivo, and 3) the role of GINS protein Psf1 on CMG stability and function. The PI has a strong record of accomplishment in the DNA replication field, but overall the experimental plan devised here was limited in scope and rather disorganized.
sig_text_str: . Synthesis of DNA at the replication fork is one of the most fundamental processes in all organisms, but the molecular details in eukaryotes are poorly understood (major) . Defects in the timing and mechanism of replication give rise to a number of human diseases including cancer (Major) . CMG helicase likely lies at the heart of the eukaryotic replisome. (minor)

The additional glycerol gradient experiments described to examine interacting partners that affect CMG stability seems incremental over the existing preliminary data. (Major) . imp_text: Strengths: The translocation t(4:14) is associated with a poor prognosis in multiple myeloma, but the mechanism behind this is poorly understood. While an oncogene has been associated with this translocation (WHSC1), its overexpression dles not lead to transformation. The PI of this proposal has identified ACA11 as a non-coding RNA that is upregulated in myeloma cells containing this translocation.  The Pis lab will address how ACA11 is associated with the disease. This is significant and important because currentl patients with the translocation have a poor prognosis, and there is a need to understand the mechanism behind this translocation in order to develop new and more effective treatments.
sig_text_str: The t(4:14) translocation is associated with a poor prognosis and the mechanism behind it is poorly understood. The PI has identified a new potential mechanism by which the cells containing this translocation are transformed. This is highly significant because it has the potential to lead to a better understanding of the disease and to the future identification of new drug targets.
inv_text_str: Dr. Washington has a strong background in studying multiple myeloma and has expertise in the techniques required for this project. Dr. Magil also has expertise in the field and the two have a successful history of collaborations.
inn_text_str: This project is innovative due to the investigation of a new mechanism by which the 4(4:14) translocation leads to multiple myeloma. Previous work has focused largely on WHSC, but this has failed to yield insight into myeloma biology. The PI has identified a novel mechanism behind the translocation in myeloma.

app_text_str: In the first aim the investigators will confirm the ACA11 interacting proteins. Mutations in ACA11 will be generated, in order to determine the functional importance of these interactions. Although some nonspecific interactions could be identified, these studies will help in addressing the mechanism by which ACA11 operates. In aim 3 the investigators will test a hypothesis that overexpression of ACA11 leads to inhibition of molecular stress induced p53 regulated ROS production. This is an interesting model. It is a bit risky because a connection with p53 has not been established. Nevertheless, p53 is a good candidate, as p53 has an important role to play in the response to nucleolar stress.
app_text_wkn: Much of the study is based on the idea that ACA11 is a located in the nucleolus. However, this appears to have been test only by overexpression, and it was not assessed in MM cells. This will be remedied in the proposal, but it would have been good to have these localization studies before proceeding with the studies in the proposal. Another potential problem is the reliance on MM cell lines rather than primary cells, but the authors do explain why this is not possible in the present study. Aim 2 involves identifying RP RNA targets of ACA11 snRNP. This will include a section that will entail deep sequencing of RNAs pulled down from cross-linked ACA11 knockdown and control cells. While this may yield important results, it could lead to the identification of  many potential targets and it is thereby lead to results that are difficult to interpret. imp_text: Strengths: This is a straightforward proposal, designed to study miRNAs and oncogene induced senescence, focusing on the microRNA miR-30. Oncogene induced senescence is an important mechanism by which cells avoid cancer. The idea of the role for microRNAs in the avoidance of this process is new, and provides new insight into the role for microRNAs in cancer. As such, the experiments in this proposal will lead to significant new information. Weanesses: Oncogene induced senescence itself is not a particularly new field, which reduces the overall impact this study will have.
sig_text_str: MicroRNAs have been found to have increasingly important roles in cellular functions. While they are well known to play a role in cancer, their role in oncogene induced senescence is a relatively new area of investigation. In this sense, the proposal is significant, because it addresses a new biological area, and one that is important for cancer.
sig_text_wkn: The weakness is that senescence has been studied a great deal in the past, although as indicated above, the role for MicroRNAs in the process is quite new.
inv_text_str: . The investigator has a solid publication background in cell signaling and studying microRNAs. The investigator is an Associate Professor at Scripps, and has been there since 2010.
inn_text_str: The study of miRNA in cellular senescence is a relatively new area of investiagtion. Furthermore, the idea that the investigator proposes, that one miRNA can globally inhibit other miRNAs and thereby disrupt senescence, is a new concept.
inn_text_wkn: Many of the techniques proposed are standard techniques. Aim 3 is the least innovative, and involves standard techniques and the possibility of somwhat ambiguous results.
app_text_str: Score (1-9):  In aim 1 the investigator will test the hypothesis that CHD7 binds to the p16INK4a promoter and regulates its activity. This could help explain how downregulation of CHD7 mediates senescence by miR-30, since p16INK4a has an important role in Ras induced senescence. While there is a possibility that the effect of miR-30 on p16INK4a is indirect, and that the investigators will not find a  promoter or enhancer binding site, the PI acknowledges this and presents reasonable alternative plans. In aim 2 the investigator will test the hypothesis that downregulation of TNRC6A (also regulated by the miR30), leads to global downregulation of miRNAs, thus leading to disruptio of senescence. This is well planned out and alternative plans are included. .
app_text_wkn: One weakness with aim 2 is that while the results will inicate whether TNRC6A downregulates miRNAs, it will be difficult to difinitely conclude that this is the actual mechanism by which it inhibits senescence. The third aim involves studying whether miR30 is directly associated with cancer. This is important, because it forms the basis of the rationale for studying miR30’s role in senescence. It may be more effective to carry out this aim first, to in order to provide more of a rationale for the other studies. The use of cancer cells for these experiments does not seem necessary, because they are already highly transformed. Experiments that they propose for fibroblasts will be more useful. Finally, studying the miR-30, CHD7, and TNRC6A levels in cancer cells is important, but it is not particularly innovative, and it is likely to lead to quite a bit of variability in the results. .

imp_text: Strengths: The goal of this proposal is to study the mechanism by which AKT is activated in cancer cells, focusing on breast cancer cells. The long term goal is to develop inhibitors that will block AKT without using PI3 kinase inhibitors, which have been known to have side effects in normal cells. To this end the inestigators will define upstream regulatory pathways of AKT including CDK2/CyclinA, Skp2, and somatic mutations in AKT genes. If succesful, these studies will provide important information for the development of new clincal therapies for the treatment of breast cancer, without relying on PI3 Kinase inhibitors. Weanesses: Overall this is a strong proposal. It is quite ambitious in its scope, so one concern would be accomplishing all of the goals, particularly aim 3, in the timeframe of the proposal.
sig_text_str: . The PI3-Kinase/AKT pathway is clearly an important target for cancer. However, there is a strong need for PI3-Kinase inhibitor independent treatments, in part due to side effects, or ineffectiveness, or cellular resistance to current treatments. In this respect the proposal is highly significant because novel mechanisms of AKT will be explored, leading to the rationale for developing new treatment options.
inv_text_str: . Both Dr. Brian and Dr. Wan are well accomplished and have numerous publications in their fields. They are well suited to carrying out the projects.
inn_text_str: . This project is innovative because it aims to address innovative new methods for inhibiting AKT. Rather than relying on current treatments, the investigators will explore new, PI3-Kinase independent, mechanisms of AKT activation, and in turn identify new potential targets for inhibition in cancer.
app_text_str: In the first aim the PI will study the activation of AKT by Cdk2/CyclinA. They will also determine whether inhibition of Cdk2/cyclinA suppresses breast cancer development by blocking Akt activation. The last part of the aim is an ambitious section in which the investigator will use transgenic mice containing a non-phosphorylatable AKT mutant, to assess the significance of AKT phosphorylation in breast cancer. Aim 2 addresses PI3-Kinase independent mechanisms of AKT activation in breast cancer cells. They focus specifically on Skp2, as well as AKT somatic mutations, as mechanisms of AKT activation. These are strong studies, and they suggest that Skp2 and AKT may be new targets for intervention in cancer treatment. Furthermore, this aim is important because preliminary studies for this aim emphasize the need for new inhibitors other than those specific to Pi3-Kinase.
app_text_wkn: Although it is expected that AKTactivity wil be regulated in all of the cell lines by Cdk2/CyclinA in a cell cycle dependent manner, more detailed alternative plans should be discussed in case this is not the case in all cells. The transgenic mouse section, while it has the advantage of assessing the significance of phosphorylation, it focuses on Ras and Her2 induced tumorigenesis. This is by necessity because of available models, but it may not be directly relevant to all types of breast cancer. In particular, it is still not clear whether Ras overexpression has biological relevance in breast cancer. Furthermore, some of the authors preliminary studies were carried out with triple negative cells, which would not be represented by this system. While Aim 2 has important impications in the identification of new mechanisms for AKT activation, it is quite ambitious for one aim. It may be better to focus on Skp2 here, and to address AKT somatic mutations in more detail, in a 3rd aim. .

imp_text: The overall goal of this grant is to functionally dissect how the small noncoding Aca11 influences oxidative stress-­?induced cell death and snRNA activity. Multiple myeloma patients with poor prognosis correlates with the incidence of characteristic translocation t(4:14) that leads to the overexpression of the candidate oncogene WHSC1 (MMSET), a relatively uncharacterized chromatin modifying enzyme with a SET domain found in histone methyltransferase enzymes. Overexpression of WHSC1 alone though does not lead to any oncogenic phenotypes, leading to the question whether it indeed is an oncogene. The researchers have identified and characterized a novel non-­?coding RNA ACA11 that is also overexpressed due to the t(4:14) translocation and appears to be involved in the cellular response to reactive oxygen species (ROS). Further localization and association experiments of ACA11 also indicate its association with the nucleolus, and potential role in regulating small nucleolar RNAs (snRNA). The work proposed here will extend preliminary studies on how overexpression of ACA11 from the t(4:14) influences snRNA, identifying distinct targets, characterizing its effect on snRNA abundance, nucleolar structure and ribosomal structure and function. They will also extend studies in to how ACA11 OE affects the cellular response to ROS, cell viability and chemosensitivity. The studies are clear, understandable and achievable and I recommend funding. Relevant to public health: yes.
