imp_text: Strengths: This grant by an established investigator explores very interesting mechanisms of how the miRNA, miR-30, allows the bypass of oncogene-induced senescence which represents a significant barrier to tumorigenesis.  Significant preliminary data is presented justifying the experimental approaches that will be taken. Weaknesses: The grant is not particularly well-written.  The organization can be confusing at times and the grant should be read over to correct multiple typos.  There is a significant amount of space used to describe alternative approaches.
sig_text_str: . The discovery that miR-30 induction allows the bypass of oncogene-induced senescence and the mechanisms involved may allow for the development of novel therapeutic strategies.
sig_text_wkn: . The clinical application of restoration of the senescence barrier either as a prevention or therapeutic strategy is currently unknown.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Brad O’Brian, Associate Professor at TSRI has extensive experience studying oncogene-induced senescence including mediation by p38 MAPK and the role of the miR-17-92 cluster.  He is well-published and is currently supported by two R01s.  Collaborator Dr. Bai Rao is an epigenetics expert who will help with ChIP and ChIP-seq experiments and analysis.  Dr. Dennis Sigel at Scripps Clinic will provide clinical samples and assistance.
inn_text_str: . The study of miRNA function in oncogene-induced senescence is largely unexplored.  This is a novel function for miR-30 and new targets are described.
inn_text_wkn: . Cancer therapies targeting cellular senescence have not been applied as a useful approach.  miRNAs including miR-30 are well-studied in cancer.
app_text_str: . Strong preliminary results including miR-30 identified as a top hit in a screen for miRNAs that inhibit ras-induced senescence and data implicating CHD7 and TNRC6A as direct miR-30 targets in senescence bypass.  Pitfalls and solutions are nicely addressed.
app_text_wkn: . The alternative approach for Aim1 is rather extensive.  Power calculations justifying animal numbers are not presented.
env_text_str: . The O’Brian lab at the Scripps Research Institute represents an outstanding environment to carry out the proposed research plan.

imp_text: Strengths: This is a very well-written proposal by an early investigator with nice outline figures/flowcharts presented for each aim.  This work is likely to lead to both discovery of lncRNAs that are differentially expressed during tumorigenesis and also hits that are functionally important. Weaknesses: The proposal is ambitious with several in vivo screens planned.  The main concern is how many hits can be followed up on and no detailed mechanistic studies are planned here.
sig_text_str: . The study of lincRNAs in pathogenesis of B-cell lymphomas and other cancers is in its infancy and this study is likely to greatly expand our knowledge in this area.
sig_text_wkn: . Studies are primarily planned in mouse and conservation of lncRNAs is likely to represent a significant hurdle.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Jamal Robinson is a physician-scientist and promising early investigator at MSKCC.  He is well-trained including a postdoc with Tyler Jacks.  Currently well-supported including an R01 focused on miR-17-92.  Charlotte Leisey will serve as a collaborator to perform computational analyses on NGS experiments.  Steve Loew has developed the in vivo RNAi screening platform on coding genes which will now be applied for lncRNAs.
inv_text_wkn: . A biostatistician could be very useful to this proposal.

imp_text: Strengths:  If successful, this work has the potential to inform the use of current targeted therapies and combinations, and to aid in the development of new agents in breast cancer.  The proposal is well-written and the approach is well-developed.  Significant preliminary data provides support for the experimental approaches. Weaknesses:  No significant weaknesses.
sig_text_str: . This proposal addresses questions of mechanisms of Akt activation in breast tumors and reactivation of Akt activity following PI3K inhibition in a subset of breast cancer cell lines.  Skp2 can promote the reactivation of Akt in a PI3K-independent manner.  This evidence may provide rationale for exclusion of the use of rapalogs or PI3K inhibitors in patients that have tumors with high Skp2 levels.  With new promising targeted agents for the PI3K, Akt, and Cdk2 pathways entering the clinic, it is important to understand the mechanisms driving tumor growth and cross talk between pathways.
sig_text_wkn: . No significant weaknesses noted.
inv_text_str: . The co-PIs have synergistic expertise when it comes to this proposal. Dr. Greg Ryan, Professor of Pathology at BIDMC, and his group have significant experience working on signaling pathways in cancer including PI3K/Akt.  Dr. Ryan is well-published and well-supported.  Completed R01 on Akt and NFAT pathway in 2012.  Dr. Weimin Wan, associate professor of Pathology at BIDMC, has expertise in studying cell cycle regulations and is well-published in this area.  They have added additional strong collaborators to their team.  Dr. Louis Cantell bring tremendous experience as a collaborator and will contribute access to single cell Akt reporter system.  Dr. Pere Primo Pandolfo will provide guidance and resources related to the animal studies and crosses.
inn_text_str: . Akt activation directly coupled to cell cycle progression (through Cdk2/Skp2) represents a novel mechanism in breast cancer oncogenesis and possibly therapy resistance.  Novel mechanism for PI3K independent Akt reactivation in subset of TNBCs depending on PIK3C2 and/or Skp2.  The E17K Akt2 mutation has not been well-studied.
inn_text_wkn: . No significant weaknesses noted.
app_text_str: . Significant preliminary data is presented providing the molecular basis and rationale for the proposed studies.  The expected results, pitfalls, and alternatives are nicely laid out for each subaim.
app_text_wkn: . In specific Aim 1.5, caveats related to compensation by other Akt family members are not addressed in animal experiments.  Lack of clinical/pre-clinical experiments beyond cell lines and mouse models.
env_text_str: . The Ryan and Wan laboratories and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center are an excellent environment with the proper facilities to carry out the proposed work.

imp_text: This proposal is designed to evaluate if c-Abl, a ubiquitously expressed nonreceptor protein tyrosine kinase, may serve as a tumor suppressor to inhibit the development and metastasis of TNBC, to investigate the mechanisms that govern c-Abl functions, and to determine the activity of a c-Abl-targeting bioactive agent in inhibiting TNBC. This project is considered highly significant and its successful completion may have important impacts on TNBC therapy. The preliminary studies provide compelling experimental evidence to support the proposed research. The PI has an excellent track record of publication, has extensive experience in the proposed research field, and has assembled a qualified research team. The research environment is excellent and all research related methods are readily available. On the other hand, the experimental approaches are not carefully designed in some aims;  the rationale of using particular xenograft models is not adequately justified; the experimental designed is not appropriate for testing the synergistic effect of combination treatments; the statistical analysis methods are not adequately discussed for data analysis and for sample size estimation.
sig_text_str: . Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most aggressive and metastatic phenotype of breast cancer, and is the major cause of breast cancer death; there has been no targeted therapeutics against TNBC. . This proposal is to investigate the role of c-Abl in the development and metastasis of TNBC and to elucidate the molecular mechanisms that regulate c-Abl expression and activity. Successful completion of this project may lead to identification of an effective molecular target for designing therapeutic strategies against TNBC. . The proposed project may also identify a natural compound that inhibits TNBC effectively.
sig_text_wkn: . c-Abl has also been shown to promote tumorigenesis in some other cancer types, such as chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML), and its antagonist has shown clinical efficacy against CML.
inv_text_str: . The PI, Dr. McCarthy, is an Associate Professor, Co-Director of Breast Cancer Program, and Leader of the TGF-b Focus Group at Case Western Reserve University and its Comprehensive Cancer Center. The PI has extensive experience in the proposed research fields. . Other investigative team members and collaborators also have complimentary expertise in the fields needed for the proposed research.
inn_text_str: . C-Abl may serve as an important tumor suppressor against TNBC. . A novel real-time intravital imaging of TNBC will be used in the in vivo studies. . An effective natural compound may be identified to inhibit TNBC.
app_text_str: . A large body of preliminary results provides strong experimental evidence to support the hypotheses to be tested. .  The experiments in aim 2 are well designed to determine the role of a novel c-Abl-p53-p21 signaling axis in TNBC. .
app_text_wkn: . In the experiments in Aim 1, it is unclear if the MCF-10A progressive series cancer cells are TNBC (Aim 1A), and if the rigid or compliant status of Matrigel can be maintained during tumor development and progression in the in vivo model (Aim 1B). . The experimental approaches in aim 3A are not carefully developed. Basic information of cell lines (D2-HAN, D2-OR, etc) is not provided, and the rationale of using those cell lines is not justified; the rationale to resect the primary tumors in the xenograft model is unjustified (Aim 3A) and the frequency of recurrent and metastatic tumors in the model are not provided; sample size seems too small and is not statistically estimated. . The experiments in Aim 3B only study the effect of c-Abl on mediating the response of non-TNBCs to docetaxel in vitro, but not in vivo. . Aim 3C, the specimens which were from patients with metastatic BCs underwent chemo-drug combination therapies may not be appropriate to determine the association between c-Abl status and response to docetaxel. . The experiments in Aim 4 are also not carefully planed; the experimental design is not adequate for determining a synergistic effect between Securinine and docetaxel; doses are not justified, and no dose-dependent effect will be evaluated; sample size (n=5/group) is not statistically justified and seems insufficient for detecting statistical significance. . Statistical analysis methods are not adequately described.

imp_text: This application is designed to investigate the functional role of Net1 in mobility and metastasis of breast cancer cells and to elucidate the underlying mechanism of Net1 actions. This project is considered significant as verification of the functional role of Net1 in breast cancer metastasis and understanding of the mechanism how Net1 activity is regulated may lead to identification of an important functional target to design therapeutic strategies against breast cancer progression and metastasis. study_section: Tumor Progression and Metastasis Study Section
imp_text: This R01 application aims to study the role of Sox2 in regulation of cell survival and growth in an androgen-deprived environment in prostrate cancer. Sox2 is a transcription factor that plays an important role in maintaining the survival and pluripotency of embryonic stem cells (ESCs). The PI showed that Sox2 is an AR-repressed target gene that promotes castration-resistant prostate cancer tumor growth, and that inhibition of Sox2 in castration-resistant prostate cancer cells causes cell death. The PI also showed that Sox2 co-factors including Oct4 and Nanog that are normally expressed in ESCs are not detected in prostate cancer cells. In addition, the PI showed that expression of Sox2 in human prostate tissues increases with tumor grade, and the majority of prostate cancer metastases are Sox2-positive. Therefore, the PI hypothesizes that Sox2 functions as an oncogene by regulating a novel set of gene targets to promote cancer cell survival and proliferation, and not via mechanisms of inhibiting differentiation and promoting pluripotency. Three aims are proposed: 1) Determine whether Sox2 is necessary and sufficient to promote castration-resistant prostate cancer cell survival and metastasis; 2) To elucidate the mechanism of Sox2 function in prostate cancer cells; and 3) To establish that prostate tumors derived from Sox2-positive cells are metastatic and castration-resistant, while tumors derived from Sox2-negative cells are not. Identifying the role of Sox2, a stem cell regulator, in castration-resistance in prostate cancer via a mechanism that is independent on Oct4 and Nanog may have an important application for developing novel therapies prostate cancer. Thus, potential impact from the proposed study is high.

imp_text: This R01 application aims to study the regulatory mechanisms that control the subcellular localization and activity of Net1 in breast cancer cells, and their roles in breast cancer cell motility in vitro and metastasis in vivo. Net1 is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor. The preliminary data from the PI’s lab showed that co-expression of Net1 with the ß4 integrin subunit in human breast cancer is predictive of decreased metastasis free survival. The PI also showed that Net1 expression is required for ligand stimulated breast cancer cell motility and invasion in vitro. In addition, the PI showed that acetylation of Net1 controls its localization outside the nucleus, and that the action of specific deacetylases is critical to suppressing Net1 activity. Therefore, the PI hypothesizes that acetylation dependent, dynamic regulation of Net1 localization to focal adhesions, and that the plasma membrane is required for temporal and spatial regulation of RhoA activation that underlies breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis. Three aims are proposed: 1) demonstrate how acetylation controls the subcellular localization of Net1, identify the acetylases and deacetylases that regulate Net1, and determine how this impacts breast cancer cell motility and invasion; 2) identify the molecular mechanism by which Net1 and FAK exert reciprocal control, and demonstrate how this impacts focal adhesion dynamics and function; and 3) will test the consequences of Net1 isoform depletion on human breast cancer cell tumorigenesis and metastasis in mouse xenograft assays. Metastasis is the major cause of deaths in breast cancer, identifying a role for Net1 in breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis is novel and significant. Since the signaling pathways governing focal adhesion dynamics and actin cytoskeletal organization are complex, the role for Src in Net1-mediated proposed function is not well explained. In addition, no experiments are proposed to test how Rac1 affects Net1 acetylation. Therefore, these deficiencies diminish the enthusiasm of this application.

imp_text: This R01 application aims to study the interaction between hormones and stromal density in the development, progression and therapeutic resistance of estrogen receptor positive (ERa+) breast cancer. The preliminary data from the PI’s group showed that elevated collagen density alone can shift the spectrum of PRL-induced signals away from STAT5 and toward ERK1/2, which is associated with pro-proliferation/ invasion signals, and reduce estrogen responsiveness. Therefore, the PI hypothesizes that stiff extracellular matrices switch the balance of hormonal signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic, thereby establishing a feed-forward loop in breast cancer. Three aims are proposed: 1) determine how the stiffness of the extracellular matrix shifts the spectrum of PRL- and estrogen-induced signals in breast cancer cells; 2) examine how PRL and estrogen regulate matrix deposition in stromal fibroblasts; and 3) elucidate the interactions of PRL, estrogen and extracellular matrix density in vivo in the development and progression of breast cancer. Understanding the interaction between tumor cells and their environment in the context of estrogen and prolactin has an important application for developing a novel therapy for ER+ breast cancer. However, the direct mechanism involving the ERK pathway is weak, which diminishes the enthusiasm of this application.

imp_text: This application by a young investigator seeks to test the hypothesis, “that Sox2 functions as an oncogene by regulating a novel set of gene targets to promote cancer cell survival and proliferation, and not via mechanisms of inhibiting differentiation and promoting pluripotency. This mechanism of Sox2 function occurs via interaction with transcriptional co-regulators unique to adult epithelial cells, and not Oct4 or Nanog”. The PI proposes to test this central hypothesis in three specific aims. First specific aim is to examine requirement of Sox2 in promoting and sustaining castration-resistant prostate cancer cell survival and metastasis. In this aim they propose to evaluate oncogenic function of Sox2 as it related to promotion of AR-independent cancer cell survival. They will also investigate the critical requirement of FGF5 in mediating the oncogenic function of Sox2. The second specific aim is to test the hypothesis that, “Sox2 directly promotes pro-survival and represses pro-apoptotic genes in prostate cancer cells to promote a poor prognosis tumor phenotype”. The third specific aim of the proposal is to test whether the prostate tumors derived from Sox2-positive cells are castrate-resistant and metastatic. Over all the central hypothesis is quite interesting, but the experimental plan is very diffuse and does not completely address the central hypothesis of the proposal. Throughout the application the PI has mixed up definitions of castration-resistant with AR-independent and metastasis, which is a concern, while many of these phenotypes may co-exist, but these phenotypes also exist independent of each other. The central hypothesis is deficient in terms of role of SOX2 in normal adult prostate cells vs prostate cancer cells. Use of TCGA expression data would be helpful. If Sox2 was sufficient to drive metastasis, one wonders why normal adult prostate cells that have Sox-2 are not malignant? These concerns dampen the enthusiasm for this application.

imp_text: Proposed studies stem from the data from several laboratories including the data from PI’s laboratory that  indicate the RhoGEF neuroepithelial transforming gene 1 (Net1) is a critical regulator of breast cancer motility and invasive potential and that acetylation of Net 1 determines its subcellular localization. Now the proposed studies aim to test the hypothesis that, hypothesis that acetylation-dependent, dynamic regulation of Net1 localization to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane is required for temporal and spatial regulation of RhoA activation that underlies breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis.” The proposal studies will test these hypotheses in three specific aims. In the first specific aim, the investigators propose to identify the acetylases and deacetylases that regulate Net 1 acetylation and control of Net 1 sub cellular localization and breast cancer cell migration and invasion.  In the second aim the investigator plans to study the mechanism and impact of Net 1 and FAK reciprocal regulation in focal adhesion dynamics and function. Finally the experiments in the third aim will evaluate the effects of Net 1 function on mammary gland tumorigenesis and metastasis in mouse xenograft assays and in Net1 conditional knockdown mice. The application is well written and experimental plan is well thought of and pit falls and alternate stratigies are included for each aim. Other strengths include a well-trained investigator who has studied Net 1 over several years, strong supportive preliminary data and first description of Net1 knockout mouse model system. One minor concern is that the proposed studies do not take into consideration contribution of other known interactions of Net 1, which makes data interpretation somewhat difficult. The Pi also brushed aside the interplay between Net1 phosphorylation and Net1 acetylation, that could have added an additional dimension to the complexity of Net 1 regulation. The PI believes that LPA or integrin mediated Rac1 activation stimulated the acetylation of Net 1 around the NSL sequence, thereby preventing nuclear localization. This simplistic model however true falls short on explaining the exact mechanism by which Net1 would move out of nucleus, although it does explain how acetylation on NSL might prevent nuclear import. Despite these minor concerns enthusiasm for the proposed studies is quite high.

imp_text: This multi-PI application seeks to test the hypothesis that,  “Stiff extracellular matrices switch the balance of hormonal signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic, thereby establishing a feed forward loop in breast cancer.” The proposed hypothesis stems in part from the preliminary and published work that demonstrated that elevated collagen density could shift the spectrum of PRL-induced signals away from STAT5 and toward ERK1/2. The investigators suggest this shift is associated with pro-proliferation/ invasion signals, and reduce estrogen responsiveness. The proposed studies have three specific aims. First aim is to investigate the underlying mechanisms by which stiffness of extracellular matrix shifts spectrum of hormonal signals in breast cancer cells, using 3D culture system to modulate mechanical stress. The second aim is to examine regulation of matrix deposition in stromal fibroblasts by estrogen and prolactin utilizing CAFs and NMFs. The third aim is to examine the interactions estrogen and prolactin with extracellular matrix density in vivo breast cancer development and progression. The experiments in the first specific aim to probe the PRL and PRL and estrogen induced signals in breast cancer cells growing in 3D matrices of various stiffness is straight forward and is an extension of the preliminary studies. The experiments in the second aim to evaluate the effects of  estrogen and PRLs on CAF and NMFs under conditional matrices of various stiffness are also straight forward. One concern though not addressed by the applicants is whether CAFs and NMFs can grow under these conditions. The rationale for these experiments is limited although experiments in 2C present a better approach  as co-culture studies of BCa cells with CAFs and NMFs. The experiments proposed in third specific aim are also extension of the studies in other two specific aims. In general the application is limited by relatively narrow and somewhat skewed focus on shift of signaling from activation of STAT5 to ERK1/2 in response to PRL and estrogen. The investigators are missing a huge opportunity to probe other signaling events that could be critical drivers here. They are also missing the other signaling events known to be activated by sheer stress and interaction of those pathways with estrogenic and PRL induced events. The studies as proposed will only have a limited impact as they are mostly correlative rather than mechanistic by design.

Epub 2013 Jan 11.), and the PI is not co-author for this publication. 3. This grant proposal is poorly written. For instance, in the specific aim page, no research strategy was described under each specific aim. 4. imp_text: Molecular mechanisms controlling metastasis in breast cancer are not well understood. The PI proposed to investigate the role of Net1, that regulates RhoA GTPase activity, in cell mobility and metastasis of breast cancer. The PI hypothesized that acetylation dependent, dynamic regulation of Net1 localization to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane is required for temporal and spatial regulation of RhoA activation that underlies breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis. The major concerns are listed below: 1. Net1 is one of GEFs in regulating RhoA GTPase activity and cell motility. The cell signaling network in regulating cell motility is highly complicated, and there are numerous players in the signaling pathway. Additional GEF, such as Vav3, is also overexpressed in breast cancer and modulates cell motility. The PI did not address why Net 1, relative to Vav3 or other signaling molecules, is critical for cell motility and cancer metastasis. 2. Aim 1, in figure 3G, due to poor quality of the data, it is not convincing to state that TSA and Tenovin-1 stimulate acetylation of endogenous Net1 proteins in MCF7 cells. 3. Aim 2, the PI proposed to screen for interacting proteins of Net1 isoforms with common SH2 domain. The complexity of signaling transduction network undermines the significance of the proposed experiments. This is an open-ended approach, which is unlikely to generate any conclusive data. 4. Aim 3, the research team is not sufficient to carry out the proposed experiments. There is no expertise in mouse model of breast cancer. Breast tumor in the mouse model can not be well analyzed without pathologist.

imp_text: Based on the clinical observation that elevated density of the extracellular matrix (ECM) is associated with tumor progression and metastasis, the goal of the proposal is to investigate that stiff extracellular matrices switch the balance of hormonal signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic in breast cancer. The PIs have extensive experiences in the related research field. The proposed experiments and animal models are available. There are a few critical concerns regarding this proposal: 1. In preliminary data, the PI only showed the altered gene expression in response to ECM stiffness at the mRNA level, but not at the protein level. It is well known that moderate alteration of gene expression at the mRNA level may not lead to a significant change at the protein level. The preliminary studies do not strongly support the hypothesis of this proposal. 2. The action of estrogen on stromal fibroblasts and on the paracrine cross-talk between tumor cells and fibroblasts was proposed, while fibroblasts usually do not express ER. In addition, no preliminary data indicates that fibroblasts express PRLR. Therefore, the experiments proposed in aim 2 may not lead to any conclusive result.

This study will reveal the underlying molecular mechanisms contributing to breast cancer progression.

imp_text: Overall Impact Score (1-9): Overall objective of the proposed research is to test the hypothesis that measures capable of promoting c-Abl expression/activation will alleviate TNBC development and metastatic progression. In four proposed aims, PI will determine the role of oncogenic TGF-b signaling and mechanotransduction to inactive c-Abl (aim 1); determine the role of p53 members in mediating tumor suppressive actions of c-Abl (aim 2); assess the utilty of c-abl as a predictive biomarker for chemo response (aim 3); and assess the therapeutic efficacy of securinine for treatment of TNBCs (aim 4). Strengths of the proposal are the significance of the clinical problem, potential to generate novel mechanistic insight on the role of c-Abl in TNBCs, strong PI and team, supportive preliminary data and well laid-out research plan and a very supportive research environment. Weaknesses include lack of clarity about c-abl action in the metastasized TNBCs, lack of mechanistic focus while establishing association of c-abl with docetaxel response and slightly diffused nature of aim 4. Overall, the proposal is judged to be of high to moderate impact. Budget is appropriate.

imp_text: The goal of proposed research is to test the hypothesis that acetylation-dependent dynamic regulation of Net1 localization to focal adhesions is required for Rho activation, and thus breast cancer invasion and metastasis. The hypothesis is supported by strong preliminary data and PI has proposed a well thought out research plan to test the hypothesis. If successfully completed, proposed research will deliver novel insight into mechanisms of action of Net1 activity and thus establish it as a novel molecular target for metastatic breast disease. There is innovation at both conceptual and technical level and PI is well qualified to lead the project. The weaknesses include the lack of a pathologist and a biostatistician in the investigative team as well as some other minor concerns in the research plan. Enthusiasm is also somewhat dampened by the fact that the acquired novel insight into Net1 involvement in breast cancer metastasis may not be translated clinically until it is established that its aberrant activation rather than overexpression is clinically significant. HDAC and HAT are already established targets for anti-cancer therapy though the proposed research may provide information regarding their novel mechanisms of action through Net1. Scientific environment and resources are appropriate at UTHSC and budget is justified.

imp_text: Considering the importance of ECM density and hormonal signaling in breast cancer pathogenesis, PIs propose to investigate how ECM density alters the actions of hormone signaling (PRLR and ER) in three specific aims. In aim 1, they will examine how the ECM stiffness shifts the spectrum of PRL- and ER –induced signals in breast cancer cells. In aim 2, they will determine how PRL and ER regulate matrix deposition in stromal fibroblast cells. Finally, in aim 3, they will study the interactions of PRL, ER and ECM stiffness in breast cancer in vivo.  The key strengths of this application are strong PIs, supportive preliminary data, innovativeness of the hypothesis and focus on tumor and stromal cells as well as supportive environment. The weaknesses include lack of rationale for the sole focus on ERK pathway along with lack of details and some supportive preliminary data as listed for the proposed approach, which somewhat decreases the overall enthusiasm for this project.

study_section: Tumor Progression and Metastasis Study Section
imp_text: The proposed project is based on a hypothesis that measures capable of promoting c-Abl (ABL1) expression and activation will alleviate TNBC development and metastatic progression. The ideas that c-Abl may function as a tumor suppressor in TNBC and that its activation may serve as a therapeutic strategy for treatment of TNBCs are innovative and has not been studied previously. Historically, Abl tyrosine kinase has been studied as a proto-oncogene whose activation and mutation is a causative event for human and feline leukemia. A role of Abl family kinases, c-ABL (ABL1) and Arg (ABL2), in promoting BC development and metastasis has also been reported. Therefore, the proposed research will contribute significantly to our understanding of this important, yet somewhat controversial, question. Additionally, the proposed project will examine the potential of Securinine as a novel chemotherapeutic agent against disseminated TNBC and, if successful, will deliver a translational advancement to TNBCs treatment. The PI has all reagents that are required for the project, including an Abl activator DPH and an expression vector for constitutively active cAbl. The assays needed for the project, especially an innovative 3D-organotypic culture system, have also been established. However, there are some weaknesses in this application. Although the applicant’s hypothesis is supported by preliminary studies, most of these studies focus on a limit of cell lines such as 4T1. Since breast cancer is a heterogeneous disease, similar studies used in 4T1 may need to be extended to a cohort of human breast cancer cell lines and this is not considered in the proposal. Also, because Abl’s function mainly relies on its kinase activity, an assessment and comparison of Abl kinase activity in various TNBCs seems to be needed.
sig_text_str: . Abl tyrosine kinase plays an important role in regulation of cell growth and motility. While its role in leukemia development has been well studied, less is known about the function of Abl in solid tumors. The proposed research will help to elucidate the function and signaling mechanism of c-Abl in TNBCs, in which the controversial studies have been reported with regard to Abl’s function and regulation; . The proposed research has potential to develop novel therapeutic strategy for treatment of human TNBCs; . The research may also have potential to identify c-Abl as a biomarker that distinguish TNBCs from other BC subtype and that predict TNBC response to Docetaxel.

imp_text: This study focuses on the role of Sox2, an important embryonic stem cell regulator, in prostate cancer metastasis and progression to castration-resistance. By genomic pathway analyses of seminal vesicle and prostate epithelial cells, the applicant identified Sox2 as a gene that is highly expressed in adult prostate epithelial cells as well as in castration-resistant prostate cancer cell line CWR-R1. Importantly, Sox2 expression is down regulated by AR stimulation and ectopic expression of Sox2 in a castration-sensitive PC cell line (LAPC4) confers it castration-resistance. Because the adult prostate epithelial and prostate cancer cells do not express ES cell specific Sox2 co-factors Oct4 and Nanog, the applicant hypothesizes that Sox2 may function in PC cells with different co-factors than Oct4 and Nanog to regulate a different set of genes that are important for cell survival. This hypothesis is further supported by a pilot experiment in which the applicant analyzed the expression of 84 ES cell associated genes in LAPC4-Sox2 cells and found that the expression of 18 genes including FGF5 is changed by ectopic Sox2 expression. However, none of these genes are known Sox2 target in ES cells. To test his hypothesis, the applicant propose to determine whether Sox2 is necessary and sufficient to promote castration-resistant prostate cancer cell survival and metastasis; to elucidate the mechanim of Sox2 function in prostate cancer cells; and to establish that the prostate tumors derived from Sox2 positive cells are metastatic and castration-resistant. The strengths of this proposal include a well formulated hypothesis that is novel and is supported by preliminary studies, a new concept that challenges existing paradigms of stem cell gene function in adult tissues, and potential impact on current prostate cancer prognosis and treatment. Minor weaknesses include the lack of description of experimental design for disruption of Sox2 expression in Aim1.1 and preliminary data in Aim1.2. It is also not clear whether the PI has all techniques and assays established.

imp_text: Neuroepithelial transforming gene 1 (Net1) is a RhoA subfamily-specific GEF and is over-expressed in human breast cancers. Its co-expression with the ß4 integrin subunit in human breast cancer has been reported as a predictive of decreased metastasis-free survival. While in vitro studies have shown that Net1 is required for breast cancer cell migration and invasion, it is not clear whether and how Net1 contributes to breast cancer development and metastasis in vivo. Subcellular localization of Net1 is a key determinant of the oncogenic potential of Net1, however, mechanisms controlling the localization of Net1 proteins have not been described. This study will test a hypothesis that acetylation-dependent, dynamic regulation of Net1 localization to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane is required for temporal and spatial regulation of RhoA activation that underlies breast cancer cell motility, invasion, and metastasis. The in vitro studies are proposed to elucidate how acetylation controls Net1 localization and function and how Net1 interacts with FAK and Src to regulate focal adhesion dynamics and function. Two loss-of-function methods, one using conventional RNAi knockdown and mouse xenografts model and the other using a unique Net1 conditional knockout mouse model created in PI’s lab, will be employed to determine how Net1 function impacts breast tumorigenesis and metastasis in vivo. The strengths of this application include a well-formulated hypothesis that is conceptually innovative, testable, and is supported by preliminary studies and, availability of a unique conditional knockout animal model that makes the team well positioned for proposed studies. The application is clearly and logically written, and appropriate alternative approaches are well described. A little more discussion about possible lethal effect of Net1 knockdown on BC cells for xenograft model may be needed.

imp_text: This is an application for a new submission of a 5-year R01 grant.   It purposes to ascertain the effect of c-Abl, a non-receptor protein tyrosine kinase, as a suppressor of oncogenesis. The authors propose that c-Abl forced expression in Triple Negative Breast Cancer (TNBC) will alleviate metastasis in vivo. Further observation, from the applicant stated that c-Abl expression levels is inversely related to TNBC tumorgenicity and its response to docetaxel therapy. Their hypothesis, that re-expression of c-Abl will block progression and development of TNBC. Furthermore, the authors state that TGF-ß signaling can be utilized to determine the tumor suppressor function of c-Abl in TNBC. The applicant’s preliminary data illustrates that: 1) targeting c-Abl via constitute-active c-Abl (CST-Abl) a mutant form, can both in vitro block EMT and in vivo tumor growth, 2) that TGF-ß signaling mediate loss of p53 can be reverted by CST-Abl, 3) c-Abl expression correlates with “responders” to docetaxel therapy and 4). The authors proposed the following four aims: (1) determine the role of TGF-ß-signaling to inactivate c-Abl tumor suppressing functions (2) determine the role of p53 in mediating tumor suppressor activity of c-Abl (3) determine the value of c-Abl expression to predict response to docetaxel response and 4) determine the efficacy of Securine, a natural product, to kill TNBC and assess p53 and c-Abl expression. The overall principles are intriguing and may be of a high impact but the proposal fails at several levels to illustrate this potential. If all the aims are met for the grant it will have a moderate impact to move the field forward due to several short comings listed below.

imp_text: This is an application for a new submission of a 5-year R01 grant.   It purposes to ascertain the role of the extracellular matrix (ECM), associated with increase mammographic density, which in turn alters “stroma” and becoming “stiff” and thus promote tumor progression and metastasis. The authors propose that stroma-alterations (i.e. increased high density (HD) collagen) has an effect of the ECM-deposits from fibroblast cells and “shifts” the spectrum of prolactin (PRL) signaling. Normally, PRL-activated STAT5 signaling is anti-estrogenic but HD-collagen alters PRL signaling towards ERK1/2 activation. The “shift” of ERK1/2 is known to be associated with both enhanced proliferation and invasive signaling and reducing estrogen responsiveness in women diagnosed with ER+ breast cancers. The authors would argue that this is the reason why in ~25% of the ER+ breast cancers cases, there is no response to therapy. Their central hypothesis, stiff extracellular matrices switches the balance of hormonal signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic, thereby establishing a feed-forward loop in breast cancer.  The applicant’s preliminary data illustrates that: 1) HD-collagen increases a “shift” in PRL signaling to ERK1/2 from that of STAT5, 2) PRL signaling increases MMP2 expression in HD-collagen causing greater invasive phenotypes, increasing both focal-adhesion and integrin-expression that modulates estrogen responses, 3) HD-collagen elicits fibroblast cells to increase their  ECM-deposits and 4) utilizing a mice knocked-in for a non-cleavable form of Col1a1 protein elicits increases of the  ECM  causing increased stiffness which shortens tumor-latency associated with increases in metastasis. The authors proposed the following three aims: (1) determine is how a shift in ECM stiffness alter both PRL and estrogen signaling (2) determine the effects of PRL and estrogen on matrix deposition in stromal fibroblast and (3) determine in vivo the interaction of PRL and estrogen on ECM and its effect on cancer progression in therapeutic setting. The overall principles are intriguing and if all the objectives are met for the grant it will have an impact to move the field forward and understanding why some ER+ breast cancer are non-responsive to hormone-therapies. imp_text: This is an application for a new submission of a 5-year R01 grant.   It purposes to ascertain the role of the extracellular matrix (ECM), associated with increase mammographic density, which in turn alters “stroma” and becoming “stiff” and thus promote tumor progression and metastasis. The authors propose that stroma-alterations (i.e. increased high density (HD) collagen) has an effect of the ECM-deposits from fibroblast cells and “shifts” the spectrum of prolactin (PRL) signaling. Normally, PRL-activated STAT5 signaling is anti-estrogenic but HD-collagen alters PRL signaling towards ERK1/2 activation. The “shift” of ERK1/2 is known to be associated with both enhanced proliferation and invasive signaling and reducing estrogen responsiveness in women diagnosed with ER+ breast cancers. The authors would argue that this is the reason why in ~25% of the ER+ breast cancers cases, there is no response to therapy. Their central hypothesis, stiff extracellular matrices switches the balance of hormonal signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic, thereby establishing a feed-forward loop in breast cancer.  The applicant’s preliminary data illustrates that: 1) HD-collagen increases a “shift” in PRL signaling to ERK1/2 from that of STAT5, 2) PRL signaling increases MMP2 expression in HD-collagen causing greater invasive phenotypes, increasing both focal-adhesion and integrin-expression that modulates estrogen responses, 3) HD-collagen elicits fibroblast cells to increase their  ECM-deposits and 4) utilizing a mice knocked-in for a non-cleavable form of Col1a1 protein elicits increases of the  ECM  causing increased stiffness which shortens tumor-latency associated with increases in metastasis. The authors proposed the following three aims: (1) determine is how a shift in ECM stiffness alter both PRL and estrogen signaling (2) determine the effects of PRL and estrogen on matrix deposition in stromal fibroblast and (3) determine in vivo the interaction of PRL and estrogen on ECM and its effect on cancer progression in therapeutic setting. The overall principles are intriguing and if all the objectives are met for the grant it will have an impact to move the field forward and understanding why some ER+ breast cancer are non-responsive to hormone-therapies. The study of TNBC is a strength given the limited therapeutic options in this disease. Given the disease and therapeutic implications, this research may influence the field, but as proposed, too many ambitious aims/subaims weaken the flow of ideas and rationale for the goal of the project.

imp_text: This proposal aims to determine define regulatory mechanisms that control the subcellular localization and activity of Net1 in breast cancer cells, and demonstrate how this affects breast cancer cell motility in vitro and metastasis in vivo. Metastasis is an important area of research and there are multiple areas of innovation in the proposed project, including identification of novel molecular mechanisms underlying metastasis, new mechanistic insights as well as innovative in vivo models that make this project have the potential to impact therapeutic strategies in humans. If completed, this research has a high probability of exerting a sustained, powerful influence on the research field.
sig_text_str: • Tumor metastasis is the primary cause of death in breast cancer patients and there are currently no treatments to prevent its occurrence. Thus, understanding signaling mechanisms governing metastasis in order to develop effective therapies makes it an important area of study. • The study aims to understand how the activation of the RhoGEF, Net1, may be  a critical factor in determining the metastatic potential of breast cancer cells • Net1 contributions to mammary gland tumorigenesis and metastasis in vivo will be assessed.

app_text_wkn: . For Aim 1, the rationale for arguing that TGFB inactivates c-abl appears to be based on abl protein levels and not phosphorylation levels.  The statement in Aim 1A that src promotes ubiquitination and degradation of abl through phosphorylation of Tyrs 245 and 412  is accurate but ignores the fact that this is concomitant with abl activation and is likely a feedback mechanism to control active abl levels.  Determination of whether abl is activated rather than inhibited, and the possibility that downregulation of abl at the protein and mRNA level reflects its strong activation does not seem to be considered. . For Aim 2, the concern with the constitutively active (CST) Abl overexpression studies is whether the level of abl activation is far greater than normally seen in cells – an imbalanced activation can drive a cell into p53-mediated senescence or apoptosis without this reflecting a process seen in cancer or normal cell biology. . Overall the majority of the studies in Aims 1 and 2 focus on using 4T1 and its related lines, raising concerns about how relevant this is to human breast cancer.  Aim 3 has a more balanced distribution but there are no preliminary data with human lines. . Aim 4 seems potentially unrelated to the fundamental mechanisms being studied in this grant, and there seems to be potentially some misunderstanding between the PI and Werdman regarding their roles (Werdman cv saying he is a co-investigator, with no supported provided in the budget justification).

imp_text: Overall Impact Score (1-9): The overall premise of the proposal is that neuro-epithelial transforming gene 1 (Net1) is a critical regulator of breast cancer aggressiveness and its subcellular localization and post-transcriptional modification is determinant of its oncogenic potential. Overall, the strengths of the application is the convincing preliminary data for each aim, well presented with clear line of ambitious experiments. Other strengths include the experience and long-term interest of the PI in this area of research. Some weaknesses include that the biological relevance of these studies in breast cancer remains uncertain. From the working hypothesis and preliminary data it seems that post-transcriptional modification of Net1 needs the cooperation of other molecules to function; hence, the rationale for depletion of this molecule (Net1) needs to be better developed. Whether Net1 is an oncogene is a fundamental question? Further, no attempt has been made to study the expression of Net1 in breast cancer and the studies lack novelty as similar work has been conducted in other cancers. These concerns limit the potential impact of the work.
sig_text_str: • The project addresses a potentially important problem in the field of breast cancer metastasis and the role of neuro-epithelial transforming gene 1 (Net1) as a critical regulator of breast cancer motility and invasiveness. • Net1 is an important regulator of RhoA activation participating in cell migration. • The PI has demonstrated that Net1 plays a role in breast cancer invasion and migration.
sig_text_wkn: • No preliminary data is compelling that Net1 is biologically inactive in breast cancer. • This work appears to be more incremental than transformative. • The likelihood of generating novel and profoundly significant advances in breast cancer seem less likely than achieving logical next steps in the understanding of breast cancer progression.
inv_text_str: • Dr. Greg McCarthy will serve as PI on this application. Dr. McCarthy is presently an Associate Professor in the Department of Integrative Biology and Pharmacology at the University of Texas Health Science Center, Houston. He is experienced investigator working in the area of Rho family small GTPases in breast cancer initiation and progression. His skills and experiences appropriate to conduct proposed specific aims. • A number of qualified collaborators will make important contributions to the proposed work.

imp_text: The focus of this application is on c-Abl tyrosine kinase, which has been implicated in multiple aspects of cancer progression. In the proposed studies, Dr. Jackson wishes to explore the tumor suppressor role of c-Abl in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). It is quite interesting that depending on the context c-Abl could be a promoter or a suppressor of tumorigenesis, and therefore understanding the mechanisms behind this paradox in TNBC may provide important insights into the differential regulation of signaling pathways by c-Abl. In fact, the P.I. found that TNBC tumorigenicity is inversely related to c-Abl expression levels, and that c-Abl also predicts the response to the anticancer agent docetaxel. In addition, he speculates that promoting c-Abl expression and activation could prevent breast tumor formation as well as metastatic progression. These are very interesting scenarios that the P.I. will hope to address by means of molecular and pharmacological approaches, both using cell culture and in vivo models. There are a number of strengths in this application that lead to its excellent overall impact. The applicant will manipulate the expression of c-Abl through gain- and loss-of-function approaches to determine if promoting c-Abl expression and activation will alleviate TNBC development and metastatic progression. The use of a c-Abl small molecule activator (DPH) may set the basis for the rational design of analogues capable of impairing TNBC cell tumorigenesis and/or metastasis. Another strength is that these studies may reveal downstream mechanisms that mediate tumor suppression by c-Abl, namely members of the p53 family. Another strength relates to the determination of c-Abl as a predictor for docetaxel responses in TNBC. The hypothesis that oncogenic TGF-beta signaling drives TNBC development and metastasis by inactivating c-Abl is certainly provocative, and if true, it may have strong impact on the mechanistic basis of epithelial-to-mesenchymal (EMT) transition.  Investigator, together with the outstanding collaborators, composed a very strong team. There are also a number of weaknesses that reduced the overall impact of the proposed studies. One is that the proposal is somehow unfocused and lacks integration. The applicant will study multiple mechanisms related to focal adhesion and mechanotransduction in Aim 1 that do not integrate well with mechanistic studies on p53 proposed in Aim 2. Another weak aspect in the application relates to the studies using the ancient Chinese herb Securinine, for which there seem to be no clear information on its cellular target or mechanisms of action.
sig_text_str: . This application deals with TNBC, which is a deadly form of breast cancer for which there are little therapeutic approaches available. If successful, the P.I. may be able to establish a novel target for breast cancer. . The proposed studies may reveal insights into the paradoxical roles of c-Abl in breast cancer. . In addition, the application has potential therapeutic significance, as activating c-Abl may lead to sensitization of breast cancer cells to chemotherapeutic agents. . Studies may reveal unknown mechanistic aspects of EMT and specifically a role for c-Abl in TGF-beta signaling. . If successful, this application may serve as proof-of-principle for the development of c-Abl activators as anticancer agents.
sig_text_wkn: . The significance of the studies using the ancient Chinese herb Securinine is unclear. Whether there is a causal association between the effects of this drug and c-Abl activation remains unclear and there is limited basis for the proposed studies. . Another weakness in this application relates to the relationship of mechanotransduction with c-Abl signaling. Studies in Aim 1 are underdeveloped. . Significance could have been higher if appropriate mouse models were developed to assess the role of c-Abl in mammary tumorigenesis.

imp_text: This is a very interesting application in which the transcription factor Sox2 is characterized as a driver of prostate tumorigenesis and metastatic dissemination of prostate cancer cells. The applicant presents very interesting preliminary data in which he shows that Sox2, which is an established transcription factor in stem cell maintenance and differentiation, is also expressed in prostate cancer, and interestingly, it does not correlate with the expression of co-factors such as Nanog and Oct4. This suggests that Sox2 may have functions specifically related to adult somatic cell functions in prostate cells. A focus is on the identification of Sox2 effector genes, particularly FGF5, as well as on novel effectors to be yet identified. The proposal, which is very well written, is mechanistic and has potential translational implications. The major strengths include the strong and convincing preliminary data, the novelty of the hypothesis in prostate cancer, the mechanistic aspects of the application, and the potential of identifying relevant biomarkers for the disease. There are relatively minor weaknesses, such as some controls missing in preliminary experiments, and the fact that some experiments are not well justified. Nevertheless, overall this is a strong application with high mechanistic and prognostic impact.
sig_text_str: . A major strength is that the proposed studies may reveal important insights into the role of Sox2 in prostate cancer independent of its role in stem cell biology. . The author already identified potential target genes for Sox2 in prostate cancer that could be pharmacologically targeted. . The proposal is highly mechanistic. . In addition, the proposed studies have significant prognostic relevance, as Sox2 may potentially serve as biomarker for disease progression as well as for therapeutic response and resistance to therapy.
sig_text_wkn: . There is a chance that Sox2 may not turn out to be a crucial determinant of progression, particularly of metastasis, as there is no evidence of a link with invasion that unambiguously suggests a role in dissemination.

He has an excellent record of publication for somebody at his level, and from those publications it is clear that he has significant expertise in the field of prostate cancer. He already received funding from the American Cancer Society and other private foundations, as well as from an internal source.

The identification of Sox2 targets unrelated to stem cell biology and possibly involved in cell death/survival represents a novel aspect of this application. . Experiments may identify novel Sox2 binding sites in a number of survival/apoptotic genes, therefore revealing mechanistic links between Sox2 expression and prostate tumorigenesis.
inn_text_wkn: . Sox2 has been extensively studied in many cancers and in the context of stem cell differentiation, and many target genes have been already identified.

This application has 4 aims, which are very well developed and described in great detail, with significant attention to potential outcomes, problems, and alternative strategies or interpretation. . Strong preliminary data is presented in most cases for each of the aims, which strongly support the proposed science. . Statistical analysis is proposed and appropriately described throughout the application. . Aim 1 is designed to determine whether Sox2 is necessary and sufficient to promote cancer-resistant prostate cancer survival and metastasis. Data from Figures 2 and 3 strongly justify the proposed experiments. The experimental models are generally appropriate, such as the use of SOX2-negative and SOX-2 positive cell lines to assess growth and tumorigenicity. The use of inducible expression/RNAi is a good approach to manipulate expression in the different cell lines. . Aim 2 is highly mechanistic. The applicant will conduct Sox2 ChIP and high throughput sequencing (ChIP-Seq) to identify genomic binding sites that could be then tested using promoter-based reporter assays. Preliminary data showing differential expression of Sox2 in normal prostate and prostate tumors gives strong feasibility to the studies, as they will be carried out in human specimens. The use of Affimetrix arrays, pathway enrichment, and dataset analysis should reveal important correlations of target genes with cell survival and patient prognosis. . Studies in Aim 3 are challenging but highly relevant in the context of this application, as they will use prostate epithelial cell cultures, for which the P.I. has previous experience, that will be transformed with specific oncogenes.

imp_text: In this application, Dr. Baker will study the involvement of the RhoGEF Net1 in breast cancer, focusing on tumorigenicity and metastasis. This exchange factor seems to be overexpressed in human cancers and according to expression analysis it co-expresses with b4 integrin and most importantly, it is predictive of decreased metastasis free survival. One unusual property of this Rho-GEF is that it is expressed in the nucleus, and therefore it it clear that in order to activate RhoA in the cytoplasm it depends on a mechanism that prevents its nuclear sequestration, which seems to be acetylation. Therefore, the applicant hypothesizes that acetylation-dependent, dynamic regulation of Net1 to its sites of action (plasma membrane and focal adhesions) is key for its ability to activate the Rho GTPase and therefore impact on breast cancer cell motility, invasion, and metastasis. What is unclear from this hypothesis is whether nuclear Net1 has any role in metastasis, which could potentially involve RhoA-independent pathways. From the application, it is unclear whether Net1 can activate other small GTPases, either RhoA-related GTPases or other unrelated ones, or whether it could have other activities that are not mediated through their RhoGEF domain, and therefore are independent of the nucleotide exchange activity. Some strengths in the application involve the experience of the P.I. in the field of signaling and specifically on Rho GTPases, and appropriate collaborators. The hypothesis is based on preliminary data that supports in large most of the proposed experiments, the conceptual innovation (particularly the regulation of Rho signaling by acetylation as a post-transcriptional mechanism), the potential identification of acetylases involved in this pathway, and the mechanistic nature of experiments in aims 1 and 2. Aim 3 should provide insight into the role of Net1 in breast tumorigenesis and metastasis in vivo, and therefore these experiments may potentially reveal important functions of the RhoGEF in breast cancer progression. There are several weaknesses in this application. One of them is that some of the preliminary experiments are not well controlled, and it is unclear what is the reproducibility of the data. The applicant does not provide data using mutants of the acetylation sites (although he proposes experiments), which would have provided confidence in the model proposed here. As proposed here, it would be still unclear if nuclear Net1 has a role or not in breast tumorigenesis and metastasis. Some experiments are unfocused, such as the determination of SH2 domain binding partners. If binding partners are identified, it would be complex to determine at a mechanistic level whether this has any impact in Net1 biology, particularly because these proteins (such as p85, PLCg, Shc, and Grb7, or maybe others) have complex roles in signaling. Experiments in vivo are definitely important. The models the applicant proposes to generate are quite complex and may present a number of complications (some of them acknowledged by the applicant). Overall, this application has significant potential to uncover novel mechanistic aspects of breast tumorigenesis and metastasis, but there are still issues that need to be solved in order to have a cohesive hypothesis and compelling data based on rigorous preliminary data.
sig_text_str: . The mechanisms driving metastatic dissemination of breast cancer cells are only partially understood. Therefore, elucidating the role of Net1 in breast cancer may reveal novel insights into the tumorigenic and invasive mechanisms as well as the functional associations between distinctive members of the Rho GTPase family. . Studies proposed in this application may reveal a novel mechanism of activation of small GTPases through temporal and subcellular compartmentalization that involves acetylation. . The applicant will generate mouse models, particularly a conditional Net1 knockout line, that may reveal important functions of this RhoGEF in vivo. . There is important mechanistic information that can be learned from the proposed studies, in particular the acetylation regulatory processes that control Net1 activity/localization and a potential regulation of focal adhesion dynamics by Net1 that involves the direct interaction of the RhoGEF and FAK. In addition, a negative regulation of Net activity by Src-dependent phosphorylation may limit Net1 activity and function.
sig_text_wkn: . It remains unclear whether Net1 is actually overexpressed in breast cancer, and in what subtypes. This would enhance the significance of this study as it may allow a better understanding of the mechanisms implicated in subsets of the disease and potentially for prognostic purposes. . It is unclear whether Net1 could be mutated in breast cancer, which may potentially represent a mechanism of hyperactivation leading to enhanced Rho activity.

A second innovative aspect is the hypothesis that acetylation regulates the localization of Net1, therefore representing a novel mechanism of regulation of a RhoGEF that has not been previously identified. . There are several mechanistic links that may be deciphered through the proposed experiments. . A novel mouse genetic model will be develop to study Net1 in an in vivo context.
inn_text_wkn: . Some of the proposed hypotheses need more rigorous data, and therefore one may question that without solid supportive experiments the conceptual innovation, at least at some level, could be questionable.
app_text_str: . Most of the approaches to study acetylation, subcellular localization, focal adhesion function, and motility, are readily available. . Proposed experiments may reveal important mechanistic links, and approaches, particularly those using cell lines, xenografts and metastasis assays are feasible. . The development of a mouse model represents a major strength.

For example, in some cases RNAi studies are based on the use of a single sequence, and therefore “off-target” effects cannot be ruled out. Multiple RNAi sequences and/or rescue experiments with RNAi insensitive mutants should be used for preliminary data and proposed for the different experiments. . Likewise, reduction in protein expression after RNAi is not shown, such as in Figures 2 and 3. . It remains unclear what is the difference in function and expression among the two Net1 variants. Do they have different roles in breast cancer biology? . Studies using imaging do not give a sense of reproducibility, as single cells are shown in some cases. . It is unclear how Net1/Net1A activity is determined, such as in experiments in Figure 4G, and how these experiments are controlled and their reproducibility. . Experiments using mutants of the acetylated sites should have been important as preliminary information to support the experimental hypothesis. . The use of alternative techniques such as FRET could have been highly beneficial to study the dynamic interaction between the different components of the pathway. . Studies on Aim 2 regarding tyrosine phosphorylation remain diffuse. It is unclear what are the potential tyrosine phosphorylation sites. Likewise, studies on SH2 binding domains are open ended and may be hard to interpret. . The mouse model to be generated is interesting and the rationale for developing this line is solid. However, it involves multiple crosses, and may not be that easy to generate. . In Aim 3, the proposed analysis of circulating tumor cells is not clear. This requires significant expertise that the applicant does not seem to have.

imp_text: Triple negative breast cancer is lethal and there is no cure. This proposal is based on an innovative idea that in contrast to common views, c-Abl kinase is actually a tumor suppressor in TNBCs. The PI argues that this may explain the failure of certain c-Abl inhibitors in clinical trials, therefore this kinase signaling needs to be activated, not inhibited, for the treatment of TNBCs. If the idea can be proven, it should have significant impact in drug development. The strengths include a novel hypothesis, a comprehensive plan to investigate the mechanism of TGF-beta-c-Abl-p53 signaling, the clinical value of this signaling in the prediction of docetaxel response, and the use of a natural compound with an effort to target this pathway. The PI is highly qualified, and the research team provides strong support. Weaknesses are identified as the lack of convincing clinical evidence suggesting the role of c-Abl as a tumor suppressor, and most preliminary data are obtained from murine cell lines. The proposed models, although complicated, are not focused. The Aim 4 may not be relevant. Overall this proposal has moderate impact in the field.

app_text_str: A comprehensive research plan to investigate the involvement of c-Abl in TNBCs. Aims 1 is to study the conversion of c-Abl functions in response to TGF-beta and mechanotransduction environment. Aim 2 will look at the involvement of p53 family in mediating the tumor suppressive function of c-Abl. They will also test if DPH, a c-Abl activator, can inhibit TNBCs. Aim 3 is particularly important in term of its potential in identifying new biomarkers for docetaxel response. The approach of using a natural compound to interfere with c-Abl-p73 signaling and treat TNBCs in Aim 4 is interesting. Human breast cancer cell lines will be used in the proposed studies. Potential problems and alternative approaches are provided.
app_text_wkn: Most preliminary data are from murine system, including a mouse tumor line 4T1. The function of c-Abl in inhibiting EMT is done on normal human/mouse epithelial cell lines, which may be different from human cancer cell lines. Although it’s an attractive hypothesis that the tissue compliance dictates tumorigenicity, it is not clear how these knowledge obtained from cell cultures can be translated into human setting, in which the tumor heterogeneity may cause complicated microenvironment changes and thereby it’s difficult to determine the overall role of TGF-beta-c-Abl signaling as oncogenic or tumor suppressive. Aim 4 is to use securinine to target c-Abl, the rationale is weak. From Aim 2, p73 may not a major effector of c-Abl. It appears that securinine is only thrown into this Aim since there are some data from collaborators showing this compound may target p73 in colon cancer. Actually, just as shown in Fig.16, it’s very likely that p73 uses an independent pathway from c-Abl, and therefore the efficacy of securinine may have little relevance to c-Abl activation.

imp_text: Failure to androgen deprivation therapy is a major problem in the treatment of prostate cancer and represents an unmet medical need. This proposal hypothesized that Sox2 is an oncogene promoting castration-resistance in prostate cancer via a mechanism independent of its role in differentiation and pluripotency in embryonic stem cells. The major strengths of the application are the expertise of the PI in prostate cancer cell signaling, the novel finding that Sox2 is an androgen-repressive gene that exerts adult somatic cell functions in tumorigenesis, and the clinical evidence indicating Sox2-positive tumors are associated with Gleason scores. The weaknesses include the lack of clear rationales in some proposed experiments, a too simplified working model (Sox2-FGF5) for explaining the effects of Sox2 in prostate cancer progression, and concerns over the proposed model systems. Overall this proposal has moderate to high impact in the field.

imp_text: Since no FDA approved drugs are available for Triple-negative breast cancers (TNBCs), the significance of its exploration was highlighted in recent years. As a non-receptor tyrosine kinase, c-ABI is inactivated in TNBCs due to the TGFbeta-mediated downregulation. Therefore, the PI hypothesized that restoration of c-ABI could alleviate TGFbeta-mediated cell metastasis and cell survival. Mechanistically, the PI planned to uncover the underlying details of how c-ABI is downregulated and what are the downstream effectors of c-ABI signaling. Moreover, the PI also wanted to test the association between c-ABI loss and docetaxel resistance, and the therapeutic effect of novel c-ABI activator, Securinine, on TNBCs tumors. Overall, this comprehensive study will help us to better understand the c-ABI role in TNBCs and assist future drug development for TNBCs. However, some weaknesses existed in this proposal: 1) Previous study demonstrated that c-ABI has a highest activity in human triple negative breast cancers compared to ER/PR/HER2 positive breast cancers, which is contradictory to PI finding in murine cell lines. 2) The signaling pathway of TGFbeta/Src/c-ABI/tumorigenicity should be stronger by manipulating Src and c-ABI expression. 3). The PI should propose to find a new upstream molecule which could mediate c-ABI downregulation rather than focus on Src 4). The mechanism of c-ABI/p53/p21 is well known. The PI might propose other signals including miRNA array to discover novel c-ABI downstream effectors. 5). The contribution of c-ABI to docetaxel resistance needs to be discussed, at least docetaxel resistant cells should be established to check c-ABI expression; 6) the specificity and the side effect of Securinine are unknown in Aim4.

imp_text: Overall Impact  3 Neuroepithelial transforming gene 1 (NET1) belongs to a subfamily of Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factors (RhoGEFs). NET1 can activate Rho GTPase and promote tumor cell motility and invasion. However, the mechanism of how NET1 activates the Rho GTPase signaling is still unknown. The PI plans to dissect the mechanism of how NET1 activates the Rho GTPase signaling. In Aim1 PI plans to define how acetylation controls the subcellular localization of NET1, identify the acetylases and deacetylases that regulate NET1, and determine how this impacts breast cancer cell motility and invasive capacity. In Aim 2 PI plans to define the molecular mechanism by which NET1 and FAK exert reciprocal control and demonstrate how this impacts focal adhesion dynamics and function. In Aim 3 PI plans to determine how NET1 function impacts breast tumorigenesis and metastasis in vivo. The PI has already generated a conditional knockout allele of Net1 in mouse, which can be used to investigate its role in mammary tumor formation and metastasis in vivo. This is a comprehensive study for the NET1 role in breast cancer cell migration and invasion and if successul will help us to better understand the mechanism of cancer progression and metastasis as well as providing potential targets for intervention in metastatic breast cancer. However, some weaknesses existed in this proposal: 1. There are many regulators of Rho family of GTPase for cell migration and invasion, yet PI did not explain well wny he picked up MET1. It is also not clear whether the tools used, shRNA and overexpression, can be sufficient to dissect the specific nucler vs cutosol role of NET1 in breast cancer invasion and metastasis. 2. Although it was found that beta4integrin and NET1 expression can be linked with enhanced breast metastasis, the mechanistic analysis failed to connect the molecular mechanism to this clinical finding. Integrin can activate FAK which can suppress NET1 function. 3. There is no preliminary data to demonstrate that NET1 is required for tumor formation or metastasis in vivo. It is possible that other RhoGEFs can compensate for NET1 function thus not yielding a clear outcome.
sig_text_str: . Hypothesis that aberrant activation of NET1 is a critical factor in determining the metastatic potential of breast cancer cells. . Use inducible knockout and overexpression both in vivo and in vitro to control the gene expression. . Use two different approaches to demonstrate how NET1 contributes to breast cancer cell motility and invasion in vitro.

It is not clear that NET1 can promote breast cancer metastasis in an experimental model, although in vitro and human clinical samples indicated that integrin and NET1 in combination can be predictive of the breast cancer metastasis. But NET1 alone fails to show such significance. . It is not clear that NET1 solely functions in the cytoplasm thus the control of its localization through acetylation is only significant for its localization. There is nuclear RhoA and it is possible that NET1 can regulate nuclear RhoA function.

One quarter of these patients eventually succumb to anti-estrogen-resistant cancer. PRL exposure is associated with the development of ERa+ cancers. Also, PRL and E2 contribute to collagen deposition/breast density, also breast cancer risk. The key preliminary data PI claimed: Elevated collagen density alone can shift the spectrum of PRL-induced signals away from STAT5 and toward ERK1/2, which is associated with pro-proliferation/ invasion signals, and reduce estrogen responsiveness. The major hypothesis: Stiff extracellular matrices switch the balance of hormonal signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic, thereby establishing a positive feed- forward loop in breast cancer. PI plans to study (1) PRL and E2 contribute to collagen deposition/ECM stiffness. (2) ECM stiffness shift PRL signals away from STAT5, then toward ERK1/2. invasion, less responsive to anti-E2 therapy Three Aims are proposed Aim 1. Determine how the stiffness of the extracellular matrix shifts the spectrum of PRL- and estrogen-induced signals in breast cancer cells Aim 2. Examine how PRL and E2 regulate matrix deposition in stromal fibroblasts Aim 3. Elucidate the interactions of PRL, E2 and extracellular matrix density in vivo in the development and progression of breast cancer. PI will breed the PRL-induced cancer in syngeneic mice with different Col1a1 background to check how the ECM level influence the outcome. imp_text: This application proposes to understand the mechanism by which c-Abl acts as a tumor suppressor and to develop c-abl agonist as a novel therapeutic for treating triple negative breast cancers (TNBCs). There are several strengths of this proposal including (1) identification of a tumor suppressor role for c-Abl in TNBC; (2) identification of the involvement of p53 family members in mediating c-Abl tumor suppressor function and (3) proposal to develop Securinine as a drug for treating TNBCs. However, lack of focus (kitchen sink approach), overambitious nature of the proposal and lack of convincing rationale and supporting evidence for using c-Abl as prognostic marker for docetaxel responsive in TNBC patients somewhat dampen the enthusiasm for this otherwise exciting proposal.
sig_text_str: 1. TNBC is an aggressive malignancy with fewer treatment options. Therefore, PI’s effort to target TNBC with novel therapeutics is significant. 2. C-Abl is known to have tumor-promoting role in CML, however, in this application PI provides convincing evidence that c-Abl may act as a potent tumor suppressor in TNBCs. It is important that PI proposes to exploit the tumor suppressive function of c-Abl to develop treatment for TNBC growth and metastasis.

app_text_wkn: 1. In Aim 1, PI proposes to explore the connection between downstream effectors of TGFß1 and c-Abl inactivation in TNBC. Given that each downstream effector has somewhat different mechanism of action in regulating TNBC progression, it is likely that PI may encounter mixed message and conflicting outcomes. A more focused approach will go a long way. 2. PI claims that aim 1 will establish the developmental stages at which TNBC becomes sensitive to oncogenic activities of mechanotransduction. However, there is no follow up study proposed that will address this. 3. It is not clear whether and why c-Abl will be more relevant to TNBC. 4. In Aim 2C, PI proposes that derivatives of DPH will be generated but does not provide any follow up study, what chemical modifications will be used and why? More importantly, PI needs to clarify whether PI would like to see less toxicity and or more potency with new derivatives. I believe that this sub-aim is a whole aim in itself. 5. Sub-aim 2D seems to be out of place. There are several different themes that PI is trying to target in Aim 2, which make this aim rather diffuse and highly overambitious. 6. Aim 3: Fig. 14 is preliminary and the association is not strong. It is not clear whether or not this correlation or c-Abl docetaxel sensitizing effect is specific to taxol. What is the mechanism behind it? PI needs to test his hypothesis with drug resistant cell lines. Overall, the supporting evidence and proposed experiments don’t seem to justify the claim that c-Abl may serve as a prognostic marker for docetaxel response. 7. Aim 3C: it is not clear how PI can be sure about c-abl being a prognostic marker for docetaxel response as these patients must have been treated with combination of chemotherapy drugs. 8. Aim 4: This aim is in itself a grant proposal. PI tries to test too many drugs. Since each drug has different mechanism of action, it is not clear what is the rationale of testing securinine with these drugs as a therapeutic adjuvant.

imp_text: Identification and characterization of factors that play a causal role in breast cancer metastasis are critical for developing novel therapeutics.  This proposal will determine the mechanism by which neuroepithelial transforming gene 1 (Net1), which is a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor family member, plays a role in breast cancer metastasis. There are several strengths of this proposal including (1) identification of novel signaling cascade that involves Net1/FAk and Src to play an instrumental role in breast cancer metastasis and (2) data showing co-expression of Net1 and b4 integrin as prognostic markers for decreased distant metastasis free survival in ER+ breast cancer patients. However, lack of thorough investigation in multiple cell lines, choice of mouse models that may not be the best models for metastasis study and lack of clarity on the choice of small molecules are limitations of this grant proposal.
