imp_text: This is a first submission for a new multi-PI R01 grant from Drs. Baker and Keat. PIs want to investigate whether rigidity of extracellular matrix regulate prolactin and estrogen-mediated signaling in breast cancer growth and progression. They propose three specific aims to explore this possibility: (1) illustrate the mechanism by which matrix density shifts the balance from PRL-and estrogen-mediated pro-differentiation signaling to a pro-proliferation and pro-invasion signaling; (2) to determine the effect of ECM rigidity on stromal fibroblasts; and (3) to examine the interactions of PRL-estrogen and ECM density in the development and progression of breast cancers using genetic mouse models, and to determine whether ECM-PRL/estrogen signaling can predict clinical outcome in breast cancer patients. There are several strengths of this proposal including potential to identify molecular events that may alter actions of endogenous hormones PRL and estrogen from normal mammary gland development to breast cancer growth and metastasis. The limitations of this grant include proposed study being incremental and lack of use of patient-derived CAFs for interaction study.

imp_text: This is an ambitious new application from an established investigator examining the role of the tyrosine kinase, c-Abl, in breast cancer. Contrary to c-Abl’s known oncogenic role in hematological cancers, several studies including work from the PI’s laboratory have demonstrated that c-Abl can function as a tumor suppressor in solid tumors such as breast cancer. This innovative application seeks to elucidate the mechanisms through with these tumor-suppressive effects occur and test whether c-Abl’s activation can stop breast cancer progression. Excitingly, the investigators also provide evidence indicating that the levels of c-Abl in patient samples may be able to predict clinical response to docetaxel. There are numerous strengths of this application including the high significance of identifying and potentially exploiting a new tumor suppressive pathway in breast cancer and determining whether this pathway can predict response to a commonly used chemotherapeutic drug. Conceptually this is innovative because it explores a largely ignored tumor suppressive role for c-Abl in cancer. The PI and assembled team of investigators are excellent and have put together a well-written and thoughtful experimental approach that includes a number of defined cancer progression models and corresponding controls. While there is some concern with the inherent difficulties of pharmacologically targeting a tumor suppressor and the potential off-target effects of the herbal extract securine proposed in Aim 4, these concerns are largely outweighed by the numerous strengths. As such, the overall impact of this application is viewed to be high.
sig_text_str: . This study has the potential to provide novel biomarkers and treatment options for patients with triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). . This proposal addresses a very understudied but potentially important role for c-Abl in multiple subtypes of breast cancer with an initial emphasis on TNBC. . While docetaxel is one of the most effective chemotherapies in use for breast cancer, docetaxel resistance is a significant problem. The experiments described in this study may help to identify which patients will be the best responders to this treatment.
sig_text_wkn: . It is inherently difficult to therapeutically target a tumor suppressor. For example, if c-Abl’s expression is decreased in breast cancers, it will be difficult to drug a protein that is not there. . While this is likely beyond the scope of the work proposed here, it will still not be mechanistically clear at the end of this study why c-Abl would sensitize cells to docetaxel.

He is the co-Director of the Breast Cancer Program and Leader of the TGF-ß focus group at this institution. Dr. McCarthy has received numerous awards and recognition for his service and accomplishments in these fields over the years and as such is well suited to lead this ambitious project. . The PI has surrounded himself with expertise in biostatistics (Babcock-Loane), pathology (Gilden), drug development and biomarker validation (Dalton), breast cancer clinical oncology/translational research (Harford), chemistry and MRI imaging (Lee), protein tyrosine kinases (Smith), and securine (Werdman) that will all help ensure the successful completion of this study.

imp_text: This is a new submission from an experienced investigator examining the role of the Rho guanine exchange factor (GEF) Net1 in breast cancer. The PI has previously identified Net1 and its splice variant Net1a as potential oncogenes in clinical samples. Here, the PI provides preliminary data indicating that Net1 activates RhoA, driving breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis. The PI puts forth a conceptually innovative hypothesis that acetylation-dependent dynamic regulation of Net1 subcellular localization to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane is required for temporal and spatial regulation of RhoA-mediated breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis. This proposal has considerable strengths including strong rationale and significance, high conceptual innovation and a solid experimental approach that combines various in vitro and in vivo models. The major weaknesses of this proposal are the potential choice of models and whether the most relevant oncogenic pathways are being examined (ex. Is LPA the best oncogenic driver of breast cancer?), that none of the in vivo models proposed address the role of Net1 acetylation, and the moderate recent productivity of the PI. However, the significance, innovation and overall approach still largely overshadow these deficiencies and as such the overall impact of this study is viewed to be high.
sig_text_str: . This proposal will help delineate the signaling mechanisms governing metastasis in order to develop effective therapies. . This work is significant because it is currently unknown which RhoGEFs contribute to breast cancer in vivo. . The studies here will provide novel insight into how the microtubule and actin cytoskeleton are regulated during cell movement in cancer. . This work will highlight a new role of specific HDACs and HATs in breast cancer. Given that multiple HDAC inhibitors are currently under clinical investigation, this work may have a translational impact.
sig_text_wkn: . It is not clear if this study addresses the most relevant oncogenic pathway in breast cancer. For example, the model presented by the PI indicates Net1 signaling is initiated by LPA. However, the oncogenic role of LPA in breast cancer is not well defined. Could Net1 signaling also result from more common oncogenic cues such as PI3K-Akt or Myc signaling?
inv_text_str: . The PI of this application, Dr. Robinson, is an Associate Professor at UT Health Science Center who’s laboratory is focused on understanding the contributions of Rho family small GTPases to breast cancer and in particular in the areas of cell motility and invasion, areas directly relevant for this proposal. . As collaborators (albeit with no effort listed), Drs. Beauchene and Dempsey have provided letters of support to help give guidance for the animal studies proposed in Aim 3.
inv_text_wkn: . The PI appears to have had only moderate productivity recently with no senior authors publications since 2009.
inn_text_str: . This is the first data demonstrating a functional role for Net1 in breast cancer motility, invasion and metastasis. . The finding that acetylation of Net1 prevents its nuclear localization and therefore regulates its function is particularly innovative. . This proposal addresses a potential new feedback mechanism involving Net1, FAK and Src that will help explain the temporal and spatial control of this signaling cascade. . This will be the first examination of Net1 function in breast cancer in vivo. . This is the first time any RhoGEF will have been tested for its contribution to breast cancer in vivo. . The investigators have created the first Net1 knockout mouse strain.
inn_text_wkn: . Roles for Net1 and RhoA in breast cancer have previously been described.
app_text_str: . There is a large amount of preliminary data presented that demonstrate a convincing functional role for Net1 and Net1a in RhoA activation and breast cancer cell migration. . There is strong rationale to support a role for acetylation of Net1 in controlling its subcellular localization. . Aim 3 proposes to use a combination of xenograft and genetic mouse models and should have some translational significance.
app_text_wkn: . The preliminary data is largely limited to 1-2 cell line models. . Much of the approach is limited to the use of only MDA-MB-231 cells and thus could fail to capture the heterogeneous nature of breast cancer. . There are no in vivo studies proposed in Aim 3 to address the role of Net1 acetylation, one of the major unique aspects of this study. . While reasonable rationale, there is no data to support that the described HDACs are indeed regulating Net1. . Minor concern--If the indicated HATs and HDACs do not end up playing a significant role, Aim 1 becomes considerably more open ended.
env_text_str: . The environment at the University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston is excellent and has all the resources necessary to ensure the successful completion of this project. . There are existing collaborators nearby that can provide guidance for the animal studies proposed in Aim 3.

imp_text: This is a new application from an established investigator examining the interaction of the extracellular matrix and hormone signaling (prolactin and estrogen) in breast cancer. Specifically, the investigators hypothesize that stiff extracellular matrices (ECM) switch the balance of hormone signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic, thereby establishing a feed-forward loop in breast cancer as the hormone signaling is then thought to exacerbate the dense extracellular matrix. Aims 1 and 2 examine the potentially interdependent roles of the ECM and hormone signaling in breast cancer cells (Aim 1) and stromal fibroblasts (Aim 2). These interactions are then examined in vivo in Aim 3. Collectively, this is fairly innovative proposal that has strong significance as it examines an understudied aspect of breast cancer, breast density. The proposed studies should provide shed new light on the regulation and role of the extracellular matrix in breast cancer and may highlight potential new therapeutic avenues. However, several weaknesses were also noted. It is still unclear (and will continue to be so after the study), exactly how increased ECM stiffness alters hormone signaling. In other words, how does a change in the mechanical properties of a tumor lead to altered signaling? In addition, it is not clear from the preliminary data that prolactin and estrogen signaling lead to true changes in the ECM. Further, there is no model of ER+, tamoxifen-resistance in Aims 1 and 2 which is a major focus (and part of the rationale) of this project. Hence, at this time this proposal is viewed to have a moderately high impact.
sig_text_str: . The role of the ECM in altering hormone-responsiveness is an understudied area. . The in vivo experiments described in Aim 3 may have translational significance both for purposes of developing new diagnostics as well as potentially highlighting new druggable targets.
sig_text_wkn: . It is unknown, and will still be unknown following the conclusion of this study, exactly how the mechanical changes that result from the stiffened ECM adjust hormone signaling. At present, only signaling downstream of the hormone receptors will be examined and so the initial part of the mechanism of action will remain unknown. . Prolactin and estrogen are already known to contribute to breast cancer and breast density. Breast density is known to associate with poor prognosis. As such the work described here may offer limited conceptual advancement. . Since matrix density influences both ER+ and ER- breast cancers, ER may have minimal involvement in the oncogenic effects of a stiff matrix.
inv_text_str: . The main PI of this proposal, Dr. Baker, is an expert in hormone signaling, including estrogen and especially prolactin, in breast cancer. Over the years, he has developed a number of models to investigate the roles of these hormones in the disease. He is well suited to co-lead this study. . The co-PI, Dr. Keat, has expertise in signal transduction and receptor/ligand interactions as they relate to the extracellular matrix. Her laboratory in particular is interested in collagen reorganization at the tumor/stroma boundary, an area that is directly relevant for this proposal. imp_text: This proposal seeks to define the role of Sox2 in aggressive prostate cancers and CRPC. Strengths include: (1) the goal of identifying a novel mechanism by which Sox2 may regulate aggressive PC and CRPC; (2) strong preliminary data demonstrating that elevated Sox2 expression can confer CRPC growth and survival and Sox2 drives the non-canonical expression of select genes. Weaknesses include: (1) an unclear model of how Sox2-positive epithelial cells become Sox2-positive CRPC, which seems at odds with some of the preliminary data; (2) a lack of clarity for how genomics results will be integrated into a clear set of Sox2 targets; and (3) some feasibility issues surrounding the normal prostate epithelial studies outlined in Aim 3. The disparate observations presented regarding the potential role of Sox2 in aggressive PC are difficult to reconcile with some of the proposed hypothesis. Therefore, the overall impact of the proposed studies is unclear, and likely to be modest.
sig_text_str: . Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related mortalities among American men, most often due to relapse of prostate cancer CRPC. . Preliminary data suggest that elevated Sox2 expression can confer CRPC growth and survival. Understanding how Sox2 induces CRPC growth would provide new information for targeting this aggressive disease. . Defining a specific cell-of-origin for PC development has been controversial, the hypothesis that Sox2-positive prostate basal epithelial cells are the cell of origin for more aggressive PC that advance to CRPC is intriguing.

Conflicting preliminary data and a confusing model of Sox2 regulation during transformation (does it remain expressed, or become repressed?) and emergence of CRPC (does it become re-expressed?), clouds the potential significance. . The expression of Sox2 and downstream effectors in normal basal epithelial cells (as well as other normal cells) may restrict therapeutic targeting, as impact on normal tissues may be significant.

Dr. Baker has experience in stem cell biology, molecular biology, animal models of prostate biology and translational research and has published a number of mid-tier first author publications in these areas. . app_text_str: . Some of the preliminary data presented are clear and robust: (1) overexpression of Sox2 in castration-sensitive PC cells induces CRPC; (2) the growth of CRPC tumors following castration results in significantly elevated levels of Sox2 and FGF5 mRNA (protein expression should also be included). . The studies to identify Sox2 co-factors and Sox2-dependent genes proposed in Aim 2 are important. . The approach includes a well-written description of the models and statistical approaches that will be used. Anticipate results, potential pitfalls and proposed solutions are discussed throughout. .
app_text_wkn: . The overall progression model for how Sox2-positive epithelial cells become Sox2-positive CRPC is not clear. The observations presented in the preliminary data are that: (1) Sox2 is high in normal basal cells; (2) Sox2 is not expressed in most PC (including cell lines and primary PC at early stages); (3) Sox2 is re-expressed again in CRPC. This is inconsistent with the overall hypothesis that “Sox2-positive prostate basal epithelial cells derive Sox2-positive tumors that progress to metastatic and castration-resistant prostate cancer”. Moreover, the preliminary data suggest that Sox2 is not expressed in castration-sensitive PC, and becomes re-expressed as CRPC develops. In patients, 10% of GS6 tumors are Sox2-positive, and yet the vast majority of patients that are not cured surgically will eventually progress to CRPC, suggesting that the tumor evolves. These disparate observations are difficult to reconcile with the proposed hypothesis. . AR often remains active in CRPC due to mutation, amplification, alternative splicing, or increased protein stability. It is therefore unclear how a Sox2-positive cell (which expresses Sox2 prior to transformation, per the above mentioned hypothesis) utilizes Sox2 differently to promote CRPC. . It is highly likely that a vast number of genes change as Sox2 levels change. The discovery of FGF5 as a Sox2 target gene using a targeted array does not make it the best candidate for analysis. The ChIP seq and microarray analysis proposed in Aim 2 are an unbiased approach to address Sox2-dependent genes. Having this information as preliminary data would allow more relevant analysis of downstream Sox2 effectors (replacing or in addition to FGF5) in Aim 1. . There is little rationale provided for why Sox2-positive PC cells would be resistant to docetaxel. . To support Aim 3, preliminary data should be included demonstrating that the different PrECs can be transformed and maintain their respective Sox2 +/- status. If transformation with the genetic elements described result in the loss of gain of Sox2, or if the cells do not respond to androgens (or androgen ablation) as expected, the proposed studies will not be feasible.

study_section: Tumor Progression and Metastasis Study Section
imp_text: This proposal seeks to define the regulatory circuitry that engages RhoA-mediated migration, with a specific focus on Net1, a Rho-guanine exchange factor. The studies examine a number of aspects of Net1 regulation, including acetylation of Net1, activation of FAK by NET1, activation of SRC by FAK, and inhibition of Net1 upon SRC activation. Strengths include: (1) the innovative proposed regulation of Net1 by HATs/HDACs; (2) the subsequent regulation of FAK/SRC by activated Net1, and the negative feedback regulation the controls overall migratory potential; (3) a logical plan to assess each of the components involved in the complex regulatory pathways, in an orderly manner; and (4) novel mouse models to assess the importance of Net1 in vivo. Weaknesses include: (1) the frequent use of transfection experiments and a limited set of BC cell lines; and (2) the lack of key preliminary data confirming that Net1 knock-out changes the biology of mammary tumorigenesis. Overall the strengths outweigh the weakness, and the study will biochemically assess the proposed pathways and regulatory mechanisms in detail, providing an expanded understanding of cancer cell migration. Yet, because this is a mechanistic study more so than a biological study, the impact on translational studies aimed at improving patient care are less clear.
sig_text_str: . Metastasis is responsible for the vast majority of cancer deaths, particularly with breast cancer. . While long studied, the molecular mechanisms governing cell motility leading to metastasis are still not fully elucidated, and likely differ among cancers and even sub-types of cancer. . RhoA is a critical factor regulating motility, and the focus of the proposal, Net1, is an emerging modulator of RhoA activity. Understanding the regulation of Net1, including its nuclear-cytoplasmic-membrane localization, the posttranslational modifications, and the reciprocal regulation of Net1 and FAK/SRC would add another level of understanding to how Net1 functions. Understanding how these components interact to regulate focal adhesions would provide new mechanistic information on how cellular motility, and thus metastasis, is regulated and has the potential to impact future therapies aimed at disrupting these signaling interactions.
sig_text_wkn: . The likelihood that Net1 regulates metastasis in all tumor types, or even all sub-types of breast cancer is unlikely. While Net1 focuses on BC, there are vastly different subtypes that have different biological properties (Luminal, Her2+, TNBC) and even sub-types within the sub-types. Some distinction of where Net1 plays a critical role would help define better the significance of the proposed studies to breast cancer patients.

study_section: Tumor Microenvironment Study Section
imp_text: This proposal seeks to define how matrix density enables hormones to drive tumor progression (proliferation, invasion, dedifferentiation). Strengths include: (1) the use of complex 3D culture systems, including co-culture with CAFs and HMFs (which are more relevant to BC matrix than traditional culture); (2) the use of novel mouse models to assess how collagen-mediated tumor stiffness impact tumor development and progression; and (3) the assessment of key findings in human BC specimens using innovative imaging techniques. Yet, while the overall hypothesis that ECM and collagen organization shift the hormonal response to tumor promoting (and less responsive to anti-estrogen therapy) has elements of innovation, the mechanistic details proposed for study are not particularly innovative, and seem highly predictable given prior studies. The fact that there a no new paradigms being pursued here is the weakness of the proposed studies. This weakness is tempered by the potential to identify ways to negate the impact of high-density ECM on tumor growth and anti-estrogen therapy, and improve treatment options for non-responsive ER+ tumors.
sig_text_str: . Anti-estrogen resistant ER+ cancers represent a significant clinical challenge. . Cross-talk between tumor cells and non-tumor stroma plays an important role in various aspects of cancer cell behavior, and likely influences the response of ER+ tumors to anti-estrogen therapies. . Understanding tumor/stroma interactions, and their influence on cancer cell signaling and ECM components would provide important new information about how the detrimental cross-talk, influencing tumor growth, metastasis, and therapeutic resistance, can be combated.
sig_text_wkn: . There are many studies addressing this significant topic. While these published studies do not yet provide a complete picture of how tumor/stromal interactions influence cancer cell signaling, they have provided some important foundational concepts built upon in the current proposal. Thus, at times, the proposal reads as an incremental step forward in our knowledge.

Many of the pathways being assessed have been studied and described following PRL stimulation, and were expected to play a role in the described phenotypes. app_text_str: . The approach is well-written, with well-stated hypotheses, and straight-forward experimental designs to test the contribution of specific pathways to specific outcomes. . Aim 2B/C will assess the impact of co-cultured CAFs or CAF-associated matrix deposition on ER-responsiveness (and anti-estrogen therapy), as well as TNBC responsiveness (and intriguing addition to the studies). Assessing the impact of anti-estrogen therapy on TNBC cells cultured with CAFs would have been an interesting experiment as well. . Aim 3 is well organized, and will complement the in vitro/cell line studies. The NRL-PRL and cola1 mouse models provide a highly relevant, in vivo system to test the hypothesis that enhanced ECM stiffness drives changes in ER+ BC progression, metastasis, and resistance to anti-estrogen therapies. . The human BC studies aimed at assessing the impact of ECM deposition and collagen structure on ERK/STAT5 signaling and patient outcomes is appropriate and will provide necessary translational relevance to the observations of the in vitro and in vivo studies.
app_text_wkn: . While the hypotheses are focused, they are focused because of preliminary and published data that strongly suggest that the hypotheses are correct, particularly in Aim 1 and 2A. For example, the role of high collagen density in causing a switch from PRL-activated STAT5 to ERK, thus changing biological outcomes (invasions, growth) is supported by the preliminary data. . Many studies have assessed CAFs compared to HMFs, thus, some of the proposed studies seem highly predictable, and assess minor variations of the same pathways/effectors known to function upstream or downstream of this switch, and seem incremental. . In Aim 2A, studies of the impact of anti-estrogen therapies on the CAFs would be an important complement. In addition, targeted assessment of specific ECM proteins may fail to identify key driver components. While a mass-spec approach is acknowledged as a potential in the alternative methods section, it would have been an innovative addition to the Aim. The origin and number of CAF cultures to be tested is not described (for example, will these be from luminal B tumors?). . Observations that cola1 mutant mice impact the aggressiveness of additional BC models, not driven by ER suggest that the impact of stiffness on tumor aggressiveness may be through ER-independent mechanisms, and a more general phenomenon that proposed here. Additionally, this model will only assess the impact of collagen-mediated stiffness, which may not be the key driving factor behind the observed phenotypes.

imp_text: The application is presented by an Associate Professor at Case Western Reserve University who propose to characterize the role of c-Abl and associated signaling in triple-negative breast cancer development and metastasis. C-Abl was demonstrated by the group with a novel function in breast carcinogenesis different from its role in hematopoietic system. The project focuses on the molecular mechanisms of how activated c-Abl acts as a tumor suppressor. The goal of the current project is to test the hypothesis that measures capable of promoting c-Abl expression and activation will alleviate TNBC development and metastatic progression. The specific aims are (1) determine the role for oncogenic TGF-ß signaling and mechano-transduction to inactivate the tumor suppressing functions of c-Abl in TNBCs; (2) determine the role for p53 family members in mediating tumor suppression by c-Abl in TNBC; (3) determine the value of c-Abl to predict TNBC response to docetaxel; and (4) determine the therapeutic effectiveness of securinine to eradicate TNBCs. Metastasis is a major cause of cancer-associated deaths and the underlying mediators of this process are poorly understood, thus justify the significance of this research. PI assembled a strong team qualified to conduct the proposed studies, and the PI has published extensively in TNBC, TGF and metastasis fields.  The experimental approaches are comprehensive and form a logic progression and are expected to demonstrate the novel role of c-Abl in breast tumorigenesis and the translational value of activating c-Abl and associated signaling for effective TNBC treatment. The entire plan is nicely described, logic and potentially problems and alternative strategies are adequately addressed. All aims are relatively independent but intervened intrinsically.

imp_text: The PI is an associate professor who proposes to characterize the role of Net1, a RhoGEF, in breast carcinogenesis and metastatic progression. The project focuses on the molecular mechanisms by which NET1 contributes to regulate breast cancer cell mobility and invasion. The goal of the current project is to test the hypothesis that acetylation dependent, dynamic regulation of Net1 localization to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane is required for temporal and spatial regulation of RhoA activation that underlies breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis. The specific aims are (1) to demonstrate how acetylation and what (acetylases and deacetylases) controls the subcellular localization of Net1, (2) to identify the molecular mechanism by which Net1 and FAK exert reciprocal control and impacts focal adhesion dynamics, and (3) to test the consequences of Net1 isoform depletion on mammary tumorigenesis and metastasis in mouse xenograft models. Distant metastasis is a major cause of cancer-related deaths, and the mediators od this process are poorly understood. For such reason, the goals of the project have considerable significance. imp_text: Estrogen receptor-positive (ER+) breast cancers (BCs) account for the majority of BCs. A significant portion of this subtype does not respond to hormonal therapies and still develop metastatic disease, constituting a significant challenge in breast cancer care.  This application proposes to understand how ER+ BCs develop and progress to metastasis, and will test the hypothesis of “Stiff extracellular matrices switch the balance of hormonal signals from pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic, thereby establishing a feed forward loop in breast cancer”. The project focuses on the prolactin and E2 signaling on breast cancer cells, and C+BC-associated stromal cells, followed by in vivo validation on disease progression, metastasis and therapeutic resistance. The goal of the current project is to illuminate the contribution of theses factors and cells to ER+ BC carcinogenesis.  The specific aims are (1) Determine how the stiffness of the extracellular matrix shifts the spectrum of PRL- and estrogen-induced signals in breast cancer cells, (2) Examine how PRL and estrogen regulate matrix deposition in stromal fibroblasts, and (3) Elucidate the interactions of PRL, estrogen and extracellular matrix density in vivo in the development and progression of breast cancer. The MPIs and collaborators are qualified to carry out the proposed studies, and the MPIs have a long record of publishing in breast carcinogenesis and Era signaling. The experimental approaches include in vitro cell models and in vivo animal models which are comprehensive in a logic progression. The outcomes are expected to inform the potential mechanisms in ER+ BC development and progression, and reveal innovative insight discovery. All aims are relatively independent and intrinsically connected.

It is more practical to perform the profiling array on the prostate cancer cell lines with orverexpression or knockdown of Sox2, to identify the potential Sox target genes. It is unclear if the Sox2 antibody has sufficient quality for the ChIP-seq study and if the PI has the previous experience in the ChIP-seq study. Aim3 proposes to transform the Sox2-positive or –negative prostate cells with combination of oncogene. It is unclear if the transformation models with oncogenes can reflect human prostate cancer tumorigenesis, and if the PI is able to establish the in vitro transformation model for the studies proposed in the Aim 3. imp_text: This proposal focuses on U12 dependent splicing which seems to depend on different factors than the more common U2 dependent splicing.  One of these factors is U4atac, which in the disorder MOPD I, contains several point mutations. Patient derived cell lines with U4atac alleles show reduced splicing. The proposal takes multiple approaches using a patient derived cell line with one known SNP change but uses transfected cells lines to perform an in vivo snRNA functional assay.  In addition, this proposal incorporates an aim to determine transcriptome changes associated with the SNP change 51G>A.  This proposal is a good example of performing both the basic science to determine the mechanism of U12 dependent splicing and research into the more direct cause of the MOPD I and similar diseases. imp_text: This project was designed to investigate function and clinical impact of Sox2 expression and its association with androgen receptor (AR) in primary, metastatic, and castration-resistant prostate cancer in prostate cell lines with different status of Sox2 expression, castration-resistance, and AR inhibition and docetaxel sensitivity in vitro and in mouse models. The Sox 2 is an essential transcription factor for maintaining the survival and pluripotency of undifferentiated embryonic stem cells (ESCs), and has an emerging role as an epigenetic reprogramming factor and oncogene. The goal of this project is to elucidate the signaling pathways regulated by Sox2 for predicting prostate cancer progression and identifying new therapeutic targets in advanced prostate cancers. The objective of this proposal is to define the mechanism of how Sox2 promotes cell survival and growth in an androgen-deprived environment. The proposed studies will elucidate the role of Sox2 in castration-resistant tumor growth and could implicate Sox2 and associated genes as therapeutic targets and as biomarkers for prediction of prostate cancer progression. The proposed work will elucidate the adult somatic functions of Sox2 in both normal and malignant prostate cells and thus, could fill a gap in understanding function of the ECS-associated core transcription factors including Sox2 in adult tissues. The proposed work will determine whether the progressive prostate tumors arise from Sox2-postive basal epithelia and this could directly address the role of Sox expression in tumor progression and confer its prognostic value in overall prostate cancer development and progression.

imp_text: Activities of RhoA GTPase and associated Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (RhoGEF) family proteins are shown to be essential for cancer cell motility, invasion of extracellular matrices, and metastasis, and are consistently upregulated in human breast cancer. The proposed studies are directly related and extended from PI’s currently awarded RO1 and CPRIT grants, which are close to the end of funding periods. This new application will investigate regulatory mechanisms that control the subcellular localization and activity of the RhoGEF Net1 in breast cancer cells and demonstrate how it affects breast cancer cell motility in vitro and metastasis in vivo. Completion of these studies could provide a mechanistic understanding of how Net1 contributes to breast cancer cell motility and invasive potential and identify novel Net1-assocated targets for intervention in metastatic human breast cancer.
sig_text_str: • The small RhoA GTP binding protein controls many cellular processes such as cell motility, extracellular matrix invasion, mesenchymal and amoeboid types of movement. imp_text: This project is based on their previous findings that changes in aligned collagen could serve as a signature for patients at risk for metastasis and poor outcome, especially those with estrogen receptor positive (ERa+) breast cancer. The proposed studies will use a combination of in vitro 3D cell culture system, a unique hormonally-induced murine model of aggressive breast carcinoma, and clinical samples to further dissect how extracellular matrix (ECM) density alters the actions of hormones including prolactin (PRL) and estrogen in breast cancer. They will also examine how these actions of hormone on tumor microenvironment (TME) contribute to the development, progression and therapeutic resistance in breast cancer. The proposed studies could bringing together perspectives on hormone action, cell responses to mechano-stimuli, establish the links between the density of the ECM and pro-tumorigenic hormonal responses, and elucidate their interaction and mechanisms of action. Findings from these studies should reveal new potential therapeutic targets for ERa+ breast cancers that are resistant to anti-estrogen therapies, which are constituting to the majority of breast cancer deaths, and will have a significant impact on improving breast cancer therapy and patient care.
sig_text_str: • The propose studies will address the important need in a better understanding the role of the ECM in altered hormonal responsiveness leading to the de novo or acquired anti-estrogen resistant breast cancer. • The propose work on investigating whether altered ECM and collagen organization shift the hormonal response of breast tumor cells towards tumor progression could elucidate novel mechanisms by which pathologic processes alter hormonal actions and reveal new potential therapeutic targets for ERa+ breast cancers that are resistant to anti-estrogen therapies.
sig_text_wkn: • Need to explore novel therapeutic strategies that could intervene the ECM and hormone interaction to overcome resistance to anti-gene therapies in preclinical or clinical models based on these proposed mechanistic studies.
inv_text_str: • Dr. Jackson is an expert in hormonal actions in normal mammary function and breast cancer. His laboratory has developed unique in vivo and in vitro models to elucidate the role of prolactin and its crosstalk with estrogen and growth factors in breast cancer development and progression. He has assembled an outstanding multi-disciplinary research team with to examine mechanisms that underlie the interplay between hormones, stiffness of the extracellular matrix, and the development, progression and therapeutic sensitivity of ERa+ breast cancer. The proposed research is a true integration of the ideas and expertise of these investigators.
inn_text_str: • Proposed studies will address the novel hypotheses that the stiffness of the ECM leads to a change in hormonal signals that in turn drive breast cancer progression and these same hormones are also agents that alter the matrix. If the hypotheses is proven it could potentially change the paradigm of how we view hormone actions and resistance in breast cancer. • The proposed studies to examine the action of PRL and estrogen on stromal fibroblasts in TME  with established in vitro 3D tumor cell-TME interactive culture system and a transgenic mouse model (NRL-PRL) are conceptually and technically novel.
inn_text_wkn: • Lack of novel therapeutic intervention models and target evaluation strategies.
app_text_str: • The approaches to proposed 3 specific aims are well integrated by examining the effects of increased stromal density on PRL and estrogen signals individually and together in ERa+ breast cancer epithelium (Aim 1) and on stromal cells themselves and crosstalk with tumor epithelium in a defined system in which we can manipulate the ECM stiffness (Aim 2), and by determining the outcome of this interplay on disease progression, metastasis and therapeutic responsiveness in a more complex and relevant context in vivo (Aim 3). • Aim 1: They will determine how the stiffness of the extracellular matrix shifts the spectrum of PRL- and estrogen-induced signals in breast cancer cells using a defined in vitro 3D culture system with matrices of different densities of collagen I. The different collagen densities could mimic low and high density stromal environments, and have known corresponding mechanical stiffness. This is a very useful system for the proposed in vitro studies. The experiments are well designed to answer important questions on how dos the density of the collagen matrix affect PRL-initiated signaling cascades and the density-modulated PRL signals modulate cell behavior; what is the effect of matrix density on PRL-estrogen crosstalk regulation of proliferation/ survival and anti-estrogen responsiveness and on the outcome of PRL-estrogen crosstalk on invasion and differentiation? • Aim 2: They will examine how PRL and estrogen regulate matrix deposition in stromal fibroblasts and this altered ECM affect the response of mammary carcinoma cells to hormones and anti-estrogen therapies. They will determine the changes in matrix deposition induced by PRL and estrogen in carcinoma-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) compared to normal mammary fibroblasts (NMFs) in vitro and investigate the effect of substrate stiffness on HMF and CAF signaling pathways mediated by PRL and estrogen and by their cross-talk vitro. • Aim 3: They will elucidate the interactions of PRL, estrogen and the stiffness of the ECM in breast cancer tumor xenograft and genetically engineered mouse models in vivo. They will determine the role of stromal cells on PRL-induced tumor growth, progression and therapeutic resistance in human carcinoma xenografts with PRL-overexpressing T47D and MDA-MB-231 cells. They will also determine the effect of increased ECM stiffness on PRL and estrogen crosstalk in the development, progression and therapeutic sensitivity of luminal cancers in vivo using an innovative transgenic mouse model (NRL-PRL) developed in PI’s lab. These are very useful approaches that could reveal biological and preclinical relevance of all above proposed in vitro studies.
app_text_wkn: • The proposed studies in Aim 1 to investigate the roles of elevated basal pERK1/2 and the predominant signals initiated by PRL in LD and HD matrices (STAT5, ERK1/2) using multiple complementary small molecule inhibitors and siRNAs lack strong rationale and a little diffused. • Similarly, the proposed studies to determine the association between clinical outcome, hormone receptors, and ECM signatures in a breast cancer tissue microarray by IHC are highly risky due to the complicated temporal and special expression and activation and inactivation, protein-protein interaction, and cellular translocation status. A novel multi-color immunofluorescence imaging analysis may be a more plausible approach.

imp_text: This is a new proposal from a new investigator focused on identifying structural features of several key factors involved in meiosis 1. My enthusiasm for this grant is driven by several factors including: 1) an emphasis on detailed characterization of key proteins at molecular resolution 2) A well-blended experimental plan taking advantage of any methodology that will aid the study, and 3) the investigator and the team of collaborators assembled are clearly productive experts. This score could have been higher if the proposal addressed the degree to which these assorted proteins are thought to be conserved outside of fungi, or if the proposal had provided a more rigorous description of how learning binding properties and structures can inform the overall field and move it forward.
sig_text_str: . Meiosis is obviously critical for sexual reproduction, period. . Dozens of proteins govern the organization of chromosomes during this well-orchestrated process, yet the molecular details of these proteins remain largely unclear. . To understand defects in meiosis (resulting in aneuploidy and spontaneous abortion), we must understand the details of the processes involved.
sig_text_wkn: . The proposal repeatedly references fungal specific domains or proteins, but the extent to which understanding these proteins is relevant to other species in not at all clear. In one case, the PI notes that the human Hop1 orthologue is not applicable to the yeast protein. This is not good. . There is a lack of illustration of why the structure of these factors matters. In general, knowing structural information is not necessarily going to move a field. This potential challenge can be addressed directly by the proposal.
inv_text_str: . This new investigator has been productive at all stages of training and is well positioned to start an independent career. . Diverse experimental approaches are supported by an expert group of collaborators. . The PI notes independence from his mentor, directly.

Aim one is focused, largely on differentiating between two models for monopolin function. The effect of geometry on protein function is well described in defense of the aim. . To characterize dimerization and protein:protein interface, the proposal deploys many methods, including NMR, which could yield high resolution insight, if performed correctly. . The aims focus on distinct protein complexes, each endeavoring to bring some level of structural insight into the known functions of these proteins.
app_text_wkn: . There is minimal effort devoted to alternative considerations. Interlaced in the approach, there are occasional technical issues addressed with solutions, but alternative explanations for the data are not clearly described. . Loose use of terms like behavior (e.g. “well behaved proteins”) and biochemistry (e.g. measure the “biochemistry” of a complex) does not instill confidence in the rigor with which data will be interpreted. . In many places, fungal specific features are mentioned without reference to general application of findings. Yeast is a great model system, but there is little reason to invest in hi resolution definition of yeast-specific features. It is likely that much of the proposal is directly applicable to higher organisms, but it is not described in the proposal. . imp_text: This proposal builds on an established investigator’s long standing interests in the mechanisms that govern mRNA splicing. Most of the reviewer’s enthusiasm for this proposal stems from the clever integration of a relevant defect in human U12 splicing that derives from mutation of the U4atac snRNA. This mutation causes a rare recessive disorder called Microcephalic Osteodysplastic Primordial Dwarfism type I (MOPD I). In this proposal, the PI employs patient samples and iPS cells derived from affected patient cells to characterize the effects of this mutation in a secondary splicing pathway snRNA on mRNA profile and splicing capacity for individual mRNAs. The PI provides substantial description of preliminary and published data that support the likelihood of success for the proposed studies. Furthermore, the proposed experiments blend classical biochemical assays, partially reconstituted activity assays, and modern mRNA sequence analyses to address the questions proposed. The greatest strength of this proposal is the perfect use of a natural human disorder to serve as a mechanistic model to characterize a fundamental cellular process. The greatest weakness of the proposal is the lack of thoughtful consideration of alternative outcomes or strategies or potential benefits of this study for the field. Nevertheless, this proposal holds great promise for promoting our understanding of U12-dependent splicing in humans.

imp_text: This is a proposal to develop and apply new methods in natural products (secondary metabolites) to enable more efficient and high throughput drug discovery. The field of natural products drug discovery is in flux, and the proposed methods here are aimed at improving the efficiency of natural product drug discovery. The approach provides incremental improvements in identifying lead natural products, but does not address the intrinsic requirement that such discoveries are based on phenotypic screens for function that limit the overall approach. The research plan is disorganized seeming to hit on several approaches without on overall view. The issue of co-culturing organisms is novel and provides hints of developing novel natural products, but the supporting rationale for this approach is not described in enough detail to provide a rationale. imp_text: This is an outstanding proposal from a new investigator to develop and apply new methods in cryo-EM & x-ray crystallography to important problems in the structure and mechanism of kinesin motors. The uncertainties in our current understanding of the mechanism of action, and the limits of detection regarding microtubule associated molecular motors are well laid out. The proposed solutions are novel and elegant. They will extend the state-of-the-art in cryo-electron microscopy and image-processing methods, as well as the specific mechanisms of this system. The project may be considered high-risk but should the experiments outlined succeed there will be an attendant high-reward.

imp_text: The investigators propose a detailed structural and functional investigation of the transport of LPS from the inner to outer membranes in bacteria.  The proposal builds on the known structure of LptA and nice sets up a bridging hypothesis that contrasts with a shuttling hypothesis.  There is evidence that LptA multimerizes (to make a bridge), but the important interaction with LPS is not well understood.  Hence, a focused mutagenesis investigation into LptA will be followed by spin labeling and LptA-LPS interaction studies.  These aim 1 and 2 experiments are very logical and comprehensive and fall within the expertise of the investigators.  There was less enthusiasm for Aim 3, which uses similar techniques to investigate the interaction of LptA with LptC and LptD and E.  These interactions are key to delineating the transport mechanisms, but the experiments proposed are really a first cut at many of the questions.  Arguably, this is necessary based on the state of knowledge.  Overall, the significance is high both because of the potential for developing antibiotics that target LPS transport, and also because the state of structural and functional knowledge of this LPS transport system sets the stage very nicely for the proposed work.  Hence, if successful, the work is expected to have a strong impact on the field.  The investigators have expertise, and the environment is appropriate.

imp_text: Overall Score:  6 PI proposes to develop new approaches to natural products discovery by evaluating natural product library design. They will apply LCMS-based untargeted metabolomics to help guide library design and utilize metabolomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics to investigate interspecies interactions. The outcomes of this proposal will be: (i) a template for producing natural product libraries enriched in new/novel small molecules with drug-like properties; and (ii) a platform for rapidly determining organisms where interspecies interactions change secondary metabolite production. Overall this proposal is both overly ambitious and poorly planned. The PI spends ample time describing how they will generate libraries but it is not clear why several of the proposed topics will be pursued. For example, which is comparison of hit rate to commercial small molecule libraries and entire aim of this grant? It is generally appreciated that NP libraries are effective so it’s not clear what major outcomes this will have. It is also not clear how effective PCA plots with just two parameters will be. Finally, the third Aim is extremely under developed. The amount of work proposed in this Aim is dramatically understated and not well defined in terms of which systems would be extensive studied.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry A Study Section
imp_text: PI proposes to further pursue the development of light-gated technologies to address existing limitations and enable targeting of specific tissues within seconds with caged oligonucleotides. These are powerful tools as they can be triggered with spatiotemporal precision and act in a sequence-specific manner. They propose to develop a universal approach for MO photocontrol with caged MOs (cMOs) that adopt single- or double-lariat conformations. Each of these novel structures utilizes a single light-cleavable tether to achieve terminus-to-backbone (Specific Aim 1) or terminus-to-base (Specific Aim 2) linkages. They will explore different conjugation sites within the MO oligonucleotide and various linker structures to optimize lariat cMO function, guided by in vitro assays of RNA function and well-characterized zebrafish models. They will also evaluate different caging chromophores to establish combinations that allow simultaneous or sequential gene knockdowns (Specific Aim 3). Overall this proposal puts forth an exciting strategy to generate tools for specific gene inactivation. They have good preliminary data and have given thorough description of their path forward. It was not always clearly why both classes of compounds are necessary or if they simply represent alternatives to one another.

imp_text: PI proposes to further study the kinesin motor and have made several relevant breakthroughs in recent work. 1) using a combination of state of the art cryo-electron microscopy instrumentation and a novel image-processing methods, they solved a 3D reconstruction of the kinesin-microtubule complex at ~5-6Å resolution. 2) They have devised a novel algorithm for producing high-resolution 3D reconstructions from cryo-EM images of imperfectly decorated, heterogeneous assemblies of kinesin with microtubules enabling them to the first 3D reconstruction of a kinesin dimer as it steps along a microtubule. The proposed Aims largely describe a continuation of this work and don't provide substantial detail about what makes their approach innovative or significant information about what they will do with the information that is obtained in these studies. The grant reads more like information gathering than obtaining the information to inform future studies of these systems. What is the motivation behind these studies? Essentially, they will use better equipment and generate data processing strategies – need much more clarity on what they are doing that cannot be done by others.

imp_text: This project  is on discovering new drug analogs or leads from natural products from marine bacteria residing in sponges.  Focus on marine bacteria is  a strong point of the proposal. If indeed new drug candidates are found,  either antibiotics or  notch-! pathway activators, the impact of the effort will be great. Overall approach is also somewhat unique in that the project is focuses on using metabolomics to identify secondary metabolites produce by bacteria either alone or in communication with other types of bacteria. Primary analytical technique  to be used  LC-MS is a good method for analyzing small molecules  from their MS spectra. Using principal component analysis (PCA) to group the observed molecules has been developed by the PI and has the potential to differentiate beween classes of  secondary metabolites. There is some preliminary data to show that the technique has promise. Another positive aspect is identifying molecules produced only in co-cultures. Against these positives there are some questions int his reviewers mind. One of the negatives is that drug like molecules will be identified by similarity to existing synthetic molecular libraries, this method will exclude radically different secondary metabolite molecules which may indeed be excellent drug candidates.  Since discovery of new drugs which make it to the market is a very long and difficult process any new approach which increases chance of identifying new natural molecule based drugs will have significant impact. Overall the positives of the proposal make it worthy.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry B Study Section
imp_text: This is a potentially impactful proposal from a new investigator dealing with improving methods for screening natural products for drug development. The proposal presents extensive preliminary data and ambitious research plan. The PI and collaborators form a strong team, although the exact roles of collaborators are not well-defined. The importance of the problem, expertise of the team and efforts to seek novel approaches are the strengths of the proposal. These are outweighed by diffuse and poor description of proposed experiments and methods. The research plan is verbal, but unfocused and uses mostly general statements while lacking technical details and clear explanations. This problem propagates all the way from introductory paragraphs to preliminary results and throughout description of aims.
sig_text_str: . Discovery of new drug leads from untapped sources of natural products is an important goal. . Focus on two disease areas with urgent unmet need for new therapeutics: antibiotics and neuroendocrine cancers.
sig_text_wkn: . As the PI points out, the chemical collections of most large pharmaceutical companies have been panned for possible antibacterials. Screening of natural products faces similar problems. While the PI claims that his new approach will enhance the chemical diversity of natural products, it is not clear how significant this enhancement will be. In fact, the proposal does not describe at all why there should be any enhancement. . PI’s optimism hinges on an assumption that the pool of secondary metabolites will provide untapped source of chemical diversity and drug leads. While this is not an unreasonable expectation, the PI’s preliminary results do not provide compelling evidence that the new structures will represent truly new drug candidates and not just variations on common themes. . Search for new antibiotics in the pool of microbial metabolites is inherently plagued by resistance problems as the microbes carry the genes of resistance to their own weapons.
inv_text_str: . The PI is well trained and has been productive during his graduate and postgraduate years. . The PI has enlisted an excellent team of collaborators with complementary broad expertise.
inv_text_wkn: . The PI has only one independent publication in JOC since starting his independent career three years ago. Most of previous publications are also in medium impact journals. . The exact role of collaborators is not addressed in the proposal. What will be their contribution remains unclear. . The PI collaborators have not published joint papers. The PI has funded collaboration with Dr. Corrie but no shared publications are listed.
inn_text_str: . New metabolomics approach for natural product drug discovery is claimed, although precise details are not discussed.
inn_text_wkn: . The discussion of innovation is diffuse and unfocused. The PI fails to explain how exactly their approach will be fundamentally different compared to traditional ones.
app_text_str: . Extensive preliminary data provide strong support for proposed ideas and feasibility of approach. . Overall, the proposed approach is logical and focused on current bottlenecks in the field.
app_text_wkn: . While extensive, the preliminary data are not well described. For example, it is not clear how the results in Figures 4 and 5 were generated. . Aims 1 and 2 fail to explain why and how collecting more sponges and performing LCMS-PAC will enhance the diversity of natural products being discovered and give new drug lead hits that would not be detected otherwise. . The technical details of LCMS-PAC methodology are not described. Lack of technical details prevents critical evaluation of the potential advantages and shortcomings of the proposed research. This also casts doubts on claimed innovation and potential impact. . Aim 3 proposes some interesting experiments on co-culturing of bacterial, but suffers similar shortcomings as the rest of proposal.
env_text_str: . The PI and collaborators share outstanding resources. The team has everything they need to succeed. . The Pi enjoys high quality mentoring environment. One of the mentors, Dr. Lienhua Leee is listed as a collaborator on this proposal.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry A Study Section
imp_text: This is a strong application from a very capable and highly qualified team of collaborators. The significance is in development of novel and potentially more effective caged morpholono oligonucleotides (MO). The innovation is relatively modest as the work is a logical and somewhat incremental continuation of PI’s and collaborators’ previous efforts in this area. The research team is almost too strong for the scope of proposed aims; the need for the massive collaborative effort is not clearly justified. The aims are well developed and propose solid experiments many of which are routinely performed in PI’s and collaborators’ laboratories. There is some concern that the lariat shaped MO caging may not be better than the previous generation of cyclic MOs; neither preliminary data nor theoretical arguments are compelling. Overall, this is a strong application, but the enthusiasm is somewhat reduced by limited innovation and lack of strong support for the MO design.
sig_text_str: . Development of novel caging techniques for morpholino oligonucleotides (MO) is important. Especially, the ability to do multi-wavelenght parallel uncaging is expected to have significant impact on the field of light controlled oligonucleotide probes.
sig_text_wkn: . The exact problems with current design of caged morpholino oligonucleotides (MO) are not well explained.  It is not clear that the massive effort of two research groups is fully justified by problems that cannot be solved using current caged oligos.
inv_text_str: . The PI, Prof. O’Brian is highly qualified to lead the proposed project. Prof. Decker is a strong collaborator with relevant expertise. . The PI and collaborator have been remarkably productive with many papers in top-notch journals. . Enlisting Prof. Lee as a consultant further strengthens the team.
inv_text_wkn: . Both PI and collaborator have significant overlapping expertise in designing and synthesizing of caged MOs. While the collaboration certainly strengthens the team, it is not immediately obvious why the PI could not accomplish the aims with her own resources. . The PI and collaborator have not published together.
inn_text_str: . New caging approach to deactivate MO.
inn_text_wkn: . The proposed project is a relatively incremental advance of the research that has been ongoing in the PIs labs for some time. It is not obvious that the new caged MO will be significantly better than the previous versions. . The innovation section is terse and not well developed. While the new lariat design is interesting, the idea is not breaking new ground in this field.
app_text_str: . Strong preliminary results support use of caged MO in proposed biological studies. . The specific aims are well developed. The previous track record of PI and collaborator inspires confidence that the experiments will succeed and the aims will be achieved. . Proposed uncaging at >400 nm will yield new and useful tools for broader applications. . Targeting the ntla gene gene is a great biologically relevant method for qualitative and quantitative measures of MO function.
app_text_wkn: . The preliminary results do not have examples of lariat MO and do not provide strong support that the lariat caging will necessarily be advantageous over other designs.  The comparison with cyclic MO of different size is not directly relevant as small cycles and lariats having small cycles are different structures and have significant single stranded end.The PI claims that lariat MO will be significantly more efficacious and versatile than current variant of caged MO are not well supported by either theoretical arguments or preliminary data. . It is not obvious that the lariat caging should be more deactivating than the cyclic design. Although the cycle is becoming smaller, at the same time the lariat features longer single stranded tail. The region of MO available for helix formation may actually be larger in lariat than in cyclic oligonucleotide. . Potential problems (such as mentioned above) are not sufficiently considered and alternative strategies are not discussed. . There is some confusion of name N-methylthioquinoline and actual structures shown in Figure 17. . While potentially interesting experiments using pdx1 and mnx1 MOs are proposed in Aim 3, they are not well described. It is not clear exactly how the two MOs with different decaging wavelength will be used to determine the spatial domain and temporal window of pdx1 and mnx1 activity.

imp_text: This is a good proposal that explores the role of LptA protein in transport of LPS in Gram-negative bacteria. It is expected that the results may help advancing new antibacterial approaches against LptA. While this is an important goal, the PI does not provide any discussion on how exactly the obtained results will be used to foster discovery of new antibiotics. The innovation is relatively modest. The aims are well developed and propose solid experimental approaches to reveal biological function of LptA; however, the link with antibiotic development is weak, which reduced the enthusiasm about the proposed studies. If successful, the proposed research will contribute to our understanding of biosynthesis of bacterial cell membrane.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry B Study Section
imp_text: The authors of this proposal aim to implement a secondary metabolomics platform to uncover structurally diverse and bioactive natural products from cultured organisms. The hypothesis supporting this research is that rapid, sensitive analytical chemistry techniques will enable the discovery of novel, non-structurally-redundant, natural products, thereby expanding the range of medicinally useful compounds in screening libraries. In turn, they expect to make screening efforts more efficient through rational library optimization. The infrastructure described in the proposal, along with validation of the platform, are robust and well thought-out. Inclusion of LLOD and scalability tests clearly indicate that the authors have the capacity to scale this screening paradigm to a larger number of samples in future studies. The authors have focused on a number of “stress tests” for the platform in order to validate the discovery paradigm and provide supporting manuscripts (including some in preparation) to validate the work. The main weakness of the approach lies in the fact that much of this work has been performed in industrial settings, and a number of challenges lie ahead, which remain unaddressed by the proposal. This does not represent a weakness in the authors knowledge of the subject matter because many of these studies have, unfortunately, not been published (outside of patent literature). One major assumption is that bioactive metabolites identified at the first-order screening level will make good drug candidates. This is untrue, companies such as Diversa uncovered thousands of novel secondary metabolites using similar strategies but none turned out to be pharmacologically relevant.  I believe the research described in the proposal will uncover novel secondary metabolites, but think the authors should focus their infrastructure on studying one organism under a variety of conditions (e.g. Aim 3) highlighting basic research studies vs. applied science/drug discovery. The proposal would be much stronger focusing on just a single system and understanding, at the molecular level, why and how (mechanistically) a co-cultured metabolite is stimulating production of a novel secondary metabolite. These findings could have a much broader impact on basic research and development vs. aiming to improve upon industrial drug discovery efforts. One of the large outstanding questions in natural product research is understanding when/why/how these molecules are produced and why so many gene clusters appear to be silent under laboratory conditions. The research described in this proposal presents a system that is capable of answering these fundamental questions but instead focuses on the pharmacological utility of these as-yet-undiscovered compounds. Discovering natural products for commercial applications is fundamentally a screening endeavor, no matter how diverse your starting library. Screening should be a means to follow up with additional basic research in this setting. In summary, I think the whole proposal should focus exclusively on aim 3.
sig_text_str: . There is a pressing need to identify novel bioactive natural products, especially in the context of small molecule antibiotics. There are a number of parallel efforts, which the authors point out in the writing of the proposal, which include genomics-guided discovery. I view this proposal as a complementary and powerful strategy to “fully mine” the novel secondary metabolome vs. focusing on specific gene clusters.
sig_text_wkn: . The main weakness of this proposal is that it focuses on applied discovery of pharmacologically relevant natural products. There is no a priori information suggesting these novel molecules will have applications in the therapeutic space. This will only be uncovered after screening/development/process engineering/cost-modelling/etc.. all of which are challenges that lie outside of the scope of this proposal and of an academic laboratory. Second, cultured organisms represent a minor fraction of the biodiversity available in our environment. Monoculture and co-culture with 2 organisms are fundamentally artificial environments in which to study these microorganisms, especially when trying to gain an understanding, at a basic research level, of when/why these molecules are produced. The proposal does not dig deeply into mechanistic and molecular detail for successes in the research program. I think it would benefit tremendously to dive into one model system that does, for example, show promise during co-cultivation in Aim 3. This could uncover general elicitors of secondary metabolite production, new induction systems that could be ported and more generalizable, and new biochemistry/gene regulation. The goal of finding bioactive drugs is extremely difficult for an academic group to undertake. I think the grant would benefit highly from focusing on mechanistic details that will undoubtedly be uncovered in this research program.
inv_text_str: . The investigators have a strong track record and understanding of the field. There are no concerns that the team presented in this proposal can accomplish all of the goals outlined in the proposal. The combined experience managing large research programs/grants is excellent.
inn_text_str: . The metabolomics pipeline described in the proposal represents a powerful way to perform comparative profiling of large numbers of cultured micro-organisms. The authors went through an extensive number of tests to validate the LLOD and sensitivity of the assays used in the proposal, in additional addressing the scalability of the technique in the context of the grant.
inn_text_wkn: . One common question/theme that kept arising while reading the grant is that the authors, and others, stress the low percentage of organisms that can be cultured effectively in laboratory settings. This grant does not address this fundamental barrier. While there remain an enormous number of cryptic/silent gene clusters in cultured organisms, there needs to be more effort placed on determining what the factors are that cause secondary metabolite induction, for example, by building a proposal around Aim 3 and diving into much more detail. The understanding and elucidation of new signaling molecules, which could be applied universally to other cultured organisms, would have an enormous impact vs just screening pairwise combinations of organisms, hoping to stimulate compound production. In addition, these efforts have been pursued in industry (circa 1990-2000) although, sadly, not publicized widely. Some examples include Diversa, Ecopia, One Cell Systems, et al. Co-culturing and stimulated production of novel metabolites is an established approach, however, the likelihood that a usable compound collection will be derived from this approach is not high. Stimulating sufficient production for functional exploration is extremely difficult as coculturing efforts cannot be easily scaled due to stochastic growth conditions in a fermenter. For example, one strain almost always dominates the culture through the course of a fermentation (with thousands of doublings). Although some systems can be derived to address this nutrient exchange through fermenter barriers is one example, they represent very costly efforts to obtain quantities of molecules that have unknown efficacy in more complex models. I would focus on Aim 3, dig into the science at much higher resolution, and avoid making connections to drug development and industrial applications.

I would focus solely on Aim 3 as a means to uncover basic science to study.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry A Study Section
imp_text: The authors of this proposal aim to develop a series of novel caged morphlinos (MOs) that have the potential to complement a number of genetic tools currently in use. Briefly, the development and application of temporally and spatially controlled genetic tools enables scientists to study dynamic cellular processes in ways which are impossible using traditional, constitutive forward genetics. This proposal aims to develop, implement, and test a structural modification to caged morpholinos which has the possibility of overcoming some limitations of current forms. These limitations include toxicity, stability, and other negative features which impact their utility. The proposal is very well written and the hypotheses and detail are supported thoroughly throughout the grant. One question I have, based on recent developments, is whether alternative systems based on temporally and spatially controlled activation of gene expression would work similarly for embedded Cas9 systems under tightly controlled promoters, for example. I have not seen many examples of this but I suspect there must be groups working/developing that approach as well. The morpholino approach promises to be faster, allowing for direct targeting of a tissue of interest, without requiring a preliminary genetic engineering step (highlighting an advantage over the aforementioned approach). Importantly, these reagents overcome many bottlenecks that currently hinder MOs from being used in broader contexts. The funding request is actually quite modest and I recommend resourcing the project with additional FTE’s and research budget if possible in order to de-risk the successful completion of the grant. The PI is well versed in the research and there is no concern about completion of the outlined objectives. The proposal represents an excellent combination of high-risk (it is an unknown but outstanding question whether alternative structures for morpholinos will overcome all of the pre-existing limitations) but high reward proposal that should be funded in order to answer fundamental questions about these tools. The ability to multiplex the activation of the cMOs using differential wavelengths expands upon the possibilities for studying dynamic cellular processes and represents a powerful extension of the work, if successful. I highly recommend funding.

The significance of the work is high in light of this potential impact. study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function C Study Section
imp_text: The authors of this proposal aim to characterize, using cryo-EM, the mechanistic details of kinesin motor protein interactions with microtubules. To date, these details remain unclear as previous efforts to use other structural characterization techniques have been confounded by the physical properties and heterogeneity of these complexes. This has led to a number of opposing hypotheses and models describing kinesin duty cycles. While biochemical and biophysical studies have generated indirect evidence of the mechanistic characteristics of kinesin-MT interactions, much detail remains unresolved, especially at the atomic level. The authors have performed a series of preliminary experiments which suggest several unexpected modes of interaction during intermediate states for kinesin/MT interactions. The goal of this proposal is to test these hypotheses using state-of-the-art structural elucidation techniques centered around cryo-EM. I found the proposal to be very well written and supported, and believe that the authors did an excellent job explaining how the methods and approaches developed through the course of this proposal would have a broad impact on resolving other, similarly cryptic molecular processes (e.g. other motor protein/scaffold complexes). The resource allocation in the grant seemed slightly incronguous and the grant could benefit from more robust descriptions of contingency plans, but these are minor criticisms and the author was likely space-constrained. Overall, the proposal was very strong and I fully endorse funding.
sig_text_str: . Kinesin/MT interactions form the basis of fundamental cellular processes (e.g. cell division) that are required by a wide range of organisms. Despite the importance of these interactions, all mechanistic, biochemical and structural studies performed to date have been confounded by innate features of microtubule/kinesin complexes. The authors have developed an approach which circumvents many of the roadblocks that exist from a technical perspective. The strength of this proposal lies in the fact that this model is representative of many other types of motor protein/scaffold interactions and the approaches developed during the course of this research can be applied to elucidate a wide range of fundamental cellular processes.

inn_text_str: . Kinesin/MT interactions have been studied using a range of biochemical and analytical techniques over the past several decades. All of these studies have failed to uncover certain aspects of the kinesin duty-cycle, leaving several fundamental questions unanswered. This proposal aims to use, for the first time, a novel array of cryo-EM structural elucidation approaches to shed light on these details.  The proposal has the potential to uncover critical details describing the kinesin duty-cycle which all other methods have failed to generate thus far.

imp_text: This is a well-written proposal from an established investigator with expertise in the role of angiogenesis and inflammatory macrophages during ischemia-reperfusion model. The proposal addresses a highly significant scientific question namely the role of IL-19 in angiogenesis or M2 polarization of macrophages during the ischemia-reperfusion. The proposal has several innovative and elegant approaches that address multiple facets of IL-19 biology in ECs, VSMCs or M2 macrophages in this process, using genetic approaches in mice as well as multiple in vitro studies. The enthusiasm for the study is somewhat diminished by Specific Aim 3 which seems to be quite risky and problematic in the approaches proposed by the investigator. This aim seems to lack a good discussion of potential pitfalls and alternative approaches. Nevertheless, this is a good proposal that will reveal important findings for pathophysiology of ischemia-reperfusion and the contribution of various cells in this process.

This is a highly significant study that addresses an important question regarding the role of IL-19 in the pathophysiology of angiogenesis following ischemia – reperfusion model and its contribution in M2 macrophage differentiation and their role in this process. The completion of this study will enhance the understanding of the role that IL-19 plays in angiogenesis versus M2 macrophage-mediated inflammation and or vascular remodeling during neo-angiogenesis in the ischemic – reperfusion model.
inv_text_str: . This is an excellent team of investigators. The PI has expertise in the role of Th2 interleukins in angiogenesis in the context of ischemia – reperfusion and adoptive transfer models.
