inn_text_str: . The in vivo studies with LOF and GOF of IL-19 in the ischemia reperfusion model coupled with Laser Doppler Imaging are quite innovative. In addition, the adoptive transfer studies to dissect out the role of IL-19 is ECs, VSCMs, versus M2 macrophages are very innovative.
inn_text_wkn: . Previous studies from the PI have already addressed the role of IL-19 in angiogenesis,  proliferation, migration, Rac1 activation and STAT3 activation in ECs versus VSMCs. Therefore, the hypothesis is not completely novel and it has been published before in several studies.
app_text_str: . This is a well-prepared application that will test an important hypothesis (the role of IL-19 as a novel angiogenic and anti-inflammatory cytokine during hypoxia-reperfusion and neo-angenesis). . The preliminary data support the hypothesis. . The investigator proposes multiple complementary approaches in various specific aims to test the role of IL-19 in angiogenesis or anti-inflammation during hypoxia-reperfusion. . In Specific Aim 1, the investigator will use both LOF and GOF approaches to ablate or overexpress IL-19 and test its role in angiogenesis in the hind-limb ischemia model. This is an important model to understand the pathogenesis since ischemia drives multiple processes. . In Specific Aim 2, the investigator will use adoptive transfer to determine which cells, ECs, VSMC, or M2 macrophages play an essential role in this process. . In Specific Aim 3, the investigator will test the role of 4 downstream molecules (IL-1b, CXCL1, IL-8 and HGF) identified in preliminary data in this process in vitro and in vivo using mouse strains deficient for these factors. . In Specific Aim 4, the investigator will test if the differential expression of IL-20R2 in ECs versus VSMCs regulates differential responses to IL-19.
app_text_wkn: . In Specific Aim 1, how will the Laser Doppler Imaging be quantified? The image provided in Figure 11 does not describe the method for quantification. . There are a lot of mice proposed for this experiment and its not clear if this is the best approach as it is likely that they may have redundant roles. The experiments 2 and 3 will use these mice for various assays to define their roles in angiogenesis and macrophage polarization. .  If these four factors function downstream of IL-19 to mediate its effects, a better approach in Specific Aim 3 would be to test which of these factors may rescue IL-19 deficient mice in all these assays prior to continuing with individual knockout mice. . The potential pitfalls and alternative approaches for this specific aim are not well-discussed.

imp_text: Overall, this is an excellent proposal from an established investigator that addresses an important question such as the mechanisms of vascular aging and aging-associated hypertension in particular the contribution of mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) in VSMC, its regulation by AngII and its role in Cav1.2 and Nox2 expression that lead to sustained VSMC contraction and oxidative stress related to age-dependent increase in BP. The knowledge from this proposal will increase our understanding of the age-dependent increase in BP and the role of AngII-dependent activation of MR in this process as well as its downstream effectors. The investigator proposes 3 independent specific aims that will test the role of each component, PKCdelta, Cav1.2 and Nox2 in this process downstream of AngII-mediated MR activation in VSMCs. Overall this is an excellent proposal; however the potential interactions of Cav1.2 and Ca++ in promoting Nox2 expression and regulation of ROS activity have not been explored in Specific Aim 3. This reduces somewhat the enthusiasm for this proposal.

This is an excellent proposal that addresses a significant scientific question and novel hypothesis to address the mechanisms of AngII signaling in the aging vasculature in specific the role of mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) in mediating activation of Cav1.2 channels and Nox2 to promote contraction and oxidative stress leading to increased BP. . The investigators (PI and collaborator) propose a diverse number of approaches both in vitro and in vivo to address the three specific aims of the proposal. . The preliminary data support the hypothesis of the proposal, except for Figure 4 that addresses Specific Aim 3. . In Specific Aim 1, the investigator will explore the direct link between AngII-MR activation and PKCdelta phosphorylation using a variety of in vitro assays on VSMCs that include LOF and GOF with siRNAs and overexpression, pharmacological inhibitors and measurement of MR activity with a MRE element fused to luciferase. The approaches in this aim are quite elegant and the investigator discusses extensively potential outcomes and pitfalls, as well as alternative approaches. . In Specific Aim 2, the investigator will focus on analysis of Cav1.2 as a potential downstream target and analysis of its function in VSMCs. These experiments will be conducted by the collaborator who has expertise with electrophysiology of Ca++ channels and measurement of Ca++ changes using Ca++ loading dyes. The last experiment of this aim will address this question in vivo in mice (SMC MR-KO mice). The experiments proposed for this aim are very elegant and potential outcomes, pitfalls and alternatives are discussed in great detail. . In Specific Aim 3, the investigator will explore the effects of AngII-MR activation on Nox2 expression and Nox2-dependent ROS activation in VSMCs in culture and in vivo in young and aged mice.

However, when you compare young and aged mice, there is a smaller, but not significant change in Nox2 or fluorescence staining. This suggests that MR contributes to AngII-induced ROS regardless of the age since there is an effect on young mice, in addition to the aged mice. . It’s possible that Ca++ changes may affect Nox2 levels in the aged VSMCs; yet this is not explored or discussed in Specific Aim 3 as a potential issue. . How sensitive is the DHEA staining in measurement of oxidative stress?

imp_text: This is a well-written proposal that investigates a highly important question in genetic and molecular mechanisms that lead to cardiac hypertrophy. The investigator will test if genetic interactions between RAF-MEK1 and Hippo-YAP-1 (yorkie) regulate cardiac hypertrophy in both flies and mice and examine structural domains in YAP-1 that confer its ability to regulate cell number versus cell size during cardiac hypertrophy. The investigator has a lot of expertise in Drosophila genetics and has developed several innovative physiological measurements (OCT) to examine heart function in Drosophila. In addition, the investigator has gathered a team of scientists with expertise in other areas such as viral production and cardiomyocyte isolation, genomic comparisons, and mouse genetics, mouse models for disease and physiology that will provide help for several aspects of the project. The project is highly innovative and likely to produce significant important findings to elucidate the role of these pathways in cardiac hypertrophy and identify novel downstream targets. The enthusiasm for the project is dampened by approaches in Specific Aim 2 that do not necessary address several caveats of potential organism-specific interacting factors that may confer YAP-1 (but not yorkie) its ability to regulate cell number and size. In addition, Specific Aims 2 and 3 lack a very detailed description of potential caveats and alternative approaches that reduce the overall impact of the project.
sig_text_str: . This is a highly significant study that addresses an important question regarding genetic interactions between two signaling pathways and molecular mechanisms that lead to cardiac hypertrophy and cardiac failure. The investigator will initially elucidate genetic interactions between Raf-MEK1 signaling and Hippo- YAP-1 (yorkie) signaling in cardiac hypertrophy in Drosophila melanogaster. He will then pursue studies in mice to test whether interactions between these two pathways produce similar effects. The outcomes of this study regardless of the presence of some caveats are likely to reveal important genetic players that control cardiac hypertrophy and may influence heart failure.
sig_text_wkn: . The role of Raf-MEK1 and Hippo-YAP-1 pathways in cardiac hypertrophy has been elucidated in the past. However, potential interactions and downstream effectors remain unknown.

In addition, he has established excellent collaborations with several experts in the mammalian heart physiology, mouse models of TAC, mammalian cardiomyocyte isolation and genomic approaches that will provide their expert help with various aspects of the proposal.

inn_text_str: . The hypothesis of the proposal and approaches are very innovative. The investigator will test a novel hypothesis that Raf-MEK1 pathway and HIPPO-YAP-1 pathway genetically interact with each other to control cardiac hypertrophy. The investigator will use genetic approaches in two model organisms, Drosophila melanogaster and Mus musculus to uncover interactions between these two pathways for cardiac hypertrophy coupled with elegant physiological measurements of heart function such as OCT in Drosophila heart or physiological measurements of cardiac output in mice in addition to conventional histological methods. The investigator has also generated some novel Drosophila lines (tinC-nuclearRFP) to detect changes in the number of cells under conditions where the activity of these pathways is modulated in flies in order to examine if the genetic manipulations affect cell number or cell size. Moreover, in Specific Aim 2 the investigator will perform some structure-function analysis between yorkie and YAP-1 to figure our domains that confer YAP-1 ability to regulate both size and number of cells. These wide-range elegant approaches will likely allow the investigator to identify novel molecules or protein domains that regulate the size and number of cardiomyocytes.

imp_text: Overall Impact Score (1-9):  5 This is an application from an established investigator to address if IL-19 can enhance angiogenesis and improve perfusion of ischemic tissue.  This application is based on recent publication in ATVB that IL-19 has unexpected pro-angiogenic effects in endothelial cells. The strengths of the application are the well-trained PI; investigation of angiogenesis, re-perfusion of ischemic tissue; potential importance of IL-19 to polarize macrophage phenotype; and the strong research environment. Weaknesses relate to lack of convincing preliminary data and the lack of biochemical data. Thus, the proposal has many weaknesses which mostly relate to the experimental design and also to the weak preliminary data. Hind limb ischemia (HLI) in C57BL/6 mice is not a suitable model to study angiogenesis. Thus, the proposal is judged premature.
sig_text_str: . Ability of IL-19 to induce angiogenesis and induce re-perfusion of ischemic tissue is a clinically relevant topic. . Potentially implicate a Th2 interleukin as a novel anti-inflammatory, pro-angiogenic cytokine expressed by inflamed resident vascular cells to promote neovascularization. It could identify IL-19, or IL-20 receptor agonists as potential therapy to restore blood flow in ischemic tissue.

imp_text: High blood pressure (HBP) is common problem with aging and contributes substantially to promoting heart attack and stroke in the elderly. The vascular aging in animals and human, is characterized by (a) enhanced angiotensin II (AngII) signaling, (b) increased vascular oxidative stress, and (c) increased vascular contraction. The agents driving these age-related vascular pathologies are less known and there is no pharmacotherapy to retard or delay arterial aging in humans. In this application the PI will address the role of Smooth Muscle Mineralocorticoid Receptors (MR) in Vascular Aging and Hypertension. The strengths of application include a track record of publication in highly visible journals. Detailed understanding of Smooth Muscle MR function is considered highly relevant especially since this receptor is linked to hypertension in vascular aging. Further, the PI has all the correct mouse models and the expertise to address this important problem. The strengths also include the environment and the collaborator (Martin Hall).

app_text_str: PI will address the novel hypothesis that in the aging vasculature, SMC MR is directly activated by AngII via PKCd-mediated phosphorylation and regulates Cav1.2 and Nox2 expression and activity, promoting the age-associated increase in vascular oxidative stress and vascular contraction, thereby contributing to increased BP. To test this hypothesis, PI proposed 3 specific aims: • AIM#1 will address the mechanism of AngII activation of vascular SMC MR. Using human coronary artery and mouse mesenteric SMCs, PI will address if AngII activates MR via PKCd-mediated phosphorylation of the MR AB-domain using an MR-responsive reporter assay, siRNA knock down of specific PKC isoforms, and targeted mutation of predicted conserved PKC phosphorylation sites in the MR. • AIM#2 will explore SMC MR regulation of vascular Cav1.2 expression and channel activity and the resulting impact on vascular tone and contraction. Using isolated mesenteric SMC and vessels from old compared to young SMC MR-intact and –deficient mice. MR-mediated regulation of Cav1.2 will be explored by qRT-PCR, immunoblotting, promoter/reporter and chIP assays. Channel function will be determined by single cell patch clamp and cellular and whole vessel Ca imaging techniques. Mesenteric vessel pressure myography will measure contractile function and spontaneous tone in the presence of specific Ca channel agonists and blockers. • AIM#3 will test SMC MR modulation of vascular oxidative stress with aging and the role in vascular tone, contractile function, and BP. Using isolated SMC and mesenteric vessels from old compared to young SMC MR-intact and –deficient mice. In cells and vessels, SMC MR regulation of Nox2 expression, membrane translocation, and activity after activation with Aldo or AngII will be assayed by RT-PCR, promoter-reporter, ChIP, immunoblotting of cell fractions and quantification of ROS production assays. Mesenteric vessel contractile responses and myogenic tone generation will be assayed by pressure myography in the presence of anti-oxidants and NADPH oxidase inhibitors. The role of oxidative stress in modulating Ca channel activity with aging will be explored by patch clamping of SMC and mesenteric vessel function studies after treatment with antioxidants in vitro and in vivo. The role of this mechanism in aging-associated BP elevation will be explored using long term telemetric BP monitoring in mice treated with MR antagonists, antioxidants, and/or calcium channel blockers. • Thus, PI will use a new mouse model to explore novel mechanisms for vascular aging and the age-associated increase in BP. Studies will address the role of SMC MR in modulating blood pressure, support novel vascular mechanisms for the protective effects of AngII and MR antagonist drugs in human clinical trials, and identify SMC MR-regulated pathways as novel targets to prevent vascular aging and to treat hypertension specifically in the growing high risk elderly population. • Preliminary data show that AngII activates SMC MR in a PKCd-dependent manner in human SMC suggesting a novel mechanism in which SMC MR mediates enhanced AngII signaling with aging (includes published data in Circ Res, 2005; ATVB, 2007, and Nature Med. 2012). • Vessels from aged SMC MR-deficient mice have decreased spontaneous vascular tone, contraction to L-type calcium channel (LTCC) agonists, expression of the LTCC Cav1.2, and lack the age-dependent increase in mesenteric contractile responses to calcium channel-activating vasoconstrictors. • Further analysis of vessels from aged SMC MR-deficient mice revealed decreased expression of the NADPH-oxidase subunit Nox2, and lower basal and AngII-induced oxidative stress. • Collaboration with Martin Hall, Professor of Medical Pharmacology and Physiology and Associate Director of the Dalton Cardiovascular Research Center at University of Missouri-Columbia – mostly for patch clamp studies. • Pitfalls and Alternative strategy are described adequately.

imp_text: This is new RO1 from a NEW INVESTIGATOR. The PI received excellent training, he had been a productive postdoct, he has supportive environment and colleagues, and importantly addressing a very important topic. The PI will explore decreased cardiac contractility contributes to Heart Failure (HF), the contractile deficit is due to a reduction in cytosolic calcium (iCa2+) transients and a decrease in sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ content. Cardiomyocyte mitochondria isolated from HF patients have shown a reduction in mitochondrial calcium uniporter (MCU) current. These findings suggest that mitoCa2+ content is diminished in HF despite elevations in diastolic iCa2+. The mitoCa2+ microdomain influences energy production and cell death. HF is characterized by metabolic dysfunction and gradual cell dropout, both of which are intimately linked with the mitoCa2+ microdomain. The strengths of this application include the use of genetic mutant mouse lines and to elucidate the role of mitoCa2+ signaling in the development and progression of HF and direct future studies towards therapeutic application. Together, the PI will address the role of mitoCa2+ signaling in the development and progression of HF and direct future studies towards therapeutic application.

app_text_str: • The goal of this research will be to examine if reducing mitoCa2+ efflux protects against gradual cell dropout and adverse remodeling in heart failure (HF) by enhancing cardiomyocyte metabolic and redox capacity. • AIM#1 will analyze biophysical propertise of mitoNCX (Slc24a6 gene) in cardiomyocytes. A recent report identified Slc24a6/NCLX as the long sought after mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger in cell lines, yet these findings have not been extended to cardiomyocytes where iCa2+ is dynamically regulated unlike any other cell types. PI will use mutant mice with conditional cardiomyocyte-specific deletion and overexpression of mitoNCX coupled with high-fidelity genetic reporters to simultaneously measure iCa2+ and mitoCa2+ flux in paced adult cardiomyocytes. PI will manipulate distinct sub-cellular Ca2+ pools (e.g. SR) and intracellular ion concentrations (elevated iNa+, iCa2+) recognized to contribute to pathological signaling associated with the development and progression of HF and examine mitoCa2+ exchange under these conditions. • AIM#2 will examine the function of mitoNCX in myocyte metabolic regulation and cell death. It is postulated that cardiomyocyte workload is integrated with energy production via mitoCa2+ exchange. Cytosolic Ca2+ cycling during excitation-contraction coupling facilitates feed-forward signaling to the mitochondria to ensure that ATP production meets functional demand. The mitochondrial matrix contains multiple Ca2+ control points to modulate oxidative phosphorylation including Ca2+-dependent dehydrogenases and direct action on components of the electron transport chain (ETC). In addition, it is widely recognized that mitoCa2+ can directly influence cell death by activating the permeability transition pore and secondarily through its effects on ATP availability. The tight coupling of these two contrasting processes makes it a necessity to experimentally evaluate both metabolism and cell death in the context of altered mitoCa2+ exchange. • PI will utilize both in vitro and in vivo gain/loss-of-function approaches to molecularly dissect the involvement of mitoNCX in these physiological processes. • AIM#3 will determine the role of mitoNCX in the development and progression of heart failure. HF is characterized by metabolic dysfunction and cell death, both of which are significantly influenced by mitoCa2+. We have previously shown that alterations in mitoCa2+ (Ppif-/-) can lead to significant metabolic reprogramming (loss of substrate flexibility) and predispose mice to HF. Therefore, we will subject mitoNCX mutants (conditional cardiac-specific deletion and overexpression) to pressure-overload and myocardial infarction models of HF and evaluate a multitude of indices to discern if mitoNCX plays a causative role in the development and progression of disease. In addition, we will cross mitoNCX mutant mice to a genetic model of Ca2+-overload (overexpression of the ß2a subunit of the L-type Ca2+ channel) in an attempt to rescue cardiac pathology. • This model will allow for a more focused assessment of Ca2+-driven pathology, void the complex milieu associated with traditional surgical HF models. • Some good preliminary data and some mutant mouse lines are in hand.

imp_text: Peripheral artery disease is a significant clinical problem, with a pressing need for improvement on the limited current therapeutic strategies. Overall, this application proposes to study a novel mechanism of angiogenesis; namely, IL-19/IL-20 receptor mediated mechanisms. The PI is only modestly productive. The investigators are qualified to perform the proposed experiments; however, addition of bone marrow transplant expertise would strengthen the proposal. The environment is very good. The approach is good, but a few gaps still remain in the experimental rationale; in particular, the in vivo studies do not parse the EC versus VSMC mediated mechanisms, which seem to be very different.

imp_text: The current proposal addresses a highly novel and potentially paradigm-shifting question, namely a possible role of mineralocorticoid receptors in smooth muscle in regulating vascular resistance (in addition to their normal role in the control of renal sodium excretion). The study also has substantial clinical relevance, in view of compelling preliminary data suggesting that the mineralocorticoid receptor plays a role in the development of elevated blood pressure, oxidant stress, and altered vascular reactivity in aging subjects; and in mediating the increasing influence of angiotensin II on blood pressure and oxidant stress in aging subjects.  The experimental plan is exceptionally well developed and addresses important questions on multiple levels ranging from the molecular to the whole animal level. The anticipated results and experimental limitations of each specific aim are addressed in detail, and solid plans and alternative approaches are in place to address each limitation. There is some concern regarding the applicability of the mouse renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system to humans, but this is offset to a large extent by preliminary data supporting a role for the mineralocorticoid receptor in human vascular smooth muscle cells. The usual concerns regarding phenotypic changes in cultured cells and their relevance to in vivo physiological conditions is offset by extensive validation of a role of the receptor in isolated resistance arteries.  The extremely comprehensive and well-designed experimental protocols, the novel and potentially paradigm-shifting information that should be obtained from the experiments and the potential clinical relevance of the studies suggest that the present project could have a sustained and powerful impact at both the basic science level and the therapeutic level.

imp_text: The proposed studies address an important area where new avenues of progress are opening due to the identification of the mitochondrial sodium/calcium exchanger (NCX).  The rationale and theoretical framework for the study are well-developed, and several mouse genetic models are available to investigate the questions at hand. In general, the proposed experiments are supported by strong preliminary data.  Important fundamental questions to be addressed include the precise role of the mitochondrial NCX in maintaining calcium homeostasis in the heart and whether higher levels of calcium in the mitochondria help to protect the myocytes during stressful conditions or predispose the myocytes to cell death. Main concerns involve potential phenotypic changes in culture, especially in neonatal versus adult myocytes; and, to a lesser extent, the relevance of chosen stressors applied to cultured myocytes (for example hypoxia/reoxygenation) to in vivo conditions.  Some components of experimental plan and alternative approaches are overly ambitious and not clearly developed, for example evaluation of the role of the mitochondrial calcium uniporter in regulating mitochondrial calcium levels.

imp_text: This application addresses an important area of investigation to demonstrate the role and mechanisms of IL-19, a TH2 interleukin, on blood vessel growth during hind limb ischemia.  The study will extend results of a recent publication that showed IL-19 is expressed by endothelial cells (EC) and induces EC proliferation, chemotaxis and MAPK and Rac 1 signaling in EC in vitro and angiogenesis. Importantly, the PI has shown its effects are independent of the known angiogenesis factors VEGF and bFGF, which is novel and significant. The effects on IL-19 on EC and M2 polarization of macrophages have complimentary roles in models of angiogenesis associated with chronic inflammation.  This proposal will now determine the influence and mechanisms of IL-19 on collateral blood vessel growth in the ischemic hindlimb model, investigate the relative contribution of IL-19 on effector EC and macrophages that participate in vessel growth in ischemic limbs, and identify IL-19 inducible factors that mediate effects on angiogenesis and SMC incorporation in developing blood vessels.  Lastly, the results will elucidate mechanisms for the divergent IL-19 responses of vascular cells, EC versus vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC), involved in angiogenesis or arteriogenesis.  This proposal is likely to identify a novel role for a Th2 activator that regulates angiogenesis in ischemic tissues and may lead to new treatments for critical limb ischemia or other chronic inflammatory diseases that involve pathologic angiogenesis and TH2 activation. The PI has investigated lymphocyte activation and cytokine effects on vascular cells in disease models of angiogenesis, atherosclerosis and allograft vasculopathy. The PI will collaborate with Dr. Edwin Chang who has expertise with surgical models of ischemic revascularization. Innovation in this proposal stems from the exploration of a novel angiogenesis pathway that could augment conventional angiogenesis factors. The approach is excellent and feasible. The proposed Aims are supported by strong preliminary data and will use existing mouse strains to investigate revascularization in vivo and use bone-marrow chimeric mice to determine IL-19 effects on EC and macrophages during ischemia-induced angiogenesis. Some weaknesses arise in the aortic ring explant model because the experiments do not distinguish effects of resident immune cells in the aorta versus the bone marrow derived macrophages added to the cultures. Aim 2 studies that explore differential IL-19 responses by EC and SMC based on their differential expression of IL-20 receptor and Stat activation will be examined in cultured human EC and VSMC, but are not confirmed in developing blood vessels of ischemic tissues generated in the other Aims.

imp_text: This study addresses the role of smooth muscle cell (SMC) mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) in vascular aging and hypertension, which is a significant and clinically relevant problem. The PI has previously shown that angiotensin II (Ang II) activation of angiotensin 1 receptor (AT1R) activates MR-mediated gene regulation (Ref 17).  Furthermore, SMC-specific deletion of MR attenuates AngII-induced hypertension and blocks its enhanced response with aging (Ref 18). Dr. McCarty now proposes to investigate the downstream signaling mechanisms of Ang II-AT1R activation that induce MR gene targets in vascular SMC and may participate in vascular aging and hypertension.  The Aims will identify specific PKC isoforms that modify Ang II activation of MR gene expression, explore how SMC MR regulation of calcium channel expression and activity influences contractile function of isolated blood vessels and characterize SMC MR regulation of vascular oxidative stress with aging. Overall impact is reduced by preliminary data that relies on the effects of less-specific inhibitors on cultured SMC and the descriptive results of proposed studies.  Understanding the effects of Ang II signaling on vascular cells and blood vessels in vivo is important, but the studies of calcium channel activity and vascular oxidative stress are not novel targets and do not specifically identify how MR activation is changed by aging. Innovation is limited.  Some Aims are descriptive and do not elucidate how aging impacts MR activation of how its target genes modify vascular aging in vivo.

imp_text: This proposal aims to address the role of hippo pathway in Raf/Mek-mediated cardiac hypertrophy. Although this is an interesting concept, most experiments will use Drosophila as the model system. Drosophila is a powerful tool to study the functionality of genetic mutations and role of genes in development. However, as the PI showed in the application (differences in Yap domains, differences in the role of Erk), there are multiple differences between mammals and flies. Therefore, studying cardiac hypertrophy pathways in drosophila to translate to humans will require these experiments to be repeated/confirmed in mammals, especially the role of hippo in a system that does not require Erk for a hypertrophic response. In addition, the use of 3 model systems and cells vs whole organ will make result interpretation more difficult.

Specifically, the applicant will determine if IL-19 can restore blood flow in ischemic tissue, if the major effector cell is endothelial or M2 macrophage, what soluble factors mediate IL-19 effects, and the molecular mechanisms and mediators of IL-19 differential effects in EC and VSMC.  This is a very interesting project, from a strong investigator.  Some minor weakness exist, particularly regarding lack of preliminary data for some aims, but overall, given the investigator expertise and strong preliminary data overall, this is considered a very strong proposal.

sig_text_wkn: • Because cytokines with pro-angiogenic and anti-inflamatory effects have been studied previously, proposal significance is somewhat diminished.

inn_text_wkn: • This is one of many known cytokines, so there is some overlap between this study and previous studies performed in IL-19 and other cytokines. Notheless, the argument that IL-19 maybe a better treatment target is significant.

Experiments are reasonable and will like yield important information. • Aim 3 is based on strong preliminary data of cDNA microarray analysis.  The applicant proposes and extensive study of the role of 4 soluble factors using individual KO animals.  This is an interesting mechanistic aim. • The applicant will test an interesting hypothesis that differential expression of IL-20 receptor subunits account for differential effects of IL-19 in VSMC compared with EC.  This will be tested bysiRNA knock down of IL-20 receptor subunits, over expression, and add-back in both EC and VSMC from IL-20R-/- mice.

study_section: Cardiac Contractility, Hypertrophy, and Failure Study Section
imp_text: This proposal studies the hypothesis that reducing mitoCa2+ efflux protects against gradual cell dropout and adverse remodeling in heart failure by enhancing cardiomyocyte metabolic and redox capacity.  First the applicant will characterization of mitoNCX (Slc24a6 gene) in cardiomyocytes by utilizing mutant mice with conditional cardiomyocyte-specific deletion and overexpression of mitoNCX coupled with high-fidelity genetic reporters to simultaneously measure iCa2+ and mitoCa2+ flux in paced adult cardiomyocytes. In addition, he proposes to manipulate distinct sub-cellular Ca2+ pools to examine mitoCa2+ exchange under different conditions.  Second, the applicant proposes to examine the function of mitoNCX in myocyte metabolic regulation and cell death. For that, the PI will utilize both in vitro and in vivo gain/loss-of-function approaches to molecularly dissect the involvement of mitoNCX in these physiological processes.  Finally, the role of mitoNCX in the development and progression of heart failure will be determined.  For that, the applicant proposes to use pressure-overload and myocardial infarction models of HF and conditional cardiac-specific deletion and overexpression mitoNCX mice, we will evaluate a multitude of indices to discern if mitoNCX plays a causative role in the development and progression of disease. In addition, we will cross mitoNCX mutant mice to a genetic model of Ca2+-overload (overexpression of the alpha2a subunit of the L-type Ca2+ channel) to rescue cardiac pathology.  This is an interesting grant, from a well-trained young investigator, but concerns exist.  The major concern about this grant is its overambitious nature. In particular, the extent of experiments proposed decreased enthusiasm for the grant.  A more focused approach would increase enthusiasm.

imp_text: This application proposes to examine the Raf-MEK1 pathway and the activation of yorkie in cardiac hypertrophy. First the applicant will determine whether Raf-MEK1-mediated cardiac hypertrophy occurs via the Hippo-yorkie pathway in flies.  Second, he will identify the specific modular domains in mammalian YAP1 (homolog of yorkie) that drive cardiomyocyte hypertrophy or proliferation.  Third he will determine whether a reduction in YAP-1 modifies the severity of cardiac hypertrophy or heart failure in RafL613V/+ knock-in mice or wild-type mice after TAC-induced pressure overload.  Although this is considered a very strong proposal, lack of preliminary data regarding YAP-1 mutants in drosophila and mammals increase concerns about feasibility and decrease enthusiasms for the proposal.

imp_text: This proposal is focused on the role that the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-19 may have on the angiogenesis associated with tissue ischemia. Successful completion of the proposed work should enhance our knowledge of the mechanisms by which anti-inflammatory cytokines participate in revascularization. The proposal addresses an important issue associated with cardiovascular diseases, as angiogenesis and revascularization are important process that impact recovery and resolution of multiple tissue pathologies. In addition, successful completion of the studies proposed has the potential to create a paradigm shift on our understanding of how pro- and anti-inflammatory cytokines participate in the recovery of blood circulation in damaged tissues. It also has the potential to drive new therapeutic strategies for improving tissue vascularization and ameliorating ischemic conditions.
sig_text_str: . Understanding the mechanisms that control angiogenesis, that is the sprouting and formation of new capillaries and blood vessels from ones that already exist, is a highly significant goal with applicability to many pathophysiological conditions. . Provides new insights as to how pro- and anti-inflammatory pathways control angiogenesis and revascularization in ischemic tissues. . Develop a new paradigm for the role of IL-19 in angiogenesis. . Provide new avenues for therapeutic approaches to control angiogenesis in multiple scenarios.
sig_text_wkn: . While the proposal is focused on the pathways that control angiogenesis in an ischemic tissue, it is not clear how or why IL-19 signaling may be prevalent only in ischemic tissue. This may reduce the applicability of the findings to other angiogenesis conditions such as those seen in cancer development.

imp_text: This proposal is focused on the role that signaling through the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) in vascular smooth muscle cells may have on vascular aging and hypertension. The proposal addresses a very important issue associated with the increasing elderly population and their overwhelming incidence of hypertension. It also advocates for a paradigm shift on our understanding of the role that MRs play in the development of hypertension and the control of blood pressure. Successful completion of the proposed work should enhance our understanding of the etiology of hypertension and should provide new avenues for the treatment of elderly hypertensives, particularly those that are resistant to currently available antihypertensive medications.

imp_text: Successful completion of the proposed work should enhance our knowledge of the pathways associated with cardiac hypertrophy and dysfunction. In particular it should shed light on the differential roles that specific pathways downstream of RTK play on cardiomyocyte hyperplasia or hypertrophy in genetic- and increased afterload-associated cardiomyopathies. The proposed work has the potential to create a paradigm shift on the pathways that induce cardiac hypertrophy as well as on the use of flies as models to expedite molecular analyses of pathways associated with cardiovascular pathologies. The risks for pitfalls, however, are high and the procedural cascades make the goals highly interdependent. In addition, considering the multiplicity of alternate routes the studies proposed may have to endure, the proposal is considerable overambitious.
sig_text_str: . Understand the mechanisms that control cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and hyperplasia in the setting of genetic and pressure overload cardiomyopathies. . Provide new insights on the interaction that alternative pathways downstream of RTK play on determining the fate and phenotypic characteristics of cardiomyocytes under different pathological conditions. . Develop novel strategies for expedite analyses of potential pathways associated with human cardiovascular diseases in flies.
sig_text_wkn: . The proposal is focused on the pathways that drive cardiomyocyte hyperplasia or hypertrophy in conditions such as Noonan syndrome and augmented cardiac afterload. However, it is uncertain how the experimental models really resemble those conditions. . Although use of flies as a model for the expedite analysis of potential pathways associated with human cardiovascular diseases through large genetic screening is an innovative strength of the proposal, it has to be recognized that is a potential weakness in the overall significance of the study.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Baker has assembled an excellent team of investigators with complementary experience and expertise that is well qualified to carry out the research proposed.

imp_text: The new proposal from an established investigator will elucidate the role of IL-19 in mediating angiogenesis and improve perfusion of ischemic tissue. This proposal aims to focus on endothelial cells and M2 macrophage in restoring blood flow in ischemic tissue. They also aim to dissect the pleotropic function of IL-19 in EC and VSMC. The enthusiasm in the proposal is buoyed by the excellent investigator, experimental design is detailed and largely sound, and is supported by preliminary data. Though the project aim to use a number of mutant mice, some of the readout seems to be difficult. Moreover, they provided little information about the mice phenotype and knockout type of the proposed mice i.e. conditional vs global knockout. Thus, there are several important concerns with this proposal in its present form which place the enthusiasm in the moderate-high range.

imp_text: This is an outstanding proposal from an extraordinary accomplished young scientist who has been productive at every stage of his career. The PI aim to define the mechanisms of mitochondrial calcium exchange in heart failure in this grant application. The central hypothesis is that reducing mitoCa2+ efflux protects against gradual cell dropout and adverse remodeling in heart failure by enhancing cardiomyocyte metabolic and redox capacity. In specific aim 1, a biophysical characterization of mitoNCX (Slc24a6 gene) in cardiomyocytes will be performed. In specific aim 2, the mechanistic function of mitoNCX in myocyte metabolic regulation and cell death will be elucidated. Finally, specific aim will define the role of mitoNCX in the development and progression of heart failure. The outlined mechanistic studies will greatly aid in our understanding of how the mitochondria regulate calcium efflux. The enthusiasm in the grant proposal stands the outstanding and productive candidate, the stellar institutional environment, and the innovative research plan that aims to investigate molecular mechanisms with potentially high significance for heart disease. I am highly impressed with the grant application.

imp_text: This is a proposal written by Dr. Washington to evaluate the role of IL-19 on angiogenesis. This work is purported to provide new mechanisms governing ischemia-driven angiogenesis particularly as it pertains to peripheral arterial disease.  Defining a role for IL-19 in angiogenesis may assist in the development of therapeutics in severe limb ischemia.  The investigators have found that IL-19 is found in inflamed but not quiescent endothelium, and that it can promote polarization of macrophages to M2 phenotype.  Additionally, lack of IL-19 in knockout mice results in less angiogenesis in vivo than in wild type mice.  While the preliminary data is promising, the proposal itself is largely descriptive with very little mechanistic information.  Additionally, the proposal of four specific aims appears to be difficult to accomplish in the given time, and may actually represent a broader but less in depth evaluation of the mechanism of action.

imp_text: This is a grant submitted by Dr. McCarthy to evaluate the role of mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) and Ang II on mediating vascular smooth muscle cell contraction, and thus contribution to vascular aging. The PI proposes that this research proposal is paradigm shifting, emphasizing the role of SMC MR in regulating BP. At times it is difficult to discern whether the proposal is about hypertension or aging.  There is already an understanding that smooth muscle cell tone is a regulator of BP, partly due to the effect of mineralocorticoids and their downstream signaling molecules. Thus the novelty of this particular grant is diminished. Furthermore, the PI is investigating the role that SMC MR plays in aging –induced hypertension, although the in vitro experiments do not describe a phenotype that convincingly reflects aging. The in vivo experiments use mice that range from 3-4 months and 9 months. Most aging experiments utilize mice that are much older (1-2 years). While they have seen differences in BP at the proposed age groups, it would be very useful to include animals that are older than nine months.  Addition of samples from patients may also be illustrative.

imp_text: This is a grant submitted by Dr. McCarthy to determine the role of a Ca2+/Na+ exchanger in mitochondria  (SLC24A6) in the pathophysiology of heart failure. The grant involves knockout of the transporter both in cells as well as in vivo to determine the effect on cell death and cardiac dysfunction. Overall, the experiments appear well thought out and represent a novel area of investigation. In the first aim, the investigator will evaluate the role of mitoNCX in calcium flux within cardiomyocytes. In the second aim, the investigator will determine how alterations in mitoNCX results in cell death and changes in metabolism. Finally, in the third aim, the investigator will determine how genetic absence of mitoNCX will affect heart failure in response to overload and ischemia.  There is a possibility that the other means of calcium transport within cardiomyocytes will make interpretation of the results difficult.  The investigator clearly acknowledges this and provides some control for it. The grant could certainly benefit from more clinical correlation, perhaps by collaborating with clinicians that can provide heart failure samples. Furthermore, in Aim 3, which is fairly clear and easy to follow, the investigator still has to determine the baseline characteristics of their knockout mouse, which may jeopardize the whole aim. Finally, the grant does not focus on how common causes of heart failure including overload and ischemia might affect the function of the mitoNCX. imp_text: This is an outstanding application to study a potential role for mitochrondrial calcium and its recently identified regulatory protein mitochondrial Na-Ca exchanger (mitoNCX) in the development of heart failure.  This proposal has great strengths and very few weaknesses.  The strengths include the significance since the role of mitoCa is a very hot topic and is very poorly understood.  Very little of the current literature provides a good compelling explanation for how mitoCa is regulated and how this could go wrong in HF. This proposal describes an extremely elegant and creative approach to addressing this important problem.  Now that the mitoNCX has been identified (Slc24a6 gene), the current experiments describe a plan of clever well-designed, comprehensive experiments that are highly likely to provide clear answers to this problem. There is a clear plan to characterize the properties of the mitochondrial in the first specific aim, then explore the role of the mitoNCX in calcium regulation during normal cardiac excitation-contraction coupling using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in mouse models in the second aim and finally to investigate the role of mitoNCX in the development and progression to HF in the last aim. The research plan is very well-thought out, the PI is perfectly positioned to perform this work, there is an excellent team and environment and there is every expectation that the PI will be able to achieve the aims of this outstanding research project.

imp_text: This is a very interesting grant using molecular and genetic observations in Drosophila to investigate mammalian hypertrophic signaling. The goal is to use epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling pathways common to Drosophila and mammals in order to use the fly as a model system to then study the molecular signaling pathways (in particular those associated with the Raf-MEK1 pathway) to investigate whether or not the mammalian YAP1 protein regulates the severity of hypertrophy. Strengths include the investigator and the team she has assembled to study molecular signaling in flies and in mice, the scientific and institutional environment, and some elements of the experimental design.  Weaknesses include too much focus on the signaling in fly and the mouse and not enough on translation to humans, innovation is modest, significance is also only modest and there is nothing really exciting about this project.  It is overall a good idea with sound experimental approaches but does not really advance the field of hypertrophic signaling in any significant and important way.

sig_text_wkn: . In the fly the pathway of interest (Hippo/Yorkie) is responsible for both hypertrophy and hyperplasia. The fact that this is involved in cardiac development is not relevant to mammalian heart so is a distraction from the hypertrophic role it also serves. . As stated in the Aims page “My central hypothesis is that crosstalk between the Raf-MEK1 and Hippo-YAP1 pathways drives cardiomyocyte decisions towards hypertrophy or hyperplasia.” There is too much discussion of cell proliferation/hyperplasia as stated goals of the project and a focus to distinguish this process from hypertrophy.  These may be significant problems in the fly, not in mammals. . Specific aim 2 includes the working hypothesis that “Whereas the activation of mammalian YAP1 causes cardiomyocyte proliferation, fly yorkie drives cardiac hypertrophy. Therefore, I hypothesize that protein motifs unique to mammalian YAP1 direct specific subsets of signals and are responsible for dictating cardiomyocyte proliferation vs. hypertrophy.” This statement is emblematic of the problem that there is too much focus on cell proliferation which is not part of the problem of hypertrophy in mammals. . Not clear how important or unique the results would be even in best case of finding role for YAP1 in mammals.  Very little discussion about role and significance in human because little is known in human heart.

imp_text: This is an R01 proposal to study the potential role of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-19 in angiogenesis and potential benefit of tissue repair in ischemic injury.  The studies are important and somewhat new.  However, the scope of the application is somewhat narrow.  The effects of IL-19 on angiogenesis may not be specific, and IL-19 may have other effects not related to angiogenesis.  The efficacy of IL-19 as a proangiogenic factor should be compared with known angiogenic factors such as VEGF. imp_text: This project takes advantage of previous work by the author showing the potential of IL-19 to exert an angiogenic effect on vascular angiogenic cells. In this work Dr. McCarthy seeks to identify some of the cell-specific mechanisms through which IL-19 is produced and accomplishes this, in 3 aims. The fourth Aim will  determine the basis of pleiotropic effects of IL-19 in vascular smooth muscle versus endothelium. The proposal begins with some novel and interesting work, but this work is not transformed into exciting or ground-breaking new information, despite the fact that that capability is there. This affects the Significance and the Innovation categories such that they do not rise above an average score. Much of the research plan is interesting and experiments are usually well-designed, but they also mostly lack the significance and innovative characteristics that are missing from the other components of the proposal. The one exception to this is Aim #4, which is novel and moves the project in a truly innovative direction, however this Aim lies outside of the direction taken by the other Aims. Overall, the four aims in the proposal make it over-ambitious. The research team has significant needed expertise but lacks evidence that Dr. McCarthy and his surgical collaborator have done any work together as yet. The proposal is further weakened by a lack of description in the Animal Welfare section of the surgical procedure, or the animal protections that will be used with the surgery.
sig_text_str: . Novel findings of IL-19 having pleiotrophic effects, anti-inflammatory in ischemic tissue and pro-angiogenic on endothelial cells, but suppresses vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation and migration. . Promotion of vasculogenesis is a novel function for a cytokine in wound healing
sig_text_wkn: . The contrasting findings of IL-19 need to be worked through to determine what is more dominant for wound healing. . It is clear that information is needed to learn more about IL-19 mechanisms. What is not emphasized is why this work is significant, i.e. what major advances in wound healing biology will be obtained? Why are the proposed studies the best questions to ask at this time, and how will their outcomes make significant progress that moves this project towards a clearer model of vascular growth to maximize wound repair? . Dr. McCarthy emphasizes the dual nature of cytokines as inflammatory mediators and repair molecules in injury, the lack of a consistent understanding of how these opposing activities can be reconciled, and the in general terms potential value of gaining such understanding. He does not show how this proposal will contribute to such an understanding.

Experiments to demonstrate angiogenic potential in vivo are amply supported by the in vitro data shown in preliminary data. . Experiments in Aim #4 are powerful and likely to produce significant results. However, as mentioned, the rationale for these experiments does not follow the same line as Aims 1 through 3, so this Aim is isolated and contributes less to the overall project than it potentially could if it accompanied Aims with goals more in line with this. imp_text: This proposal to examine the mineralocorticoid receptor as a regulator of hypertension in aged individuals, and to identify the mechanisms by which signaling through the receptor accomplishes this is quite strong in concept and design. The Significance and Innovative nature of the proposal are very strong, with only minor weaknesses. The Investigators and Environment are similarly impressive. The Approach is in general also very well developed, complete and rationally explained. However the failure to explain the source of human tissue is an unfortunate oversight which represents an important concern in the Approach and  affects the overall enthusiasm of the proposal
sig_text_str: . Hypertension with aging is a major and common problem in the elderly population. It is difficult to treat and control, and is a leading cause of death. . Previous work from Dr. Washington showed the role of the mineralocorticoid receptor in mediating blood pressure in aging animals, and that removal of the receptor (transgenically) resolved age-associated hypertension. These were landmark studies. . This proposal follows those findings to a logical next step by seeking to determine the global significance of blood pressure regulation by aldosterone-mediated mineralocorticoid receptor activation and determine the mechanisms by which this is mediated.
sig_text_wkn: . The ability to examine both mouse and human coronary arteries (Aim 1b) to establish relevance is an excelletn strategy. However, it is not continued in Aims 2 and 3, parts of which would also lend themselves to similar correlative studies.

He is currently situated at the University of Missouri-Columbia. He is highly capable to carry out his components of the project. Novel transgenic vascular smooth muscle mineralocorticoid receptor knockout mouse developed for these studies.

imp_text: This is a very strong proposal from Dr. McCarthy whose lab has been focusing on the role of IL-19 on angiogenesis. The PI has previously demonstrated that IL-19 possesses suppresses vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC) migration and proliferation of SMCs. Recently, the lab has unexpectedly identified IL-19 as an angiogenic factor in ECs. Furthermore, They discovered that IL-19 polarizes the macrophages to the M2. Based on these observations, the PI hypothesize that the differential actiivity of IL-19 on angiogenesis between SMCs and ECs is due to differential expression of IL-19 receptors, IL20R1 and IL20R2. Four aims were proposed: 1) To test the hypothesis that IL-19 expression regulates angiogenesis, the PI will determine if absence of IL-19 attenuates, and if over expression of IL-19 promotes angiogenesis, 2) To determine if IL-19 regulation of angiogenesis is by primarily facilitated by direct effects on vascular cells, or by macrophage M2 polarization, 3) To identify and characterize IL-19 inducible factors necessary for IL-19-driven angiogenesis in vivo, the PI will identify if these factors are primarily secreted by IL-19-stimulated EC or by IL-19-stimulated M2 macrophage and 4) To test the hypothesis that differential expression of IL-20 receptor subunits account for pleiotropic effects of IL-19 in VSMC compared with EC. Success of this proposal will implicate a Th2 interleukin as a novel anti-inflammatory, pro-vasculogenic cytokine expressed by inflamed resident vascular cells to promote neovascularization. Thus, this proposal is potentially of significant.

imp_text: This is an excellent application from a junior physician scientist at Duke University. The PI has provided strong preliminary data which support a role of Hippo signaling and its downstream effect yorkie (YAP1 in mammalian system) in the control of cardiac hypertrophy, a mechanism that is known to be regulated by the EGFR/Ras pathway. Three aims were proposed. Aim 1 will determine whether Raf-MEK1-mediated cardiac hypertrophy occurs via regulation of the Hippo-yorkie pathway in flies and identify signaling pathways that function downstream of yorkie. Classic fly genetics will be employed to quickly evaluate the role of specific components of this signaling pathway in the development of cardiac hypertrophy. Using a series of deletions and mutations of mammalian YAP1, the PI will determine the specific modular domains in mammalian YAP1 that drive cardiomyocyte hypertrophy or proliferation. In Aim 3, the PI will determine whether a reduction in YAP-1 alters the severity of cardiac hypertrophy or heart failure in RafL613V/+ knock-in mice or wild-type mice after TAC-induced pressure overload. Regarding the association between Raf and Hippo, the PI demonstrated that overexpression of Raf and Hippo interact in HEK293 cells, but did not elaborate whether this physical interaction is functional by mutation analyses. A minor but important piece of data will be showing interaction between endogenous proteins. Overall, the application is well-written and novel. Success of this application will shed new light on our understanding of the crosstalk between EGFR/Ras and Hippo pathways.

imp_text: This new proposal from an established investigator aims to demonstrate that Interleukin-19 (IL-19), an anti-inflammatory Th2 interleukin, promotes angiogenesis and improves perfusion of ischemic tissue. Preliminary/published data support the main goal of this proposal: the PI documented recently that IL-19 has unexpected pro-angiogenic effects in endothelial cells (EC). This is a novel concept that is potentially paradigm-shifting and has implications for wound healing and vascular biology. The application now proposes to uncover molecular mechanisms of these effects. The strengths of the application are: 1) the PI has an excellent track record in the area of the proposal, displays authoritative grasp of relevant literature, and provides ground work to validate its main premises. 2) Angiogenesis is a multi-step process that involves endothelial cell activation, proliferation, migration, and vessel formation, and the PI demonstrates that IL-19 participates in EC activation by effecting all of these steps; significance of these findings, therefore, is high. 3) Novel conceptual and technical approaches to elucidate the unexpected and intriguing role of IL-19 in angiogenesis. 4) Invaluable experimental tools (mice with downregulation of IL-19, etc) are at the disposal of the PI. 5) Excellent academic environment and research team to conduct this research. Weaknesses relate to the overambitious nature of the research design, with an overwhelming number of experiments to be conducted. However, given the track record of productivity of the PI, this weakness detracts modestly, only, from an overall high enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: . Peripheral vascular disease is a significant medical and socioeconomic problem contributing to mortality of multiple diseases including myocardial infarction, diabetes, and peripheral vascular disease. It will only worsen with an increasing co-morbidity such as metabolic syndrome and Type 2 diabetes, which are reaching epidemic proportions. Research to improve vascularization is therefore urgently needed. . Neovascularization is repair mechanism to preserve tissue and organ viability in response to ischemic conditions in peripheral limb vasculature and in ischemic myocardium. Consequently, a better understanding of mechanisms of angiogenesis and in particular the role of inflammatory cytokines which regulate this process will lead to new treatment modalities.

imp_text: This new proposal from a young investigator aims to elucidate the mechanisms by which smooth muscle cell (SMC) mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) regulate blood pressure (BP). The strengths of the application are many and easily outweigh its minor weaknesses: 1) the PI previously identified MRs in SMC and provided evidence that their downregulation prevents the age-dependent increase in BP and other aspects of vascular aging; she is therefore highly qualified to conduct this research. 2) The presence of functional MR in SMC and their significant impact on BP challenge the notion that the latter is exclusively controlled at the renal level and provides a new platform for the treatment of hypertension in the older population; this novel conceptual framework is an appealing aspect of this research program. 3) A mouse line with downregulation of MRs exclusively in SMCs is available to the PI and constitutes an excellent experimental tool. 4) Critical preliminary data support the feasibility of most of the proposed experiments. 5) As hypertension contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality in the aging population by mechanisms incompletely understood, the proposal is timely and highly significant. The only perceived weakness relates to the vast number of experiments proposed and overly optimistic outcomes. This weakness, however, is minor and does not detract significantly from a high enthusiasm for this research program. This is an outstanding proposal

imp_text: This new proposal from a young investigator aims to elucidate the role of the mitochondrial Na-Ca exchanger (mitoNCX) in normal conditions and in heart failure. The PI has developed animal models with mitoNCX gain- and loss-of-function, as well as others that modulate other mitochondrial calcium transporters, that constitute valuable experimental tools for this goal. Preliminary/published data support the main hypothesis of this proposal: reducing mitochondrial calcium efflux (mainly by decreasing mitoNCX activity) protects against cell death and adverse remodeling in heart failure by enhancing cardiomyocyte metabolic and redox capacity. This is a novel concept that runs counter to some established dogmas regarding the role of mitochondrial calcium fluxes in disease and one that warrants a systematic testing. The strengths of the application are numerous, including: 1) the PI has an excellent track record in the area of the proposal and provided ground work to validate its main premises; 2) although a multitude of factors contribute to heart failure pathogenesis, abnormal intracellular calcium signaling and mitochondrial calcium transport are commonly found; significance of the findings, therefore, is high. 3) Novel conceptual and technical approaches to elucidate the role of an elusive mitochondrial calcium transporter. 4) Invaluable experimental tools (mice with downregulation and up-regulation of mitoNCX function in heart) are at the disposal of the PI. 5) Excellent academic environment to conduct this research. Weaknesses detract modestly from an overall high enthusiasm for this proposal and relate to the lack of critical preliminary data for most (but not all) of the specific subaims and a diffuse plan to integrate the mitoNCX role with that of other mitochondrial calcium transporters (especially the MPTP).
sig_text_str: . Intracellular calcium signals that drive contraction and other essential processes of the cardiomyocyte are quickly integrated into mitochondria, thereby regulating energy metabolism and ATP production. Although some major concepts in this general process have been elucidated, the precise role and hierarchy of mitochondrial calcium transporters are incompletely understood. . The role of mitoNCX in heart failure has not been systematically studied. It is essential to know if the reduced mitoNCX expression that occurs in heart failure is causative or adaptative in HF, to guide novel therapies.

imp_text: The overall goal of this proposal is to establish whether IL-19 is a novel interleukin with both pro-angiogenic and anti-inflammatory properties that may become activated under conditions of ischemia. Moreover, the authors propose to establish whether the main mechanism is through macrophages activated into an M2 (anti-inflammatory) phenotype or whether the effect is mediated by a direct effect on the vascular endothelium itself. The strengths of the study are its novelty – in the identification of a little-studied potential drug target for improved vascularization, and its approach – in the thoughtful use of knockout animals to delineate the relative contribution of endothelium versus macrophages. The results are potentially very significant, but only if the results prove positive for most aims. The preliminary data is adequate to support the initial aims, but some of the more mechanistic hypotheses are hard to gauge based on limited data. In particular, the link between the systemic phenotype (using knockout mice or systemic injection of IL-19) and the putative mechanism of action locally (via endothelial cell activation) is rather tenuous. There is also a substantial amount of grammar errors and typos, that significantly hamper the clarity of the proposal.

The authors do not discuss the approach to be taken if physiological data is inconsistent with the angiogenic or inflammatory profile based on histology or gene assays. . It’s unclear if the systemic effects (obtained via whole-animal knockout or systemic injection of drugs) may be occurring solely through mechanisms centered on the ischemically-activated endothelial segment or via more indirect mechanisms. An approach using viral-mediated knockdown or knockout specifically in the target segment (as in Aim 4, but in vivo) may be more useful. Similarly, more localized injection of drug may also help narrow this effect down. . The authors plan to use multiple knockout animals, but there is absent preliminary data to suggest that these animals will behave in the expected fashion or that adaptive transfer will be successful in these genetically-modified animals, and what contingency plans the authors have if the animals behave unexpectedly. . Similarly, the authors focus on four factors that are transiently overexpressed following IL-19 stimulation of EC. However, it’s unclear if such transient expression correlated with actual protein abundance, and whether, as the authors suggest, expression of factors stimulated by IL-19 in other cells may also be part of the effect.

imp_text: In this proposal, the PI proposes to elucidate the contribution of mitochondrial calcium transport to cardiomyocyte function, how such transport is disrupted in heart failure, and whether altering calcium transport can be potentially therapeutic in mouse models. The experimental approach focuses on genetic manipulation of the mitochondrial Na+-Ca exchanger, the main mechanism for mitochondrial ca efflux.  The proposal is quite strong in terms of the methodologies proposed, combining studies in isolated cells / mitochondria to investigate molecular mechanisms with whole-animal physiology to investigate the contribution to disease. The PI seems uniquely qualified to carry out this project given his background and expertise with mouse genetics. The genetic models proposed have been carefully chosen and preliminary data show that they are viable and likely suitable for the proposed experiments. The main concerns for the proposal are the absence of a clear hypothesis regarding mitochondrial calcium handling that will be the basis for interpreting results. The authors review previous data regarding calcium as a beneficial stimulator of ATP synthesis versus calcium overload leading to cell death, but do not appear to have a clear sense to which end of the spectrum their data is relevant.  This can complicate the interpretation of the results. Secondly, although the authors are interested in querying mitochondrial calcium handling, their proposal largely rests on the effects of modulating calcium efflux, so it is unclear how generalizable the results will be (though they have the potential to be quite meaningful from a therapeutic standpoint). Finally, the assays they choose to assay mitochondrial calcium efflux may be affected as well by changes in calcium buffering or calcium uptake, and the authors fail to propose careful experiments to distinguish between these competing mechanisms.

imp_text: The overall goal of this proposal is to assess whether cardiac hypertrophy in animal models is caused by crosstalk between two signaling cascades – EGFR-Ras-Raf-Mek and Hippo-Yap. The proposal takes advantage of novel phenotyping tools possessed / developed by the PI to harness Drosophila genetics in trying to delineate such crosstalk, and this is the strongest portion of the proposal. Aim 2 focuses on the apparently differential action of Yap1 in mammals versus yorkie in Drosophila. The main hypothesis here is that differences in protein structure are the main driver, but alternative mechanisms are not sufficiently considered. Although some effort is made to test whether the differences are due to timing, other alternatives (such as differential interactions with transcription factors in Drosophila versus mice) are not considered, and the purely cell culture-based assessment of the timing mechanism may have limited results. The last aim focuses on modulating Yap1 function in heart failure models, and will be informed by the results of the prior two aims. The main concern here is that the PI has apparently very limited experience with these techniques, and there are a substantial number of different techniques and transgenic lines involved.  Thus, in the absence of preliminary data showing familiarity with these models, it is unclear how the PI will reasonably perform these experiments without outsourcing them to his collaborators.

Given the high rapid mortality associated with TAC, it may not be the best model for the mechanisms of hypertrophy, but rather of end-stage cardiomyopathy following pressure-overload.

imp_text: This application proposes to use x-ray crystallography to investigate the physical mechanisms of chromosome segregation in meiosis I in the yeast S. cerevisiae, with three goals: (1) examining the architecture of the monopolin complex, including the binding structures of the proteins Mam1, Hrr25, Csm1, and Tof2. Additionally, the role of kinetochore cross-linking will be tested by engineering a one-headed version of the Csm1:Lrs4 complex, and seeing if it can still coorient kinetochores in MI.  (2) Purify and characterize the Hop1 HORMA domain to examine its interactions, using its homology to Mad2 as a guide, by making point mutations to conserved residues and examining their interactions and crystal structures. (3) Characterizing the structure and properties of the S. cerevisiae transverse filament protein Zip1.  Given the PI’s previous successes in elucidating crystal structure, the odds of success for these aimsare good, and the determination of structural protein mechanics will improve our physical understanding of the events of meiosis.  One potential weakness with Aim 3 that was not discussed can be seen in work done on the Drosophila functional homolog, c(3)G. Many of the constructs made to examine changes in this protein were found to form large insoluble aggregates, which could renderanalysis of the crystal structure impossible.

imp_text: This study extends the PIs long term investigation of pre-mRNA splicing events. Focusing on a rare autosomal recessive disease (MOPD I) caused by mutations in the RNU4ATAC gene, which greatly reduced splicing rates in U12-dependent introns, this study attempts the following experimental goals: (1) Biochemical analysis of mutant snRNAs, to determine the effects of the disease-causing variants on normal RNA splicing. (2) Identification of the downstream regulatory targets of the RNU4ATAC gene, by identifying changes in the transcriptome cause by these mutations, in comparison of patient lines to control cells. These results will be validated by both knockdown (morpholino) assays and rescue with wildtype rescue validation, and any identified target genes will be investigated for potential roles in causing pathology. (3) Investigation of the effects of existing polymorphisms in snRNA genes, to see if these are additional candidate disease genes.  As the study already has multiple patient cell lines and identified polymorphisms to work with, and a rigorous quantitative assay to determine the rate and extent of splicing, the odds for this study to be successful are very high.

imp_text: This study seeks to investigate the mechanisms by which the eukaryotic ribosome is formed. Specifically, by investigating how essential proteins mediate the processing of pre-rRNA into the final mature ribosome.  The overall idea is that Bud23 exerts quality control, ‘testing’ ribosomes for successful formation before activating Ecm16, to ensure that rRNA transcription and folding are complete. They specifically seek to test (1) whether Ecm16 dissociates U3-pre-rRNA interactions, (2) whether Bud23 activates Ecm16 activity by methylation, (3) whether Imp4 stabilizes these interactions, and (4) whether Rps2 helps stabilize the CPK to enable folding. Improving our understanding of ribosome biogenesis has the potential to provide therapeutic targets for cancer treatment, as many cancers have upregulated ribosome formation, and homologs of some genes targeted in this study have known homologs (e.g. BUD23/WBSCR22) with known associations to human diseases.  However, one weakness with this proposal is that a number of the proposed experiments are high risk (e.g. the mutant screen in aim 4.1b) with few discussions of possible alternative experiments.

imp_text: This proposal is based on PI?s novel finding that vascular smooth muscle cell (SMC) mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) is directly activated by Angiotensin II (Ang II) which was shown to be responsible for age-??related increase in hypertension, expression of L-??type calcium channel component and activity, increased oxidative  stress and  vasoconstriction.  The  PI proposes, ?understanding the direct  role  of  SMC  MR  in  modulating  blood  pressure  will  fundamentally  change paradigms in the  field  of RAAS-mediated  cardiovascular disease, support novel vascular mechanisms  for the protective effects of AngII and MR antagonist drugs in human clinical trials, and identify SMC MR- regulated pathways as novel targets to prevent vascular aging and to treat hypertension specifically in the growing high risk elderly population?.   The strengths are that the study is based on a novel finding that     SMC MR regulates the AngII mediated increase in BP in aged animals which is very different from what     has  been  conventionally  practiced  with  RAAS  (Rennin-angiotensin-aldosterone  system);  A  transgenic animal model where MR could be knockdown specifically in SMC in temporal manner; and the logical approaches  described  under  each  specific  aim.  Some  of  the  weaknesses  include  lack  of  preliminary support for the proposed experiments (see approach).
sig_text_str: Current pharmacologic therapies to control hypertension are inadequate in about 50% of patients over 60 years of age. Therefore, understanding of the mechanisms of the age-dependent increase in BP is expected to yield novel therapeutic targets to prevent or improve the treatment of hypertension. The PI proposes a new concept which is different from what is conventionally practiced. That is, it is well known that in the RAAS, Angiotensin-II act on Ang receptor-I (ATR1) in kidney epithelial cells for the release aldosterone that leads to sodium retention and vasoconstriction. Previous studies show that the effect of ACE inhibitors and ATR1 blockers that improve patient survival were accompanied with only modest changes in renal natriuresis. The PI?s earlier work and preliminary studies indicate that the reduced BP by the RAAS inhibitors may also be mediated through reduced SMC MR activation. The loss of SMC MR activation by the RAAS inhibitors might significantly contribute to the reduced levels of oxidative stress, calcium channel activity and vasoconstriction. Thus the proposed studies on SMC MR are expected to identify novel mechanisms and pathways responsible for the increased levels of oxidative stress and vascular age-related adverse changes. Therefore, studies proposed in the application are expected to reveal new potential drug targets for treating BP.

inn_text_str: 1. The conventional paradigm for BP increase is that the changes in RAAS mediate renal sodium retention and systemic vascular resistance. However, studies by the PI and others strongly indicate that direct regulation of vascular tone contribute to systemic BP. The PI?s compelling work supports that SMC MR can directly regulate vascular Ca channel function, vascular tone, and systemic BP even in the absence of changes in renal sodium handling. In particular, the PI?s lab has previously shown that ATR1 activation by AngII in human SMC results in a direct activation of MR-mediated gene regulation. This activation was shown to occur independent of the MR ligand, but is still inhibited by MR antagonist. Therefore, the PI proposes a crosstalk between AngII and SMC MR which is a novel mechanism, independent of MR ligand and will change our current views on RAAS and its antagonist drugs. Thus, the new mechanism proposed by the PI, which challenges the existing dogma on BP regulation is novel. 2. The PI has characterized and used an innovative mouse model system to knockdown spatially and temporarily MR in vascular SMC.
inn_text_wkn: The PI describes the transgenic mouse by cross breeding floxed MR mouse and a-SMA-Cre-ERT. This being an inducible mouse system, tamoxifen treatment and clearance are required for spatial and conditional deletion of the floxed gene. As tamoxifen is known to modulate estrogen receptor, its treatment in adult male mice has been found to have side effects. Although PI has used these mice previously, it is not mentioned in the proposal how the PI will overcome this situation. Furthermore, it is not clear how unique is this knockdown in vascular a-SMC as activated fibroblasts also express a-SMA.

The data with MR knockout mice showing reduced BP is very convincing that MR in aSMC participates in the regulation of BP. Collaborative work with Dr. Hall laboratory is a strength to study the relationship between SMC MR and LTCC activity. In Aim2, the studies using transgenic MR KO mice that show a link between MR and Cav1.2 and a decreased sensitivity of vessel contraction to LTCC agonist are strong and supportive of the hypothesis. In SA1c, the PI proposes to construct adenoviruses for the expression of mutant MR in the AB domain, based on some potential sites for phosphorylation by PKCd. While this approach may be a valid one, the PI needs to show first whether AngII stimulation results in MR phosphorylation. This could be done through Mass spectrophotometry. The PI proposes to take this as an alternative approach. However, identifying the phosphorylation site in the presence or absence of PKCd inhibitor (rottlerin) will bring a significant strength to this specific Aim.
