imp_text: This proposal is based on the idea that in patients with heart failure (HF), mitoCa2+content is severely reduced although cytoplasmic Ca2+ level is increased. The PI’s lab has developed transgenic mouse models targeting a newly characterized mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (mitoNCX).The regulation of mitoCa2+ draws much attention in HF due to its significant influence in energyproduction and cell death. The central hypothesis that drives this project is that “reducing mitoCa2+efflux protects against gradual cell dropout and adverse remodeling in heart failure by enhancingcardiomyocyte metabolic and redox capacity”. The PI proposes to use gain-and loss-of-functionapproaches on the exchanger to explore its role in the development and progression of HF which isexpected to have therapeutic application. This application has several strengths: The PI shows key preliminary data that in heart samples from ischemic heart failure patients, the decreased level ofmitoCa2+ is accompanied with increased expression of mitoNCX (.Ca efflux), decreased level of MCU (.Ca influx) and increased level of MICU1 (.Ca influx). The PI proposes whether these changes in thegene expression are part of a compensatory process or play causative role in the progression of heart failure. Therefore, addressing the importance of these changes in the microdomain handling of mitoCa issignificant in understanding HF. Secondly, the PI has generated and tested several transgenic mouse linescritical for the study. Overall, enthusiasm was high for this application.
sig_text_str: Reduced levels of mitoCa2+ in failing cardiomyocytes have been found in animal models of pressure-overload hypertrophy and genetically created cardiomyopathies. Previous studies show increased levels ofintracellular Na impairs mitochondrial mitoCa2+ uptake. The PI shows striking preliminary data that inheart samples from ischemic heart failure patients, the decreased level of mitoCa2+ is accompanied with increased expression of mitoNCX. These data strongly indicate that mitoNCX plays a primary role for thereduced mitoCa2+ in failing hearts. The central idea of this application that reducing mitoCa2+ effluxwould protect against the loss of cardiomyocyte metabolic and redox capacity and cell dropout has strong clinical significance. Importantly, characterizing the role of mitoNCX in maintaining mitoCa2+ usingseveral transgenic models that the PI has generated will address the hypothesis and identify new targets toimprove ventricular function in HF patients.

imp_text: The PI proposes that complex signals from Ser/Thr kinases c-Raf and MEK, independent of ERK, influence the development of cardiac hypertrophy. The PIs suggests that the components of Hippo pathway identified in flies, consisting of Ser/Thr kinases, adaptor proteins and transcriptional co-activator function downstream of Raf/MEK signaling in mediating either cardiac hypertrophy or cardiomyocyte proliferation. The PI states that a clear understanding of how Raf1/MEK/Hippo signaling switches from proliferative signaling to hypertrophic signaling will have significant impact to provide new insights into therapies to treat cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure. For initial work, the PI proposes to use invertebrate model system where fruit fly hearts will be used to evaluate the signaling mechanism. The PI emphases that invertebrate models, although receives skepticisms for their use in studying mammalian organ function, have identified several evolutionarily conserved genes and pathways that have strong impact on mammalian systems. The PI lab used the invertebrate system to study EGFR role in post developmental processes of the heart where the loss of EGFR function leads to dilated cardiomyopathy in flies. Furthermore, invertebrate genetic model system such as Drosophila genetics has several advantages over animal model systems while we perform large-scale genetic screens. In particular, genetic screening in flies has identified the signaling components involved in receptor tyrosine kinase (RTKs) pathways that primarily promote cell proliferation. However, RTKs in the post mitotic heart muscle cells promote hypertrophic growth. Therefore, the contention of the PI is that there might be some cardiac-specific genetic modifiers that divert the proliferative signaling involving Raf/MEK/Hippo pathway into hypertrophic growth signaling. The overall goal is to use both invertebrate and vertebrate models to characterize intermediary pathways that commit cardiomyocytes to undergo either hypertrophy or proliferation. Overall, this is a well-written proposal and the PI has the knowledge and experience and assembled talented group of scientist to successfully complete the work.
sig_text_str: A great strength of this proposal is showing a link between Raf/MEK and Hippo-yorkie pathways. While these pathways promote hyperplastic growth in other cell types, they promote hypertrophic growth in cardiomyocytes. The proposed experiments to use both invertebrate and vertebrate models to characterize regulatory components of this pathways that are responsible to turn proliferative signaling into hypertrophic is also expected to have significant impact on cardiac hypertrophy and congestive heart failure.
sig_text_wkn: Although the PI has previous experience with fruit fly model system and show the link between Raf/MEK and Hippo-yorkie pathway, it is not clear what accessory proteins are involved specifically in post-mitotic cardiac muscle cells that contribute to hypertrophic signaling instead of proliferative signaling. It is conceivable that the post-mitotic processing would involve multiple proteins where eventually even the proliferative signals are simply responded by these cells as an hypertrophic phenomena. The PI needs to provide preliminary evidence on one or more unique players that could divert proliferative effect of Hippo-yorkie into hypertrophic signaling.
inv_text_str: The PI has a strong publication record and expertise in using Drosophila genetic models to characterize signaling pathways related to cardiac diseases. The PI and the team have the ability and resources to complete the proposed work.
inv_text_wkn: Studies and publications using animal models from PI’s lab are modest.
inn_text_str: All published and proposed work using the Drosophila model system indicates that c-Raf and possibly MEK mediated signaling is linked to Hippo-yorkie pathway that contribute to cardiac hypertrophy and maladaptive ventricular remodeling. The PI’s work showing a link for the first time between c-Raf and the Hippo pathway is novel. Furthermore the use of Drosophila model system has several advantages over the conventional mouse transgenic models. It is very effective in terms of cost and time to perform large-scale genetic screening.
inn_text_wkn: An inherited weakness is that one or more key molecules identified in the pathway may be unique to the Drosophila model. For example, the functional domains in mammalian system that are proposed to be characterized using Drosophila system in Specific Aim-2 may be unique only to the later model due to specific protein-protein interaction.

These studies will establish for the first time that Raf1-MEK pathway is tied into Hippo Yorkie pathway to mediate cardiac hypertrophy or dilation and identify expression of specific genes mediated by this unique pathway. 2. The approach to identify the importance of unique domains in mammalian Yap using Drosophila is one of the strengths of this application. The rationale, hypothesis and proposed experiments are described well. 3. Specific Aim-3 is a logical extension where the PI will evaluate whether PO-induced cardiac hypertrophy in WT and active c-Raf or MEK1 transgenic mice requires YAP1. Resources to generate transgenic mice that express active c-Raf or MEK1 with YAP1 knockout background are available to PI.
app_text_wkn: 1. Since MEK1 is a critical downstream mediator of Raf1, showing data that MEK1 functions upstream of Hippo pathway would strengthen the application. Since PI shows a direct complex between Raf1 and Hippo, they could have analyzed if MEK1 is also present in the complex. It is possible that Raf1 mediates Hippo signaling independent of MEK1. 2. The PI needs to generate at least one key evidences that the expression of active (S127A) mYap1 expression alters substantially the native phenotype of Drosophila present under the Yorkie background. That is, only if the cardiac function and morphology are altered following the expression of full-length active mYap, then the rest of the proposed experiments (under Specific Aim-2 (1)) with the deletion mutants make a whole of sense. Validation of such an initial experiment is critical that will allow the PI to truncate and characterize the importance of each of the specific functional domains in Yap. It is not clear at the moment whether expression of active mYap in flies will alter the morphology and function under the background of native Yorkie. 3. In Specific Aim-2 (2A), the PI proposes to develop several adenoviral constructs for the expression of various YAP1 mutants in neonatal and adult cardiomyocytes. Construction and characterization of these viruses are a time consuming effort. 4. Although the PI shows the availability of various transgenic mice to generate double transgenic mice exhibiting YAP1 deletion under the background of active Raf or MEK1, this specific mouse line has yet to be generated by crossbreeding and genotyping. Similarly, the generation of YAP1flox/flox/a-MHC cre mice and the use of tamoxifen to induce YAP1 deletion temporarily and spatially in cardiomyocytes have yet to be established. Given the fact tamoxifen treatment often poses deleterious effects in mice including ventricular function, preliminary data showing the feasibility on the generation and use of these mice would be helpful. The entire Specific Aim-3 is dependent on the availability of such transgenic mice.

imp_text: The subject of this grant – the potential role of amylin and its metabolites in diabetic heart failure – is an important one and the investigator shows convincing data for the potential role of amylin in this process.   In contrast to the Jackson grant these studies in rats are more relevant because they are using human amylin and in the first aims studyingmetabolic processes that are similar in rats and humans.  Thus there is potential for relevance in humans and possible therapeutic targets.  The problem is that a huge series of broad experiments are proposed with little detail on methodology and no discussion of power or limitations.
sig_text_str: . Cardiac changes in diabetes lead to significant morbidity and mortality;  the investigator presents plausible data that amylin may be involved in these processes.  Exploring the metabolic effects of amylin could help understand the cardiac abnormalities of diabetes and potentially lead to strategies for intervention

imp_text: Lipin 1 is emerging as a critical regulator of intermediary metabolism. However, very little is known regarding the effects of lipin 1 on energy metabolism and glycerolipid homeostasis in the myocardium. This study tries to investigate the factors that regulate accumulation of lipid within the cardiac myocytes and to find the strategies for the treatment of diabetic cardiac disease. Using transgenic models, the applicant will investigate how lipin 1 translocate from cytoplasm to nucleus; as well as what is the bi-function of lipin 1 as a lipid phosphatase at the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and as the genes encoding mitochondrial enzymes in the nucleus. Finally, the relationship of localization of lipin 1 and cardiac lipid metabolism, signaling pathway and cardiac function will also be investigated. This project may provide new sight into the mechanisms leading to cardiac lipotoxicity and potential identify new therapeutic targets and strategies. Dr. Murphy is a productive assistant professor at the Division of Geriatrics and Nutritional Science. The research environment in Washington University School of Medicine is excellent. The proposal is written smoothly; experiments are well designed. However, the research team is a little bit weak.

It has been indicated that the translocation of lipin 1 depends on the activity of mTOR, concentration of fatty acid and PA. Three aims are designed: • Aim 1. The applicant will first investigate whether the dietary nutrient will manipulate lipin-1 expression, activity and sub-cellular localization in cardiac myocyte. They will test three types of HFD and employ mice overexpressing PPARa which are sensitized to HFD and increased mTOR signaling in their in vivo studies. They will also treat neonatal rat ventricle myocytes (NRVM) with various fatty acids to assess lipin 1 localization and PAP activity. To directly investigate the attenuated effect of mTOR on the unclear transcriptional regulatory effects of lipin 1, applicant will use NRVMs to overexpress or knockdown lipin 1. These cells will be treated with various types of fatty acid under presence of pharmacologic inhibitor of mTOR or activation of mTOR. The effectiveness of the mTOR manipulations will be confirmed by assessing phosphorylation of mTOR and its target proteins. • Aim 2. Following feeding with HFD for 4 ~ 12 weeks, unbiased transcriptional profiling will be performed using RNAseq technology. Mitochondrial function, morphology and signaling pathways, as well as cardiac function will be tested. • Aim 3. The applicant will examine the effect of reactivating nuclear lipin 1 activity in heart by overexpressing a phosphorylation-deficient lipin 1 allele (21XA). The endpoints will be similar to Aim 2. imp_text: Human myocardium reveals significant accumulation of amylin oligomers, fibrils, and plaques in failing hearts from obese and type-2 diabetes patients, The aim of proposed study is to decipher a possible role of hyperamylinemia in diabetic heart failure. The applicant have performed a plenty of preliminary experiments and submitted a manuscript to Circulation Research. Based on the preliminary data, they will use two rat models: rats expressing amyloidogenic human amylin in the pancreas (HIP rats) and rats expressing only native non-amyloidogenic rat amylin (UCD rats), to test the hypothesis that amylin buildup in the heart accelerates the onset of diabetic heart failure by altering cardiac structure and metabolism. This research will clarify whether amylin oligomers i) disrupt sarcolemmal integrity, ii) activate Ca2+-dependent pathways for hypertrophic signaling and remodeling, iii) impair glucose and/or fat metabolism (or their balance), and iv) induce oxidative stress. In addition, by using membrane sealants and scavengers of circulating amylin oligomers in pre-diabetic HIP rats, the applicant will disrupt the deposition of oligomeric amylin in the heart to recover sarcolemmal integrity and improve cardiac function. This proposal has very high significance on finding a key contributor of pathogenesis in diabetic heart disease. The use of a “humanized” rat model of hyperamylinemia will provide critical insight into the molecular mechanisms linking insulin resistance and cardiac dysfunction. The design of this proposal is very systematically and thoroughly. The research team is strong and the environment is excellent.

app_text_str: It is proposed that amylin buildup is a key contributor to diabetic heart disease. To decipher the mechanism(s) underlying the cardiotoxicity of hyperamylinemia, two rat models will be used: 1) HIP: the rats expressed amyloidogenic human amylin in the pancreas; 2) UCD rats, pre-diabetic rats bearing only the non-amyloidogenic rat amylin. The cardiac structure, metabolism, and function will be compared between these two types of mice. Three aims are designed: • Aim 1A. To test whether oligomeric amylin disrupts sarcolemmal integrity, including ultrastructural analysis of cardiac myocytes, passive trans-sarcolemmal Ca2+ and Na+ leak, dye leakage and resting membrane potential and action potential configuration. • Aim 1B. To test whether oligomeric amylin activates Ca2+-dependent pathways signaling, including Ca2+-dependent CaMKII-HDAC and calcineurin-NFAT hypertrophic pathways. In addition, cardiac amylin deposition and state aggregation will be assessed. • Aim 2A. To test whether oligomeric amylin impairs glucose and/or fat metabolism, they will assess i) binding of amylin oligomers to insulin receptor, glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4), and/or fatty acid translocase (CD36), ii) insulin-mediated activation of PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, and iii) translocation of GLUT4 and CD36 in hearts. • Aim 2B.  To test whether oligomeric amylin induces oxidative stress, amylin oligomer-induced lipid peroxidation, mitochondrial damage and the activation of receptor for Advanced Glycation End-Products (RAGE) will be evaluated. Moreover, the related mechanisms—alterations in mitochondrial Ca2+ and insulin signaling will be analyzed. • Aim 3. Investigate whether limiting amylin buildup by using membrane sealants reduce Ca2+ leak or by blocking amylin oligomerization and attachment to the sarcolemma to improve heart function in HIP rats.

imp_text: Circulating platelets play an important role in the pathogenesis of these diseases. During vascular injury, pro-stimulatory mechanisms, such as signaling by various physiological agonists, override the anti-stimulatory machinery to achieve platelet aggregation. The preliminary data suggest that ASK1 (Apoptosis Signal-regulated Kinase 1), a novel platelet protein, is rapidly activated during platelet stimulation by a variety of platelet agonists. Genetic ablation of Ask1 results in a strong anti-thrombotic phenotype in an array of in vivo models of thrombosis. Therefore, it is hypothesized that ASK1 senses stress and/or pro-stimulatory signals initiated by agonists and transmits signals to the platelet fibrinogen receptor complex and helps in coordinating stimulatory signals that regulate platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. The applicant will investigate whether ASK1 plays a key role in regulating multiple distinct signaling events downstream of platelet agonists and elucidate whether ASK1 functions downstream of GPCRs and exerts its effect through activation of p38 and ERK2 MAP kinases. It is first time to characterize ASK1 as a novel protein kinase to regulate stress-induced MAP kinase cascades in platelets. The proposed study may define new targets for developing potential therapeutic agents toward thrombotic disorders. The design is reasonable. Research team is strong and environment is excellent.

imp_text: Previous work from the same laboratory demonstrated that lipin 1 acts in the nucleus to regulate the expression of genes encoding mitochondrial enzymes by interacting with DNA-bound transcription factors and coactivators such as PPARa and PGC-1a. It is hypothesized that chronic caloric and lipid excess will lead to increased phosphorylation and cytoplasmic localization of lipin 1 in the cardiac myocyte. It is also hypothesized that abnormalities in the regulation of cardiac lipin 1 activity will promote glycerolipid synthesis and reduce its pro-catabolic actions, contributing to the lipotoxic cardiomyopathy that develops in states of chronic caloric excess. The proposed work will investigator the myocyte lipin1 expression, and the role of lipin 1 in regulating cardiac metabolism by using both gain of function and loss of function approaches. Overall, this is a good proposal from an established investigator who has expertise in investigating lipin 1 in lipid and glucose metabolism in various cell types, as well as the experience in myocardial metabolism. However, the concept of lipin 1 in regulating lipid metabolism is anticipated, the proposed work is generally descriptive. The proposed work may only generate new data that has moderate impact to understand the abnormal cardiac metabolism in the failing hearts.  In addition, the translational significance is not clear.

imp_text: These investigators hypothesize that amylin buildup in the heart accelerates the onset of diabetic HF by altering cardiac structure and metabolism. Limiting accumulation of amylin oligomers in the heart may slow the onset of diabetic HF. Hence, our study aims to decipher the mechanism(s) underlying the cardiotoxicity of hyperamylinemia and to find ways to prevent/reduce it. They will investigate cardiac structure, metabolism, and function in HIP versus UCD rats to test the following major hypotheses: (i) Oligomeric amylin alters cardiac function by remodeling the myocytes; (ii) Amylin buildup accelerates diabetic heart failure by impairing cardiac energy substrate; (iii) Limiting amylin buildup and its cardiac effect delays heart failure in pre-diabetes. Specifically, they expect that disrupting accumulation of oligomeric amylin in the heart and recovering sarcolemmal integrity, increase intracellular calcium, impair glucose and fatty acid metabolism, and increase oxidative stress by using HIP rats (rats that express amyloidogenic human amylin in the pancreas). This is a strong research proposal from a highly motived young investigator who is supported by a group of outstanding senior investigators. The concept that amylin oligomer accumulation contribute to the abnormal cardiac metabolism and function is novel.   The proposed work is addressing an important research question. The central hypothesis is supported by strong preliminary data.  The proposal study will elucidate an early and direct pathogenic mechanism of amyloids in T2D with cardiac disease, and identify the inhibition of cardiac amyloids as a therapeutic target.

imp_text: This proposal addresses an important protein Lipin-1 and its role in cardiomyopathy. It has direct relevance to populations that suffer from obesity and diabetes induced complications of the cardiovascular system. Since both diabetes and obesity are increasingly prevalent in developed countries the proposed research is extremely significant. Lipin 1 has only recently been receiving attention for its role in regulating anabolic and catabolic pathways and the present researchers have preliminary work and experience in this area. They also have a very strong supporting infrastructure at Wash U and excellent facilities to make progress in the work. The significance and potential impact of the work is therefore very high. The authors have preliminary data on Lipin activity and have already worked with mice models, including producing lines of mice with specific characteristics. So they are well set up to attack the specific aims of the proposed project. The hypothesis to be examined are well developed and specific, i.e. they can be achieved by the methods developed in the project. The research plan is well constructed. First the effect of high fatty acid diets on Lipin 1 will be shown. Then the Lipin 1 loss of function impacts on cardiac lipid metabolism, signaling and function will be demonstrated. Several state-of-the-art experimental techniques are to be used in identifying mitochondrial function and activity of mTOR, insulin etc to delve deep into their roles and signaling pathways. Third, the effect of reactivation of lipin-1 will be studied and may provide insights into the treatment of patients with cardiovascular problems in the future. The project is well conceived yet ambitious and has great future potential in terms of clinical treatment of diet/diabetes induced cardiovascular problems.

While these goals are important they movement of Lpin 1 has been studied in the liver, as noted by the applicant, and this movement between the nucleus and membrane of the endoplasmic reticulum is in response to caloric/lipid excess. Therefore this part of the central hypothesis, while important, has reduced innovation. Part 2; that abnormalities in the regulation of Lpin 1 activity promote glycerolipid synthesis and inhibit pro-catabolic action. This goal is much more complex and a better overall hypothesis. The applicant has loss of function model (fld) as well as a partial loss of function mutations in Lpin 1 (sc-Lpin 1) that removes the PAP activity of Lpin 1 but maintains the transcription factor (PGC-1a) binding motifs. study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: The problem being addressed is important and the generation of a relevant clinical model for the deposition of amylin oligomers in the heart of a rat model of type 2 diabetes (T2D) is important. The major difference between human and rats with respect to amylin is the lack of oligomerization in the rat peptide due to proline substitutions at several positions. So the development of a relevant rat model of T2D that has amylin deposition in the heart is important because it better reflects the human condition. Without this model it would be difficult to test the central hypothesis: that amylin buildup in the heart accelerates the onset of diabetic HF by altering cardiac structure and metabolism. The goals are to understand the mechanism of cardiotoxicity that results from amylin oligomerization in the heart and to find ways to prevent this buildup in their T2D model. The transgenic rat model recapitulates the secretion of human amylin from the pancreas and accumulation in the heart. It was shown that human amylin is not expressed in the transgenic rat heart. The aims follow logically; AIM 1: Amylin oligomers alter cardiac function by remodeling. Amylin oligomers are present in the heart of rats disrupting sarcolemmal integrity. Amylin oligomers activate Ca2+ dependent pathways leading to hypertrophic signaling and remodeling. AIM 2: Amylin buildup accelerates diabetic heart failure Oligomeric amylin impairs glucose and/or fat metabolism Amylin oligomers induce oxidative stress Aim 3: Limiting buildup delays failure Using membrane sealants Disrupting amylin oligomer accumulation improves heart function. The successful completion of these aims has a good chance of finding a new pre-T2D marker and a target for a therapeutic molecule.

study_section: Hemostasis and Thrombosis Study Section
imp_text: The protein apoptosis signal-regulated kinase 1 (Ask1) is a 1374 amino acid protein that is expressed at moderate levels in almost all cell types. It is located in the cytoplasm. In platelets it is part of a signaling cascade and it has pro-thromobotic phenotype. Knockout of Ask1 has strong anti-thrombotic phenotype. The hypothesis is ASK1 is a novel key signaling molecule that regulates platelet function and thrombosis. In Aim 1 the applicant is going to evaluate the role of ASK1 in platelet function and thrombosis. First by evaluating tail bleeding time in Ask1-/- mice vs. wt. Then in Fig. 5 the results of bleeding time between Ask1-/- and wt mice is presented with an n=9. Second 10% FeCl3-induced carotid artery injury will be done to observe differences in the time of occlusion between Ask-/- and wt mice. Fig. 6 shows the difference in occlusion time between Ask1 -/- and wt. Third pulmonary thromboembolism model again preliminary results are present (Fig. 7) with sufficient power to see differences between Ask-/- and wt animals. Fourth reaction of platelets isolated from Ask-/- and wt animals is presented (Fig. 8) again as a preliminary result, but again in the specific aims section. In conclusion nearly all of Specific Aim 1 has been done and is presented as preliminary results, not in the Approach (preliminary results). Why should the NIH pay for data already generated?

study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: The applicant proposes to study the dynamic role of lipin-1 as a regulator of cardiac metabolism.  The hypothesis to be tested is interesting and suggests nutrition, specifically high fat, can change gene expression and sub-cellular localization through the lipin-1 protein.  The concept to be tested is novel and based on a long standing interest in lipin-1 biology.  One aspect of the work that was consistently down-played was the relevance, if any, of the other lipin proteins, 2 and 3.  The applicant makes a bold statement lipin 1 is abundantly expressed in the myocardium while lipin 2 and lipin 3 are not highly expressed in this tissue.  Proof of this statement is found in Fig 2, yet the results may suggest otherwise.  At the levels of protein loaded in Fig 2, significant lipin 3 is present.  The comparative loads of protein extracts in the lipin blots is not given, so it is a crucial experiment, but difficult to make a conclusion that supports focusing only on lipin 1’s role.  The mouse model experiments are interesting but there was concern about whether adequate strain considerations have been given.  It seems each of the starting strains are on different background, but unclear what the strain background of the to-be-generated animals will be.  An additional concern in interpretation of the preliminary studies is the use of “tended to be increased” when statistical analysis did not support a statistically significant difference.  This has left some doubt for interpretation of findings going forward.  Overall, an interesting hypothesis.  However, there are concerns for the presentation of data, interpretation of results and consideration of models to be used in the future.  Thus, enthusiasm is in the moderate range at this point.

study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: The proposal builds on a recent publication by the PI and his group documenting the accumulation of amylin fibrils in the heart tissue of patients with type 2 diabetes and heart failure.  Assuming successful completion of the studies is likely to have a significant impact defining the pathophysiology of heart failure and could potentially identify new therapeutic targets used in the management of heart disease.  This is significant.  However, the grant as written, is difficult to follow and lacks details for controls in a variety of places.  The specific aims page is very non-traditional and lacks “specific aims”, but instead lists a series of 3 hypotheses and some experiments.  Figure 1 examines via WB, tissues samples from human hearts.  Are these perfused hearts?  The PI would like to suggest the increased levels of amylin is associated with myocytes but it is unclear in the presented data what we are looking at.  Binding in Figure 4A, is it specific? imp_text: This is an interesting proposal based on strong preliminary data linking Rnd3 to heart failure.  The proposal is well written with excellent preliminary studies.  The proposal describes experiments that will further investigate the pathophysiologic responses that are Rnd3-dependent.  However, the major weakness of the current application is direct proof that Rnd3 causes heart failure or is simply a marker of the stressed heart condition.  Most of the data simply looks at the Rdn3 consequences during heart failure.  Does overexpression of Rnd3 actually improve the response during heart failure?  This could be an experiment that would more definitively establish whether levels of Rnd3 are a cause or an effect and strengthen the justification to pursue the proposed experiments.  Not well described in the application was more details on the haploinsufficiency mouse model.  Nowhere in the application were levels of Rdn3 shown to be reduced, or to what extent reduced, in this model.  This is extremely important data to fully justify why studying this animal model has merit.  The homozygous KO is lethal, but what are the protein levels in the heterozygous animal?  For a reviewer with no knowledge of this mouse model this was an omission that placed doubt on the pathophysiologic relevance of the proposed studies.  There was also concern over the budget with a modification proposed but this was not considered as a score driving factor.

imp_text: Abnormalities in cardiac metabolism are known to lead to cardiac dysfunction and heart failure. Given that Lipin-1 is emerging as a critical regulator of intermediary metabolism, therefore, this proposal testing the effects of lipin1 on cardiac lipid metabolism, signaling, and function would be very significant, as it could help us better understand the role of lipin-1 in regulating lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. Also, this proposal is expected to identify new therapies for treating cardiac disease in people with diabetes. The preliminary data are strong and supporting the hypothesis of proposal.  Three Aims are independent and logically connected. Experimental design is reasonable and the methodology is appropriate. 6 animal models proposed in this application are available. PI’s publication record on Lipin-1 is outstanding. Overall, the proposed science, PI and research environment at the Washington University in St. Louis are excellent. The impact of this proposal is high. However, the proposal appears not well-delivered. Also, it looks ambitious and diffused. Too many animal models are proposed. Aim 1 is clear and straight-forward, but Aims 2 and 3 are not easy to follow. Aim 2 should focus on testing the effects of cytosol-targeted Llipin1 on cardiac lipid metabolism, signaling, and function, and Aim 3 should focus on testing the effects of nuclear-targeted lipin1 on lipotoxic cardiomyopathy.

imp_text: Obesity and type-2 diabetes (T2D) are approaching epidemic proportions in the US and are associated with a high risk of heart disease. The pathogenesis is multifactorial and can develop independently of co-existing hypertension and coronary artery disease. To date, there is no diagnosis and treatment specific to diabetic heart failure (HF). The proposal tests the hypothesis that amylin buildup in the heart accelerates the onset of diabetic HF by altering cardiac structure and metabolism. Limiting accumulation of amylin oligomers in the heart may slow the onset of diabetic HF. Hence, this project aimed to decipher the mechanism(s) underlying the cardiotoxicity of hyperamylinemia and to find ways to prevent/reduce it, which is very significant. The preliminary data are strong and supporting the hypothesis of proposal.  Three Aims are independent and logically connected. Aim 1 is to test whether Oligomeric amylin alters cardiac function by remodeling the myocytes; Aim 2 is to test Amylin buildup accelerates diabetic heart failure by impairing cardiac energy substrate metabolism; and Aim 3 is to test whether Limiting amylin buildup and its cardiac effect delays heart failure in pre-diabetes. Experimental design is reasonable and the methodology is appropriate. PI has an interdisciplinary background and productive track record (53 papers in peer reviewed journals) in studies of amyloid formation, structure, and pathological mechanisms, attesting her outstanding. Overall, the proposal is well-developed and well-written. PI and research environment at the University of California (Davis) are excellent. The impact of this proposal is very high. The proposed work will reveal a novel therapeutic target in diabetic HF and significantly improve cardiac prognosis and diagnosis in obesity and T2D. Most importantly, the proposed work using a “humanized” HIP rat model of hyperamylinemia has great translational potential. The enthusiasm for this grant proposal is very high. This proposal is to test the hypothesis that ASK1 senses stress and/or pro-stimulatory signals initiated by agonists and transmits signals to the platelet Fibrinogen receptor complex and thereby, coordinating stimulatory signals that regulate platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. Specifically, the proposed research is to investigate the molecular mechanism through which ASK1 affects platelet functions such as granular secretion and integrin IIb 3 activation in order to induce thrombosis. This proposed study is expected to define ASK1 as a new target for developing potential therapeutic agents toward thrombotic disorders. imp_text: The primary aim of this application is to examine the role of lipin 1 in regulating anabolic and catabolic pathways in the cardiac tissue during caloric excess conditions. Under nutrient excess conditions molecular target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1)   is inactivated lipin1 is phosphorylated retained in the cytoplasm and trafficked to the ER where it converts phosphatidic acid (PA) to diacyglycerol (DAG) that are known to activate PKC and JNK. When mTOR1 is inactivated lipin1 is dephosphorylated and trafficked to nucleus where it increases the expression of enzymes that are involved in oxidative metabolism. Three aims are proposed to understand how lipin1 can either contribute to cardiotoxicity or cardiac protection. Dr. Sullivan proposes to use different genetic mice models (A) that lack lipin1 (B) cardiac specific mice expressing lipin1 deficient in conversion of PA to DAG (PAP activity) (C) inducible mice overexpressing lipin1 that lacks the phosphorylation site. Preliminary data shows that the PAP activity is increased under high fat feeding conditions and all the mice models that will be used in the study have been generated. The major strength of this application is the use of different genetically modified mice that have been generated to determine the cardioprotective and the cardiotoxic role of lipin 1 in the cardiac tissue under nutrient excess conditions. The proposal is very innovative however there are few shortcomings. Foremost if the catabolic activity of lipin 1 is cardiotoxic why the author does not propose to use or design specific inhibitors against the conserved catalytic site. Overall this is an excellent application from a PI who has a very excellent track record of publications supported by a strong environment.

imp_text: Overall Impact  This is well-written proposal from an established investigator who seeks to investigate a hypothesis that chronic caloric and lipid excess will increase lipin 1 phosphorylation and location that promotes glycerolipid synthesis, thus contributing to the lipotoxic cardiomyopathy in high fat diet induced obese model. This hypothesis is novel with strong preliminary data. The excellent research environments is considered strength of this application. Successful completion of this project will result in a meaningful discovery and advance the current understating of obese-associated abnormalities in cardiac lipid metabolisms that lead to cardiac dysfunction and heart failure in diabetes and obesity. The principal investigator has excellent research experience in cardiac metabolism and obesity. The proposed research is of significance. However, the innovation is somewhat limited because the role of lipid 1 in cell metabolism and mitochondrial function is already known although the proposed research investigates lipin1 in the cardiomyocyte in obesity. The experimental approach is modest innovative and lack of a significant cardiac phenotype in Lipin 1 knockout mice. Another major concern is using mTOR knockout mice (aMHC-mer-Cre-mer-Raptorf/f mice) which already developed heart failure after the deletion, which brought into question the outcomes of this study. Feeding a high diet on this mice may worsen cardiac dysfunction but not protects the heart. The causative relationship between lipid 1 and PAP interactions is not clearly defined, since there is no changes in lipin 1 expression, phosphorylation and no evidence of disruption of interactions with PAP in the heart of high fat diet obese mice. These limitations somewhat dampens the enthusiasm of this application.

imp_text: Overall Impact  Heart failure (HF) remains a leading cause of death worldwide, identified new drug targets to improve HF is warranted. This application propose to investigate the molecular mechanisms of a fall in Rnd3 levels in heart failure and identify potential drug targets for heart failure. A small GTPase Rnd3 has been recognized as important player in the human HF by the PI’s lab. In this application, they hypothesize that downregulation of Rnd3 results in insufficient angiogenesis by enhancing Notch activity in endothelial and weakening HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling in cardiomyocytes. The hypothesis in innovative. The experiments are well designed and clearly feasible, this is considered to be strength.  The PI is an established investigator with expertise in heart failure, complete this project is likely to produce meaningful results. Weakness of the grant is that highly focused on the contribution of Rnd3 mediated angiogenesis in heart failure without considering direct effect of impaired Rnd3 signaling in cardiomyocyte function. Cardiomyocyte size is an important determinant of microvascular density in the heart. Fall in capillary in TAC model is considered as secondary. The reduction of capillary density in the TAC model is mainly due to the pressure overload mediated cardiac hypertrophy. However, they do not consider the role of cardiomyocyte size in determining microvascular density in this model. Besides, there is no evidence that impairment of angiogenesis can causes heart failure. Angiogenesis is important for cardiac repair and recovery after myocardial ischemia/or reperfusion, considering using MI model instead of TAC will be more translational. The experimental approach and methodology is state- of- the- art but not innovative. Overall impact is medium.

This proposal explores novel molecular mechanisms that a fall in Rnd3 impairs angiogenesis and cardiac dysfunction in heart failure. 3. Exploring Rnd3-HIF-VEGF interactions and angiogenesis is novel and significant.

imp_text: Overall Impact  Circulating platelets play an important role in the pathogenesis of cardiovascular diseases, exploring the novel signaling pathway that regulates platelet function is of significance. This research proposal will test the hypothesis that ASK1 (Apoptosis Signal-regulated Kinase 1) is a novel key signaling molecule that regulate platelet function and thrombosis. Two specific aims are proposed to explore the novel molecular mechanism by which ASK1 regulates platelet function by using novel ASK1 global knockout mice and in vitro platelet functional test as well as in vivo thrombosis models. Overall, this is an interesting application with numerous strength including experience and productive investigators, novel hypothesis and well-developed methodologies. Successful completion of this project will advance the current understanding of platelets activation in cardiovascular diseases. However, the innovation of proposed signaling pathways is somewhat limited because the roles of p38 and MAP kinase in ASK1 signaling pathway are already known although the proposal research investigate platelets and thrombosis. There are some concerns with experimental approaches. One concern is that ASK1 knockout mice is global knockout not specific in platelets. Knockout of ASK1 in endothelium may disrupt the EC-platelet interactions and impair bleed time as well the thrombus formation. Since both specific aim 1& 2 dependent on ASK1 knockout mice, preliminary data to demonstrate deficiency of ASK1 in EC will not interfere thrombosis and platelets function are required. In addition, a fall in the number of platelets in ASK1 KO mice may also contribute to delay bleed time since this signaling pathway is strongly associated with cell apoptosis. This has not discussed in the application. These limitations somewhat lows the enthusiasm for this otherwise excellent application.

imp_text: This is an exciting and well written proposal by a highly productive new investigator to investigate the role of circulating amylin in the pathogenesis of diabetes-related heart failure.  The investigators show compelling preliminary data supporting their novel hypothesis.  Furthermore, the experimental plan which utilizes a humanized rodent model system is innovative and feasible with the investigative team assembled.  There is a very strong team of investigators assembled with the necessary expertise and proven track record of success.  This project is a logical extension of Dr. Murphey’s prior research which has established a role of amylin aggregates in diabetic cardiomyopathy.  Limitations are appropriately acknowledged in the context of the ability to make definitive conclusions within the framework of the model used.  One critique is that the project is quite ambitious.  This potential concern is alleviated by the strong team of investigators and recognition that even partial success will provide important insight into the role of amylin oligomers in the development of diabetic cardiomyopathy.
sig_text_str: . Heart failure remains a serious and important complication in diabetic patients . While it is likely that diabetes-related heart failure is multifactorial, establishment of a link to elevated amyloid protein is plausible and important if validated. . Validation of the amylin hypothesis could provide a useful approach to screen patients at highest risk for development and/or progression of diabetes-related cardiomyopathy. . There is potential for expanding these findings to other diseases that are influenced by oligomer formation. . The proposed studies include ambitious plans to test for therapeutic benefit by prevent adverse effects of amylin deposition in a rodent model system
sig_text_wkn: . Prior studies have frequently failed to show direct correlations between diabetes-related effects in rodent models and human subjects. Thus, appropriate caution regarding these potential effects is justified.

Dr. Murphy has had outstanding training, substantial experience in the investigation of amylin-related toxicity, and an impressive list of publications for a junior level (assistant professor) investigator . Dr. Traughott is a well-recognized and highly productive senior investigator with a proven track record of successful collaborations. He will be an outstanding member of the investigative team with expertise that will be very helpful for the proposed project. . The direct demonstration of amylin deposition in human hearts is particularly significant for the proposed project. . The humanized amylin rat model  is novel and overcomes one of the most important barriers to studying the effect of amyloidogenic human amylin in rodent systems . The proposed approach to preventing oligomeric amylin formation is unique.

While the focus of the proposed studies is on the effects of amylin in cardiomyocytes, there are several systemic effects of this protein including gastric emptying, glucagon secretion, and satiety.  It is important to consider these in the interpretation of the full study findings. . The nature of the amylin overexpressing rat model does not fully recapitulate human secretion as insulin and amylin production are not directly linked. . The proposed study of cardiac metabolism is limited and there are potential confounders that may affect data interpretation.  This includes insulin-independent mechanisms of GLUT4 translocation (cell surface levels will not be directly assessed) and changes in expression of other transporters. . imp_text: This proposal to establish a role for Rnd3 in a rodent heart failure model has potential for contributing significant advance in understanding alterations in pathways regulating myocardial angiogenesis in response to cardiac stress.  While there is merit in the overall hypothesis and intriguing preliminary data, the presentation of the rationale, approach, and particularly the potential clinical significance of this project raise questions about overall impact.   It particular, despite the repeated assertion that a patient-relevant model will be used, it is not convincing that genetic knockdown in a rodent model can recapitulate the dynamic changes in Rnd3 expression that likely occur during heart failure evolution.  As noted by the investigators themselves, translation of rodent data to humans has been a substantial challenge in this field.  Some important background information and/or data such as the temporal changes in Rnd3 expression following cardiac stress/injury in the proposed model system would facilitate the desired link between the rodent model and clinical data. Most of the proposed in vitro experiments appear logical, straightforward and feasible with Dr. Sullivan’s experience in this area. It is likely that new insight will be gained on signaling pathways influenced by Rnd3.  How this information could be used clinically is unclear as it is unlikely that pharmacologic approaches would be specific for effects in the myocardium.
sig_text_str: . There is a clear need to better understand the normal signals controlling myocardial angiogenesis and pathways altered in heart failure. . The proposed studies can provide valuable new data on the influence of Rnd3 on HIF1-VEGF signaling
sig_text_wkn: . The relationship between observed reductions in Rnd3 in tissue from human heart failure patients and the haploinsufficiency mouse model is not clear.  The same concern regarding translation from rodents to humans as seen in other attempts to influence angiogenesis remains. . The heart failure phenotype observed for Rnd3 knock town is dependent upon pressure overload.  The generalizability of this model to other factors that may impact clinical heart failure is not clearly presented.

imp_text: Successful completion of the project aims will provide demonstration of the effects of ASK1 in platelets, providing some advance in understanding of the role of MAPK pathways in these cells.  The studies themselves are clearly feasible. The preliminary data is convincing that the hypothesized responses will occur.  In many cases, these data have already established the role of Ask1 in the individual assays proposed for the first aim.  Enthusiasm is also weakened by the apparent lack of focus.  Better presentation of the key unique features mediated by ASK1 and a more ordered approach to investigation of key pathway intermediates rather than a “shotgun approach” would alleviate some of the concerns that specific conclusions on the specific role(s) in this complex pathway will be achieved.   Many questions regarding potential impact are not clearly presented.  In particular, several inhibitors of platelet activation that impact the proposed signaling cascades to be investigated in this study have already been characterized.  There is also a general lack of enthusiasm in how the elucidation of the role of Ask1 will translate into improved therapeutics.
sig_text_str: . The physiologic/pathophysiologic role of MAP kinase pathways in hemostasis and thrombosis is relatively understudied with continued gaps in knowledge. . ASK1 potentially plays a key role in regulation of platelet activation . The observation of significant differences in MAPK signaling pathways in platelets versus nucleated cells would be important . imp_text: This is a good application from the established investigator that explores the mechanism and role of lipin 1 in chronic caloric and lipid excess-mediated lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. The concept that lipin 1 phosphorylation induced by mTOR increases cytosolic lipin 1-mediated PAP activity and inhibits nuclear lipin1-medaited induction of mitochondrial oxidative metabolism-related gene is interesting and novel. Major strengths include convincing preliminary data, interesting and novel concepts, and the interesting approaches by using cs-line 1 delta 115 and 21XA transgenic mice.  There were several significant weaknesses in the approach such as no preliminary data to support the different localization of lipin 1 under HFD, the lower expression level of lipin 1 in cs-lipin 1 delta 115 mice compared to wild type mice, and no preliminary data to support the crucial role of lipin 1 modification on HFD-mediated cardiac dysfunction.  These issues significantly dampen the impact from this study.
sig_text_str: . The PI proposed the hypothesis that chronic caloric and lipid excess increase lipin 1 phosphorylation and cytoplasmic localization, increases PAP activity, catalyzes DAG production, increases glycerol-lipid synthesis, and contributes to the lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. . Since the exact molecular mechanism and role of lipotoxic cardiomyopathy remains unclear, understanding the molecular process and involvement of lipin 1 in lipotoxic cardiomyopathy both in vitro and in vivo is of major consequence.

Since the PI showed the preliminary data that nuclear lipin 1 inhibits SREBP1 expression and increase mitochondrial biogenesis via PGC-1a coactivation.  This will be a good start to detect the role of sub-cellular localization of lipin 1 in regulating cytosolic PAP activity and nuclear lipin 1-mediated transactivation of PGC-1a and PPARa and suppression of SREBP1 under high fat diet. • In aim 2, the PI will investigate the role of lipin 1-mediated cardiac PAP activity in HFD-mediated DAG and other toxic lipids accumulation. The PI will utilize cardiac specific cs-lipin1 delta 115 mice, which is catalytically inactive for PAP activity, but retains its transcriptional regulatory function.  These mice can be very useful to separate the role of lipin 1 PAP activity and its transcriptional regulatory function. • In aim 3 the PI proposed to use phosphorylation-deficient 21XA transgenic mice and detect the role of lipin 1 phosphorylation in lipotoxicity and pressure overload-mediated cardiac dysfunction. imp_text: The proposed studies will investigate whether accumulation of amylin oligomers in the heart disrupts sarcolemmal integrity, and disrupting accumulation of oligomeric amylin mediated by poloxamer P188 and plasmin/14,15-EET improves sarcommal damage and cardiac function in HIP rats.  Major strengths include convincing in vitro preliminary data, interesting and novel concepts, and productive investigator’s group.  Since amylin oligomers can accumulate membrane structure, it is not clear whether SR is the most critical target site of amylin oligomers, and how the PI will detect the interplay and hierarchy (upstream or downstream, cause or result) of SR damage, ROS production, and mitochondrial function. In addition, no pilot study of show the effectiveness of P188 and plamin/14,15-EET treatment in vivo including dose and half life in HIP rats was provided. These issues significantly detract from the overall impact of this proposal.
sig_text_str: • The PI hypothesized that accumulation of amylin oligomers in the heart disrupts sarcolemmal integrity, activates Ca2+-dependent pathway, impairs glucose and/or fat metabolism, and increases oxidative stress, resulting in diabetes-induced cardiac dysfunction. Therefore, it is also interesting to detect the role of amylin oligomers on mitochondrial-related events. • In aim 3 the PI will detect the effects of poloxamer P188, which seals damaged cell membrane and recovers cell function, and plasmin/14, 15-EET, which block oligomerization of amylin in saline solution, on Ca2+ leak and cardiac dysfunction in HIP rats. imp_text: This is the application from the established investigator that explores the mechanism and role of Ask1 in regulating platelet activation.  Since novel anti-thrombotic targets that would be effective without much bleeding or side-effects are desperately needed, understanding the molecular process and involvement of Ask1 in platelet activation can be of major consequence. Major strengths include convincing preliminary data, and the experience of the PI.  However, the PI proposed to study many signaling pathways as the possible down-stream and up-stream regulators, and it is not clear how these pathways can coordinately regulate ASK1 and platelet activation.  Without investigating the uniqueness of each pathway in regulating platelet activation it is difficult to detect exact mechanistic insights on ASK1-mediated platelet activation.  In addition, the recent productivity of the PI is modest.  These issues significantly dampen the impact from this study.

imp_text: This proposed project is to use various mouse models to confirm the in vivo function of Lipin 1 as both a transcription regulator and a phosphatidic acid phosphatase (PAP) enzymes to convert phospholipid to DAG in response to different lipid loading conditions. The main hypothesis that the nuclear lipin 1 would shuttle to the cytosol when cytosolic lipid is accumulated and the cytosolic lipin 1 will exert the PAP enzymatic function to facilitate lipid synthesis. The preliminary data are largely supportive of this hypothesis. The PI claimed that the confirmation of this hypothesis will help the development of new therapeutic target for treating lipotoxicity in the heart, such as in diabetic and obese patients. The proposed approaches include, 1) determine the effects of dietary nutrient manipulation on cardiac myocyte lipin 1 expression, activity, and sub-cellular localization to test the hypothesis that activation of mTOR and excessive cardiac lipid content will lead to cytoplasmic localization of lipin 1 and stimulation of glycerolipid synthesis in the cardiac myocyte. 2) Using two loss of function models with constitutive lipin 1 deficiency and cardiac-specific PAP-deficiency to test the hypothesis that the loss of lipin 1-mediated PAP activity may attenuate the pathogenic response to nutrient overabundance by inhibiting lipin 1-mediated synthesis of DAG, TG and ther potential lipotoxins.  3) To test the hypothesis that reactivation of cardiac lipin 1 nuclear activity in the context of nutrient excess will ameliorate cardiac dysfunction in lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. The overall hypothesis is somewhat new and will be tested in various animal preclinical mouse models. If the project works out as plan, the finding may fill some small gaps of our knowledge on how lipin 1 may be response to lipid loading condition in the in vivo condition. However, the overall impact of this grant is relatively low with major flaws in the experimental design and the unavailable of a proposed mouse model.

Finding from this proposal may help identify therapeutic targets to treat lipotoxic cardiomyopathy . imp_text: The overall goal of this study is to investigate the pathological significance and molecular mechanisms related to the Rnd3 downregulation in heart failure based on mouse models with heterozygous Rnd3 knockout, which showed no basal phenotype but developed dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) with heart failure in responsed to transverse aortic constriction (TAC) induced left ventricular the pressure overload. Based on their preliminary finding that downregulation of Rnd3 results in insufficient angiogenesis. The main hypothesisis that cardiac Rnd3 deficiency enhances Notch activity in endothelia and weakening HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling in cardiomyocytes, resulting in the insufficient angiogenesis. In Aim 1, the proposed study will explore the mechanistic role of Rnd3 in the Notch transcriptional complex in endothelial cells.  In Aim 2, the proposed study will establish the regulatory role of Rnd3 in the HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling axis in cardiomyocytes. Finally, aim 3 will investigate the feedback loop mechanism between HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling and Notch signaling and test if the introduction of a Notch inhibitor, HIF1a-VEGF agonist, and genetic reintroduction of Rnd3 into endothelia and cardiomyocytes correct the angiogenic defect. With the limited knowledge of how Rnd3 involves in the pathological development of cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure, the proposed study appears to be ready to fill this knowledge gap. The study is highly feasible with the available of the mouse models Rnd3 KO and the expertise of the team in the related area. The study is novel and clinically relevant with convincing preliminary data to support the hypothesis and the feasibility of the experimental approaches.

imp_text: This proposal is to define the role of Ask1 in platelet function and hence thrombosis. Specifically, the proposal will explore the molecular mechanism through which ASK1 regulates platelet functions by assessing granular secretion and integrin aIIbß3 activation and how the corresponding changes in platelet function would affect the induction of thrombosis. The overall hypothesis is that ASK1 is a novel key signaling molecule that regulate platelet function and thrombosis. The grant will test the hypothesis by two specific aims, 1) to evaluate the role of ASK1 in platelet function and thrombosis and 2) to elucidate the mechanism through which ASK1 is activated by platelet agonists. Overall, the idea that ASK1 is a key signaling molecule in platelet function and thrombosis is not novel, which will not likely yield significant clinically relevant findings. The two specific aims are vague and ambiguous. The research strategy is poorly described with extremely hard to follow schemes with no essential details of each experiments. Therefore, the perspective of productivity and potential impact of the proposed project is likely be disappointed.

This work is innovative in that it has identified a potential pathologic target for diabetic cardiomyopathy and seeks to define mechanism by which amylin deposits cause cardiomyopathy in addition to treating it.  The approach is sound and is centralized on use of transgenic rats that express human amylin.  The assays are reasonable and in the proposed environment can be accomplished.

imp_text: This application proposes a set of in vivo and in vitro experimental studies to elucidate the mechanistic involvement of lipin1 in regulating cardiac metabolism and in the genesis of lipotoxic cardiomyopathy in animals fed with high fat diet. The experiments are hypothesis-driven and the scientific premise and feasibility, by in large, are well-demonstrated. The strength of the proposed study resides in the Significance, Investigator, and Environment.  With modified approaches and improved vigor (see major weakness), successful pursuit of the proposed specific aims is expected to generate new information that improves the understanding of the regulation of cardiac metabolism and cardiac metabolic disease. However, failure to include the most vigorous controls for several of the genetic mouse models used in the pilot studies and to be used in the proposed experiments represents a major weakness, making it impossible to interpret the potential results of the related experiments with high confidence. This and other weaknesses identified primarily with the Approach significantly dampens the overall enthusiasm toward this proposal.
sig_text_str: • Prior studies, including work from the PI’s group, has shown that lipin plays an important role in regulating hepatic metabolism but the role of lipin1 in the regulation of myocardial metabolism, especially during diabetes remains to be elucidated. This project is proposed to fill this important gap. • This is a hypothesis-driven proposal to test hypotheses that “chronic caloric and lipid excess lead to increased phosphorylation and cytoplasmic localization of lipin1” and that “abnormalities in the regulation of cardiac lipin1 activity promote glycerolipid synthesis and inhibit its pro-catabolic actions, contributing to the lipotoxic cardiomyopathy”. • Mouse genetic models with altered lipin1 function to be created and/or characterized in this project are expected to benefit future studies on lipin1.

By feeding loss-of-lipin 1-function mice with a high fat diet (HFD) and intercrossing with PPARa overexpressing mice and examining the cardiac functional response as well as lipidomic and metabolic profiles, Specific Aim 2 will test the postulate that attenuation of lipin 1 PAP activity will ameliorate lipotoxicity in mice fed a HFD or overexpressing PPARa. . imp_text: As a member of the Rho family, Rnd3/RhoE had been primarily studied for its role in the RhoA and ROCK1 signaling pathway. The applicant’s recent work has begun to reveal Rnd3 as an exciting novel regulator of Notch signaling, promoting Notch degradation by the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS).  The proposed project will test novel mechanistic roles for Rnd3 in myocardial angiogenesis using clinically relevant in vivo mouse models and in vitro cell culture systems. The strength of this proposal resides in its high significance by tackling a clinically highly relevant important problem, in its conceptual innovation, in the PI who has demonstrated prior success in leading a productive research program and, more importantly, discovered this new regulatory paradigm of Rnd3, and in the environment which is excellent for the proposed project. The approaches are also well laid out using for the most part state-of-the-art methodologies although very minor weakness is identified. The completion of the proposed study is expected to generate exciting new knowledge regarding the fundamental biological function of Rnd3 in both vascular endothelia and cardiomyocytes while establishing Rnd3 downregulation as a potentially new pathogenic factor for defective angiogenesis in pathological cardiac hypertrophy, an important process that dominates cardiac pathophysiology. Hence, the overall impact of the proposed study is expected to be sustaining and broad.  The overall enthusiasm is very high.
sig_text_str: . Insufficient angiogenesis has been suggested as one of the critical factors responsible for the transition of the heart from compensated hypertrophy to heart failure; hence enhancing myocardial angiogenesis in a hypertrophied heart is of great therapeutic potential but this has not been effectively applied to the clinic because the molecular basis for the inadequacy remains incompletely understood. Studies proposed in this application are aimed to tackle this critical barrier. . The applicant’s preliminary data indicate that Rnd3 is significantly down regulated in human failing hearts. This project is proposed to test the hypothesis that downregulation of Rnd3 results in insufficient angiogenesis by enhancing Notch activity in endothelia and weakening HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling in cardiomyocytes, identifying Rnd3 as a novel mediator in the adaptive coronary angiogenesis program. . The hypothesis to be tested is mechanistic and strongly supported by ample preliminary data. The molecular mechanism of Rnd3’s proactive role in the HIF1a-VEGF pathway and inhibitory effects on Notch signaling will be elucidated. . A clinically relevant animal model of impaired myocardial angiogenesis will be established via coupling Rnd3 haploinsufficiency with pressure overload. . The completion of the proposed study is expected to identify a potentially new therapeutic strategy to intervening myocardial angiogenesis.

imp_text: The goal of the proposed research is to investigate the role of ASK1 in regulating platelet function. Specifically, the applicant plans to investigate the molecular mechanism through which ASK1 affect platelet functions such as granular secretion and integrin IIb 3 activation in order to induce thrombosis. The PI and the investigative team have the expertise, leadership and motivation necessary to carry out the proposed work which deems to be significant and clinically relevant. The main weakness resides in the approaches which are inadequately developed and quite diffuse and, more importantly, several critical mouse models required for the most exciting portions of the project remains to be made, which is exceedingly risky. These major weaknesses significantly dampen the overall impact of this application.
sig_text_str: . ASK1, a MAPKKK that was well studied in nucleated cells but has not been studied for its role in platelets, was found by the applicant to express in platelets. . Using mouse models of genetic modifications of ASK1, the proposed study will establish ASK1 as an important regulator of platelet activation and thrombosis, including elucidating the up- and downstream mechanism of ASK1 activation in platelets. . Applicant’s preliminary data suggest that activation of ASK1 by agonists may activate downstream MAPK pathways in platelets differentially from nucleated cells, rendering it essential to study this MAPKKK in the platelets. . Despite current availability of clinical anti-thrombotic therapies, there is still a clear need for developing new therapeutic agents for the broad spectrum of thrombotic disorders. This need cannot be met without a full understanding of the regulation of platelet function and thrombosis. The identification of ASK1 as such a regulator by the proposed study is thus expected to yield potentially important new targets for therapeutic development.

ASK1, a well-studied MAPKKK in nucleated cells, has not been studied for its role in regulating platelet function and thrombosis but will be established by the proposed study as an important regulator of platelets. . The ubiquitous nature of the ASK1 germ-line knockout model used for the preliminary studies makes it impossible to attribute the in vivo thrombotic/hemostatic phenotypes exclusively to resultant platelet defects; however, this will be overcome by using adoptive bone marrow transfer although the feasibility remains to be demonstrated by the applicant.

app_text_str: • Preliminary characterization reveals striking alterations in hemostasis and platelet activation in ASK1 KO mice, supporting much of the hypothesis. • That ASK1 is a positive regulator of platelet function and thrombosis will be conclusively determined. The thrombotic phenotype in Ask-/- mice will be characterized using a variety of in vivo thrombosis models. •  Aim 2 will elucidate the molecular mechanism of how ASK1 exerts a stimulatory effect on platelet activation. The specific platelet activation events that are compromised by Ask1 deficiency will be dissected, using state of the art in vitro and in vivo techniques as well as mutant Ask1 knock-in mice and chimeric mice generated through adoptive transfer of bone marrow cells followed by in vivo thrombosis assay to conclusively determine the exact role of ASK1 in the process of thrombosis. • Although in platelets, agonist-induced activation of MAPKs has been well documented, very little is known about the upstream and downstream signaling components of these pathways. The agonist induced signaling pathway responsible for MAPKs activation and cellular responses in platelets will be defined using Ask1-/- mice, pharmacological tools, as well as, in some cases, genetic rescues.

imp_text: The overarching goal of the proposed research is to elucidate the role of amylin in mechanistic correlation between type 2 diabetes (T2D), obesity and heart failure (HF). Although the investigator name is stated as Matthew Sullivan, from the biosketch publications it is apparent that the PI under review is Florin Despa. The research is driven by the central hypotheses that amylin deposition is enhanced in the heart of T2D patients and this negatively influences several biomolecular and cellular aspects of cardiac structure and function, leading to heart failure. The preliminary data presented strongly supports the rationale behind the hypothesis. The experimental designs are adequately described pertaining to sub-components of each aim. The clinical significance of this research is not only the elucidation of new mechanisms (and therapeutic targets) for HF in T2D based on hyperamylinemia, but also possible correlation of these mechanisms to other amylin/amyloid involved pathologies. The main drawback of the proposal is that the therapeutic aim components (Aim 3) are only valid and dependent upon the success and validation of the mechanistic elucidation aim components (Aims 1 and 2). The Aims 1 and 2, on the other hand, have several ‘hypothesis’ components under the central mechanistic theme, such that any or all of those mechanisms can affect cardiac structure and function at biomolecular and cellular levels. In that respect, it is not clear if the HF would be correlated to each of the mechanistic components independent of each other, such that, from a subsequent therapeutic context treatment of any one of the mechanisms can in essence ameliorate the HF problem. In other words, it is unclear whether establishment of any one of the mechanistic components (to be studied by virtue of Aims 1 and 2) can still lead to some therapeutic development (to be studied in Aim 3), or whether all the components of Aims 1 and 2 need to be validated in order to realize the therapeutic potential of Aim 3. Also from a diagnostic/prognostic standpoint, it is unclear how amylin deposit levels in the heart are correlated to amylin detection levels in plasma and guide therapeutic intervention, quantitatively. These factors altogether make the proposal of moderately good impact.

imp_text: The overall goal of the research is to investigate the mechanistic role of Rnd 3, a Rho GTPase, in modulating Notch signaling (in endothelial cells) and HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling (in cardiomyocytes) as components of angiogenic response to cardiac stress. Although the PI name is stated as Todd Murphy, it is apparent from the biosketch publications that the PI under review is J Chang. The clinical significance of the research is the potential to understand new mechanisms of heart failure in the context of sub-optimal angiogenic response, and thereby lead to new therapeutic (drugs, gene therapy etc.) treatment modalities for heart disease. Elucidating the role of Rnd 3 in the two signaling mechanisms correlated to angiogenic response is an important innovative aspect of the grant. The experimental approaches are well-rationalized and the aims are independent yet synergistic to establish the novel molecular mechanisms. One weakness of the proposal is that the evaluation is qualitative rather than quantitative; in other words, the findings of the aims will reveal the novel roles of Rnd3 in the angiogenic responses but may not necessarily provide insight regarding how much of Rnd3 activity leads to what level of angiogenic response modulation. This kind of information may be important down the line to develop appropriate therapeutic strategies. Also, the research approach does not provide what number of animals will be needed for each aim in vivo component validation (i.e., what statistical analysis and significance will be considered in the context of success of the aim). Barring these issues, this is a well-written strong proposal with good impact.

imp_text: The goal of this grant application is to better understand the role of lipin 1 in regulating cardiac metabolism in the diabetic heart. The PI notes that cardiac disease in people with diabetes is extremely common and abnormalities in cardiac energy metabolism have been strongly implicated in diabetic cardiac dysfunction. To that end, the PI has demonstrated that lipin 1 is an important regulator of energy and lipid metabolism. Strengths of this proposal include an innovative idea backed up with sophisticated “-omic” approaches, a highly qualified PI and an excellent environment. Weaknesses include the lack of compelling preliminary data on lipin 1 in overtly diabetic hearts, an apparent lack of focus inherent in some of the proposed studies, lack of use of overt diabetic animal models, absence of statistical analysis plan in all the Aims, and the absence of any proposed translational studies involving human diabetes tissue samples. As a result, the proposed studies are unlikely to lead to a better understanding of the role of lipin 1 in cardiac metabolism abnormalities specifically in the diabetic heart.  Additionally, the translational potential for the outcomes cannot be determined.

study_section: Hemostasis and Thrombosis Study Section
imp_text: The goal of this proposal is to better understand the mechanisms that regulate platelet function and the thrombotic process. As the applicant points out, platelet aggregation is paramount in achieving hemostasis and controlling thrombosis but unwanted activation can lead to thrombotic disorders that culminate in MI or stroke.  To that end, the applicant has presented preliminary data suggesting that Apoptosis Signal-Regulated Kinase 1 (ASK1) belonging to the MAP Kinase Kinase Kinase family is expressed in platelets and is rapidly activated during platelet stimulation by a variety of platelet agonists.  Furthermore, the applicant also presents preliminary data that genetic ablation of ASK1 results in a strong anti-thrombotic phenotype in a variety of in vivo models of thrombosis. This preliminary data strongly supports the applicants hypothesis that ASK 1 is a novel regulator of platelet function and thrombosis and is a logical extension of his previous work. Strengths of this proposal include an innovative idea, multifaceted approach involving biochemical, pharmacological, and genetic approaches, a highly qualified PI and team of investigators, an excellent environment, and translational studies involving human platelets. Weaknesses include an over-extending of some of the proposed studies/Aims leading to lack of focus, absence of statistical analysis plan in all the Aims, and some instances of improper  sentence structure indicative of inadequate proof-reading. These weaknesses dampen enthusiasm to some extent for an otherwise highly significant grant proposal that has high potential to aide in developing new therapeutic strategies to combat cardiovascular disease resulting from thrombotic disorders.

study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: This proposal from an established investigator focuses upon investigating the cellular mechanisms whereby amylin deposition in the heart causes cardiac myocye dysfunction, in hyperamylinemic conditions as observed with diabetes and obesity. The experiments build upon prior observations that elevated circulating amylin levels are found in diabetic patients with insulin resistance as a result of amylin being co-secreted along with the hypersecretion of insulin from beta cells. The investigators will utilize a rat model with transgenic expression of human amylin in the rat beta cells, to examine whether amylin oligomers disrupt sarcolemmal integrity, activate calcium signaling in aim 1; whether altered cardiac metabolism or oxidative stress is observed in aim 2; and whether proteolytic agents plasmin and 14,15 EETs reduce amylin and work synergistically with membrane sealants to attenuate sarcolemmal damage and prevent activation of calcium signaling. The studies are feasible with a strong environment and excellent collaborative expertise. A major issue with the studies is the lack of specificity of the observations in both humans and the rat models; and the lack of experiments designed to conclusively address the hypotheses proposed. This dampens the overall enthusiasm for the proposal.

Preliminary data are presented to demonstrate that amylin trimers are found at much elevated levels in both obese and diabetic patients with heart failure, but not the non-obese counterparts. Also, rat myocytes challenged with human amylin demonstrate elevated cytosolic Ca2+ levels without a change in Serca levels suggesting increased influx of Ca. This was accompanied with HDAC4 export, speculatively as a result of CAMK activation and activation of NFATc4; and was prevented by co-incubation with 4EET. The hearts of HIP rats also demonstrate elevated BNP, LV dilation and diastolic dysfunction. . Cardiac myocytes will be studied from the HIP rats (and the glucose matched non-human amylin transgenic) control rats to evaluate for evidence of membrane permeabilization with dye leakage and patch clamping assays. . In aim 3, membrane sealants will be employed to determine if the effect of amylin on cardiac myocyte sarcolemmal permeabilization can be prevented and/or blunted
