Does this indicate that even in nondiabetic individuals, amylin is deposited in the heart. If so, is this toxic? If not, why? The authors indicate that the antibodies employed are specific (and point to reference 14), without demonstrating the specificity in the specific heart tissues that are presented in the data (by either omission of primary antibody or pre-adsorption with a synthetic peptide). In fact, the validity of the entire hypothesis rests on the specificity of these antibodies. imp_text: This is a well-written proposal from an established investigator with significant expertise in investigating cardiac cellular signaling. The proposal focuses upon the role of Rnd3, a small GTPase, which was found to be essential for embryonic development in the PI’s lab. Genetic ablation of Rnd3 resulted in hyperactivation of Notch signaling with hydrocephalus. Preliminary studies reveal the Rnd3 levels are reduced by ~50% in failing human hearts as compared with controls; and mice with haplo-insufficiency of Rnd3 are sensitive to pressure overload with impaired angiogenic response, resulting in cardiomyopathy. The PI hypothesizes that Rnd3 regulated VEGFA secretion from cardiac myocytes, and de-represses VEGFA receptor expression in endothelial cells via suppression of notch signaling. Aim 1 will examine the regulatory role of Rnd3 in endothelial cells on Notch signaling via effects on NICD, and two key Notch transcription co-factors mastermind-like 1 (Maml1) and CBF1, suppressor of hairless, Lag-1 (CSL). Aim 2 will examine the HIFa-VEGF transcriptional axis in cardiac myocytes, and evaluate whether Rnd3 enhances HIF1a transcriptional activity via increasing its stability and association with co-activators. Aim3 will introduce a Notch inhibitor, a VEGF and HIF1a agonist and re-express Notch in individual cell types to confirm the hypotheses investigated in aims 1 and 2. The hypotheses are well formulated, all tools and reagents are available to the PI; and the studies are feasible. The anticipated findings and alternative approaches are adequately discussed. Overall, a strong proposal with high likelihood for success.

imp_text: This proposal from an experienced investigator proposes to examine the role of ASK1, a MAPKKK5, downstream of GPCRs in platelets activation in response to prothrombotic stimuli. The overall hypothesis is that ASK1 signaling indices platelet activation via ERK and p38 signaling. The investigators will study ASK1 null mice, as well as mice with knock-in for a threonine residue mutant in ASK1 that is expected to be loss-of-function, as well as adoptive bone marrow transfer of ASK1 positive wild type marrow in the context of thrombotic insults. In aim 2, the applicant will examine activation of ERK and p38 pathways upon ASK1 activation and the downstream pro-thrombotic effects. Preliminary data are provided to demonstrate that ASK1 is expressed in human and mouse platelets, and that AKS1 null mice have presence of fecal blood with aging, and increased bleeding time. Additionally, these mice do not develop thrombosis as rapidly in injured carotid arteries and are somewhat resistance to other thrombotic events as pulmonary thromboembolism, and in vivo laser induced thrombosis of cremastric arterioles. Under aim 2, various signaling events that connect platelet GPCRA activation to ASK1 activation; as well as subsequent ASK1 signaling steps are being examined in WT and ASK1 null platelets exposed to prothrombotic agents. Various proteins and their phosphorylation states will be assessed under this specific aim. The goal is to map out the signaling cascade whereby ASK1 signals to induce platelet thrombosis. While the environment for the proposed studies is excellent and the investigator has put together a strong team of collaborators, there are issues with the approach and lack of producvitivty on part of the investigator that diminish overall enthusiasm.

imp_text: This application aims to define the role of rnd3 in the adaptive process of cardiac angiogenesis in response to heart failure. This proposal is highly significant and innovative because it explores an understudied area of relationships between heart and its vascular endothelium in response to stress. Strengths of this proposal also included the PI - with expertise for all aspects of the project - and supportive preliminary data. However, some minor to major weaknesses reduced enthusiasm for this application. This reviewer questions why the study does not use existing human endothelial cell models to confirm the molecular interactions of rnd3 in endothelial cells. In addition, the transgenic models proposed in Aim 3 may lead to a non-physiological concentration of rnd3, and thus difficulty interpreting the clinical relevance of the results. Overall, this study is expected to have a moderate impact on understanding the role of rnd3 in mediation of crosstalk between heart and its endothelium.

imp_text: There is a clear need for identifying new players in the complex regulation of platelet signaling.  The overall objective of the proposal is to understand the molecular mechanisms that are regulated by Ask1 in order to regulate platelet activation. To do that, two aims are proposed: Aim1 will evaluate the role of Ask1 in platelet function and thrombosis by using knockdown and knockin mice models with in vivo assessment of thrombosis and Aim2 will examine the signaling pathways that activate Ask1 using human and mice cell models. Strengths of this proposal include the PI, strong preliminary data supporting the hypothesis of the proposed research (e.g. indication that Ask1 plays a role in thrombosis), and use of state of the art technologies to study platelet function in vivo.  Major concerns that diminish enthusiasm of this proposal are that the platelet may not be the sole cell type whereby Ask1 plays a key role in thrombosis, uncertainty as to which phosphorylation site is key to regulating Ask1 activities and interactions with other proteins, and a lack of confirmatory experiments to ascertain specificities of the pharmacological drugs used.

imp_text: Loss of regulation of the inflammatory response contributes to the pathogenesis of several heart diseases. This application will study the PD-L1/PD1 pathway in the modulation of myocardial inflammation. The investigators have ample experience in the field, a very strong productivity record, and have developed many of the models used for these studies. This is a clearly written proposal, although its scope may be too ample for a single R01. The aims are well defined and will independently provide novel layers of information on the roles of PD-L1 and PD1 in the regulation of inflammation on different cell types involved on myocardial inflammation. There is strong and abundant preliminary data. A major plus is that therapeutic approaches are proposed through the proposal. Aim 3 particularly focuses on the translational potential of targeting this system. However, a major concern is that accomplishing the aims in this proposal may not be feasible in the timeframe of an R01, and the many animal and human studies proposed might be overwhelming for a postdoc and a research assistant devoting 100% and 40% effort to the project, respectively. However, even partial completion of these aims will likely have a significant impact on the field.

imp_text: This is a grant by a new investigation to study the interrelationship between a subset of calcium channels redox signaling and peripheral mitochondria localized to caveolae domains in arterial smooth muscle function. State-of-the-art microscopy techniques acquired by the applicant will be used; a major concern is that most of the experiments are descriptive. Loss-of-function experiments are based on the use of siRNA and, as the applicant acknowledges, some cells may not have sufficient protein downregulation. Experiments in Aims 1.3. and 2.3. will be performed on isolated arterial segments in absence of a functional endothelium and in the presence of a nitric oxide synthase inhibitor, i.e. under-non physiological conditions. It is stated that ‘the goal of this propodal is to identify molecular components necessary for functional coupling of Ca2+ and redox microdomains….’. Howeer, it is unclar how the proposed aims will fulfill this objective. The preliminary evidence in Fig. 12 seems insufficient to justify the hypothesis that the proposed mechanisms are the underlying cause of arterial dysfunction in diabetes. Lack of genetically modified models for in vivo studies is a major concern. Thus, the outcome of the studies is unlikely to provide mechanistic insights into events underlying arterial dysfunction in obesity.

study_section: Atherosclerosis and Inflammation of the Cardiovascular System Study Section
imp_text: This application will study the role in atherosclerosis development of Kalirin, which is the product of a gene that has been associated with both coronary artery disease and stroke in humans. Previous observations by the same group indicate that Kalirin increases intimal hyperplasia but protects against atherosclerosis in mice fed a Western diet. Together, the data from human association studies and from experimental models of atherosclerosis rise enthusiasm on the potential translational applications of these studies. In animal studies, mixed effects on different cell types present in atherosclerotic lesions are puzzling, and so are the multiple protein domains that might mediate both proatherogenic and antiatherogenic effects. However, the main effect seems to be atheroprotective. So far this has been assessed in studies on heterozygous KO mice, which displayed larger lesions. A drawback is that these studies have been performed only under Western diet. Other drawbacks are that studies have only been performed using heterozygous, and that gain of function studies have not been performed, nor are proposed in this application. Given that the working hypothesis is that kalirin is atheroprotective, atherosclerosis studies under gain of function seem critical to test the hypothesis and/or its potential therapeutic potential. Overall, the application is likely to have a medium impact in the field.

study_section: Atherosclerosis and Inflammation of the Cardiovascular System Study Section
imp_text: Both applicants propose investigating the role of the PD-L1/PD-1 ligand/receptor system in cardiac inflammation using a series of conditional knockout (KO) mice to tease out which cells are responsible for T-cell tolerance. The experimental plan for creating the knockouts and testing them is provided in detail and is well thought out. Despite the extensive descriptions, the research plan could have used a flow chart to help the reader keep track of the numerous crosses of mice with the Cre/lox system the applicants propose creating (or have already created). The applicants will use a CD8+ T cell mediated model and a CD4+ model as well. In Specific Aim 1, the applicants focus on the role of the ligand, PD-L1, and the cells which would trigger an auto-immune response (specifically, endothelial cells, cardiomyocytes and dendritic cells). The applicants also propose investigating the role PD-L1 plays in chronic inflammation and ventricular remodeling. And finally, they propose investigating whether cytokine therapeutics can induce PD-L1 in the myocardium to protect against T-cell mediated myocarditis. In Specific Aim 2, the applicants focus on the role of the receptor, PD-1, in particular, if its presence on myeloid cells plays a role in protecting the heart from T-cell mediated inflammation. They also propose investigating the role of PD-1 in the immune response following ischemia and reperfusion using a standard artery ligation to create a myocardial infarction. In Specific Aim 3, the proposal takes on more of a translational goal by investigating the use of statins plus rapamycin to increase PD-L1 expression on dendritic cells and seeing if this induces CD4+ T or CD8+ cell tolerance to cardiac antigens. The proposal will also look at whether PD-L1 upregulation is specifically binding the PD-1 receptor or some other receptor to induce the CD4+ T cell tolerance. And whether KLF2 plays a role in tolerizing the T-cells. Overall, there is a lot of work here and the creation of the strains of conditional mutants will take time. The proposal calls for extensive functional investigations in the ischemia model, including echocardiography. There is some concern whether the personnel listed, a yet to be hired and trained post-doc and a research assistant are sufficient to complete the work despite the 5 year time frame. Furthermore, the proposal to gather human cardiac tissues to investigate the presence of PD-L1 upregulation in inflamed human myocardium (Specific Aim C1D) does not fit in with the overall plan. That should really be a separate grant proposal. If the experimentation proposed in the KO mice clarifies the role of PD-L1, then more informed studies can be carried out with the human tissues. However, on a positive note, this is a very worthy study that would help establish potential new druggable targets in cardiovascular indications.

The applicants have detailed their approach for creating and testing all of the conditional mutants. . The applicants are exploring several key cell types that express PD-L1. . The applicants answer basic research questions and establish a path for translational research by investigating the possible upregulation of PD-L1 in dendritic cells using statins and rapamycin. In the “Alternative Approaches” section of Specific Aim 1, the authors state: “We have proposed a more complete interrogation of lineage- specific roles of PD-L1 ( EC, CM, and DC) in the CD8+ T cell mediated cMY-mOva model, than in the CD4+ T cell mediated EAM model (BM, EC). In order to test if myocyte or DC PD-L1 regulates CD4+ T cell-mediated myocarditis in the EAM model, we would have to breed the aMHC-myosin driven Cre or the CD11C-Cre onto the BALB/c background. We will do this only if our studies in A1 indicate that myocyte or DC PD-L1 plays a regulatory role in the CD8+ cMy-mOVa model.” This statement, while prudent, highlights the delays that can occur in completing all of the specific aims. . There is a lot of mouse work proposed. The survey of human tissues to determine if PD-L1 is upregulated in myocarditis should be put into a separate grant. Possibly in a grant with a greater translational research orientation. . The applicants propose testing in a standard myocardial infarction model whether myeloid PD-1 protects the myocardium from inflammation after ischemia and reperfusion. The ligation of the artery occurs for 30 minutes, during which time the LV cavity is injected with fluorescent microspheres. Some mice are sacrificed at 24 hours, others at 48 hours after reperfusion. The applicants need to account for the possibility that the presence of fluorescent microspheres alone, regardless of injection into Pdcd1 fl/fl or wt/wt mice, will cause some inflammation. The applicants should consider having equal numbers of fl/fl and wt/wt mice as sham controls which will receive an LV cavity injection of the vehicle buffer for the flourescent microspheres. . Given the complexity of the program, the applicants should have provided a graphical timeline estimating the duration and chronological order of each sub-aim during the 5 year funding period.

study_section: Vascular Cell and Molecular Biology Study Section
imp_text: The applicant proposes a series of studies to test a model where NADPH oxidase and L-type calcium channels (in particular, CaV 1.2), in proximity to one another on the plasma membrane, create a redox and calcium “microdomain”. He hypothesizes that an increased ROS and an influx of Ca2+ results in arterial smooth muscle dysfunction. A series of well structured experiments are laid out in 3 specific aims. In Specific Aim 1, the involvement of Caveolin-1 and calveolar structures in the coupling of NADPH oxidase and L-type calcium channels is investigated using functional and structural assays. In Specific Aim 2, the role of mitochondria within close proximity to the NADPH oxidase and L-type calcium channels is investigated. In particular, the applicant wishes to determine if NADPH oxidase generated ROS help upregulate the generation of ROS by the mitochondria, in turn increasing the influx of Ca2+. Specific Aim 3, adds a translational aspect to the study by looking at obesity models in rats and investigating whether increases in the ROS and Ca2+ microdomains are a hallmark of arterial dysfunction. Overall the use of multiple complimentary methods, including pharmacological inhibition, siRNA, calcium sensors, rat obesity models, state-of-the-art fluorescent proteins, antibodies, electron microscopy and TIRF microscopy are well thought out. That is why it is perplexing to find an error that goes beyond being a simple typo. Figures 4, 5, 6 and 8 all reference the publication: “Murray et al. 2010 Circ Res; 107(8):1002-10”. When I went to look for this reference in the bibliography, I initially did not find it. All of the references are in alphabetical order, except the Murray references, which appear to have been thrown in last minute as Ref. 4, 5 and 6. When looking up these references, in PubMed, they belong to Amberg, not Murray. There appears to be more than a typographical error, since these papers have all been published by Gregory Amberg. The Murray 2010 Circ Res paper lists the authors as Murray, Evans, Glapa. Evans is actually Scott Earley. Both Murray and Evans have provided Biosketches with their names on the publication when the real authors are Amberg, Earley and Glapa. This is more than an oversight and an explanation should be provided by the applicants. Now, the names were probably changed by the committee as part of this exercise, but I’m penalizing the guy who did a sloppy job of hiding the authors’ identities.

imp_text: The applicants propose a series of microscopy studies to elucidate the structural organization of a-granules populating platelets. The project also proposes to identify a mechanism of action for the delivery of cargo proteins from the granules to the platelet surface during activation. In Specific Aim #1, the applicants propose several orthogonal microscopic techniques (conventional electron tomography, STEM tomography, and 3D-SIM super-resolution light microscopy) to address their hypothesis that a heterogenous population of a­granules does not exist, rather, the proteins are zonally distributed within each granule. In Specific Aim #2, they want to determine whether extensions seen emanating from some a­granules in preliminary data represent actual subdomains containing segregated distributions of cargo proteins. They also want to test whether these tubular extensions may be sites of SNARE and docking proteins for specific interaction with the platelet surface and the OCS. To test this “Spigot” hypothesis, they propose using platelets from several knockout mice lacking key SNARE and docking proteins in order to see if images can be captured of the a-granules in an intermediate state prior to fusion with the plasma membrane. They propose using the complementary approaches of electron microscopy, time-lapse fluorescence microscopy and protein colocalization using antibodies. Finally, in Specific Aim #3, they propose testing the hypothesis that von Willebrand Factor and cytoskeletal elements (microfilaments and microtubules) provide structural support for the Spigot mechanism. They propose using VWF deficient human and mouse platelets, as well as chemical inhibitors of cytoskeletal polymerization to elucidate the roles of each structural element. Overall, the approach is well planned and uses several orthogonal approaches to help clarify an important aspect of platelet function.

imp_text: This is an excellent proposal from an experienced and well-accomplished in the field investigator to look at the characteristics of human platelet alpha granules with an eye towards structure-function relationships. The investigators propose to do an exhaustive and elegant array of imaging techniques determine dynamics of granule makeup with regard to cargo and spatial orientation in the cell. The work will involve state-of-the-art imaging techniques. The alpha granule is the major secretory organelle of the platelet, and there is no question that new and important information relating to granule content and interactions will be forthcoming that could relate to important platelet functions, such as thrombosis. Although this probably represents elegant imaging procedures, enthusiasm for this application is tempered by the fact that that it’s all morphology and imaging. There are no correlative functional studies included. While it could be that a lot of structural hints do translate into function, others may not. What if all these granules are indeed compartmentalized but it turns out that this structure has no functional meaning; e.g. they all get released at the same time. This is not downplaying the importance of these imaging studies, and this PI has really done some elegant work in the area, but imaging not in conjunction with functional studies loses a lot of impact.

imp_text: This is a new application for an R01 that focuses on inflammatory responses in the heart. The project investigates the PD-L1/PD-1 pathway that the investigators have previously shown to modulate myocardial inflammation in mice. Aim 1 tests the hypothesis that PD-L1 produces distinctive protective functions in different cell types. Aim 2 tests whether PD-1/PD-L1 directly regulates myeloid cell inflammatory responses. Aim 3 is to develop PD-1/PD-L1-dependent methods to induce T cell tolerance to myocardial antigens as a potential new therapy for myocardial inflammation. The main strengths of this application are the investigators and the environment. Both are in the outstanding to exceptional range. The innovation was very good but it’s not clear from the proposal that the research is breaking new ground as opposed to being an incremental development of the field. The research plan provided an enormous amount of technical detail but the overall plan was difficult to follow and the impact of the work outside the immediate field was not made obvious. Another factor that weakened the overall impact was a concern that the PD-L1/PD-1 pathway may not be a major factor in human patients. The plan includes a single example of human myocardium expressing PD-L1 but there are no data showing that the pathway is differentially affected in human myocardial inflammation. This was a major weakness.

imp_text: This is a new application for an R01 that focuses on caveolae and mitochondria in arterial smooth muscle. Aim 1 tests the hypothesis that ROS and calcium signal synergistically in microdomains. Aim 2 tests the hypothesis that a subpopulation of peripheral mitochondria modulate functional coupling of redox and Ca2+ microdomains. Aim 3 studies the same mechanisms in animal models of obesity. The main strength is the environment for this work at Colorado State University where there is a strong group of investigators with relevant skills. The PI has many strengths but the relatively low rate at which he has published manuscripts as a first or senior author since starting his independent position was a minor weakness. The innovation was moderate. Although the concept that Ca2+ and ROS may interact synergistically in local microdomains is interesting, it is not very surprising. The research plan was also judged to be moderate. While it was exceptionally clear, many of the experiments were only vaguely defined. It was also unclear how the data would be interpreted and how the experiments would provide definitive information about cross-talk between ROS and Ca2+. The research was descriptive and incremental. imp_text: This is a New R01 application from a senior investigator. The central goal of the proposed study is to determine the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which Kalirin reduces atherosclerosis. Kalirin has been shown to be associated with human coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke. It contains two GEF domains and several protein-protein interaction domains. Preliminary data show that Kalirin deficiency diminishes SMC Rac signaling and Kalrn heterozygous mice develop less neointima after injury. The strength of this proposal includes the experiences of the PI in the field of EC biology and atherosclerosis, the scientific environment and the significance of the study. However, the innovation of current proposal is moderate and some of the approach proposed are not very well rationalized. Power study is missing to justify animal number.

imp_text: This is a New R01 application from a senior investigator. The central goal of the proposed study is to address a fundamental questions in platelet biology: Are platelets an active participant specifically releasing context-appropriate material from their a-granules or are they random delivery devices, and how cargo is released from alpha-granules? Three Aims are proposed to test the hypothesis: 1) test the hypothesis that human platelets contain a single major a-granule population in which individual cargo proteins are packaged into distinct zones; 2) test the hypothesis that specialized a-granule subdomains/extensions provide a spatial basis for differential membrane fusion/protein secretion to the plasma membrane/OCS in response to agonists; 3) test the hypothesis that VWF and/or cytoskeletal elements provides an organizing principle for platelet a-granule structure and function. The proposal is very significant that understanding the structure and mechanisms of protein releasing from platelets will provide a reference framework for future therapeutic design. The proposal also provides innovative hypothesis and novel methods for the field of platelet biology. The strength of this application also includes highly experienced and productive PI and research team and excellent scientific environment. The approaches are hypothesis driven and rigorously designed using state of art techniques.

imp_text: This proposal is to study biological role of Foxo (1 and 3) transcription factors (TFs) for control/regulation of T cell memory. Actually, role of Foxo TFs on all subsets of T cells for their differentiation and activation has been determined, whereas the applicant strategically pushes the study in depth to a specific T cell subpopulation (memory T cells), and links the study to viral infection-related memory to bring up clinical significance of Foxo TFs. Aim 1 is the strongest aim in this proposal to study how Foxo TFs regulate CD8 memory T cell’s recalling response in the second time CMV infection using multiple genetically manipulated mouse models, including loss-of-function (Foxo1 knockout or both Foxo1 and Foxo3 double knockout), as well as Foxo1 knockout combining with IL-7R transgenic mouse. Studies on the phenotypes in these models will lead to findings to answer the questions of a, b, c, d, e, and f, which are raised by the applicant in pages 40 – 42. These questions are gaps of knowledge and goals of each experiment in Aim 1. Aims 3 and 4 are also strong. The applicant tries to mechanistically determine how Tfh (follicular helper T cells) and TCM (central memory T cells) are programmed under the Foxo TFs’ regulation, via analyses of differentiation (Tfh and CMP – CD4 central memory precursor), formation of germinal centers, and maintenance for TCM. The applicant also tries to determine “elite controller” for control of persistent viruses. Aims 3 and 4 will use many kinds of genetically engineered mouse models as well. However, Aim 2 is relatively not as strong as the other three aims, in which the applicant tries to determine Foxo TF targeted genes in CD8 (memory) T cells. It looks like this is only a description of gene increase or decrease with a fishing method. In this proposal, the applicant included solid preliminary data, generated many different types of necessary genetically engineered mouse models via long-term crossbreeding, designed a large number of question-based experiments to address the gaps of knowledge, and invited strong complementary collaborators to enhance the applicant’s shortages. Although it is an outstanding proposal, it is still imperfect, because the proposal did not explain why the following three aspects cannot pay more attentions and provide more considerations. 1. For studying T cell memory, vaccination models should be better and closer to clinical significance than the latent viral (such as CMV) infection models that the applicant proposed to use. CMV model may not exactly reflect the immune memory, because CMV cannot be completely cleared up by immune system and the virus accumulates with host’s age. CMV persistently stimulates immune system (either lowly or highly) without a negative period. Therefore, it is hard to tell when the period of memory is, and which cells are new or old “memory T cells”. 2. The applicant will use a loss-of-function model (Foxo gene knockout) to study all the questions. If the applicant want to fully address these questions, a gain-of-function (Foxo gene overexpression) model may be necessary or complementary. 3. It looks like that Foxo TFs are required for differentiation and activation in all types of T cells (such as Treg, CD4+ T cells, CD8+ effector T cells -- throughout T cell biology). This study focuses on Foxo TFs in T memory. It is unclear whether Foxo TFs are T memory intrinsic requirement or there is any T memory cell type-specific aspect for Foxo TFs? Although the applicant will use GzmBCre or Cd8Cre (both genes are expressed in CTLs), it only provides information about that Foxo1 is required for cytotoxic CD8 T cells, but it is hard to directly link to memory specific requirement.

Studying Foxo transcription factor-regulated immune memory by linking cellular metabolism, differentiation, and immune function will provide insights into immune memory associated with vaccination and infection. . To address the gaps of knowledge in Foxo TFs’ control of T cell memory, the applicant uses a large number of question-based experimental designs. It is very impressive. . Solid preliminary data, which almost reach to a published level, strongly support the proposed experiments. . A number of elegant genetically engineered mouse models, which are many years’ efforts, are available to assist with the proposed studies. . Many experiments are elegant, such as, Foxo 1 and 3 double knockout; linking to IL-7R signaling; timing deletion of Foxo1 gene; cellular energy consume in vivo test (metabolism); three adaptive transplantation sets for study on genetic and cellular complementation, etc.
app_text_wkn: . Aim 2a is to determine Foxo dependent genes with gene array using sorted CD8 T cells from Foxo1 deficient and sufficient mice. It looks like this is only a description with a fishing method. After candidate genes are obtained, it is unclear how the applicant will validate these genes. In addition, direct target locus in these genes need to be identified, while ChIP-Seq (Aim 2b) is still a large scale of screen, but not detailed validation. Whereas, Aim 2c is to identify the binding sites on Foxo1 gene. Since Foxo1 is a transcription factor (TF) and Aim 2 is to determine this TF targeted/dependent genes, it is unclear how the applicant identifies the binding sites on Foxo1 targeted genes (rather than Foxo1 itself) and how many candidate genes are expected to be identified. . The writing is too density so that there is few experimental detail for the proposed approaches throughout the four aims. Therefore, it is hard to assess whether the experimental outcomes are able to address the questions. . It is the lack of explanations for intricate genetically engineered mouse models being used. Particularly, some models are somehow redundant without explanation about why similar mouse models will be used and how they provide what different information. For example, GzmBCre and Cd8Cre (both genes are expressed in CTLs) will be used to delete Foxo3 or Foxo1 (Aim-4, page-47). It is unclear what different outcomes the applicant anticipates? . There is no pitfall discussed, although some alternative strategies are addressed in the experiments.

imp_text: Role of actin-bundling protein L-plastin (LPL) on peripheral lymphocyte (T- and B-cell) motility has been previously known prior to the application submitted (role on T cell motility published in 2010 and role on B cell motility published in 2011, by the applicant and others). Whereas, this application tries to address role of three LPL protein domains on peripheral B-cell motility in lymph nodes (LNs) (Aim 1); and to determine the interactive proteins in integrin adhesion complex, related to up- and down-stream of kinase Pyk2 signaling, under the background of LPL-knockout B cells (Aim 2); as well as re-assess the role of LPL on B-cell motility with cell type-specific (conditional) loss-of-LPL in B cells (Aim 3). This could be an excellent project, because although the role of LPL in T and B cell motility has been known, molecular characteristics of LPL associated with its role are unknown. For example, the key LPL domain(s) (Aim 1) and LPL interactive network proteins (Aim 2) associated with the role, and role of LPL uniquely/intrinsically to B cells (Aim 3) are necessary to be investigated for the insights. However, Aim 1 is relative weak and very risky, because PI has no experience in bone marrow transplantation (BMT) and lentiviral transform of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), and no any DNA construction (for LPL domains) ready. If failure in experiment-1A, all other Aim-1 experiments (1B and 1C) will be unable to carry out (I will provide details in #4-Approach section). This reduces enthusiasm of whole project. After reading Aim 3, which will use a novel LPL-floxed/CD19-Cre conditional knockout mouse model, one will recognize that all previous experiments about role of LPL on B-cell motility are not B cell type-specific, and the data may include effect/co-effect of T or other cells on B-cell motility. The phenotype from tissue- or cell type-specific conditional knockout of a gene may provide unexpected results compared to knockout of the same gene in all tissue or all cell types. Particularly, for the LPL gene, which plays a role in both B and T cells, and B and T cells are interacting in the LNs. Therefore, it is necessary to re-assess previous findings about specific/intrinsic role of LPL on B-cell motility. Obviously, with this novel mouse model this aim will provide strong B-cell type-specific information about LPL’s role. If there is any different outcomes obtained from this Aim, the previous studies on LPL’s role in B-cell motility could be modified. It is good for updating previously known information, but could be bad for the designed experiments in Aims 1 and 2, which probably should be reconsidered or redesigned.

The applicant should show how many % she can reach; 2) Using HSCs (which will be isolated from WT mice, what molecular markers the applicant will be based on: lineage negative, ckit+, sca1+ …?) to reconstitute lethally irradiated recipient mice should accompany with syngeneic bone marrow (BM) cells to ensure survival. How the applicant design this accompanying BM cells (i.e. molecular marker usage)? 3) The applicant should also have a strategy about how to subclone these LPL domains (Table in page-45) into lentiviral arms. . In Aim 2, the applicant will determine protein-protein interaction (PPI). However, the approaches/methods that the applicant will use are very vague. For example, The applicant will determine more 15 phosphorylated proteins (kinases, GTPases, motor protein, and calcium protein) with immunoblotting (Western blot) in C.3.2.A and 2.B (page-48). It is unclear why many high throughput methods, such as proteomics and mass spectroscopy, will not be used? It is unclear whether so many phosphor-specific antibodies are available? . Aim 2 did not provide any preliminary data. At least the applicant should show she has an ability to conduct proposed experiments. For example, in Aim 2 the applicant tries to look at polarization of certain molecules in stimulated LPL knockout B cells with confocal microscope. She should show what the polarization image looks like. . Aim 3 did not provide any preliminary data as well. It is probably due to the LPL-floxed mice are not ready. Aim 3 is still in underdevelopment. Even if the model is underdevelopment, the PI still can do some pilot work. For example, in C.3.3.D, it is unclear why the applicant cannot use LPL knockout (non-conditional) mice to test West Nile Viral (WNV) infection. If this non-conditional LPL knockout mouse is more susceptible to WNV, then think about using LPL-floxed CD19-Cre conditional gene knockout mice. The PI planed to wait for 2 -2.5 years until LPL-floxed CD19-Cre ready to test this proposal. If failure, time almost runs out.

imp_text: This is a really exceptional proposal, focusing on studying signaling through chemokine receptor CXCR4 and IL-7R on regulation of developing B lymphocyte movement in and interaction with their bone marrow (BM) microenvironment. The strengths of the proposal are conceptual advance, many elegant experimental designs, solid preliminary data coinciding with each hypothesis, and concise writing style. Aim-1 will address how CXCR4 in BM stromal cell-constituted microenvironment affects B cell development, which is a current hot topic about how the “soil” regulates/controls development of the “seeds”. Although this aim is simple, it is pretty straightforward, and will address an important topic, which is neglected and contains many gaps of knowledge in either B-cell development. Aim-2 will address how CXCR4 is required for guiding common lymphoid progenitor (CLP) cells moving towards IL-7+ BM stromal cells. Although this aim is relative weak in this proposal due to unclear rationale in some experiments (I will give more details in #4-Approach section), the conceptual advance, which is that IL-7R signaling should be appropriately arranged in a spatial and temporal manner for B cell development, outweighs the minor concerns. Aim 3 is the strongest part in this proposal. imp_text: Myocardial inflammation has the potential to impair protective pathways in the myocardium in response to a variety of cardiac stressors. The goal of the current grant application is to better understand the role of innate and adaptive immunity in the heart in general and the specific role that PD-1 and PD-L1 play in multiple cell types in the heart to regulate the inflammatory response. Three aims are proposed: the first will determine which cell type mediates the PD-L1 dependent protection against T cells in the heart, how this protection occurs, and the feasibility to therapeutically target this protection; the second aim will determine if PD-1-PD-L1 pathway regulates myeloid cell inflammatory responses in the heart; and the third aim will develop PD-1:PD-L1 dependent methods to therapeutically induced T cell tolerance to myocardial antigens. The aims are overambitious and not well focused.  The look at ever possible cell with similar endpoints assessed in various parts and then focus look at one or two specific cells in other parts.  Focus on a single cell type with in depth development of experiments exploring mechanisms and therapeutics would be more useful and feasible.  There is lac of most targeted mice, since this represents a bulk of the proposed studies, it would be nice if these mice were ready to go for the proposed studies.  A MPI approach is undertaken but there is little effort to develop a rationale for why these two specific PIs are needed and what they add synergistically to the project. Overall this is a loosely focused, overly ambitious project that as proposed is likely to not yield significant new insight. As such enthusiasm is low.

imp_text: Smooth muscle contraction is regulated by L type calcium channel function, however, specifics mechanisms that regulated calcium channel function and how this is regulated in the setting of disease such as diabetes is unknown.  The goal of this project is to determine if caveolae serve to regulate and converge oxidant and calcium signaling in smooth muscle cells by creating proximity to mitochondria. Three aims are proposed.  The first aim determine if NADPH oxidase and L-type calcium channels co-localize in caveolae to couple redox and calcium microdomains. The second aim will determine if a subpopulation of peripheral mitochondria modulate this coupling. The final aim will determine if this coupling contributes to arterial dysfunction in obesity. Aims 1 and 2 largely explore the control condition with Ang II stress on the system.  The integration of obesity appears to be an afterthought to the design of the experiments and conceptualization.  This is a strong element of the proposal that is not well developed of integrated.  Aims 1 and 2 also have a number of methodological limitations and thought multiple aspect including redox and calcium signaling are to be studies the only manipulation appears to that of disrupting caveolin.  Why not also disrupt these other elements to establish a better understanding of the relationship as a whole.  The distinction of NADPH oxidase driven vs mitochondrial ROS may be problematic. The mitochondrial subpopulation hypothesis is interesting but not well developed.  It would be important to define these specific populations and how they change with pathology in vascular smooth muscle.  Aim 3 is not well integrated and a lot missing.  The PI is a junior investigator, there is some concern with lack of senior author productivity given that the PI has had some independent funding for some time. The environment is strong for microscopy but appears limited for in vivo modeling and studies. Overall enthusiasm if somewhat limited for this application.

Understanding the regulation of redox signaling and how it links with calcium signaling in the setting of vascular physiology and pathophysiology is significant and has potential for defining novel mechanisms. . Focus on vascular changes with obesity are also significant as they may help to explain vascular changes in diseases such as diabetes.

imp_text: Platelets are a major source of secreted material that has potent biological effects; however, it is unclear of this secretion random ore dependent on biological cues. The goal of the project is to determine if there is specificity to granule packaging and release in platelets. Three aims are proposed. The first will determine if cargo proteins are packaged into distinct granule compartments. The second aim will determine if there are granule subdomains that provide bias with regard to different membrane fusion/protein secretion especially in response to different agonist cues.  The final aim will determine cellular mechanisms that contribute to the organization of structure and function. The aims are well developed and described and supported by preliminary data.  The experiments are expected to yield important descriptive as well as mechanistic information. The PI is established and productive and the environment is strong. imp_text: The RO1 proposes to determine the structure-function relationship that determines how the a-granule, the major secretory organelle of the platelet is organized functionally to support agonist-diverse secretory responses.  Addressing this question seems to be important as it will provide a fundamental knowledge for how the residing proteins in platelets are packed and how they respond to stimulations. The information obtained will be important for understanding the platelet physiology critical for hemostasis as a-granules plays a critical role in aggregating in platelet plugs to seal leaks at sites of vascular injury, which in turn provide any rationale for any attempts of therapeutic design targeting clot formation.

The proposed studies proposed a novel “zonal packaging” hypothesis to explain how the proteins in the a-granules are likely organized and how they respond to stimulation.

imp_text: Cardiac inflammation is seen in a multitude of cardiovascular diseases, and there is currently drug trials being used to asses a role in modulating inflammatory conditions in combination with treatment for MI.  Thus, from a translational perspective this work is very important.  The work uses a combination of inducible knockout mice, human samples, and cell culture all focused on the role of PD-1 and PD-L1 in the heart.  The researchers have prior experience in the area, and have already made important discoveries.  Here they extend their work by determining possible roles for endothelial cells, and/or immune cells (namely T-cells).  There is significant enthusiasm in all areas for this application.
sig_text_str: . Myocardial inflammation is an important pathological development in several CV disease etiologies. imp_text: This application, submitted from a “rising star” in the smooth muscle calcium field, builds upon many years of calcium signaling in smooth muscle cells using state-of-the-art techniques.  The central hypothesis is that there is a signaling microdomain in smooth muscle cells between caveolla and mitochondria that regulates calcium dynamics, in terms regulating ROS.  This concept provided some initial enthusiasm.  However, the overall grant lacked a tangible disease focus or problem to solve, was overly reliant on calcium dynamics, and lacked an overall novelty or paradigm shift.  Indeed a lot of this work has been done in cell culture already, so the onerous is on the investigators not to simply show that it occurs in arterioles, but to expand this knowledge both functionally and at the cellular level.

imp_text: This application seeks to more fully understand platelet granule secretion and how platelets may differentially release vesicles.  The application proposes to use a large range of microscopy techniques including electron microscopy and quantitative fluorescence microscopy to elucidate their aims.  This work will be coupled with platelets from knockout mice and humans to more fully decipher the proposed mechanism.  Overall, the PI has outstanding microscopy expertise and significant research experience in exocytosis.  However, the grant is focused on a hypothesis with limited implications for human pathology.  In addition, the application is completely reliant on microscopy techniques without using molecular approaches that could better answer the question.

imp_text: Overall Impact Score (1-9):  5 This new application will examine how oxidant and calcium signals influence each other to cause contraction of blood vessels.  The project has high significance as a possible therapeutic approach for the treatment of arterial dysfunction in obesity.  The innovation in the work relates to the concept that the physiological response of vascular contraction arises from co-loalized and synergistically linked micordomains regulating reactive oxygen species generation and calcium entry.  A significant weakness is that the largely pharmacological approach is not validated with preliminary data for all three aims.  As acknowledged by the applicant, a more direct approach would use knock out mice as an important tool.  It is stated that the experiments will be performed principally on cerebral arteries but that two others would be included.  The rationale for repeating the core experiments in 3 arteries is not clearly stated and the issue of tachyphlaxis to angiotensin II is not addressed.  The overall impact of the proposed work is very good.
sig_text_str: • The overall goal of this program is to establish a more complete understanding of mechanisms underlying calcium signaling in the vasculature.  The work has high significance with respect to altered contractile properties of the vessel wall in hypertension and other cardiovascular diseases. • This research proposal addresses novel molecular mechanisms for oxidant and calcium signaling in subcellular organelles.

This is non-ligand dependent and may play an important role in experiments examining pressurized arteries. • Preliminary data supporting aim 3 is not extensive.  Additionally, this aim is over ambitious and not realistic.  Two animal models will be characterized on two different diets at 3 different ages.  Further, a dietary intervention is proposed along with sleeve gastrectomy to study weight loss. • In several places in the application, it is stated that key experiments will be replicated in caveolin-1 knock out mice.  While the rationale is clear, there is concern that this will be difficult because of the arteries will be much smaller. imp_text: This proposal aims to discover how cardiac inflammation is regulated by endothelial, myocyte, and dendritic cell PD-L1, and by myeloid PD-1. It is also very focused on complex transgenic models that may be difficult to control for, especially the bone marrow chimeras. There is a myopic focus on the role of cell type specific PD-L1 and where the immunoregulatory effects are most important for myocardial inflammation. Since it is postulated that endothelial PD-L1 is of critical relevance to myodarditis, but there are few experiments where the mechanism is truly tested. There are many experiments described to limit expression in one cell expressing PD-L1 or PD-1 but not how the ligand is signaling and delivered. How is protection conferred? A strength is the development of a number of potentially useful leukocyte conditional knockouts that may be used to tease apart mechanism at level of tissue or hematopoietic cell level. study_section: Vascular Cell and Molecular Biology Study Section
imp_text: This proposal examines Ca2+ and redox signaling and their functional relation to arterial smooth muscle regulated hypertension brought on by obesity. It is supported by an innovative approach using a combination of TIRF to quantify ROS and Ca2+ microdomains in smooth muscle cells. Also EM will provide structural evidence for a tight relationship between ROS, L-type Ca2+ channels, and plasmalemmal caveolae. While this information will provide qualitative data on the correlation between these events, they will not provide a detailed mechanism defining how these changes are necessarily a consequence of obesity and how this relates to development of hypertension beyond what is already well defined at a correlative level. The strongest element of this proposal is the wealth of preliminary data and feasibility demonstrated for the technique of coupling local NADPH redox activity with L-type Ca2+ function. Many of the studies that relate the two functions rely on pharmacological inhibitors applied to excised tissues to establish cause-effect in functional coupling NADPH redox and Ca2+ activity. For instance, simultaneous imaging of these events at the cell level are not in place and a key question is how these interact and go awry in disease. There is enthusiasm for the transgenic approaches to provide more direct evidence rather than simply imaging approaches. However, these are simply siRNA knockdown and identifying how NOX isoforms influence ROS and Ca2+ sparklets are more direct. However, there is not a firm plan in place to relate these to the observed hypertension that develops in obesity. Also a more defined disease state resulting in hypertension would provide additional evidence for the Ca2+ and ROS link to caveoli. The details and analysis in Aim 3 are not well described in the brief writeup devoted to this section.

imp_text: This proposal addresses the importance of Kalirin to determine its role in atherogenesis, which has been inferred from epidemiological and genomic screening studies. Since it contains a guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) for monomeric G proteins of the Rho family and may directly activate Rac1 and RhoA, it is implicated as playing diverse roles in atherosclerosis as a function of tissue expression. The approach describes a thorough approach using a heterozygous crossbred model that drops Kalirin expression by 50% and is associated with exacerbated athero. The strategy to examine its role in endothelium as well as macrophages and from molecular expression to cell function is a strength of this proposal and increases enthusiasm for this systems approach to defiing mechanism of action when it is increased or decreased in respective cell types associated with atherogenesis. One weakness is the lack of capacity to completely knockout Kalirin expression since the mouse have a nonviable phenotype. Not always clear how 50% expression of the protein very significantly alters atherosclerosis or provides rescue.

imp_text: The objective of this project is to understand how cardiac inflammation is regulated by endothelial, monocyte/macrophage and dendritic cell PDL-1 and myeloid PD-1.  These surface molecules vary in their extent of protection of the inflammatory heart diseases.  It is proposed that a clear understanding of these processes and expression of these molecules in different cells on the heart may lead to treatment of Myocardial inflammation.  The project will take advantage of the newly developed animal models which lack PD-1 and PDL-1.  The proposal is clearly written with limited preliminary results that support their hypotheses.  Aim 1 will determine which cell types mediate the PDL-1 dependent protection against T cells in the heart, the mechanism of protection and testing possible therapeutic modalities that may engage in these mechanisms.  Aim 2 will test hypothesis that the PD-1/PDL-1 pathway directly regulate myeloid cell inflammatory response in the heart. Aim 3 focusses on the development of PD-1:PDL-1 dependent methods to therapeutically induced T cell tolerance to myocardial antigens.  It is important to gain information on cell types that express PDL-1. The PI and his team have developed mouse models to test their hypotheses.  This is a strong investigative team.  Based on previous experience of the investigative team, it is believed that new and useful information will be obtained in treating inflammation in the myocardium.  This is therefore an outstanding application.

imp_text: The excellent application proposes to study the anti-atherogenic role of Kalirin in animal models.  The main goal of this project is to ascertain the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which kalirin reduces atherosclerosis.  The mouse models are all based on apoE null mice.  Three specific aims are proposed 1. To determine if kalirin reduces atherosclerosis via its interaction with either RhoGEF1 domain or iNOS-interacting domain or both. Aim 2 is to investigate molecular mechanisms by which EC kalirin reduces atherosclerosis and Aim 3 will determine molecular mechanisms by which macrophage kalirin reduces atherosclerosis by defining Kalirin’s Rac- and RhoGEF activity in macrophages, whether kalirin augments LPS-induced IL-10 and whether apoE-/- mice with macrophage-specific kalirin haplosufficiency induces enhanced atherosclerosis.  The application is carefully written with very good preliminary results so support specific aims.  However, since it is clear that in murine models of atherosclerosis, apoE is very important to protect against atherosclerosis, it is somewhat surprising that the PI has not suggested such experiments in LDL-R-/- mice to determine if overexpression of kalirin exerts protective effect.  It is also surprising that the PI has not suggested overproduction of kalirin in apoE null or LDL-R null mice to determine the role of apoE in kalirin-mediated inhibition of atherosclerosis.  Particularly since both apoE and kalirin play important role in the brain, role of apoE in Kalirin-mediated protection of atherosclerosis could have been addressed using LDL-R null mice. It is also surprising that discussions on lipid changes are absent, particularly since the PI states that changes are observed in high fat diet administered Kalm-/+-apoE-/- mice and not on the normal diet. Overall, the proposal is carefully written and the PI is highly qualified.  However, several concerns regarding the design of experiments somewhat dampens enthusiasm.

Furthermore, since WD fed mice but not normal diet fed mice are used for these investigations, lipid changes may be more important in protein-protein interactions.

imp_text: This is an outstanding application by a researcher who has extensive experience in defining structural organization of platelet granules.  The major question “are platelets active participants specifically releasing context-appropriate material from their a-granules or are they random delivery devises?” is timely. The investigator and his research team described in this proposal are all outstanding scientists.  Three hypotheses driven specific aims are designed to address the above question.  The techniques used in this application are unique and preliminary results strongly support the specific aims.  Aim 1 will test hypothesis that using resting human platelets contain a single major a-granule population in which individual cargo proteins are packed into distinct zones. Aim 2 utilizes mouse models from gene knockouts to test hypothesis that specialized a-granule subdomains/extensions provide a spatial basis for differential membrane fusion/protein secretion to the plasma membrane/OCS response to agonists.  Aim 3 will test hypothesis VWF and/or cytoskeletal elements provides an organizing principle for platelet a-granule structure and function.  While most of the approaches are described well, it is not clear if there are differences in the native (mobile) platelets and resting platelets in such organization.  Nor has the PI described such possible differences and how he proposes to study for example, flow (current) mediated changes in platelet a-granules secreting properties which in fact is the physiological situation.  It is also not clear which aspect of their proposal will give raise to future therapeutic design and for which specific disease conditions treatment. Despite this, these studies are very important and will lead to now insights into the platelet biology and physiology.

There is no question that myocardial inflammation is an important clinical problem, and the role of endogenous pathways in limiting inflammation is highly relevant. imp_text: This is an excellent application from established PIs seeking to investigate how cardiac inflammation is regulated by endothelial, myocyte, and dendritic cell PD-L1, and by myeloid PD-1. Successful completion of the project will provide a better understanding of the role of PD-L1 - PD-1 signaling axis in myocardial inflammation and may help develop novel therapeutic strategies for autoimmune myocarditis and ischemic heart disease. The study will take advantage of mouse lines with lineage specific deficiencies of PD-L1 and PD-1. The work proposed is built on the impressive expertise of the PIs in T cell-mediated immune responses in the heart and vasculature (Dr. Murphy) and T cell activation and tolerance (Dr. Schaffer), in an environment that strongly supports the studies that are proposed. Strong preliminary data support the hypothesis to be tested. There are weaknesses in the design of Aim 1 and 2 experiments as some subaims depend on the outcome of previous subaims. As non-hematopoietic restricted PD-L1 deficiencies had been shown to enhance myocardial inflammation, the rationale for dendritic cell PD-L1 studies is unclear. Overall, this application is outstanding in several major review criteria with weaknesses in experimental design and approaches.
sig_text_str: . Previous work of the PIs and preliminary data in the proposal demonstrated the role of PD-L1 and PD-1 in modulating myocardial inflammation. The precise mechanisms by which PD-L1 - PD-1 attenuate the inflammatory processes in the heart remain unknown. The objectives of this project is to investigate the mechanisms by which cardiac inflammation is regulated by endothelial, myocyte, and dendritic cell PD-L1, and by myeloid PD-1. . The proposed studies may reveal new targets for attenuating immune-mediated cardiac inflammation and injury following myocardial ischemia. . The proposal will also explore therapeutic strategies to stimulate PD-1/PD-L1 signaling, induce T cell tolerance, and ameliorate myocardial inflammation.

imp_text: This is a good application from a highly productive PI seeking to investigate a potential mechanistic link between NADPH oxidase (Nox)-derived reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, L-type calcium channel activity, and peripheral mitochondria function in smooth muscle cell caveolae. In vivo experiments were designed to investigate the proposed signaling pathway in the development of vascular dysfunction in obesity. Dr. Murray has sufficient knowledge and extensive research expertise to lead the proposed research, which is evidenced by numerous relevant publications. The concerns are primarily with the research plan. The proposed mechanistic link is novel but it is not clear how the research plan would change the current therapeutic approaches to improve vascular function in obesity or other vascular disorders. Some of the experiments lack specificity for the signaling pathway proposed. For example, a major weakness is that only apocynin was used to investigate the role of Nox in L-type Ca2+ channel activity. Apocynin is an ROS scavenger and not a Nox inhibitor therefore any other enzymatic sources of ROS could contribute to Ca channel activation. The authors have published data demonstrating that Nox-derived ROS colocalized with sites of L-type calcium channel sparklet activity in smooth muscle cells. The only new aspect of this proposal is that the functional link between Nox and Ca channels is localized to the caveolae. Finally, it remains unclear how the proposed work will benefit from unique features of the environment or the institutional resources available to the PI. Although some aspects of this proposal are excellent these weaknesses decreased the enthusiasm for this application.
sig_text_str: . The proposed work investigates functional coupling of Nox and L-type calcium channels in smooth muscle cell caveolae. The role of mitochondria to modulate functional coupling of redox and calcium microdomains will be also investigated. . The goal of this project is to uncover new pathways that regulate vascular tone function and identify new pharmacological targets to prevent vascular dysfunction in obesity. . The expected outcomes potentially expose AngII-induced smooth muscle cell tone through Nox/calcium channels and mitochondria that will bring new insights into basic knowledge in arterial tone regulation.
sig_text_wkn: . It is unclear how the proposed research would change the current therapeutic approaches to improve vascular function and health. Calcium channel blockers to inhibit calcium uptake by SMC, ACE inhibitors to decrease circulating AngII levels, statins to improve cardiovascular health, and antioxidants to scavenge ROS (all targets in the present proposal) are widely used therapeutics to improve vascular tone function and prevent vascular remodeling.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Murray is a highly productive investigator. Outstanding publication record is listed, such as JCI, Circ Res, JBC, and PNAS. He is the corresponding author of a Circ Res paper demonstrating Nox regulation of Ca2+ influx via enhanced L-type Ca2+ channel activity leading to smooth muscle cell contraction. . Dr. Murray certainly has sufficient knowledge and expertise to lead the proposed research. He has extensive experience studying Ca2+-activated K+ channels and L-type Ca2+ channels in vascular smooth muscle cells. . Dr. Murray has obtained research support from AHA (SDG), which ends June 30, 2010. He is a collaborator on an NIH R01 to study the role of cortical cytoskeleton in the regulation of voltage-gated potassium channels. The current proposal is his first independent R01 application. . The investigative team is well suited to the project.
inn_text_str: . The proposed research is conceptually innovative as it will investigate for the first time a reciprocal coupling mechanism in SMC caveolae between Ca2+ signaling and ROS generation. The potential role of Ca2+/ROS coupled microdomain in vascular tone regulation is unknown. . Investigating the role of functionally coupled redox and Ca2+ microdomains in arterial dysfunction in obesity is clinically important.
inn_text_wkn: . Translational innovation of the proposal is not clear. Calcium channel blockers, ACE inhibitors, statins, and antioxidants are widely used to improve vascular function in obesity and other cardiovascular disorders. . RoGFP and HyPer have been previously used to detect ROS in vascular and other cell types. The use of these ROS indicators are superior to DCF but do not represent methodological innovation. . The authors have published data demonstrating that ROS colocalized with sites of L-type calcium channel sparklet activity in smooth muscle cells (Circ Res. 2010;107:1002-1010). The authors have also demonstrated that AngII stimulates L-type Ca channel activity in isolated smooth muscle cells and contraction of intact arteries via Nox. The only new aspect of this proposal is that the functional link between Nox and Ca channels is localized to the caveolae.

app_text_wkn: . The present proposal is designed to investigate the role of Nox and L-type Ca2+ channel interaction in arterial tone regulation. A major weakness of the study is that no preliminary data were provided that Nox enzymes are actually involved in the regulation of L-type Ca2+ channel activity. Apocynin is not a Nox inhibitor in vascular cells it is an antioxidant that scavenges ROS (Hypertension. 2008;51:211-217). AngII stimulates xanthine oxidase activation, increases mitochondrial ROS generation, and induces NOS uncoupling. These Nox-independent ROS sources could also regulate L-type Ca2+ channel activity. It seems to be important to have some preliminary data utilizing specific Nox inhibitors or gene silencing approaches. . The PI proposes that subplasmalemmal ROS stimulate L-type Ca2+ channel activity. Plasma membrane Nox produces ROS outside the cell membrane. How do Nox-derived ROS regulate calcium channel activity from the outside? How extracellular ROS can regulate mitochondrial activity in the cell?  It also remains unclear which reactive oxygen species is responsible for increased calcium channel activity. . Some of the experiments lack specificity for the signaling pathway proposed.  Although the small GTPase Rac1 contributes to increased Nox activity it regulates a diverse array of cellular events independent of ROS signaling. Therefore, pharmacological inhibition of Rac1 signaling does not provide evidence that Nox enzymes are involved in calcium channel activation. In addition, lovastatin was proposed to use to inhibit Rac1 translocation to the membrane. As lovastatin decreases caveolin-1 expression it may directly interfere with Nox-Ca coupling in the caveolae independently of Rac1 signaling. Simvastatin will decrease lipid levels in obese animals and may improve vascular function independently of Nox and Ca signaling. . The lack of specific and validated antibodies against different Nox isoforms represents a major limitation in the Nox field. Have the investigators tested the isoform specificity of their antibodies for western blotting and imaging experiments. . Only imaging studies were proposed to detect ROS. Non-imaging techniques to quantify ROS, such as Amplex red fluorescence and cytochrome c reduction are recommended to confirm results.

imp_text: Arterial wall redox signaling and Ca2+ influx control artery constriction. Increased Ca2+ influx and oxidant stress are associated with hypertension, stroke, and atherosclerosis. This proposal was presented to study the interplay and regulation of redox signaling, Ca2+ influx, caveola, mitochondria, and ultimately arterial function or dysfunction. Applicant proposed three Aims: Aim 1 was proposed to test whether redox NADPH oxidase and L-type Ca2+ channels co-localize in the caveolae and produce coupled redox and Ca2+ microdomains in arterial smooth muscle cells. Applicant will test whether caveolae is required for redox and Ca2+ microdomain coupling with co-localized NADPH oxidase signaling and L-type Ca2+ channels, and whether such coupling affects arterial constriction. TIRF (total internal reflection fluorescence) microscopy and cell electrophysiology were planned. In Aim 2, applicant proposed to test the role of mitochondria to the coupling of redox and Ca2+ microdomains. Several chemicals were planned to activate (diazoxide, antimycin A, 3-nitropropionic acid) or inhibit (rotenone and CCCP) mitochondria ROS production, and the same TIRF microscopy, immunofluorescent imaging, TEM (transmission electron microscopy) techniques were proposed to localize mitochondria to caveolae, Ca2+ channel sparklet activity and ROS puncta. Arterial segments were also planned to test whether mitochondria activation or inhibition regulate arterial function. Finally, Aim 3 was proposed to test whether redox and Ca2+ microdomain coupling contributes to arterial dysfunction in smooth muscle cells from obese rat models. Same TIRF imaging and TEM were proposed to monitor redox and Ca2+ microdomain coupling. Applicant hypothesized that weight loss or DADPH oxidase inhibition with statin may decrease the coupling of redox and Ca
sig_text_str: • The oxidative stress and Ca2+ influx determine arterial wall vasoconstriction. This proposal was presented to study the coupling of ROS (reactive oxygen species) and Ca2+ microdomains, the function and regulation of such coupling. • Both caveolae and mitochondria regulate the coupling of ROS and Ca2+ microdomains. Dysfunction of caveolae, mitochondria, and their associated proteins, or inhibition of either the ROS or the Ca2+ microdomains will affect ROS and Ca2+ microdomains coupling, thereby arterial vasoconstriction and associated vascular diseases, such as hypertension, atherosclerosis, and even obesity. • Hypothesis and measurement of ROS and Ca2+ microdomains coupling on arterial vasoconstriction link these in vitro biochemical studies to human vascular diseases.
sig_text_wkn: • More relevant preliminary data are needed. Also, there is no plan to test the hypothesis in a disease model, e.g. hypertension or obesity, not only isolated arterial fragment or single cell population.
inv_text_str: • Applicant Dr. Jay C. Walsh is an assistant professor from Colorado State University. He has sufficient research experience in Ca2+ influx and vasoconstriction. PI also arranged a team of experts who can help PI with TIRF (total internal reflection fluorescence), siRNA knockdown technology, and TEM detection of mitochondria and caveolae.
inn_text_str: • If successful, planned experiments will give direct evidence that the coupling between ROS activity and Ca2+ influx activity can be regulated in caveolae and by mitochondria. • It will be intriguing to see via TIRF and TEM that the coupling between ROS activity and Ca2+ influx activity, under different conditions is associated with vasoconstriction.
inn_text_wkn: • Limited preliminary data questioned the feasibility of proposed experiments. • Lack of in vivo evidence and plans (not only isolated cells or arterial segment) greatly reduced the innovation level.
app_text_str: • Aim 1 proposed to use TIRF microscopy, whole-cell electrophysiology, and TEM to detect redox and Ca2+ microdomains in caveolae, including newly developed ROS indicator HyPer and conventional ROS indicator DCF along with fluo-5F detection of Ca2+ sparklet sites in the presence of thapsigargin to abolish Ca2+ release and nifedipine to block L-type Ca2+ channel. Few pieces of preliminary data suggested the feasibility of most planned experiments (DCF and fluo-5F fluorescence). Experiments were well planned. • Arterial segment physiology allow direct test of proposed hypothesis in controlling arterial diameter, wall Ca2+, and membrane potential. • Aim 2 proposed to test the role of mitochondria in regulating the coupling of detect redox and Ca2+ microdomains in caveolae. The same detection methodologies were planned. If successful, this plan will provide important information about how mitochondria regulates redox and Ca2+ microdomains coupling and arterial vasoconstriction. • More relevant to human diseases, applicant planned to use smooth muscle cells from obese rats to test the hypothesis of redox and Ca2+ microdomains coupling occurrence in the caveolae, regulation by mitochondria, and vasoconstriction using arterial segments.
app_text_wkn: • In Aim 1, there are some limitations in methodologies. Besides consistent Ca2+ sparklet signals from the published work, no relevant preliminary studies were provided. For example, TNF-a to stimulate NAPDH oxidase, ß-cyclodextrin to disrupt caveolae, caveolin-1 peptide to inhibit caveolin-1, use siRNA technique to block caviolin-1 activity, use Nox siRNA to block reduce NADPH oxidase activity, and use Rac1 siRNA and Rac1 peptide inhibitor to block NADPH oxidase activity, and use statin to block Rac1 plasma membrane translocation. No any preliminary data to support the hypothesis of proposed plan. Some of these siRNA-treated proteins may have gene-depleted mice available to use. Some preliminary data will help. • Although exposure of arterial segments to Ang-II or TNF-a to activate ROS and Ca2+ channels to study arterial segment physiology is very interesting, applicant did not present one single piece of preliminary data besides what have already been published. It will greatly enhance the enthusiasm if there are data to show that inhibition of NADPH oxidase activity, or disruption of caveolae, or interference of Ca2+ influx can affect arterial diameter, wall Ca2+, and membrane potential of isolated arterial segments. • Similarly, smooth muscle cells from obese rats were planed in Aim 3 to test caveolae and mitochondria involvement in coupling of redox and Ca2+ microdomains. The purpose of this part of plan is to link the studies to human diseases. However, there is no direct test of proposed hypothesis in obese rats. • The most significant weakness of this proposal is probably the lack of preliminary results that can be used to test the feasibility of proposed plans. imp_text: This proposal was presented to identify the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which the dual Rho-GEF kalirin in inhibiting atherogenesis. Applicant proposed series of in vitro and in vivo experiments and cell type (EC and macrophage)-conditional knockout mice to test the role of kalirin from these cells in atherosclerosis. In Aim 1, applicant proposed to test two activities of kalirin in iNOS inhibition and in eNOS expression up-regulation in mouse model of atherosclerosis. In Aim 2, applicant proposed in vitro experiment using cultured ECs with different methods of kalirin inhibition (e.g. haploinsufficiency, siRNA, and kalirin RhoGEF1 inhibition) to test kalirin activity in EC gene expression and protein-protein interactions. Finally, applicant planed EC-conditional KO mice to test kalirin activity in atherogenesis. In Aim 3, applicant used similar approaches to that of ECs in Aim 2 to study kalirin functions in macrophage IL10 production and secretion and planned macrophage-conditional knockout mice kalirin in mouse atherosclerosis model. Most proposed experiments have sufficient rationale and should yield important information to explain the athero-protective role of kalirin. However, it is unclear whether this applicant has sufficient commitment in basic research. His publication productivity remains unclear (name changes?). There are also several research approaches require adjustments. For example, the contribution of kalirin appears different in neointoma model versus Apoe atherosclerosis model and aorta transplant model. It may be cleaner by using only the conventional Apoe atherosclerosis model. Kalirin induces SMC proliferation and migration. This activity may confound kalirin activity on EC and macrophages. Careful consideration may be necessary when choose model system. Further, applicant focused on macrophage expression of IL10. It is possible that kalirin may affect macrophage IL10 expression as one of the anti-inflammatory mechanisms. Applicant has to consider additional roles of kalirin in inhibiting macrophage expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

EC- and macrophage-specific role of kalirin could be essential to atherogenesis, but remains untested.
