study_section: Hemostasis and Thrombosis Study Section
imp_text: This is a pure cell biology proposal presented to study how the platelet a-granules are positioned and activated. Platelets are very important blood component that determines blood clotting and thrombosis. Their activation regulation has pathophysiological significance to the cardiovascular system. Applicant and the team members are leading scientists in platelet/a-granule structures and activation. Applicant proposed three aims in this proposal. In Aim 1, applicant hypothesized that proteins (VWF [von Willebrand factor] and fibrinogen) in a-granules are packaged into distinct zones. Applicant presented a series of techniques, including electron tomography, immunogold labeling, and super-resolution light microscopy to visualize a-granule structure and VWF and fibrinogen localization from human platelets. In Aim 2, applicant proposed to use electron microscopy/electron tomography, fluorescence microscopy/super-resolution light microscopy, and time-lapse fluorescence microscopy to examine how a-granules release different proteins after stimulation with pro- and anti-angiogenic agonists (ADP and thromboxane A2 TXA2). A v-SNARE (e.g. VAMP-8, VAMP-7) pathway was proposed to mediate subdomain-specific fusion using platelets from different VAMP-deficient mice. Both v-SNARE-null mice and Munc13-2 mice were proposed to test the sequence of protein release. In Aim 3, applicant will also use the same technologies to test the hypothesis that VWF and pH changes are essential to maintain the structure of a-granules. However, many hypotheses were based on “predictions” only and there was no direct evidence or hint. It is possible that Aims 1 and 2 may yield some important information regarding a-granule components and activation pathways, given the outstanding team of microscopy scientists. That may be the maximum can get from this proposal. There is no studies to link these structures, components, and conditions to the setting of human diseases. Aim 3 is even more superficial. It is merely hypothesis that VWF expression and pH changes may affect a-granule shapes, because of the lack of preliminary data. Matrix protein may be more relevant to a-granule structures, but not planed. None of these hypotheses was proposed to be tested in disease models.
sig_text_str: • Platelets are important blood component that mediates blood clotting, thrombosis, and vasculature repair. a-granules within the platelets contain unique sets of proteins that localize into separate zones. Their structure, activation mechanisms in response to stimulations, and shape changes may determine platelet function. • Direct vision of a-granule protein distribution, protein release, and shape changes regulation by intraorganelle proteins, extracellular matrix proteins, or pH, is limited. These activities of a-granules may have pathological roles or therapeutic potential to human diseases.
sig_text_wkn: • The whole proposal is limited to physical observations of a-granules (structure, protein distribution, agonist-mediated activation, VWF and pH change-induced shape changes). There was no intention to test whether any of these visions from different kinds of microscopes has pathological relevance to human diseases.

This proposal was presented to use modern immune and electron techniques to visualize platelet a-granule intraorganelle structure, protein release pathway, and a-granule activity-related shape changes. imp_text: The proposal is significant and innovative in its exploration of the suggested link of kalirin in atherosclerosis in humans and mice. imp_text: This is a new proposal from an established investigator that will examine the protective role of Kalirin-9 in atherosclerosis. Polymorphisms of the human KALRN gene have been associated with coronary artery disease and ischemic stroke, so this proposal has considerable clinical relevance. Kalirin has two GEF domains that activate Rac and RhoA, so the specific aims are logically designed to explore the mechanisms related to activation of these GEF domains in different cell types. Kalirin also has an iNOS-interacting domain, so Specific Aim 1 will also explore the involvement of this domain separately and in combination with the RhoGEF1 domain using a pharmacological approach. Specific aims 2 and 3 will examine molecular mechanisms for Kalirin signaling in endothelial cell and macrophages, respectively using a variety of tools including Apoe(-/-) mice with EC- or macrophage-specific inducible deficiencies of Kalirin. Unfortunately, the outcome measures are somewhat descriptive, but the results of the proposed studies should yield valuable insight into the protective role of Kalirin and thereby provide potential anti-atherosclerosis therapeutic targets. However, enthusiasm is dampened by the absence of a clear overall conceptual framework that integrates results from the three specific aims. Accordingly, although the proposal focuses on Kalirin signaling, it is somewhat disjointed with apparently disparate results being obtained in each of the specific aims.

imp_text: This new application from an experienced group of investigators proposes an intriguing conceptual framework that platelets are organized into discrete a-granule subdomains by cytoskeletal structures from which platelet cargo can be selectively released via agonist activation and interaction with fusion proteins such as v-SNARE and VAMP-8. The three specific aims are logically organized as testable hypotheses. The proposed studies will use a combination of sophisticated high resolution imaging techniques together with immunohistochemistry, molecular biology and transgenic animal models. The outcome measures and their interpretation are clearly defined although there is some concern whether unambiguous results can be obtained. Overall, this is a highly innovative proposal that should yield important basic information regarding platelet physiology that could provide novel therapeutic targets. However, enthusiasm is dampened by the fact that much of Specific Aim 1 appears to have already been accomplished and published. Furthermore, the experimental design for Specific Aims 2 and 3 will not provide a clear unequivocal mechanistic answer regarding their central hypothesis.
sig_text_str: . An intriguing conceptual framework that addresses a major unanswered question in platelet physiology – are platelets organized by a-granule content? Or do they represent a single major a-granule population organized into subdomains from which platelet cargo can be selectively released. . To address this essential question, the investigators propose a logical series of specific aims. . The results of the proposed studies should provide basic information that will drive future research in this area including evaluation of potential therapeutic targets.

imp_text: This is a proposal to investigate the potential for microdomains consisting of calcium channels, caveolae, ROS and subplasmalemmal mitochondria in regulating calcium channel activation and calcium influx. The investigators are excellent and have the expertise to perform the proposed studies. They have generally collaborated together showing that they are productive together. The TRIF microscopy which allows visualization of the structural components with the functional (molecular biology) assays is a strength of the studies. There is some concern however that the pharmacologic inhibitors and ROS activators to be used will impact the cell physiology as a whole and not exclusively the subplasmalemmal mitochondria which the PI hypothesizes is primarily responsible for regulating calcium influx. This could make interpretation of the data difficult. There is inadequate discussion of unanticipated problems or outcomes. Aim 3 will evaluate arterial smooth muscle cells during obesity. While the goal of this Aim is important, as the PI is aware, there are many aspects of obesity which could impact the function of the microdomain and calcium signaling. This Aim should produce important information, but will not really indicate which aspect(s) of the total complex is most impact during obesity resulting in dusfunction. Thus, this Aim is somewhat underdeveloped.
sig_text_str: . This project investigates an important aspect of calcium signaling: namely the microdomains of mitochondria and caveolae resulting in reactive oxygen species (ROS) which activate calcium channels in the plasma membrane leading to calcium influx. The investigators have the unique ability to apply microbiology, and microscopy techniques to characterize this signal pathway.
sig_text_wkn: . While the concept of a microdomain controlling calcium signaling is both important and innovative, the use of pharmacologic activators/inhibitors will not selectively impact only subplamalemmal mitochondria but all cellular mictochondria. Thus, it may not be possible to do more than correlate the physical juxtaposition of mitochondria to caveolae.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Walsh is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Biomedical Sciences at Colorado State University. He has had a AHA Scientist Development Grant and currently has a Pew Scholar award. He is a collaborator on an R01 on ion channel functions and localizations. app_text_str: . The visualization studies in Aim 1.2 are reasonable and new and will complement the largely redundant functional studies in Aim 1.1. The PI would have been wiser to present the functional and imaging studies together rather than as separate subaims. It is unlikely that Aims 1.1 and 1.2 will produce discordant results but what happens if this occurs? The PI clearly expects both subaims to complement each other and provides no discussion of unanticipated results. . Evaluation of vessels under increased pressure (Aim 1.3 is excellent). . Aim 2 will evaluate nanocontacts between mitochondria and caveolae regulating redox regulation of calcium influx. There is some discussion that the ROS modulation may have impacts on all cellular mitochondria not just on those adjacent to caveolae and that this might have indirect impacts on calcium signaling. This is not well controlled or discussed. Aim 2.2 will localize mitochondria adjacent to caveolae but this does not itself prove that those are the only ones regulating calcium influx. How will the PI prove that it is really the subplasmalemmal mitochondria that are important? This may not be practical but the potential problem should be faced. . There is advantage in studying how physiological conditions such as obecity can impact calcium signaling. However, this is likely to be a very complex condition which can impact many aspects of cell biology from lipid composition on the membrane impacting fluidity, to mitochondria metabolism. Aim 3 is poorly developed and superficial. It will indicate whether calcium signaling is altered and confirm changes in ion channel-ROS-mitochondria localizations but will not really provide detailed information on mechanism. Nonetheless, the information might be valuable as a first step toward further investigations.

imp_text: This is a potentially highly exciting proposal which will investigate kalirin, a protein associated with atherosclerosis in several genetic screens of humans and shown buy the principal investigator to affect atherogenesis in the apoE-/- model of atherosclerosis. This makes the proposal highly significant as it provides the opportunity to determine the mechanism of kalirin action in this disease. Other strengths of the proposal are the investigative team and the research environment which are both outstanding. The general approach of the studies is reasonable but often pre-assumes the results without adequate preliminary data to justify this. While it is possible and potentially exciting that kalirin expression in SMC and EC could have diametrically opposite effects on atherogenesis, there are other potential explanations which are not apparently considered by the PI. The crucial experiment (inducible conditional EC knockdown) is proposed, but if this mouse fails to give the predicted phenotype, the alternative explanations for the preliminary results are not discussed. Similarly, while it is reasonable to study kalirin in macrophage (since this cell type expresses the protein), the assumption that any effect would involve IL-10 seems to be a major leap as no IL-10 levels were measured in kalrn+/- or SMCkalrn+/- mice compared to WT mice, and there are many other ways macrophage would impact atherogenesis. The PI should first use the kalirin knockdown specifically in macrophage to get a phenotype before proposing potential studies on mechanisms. If there is no phenotype, then Aims 3.1 and 3.2 will be irrelevant. There is little evidence that the PI has expertise in studying macrophage or immunology but this expertise is locally available and should not be a problem.
sig_text_str: . Kalirin has been associated with atherosclerosis by human genetic linkage studies and is a protein in Rho family signaling and is highly expressed in vascular smooth muscle cells (SMC) endothelial cells (EC) and macrophage. Preliminary studies using a mouse model of atherosclerosis confirm that Kalirin alters atherosclerosis susceptibility but its impact may be dependent on the type of cell expressing it with SMC kalirin suppressing atherogenesis and potentially aggravating it. If this is so, then the proposed studies would be of very high significance as it would not only identify a protein crucial to atherogenesis but caution that systemic targeting of the protein can have unintended results. This is not likely to be restricted to kalirin but other atherosclerosis-relevant molecules expressed by multiple cell types might have different biological effects in a cell-specific manner.

app_text_str: . The preliminary data showing that Kalirin expressed specifically in vascular smooth muscle cells (SMC) protects from neointimal hyperplasia is strong. Use of cell specific congenic knockouts is excellent and there is a good phenotype despite only ~60% reduction in Kalirin protein expression. The atherosclerosis data is potentially exciting. Kalirin+/-ApoE-/- mice showed increased atherosclerosis but SMC-Kalrn+/-ApoE-/- mice which should have Kalirin decreased only in SMC show decreased atherosclerosis. This indicates that different cells in the artery expressing Kalirin might have distinct effect on atherosclerosis and presumably the difference would be between the EC and the SMC, but no Kalirin levels are reported. The problem with these preliminary studies is that the EC in the SMC Kalrn+/- mice might not resemble EC in WT mice as cells communicate with each other and changes in the vascular SMC might alter the EC in unknown ways decreasing atherogenesis. In fact the decreased expression of VCAM-1 in SMC Kalrn+/- mice supports this possibility. Data is provided showing decreased NO levels in EC Kalrn+/- cells compared to WT EC and decreased migration. To truly demonstrate an in vivo role for EC kalirin in atherosclerosis, studies should use cell specific conditional knockouts. This is proposed in Aim 2.3. However, if the hypothesized disease phenotype is not observed, there is little discussion of what the unanticipated result would mean. . Aim 1 will determine if kalirin inhibits atherosclerosis through inhibition of iNOS or RacGEF. The studies will be performed using both normal low fat and high fat diet atherosclerosis models. Evaluating plaque composition is descriptive but likely to provide useful information which could lead to further studies. Why study IL-10 when there is no preliminary data that IL-10 levels are altered in Kalrn+/- mice? Use of the presumably selective 1400W iNOS inhibitor is reasonable. Are there side-effects to prolonged iNOS inhibition as there are with prolonged eNOS inhibition (kidney damage)? . Giving ITX3 in a focal model of atherosclerosis is excellent as it could help prevent systemic side-effects. Presumably there is evidence that insufficient compound is adsorbed systemically to cause problems. If ITX3 is given systemically, what are the potential side-effects and how would they be controlled? . Aim 2 will investigate the anti-atherosclerotic effects of kalirin in EC. Proposed studies will extend preliminary data on eNOS and Rac-1/PAK pathway effects. These are reasonable but involve in vitro cell culture. The crucial experiment is in Aim 2.3 using the inducible EC specific kalrn+/- knockdown mouse which should show a disease phenotype. If this mouse has WT atherosclerosis susceptibility, then the hypothesis that kalirin expression in EC is anti-atherogenic would be in question. Based on preliminary in vitro studies, this outcome does not seem likely, but a better discussion of unanticipated results would have been beneficial. The assumption that the Kalrn+/- versus SMCKalrn+/- difference reflects macrophage might be an explanation but the PI stated that grafts were taken prior to macrophage infiltration and the number of macrophage in an aortic graft ought to be minuscule compared to the potential macrophage in the graft recipients. Therefore, this explanation seems highly unlikely. . For Aim 3, the cell specific (macrophage) knock-down experiments should be the first done since if these are normal, signal pathway studies will be of less interest. As with the EC, the knockdowns should be an inducible model.
app_text_wkn: . There is no evidence that feeding a low fat diet will really eliminate iNOS contribution to atherosclerosis. There is oxLDL generation in apoE-/- mice fed a low fat diet. . Assuming that if 1400W fails to reduce atherosclerosis it is because the pharmacologic inhibitor is unstable in the pump seems to presume the results of the experiment. Controls were proposed which were supposed to determine if NO is reduced in treated animals. Giving 1400W either s.c. or in drinking water over a 4 week period is a viable alternative but how would the actual adsorption dose be determined (drinking water) or how would bolus administration of a potentially short-lived reagent impact the results? . Investigating kalirin knockdown in macrophage is reasonable. If there is a phenotype it would then be reasonable to determine what kalirin does in this cell type to affect atherogenesis but why the fixation on IL-10? Many cells make IL-10 and the immune cell most likely responsible for immunosuppressive IL-10 production in atherosclerosis could be the Tr1 cell. There are many aspects of macrophage biology which should be investigated including scavenger receptors and foam cell formation not to mention cell adhesion molecules allowing EC binding. Unless there is specific evidence that IL-10 levels differ between Kalrn+/- and WT mice, the studies should be more broadly based on macrophage biology. This is somewhat the case with the signaling studies.

imp_text: This is a proposal by an outstanding team of investigators to determine whether cargo proteins in alpha-granules of platelets are zonally organized and selectively secreted rather than having distinctive granule subtypes. The goals of the proposal are excellent and the PI has expertise in 3D-SIM imaging and the co-investigator has expertise in platelet secretion. Other investigators are identified but biosketches are not included nor are their specific roles always clearly defined. Aim 1 will use imaging to detail the 3D structure of granules and distribution of VWF and fibrinogen with other proteins such as VAMP-8, VAMP-2/3/7 or SNAREs. There is no information on how many platelets or how many granules/platelet will be evaluated. Blood drawing alone might partially activate platelets and there could be some inter-platelet variability which is not discussed. Figure 1P certainly suggests there could be inter-person variation so would studying 3 volunteers have sufficient power? Aim 2 will investigate secretion by an extension or “spigot” but alternative explanations for this extension are not discussed nor what happens if knockout of VAMP proteins either has no effect on the extension or secretion. Aim 3 will evaluate pH on cargo distribution and granule shape. Again, little discussion of potential problems, alternative results or alternative approaches is a problem which reduces enthusiasm.
sig_text_str: . The question of whether there are subtypes of alpha-granules in platelets or whether there is zonal composition of cargo in the alpha-granules with selective cargo secretion is highly significant. Preliminary data would suggest that the zonal hypothesis is more likely despite publications by other investigations to the contrary. Definitive studies conclusively deciding this point would be very valuable.
sig_text_wkn: . It isn’t certain that the proposed imaging studies will in fact decisively prove a single granule hypothesis but it should at least confirm that granules can have zonal cargo.

Dr. Murray is Professor and Director of the Imaging Core in the Department of Physiology and Biophysics of the University of Arkansas; has 111 publications including expertise in platelet granules; and has an excellent grant funding history. Dr. Woodhead is Professor of Molecular and Cellular Biochemistry with a strong publication history on platelet secretion. The investigative team is outstanding and has the expertise to perform the proposed studies.

imp_text: 3.0 Strengths PIs propose a novel strategy to target programmed death-ligand 1 pathway (PD-1/PD-L1) for cardiac protection. PD-1/PD-L1 is an important immuno-modulation pathway and PIs previously showed that T cell PD-1 and nonhematopoietic PD-L1 protect mice in a CD8 T cell dependent myocarditis. PIs have extensive expertise in T cell studies. Weaknesses The experimental approach lacks fails to determine the cell-specific role of PD-1/PD-L1 and it does not consider potential off-target pro-cancer effects of PD-1/PD-L1 pathway.
sig_text_str: • Myocardial diseases are the leading causes of death and a major economic burden. • PIs will study the role of PD-1/PD-L1 pathway in myocardial inflammation which is significantly contributes to myocardial dysfunction.
sig_text_wkn: • PD-1/PD-L1 is expressed both in immune cells and nonhematopoietic cells such as endothelium but proposal will test only PD-1/PD-L1 in CD4 and CD8 T cells.
inv_text_str: • PIs and team has extensive expertise in T cells.
inv_text_wkn: • The 0.6 moth effort for co-PI Andrea Schaffer is not adequate.

inn_text_wkn: • PD-1/PD-L1 is well known regulator of programmed death and immune check point and it is not clear what new mechanistic insight will be obtained with respect to T cell function. • PIs initially claimed to determine which cell types mediate PD-L1-dependent protection against T cells in the heart by endothelial, myocyte, and DC PD-L1, and by myeloid PD-1.; however, they do not pursue this goal rather focus only on modulation of PD-1/PD-L1 in T cells only.

imp_text: While the topic addressed in this application — which concerns how to damper inflammation during pathogenesis of the heart — is of great importance, I have significant qualms about the methodology used for this study.  The research plan suffers from its reliance on a transgenic model of myocarditis that may be a highly artificial and inappropriate system for addressing many of the questions addressed in the experimental aims.  To be specific, the investigators have generated a transgenic model of myocarditis where a membrane bound form of albumin is expressed on cardiomyocytes, to provide a target for T cells primed against this antigen.  It is not clear if the tethered ovalbumin myocarditis model triggers an overly aggressive T cell response that may not reflect the inflammation process in human disease.  Much of this grant relies on yet to be generated transgenic animals that may or may not be useful for addressing the importance of PD-1 and PD-L1 signaling.  For example, in the first aim they propose to produce a series of PD-L1 KO mice where the gene deletion is targeted to specific cell types.  The presumption is that all these animals will suffer from no change in cell phenotype and function, no change in cardiac performance, no change in the overall health of the animals, and no change in the overall immune responses, except when dealing with the myocarditis.  Little comment is given to how these gene-targeted animals will be assessed prior to testing the myocarditis model.  In addition, since the myocarditis model is artificially skewed to having immune cells directly and aggressively attack myocytes, it is not clear whether deletion of PDL1 expression on various cell types is relevant for understanding the involvement of PD1-PDL1 signaling in human myocarditis. Another issue with this proposal is that the research plan is very poorly described and its narrative poorly written.  The myriad numbers of transgenic animals are introduced in a stream-of-consciousness manner throughout the narrative.  This grant application would have helped immensely by having a table that listed all the transgenic lines, which would have indicated those that had been previously or planning to be generated, and included information on how their genetic aberrations are to be controlled (e.g., constitutive, induced, Cre-recombination, etc.).  As is, reading and critiquing this application was unnecessarily laborious.  From the introduction and background information provided by the investigators, it was also difficult to distinguish what had been shown experimentally and what was their supposition or hypothesis.

study_section: Atherosclerosis and Inflammation of the Cardiovascular System Study Section
imp_text: The proposed research investigates molecular mechanisms that influence the development of atherosclerosis.  The specific focus of their study is a novel atherogenesis candidate gene Kalirin, which has been implicated in the human disease from genetic epidemiology studies.  Thus, the subject of this proposal is both novel and pertinent to human disease.  The lack of enthusiasm for this proposal is due to concerns whether (a) the mouse Kalirin haploinsufficiency model is truly relevant to the Kalirin mutant phenotype that is associated with human atherosclerosis, (b) that the research plan is too safe and thus completion of the aims may not generate any insightful information, and (c) that the investigators did not address in there research plan how to understand why this molecule seems to promote disparate effects depending on the specific cell type that is targeted.
sig_text_str: . Human genetic epidemiology studies have identified the Kalirin gene as being associated with the development of atherogenesis.  This proposal focuses on Kalirin as a molecule whose deficiency may promote atherogenesis and thus the investigators have designed a research plan dissecting the signaling mechanisms that may underlie the anti-atherogenic mechanisms of Kalirin activity.
sig_text_wkn: . Atherosclerosis is a multifactorial disease, so it is not certain whether a single-minded focus on the effect of this one identified factor will provide useful information that can be translated into therapies for treating human disease.
inv_text_str: The PI, Dr. Walsh, has been a productive researcher on regulatory mechanisms underlying atherogenesis, and has published a series of research studies over the past 10 years on this topic in major journals.  During that time, the PI has had a consistent track record in NIH and AHA funding for atherogenesis research.  The collaborating investigator, Dr. Xiang brings his expertise in mass spectrometry/proteomics that has been incorporated into the research plan.
inn_text_str: . The innovation of this project relates to its focus on a novel molecular determinant of atherogenesis, which is Kalirin, whose deficient expression and/or mutation in humans has been shown to be associated with the progression of this disease.
inn_text_wkn: . The weakness is that the role of Kalirin is being explored primarily by its association with signaling mechanisms already known to be associated with atherogenesis.  Thus, it is uncertain whether this project — even if fully successful in completing all its aims — will offer new insights into treatments for atherogenesis.
app_text_str: • The proposed studies will investigate how physiological levels of Kalirin expression may protect against atherogenesis.  The research plan involves crossing haploinsufficient mice that have one inactive Kalirin locus with apoE KO animals (kalrn +/-;apoE-/-) and comparing their development of atherogenesis in response to an high fat Western diet to mice with apoE KO mice with normal Kalirin levels (kalrn +/+;apoE-/-).  In the first aim, mice will also be assessed for whether levels of Kalirin influence signaling activities of molecules known to influence atherogenesis, such as iNOS, Rac1 and RhoA.  Mice will also be treated with selective antagonists against either iNOS or guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) domains that are present on Kalirin, and which normally act as stimulators of Rac and RhoA activities. • The last two aims are designed to provide insights into the multifaceted roles of Kalirin in atherogenesis.  In the final two aims, the investigators plan to work with genetically altered mice where the Kalirin haploinsufficiency is targeted to either smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells, or macrophages.  Thus, SMC-kalrn +/-;apoE-/-, EC-kalrn +/-;apoE-/-, and Mf-kalrn +/-;apoE-/- mice will be compared to kalrn +/+;apoE-/- mice and examined both for atherogenic development and the appropriate targets established in previous atherogenic studies, such as eNos and IL10.  Included in this research plan is a shotgun proteomics approach, involving mass spectrometry of peptides that co-IP with Kalirin, with the goal that new targets for atherosclerosis therapy may be identified based on Kalirin’s protein-protein interactions in endothelial cells.  The rationale for the cell-specific targeted Kalirin deficiencies is that preliminary data indicate that reduced Kalirin seems to decrease atherogenesis when associated with endothelial cells or macrophages, but promotes atherogenesis when associated with smooth muscle cells.
app_text_wkn: . There are several weaknesses with the scientific approach.  First, is that the role of Kalirin is being explored primarily by its association with signaling mechanisms already known to be associated with atherogenesis.  So it is uncertain whether this project — even if fully successful in completing all its aims — will offer new insights into treatments for atherogenesis.  The second weakness concerns whether the haploinsufficiency model is a suitable stand-in for human disease that is not due to lowered levels of the protein’s expression but resulting from a mutated form of the molecule (with presumably altered functional properties).  The third issue concerns the seeming contradiction that the stimulatory or inhibitory effect of Kalirin on atherogenesis depends on the specific cell type that is targeted for haploinsufficient phenotype.  Since the human disease associated with the Kalirin mutation presumably affects smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells, and macrophages together, the investigators may have better considered experimentation that would help uncover the meaning behind that apparent contradiction.
env_text_str: . The Duke University Medical Center provides a supportive environment for these studies.  Since the laboratories of the PI and main collaborating investigator are adjacent to one other, the two groups are able to foster close scientific collaboration on the proposed research.  Moreover, active collaboration for the proposed project of the two laboratories is also cultivated by the laboratories joint weekly lab meetings.

imp_text: The proposed investigations elicit a very positive assessment.  Several factors contribute to this favorable appraisal: 1) the investigators are tackling fundamental questions in platelet biology, which they are well equipped to address; 2) they use state-of-the-art technologies, such as STEM electron tomography, for which they have developed considerable expertise; 3) all genetically altered mouse models that are included in this study have been previously generated and fully characterized, 4) the proposed use of the genetically altered mice (e.g., SNARE or VWD KO mice) serve a real purpose for the overall experimental plan; and 5) the usefulness of this study is not dependent on a particular outcome, but instead will provide important information on platelet biology and function regardless of whether the investigators’ hypotheses are confirmed or contradicted.  Moreover, this is a very well written grant application that explains in clear, lucid prose the issues to be investigated in this proposal, and the research plan and experimental approach for discovering fundamental information on platelet biology and function.
sig_text_str: . This proposal addresses fundamental questions on platelet biology and the structure and function of its a-granules, with specific aims geared to investigate how these storage and secretory organelles are organized, and differential release of its contents are regulated.

inv_text_str: . As shown by an impressive publication record and consistent external grant funding, the PI has had a very productive research career investigating secretary granules, membrane trafficking, and platelet function.  Work is also being proposed at a second institution as a subaward, headed by Dr. Woodhead, who has devoted his research to platelet biology and also has a consistent record of external funding.  In collaboration with the PI, this lab will provide a number of unique mouse strains and prepare platelets from these animals.
inn_text_str: . Research proposes to use STEM electron tomography to define the distribution and structure of a-granules, and the deposition of VWF and fibrinogen, within platelets.  Innovation is in addressing unknown aspects of the functional mechanisms of platelet function.  Successful completion of these studies may provide important insights into understanding how platelets regulate hemostasis, inflammation, and wound repair, and how to manipulate these responses for human therapies.
inn_text_wkn: . Although the proposed studies would provide the most detailed 3D resolution of platelets and a-granules generated to date, the investigators acknowledge the limitations in resolution are dictated by the present state of current technologies.
app_text_str: . Three aims are proposed.  In the first aim, electron tomography will be used to map a-granule distribution in human platelets and define the deposition of both VWF and fibrinogen within platelets.  The second aim will examine whether a- granule extensions/subdomains mediate the secretion of their contents to the open canalicular system and the involvement of different SNAREs in determining differential a- granule secretion.  These experiments will utilize KO mouse deficient in various SNARE proteins and use electron microscopy/electron tomography, fluorescence microscopy/super-resolution light microscopy, and time-lapse fluorescence microscopy as readouts.  The final aim will examine the role of VWF and other cytoskeletal elements in affecting a-granule function in secretion.  VWF deficient platelets will be obtained from both human patients and VWF deficient mice (provided via outside sources as verified from letters of collaboration) to examine the effect of this molecule on a-granule organelle shape and intragranular cargo protein distribution.  In addition, drugs affecting intragranular pH will be utilized to examine whether a-granule shape and cargo distribution can be reversibility managed.

imp_text: The primary aims of this proposal are to elucidate the biochemical and biophysical properties of protein complexes involved in chromosome alignment, recombination, and segregation in meiosis I. The investigator will perform structure-function analysis to understand the molecular mechanism of the monopolin complex (Aim 1); will determine how the structure of the Hop1 protein relates to its meiotic recombination checkpoint function (Aim 2); and elucidate the architecture of the Zip1 protein and its role in mediating synaptonemal complex assembly (Aim 3). This is a very clearly written proposal from a talented young investigator that takes advantage of many different complementary approaches to understand the function of these important protein complexes. The major positive score driving attributes are a well-trained investigator, strong preliminary data in support of the hypothesis, and a clear plan of alternative approaches should X-ray structural studies fail. The only negative attribute of this proposal (which is relatively minor) is that the Aims are only loosely interconnected, giving the impression that there are three somewhat distinct proposals.
sig_text_str: • The protein complexes chosen to be studied in the proposal are important for normal meiosis. To date they have not been well-studied in detail at the atomic level. Therefore the overall significance of the study is quite high. • The structure-function relationship of these molecules (particularly the idea of creating a one-headed monopolin complex and testing its effects in vivo in Aim 1, and the role of SUMO in the regulation of the synaptonemal complex in Aim 3) are critical questions.

imp_text: The primary goals of this proposal are to reconstitute the DNA replication machinery of human cells and understand the important of specific factors in the replication process. Namely, the PI wishes to test the hypothesis that Pol-e and Pol-d support leading and lagging strand synthesis, respectively (Aim 1); to understand the mechanism of human Ctf4 and other proteins in the regulation of the CMG helicase complex (Aim 2); and to determine the role of Psf1 in replication (Aim 3). As replication of the genome is a fundamental process in all eukaryotes, understanding the role of these factors in human cells is of some general importance, and may have some relevance to specific disease states. Nonetheless, enthusiasm for the proposal was hampered by a number of factors. An overarching hypothesis for much of the work is not clearly evident. Furthermore many of these proteins have already been studied in detail in other eukaryotic systems (e.g., Xenopus and yeast). Therefore it appears that the knowledge to be gained from these studies will only be of incremental value.

imp_text: The primary aims of this proposal are to understand the molecular steps involved in the maturation of the ribosomal 40S subunit using budding yeast as a model system. The proposal centers on identifying the biochemical and genetic functions of several key players in this process, namely: the RNA helicase Ecm16 (Aim 1), the methyltransferase Bud23 (Aim 2), the RNA chaperone Imp4 (Aim 3), and the ribosomal protein Rps2 (Aim 4). The major positive score driving aspects of this proposal are a significant amount of relevant preliminary data in support of the hypotheses, complementary genetic and biochemical approaches to the questions, and a very strong PI/Co-I team. Nevertheless, enthusiasm for the proposal was somewhat moderated by what seemed to be significant emphasis on the details of the processes at hand, which made it difficult to appreciate its overall significance. Furthermore, the notion of RNA quality control in pre-40S maturation seems to be the most innovative aspect of the proposal; however, the concept of RNA quality control, while important, is no longer very original.

imp_text: This is an impressive first application from a new and early stage investigator to dissect molecular interactions within the monopolin complex and other proteins critical for chromosomal segregation during meiosis I in yeast. The proposed studies couple structural and biochemical characterization with functional assays to evaluate the impact of disrupting these interactions on recombination and chromosomal segregation in vivo. The experiments are well conceived, logical, and often supported by strong preliminary data, but overall, the scope of the project and number of protein interactions to be interrogated may be ambitious. The PI has strong experience in protein structure elucidation and sufficient expertise to execute the genetic assays in yeast. Successful completion of this work will likely provide significant insight into the architecture and function of proteins important for meiosis I in yeast. Enthusiasm is somewhat dampened by knowledge that the monopolin complex is fungal specific, and its relevance to furthering our understanding of chromosome segregation during meiosis in metazoa unclear.

app_text_str: • Aim 1 will further define the architecture of the monopolin complex and test its kinetichore binding activity during meiosis I in vivo. The crystal structure of Mam1 bound to Hrr25 will be solved (crystals are in hand) and their association with the intact monopolin complex determined (using electron microscopy). Structural analysis of monopolin protein Csm1 with its protein binding partner Tof2 will be investigated - enabled by the clever use of engineered fusion proteins. Monovalent (i.e. one-headed) Csm1:Lrs4 complexes will be generated and characterized in vitro and their function in sister kinetochore co-orientation in meiosis I tested in vivo. • In Aim 2, the structure and function of chromosome-associated protein, Hop1, in regulating meiotic recombination and the recombination checkpoint will be investigated. Homology between Hop1 and the well characterized spindle checkpoint protein, Mad2, and a shared HORMA protein domain predominantly guide the proposed experiments. Structural analysis (by NMR then, if possible, crystallography) of Hop1 HORMA will be aided by introduction of mutations predicted to stabilize an open versus closed conformation. Interactions between Hop1 and its binding partners Rec114 and Red1 will be mapped and tested in vivo (along with HORMA mutations) for defects in recombination using well established yeast genetic assays. • Aim 3 will characterize the self-assembly properties, protein-protein interactions, and structure of synaptonemal complex protein Zip1. The oligomeric state of purified Zip1 fragments in solution will be analyzed biophysically (using SEC-MALS). Interactions between Zip1 (or Red1, a lateral synaptonemal protein) and its putative binding partner SUMO will be investigated using purified proteins and SUMO oligomers of defined length. Finally, structural analysis (by EM and crystallography) of Zip1 head-to-head dimers and Zip1-SUMO is proposed. • There is extensive preliminary data and many of the needed reagents appear to be in hand (e.g. crystals of Mam1 and Hrr25, mapped Hop1 protein interaction domains). The role of many of these protein interactions will be evaluated in vivo using established yeast chromosome orientation and segregation assays.
app_text_wkn: • The monopolin complex is fungal specific and it was not made clear how these studies will further our understanding of chromosome segregation during meiosis in metazoa. It is particularly relevant to make it clear how these studies will impact our understanding of the underlying defects leading to errors in chromosome segregation in humans. • The monovalent Csm1:Lrs4 complex required to evaluate the role of the monopolin complex in mediating sister kinetochore co-orientation may be difficult to generate and limit the ability to complete studies proposed in Aim 1. • Highly specific mutations that capture the open or closed state of Hop1 or disrupt binding to Rec114 or Red1 (Aim 2) may be difficult to identify thus limiting the ability to dissect their specific roles in meiosis.

imp_text: This is a new application from a veteran researcher with decades-long experience investigating the molecular mechanisms of DNA replication in eukaryotic cells. Proposed studies are aimed at understanding the assembly and function of the human CMG replicative helicase complex (proposed to be the protein core at the replication fork during DNA synthesis). Three aims will examine the properties of the CMG and its interactions with a number of replicating proteins (including the polymerases themselves), and how these factors influence DNA replication both in vitro and in vivo. The PI is an expert and leader in the field, and has both key reagents and unique assays to monitor DNA replication in vitro. The PI is very well positioned to perform the proposed studies and a detailed understanding of the structure and function of the CMG complex is critical for our complete understanding of eukaryotic DNA replication. Enthusiasm for this proposal is dampened however, since a majority of the studies examine interactions that have been previously observed in studies of the yeast replicative complex and/or in Xenopus cell extracts. It is unclear whether these studies will provide significant new insight into the architecture and/or function of the CMG complex.
sig_text_str: • The analysis of specific mutations in Psf1 found linked to a childhood developmental disorder and susceptibility to cancer will likely provide insight into a cellular defect that may contribute to the observed phenotypes.
sig_text_wkn: • Many of the proposed experiments are interaction and structure/function analyses proposed based on findings from studies of the yeast RPC (replisome progression complex) and/or work on the Xenopus CMG complex. While it is likely these studies will confirm interactions characterized in these non-mammalian systems, it is unclear what new information will be gained. app_text_str: • There is a significant amount of published data (both from the PIs lab and from others) and preliminary data to justify the proposed experiments. • As stated by PI, her lab has purified the key proteins involved in DNA replication from higher eukaryotes and thus has key reagents and is in a unique position to examine DNA replication and the replicative helicase complex in vitro. • Aim 1 proposes to evaluate the role of various replication factors in leading and lagging strand DNA synthesis in vitro utilizing a powerful and established primed circular template. An alternative helicase (ChIR1) will also be used to replace CMG and tested. • Aim 2 will examine interactions between the CMG complex and various replication proteins/polymerases, and the impact of these interactions on DNA replication. Particular attention will be placed upon the requirement of Ctf4 (a purported chromosome transmission fidelity factor) to dimerize and recruit Pol alpha into the CMG complex. Additional factors (Mcm10, FACT, and Tim-Tipin) will also be analyzed. These studies will employ CoIP and in vitro helicase/replication assays as well as in vivo interaction (proximity ligation assay) and functional studies (assembly on chromatin as determined by ChIP). Finally, the ability of the chaperone complex FACT to displace DNA containing nucleosomes will be evaluated in collaboration with David Readingling (letter of support included). • In Aim 3, mutations within Psf1 – a component of the GINS complex and subcomplex of the CMG - found linked to developmental and immunological defects in a number of children will be investigated. Their effect on GINS/CMG formation, CMG helicase activity, and DNA replication for a particular mutation (C152Y; that weakly supports CMG complex formation) will be evaluated. Finally, structure-function mapping of Psf1 will also be undertaken to map interactions with other GINS components as well as Cdc45 and Mcm proteins of the CMG complex. Complex formation and DNA replication will be tested in vitro, and both HeLa and patient fibroblasts will be used for in vivo DNA replication and cell cycle studies.

imp_text: This is a new application from an established investigator to study the biogenesis of the eukaryotic small ribosomal subunit in the yeast model. In particular, the role of DEAH RNA helicase Ecm16 in promoting the transition of the 90S pre-ribosome particle to the pre-40S small subunit precursor will be investigated. Four aims are proposed that couple genetic and biochemical characterization of Ecm16 function to understand key events in dissociating U3 snoRNA from the pre-rRNA and formation of the central RNA pseudoknot (a critical step for downstream rRNA processing and small subunit maturation). There is impressive preliminary genetic data to support the role of Ecm16 in various events in pre-40S subunit formation. The proposed studies are logical and nicely include both genetic and biochemical analyses. The collaboration of the PI with Cory Cobbett is key to the success of the dual approach. There is concern that the characterization of purified 40S intermediates from Ecm16 mutants (stalled and chased) may not be physiologically relevant and that the characterization of the protein composition and RNA structures within these complexes will be exceedingly difficult. Overall, while the studies are likely to shed light on an important event in small ribosome biogenesis and may identify a substrate for an essential RNA helicase, the advance to our understanding of ribosome biogenesis will be incremental.

app_text_str: • Aim 1 will investigate the role of Ecm16 in dissociating the U3 snoRNA/pre-rRNA interactions within the 90S particle. Notably, the PI has shown that ATPase-deficient Ecm16 result in a stalled pre-40S intermediate with 21S pre-rRNA still associated with U3 snoRNA. Using cold-sensitive mutants of Ecm16 (that are in hand), the PI proposes to chase these stalled complexes in vitro and biochemically characterize the resulting complexes (chased in the presence and absence of ATP) and the ability of Ecm16 to catalyze its own dissociation from the 40S complex. Technically challenging experiments to characterize the protein composition (by mass spec) and RNA structures (by SHAPE analysis) in stalled and chases complexes are also proposed. Finally, a genetic screen for extragenic suppressors of temperature-sensitive mutants of Ecm16 is proposed to identify proteins and/or RNA interactions that may act as direct substrates for Ecm16 function. • Aim 2 will characterize the ATPase and helicase activity of wild-type and mutant Ecm16 in vitro and determine whether interacting protein, Bud23, regulates Ecm16 activity. Helicase assays will be optimized using non-physiological substrates followed by testing the displacement of U3 snoRNA from pre-rRNA and dissociation of Imp3/4 from RNA duplexes. • Aim 3 will investigate whether the U3 snoRNA binding protein, Imp4, stabilizes U3 snoRNA/pre-rRNA interactions prior to formation of the central pseudoknot (CPK). These experiments are based on the finding that a majority of the suppressors of bud23. cells have mutations in IMP4, and are directed to specifically evaluate the biochemical defect of mutant Imp4 on its ability to bind U3 snoRNA and/or interact with binding partner, Mpp10, in vivo and with purified protein in vitro. Finally, the ability of mutations in U3 snoRNA that reduce its interaction with 18S pre-rRNA to bypass ecm16 or bud23 mutations will be tested. • Aim 4 will evaluate whether ribosomal protein Rps2 acts as a folding cofactor to stabilize the CPK. Preliminarily results indicate that Rps2 is a high copy suppressor of growth defects exhibited by bud23. cells. Given this, mutations in Rps2 (both directed and randomly introduced) will be tested for a role in CPK folding (as assayed by A2 position RNA cleavage) and bud23. growth as a means to identify critical contacts between Rps2 and the rRNA. These mutations will also be tested for synthetic lethality with Ecm16, Imp4 and snoRNA mutants thought to have defects in CPK formation. Finally, CoIP will be used to evaluate the interaction of wild-type and mutant Rps2 with pre-40S particles stalled at various stages in 40S biogenesis mutants. • The PI has isolated key extragenic suppressors in IMP4 and EMC16 that suppress growth defects in bud23. cells and has found that Rps2 acts as a high-copy suppressor of bud23.. These elements provide key insight and tools to investigate the physical and functional interactions between these proteins.
app_text_wkn: • A key approach is the chase of pre-40S intermediates that stall in ATPase-deficient and temperature-sensitive Ecm16 mutants. Chasing of the stalled intermediates will be done on purified complexes that likely lack protein components critical for formation/stabilization of complexes that would form in cells. There is a significant concern that the chased complexes may be physiologically irrelevant based on their formation in vitro from purified intermediates. • It is not completely clear from Fig. 7 whether epitope-tagged Ecm16 is fully functional. This is a small yet relevant concern given that the ATPase and helicase assays proposed in Aim 2 will utilize this protein purified from yeast cells.

imp_text: This study is focused on structural aspects of proteins involved in meiosis and is likely to generate significant insights as to how these proteins interact and form the architecture that catalyzes and regulates recombination between homologous chromosomes.  The main impact on the field will be a detailed picture of how these meiotic proteins position themselves on the chromosomes during meiosis.  Determination of the atomic structures of proteins and protein complexes can provide visual clarity into form and function leading to mechanistic insight that may have been previously impossible using classical genetic or biochemical functional assays. For example, proteins identified through genetic screens that are redundant or provide no apparent biochemical function using established assays may reveal their true function once high resolution structures are obtained.  Structural analysis of these meiotic proteins is critical to exert a sustained impact on the field and will complement present and future genetic and biochemical understanding.
sig_text_str: . A fundamental understanding of how meiosis is regulated is critical to human health if we are to understand the molecular defects that underlie aneuploidy, miscarriages, and birth defects.  This study will address both the molecular architecture and genetic functions of meiotic proteins which was previously unattainable through classical approaches.  Many of these meiotic proteins lack structural information and therefore, this project is poised to overcome that barrier in the field.
sig_text_wkn: . It would have strengthened the significance if the applicant had suggested how his results would impact or change how we diagnose/treat aneuploidy as a result of mis-regulated meiotic functions.
inv_text_str: .  Dr. Murray is well trained having received his PhD from UC Berkeley and post-doctoral training at Harvard with Steve Harrison (world leader in x-ray crystallography).  He is well-versed with protein purification techniques and has more than 20 crystal structures under his belt.  He is collaborative as indicated by his letters of support and is not afraid to strike out of his “comfort zone” to learn new approaches and techniques such as yeast genetics.  Clearly, he is capable of assembling a well-rounded team and all of the components to succeed in clarifying the architecture of meiotic proteins.
inn_text_str: . The key innovation is the applicants ability to purify and structurally characterize specific meiotic proteins and protein complexes that were previously intractable to this analysis.  Based on the applicant’s prior track record, there is high likelihood of success in this endeavor.  Secondly, combining genetic analysis with structural analysis is highly complementary and adds to the innovation. Again, the study of these meiotic proteins at the structural level in vitro has been incredibly difficult and the applicant has established methods to overcome these prior limitations.
inn_text_wkn: . It is not entirely clear from the innovation description how structural information will drive innovation in the yeast functional assay system.
app_text_str: . The overall approach is to purify meiotic proteins or protein complexes, such as the monopolin complex, and define their functions based on x-ray crystal structure, SAXS, or EM (or cryo-EM) depending on the yield of protein and information needed  - static picture (x-ray structure) versus tumbling in solution (SAXS). . There is a significant amount of preliminary data indicating that many of the proteins can be purified in isolation or in complexes (e.g. Mam1). . Extensive crystallization screening is used to obtain the conditions under which proteins will form x-ray diffraction quality crystals. A small molecule inhibitor is used in certain cases to rigidify the protein into a specific structure which is a nice approach to facilitate x-ray diffraction studies. . The applicant has recruited expertise to engage in EM studies if crystal structures are not obtainable. . A TnT rabbit reticulocyte system is used to define specific protein-protein interactions. . A nice approach is the deletion mutant strategy or “one-headed” monopolin complexes to determine if this protein complex cross-links kinetochores via the two heads.  These constructs will be further tested in vivo using yeast functional genetic studies and is complementary to the purified protein biochemical studies.  Several potential outcomes are given to place these experiments in context in term of what information will be gained from these studies. . Aim 2 is a characterization of the meiotic Hop1 HOMRA domain by size exclusion chromatography, NMR (support is noted from NMR collaborator) to examine conformational changes, defining Hop-1 partner interactions using in vitro (TnT) translated proteins and pull-down assays, and then using yeast genetics to study specific mutations in Hop1 on meiotic functions (spore viability,etc..).  Immunofluorescent studies will be undertaken to look in vivo at synapsed chromosomes in collaboration with Aanjay Dubey, Zhen, and Kolterman (letters of support are strong).  Finally, NMR studies will be used to guide x-ray diffraction studies of Hop1 HOMRA domain if crystals are obtained successfully.  Multiple Hop1 HOMRA homologues from different species are proposed to aid success in structural analysis. . Aim 3 is to characterize the synaptonemal protein Zip1.  The subaims are to (1) characterize Zip1 domain structure and self assembly by purification and SEC-MALS, (2) define Zip1 interactions with Red1 and SUMO using artificially synthesized SUMO oligomers of defined sizes in complex with and without Red1, and (3) use EM to determine structure of Zip1 or fragment of Zip1.  The Zip1 structural and functional studies are challenging as this protein has not been extensively characterized but worth the effort because there is a severe lack of information regarding this protein. .
app_text_wkn: . The proposal is quite ambitious but given the applicant’s strong track record, successful completion of the aims is likely.

UCSD is a world-renowned institution with significant resources, established leaders in the field of molecular biology and specifically areas related to meiosis and recombination, and a rich and vibrant intellectual environment.  Dr. Murray is in close proximity to several investigators and collaborators pursuing similar goals and has all the equipment and laboratory supplies to succeed in this endeavor. Core facilities are excellent and accessible. Technical support from cores is indicated in letters of support.

imp_text: The proposal was difficult to read and seemed mostly exploratory in nature.  The approaches and rationale seemed disjointed.  Nomenclature and acronyms used throughout the text made it incredibly difficult to follow the logic of the aims.  It was unclear how the descriptive based experiments could have a sustained impact on the field.   While interesting findings could certainly emerge from these studies, there does not seem to be a clear goal in the proposal, just a rambling assortment of experiments exploring different replication proteins using outdated methods for analysis.
sig_text_str: . Replication complexes and DNA replication are critical for cellular viability and defects in replication can lead to genomic instability.
sig_text_wkn: . Very little context and background was given to understand the significance of the aims.  While a statement is made that an altered CMG complex is linked with genetic instability and cancer, no specific examples are given. The significance section seems to be a laundry list of pre-RC and RC proteins with no clear focus on what proteins will be addressed in the proposal.
inv_text_str: . The investigator co-discovered RNA polymerase which is a seminal achievement in molecular biology.  National academy member. Vice-chairman of MSKCC.
inv_text_wkn: . Very little effort was put into writing the proposal.  Productivity seems on a downward trajectory.  No current external grant support.
inn_text_str: . Applicant claims to have unique reagents and assays for understanding leading and lagging strand synthesis with purified proteins isolated from higher eukaryotes.
inn_text_wkn: . It does not seem likely that this laboratory is “the only” one studying purified DNA replication proteins with unique assays.  In fact, Ken Marians at MSKCC has purified many replication proteins and reconstituted most of them in very innovative biochemical assays (including single molecule analysis) to understand DNA replication and pre-RC complexes.  There is no explanation why pol alpha utilizes bio-dUTP and pol delta does not and what this implies for each of these proteins.  PLA is commercially available and not innovative on its own.
app_text_str: They seem to have a unique rolling circle replication assay as well as a bio-dUTP analog for distinguishing different polymerase activities. They allude to the fact that they have a well characterized in vitro system for analyzing replication complexes however the details are unclear.
app_text_wkn: . Aim 1 is “studies on leading and lagging strand synthesis in vitro” - seems like an incredibly broad aim.  There also seems to be conflicting statements as in significance section they claim pol delta can not incorporate bio-dUTP, then here in Aim 1 they say it can and pol episilon can’t??    There doesn’t seem to be a rationale for this aim. . Aim 2 is the “interaction of CTF4/AND-1 with components of the replication fork”. Experiments are described to co-infect proteins in insect cells using baculovirus system with CTF4 but this seems like a highly artifactual method to look at protein-protein interactions.  PLA is used to test interactions in cells but the rationale in this aim does not seem defined.  Additionally, the PLA stained cells in Fig. 11 seem like non-specific total staining of nuclei rather than a specific PLA signal. . Aim 3 is “physiological effects due to alterations in GINS complex”.  Clinical mutations in Psf1 (a component of the GINS complex) are evaluated.  This aim seems to contain mostly past data and background on Psf1 mutations.  Transfection experiments are proposed with deletion mutants to test interactions and purified proteins in leading and lagging strand assays but the details are vague. .

imp_text: If successful, the project will add significant insight into the assembly and regulation of the small ribosomal subunit.  The applicant has recruited a biochemist as a co-investigator who is also an expert in the field of ribosomal biogenesis. The combined expertise of the two investigators in the ribosomal biogenesis arena coupled to strong genetics and biochemistry backgrounds ensure that the devised approaches will likely be successful.   The questions posed by the investigators address specific hypotheses: (1) Ecm16 is an RNA helicase that dissociates the U3 snoRNA allowing formation of the pseudoknot, (2) Bud23 is needed to license Ecm16 helicase activity, (3) Imp4 stabilizes the duplex target of Ecm16, and (4) Rps2 chaperones the folding of the central pseudoknot.  The rationales are clear and the multi-faceted approaches should drive findings and conclusions that will exert a sustained impact on the ribosome biogenesis field.  The only critique is that many sub-aims are proposed indicating that the applicant is quite ambitious and some of the screens may lead the research in different directions.
sig_text_str: Ribosome biogenesis is critical to cellular viability and life as we know it. Furthermore, ribosomopathies have been associated with human disease and the rapid proliferation of cancer cells require elevated ribosome synthesis to keep up with increased translational capacity. These studies will increase our knowledge of the basic mechanisms underlying ribosome biogenesis and provide insight to develop new tools for controlling cell proliferation in disease states.  The ribosome, its components, and enzymatic activity is highly conserved and thus yeast is an excellent genetic model to pursue these studies. .

In particular, the PI will examine what pathways (metabolic and others) are impacted by Foxo TFs that in turn affect the development of T cell memory.  The stages of differentiation at which Foxo TFs mediate their effects will also be determined. This application will provide in depth information on the role of Foxo TFs during T cell differentiation.  Strengths of this proposal include the preliminary data showing Foxo TFs are critical for T cell differentiation and the available mouse strains that will be critical for this study.  Humans that are elite controllers of HIV infection are known to have a deficit in Foxo TF activity.  Thus, better the results of this study could have translational applications for therapeutics. imp_text: This is a new R01 application from a promising new investigator to study the role of the actin-bundling protein L-plastin (LPL) in B cell motility, germinal center development and T cell-dependent antibody production. The strengths of the proposal are the PI’s expertise in the field, the productivity of the PI, and the interesting preliminary data. Weaknesses of the proposal are i) no evidence that LPL deficiency causes any clinical disease in humans, ii) the proposal was not hypothesis driven, iii) the proposal was not straightforward to understand why LPL is required for germinal center formation and T cell-dependent antibody production, iv) it is uncertain whether the PI will be able to complete the proposed study in Aim1 and Aim3, and v) it is unclear how the information gained from this study will help understand autoimmunity and develop therapeutic products. Successful completion of the proposed studies may generate novel information for understanding the role of LPL in humoral immunity. However, the weaknesses decreased the enthusiasm for this application.

imp_text: The proposal is from a very well trained and productive investigator. Production of high affinity antibodies requires formation of germinal centers (GC) and a defect in its formation can lead to immunodeficiency. Therefore, understanding the mechanism that regulates GC formation is of importance. The PI has found that the actin-bundling protein L-plastin plays a critical role in GC formation however, the specific role it plays has not yet been elucidated. The PI proposes to define the role of L-plastin in ”integrating the chemotactic and adhesive cues” required for GC formation. The proposed studies are of interest but not entirely novel as the function of this protein has been studied in some detail in other cells of the hematopoietic system including T cells. Studies proposed under aim-1 are relatively straight forward, the PI might be under estimating the challenges associated with efficiently transducing primary cells with lentivirus vectors. The success of the proposed experiments will largely depend on the efficiency of transduction and the sustained expression of GFP in the transduced cells. A more convincing preliminary data would be essential to demonstrate feasibility. In aim-2, a series of signaling and co-localization studies have been proposed. These studies will analyze very complex multi-protein interactions; unfortunately, as proposed the proposed studies are descriptive and unlikely to yield definitive results. Finally, aim-3 will utilize floxed mice in which L-plastin can be selectively deleted in B cells. The proposed studies are relatively straight forward and the PI is likely to find the expected results. In summary, although the team of investigators and the scientific environment are outstanding and the proposed studies are interesting, it could face technical challenges and are not particularly novel.

imp_text: This is well written and focused application from an established investigator. Thymic atrophy is associated with aging and has significant immunological implications for the continued development of T cell repertoire, particularly when given that people are likely to live longer. Therefore, understanding the molecular basis for age related thymic atrophy is important and could eventually lead to the development of therapies that can be used to slow or reverse this age-dependent physiological phenomenon. In this regard, the PI has made an interesting observation that thymic stromal cells are deficient in catalase that is required for removing H2O2. Additionally, the PI has shown that either treatment with dietary anti-oxidants or restoration of catalase expression through ubiquitous expression of a catalase transgene can slow thymic atrophy. Based on these interesting observations, the PI proposes to generate transgenic mice which will conditionally express catalase in thymic stromal cells and determine whether it can slow thymic atrophy, reduce oxidative lesions and resist ROS induced injury. These are important and worthwhile studies. However, it is not clear whether the data shown in figs-1 thru 3 were generated from older or younger mice. Only result that shows “a direct role” for catalase in preserving thymic function is through the gain of function results shown in Fig-5. However, it is not apparent if conditional catalase knockout in thymic stromal cells can result in early thymic atrophy. Moreover, the proposed studies are relatively simple and appear incremental in that catalase will be conditionally expressed in thymic stroma as opposed to ubiquitous expression used in the preliminary study.  Moreover, the proposal involves only gain of function studies and are not complemented with loss of function studies. Aim-4 is unlikely to yield definitive results. Therefore, there is only a modest enthusiasm for the proposal.

imp_text: Although much is known about the dynamics of lymphocyte trafficking into secondary lymphoid organs, similar insights on the cellular interactions that contribute to cellular differentiation and migration within the bone marrow are lacking. Similarly a considerable amount of information is available on lymphocyte intrinsic factors that contribute to lymphocyte development. However there is paucity of information on the necessary interactions that occur between hematopoietic precursors and the BM stromal cells that are required for lymphocyte differentiation. Therefore, the PI proposes to study the critical role played by CXCR4 expressed on BM stromal cells in the development of niches that are conducive to B cell development. In aim-1, the investigators will study B cell differentiation and migration using BM stromal specific CXCR4 deficient mice. In aim-2, the stromal cell niches that are critical for B cell development will be characterized. Since in later stages of development, self-reactive B cells are eliminated either by receptor editing or clonal deletion, in aim-3, the PI will study how the BM stromal cell niches influence this process using intravital microscopy and relevant transgenic mice. If successfully completed the proposed studies will likely provide new insights on how stromal cell niches are formed and how they regulate B cell development. These are conceptually novel studies that will use state of the art approaches. Although the PI appears to be capable of completing the studies, it appears that he has made no effort to take advantage of the extensive resources available at Yale University and thus appears isolated. Some of the proposed experiments are technically quite challenging and therefore, establishing appropriate collaborations is likely to make the proposed studies more feasible. In general, experimental details are lacking and thus preclude proper evaluation. Moreover, the proposal is overly ambitious, and it is unlikely to yield definitive or conclusive results.

Kelly and Spindler have many years of experience in their disciplines, and they have a number of experienced collaborators and helper who will assist with the work in different areas (transgenic mice, high throughput screen). However, the project is presented in a somewhat disorganized and complex fashion which made it difficult to follow in many places, although the overall goals were relatively clear. As a result it was not very clear how the studies would be carried out, and what the alternatives were to some of the studies proposed. The mechanism being investigated has a certain novelty, but is another of many different mechanisms by which viruses manipulate the innate responses of their host cells, so that the significance is moderate, as is the innovation.

imp_text: This project is presented by a talented investigator with skills in biochemistry and structural biology at the University of Denver, along with a collaborator in the Special Pathogens branch at the CDC who has greater skills in molecular virology. Together they have the appropriate experience in the areas of protein structure and function, and virology, and have obtained strong preliminary results that indicates that the vOTU proteins may be key modulators of the host innate immune responses by their ability to remove specific ubiquitin or ISG15 modifications, and therefore also of viral pathogenesis. The investigators have recently prepared infectious plasmid clones of one of the viruses – apparently for the first time. While the topic is likely very interesting, the proposal is very difficult to follow in places, with numerous viral variant proteins, mutants and combinations proposed. The biochemical and structural studies appear to be relatively clear and should generate a variety of interesting data about the specific effects of the proteins from different viruses on different host modified proteins. The studies of the viruses recovered from plasmids in tissue culture or mice are apparently novel but are not well described - it is difficult to understand what might be done, and what the results obtained might be. Issues of biosafety and select agents are well addressed, as are animal care. Some issues of presentation and following grant guidelines were present, and contributed to the difficulty of the presentation.

imp_text: The tradeoff between resolution and accessible timescale is a major limitation in the field of molecular dynamics and computational modeling. For very long timescale processes, such as in vivo formation of amyloid fibrils, there is currently no meaningful way to model at the molecular level. The current proposal is therefore aimed at bridging that gap by focusing on the rate limiting steps of fibril nucleation and growth. The PI is attempting to fill an unmet need in computational biology in order to better understand disease processes related to neurodegeneration. I am however not sure how the proposed dynamics studies will relate to in vivo, physiological states.  To me this is analogous to studying evolution of an organism in a vacuum, with no external pressures. As the PI acknowledges the kinetic phase diagram describing how fibril formation and growth is affected by different environmental conditions (e.g. temperature, pH, etc.), which are infinitely more complex in vivo. I am not convinced that the pathological growth of fibrils is driven by very long time scales (analogous to the Leviathan paradox of protein folding) versus simple accumulation of amyloidogenic peptides that drive fibril formation in a concentration dependent manner. Thus, the primary hypothesis being tested by the PI, while interesting, may have no relevance to in vivo amyloid formation.

imp_text: This proposal aims to investigate the structure and function of concentrative nucleoside transporters (CNTs), integral membrane proteins that belong to the solute carrier family of proteins.  CNTs import nucleosides and nucleoside-derived scaffolds into the cell for use in transcription.  Cancer cells that lack NTs are resistant to nucleoside-based drugs.  There are currently no structures of CNTs, and only limited information regarding the molecular basis of function. The current proposal has a sound, well vetted research plan with excellent preliminary results that suggest the specific aims will be accomplished.  The biggest concern is whether the lessons learned from a bacterial CNT will be applicable to the distant human homologue, although the grant does attempt to investigate this.  Overall, this is a classic, almost formulaic grant to investigate an important class of biomedically relevant membrane proteins.  The formulaic nature is not necessarily a negative here as the PI is proposing tried and true methods to tackle CNTs, which to date, have yet to yield structural information.

imp_text: Dr. Robinson is an early stage investigator who uses computational and biophysical approaches to study amyloid aggregation. She trained in top labs for her PhD and post-doctoral training and has been in her new independent position for just a few years. The problem of fibril formation is a good one and the computational methods being applied by Dr. Robinson are appropriate for the problem. Multi-timescale approaches are a good way to tackle this problem, but it is not clear given that some fo the fibril formations have very long time frames, that even this method will allow the simulations to be long enough to see what the PI wishes to see. The kinetic phase diagram concept is also of concern. Proposing to used biophysical methods (ITC) to characterize the binding of analogs to the proteins to assess mechanisms of substrate recognition and translocation. Methods are pretty standard for the field but the preliminary data indicate that the PI is very capable of completing this work. The study of the analogs is well designed. The one piece that is potentially lacking is the framework by which the data will be used to think about the design of future antiviral and anti cancer agents to avoid the efflux pumps being studied here.

These include the ambitious nature of the application especially in the aspect of drug discovery, certain experiments that are not fully justified, the absence of a medicinal chemist as a collaborator, not clear what would be source of the small molecules and peptides she plans to screen etc.  Nevertheless, this application has sufficient innovation and potential for translation, and can be expected to have a medium impact on the field.
