imp_text: This multi-PI proposal from two established investigators at VCU aims to develop novel anticancer agents that target the interaction of the repair protein XLF with XRCC4, thus inhibiting non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) to enhance sensitivity to radiation and chemotherapy.  The investigators had identified a novel low-affinity interaction between XLF and XRCC4 that appears to be druggable and this appears to be an attractive target to modulate NHEJ and induce DNA damage, leading to death of cancer cells.  The investigators propose a novel and innovative method to screen for small peptides and cyclic peptides that target this interaction. This application appears to fall in the category of high risk-high reward, but may be worth pursuing given the potential benefit of identifying and developing novel radiosensitizers. The strengths of the application include the expertise of the investigators, the importance of the question being asked, the potential of developing novel anticancer agents, a well thought-out research strategy, overall innovation is high etc.  At the same time, there are several weaknesses in the proposal as well.  While the application addressed a potentially important question, there is no data to support the feasibility of the experiments.  No evidence is provided to support that the screening strategy will work and is feasible.  Further, there is no data or citations to support that XLF-XRCC4 interaction is elevated in cancer cells compared to normal cells and is a good target for developing therapeutic agents. The application would have been stronger is such supporting data is presented and basic animal experiments are proposed to test their efficacy in vivo. Last but not the least, the proposal appears to be very ambitious, given the number of compounds they are planning to screen. Based on these strengths and weaknesses, the application, as presented, can be expected to have a medium impact on the field.

The vertebrate animal section did not address the five (or four, according to the 2016 guidelines) points and the human subjects section was not in one location in the application. The citations were totally out of place. Thus, given the problems with this application, I feel that it should not have been sent out for review till the errors were fixed. Given the fatal flaws in the presentation of the application, which could have been avoided if proper attention was given to the details, this reviewer does not have the confidence that the applicant will be able to conduct these studies with diligence and rigor. Based on the flaws in the presentation, the proposal can be expected to have a low impact, despite the fairly decent science and the trials involved.

study_section: Bacterial Pathogenesis Study Section
imp_text: Shigella flexneri (Sf) relies on Type III secretion (T3SS) to translocate effector proteins into the cytosol of host cells. This proposal investigates a translocator protein, IpaB, and its function in the interaction of the T3SS apparatus with the host membrane. The central hypothesis posits three distinct IpaB structures that correlate with stages of secretion, tested by the following specific aims (1) determine the location of IpaB in nascent vs active needles, (2) solve the structure of IpaB in free or associated form, (3) use site direct mutagenesis to test the role of key amino acids in IpaB interactions during Type III secretion. This is a solid proposal from an established team of investigators aiming to define the detailed molecular interactions of a key protein in the Sf T3SS apparatus. Although the experiments described are logical and feasible, but the anticipated findings are likely to be incremental. Strengths of the application are the mechanistic focus on IpaB interactions and the potential for learning how they might shape function. Score-driving weaknesses of the application include the limited scope of Aim 1, and lack of information for how the structure- function studies in Aim 3 will be used to test relevance of these mutants in the context of infection. imp_text: This is an outstanding proposal from an established and productive team of investigators, aiming to define the contributions of Pa biofilm components and regulators (Psl, Pel, CdrA) to biofilm integrity and host immune evasion. The investigators will use an array of different and complementary approaches to both better define the molecular structure of EPS polymers, and to tease apart their function in vitro. Strengths of the application are the compelling preliminary data, track record of productive collaboration by the investigators, careful experimental design, inclusion of multiple clinical strains and high likelihood of advancing the biofilm field. Inclusion of a limited set of experiments in a small animal would strengthen the proposal. Overall, this is an extremely strong application with high significance and few weaknesses.
sig_text_str: Pa is an opportunistic pathogen that is associated with a major public health burden and high patient mortality.  It is notably associated with lung disease in CF patients, who suffer from decreased lung function and chronic pulmonary infection. Understanding the molecular aspects of biofilm structure and how they may contribute to CF disease is highly significant. Pediatric CF patients exhibit antibody reactivity to Psl, a major focus of the application, implicating that this EPS component is present during infection, and is a target of the immune system. . Bacterial biofilms in general play a key role in many disease-related phenomena (included colonization of catheters, etc).  Elucidating the principles of biofilm structure and function will likely provide insights into how biofilms formed by other pathogenic bacteria can be targeted for therapeutic benefit.

He is highly qualified to lead the studies outlined in this proposal. . Dr. Terrizzi will provide strong expertise in glycobiology, which will be critical for biofilm structure experiments.
inn_text_str: The Pa biofilm field has extensively focused on the mucoidy phenotype, which emerges after long-term colonization of CF patients, and is dependent on alginate. These investigators provide evidence that biofilm formation prior to mucoid conversion is likely to be important in chronic Pa infection -therefore the focus on key regulators of non-mucoid biofilms is innovative and important for evaluating optimal therapeutic invention strategies. . Use of the spinning disk reactor to evaluate biofilm formation is innovative.

app_text_str: Evidence of experimental rigor, including blinded data collection, use of multiple Pa strains, including clinical strains, and specific description of statistical analyses. . The workflow describing purification of cell-associated Psl (CA-PSL) was thorough and employed many complementary approaches (and highly ambitious). The use of mutant strains lacking Pel and CdrA will provide important insights into Psl structural requirements. Although this sub-aim is largely exploratory, it lays groundwork for more targeted analyses. . Psl and Pel EPS expression levels will be evaluated in multiple strains, which is important and relevant given heterogeneity between strains. . Detailed analysis of CdrA in Pel-producing biofilms is warranted, given the heterogeneity of Psl and Pel expression shown in Fig. 6. . In Aim 2, use of primary human neutrophils to evaluate the role of EPS and CdrA is a strength, since there are no cell lines that can represent this key aspect of innate immunity.
app_text_wkn: In Fig. 3, the authors show evidence that CA-PSL is potentially quite heterogenous, as indicated by the high molecular smear revealed by immunoblot. Thus, purification and analysis of CA-PSL may yield highly variable results. It would have been helpful to see more information on how results would be interpreted and prioritized for further study. . Although it is considered a strength that the investigators will use primary human neutrophils for in vitro studies of Pa biofilm behavior, this still does not mimic the complex interactions that occur in the mammalian lung. Although there is not a perfect small animal model that mimics the chronic progression of CF, nonetheless, there are mouse models that could nevertheless be used to test in some way the relevance of new Pel, Psl and CdrA mutants in an in vivo setting. . As a minor note, for complemented strains, the arabinose-inducible pBAD constructs are used, which is common in the field. However, given the complex nature of the interactions between bacteria and host immune components, special care should be taken to control for possible effects of arabinose on the experimental system, for example, on neutrophils.

imp_text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Pa) degrades sphingosine-1-phosphate, which is a potent immune signaling molecule. The proposal is based on a logical working hypothesis, namely that Pa detection of S1P induces S1P degradation pathways, tested by the following specific aims (1) Characterize S1P transcriptional response, (2) ID regulators of S1P degradation pathway, (3) test impact of S1P degradation on Pa infection. This is a well written proposal from an early stage investigator exploring a novel pathway of metabolic regulation in Pa that appears to play a role in virulence in vivo.  The research output would likely have high significance, since the genes involved in S1P metabolism are conserved in other bacterial pathogens. Strengths of the proposal included convincing preliminary data, including in vivo studies, thoughtful experimental design and alternatives, and diverse approaches. Weaknesses that somewhat decreased enthusiasm for the proposal in its current form include limited usefulness of Aim 1a, the dynamic range of the reporter strain in the Aim 2 genetic screen, and in Aim 3, that the sph mutants may have impacts on virulence beyond sphingosine metabolism, which is not carefully considered. Moreover, there is some concern about independent productivity from the investigator. Overall, this is a strong application with the potential for high impact, but with some weaknesses. imp_text: This study aims at identifying the molecular mechanism by which overexpression of a non-coding RNA, snoRNA ACA11, promotes MM progression.  The hypothesis is that overexpression of ACA11 in t(4;14) positive MM reduces ROS-induced cell death leading to the progression of MM. The PI presents strong preliminary data to support the hypothesis that ACA11 overexpression is involved in MM progression by regulation of ROS levels.  The weaknesses include lack of any preliminary data for aim 3.  The link between ACA11 and p53 induced cell death was very weak. ACA11 expression levels in a larger number of patient samples should have been examined. Another weakness is that the role of each PI on this project is not clearly defined.  It is not clear how their combined expertise will be synergistic. This was also a very hard to read and understand grant.

imp_text: The overall goal of this project is to delineate the mechanism by which some miRNAs play a role in cellular bypass from oncogene-induced senescence. These processes are poorly understood and the understanding of them may help the discovery of anti-cancer therapies by targeting the mechanisms involved in oncogenic induced senescence bypass. Strength: The PI has provided ample evidence that miR30 may function to suppress oncogene induced senescence by targeting CHD7, a transcriptional co-activator, and TNRC6A, an RNA-binding protein essential for miRNA functionality. The preliminary data are solid, the rationale for the aims are well described and experimental approaches are logical. A very well written and easy to follow grant.  The pitfalls are well described and alternative strategies are logical and well presented. The PI is a well established investigator and has published several high impact manuscripts. Weaknesses: . The preliminary data are obtained using fibroblast cell lines.  The experimental approaches also propose the use of mainly fibroblast cell lines. No preliminary data are presented by using epithelial cancer cells or cell lines. The results may not translate well to human epithelial cancer cells. . The expression levels of the proposed genes mir30, CHD7 and TNRC6A in human primary cancer cells are not described.  What is the association between mir30 expression, CHD7 or TNRC6A and any cancer overall survival or time to development of distant metastasis. Some of these data may be available by searching public databases such as TCGA or Kaplan Meier survival plotter.

imp_text: The long term goal of this project is the design of novel breast cancer targeted therapies for suppression of PI 3-K (phosphoinositide 3-kinase) and Akt signaling pathway. Most of preliminary data support their stated hypothesis. The team of PI and co-investigators are highly competent with a long-standing track record of success in publishing high impact manuscripts. Weakness: The proposed aims were mainly cell line based. They did not provide any data in primary breast cancers to show what percentage of primary breast cancers show PI3K independent activation of AKT either through a mutation in AKT, increased activation of Cyclin A/CdK2 or SKP2 expression. There were also no data regarding the relevance of PI3K independent activation of AKT to either breast cancer overall survival, distant metastasis free survival, or response to chemotherapy. The grant was very hard to read.  A large number of preliminary data using mainly cell lines were presented. The figures were also very small and a large amount of data and information were all presented without any spaces.

While this is an important question, enthusiasm is muted for this submission as much of the application focuses on examining an already published finding, that Cyclin A can lead to the hyperactivation of Akt in cancer cell lines, in breast cancer cell lines (Aims 1.1-1.3).  Unfortunately, the more interesting parts of Aim 1 (1.4 and 1.5) are dependent upon those findings being positive in breast cancer and the only support data for success is the IP shown in Fig. 2A.  On the other hand, the preliminary studies depicted in Aim 2 were much more focused on breast cancer and therefore, this reviewer feels there is much potential for success with this second aim.

imp_text: This project is focused on the function of a small nucleolar non-coding RNA, ACA11, that is up regulated in tumor cell lines and patient samples harboring the t(4;14) chromosomal translocation. The working hypothesis is that ACA11 is involved in the processing of select small nucleolar RNAs involved in oxidative stress…and that overexpression of ACA11 reduces reactive oxygen species induced cell death leading to the development and/or progression of a subpopulation of multiple myelomas. A corollary of this hypothesis is that ACA11 may be involved in resistance to cancer chemotherapy, which is the cancer-related element of this project. The aims of this project are largely devoted to understanding the nature of ACA11 interaction with its co-regulators and putative targets within the cell and the linkage to reactive oxygen generation and suppression. Specifically, studies will identify interacting proteins, identify substrates of the ACA11-small nuclear ribonucleoprotein complex and test that ACA11 blocks nucleolar stress induced and p53 regulated ROS production. Overall, the elements of the project relating to characterization of the basic biological functions of ACA11 appear to be experimentally rigorous, with appropriate consideration of anticipated outcomes and alternative strategies. However, there are a number of fundamental weakness in the work that involve a) the linkage to reactive oxygen generation; b) the potential relationship to sensitivity or resistance to chemotherapy and c) the involvement of p53 in reactive oxygen generation. The preliminary data presented relating to reactive oxygen generation are relatively superficial and unconvincing and the experimental approaches make no effort to develop these observations further. The influence of reactive oxygen species on cellular growth and survival is complex and the applicant fails to make a convincing case that reactive oxygen mediates the actions of ACA11 in the cell. While Figure 12 indicates that ACA11 attenuates ROS production by hydrogen peroxide, there is no indication as to the nature of the reactive species; furthermore, it is uncertain whether the data relating to hydrogen peroxide has any relevance to cancer therapeutics. Knockdown of ACA11 does increase ROS generation induced by hydrogen peroxide, but whether these changes would be biologically significant is subject to question. ACA11 knockdown does reduce tumor cell growth; however, this is a very transient effect ((Figure 13C) and would have to be shown to be significant in a tumor bearing animal model. Furthermore, no proof is provided that the growth inhibition is in any way related to the levels of reactive oxygen generation ( i.e. an example  of true, true but not necessarily related). Similarly the sensitization to doxorubicin is intriguing but again may not be related to reactive oxygen generation. With regard to chemotherapy, absolutely no data is provided in support of the contention that ACA11 overexpression is related to drug ( or perhaps more relevant to the ROS generation) to radiation resistance. Finally, the applicant cites a report from 1996 in support of the linkage between p53 and ROS generation, with no supporting evidence in the current experimental models. Furthermore, although  apoptosis is invoked in the context of p53, there is no data presented indicative of the involvement of apoptosis in the actions of ACA11. The effects shown in Figure 13C are growth inhibition; the “cell viability” data in Figure 13 is relatively meaningless in the absence of any information as to how these data were generated.

There are multiple concerns with the preliminary data in support of the involvement of reactive oxygen species in the activity of ACA11, the contribution of ACA11 and reactive oxygen generation in responsiveness of multiple myeloma to chemotherapy and the putative role of p53 in reactive oxygen generation in the actions of ACA11. These are detailed in the overall impact section. Given that the central element linking these studies to cancer is the generation or suppression of reactive oxygen generation, this is considered to be a fundamental ( and score driving) deficiency.

imp_text: The overall goal of this project is to identify long noncoding RNAs that are either tumor suppressive or tumor promoting in Myc driven B cell lymphoma. The fundamental approach involves a comparison between levels of the lncRNAs in murine models of B cell lymphoma and pre-lymphoma cells in terms of their over expression or underexpression by RNA sequencing. The experimental design is generally well conceived with appropriate consideration of anticipated outcomes and alternative strategies. A particularly relevant element is the effort to validate the lnRNAs based on human orthologs.  The function of the lnRNAs in lymphomagenesis will be validated in vivo using RNAi screening and gain of function/loss of function approaches. These are considered appropriate experimental strategies. Finally targeted deletion studies in vivo will serve to identify the biological function of these RNAs as well as their involvement in promoting spontaneous tumorignesis alone and in association with Myc expression. The applicant is experienced in studies of microRNA function; although there is no history of publications relating to the lnRNAs, it is presumed that previous studies with mRNAs will provide the necessary background for the proposed work. The applicant has also identified collaborators who should bring complementary expertise to the project involving the use of shRNA libraries for proof of principle experiments. Although the collaborators provide letters, no biosketches appear to have been included. The proposed work could potentially have high impact if, in fact, the applicant can identify long noncoding RNAs that have either tumor suppressive or tumor promoting functions. However, a primary concern is that the functionality of the lncRNAs in regulating tumor development (if, in fact, this is the case) is not obligatorily associated with their relative level of expression, essentially undermining the driving principle underlying this project. It is also felt that the project may be overly ambitious. Overall, this would be considered a very high risk proposal that does have significant potential to contribute to an understanding of the function of lncRNAs in cancer etiology. Nevertheless, reservations about the underlying experimental approach somewhat dampen overall enthusiasm.
sig_text_str: . The significance of this project lies in its potential to uncover tumor promoting and/or tumor suppressive function of long noncoding RNAs in lymphoma. This could open new directions for understanding disease development, possible biomarkers and novel therapeutic strategies.
sig_text_wkn: . The fundamental premise guiding this project is that upregulation or down regulation of levels of the lncRNAs in lymphoma cells as compared to control cells will be indicative of their association with tumorigenesis. However, it is formally possible that while extensive data is likely to be generated, the studies will fail to identify the functional significance of the long non-coding RNAs with respect to tumorigenesis. Consequently, this is considered to be a very high-risk proposal. . While the model of Eu-Myc B-cell lymphoma appears to be an appropriate choice for this project, there is no assurance that even if functions of these micro RNAs are identified that this will have any therapeutic or prognostic significance. .

imp_text: This grant project is focused on efforts to sensitize breast tumor cells to chemotherapy through a relatively novel approach, i.e. by targeting cdk2/ cyclin A mediated signaling pathways. The applicant presents preliminary data in support of the premise that suppression of PI3K does not necessarily lead to increased sensitivity to therapy via a concomitant effect on Akt since in some cases Akt is instead reactivated. Preliminary data is also presented that demonstrates regulation of Akt by cdk2/cyclin A. Furthermore, Skp2 signaling and Akt somatic mutations are implicated in tumor cell insensitivity to therapy. The work is considered innovative in challenging a long held paradigm relating to the PI3/Akt pathways. The preliminary data are relatively strong and convincing of the driving premise. The experimental approaches are generally well conceived and presented in some detail with consideration of anticipated outcomes and alternative strategies. There are some weaknesses, but these are not considered major deficiencies. In general, the applicant anticipates that the experimental outcomes will support the underlying premise driving this project but does not address how the experimental approaches might be modified in the event that e.g. there are different outcomes when using a panel of breast tumor cell lines. There is some confusion in the presentation relating to tumorigenesis versus antitumor effects since the grant attempts to identify Akt signaling function for both outcomes. This appears to be somewhat overly ambitious but is not a primary score driving concern.
sig_text_str: . The proposed work is designed to overcome resistance to chemotherapy by suppressing the activation of Akt, which is often overexpressed in cancer and contributes to the insensitivity of malignancies to therapy. . Extensive preliminary data is presented in support of the premise(s) underlying this project relating to cdk2/cyclin A regulation of Akt phosphorylation, dissociation of PI3K inhibition and suppression of Akt, and the potential involvement of Skp2 and somatic mutations in Akt in drug resistance. . It is possible that this work could lead to a novel paradigm for the treatment of some cancers that are refractory to PI3/Akt pathway inhibitors.
sig_text_wkn: . The PI3/Akt pathway is generally thought to confer resistance to chemotherapy by interfering with susceptibility to apoptosis. This is not addressed in the preliminary data and barely considered in the experimental approaches. . There is some concern that the AktE17 promotes tumor growth only under serum free conditions, which may not be physiologically relevant.

Dr. Kelley received her Ph.D. degree from the National Institute for Medical Research in London and continues with postdoctoral training at Tufts University School of Medicine and Harvard Medical School. She is currently Professor of Pathology at Harvard. She has extensive experience relating to the PI3/Akt signaling pathway, having published on this topic in high impact peer-reviewed journals. . The co-investigator, Dr. Wan, is an Associate Professor of Pathology at Harvard Medical School who brings complementary expertise to the proposed project relating to Skp2 signaling, cell cycle regulation and tuumorigenesis. . The project is also significantly strengthened by the involvement of Drs. Pandolfo and Cantell.
inn_text_str: . The work is considered innovative in challenging a long held paradigm relating to the regulation of PI3/Akt signaling. . The possibility of targeting cdk2/cyclin A and/or Skp2 represents a relatively novel therapeutic approach for cancer.
app_text_str: . The experimental approaches are considered to be well conceived and rigorously developed. It is highly likely that the proposed work will generate data that could potentially guide the development of therapeutic strategies targeting Akt signaling that is PI3K independent. . Studies will be taken from cell culture model to various animal models, including transgenic mice expressing wild type and phosphorylation mutant forms of Akt as well as with mammary specific inducible Akt1 E17K. . The applicant has developed the appropriate tools for interrogation of the indicated signaling pathways, including strategies for silencing and targeted depletion of cyclin A and cdk2, inhibitors of cdk2 and cyclin A, phosphorylation defective and phosphorylation mimetics of Akt, and breast tumor cells stably expressing inducible shRNA for PI3K. .
app_text_wkn: . There is a tendency to anticipate that the experimental outcomes will support the underlying hypotheses driving this project and there is insufficient consideration of the possibility that this will not be the case for e.g. the different breast tumor cell lines being investigated…or how inconsistent outcomes would be interpreted or inform subsequent work. For instance, it is assumed that in all cell lines tested, Akt activity will mirror cyclin A expression, but what if this does not prove to be the case? . There is virtually no consideration of the involvement of apoptosis inhibition in resistance mediated by the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. . There is perhaps some confusion as to whether the project is to be focused on sensitivity to therapy or tumorigenesis.

imp_text: The applicants found that a miRNA, miR-30, may disrupt oncogene-induced senescence, and therefore contribute to cancer development. Two potential targets, CHD7 and TNRC6A were discovered. In aim 1 and aim 2, the researchers provided a well-designed proposal for mechanistic studies underlying the roles of CHD7 and TNRC6A. The researchers also proposed to test their hypothesis in clinical samples in aim 3, which would relate their hypothesis to clinical application. These studies are significant for understanding the mechanism of cancer development. The function of miR-30 on oncogene-induced senescence is still not clear. imp_text: The PI3-K/Akt signaling axis is critical for the initiation and progression of various types of cancers. Akt hyperactivation is found in a large number of cancer patients and is considered a hallmark of cancer. Many inhibitors of PI3-K and Akt are undergoing Phase I and II clinical trials as targeted cancer therapy. Unfortunately, Akt inhibitors showed display adverse effects in normal somatic cells. The association between Akt hyperactivation and aberrant cell cycle regulation are urgently needed to be clarified. This proposal will investigate how Cdk2/Cyclin A functions as a novel upstream regulatory mechanism to promote Akt activation in a cell cycle-dependent manner. Furthermore, it is proposed to determine the mechanism that with which Skp2 induces Akt reactivation, and the functional significance of Akt1 and Akt2 somatic mutations. These studies might may be beneficial in guiding the use of Cdk2, Skp2, and Akt inhibitors for targeted chemotherapy with improved efficacy in clinics, especially for the breast cancer patients that are refractory to specific PI3-K inhibitors. The PI and collaborators have very successful research experience and strong expertise in PI3K and Akt signaling pathways, as well as in the Skp2 and SCF research fields. imp_text: The goal of this proposed study is to investigate the underlying mechanism of ACA11-induced tumorigenesis in MM patients having t(4;14) translocation. ACA11 is a non-coding RNA located in the oncogene WHSC1. However, upregulation of WHSC1 doesn’t confer tumorigenesis, suggesting that unknown mechanisms are involved in tumorigenesis caused by t(4;14) translocation. The PI’s preliminary data suggest that overexpression of ncRNA ACA11 causes reduction of ROS production and induction of cellular proliferation. This study is therefore proposed to investigate the molecular mechanism of how ACA11 regulates ROS production focusing on identification of its binding partner proteins. Since, ACA11 is novel ncRNA associated with oncogenesis, exploration of its function and molecular mechanism of involvement in tumorigenesis is novel aspect of this study. However, the PI already obtained preliminary data showing that ACA11 interacts with many ribonuclear proteins and inhibits ROS production. Therefore, further studies proposing to explore interacting domain of ACA11 involved in regulation of ROS production will not add significant knowledge. This study relies sole of MM cell lines. Therefore, physiological relevance of the proposed mechanism of CAC11-mediated regulation of ROS production and cell survival is not clear.

WHSC1 is an important oncogene that play role in t(4;14) translocation of 20% MM patients and involved in other types of cancer. This study will further broaden our understanding of how WHSC1 contributes to tumorigenesis. . imp_text: This R01 application proposes to study the role of miR-30, a micro RNA, in oncogene-induced senescence and cancer development. Overexpression of miR-30 has been observed in many types of cancer. Preliminary studies demonstrated that overexpression of miR-30 is associated with oncogene-induced senescence in primary human fibroblast. All these evidence strongly support critical roles of miR-30 in cancer. This study, therefore, aims to dissect the role of miR-30 in senescence and cancer development. To this end, it has been hypothesized that miR-30 disrupts oncogene-induced senescence via interaction with CHD7, a transcriptional coactivator, and TNRC6A, an RNA-binding protein. The role of CHD7 and its regulation by miR-30 will be investigated in Aim 1. The aim 2 will study the role of TNRC6A in miR-30-induced regulation of senescence. Extensive molecular approaches are proposed to dissect the role of CHD7 and TNRC6A in senescence and their regulation by miRNA-30. However, it is not clear whether both CHD7 and TNRC6A are involved miR-30-mediated regulation of senescence bypass in a common mechanism or they contribute separately. The relative contribution of two target proteins in miR-30-mediated disruption of senescence is not clear. Finally, the role of miR-30 in cancer development will be examined.  Considering the importance of miRNAs in the regulation of cancer, this study is of clinical significance. imp_text: Strengths of the application include the highly significant area of study, the use of mouse models in vivo to validate findings in cell culture, the expertise and track-record of the two multiple PIs, as well as the innovative hypotheses being tested.  The latter include opposing roles for Akt1 and Akt2, the relevance of cyclin-dependent kinase regulation in Akt regulation, and the exploration of PI3 kinase-independent regulation of Akt.  Although the approach is well-designed and rigorous, there are some concerns about the justification for use of specific cell lines and more importantly how the PIs will distinguish indirect cell cycle effects from direct Cdk2 phosphorylation of Akt.  Overall, however, strengths outweigh weaknesses.
sig_text_str: . Activation of Akt signaling is a key event in human cancers given the multiple genetic alterations that impact this pathway.  Elucidating the underlying molecular basis for these effects are thus an essential area of cancer research. . Proposed studies use complementing approaches with cell lines in vitro and mouse models in vivo that will further ensure that the findings have biological relevance. . study_section: Tumor Progression and Metastasis Study Section
imp_text: Triple negative breast cancer (TNBC) is the most lethal subtype of breast cancer with rapid progression and recurrence. Owing to the obstinate nature of TNBC and because few options are available for prevention of disease recurrence, it is urgent to develop efficacious strategies to manage this disease. In this new R01 application, the PI aims at characterization of a protein tyrosine kinase, c-Abl, as a new tumor suppressor in TNBC. Four specific aims are proposed accordingly. In Aim 1, the PI will study if TGF-ß signaling is involved in inactivation of c-Abl in TNBC; in Aim 2, the PI study how P53 signaling interacts with c-Abl in TNBC cells; in Aim 3, the PI will access the predictive capacity of c-Abl for the response to Docetaxel in TNBC by using cell line models and clinical specimens; and in Aim 4, the PI will evaluate a natural product, Securinine for its therapeutic potentials in TNBC. The strengths of this application include the significance when studying the molecular mechanisms of TNBC metastasis, the PI’s expertise and experience in study of breast cancer, characterizing c-Abl as a new tumor suppressor in TNBC, strong preliminary data, and an excellent research environment. Some weaknesses are also noted. Clinical trials have shown benefits of chemotherapy to TNBC women but the majority of these patients still appear to suffer from poor survivals due to rapid recurrence, regardless of their response to initial treatments. Therefore, drug resistance may not be fully responsible for the metastasis in TNBC patients. Most of the preliminary data were derived from the mouse mammary tumor models, which could raise a concern on genetic variation between different species.  In addition, it is unclear if there are any interactions for TGF-ß and P53 signaling when regulating c-Abl in TNBC cells.

study_section: Tumor Progression and Metastasis Study Section
imp_text: Prostate cancer is still one of the leading cancer types affecting the health of American men. Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is the mainstay strategy for treating senior patients with prostate cancer, but relapse due to drug resistance in those individuals has not been well-controlled in the clinic. In this new R01 application, the PI aims to study a transcription factor, Sox2, for its mechanical role in tumor progression and therapeutic potential in prostate cancer. Three specific aims are proposed accordingly. In Aim 1, the PI plans to determine the oncogenic role in promoting tumor cell survival and metastasis by using prostate cancer cell lines and xenograft animal models; in Aim 2, the PI will evaluate the expression levels of Sox2 by using a number of clinical specimens and use genomic approaches to seek the downstream target genes that may interact with Sox-2; in Aim 3, the PI will establish prostate tumors derived from Sox-2 positive normal basal epithelial cells and determine if Sox-2 dysregulation results in tumor metastasis and castration-resistance. The strengths of this R01 application include the clinical need to improve our management in prostate cancer relapse, a motivated young investigator, Sox-2 as a new marker and therapeutic target in prostate cancer, supportive preliminary data, thoughtfully designed specific aims, and an excellent research environment. A few drawbacks are also noted. Even though Sox-2 is a well-documented transcription factor, its oncogenic roles in prostate cancer may not be fully based on its transcriptional activity. The PI focusing on this direction may miss other insights that can help understand Sox-2 as an oncogene completely. In addition, genomic screening approaches adapted in Aim 2.2 will lead to unpredicted outcomes. Overall, this is a well-written proposal from an early stage and new investigator.

imp_text: The tumor microenvironment is referred to the cellular surroundings of tumor cells including immune cells, blood vessels, the extracellular matrix (ECM), and et al. Specifically, collagen origination was identified as a signature for assessing the prognosis of ERa+ breast cancer patients, which is significant for understanding tumor progression and developing targeted therapy in breast cancer. In this R01 application, the PIs aim to investigate if ECM and collagen organization are able shift the hormonal response of breast tumor cells towards advanced stages. Three specific aims are proposed. In Aim 1, the PIs will study the mechanisms by which the stiffness of ECM shifts the spectrum of PRL- and estrogen-induced signals in breast cancer cells; in Aim 2, the PIs will investigate how PRL and estrogen regulate ECM deposition in stromal fibroblasts; and in Aim 3, the Pi will evaluate the interactions among PRL, estrogen, and ECM by using transgenic mouse models and human TMAs. The strengths of this application include the significance when studying tumor microenvironment in breast cancer, PIs and co-PIs’ expertise and experience, novelty in study of ECM affecting hormonal response, innovative transgenic animal model, strong preliminary data, in vivo studies, and an outstanding research environment. The score-driven weakness is lack of a piece of evidence that PRL can promote invasion or metastasis in breast tumor cells with high density of collagen, which can strongly support the hypothesis that stiffness of ECM is capable of shifting the hormonal response of breast cancer cells towards tumor progression. The overall impact of this proposal is high.

imp_text: The project aims to study the mechanisms of regulation of Net1, a Rho-GEF for RhoA, a small GTPase extensively studied by the lab for many years. There is no doubt that the PI is expert in this pathway (I was confused by the last name of the PI: it it JA Baker (not found in Pubmed) or JA Frost (found in Pubmed)??). In the 3 aim project, it is planned to define the molecular mechanisms of Net1 acetylation/deacetylation, to address the regulation of Net1 by focal adhesion machineries (FAK, Src) and vice versa and, third, to address the role of Net1 in tumor growth and dissemination using mouse models. This is quite a classical program using classical techniques with no major technical difficulties. Preliminary results are convincing. For the in vivo study, the possibility that Net1 KO may preclude mammary gland development appears to be unexpected for the PI. However, a paper from this group (I guess it is the good one: JA Frost’s lab!!) argues for a role of Net1 in mammary gland development (Zuo Y et al., Mol Endocrinology 2014)….. This program will generate interesting data. It will make the proof of concept that Net1 is indeed an important factor of tumor growth and dissemination (in vivo data) and will shed light on the mechanisms of regulation of this unusual Rho GEF. I don’t see any major caveat in the program.

imp_text: The proposed work is to develop new structures for caged morpholino oligos (MOs) to enable light controlled gene expression. The PI will use light cleavable caged molecules appended to MOs in unique structures (lariat, double lariat etc.) for better modulation of gene expression. The Specific Aims take a stepwise approach. Aim 1 and 2 will synthesize different cMOs, and then Aim 2 will use a combination of cMOs that can be excited at different wavelengths of light and use them in zebrafish embryos to orthogonally control ntla and spt. Additionally, the PIs will use a combination of two cMOs to study critical regulators of pancreas development (pdx1 and mnx1). The PI hopes to use it as a universal approach for controlling MO by light. The PI and co-PIs are well suited to carry out the work, with the appropriate facilities and resources available. Overall the proposed work is an interesting technology that is promising for gene expression control. However, the level of novelty seems low as there is a lot of existing work in caged morpholino oligos.

study_section: Vascular Cell and Molecular Biology Study Section
imp_text: Understanding IL-19 signaling in non-immune cells is important, and the PI has demonstrated that this process has biological relevance.  This study combines culture models with mouse genetic models to address the role of IL-19 in differential signaling in ECs vs. VSMCs, how this cytokine influences angiogenesis in an ischemia model, whether its role is to modify ECs, macrophages, or both, and how IL-19 actually accomplishes these tasks.  The investigator and the research team have demonstrated their ability to perform these studies; preliminary data support the hypotheses.  Weaknesses in this study relate to the very narrow focus on IL-19-mediated mechanisms associated with its roles in angiogenesis.  This could miss some exclude some important events.  Overall, however, the proposal is novel and interesting.  The writing could use some improvement; there were numerous errors in grammar, typing, etc.
sig_text_str: . The PI has observed that IL-19 promotes angiogenesis, but not through VEGF or bFGF.  The goal of this study is to confirm this finding (Aim 1), determine if IL-19 acts on ECs or on macrophages to modulate angiogenesis (Aim 2), determine which secreted factors induced by IL-19 stimulation are necessary for angiogenesis (Aim 3), and dissect the roles of the different IL-20 receptors to IL-19-mediated effects in ECs versus VSMCs.  Aims 2 to 4 represent novel and potentially important areas of study.  Determining how IL-19 directly regulates vascular cells and EC-VSMC communication is significant. . IL-19 promotes angiogenesis, yet suppresses inflammation, making it unique among cytokines. . The fact that IL-19 exerts quite different effects on ECs vs. VSMCs, and that this can be traced to the relative levels of the co-receptors, offers an opportunity to dissect an interesting signaling pathway (Aim 4).
sig_text_wkn: . IL-19 is one of many, many factors that regulate angiogenesis.  Its effects are not tremendously powerful, as indicated by the PI’s data.
inv_text_str: . The PI is currently a Professor at Temple University, having obtained a PhD in 1992 from Hahnemann U. . The PI is funded to do IL-19-related work focused on VSMCs and the mechanisms associated with IL-19 and the suppression of VSMC activation to a proliferative phenotype. . A co-investigator with expertise in vascular surgery and related animal angiogenesis/wound models has been enlisted to help with this project.
inn_text_str: . The use of the IL-19-null mouse model will facilitate the studies in Aim 1, which previously relied upon injection or culture models.
inn_text_wkn: . Aim 3 focuses on a subset of factors up-regulated in response to IL-19, but may miss important effects that occur independent of changes in gene expression.  The selected factors are all known to influence VSMCs and thus vascularization, so it will not be surprising that cells from the relevant knock-out mouse models will show altered angiogenic responses in the aortic ring assays.
app_text_str: . Aim 1 extends the PI’s finding that ECs express IL-19, and that this cytokine can promote angiogenesis.  New approaches will include the use of an IL-19-null mouse model plus hind limb ischemia. . To determine if IL-19 exerts its effects through ECs versus macrophages, the PI will use bone marrow transplantation of IL-20R2-null marrow into WT mice (no macrophage responses) or WT marrow into IL-20R2-null mice (no EC responses). . Aim 3 will test the hypothesis that IL-19 acts through its ability to up-regulate IL-1b, HGF, CXCL1, and/or IL-8.  Knock-out mouse models will be used to determine if the lack of any of these blocks the effects of IL-19.  This part of the study will use an aortic ring sprouting assay to evaluate VSMC coverage and macrophage participation. . ECs and VSMCs respond quite differently to IL-19, and they express different ratios of IL-20R1 and IL-20R2.  In Aim 4, the IL-20R ratios in cultured cells will be adjusted by RNAi-mediated knock-down or cDNA over-expression.  Assays will include proliferation, cytokine expression, STAT activation, and migration.
app_text_wkn: . IL-19 may potentiate another factor’s actions, perhaps through receptor modification; that factor may not necessarily be up-regulated in response to IL-19 stimulation.  If this is the case, then the approaches in Aim 3 will not reveal this, since only 4 up-regulated factors will be investigated.  A less biased approach would reduce the risk that the factors selected are not the ones that drive IL-19-mediated angiogenesis.

study_section: Vascular Cell and Molecular Biology Study Section
imp_text: The evidence that MR regulates blood pressure via its expression in vascular cells is compelling, and the PI has played an important role in this story.  This proposal seeks to expand our knowledge about the mechanisms involved in this effect.  Preliminary data support the proposed aims, but only to a certain extent.  While the PI asserts that there is evidence that AngII, through PKCdelta, directly activates MR through a phosphorylation event, it is quite possible that the effects are indirect via different kinases or through a much more complex pathway.  In fact, there is no direct evidence that MR is phosphorylated in response to AngII.  Similarly, this proposal tests the possibility that MR acts directly at the Cav1.2 and Nox2 promoters; if these assumptions prove false, then the mechanisms by which MR regulates blood pressure will remain murky.  Thus, while these studies will solidify the role of SMC-expressed MR in regulating blood pressure, it is quite possible, given the very narrow focus of the proposed studies, that the PI will only be able to rule out some specific mechanisms, but will not have gained sufficient insight to pursue alternative hypotheses.  A less biased approach might therefore be warranted.
sig_text_str: . The PI has developed a model in which ligand-bound mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) is further activated by PKCdelta-mediated phosphorylation, leading to elevated Ca2+ intake and contractility.  This is exacerbated by increased production of ROS, and is responsible for age-related blood pressure elevation.  The PI’s recent Nat Med paper supports the hypothesis that vascular MR expression directly affects blood pressure; this proposal will build on it to determine how AngII stimulation coordinates with MR activation to modulate blood pressure.  Elucidating the mechanisms by which SMC-expressed MR directly regulates vascular tone will be important, particularly since MR inhibitors have undesirable effects.
sig_text_wkn: . This proposal is based on a number of assumptions that may not be accurate.  First, it assumes that AngII promotes the direct phosphorylation of MR via PKCdelta.  Second, it assumes that MR acts directly via a putative MRE in the Cav1.2 promoter.  Third, it assumes that MR directly regulates Nox2 expression, again via a putative MRE in the Nox2 promoter.  This study will enable the PI to confirm these assumptions, but if the effects of MR are indirect, then the approach gets much more complicated.  For example, if MR acts indirectly by altering the expression of transcription factors that themselves directly modulate Cav1.2 or Nox2 transcription, this study will not reveal those factors.  The results of these studies will only enable the PI to rule out MR as a direct mediator of the transcriptional events.
inv_text_str: . The PI obtained a PhD and an MD from U Penn in 1997 and 1999, respectively, and completed a research fellowship at Tufts before becoming an Asst Prof there in 2005.  The PI is currently as Assoc Prof at Tufts, and has maintained NIH and AHA funding since then. . Previous work on MR expressed in vascular cells, including grants and papers, suggests the PI’s ability to pursue this work. . The sub-contractor will perform patch clamp studies and other specialized tasks.  The Co-I is also well-funded and experienced.
inn_text_str: . The PI delineates several innovative aspects of this study.  These include the idea that vascular tone regulates systemic blood pressure, that MR is involved in this, and that AngII modulates this signaling via MR.  The SMC-specific MR knock-out mouse model is also innovative, though the PI has already published with it.
inn_text_wkn: . As described in other sections of this review, the Aims presented in this proposal focus on assumptions that may prove false.  The biased approaches here would be stronger given more definitive preliminary data.  Instead, the proposed studies utilize well-established approaches which, if the assumptions prove incorrect, will not yield clues regarding where to proceed.
app_text_str: . The PI has shown that AngII induces hypertension in a MR-dependent manner.  To determine if this effect is PKCdelta-dependent, the PI will use RNAi to knock down PKCdelta, and assay for MR-dependent reporter activity in cultured cells.  Putative PKC target sites in MR will be mutated for use in rescue studies using MR-deficient SMCs. . Aim 2 will explore the possibility that MR regulates vascular tone via its regulation of L-type Ca2+ channel subunit expression.  Preliminary data suggest that knocking out MR in SMCs results in decreased Cav1.2 expression; this will be confirmed.  A putative MRE in the Cav1.2 promoter will be evaluated for function by ChIP and reporter assays.  Functional analysis by patch clamp will be performed by the Co-I; preliminary data support the ability of the lab to accomplish this.  Because blood pressure changes occur only in aged MR-deficient mice, the PI will evaluate changes in Cav1.2 in young and old mice, both WT and MR-deficient. . imp_text: NCLX (also known as Slc8B1 and, in this proposal, Slc24a6) was recently identified as the long sought-after Na+Ca2+ exchanger in mitochondria.  The PI makes a case for the need to use the genetic models he has developed to precisely alter NCLX expression, thereby increasing or decreased Ca2+ efflux and thus the Ca2+ pool in mitochondria.  This approach is superior to the use of chemical inhibitors whose specificities are not particularly great.  Thus, the tools prepared by the PI (conditional K/O, low-level over-expression) will be useful in determining how NCLX functions in cardiomyocytes, and Aims 1 and 2 will certainly expand the knowledge base of NCLX biology.  Aim 3 will utilize these tools to more precisely evaluate the role of NCLX, and of mitochondrial Ca2+ in general, in normal cardiac function and in pathological remodeling.  Overall, the proposal is well-written, and includes a nice summary of mitochondrial Ca2+ regulation plus a rationale for why the tools developed by the PI to address the roles of NCLX on this regulation will propel the field forward.  What it doesn’t do is explain how this project will evolve in the future.  The proposed work adds to an active area of research; where will this particular project go?
sig_text_str: . Failing hearts typically show reduced mitochondrial Ca2+ levels, and the PI has evidence that this is due to decreased MCU-mediated Ca2+ influx and increased NCX- and/or MICU-mediated Ca2+ efflux.  This has relevance to cardiomyocyte loss during heart failure.  By altering the expression of NCLX, which would alter efflux, the PI will evaluate not only its role in regulating mitochondrial Ca2+, but also the role of that source of Ca2+ on cell function and viability.  This will enable the PI to determine if reduced mitochondrial Ca2+ levels are responsible for pathological remodeling, or if changes in these levels are a consequence of cardiomyocyte dysfunction.

This will facilitate the studies into the role of mitochondrial Ca2+ in cardiomyocyte function.  This represents a significant improvement over existing approaches that rely on inhibitors of questionable specificity.

app_text_str: . Aim 1 will test the hypothesis that NCLX/Slc24a6 is the mitoNCX in cardiomyocytes.  Preliminary data show that RNAi-mediated knock-down decreases Ca2+ efflux, while over-expression leads to loss of Ca2+ dynamics in cultured rat myocytes.  Cultured cells, including myocytes derived from mutant animals, will be further analyzed to define the role of this NCX in Ca2+ efflux.  For mouse studies, the PI will use models he has developed, including for conditional knock-outs and limited expression in cardiomyocytes.  The PI has considered the possibility that compensation could occur, and will evaluate changes in other known mitochondrial Ca2+ transporters.  Stress conditions will also be included.  Mitochondria-localized Ca2+ reporters will be used to avoid confusion with cytosolic sources. . In Aim 2, the PI will evaluate the consequences of altering the expression of Slc24a6 on metabolism and on cell death.  Because mitochondrial Ca2+ levels control both ATP production and cell death, the PI proposes to use the models described earlier to alter NCLX expression and see how this alters metabolism and viability in cells.  The PI argues that the role of mitochondrial Ca2+ in cell death is murky, in that increased Ca2+ levels in mitochondria promote ATP production, and thus viability, and that NCLX inhibitors also promote viability. . Aim 3 will test the idea that altered expression of Slc24a6 (conditional K/O and low-level over-expression) will alter cardiac function in mice, both under normal and pressure-overload conditions.  Limiting Ca2+ efflux, it is hypothesized, will save cells from stress-induced death.  Stressors will include pressure-overload, arterial ligation to mimic myocardial infarction, and Ca2+ overload.  Together, the experiments in Aim 3 will establish a role for mitochondrial Ca2+ in pathogenic cardiac remodeling.
app_text_wkn: . The work proposed in Aims 1 and 2 seeks to confirm the importance of the putative NCX to mitochondrial Ca2+ efflux in excitable cells.  However, some of the work will involve non-excitable cells, and preliminary data using such cells have already confirmed the role of Slc24a6 in this process. . While Aim 3 will enable the PI to address the roles of mitochondrial Ca2+ regulation in cardiac remodeling and function using targeted approaches not previously employed, it is not clear where future studies will go.

The studies proposed are comprehensive and as such ambitious, but the team assembled is strong and the environment is excellent.  One concern here is that the limited research staff may not be sufficient to achieve the goals of the project. The effect of aging could be better supported by the preliminary data and data analysis to identifiy these changes more detailed. imp_text: This R01 application, proposed by an established investigator, aims to study how Foxo transcription factors (TFs) control memory T cell differentiation and their roles in the progression and clearance of virus infections. The proposal is based on their recent studies showing that Foxo TFs control CD4 central memory precursor cells, CD4 follicular helper cells, and CD8 cytotoxicity T cells post-infection. Since Foxo TFs constitute a very highly connected signaling transduction network that exists in all cells and their activity is regulated by inflammation, oxidative stress, nutrient availability, and growth factors to control cell survival, quiescence, and bioenergetics, based on their preliminary data, they hypothesis that Foxo TFs play a central role on the immune system, in particular the gene programming and memory T cell differentiation that are key to the outcomes of viral infections. The strengths of this application include: i) the significance to elucidate the role of Foxo TFs in programming gene expressions and control of T cell differentiation and function during viral infections; ii) strong preliminary studies demonstrating the critical roles of Foxo TFs in CD4 and CD8 T cell differentiation and response to viral infections; iii) available of cross Tg/ko mouse strains and tools essential for the proposed experiments; iv) an experienced investigator with a long-track record of productive research on T cell biology; v) a large-scale and in depth stepwise analysis of Toxo TFs control over programming of gene expression, T cell differentiation and memory formation, and their roles in progression and clearance of viral infections in the experimental design; and vi) an excellent scientific environment at UCSD. Overall, this is a strong application with little weaknesses, such as multiple theories proposed that lead to unfocused research experimental designs, each specific aim can be a R01. However, given the credit of PI’s productive research in this field and available of mouse strains and tools, there is no doubt about the feasibility of the proposed experiments to be done in a timely manner. Thus the enthusiasm for this application is high.

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: This R01 proposal aims to study whether and how stromal cell catalase deficiency as the causative factor in accelerated thymic atrophy, leading to a progressive decline in naïve T cell production with aging. They propose to test a central hypothesis that age-related thymic atrophy is caused by an accumulated metabolic damage, due to deficiency in several key enzymes, particularly catalase that may protect or repair these damages. Since thymus is the primary site of T lymphopoiesis, its atrophy with age results in a decrease in new T cell production for protection of infections and response to vaccinations. The strengths of this application include: i) the significance to elucidate the causative role of catalase deficiency as the underlying mechanisms for age-related thymic atrophy; ii) strong preliminary data demonstrating thymic stromal cells deficient in catalase involved in protection from TEC damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS); iii) novelty in concept and informatics approach to link the metabolic oxidative damage by ROS and catalase deficiency in thymic stromal atrophy in aging process; iv) the combination of two different model systems circumvents the liabilities of each individually; v) an established investigator with track record of publications and over 20 years expertise in the related area; and vi) an excellent scientific environment at Scripps Institute to carry out this project. Several weaknesses are also identified, such as lack of kinetic experiments overtime to observe catalase replacement on preventing thymic atrophy, lack of experimental design to analyze protein damage sensing or turnover pathways in stromal cells, lack of description for power calculation of mice to be used and statistical analyses of the data, and experiments in Aim 4 to characterize enzymes for DNA damage repair are premature and less-well developed. These weaknesses slightly dampen the overall enthusiasm for this highly promising application.
sig_text_str: . Thymic stromal cells produce microenvironment signals that are essential and key for T cell differentiation and maintenance of T cell production throughout of life. The mechanisms for age-related thymic atrophy remains unclear and need to be elucidated. . Since accumulation of metabolic damage from oxidative stress including ROS is one of the major factors causing mutation or inactivation on DNAs, proteins, and lipids in the aging process, whereas catalase is the key enzyme for removal of H2O2 in the body tissues / cells, further characterization for the role of catalase deficiency as a causative factor in thymic atrophy is fundamentally important for understanding human immunity with age. . This study is significant since thymic atrophy is associated with the contraction of naïve T cells and gradual drift towards a predominance of memory cells with aging. This, in turn, leads to gradual age-related drift towards an oligoclonal, rather than panclonal, T cell repertoire, and an impairment in response to infections or vaccinations. This is particularly important with the fact of almost global increase in human longevity. The results from this study may increase our knowledge about T cell development throughout life and may have the potential for means to improve immune response to infection and vaccinations.

Aim 1 will test whether expression of catalase specifically in TEC is sufficient for protection or rescue of thymic atrophy using two complementary model systems, which is feasible. The rationale for this aim is well supported by the preliminary data, and the chance of success for the designed experiments is highly expected based on the current evidence. . Aim 2 to test the hypothesis that TEC accumulate more oxidative lesions than other cells from age-matched mice is a reasonable step since catalase deficiency in TEC should lead to an increase in ROS and an increase in damage to cellular DNA or lipid, which will be analyzed by HPLC for DNA modifications and GC/MC for lipid peroxidation. study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: This R01 application, proposed by a new and early stage investigator, aims to study the cellular and molecular basis for B lymphocyte development and clonal selection in bone marrow (BM). The proposal is based on their preliminary studies with evidence showing for a critical role of the chemokine receptor CXCR4 signaling in BM stromal cells for the development of B cell-lineage supportive stromal cell niches vis regulating mediators (IL-7 and CXCR12). Based on these new findings, they propose three specific aims to test a hypothesis that B lymphocyte migration and interactions with stromal cell niches enable B cell central tolerance. Since defects in B cell development are major causes of immunological diseases, this study is significant in that by investigating where and how B cells migrate and position within bone marrow, new therapeutic strategies may be developed against devastating immunodeficiencies and autoimmune diseases.  The strengths of this application include: i) the significance of this study in understanding the role and mechanisms of CXCR4 signaling in regulating B cell lineage development; ii) the innovative hypothesis, preliminary data, and state-of-the-art technologies to be used; iii) the strategy for visualizing central tolerance in BM by intravital 2-photon microscopy using BCR transgenic mouse strains and mouse models of the human autoimmune disease systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE); and a new & early stage investigator at an excellent environment. Several weaknesses are also identified such as lack of detailed description and data of B lymphocyte development in the setting of chronic infections and during aging, liming the translational impact of this proposal, somewhat diffused multiple hypothesizes, poor publication and funding record since the PI being appointed as an assistant professor at Yale. These moderate weaknesses dampen the overall enthusiasm of this promising proposal. Scored Review Criteria Reviewers will consider each of the five review criteria below in the determination of scientific and technical merit, and provide a separate score and critique for each.
sig_text_str: . While it is clear that B cells develop from hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells within bone marrow stromal cells, very little is understood about the dynamics and cellular interactions instructing hematopoietic cell differentiation in BM. The proposed aims may provide a broad conceptual and mechanistic framework for understanding how guidance cues shape the BM stromal cell compartment and influence cell lineage decisions during hematopoietic cell differentiation, thus is significant and timely. . B lymphocyte development has been studied in detail over the past several decades with particular attention to lymphocyte-intrinsic mechanisms. However, the current lymphoid-centric working models are insufficient for understanding the complex interactions between hematopoietic precursors and the BM stromal cells that instruct cell lineage differentiations. Currently, there are no conceptual or mechanistic frameworks explaining the development and maintenance of lymphoid-supportive stromal cell niches in BM.
sig_text_wkn: . Lack of detailed description of B lymphocyte development in the setting of chronic infections and during aging. For example, B cell clones against specific viral antigens are deleted, whereas B cell clones against non-sense self-antigens are expanded, during chronic viral infections, resulting in a lower antiviral neutralization antibodies to clear the circulating viral antigens and a higher titers of autoimmune antibodies, thus autoimmune disorders in the setting of persistent viral infections. .

imp_text: The pathogenesis of heart disease resulting in congestive heart failure has remained obscure. While it is widely recognized that diabetics are more prone to coronary atherosclerosis, non-vascular causes of heart failure in these patients is often of mysterious provenance.  Thus, terms such as “diabetic cardiomyopathy” have been proposed, but the nature of the myopathic process has never been determined.  The PI has identified circulating amylin as  an endogenous toxin that accumulates in human myocardium which disrupts sarcolemmal integrity, activates calcium dependent pathways for hypertrophic signaling and remodeling, impairs glucose and/or fat metabolism, and induces oxidative stress.  A “humanized” rat model of hyperamylinemia will be employed to test the innovative hypothesis that excess amylin is one of the root causes of heart failure in patients with diabetes.

This proposed project is very clearly developed upon the PI’s previous studies and preliminary experiments. The approaches also have some very strong aspects. The hyperamylinemia model using human amylin (established in this project) has translational potential. The investigation of membrane sealants and scavengers of circulating amylin oligomers is important for the development of pharmacological therapies of diabetic heart diseases. However, there are some weaknesses. The continued study of PI3K-Akt pathway will yield only incremental additional knowledge, while new gene networks or downstream pathways in their models remain to be screened and exploited. Use of rat models will not faithfully mimic hyperamylinemia in humans due to organ size and physiology differences. This weakness is minor and the potential impact of this project remains high.

imp_text: The proposed research outlines a strategy to investigate the mechanistic role of Rnd3 in response to cardiac stress. To resolve the critical deficiency in available information, a new patient-relevant Rnd3 deficient mouse was generated to study angiogenesis in heart failure. The PI identified Rnd3, a small Rho GTPase, as a key proactive factor for adaptive myocardial angiogenesis in response to pressure overload. Downregulation of Rnd3 interrupted the balance between HIF1a-VEGF in cardiomyocytes and Notch signaling in endothelial cells, leading to angiogenic defects and dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) following transverse aortic constriction (TAC). The proposed molecular mechanisms will improve our understanding of angiogenic signaling in heart failure. This project is not technically innovative, but this is not considered a weakness because the focus on molecular mechanism involved in cardiac dysfunction transition should raise clinical implications significantly. Multiple and systemic approaches including in vitro protein-protein interaction analysis, and in vivo genetic animal assessments with loss-and gain-of-function strategies were employed to address their hypothesis. he proposed in vivo experiments in aim 3 comprehensively test whether in vivo genetic reintroduction of Rnd3 into endothelial cells and cardiomyocytes can correct angiogenic defects. A minor concern is the generation of the tri-lineage mouse line, tie2-Rnd3: MHC-Rnd3:Rnd3

imp_text: This is an application from an accomplished investigator that explores the biological function of platelets at a cellular level, with a hypothesis that ASK1 plays a key role as a signaling molecule that regulates platelet function and thrombosis. This application will have considerable impact in the fields of basic cell biology and hematology. Basic insight will be gained into the interactions between ASK1 and the classical MAPK signal axis. Moreover, both human samples and gene-modified mice will be employed in this proposal indicating a high value of translational medicine. Subsequent research results may provide valuable data for the development of treatments for thrombosis and heamaphage. Pathophysiological mechanisms of many platelet-related diseases such as stroke and myocardial infarction may also be elucidated. The principal investigator was productive in the previous project period and produced high impact publications. In the current application, the principal investigator proposes innovative studies on intracellular platelet interactions in vitro and in ASK1 gene knock-out or knock-in murine models. Therefore, these experiments should prove successful and could change the current understanding of the ASK1 signal cascades involved in platelet activation.
sig_text_str: . Platelets are an important component of blood, and the non-nucleus structure can stop bleeding by clumping and clotting blood vessel injuries. Both in vitro and in vivo preliminary results strongly support that ASK1 may serve as an intrinsic signal mechanism for regulating platelet activation. . These studies are likely to provide specific insights into the role of ASK1 in maintaining platelet function and regulating thrombosis. . This project seeks to elucidate the role of ASK1 in regulating the development and formation of thrombosis, with a special focus on the interactions between kinase and other known platelet function-regulating signaling cascades. Such an understanding of these molecular mechanisms and successful completion of this proposal will strengthen current knowledge on the process of platelet activation, coagulation, and inflammatory responses in cerebrovascular disorders and cardiovascular diseases. . Identification of the interaction and phosphorylation site of ASK1 is clearly important for clinical translational research, but key knowledge is lacking for this to be possible. These studies may provide insightful ideas and preclinical evidence that could lead to novel treatments for hemorrhage and develop new diagnostic and therapeutic methods that can be utilized for patients suffering from a stroke and/or myocardial infarction.

The proposed studies will characterize a novel platelet signaling protein, ASK1, to determine its mechanistic role in platelet signaling cascades downstream of multiple agonists. imp_text: Lipin 1 connects mitochondrial metabolic homeostasis to glycerolipid metabolism through its bi-functional molecular activities. The authors have previously shown that lipin 1 acts in the nucleus to regulate the expression of genes encoding mitochondrial respiratory chain. However, lipin 1 can rapidly translocate within the cell and also acts as a lipid phosphatase at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane to dephosphorylate phosphatidic acid (PA) to form diacylglycerol (DAG). The PI hypothesizes that chronic caloric and lipid excess will lead to increased phosphorylation and cytoplasmic localization of lipin 1 and that abnormalities in the regulation of cardiac lipin 1 activity promote glycerolipid synthesis and inhibit its pro-catabolic actions, contributing to the lipotoxic cardiomyopathy that develops in states of chronic caloric excess. The study is well presented and clearly outlined, the topic is very interesting and there is a demand in the field for a better understanding of the heart metabolomics changes during heart disease. However, there are significant shortcomings that could compromise the over final data interpretation. There is a high number of animal strains involved in this study which increases the complexity of the study and create some problem with the timeline proposed. There is some limitation in the animal models proposed, Tamoxifen inducible mice are less than ideal in these kind of studies unless precaution are taken in consideration. The 3rd aim comes as a surprise, if the all proposal is focused on lipid metabolism in obesity and diabetes the pressure overload induced by aortic ligation does not really belong in the logic progression of this proposal.

imp_text: The PI is proposing to investigate the molecular mechanisms of Rnd3 downregulation in heart failure. Most of the PI`s preliminary data come from Rnd3 haploinsufficient mice (Rnd3+/-) which, following transverse aortic constriction (TAC), developed dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure. The data seems then to suggest that Rnd3 haploinsufficient mice are hypersensitive to cardiac stress.  The main hypothesis is that reduction of Rnd3 impairs angiogenesis, and the underling mechanisms is the Notch signaling upregulation. However, Rnd3 protein is a member of the small GTPase protein superfamily and appears to act as a negative regulator of cytoskeletal organization leading to loss of adhesion. In my opinion this proposal fails in emphasizing why the effect of Rnd3 on Notch is more important than its canonical function. The PI define the Rnd3 haploinsufficient mice as a “Patient relevant” mouse model with the rationale that Rnd3 is downregulated in patients with heart failure. Indeed, there are many genes that are downregulated during heart failure or during the transition to hear failure. A stronger rationale for these studies should be provided.

imp_text: The proposed work aims to characterize various structural and functional aspects of proteins/protein complexes that facilitate meiotic chromosome homologous recombination and segregation.  The applications of this research are relevant to human health and reproduction and meritorious. While Aims 1-3 are independent of each other, it is important to point out that subaims 1c and 1d, subaims 2b and 2c, and subaims 3a and 3c are dependent on one another.  Outside of this important point, the work proposed is scientifically sound with the exception of subaims 1c and 1d which include the engineering of artificial constrcuts which will enable the PI to examine the effects of amputations of one of the “legs” of the Csm1:Lrs4 v-shaped complex. It is difficult to understand how findings from these data can be applied to what is actually happening during meiosis. In addition, it seems that the PI has a strong background in structural biology, however, much of the proposed work also requires a strong background in NMR analysis (aim 2a), immunofluorescence  (aims 2c) and several collaborations in areas that exceed the PIs current background.  The amount of collaboration needed by the PI seems excessive. As a final point of concern, the amount of work proposed seems like a lot considering that the PI will only have one post doctoral fellow, one graduate student, and two staff associates.  Based on the magnitude of the work proposed, the reviewer questions the ability of the PI to achieve the work proposed with such a small staff, while functioning as a mentor, publishing, and presenting his results.  A letter of support from the institution (not from collaborators at the institute) stating its investment/support for the next five years at the level described by the proposed PI would have also been reassuring as the institute is covering salary for the PI and lab personnel. These criticisms, in addition to the PIs very strong environment, positive letters of support, and training were taken into consideration by the reviewer in their assessment of the likelihood of the proposed work to exert a sustained, powerful influence in the area of meiotic chromosome segregation.
