imp_text: The proposal is to use structural biology combined with yeast genetics and biochemistry to understand the contribution of different protein complexes to the 3D orientation/positioning of sister chromatids during meiosis I prior to meiotic recombination. As advertised, the proposal draws on a multi-disciplinary approach to the problem, and seeks to structurally characterize 3 different protein complexes important for meiosis I, one for each Aim. With each structural characterization there is a series of unanswered questions that the proposal seeks to address. Although the biological question is important, the project is unfocused and too broad. Any one of the aims could give rise to a full five years of investigation. Furthermore, the approach suggested may or may not be feasible based on the presentation, and even if successful, it is not clear to what extent the results will illuminate the large question of how things are arranged in order to have successful chromosome recombination and subsequent segregation.
sig_text_str: . The major question in the field as presented is significant and surprisingly largely unanswered. The answer to the question could impact a major detriment to successful reproduction, or reduction of birth defects. . The chosen targets for the study are likely critical components of the assembly required for successful meiotic recombination.
sig_text_wkn: . The study focuses in part on a fungal specific complex, when the significance statements reference defects or malfunctioning in human meiosis machinery. . The study is too broad and therefore likely will not result in significant depth in study. . It is not clear how the study as proposed would elucidate the 3D organization during meiosis 1 to the extent necessary to answer the major question.
inv_text_str: . The PI has strong experience in structural biology and protein biochemistry. . The PI has a vast array of support from personnel outside of her assembled team of investigators.
inv_text_wkn: . The lab is not experienced in yeast genetics and cell biology at the level required for some of the experiments proposed. A strong collaborator (PI/Co-PI) would strengthen confidence in the project’s success.
inn_text_str: . The complexes described in the proposal have not yet been explored structurally.
inn_text_wkn: . The approach is typical structure determination followed by functional analysis of mutants.
app_text_str: . The proposed structural biology work is in progress and has yielded initial crystal hits. . The approach to looking at complex formation, stoichiometry and biochemistry is multidisciplinary and will include in vivo functional analysis. . Engineering of the one-headed monopolin complex will likely illuminate the model for its involvement in kinetochore positioning.
app_text_wkn: . The extent of work described in the proposal is too large for the time period described and the personnel requested, especially in the absence of invested collaborators. . Despite crystal hits shown for Hrr25/Mam1 complex, the lack of report on diffraction data is concerning since this may be the most significant hurdle for successful structure determination. . Has it been shown that the kinase activity of Hrr25 is necessary for function in this context? . Preliminary data has not been provided to support the feasibility of the proposed genetics-based assays.

env_text_wkn: . The team could use some help from a co-PI with yeast cell biology experience.

imp_text: The proposal describes a project that seeks to impact the understanding of a U12-dependent splicing, which is a minor class secondary to most splicing which occurs in a U2-dependent manner. Splicing via this pathway utilizes specific small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs). One of these snRNAs is mutated in a rare disease known as microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type I (MOPD I). The investigators will employ several approaches to unravel the mechanism by which these snRNA mutations and others result in loss of function and pathology. Furthermore, they will expand the study in this area by looking at the consequences of SNPs in the U12-dependent splicing snRNAs. The group has access to a cell line derived from a patient with one of the MOPD I causing mutations, and has developed methods to look at other mutations in the affected snRNA. In addition, the group has developed robust methodology to address each of the questions posed in the proposal. The project will undoubtedly shed light on a largely unknown area of biology in the secondary splicing pathway, and will also illuminate how snRNAs play a role in gene expression regulation and disease. The team has experience and convincing preliminary data was provided in the proposal. This is an exciting proposal, which will deliver much needed insight in this RNA biology area.
sig_text_str: . The project will investigate an important problem in biology, splicing, which is essential for proper gene expression. Defects in this process results in severe disease phenotypes. . The work is centered upon disease (MOPD I)-linked genetic mutations in an snRNA. The mutation is known, and cell lines have been established harboring this mutation . There is a gap in the knowledge with regards to the function of the secondary splicing pathway. This proposal directly addresses this gap on multiple fronts – protein interactions, snRNA stability, complex formation, transcriptome analysis, SNPs. . As designed, the project will likely elucidate mechanisms by which disease mutations result in disease phenotypes. . Although the study is focused on mutations resulting in MOPD 1, the study of mutations or polymorphisms affecting snRNA function will likely have impact on other diseases in which they have been shown to play a role.

imp_text: The proposal seeks support for studies designed to characterize the interactions of the replicative DNA helicase and other replication proteins. The research team is experienced and the group has developed technology to allow an innovative approach to the first aim. Although the aims of the applications are clearly stated, it is not clear how these aims address a major question or set of questions, or a gap in the field. Furthermore, the presentation of the approach was not sufficiently developed to allow confident evaluation of the feasibility of the project and the significance of the outcomes.

sig_text_wkn: . Questions addressed by this proposal not clearly indicated. There is a postulate that the CMG complex interacts with several other replication proteins, however, this is vague and does not lead to any mechanistic insight. . Other than the potential to understand how disease mutations affect DNA replication, it is not clear that this work will significantly advance the field. . Aim 2 seeks to confirm interactions in the contexts of Xenopus and human DNA replication that have been shown to occur in yeast RPC. Although this is important to establish this, there does not seem to be effort to extend knowledge beyond this previously determined information.

inn_text_str: . The identification of differential utilization of bio-UTP by Xenopus Pols allows for an innovative approach in the project. Also, the use of the PLAs to look at components of the DNA replication complex is novel.

app_text_str: . The lab has developed a unique approach to analysis of factors affecting leading strand vs lagging strand synthesis. They have observed that biotin-UTP is incorporated selectively into DNA strands by Pol a and d but not Pol e in Xenopus extracts. This will allow the determination of which Pol is responsible for which replicative strand, and also allow an assay for factors that differentially affect the strand synthesis. . The lab has used proximity ligation assays, which utilizes ligation of oligonucleotides linked to antibodies bound to interacting proteins followed by rolling circle amplification and fluorescence detection, to detect the interaction of proteins within the CMG complex. They will use this assay to look at binding of proteins to CMG in vivo. . The group has isolated the components to perform in-vitro replication including the CMG complex and will use this assay to investigate interactions and leading strand/lagging strand synthesis.

imp_text: The applicants designed experiments to address the mechanistic consequences of snRNA mutations, especially mutation in human U4atac.  Aim1 aims to analyze the biochemical function of mutant U4atac.  The applicants majorly will focus on the mutant U4atac stability and its binding partners in comparison to the wild type.  In Aim2, the authors will interrogate the RNA profiling in patient-derived iPS cells.  In Aim3, the applicants will employ the “orthogonal spliceosome” assay to measure the splicing efficiency in presence of various of U4atac mutations.  We believe the proposed experiments are reasonable and doable, and the future achievement from current proposal will move the field forward.  Unfortunately, the applicants did not address the major concern in the field, the biological consequences of mutant U4atac found in MOPDI at entire animal level.  In addition, the design in Aim2, if we argue, needs perfect wild type control (isogenic control) to gain insights into the global splicing changes.  The other caveats for the Aim2 design is the heterogeneous feature of individual iPS cell lines, even though they were derived from the same patient.  We recommend it might be feasible to apply Crispr/Cas9 approach to introduce the MOPDI mutant U4atac into human cells, in order to back up the designs.  Our overall impact score for this application is 2.

imp_text: DNA replication is a precise, complex biological process, characterized by producing two identical replicas of DNA from one copy. Although structural and biochemical studies have delivered much knowledge according to this process in lower organism, some details were still unidentified, especially for high organism like human, not mention to in disease conditions. Here, the applicants plan to address the properties of human CMG complex and its interacted protein partners. The solid biochemical background and abundant experience in DNA replication let the applicants generated three readily goals and comprehensive strategies and methods to achieve the goals. Firstly, they focus on the functions of Pol e and Pol d in leading and lagging strand synthesis, by using rolling circle replication reaction with bio-dUTP. Then, the authors will identify the human replication proteins that interact with the CMG complex. At last, the authors will study how the Psf1 mutations, which have found in human disease, affect formation of hCMG complex, DNA replication, and cell cycle progress. The significance displayed in this proposal is the detailed mechanisms of human DNA replication, as well as how disease-associated mutations affect the processes.  However, the conceptual breakthroughs in DNA replication field, we believe, will hardly to make from current proposal, in contrast to the existing knowledge we have gained from yeast studies.   Our overall impact score for this application is 2.

imp_text: As aneuploidy is a leading cause of miscarriage and developmental disorders in humans, the overall topic is of high interest and the research proposed will likely have a significant impact on our understanding of meiotic chromosome segregation.  Importantly, it will explicate the biochemical nature of this process, which is not well understood.  The proposal primarily focuses proposes use of in vitro assays which are complemented by in vivo experiments utilizing the model Saccharomyces cerevisiae.  The overall goal of the proposal is to define meiotic chromosome interactions, an area of research that has been characterized extensively at a cellular and genetic level, yet is not well understood at the structural level, given the technical difficulty of these types of experiments.  Aim 1 is an extension of Dr. Murray’s postdoctoral work, which uses several biochemical approaches to determine structural interactions between monopolin complex members and will test two competing hypotheses regarding its function. Either outcome would yield results that would be of high interest to the scientific community and would result in several well laid follow-up studies.  The experiments in this aim are sound, hypothesis-driven and supported by extensive preliminary data.   Aims 2 and 3 focus on defining the structural nature of the HORMA domain axis protein Hop1 and the synaptonemal complex component Zip1; both of these have been extensively studied by geneticists and are of significant interest to researchers studying meiosis and recombination.  While preliminary data is included to support both aims, neither is hypothesis-driven, and the future implications of these anticipated findings are not clearly identified. However, given the Dr. Murray’s outstanding training and the collaborative environment with numerous researchers studying related projects at Ludwig, it is likely that the completion of these experiments will be successful and will generate considerable insight that will undoubtedly advance the field.

imp_text: This is a complex and ambitious proposal is from an expert in the field of DNA replication whom has already made significant contributions to the field.  Her proposed experiments involve a combination in vitro and in vivo assays to explicate how components of CMG, a replicative DNA polymerase complex, interact and are targeted to replication forks.  Findings from her studies could reveal how dysregulation of CMG contributes to genomic instability and cancer.  The proposed work is a continuation of prior research efforts to tease out specific function for each replicative polymerase as well as other proteins at the replication fork.  Notably, it will utilize several innovative techniques that will elucidate the molecular mechanisms driving lagging strand synthesis in vitro, clarify the function of human chromosome transmission factor hCtf and its interactions with hCMG, and will identify new replicative factors involved in these processes. Although the aims are not strongly hypothesis driven (a central hypothesis is not mentioned anywhere in this proposal) the overwhelming strength of the proposed work is the extensive preliminary data and expertise of the PI, which leaves little doubt that the experiments will be carried out and will generate substantial data that is of wide-spread interest to the scientific community.

imp_text: • This is a competitive R01 renewal for an established PI.  The proposal itself is exceptionally well-organized and addresses four hypothesis driven questions, all of which are supported by strong preliminary data generated as part of the prior funding period for this renewal.  The proposed experiments will identify functional interactions among ribosomal components and elucidate ribosome biogenesis pathways in S. cerevisiae, focusing on the role of RNA helicase Ecm16. Aims 1 uses cellular and genetic assays to determine its function. Aim 2 uses several in vitro approaches to test its activation and helicase activity.  Aims 3 and 4 examine functional interactions among components of the central pseudoknot, the assembly of which is not well understood.  The findings from studies will likely be of broad interest to researchers studying RNA helicases and RNA metabolism in general.  The strengths of this renewal application are that it experiments are very clearly articulated, it is strongly hypothesis-driven and is supported by preliminary data.  Limitations are the large number of experiments listed which include several genetic screens; it is not clear whether these will be able to be accomplished within a 4-year time frame.  Additionally, the experiments themselves, while well-articulated, are repetitive and the research plan as a whole lacks innovation.

imp_text: Dr. Washington has the necessary background and expertise to carry out the studies proposed in this application. The aims in this proposal describes using structural/biochemical approaches to understand the functions of several key proteins involved in meiotic chromosome recombination and segregation in yeast. Preliminary data presented is strong suggesting that some of the aims are feasible.  However, as noted below, preliminary data demonstrating that some of the proteins/protein complexes of interest can be purified and are functional is lacking. Furthermore, while this type of approach would likely provide unique prospective into the functions of proteins in yeast (if the aims were accomplished), it is unclear how the data generated from these studies would be applied to higher eukaryotes.
sig_text_str: • The aims of this proposal are significant as they attempt to address the poorly understood molecular functions of proteins involved in meiotic recombination and chromosome segregation. Understanding these processes are highly significant as errors in the meioses pathway have been shown to contribute to aneuploidies, resulting in miscarriage and severe developmental disorders in humans.
sig_text_wkn: • A significant weakness of the proposed studies is that they are all centered around the model organism S. cerevisiae. If the aims are achieved valuable mechanistic information will likely be obtained from these studies. However, the investigator makes no attempt to describe how these results could be extended to higher eukaryotes and thus help explain aneuploidy pathologies. If understanding human disease is indeed a point of significance for the proposed studies, the investigator should include some information regarding the known similarities and differences in meioses in yeast and other higher eukaryotes and specifically on whether or not homologs/orthologs of the proteins under investigation are present in higher eukaryotes.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Washington is a new investigator that has published numerous manuscripts as both a graduate student and a post-doctoral researcher. Dr. Washington clearly has the expertise in structural biology and yeast biochemistry/genetics necessary for the proposed work.
inv_text_wkn: . A significant weakness is that Dr. Washington currently only has two lab technicians and one graduate student to work toward completing the rather ambitious goals described in this proposal.
inn_text_str: • The innovation of the proposed research lies in the structural and biochemical approaches that the investigator intends to use to study a system that has traditionally been studied using genetics and microscopy. The investigator has demonstrated the ability to reconstitute and biochemically characterize proteins and protein complexes involved in various aspects of meiosis which are notoriously difficult to work with in vitro. Thus these studies have the potential to generate unique prospective to understanding the molecular details of meiotic chromosome segregation in yeast.
inn_text_wkn: . Some concerns exist regarding in vitro experiments using purified truncated rather than the full length proteins as well as in vitro experiments described for proteins that have not yet been purified.

For Aim1a preliminary studies are encouraging, demonstrating that the proteins of interest can be purified and that the 3D structure of a similar complex (Csm1-Mam1) has been solved. . The experiments proposed for Aim2a-c seem reasonable and will likely generate valuable information regarding the function of Hop1 even in the event that the 3D structure of the Hop1 HORMA domain cannot be determined (Aim2d). . The experiments proposed for Aim3a seem reasonable and will likely generate valuable information regarding Zip1 and Red1 domain structure.
app_text_wkn: . For Aim1a the investigator proposes to determine 3D structures of truncated Hrr25 (residues 1-394 of 494). It is not clear why studies are not aimed at trying to characterize the full length protein. . For Aim2b the investigator proposes to determine 3D structures of a truncated Tof2 (residues 388-404) fused to Csm1. Again it is not clear why studies are not aimed at trying to characterize the full length protein rather than only a very small segment of Tof2 fused to Csm1. It would seem reasonable to at least attempt crystallization with the full length protein before using truncated fusions. . For Aim1c the proposed strategy to engineer artificial constructs that alter the Csm1:Ls4 stoichiometry seem precarious as these alterations may disrupt global structure of the complex, possibly complicating data analysis for Aim1d. Furthermore, the investigator has not demonstrated that this complex is stable or functional which is necessary for completion of Aim1d. . For Aim2b the investigator points out some ambiguity with the results of pulldown assays that attempt to identify the binding region of Hop1 for Red1. . Preliminary data demonstrating that the C-terminal SUMO-binding region +/- the coiled-coil region of Zip1 or the full length protein can be purified would be preferred to demonstrate the feasibility of Aim3b-c.

imp_text: Dr. Murray has made significant contributions to the splicing field and has demonstrated that he is able to manage a productive laboratory.  Aims 1 and 3 of this proposal describe feasible experiments that will likely shed valuable insights into the U12 spliceosme biogenesis pathway and the effect of disease causing SNPs and point mutations in the U12 snRNAs.  The data obtained from the proposed studies will likely serve as a foundation for understanding genetic diseases caused by defective splicesome components. Dr. Murray has also proposed transcriptome analysis of MOPD 1patient cells in an attempt to identify downstream target genes. While these studies do have some promise, preliminary experiments need to be carried out that demonstrate likelihood for success.
sig_text_str: . The aims described in this proposal are highly significant as they attempt to elucidate how components of the less well understood U12 dependent splicesome contribute to assembly and function. . In addition these studies are also significant as they will attempt to explain how SNPs and point mutations in U12 snRNAs cause disease.
sig_text_wkn: . A modest weakness is that these studies are aimed at describing how U12 dependent splicing defects cause a single and rare disease (MOPD 1). Though as the investigator states the proposed studies and techniques do have the potential to be extended to other human diseases caused by splicing defects.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Murray has an excellent research record in the field of RNA processing and has developed in vitro and in vivo systems for studying pre-mRNA splicing. He has also made significant progress toward understanding the mechanism of the minor U12 dependent splicing pathway. Furthermore these investigations have produced numerous publications in excellent journals. . Dr. Scott is highly experienced in both the laboratory and clinical settings. Dr. Scott is also well versed in various techniques relevant to studying mammalian genomics and human disease and is thus well suited to carry out the deep sequencing studies outlined in this proposal. . Dr. Asano has a strong background in analyzing sequencing data sets using various computational techniques and a strong publication record. Dr. Asano’s experience makes her an ideal resource to carry out the bioinformatics analysis of the deep sequencing data that would be generated by the transcriptome studies described in this proposal.

imp_text: In this application, an early career PI proposes solid aims to understand the structural biology of meiosis, an important aspect of basic biology. The PI is well trained, with a good track record, a fantastic environment, and really good collaborators. There is little doubt that the PI will have success in his laboratory’s structural biology projects. The overall significance of this project is moderate. The project is not highly innovative, nor are there obvious and immediate applications of this research. However, these criticisms apply to much of academic and basic research, and are not particular problems with this proposal.
sig_text_str: . Meiosis is an important aspect of biology; and the structural biology approaches outlined here offer important insights into the mechanism of meiosis in eukaryotes.
sig_text_wkn: . These studies will, if successful, be additional pieces to a puzzle that will include molecular biology and genetics approaches from other investigators. There are no immediate applications of the proposed research to human disease or problems of infertility or aneuploidy.
inv_text_str: . The PI had a very successful training period, making important structural biology contributions. His background in structural biology of meiosis as a postdoctoral fellow is also important. He has several top-notch collaborators.
inv_text_wkn: . The PI has not yet shown the ability to lead a laboratory. While this is not a weakness, per se, it is not yet a strength.
inn_text_str: . The PI has a good grasp of structural biology and basic in vitro biology. Should structural biology obstacles appear, he and his group should be able to apply advanced techniques, and even perhaps develop novel techniques to solve the problems.
inn_text_wkn: . The PI’s approach: Make recombinant proteins of varying lengths, mutations, combinations, then solve the structure, is solid, respectable, but is not highly innovative. Although some more innovative ideas and techniques are presented in the proposal, these are clearly not in the PI’s wheelhouse.
app_text_str: . Based on the PI’s past success in solving crystal structures, and the proposed structural biology in this proposal, he is capable of putting together a highly competent structural biology approach.
app_text_wkn: . The scope of work presented here seems too broad. It would be surprising if one half of the proposed work could be accomplished within the funding period. One worries about the possibility of becoming spread too thin.
env_text_str: . UCSD is a top-notch research institution. The equipment, access to collaborators, etc., is second to none.

imp_text: This is a highly significant area of research. Understanding the connection between snRNA mutations in the minor U4atac snRNA and disease (MOPD I) are highly relevant. The PI is highly experienced in biochemical techniques to understand mRNA splicing. However, it isn’t clear from this application that the approach is sufficiently well thought out to be able to clearly dissect the mechanism(s) whereby mutations lead to disease in this setting. Better, more precise assays need to be developed and demonstrated.
sig_text_str: . Mutations in U4atac snRNA, responsible for mRNA splicing by the minor spliceosome, were recently shown to cause MOPD I. The mechanistic consequences of these mutations are unclear, and the target genes affected and, presumably, contributing to disease, are unknown. This area of research has direct connection to understanding disease, and has a high probability of applicability to translational science, both to MOPD I specifically, and splicing-related diseases in general.

imp_text: This is an application by an enthusiastic researcher that has demonstrated great talent and dedication to understanding the immune system.  Her passion can be seen in this grant application, which is easily one of the best and most comprehensive grants I have ever read. The goal of the proposed research is understand the basis for memory T cell differentiation, and how memory T cells influence the progression of acute and chronic viral diseases.  The focus of the grant is on the role of FOXO transcription factors and how they control immune memory.  She presents novel data showing Foxo1 deficient CD8 cytotoxic T cells stay in an activated state. In addition, the absence of Foxo1 promotes the appearance of CD4 central memory precursor cells, and CD4 follicular helper cells able to produce IL-21.  She proposes that Foxo TFs play a central role in the formation of memory T cells and the progression or decay of persistent viral infections.  In this application she proposes to examine the role of Foxo TFs (1 and 3) in metabolic changes and gene expression in CD8 T cells.  She will examine the mechanisms of how T follicular helper cells are programmed by Foxo1 and ultimately, how foxo1 is altered and its effects during persistent viral infection.  This application offers a very comprehensive background of Foxo TFs in Tfh and CD8 T cell development and programming.  While it was dense to read at times, it presented a very compelling story.  The experiments proposed in this application should greatly advance our knowledge of the regulation of immunity post infection.
sig_text_str: . The application offers a comprehensive analysis of two specific FOXO transcription factors.  The role of the TFs are tested by a series of novel and testable hypotheses.  The experiments employ genetic, cellular, and molecular tools that will directly test the hypothesis and provide novel and high impact contributions in the understanding of FOXO transcription factors in T cell differentiation. .

imp_text: This is a well-written grant by a PI that has years of expertise in studies revolving around the thymus and T cell differentiation.   In this application, the PI presents novel and compelling data demonstrating that thymic epithelial cells (TECs) have reduced expression of catalase.  Moreover, restoration of catalase through transgenic mice or drug administration reduced age associated thymic atrophy.  This leads them to hypothesize  that early thymic atrophy is caused by an accelerated accumulation of the canonical lesions of metabolic damage, due to innate deficiencies in these enzymes, particularly Catalase.  They propose to test the hypothesis through 4 specific aims using in vivo and in vitro models.  The aims are simple and testable.  While they are likely to produce a positive outcome, there are several factors that reduce excitement regarding this proposal.  Most importantly, the aims lack a functional component.  Specifically, they do not address why catalase is decreased in the TEC populations.  Given the specificity of TECs in T cell development, it is possible that decreased catalase is required for antigen or MHC presentation on TEC cells and thus vital for T cell positive and negative selection.   Since the PI seems to be proposing that restoring catalase or protecting from ROS may help in reducing thymic atrophy, understanding why the TECs are different is therapeutically important.
sig_text_str: . Thymic involution is one of the earliest age related changes to manifest itself, however the reasons for these changes, as well as the impact of these changes on the immune system are still debated.  The discovery of how the thymus deteriorates can potentially lead to therapies that may reduce age related changes in immunity . The PI offers compelling data suggesting that TEC populations have decreased catalase gene expression and that administration of antioxidants or constitutive expression of catalase promotes thymic cellularity.
sig_text_wkn: . The proposed studies seem observational with little emphasis on what the outcomes of the research ill mean in the context of therapy. . It is assumed that decreased levels of catalase are a negative thing.  Teliologically speaking, these cells have evolved to do very specific tasks important in maturing the immune compartment.  The decreased levels of catalase (and subsequent increased levels of other antioxidants that are involved in cell signaling such as prdx1 and SOD) may be required for TEC populations to positively and negatively select T cells.  The outcomes of these studies do not address what increased oxidation means in context of the immune compartment.
inv_text_str: . The PI is well established in thymic function and its role in immune cell differentiation.  He has multiple publications in top tier journals and a strong funding track record.
inv_text_wkn: . There are no weaknesses to note.
inn_text_str: . The innovation of this grant is conceptual.  To date, there have been no studies demonstrating deficiency in TEC catalase and correlating these with the changes that occur during aging and thymic involution. . The investigators will use a TEC specific catalase transgenic mouse which is novel.

Moreover, the use of an antioxidant or overexpression of Cat increases thmyic cellularity and size. The PI proposes a number of simple experiments designed to test the hypothesis that the reducing oxidative stress by restoring catalase levels will reduce thymic atrophy.  The proposed experiments are reasonable and testable and will likely give positive outcomes. . The use of the Foxn1-cre catalase tg mouse will provide useful data that as to the role of catalase in reducing thymic atrophy.
app_text_wkn: . The reduction in catalase seen in TECs is unique to these epithelial cell populations and probably happens for a reason.  Evidence for this is the expression of Cat in what the PI is calling immature MTECs and regions of thymic progenitor cells is higher than in mature TECs.  Thus, catalase expression may be decreasing with TEC differentiation.  An important question to ask is why is this occurring?  Specific aim 1 focuses strictly on what overexpression of catalase does to cell numbers and atrophy but does not examine what is happening in to the function of the thymus.  Recent thymic immigrants, autoimmune regulator gene (AIRE) expression and tissue restricted antigens all need to be examined to determine if augmentation of catalase changes the function of the thymus.  It is quite likely that the reduction in catalase is important in the function of antigen and MHC expression in TEC populations. . Catalse is a key component of the peroxisome.  This organelle is integral in autophagy which is important in antigen presentation to T cells.  As such, catalase numbers an function should be assessed as well as autophagy in the TEC cell populations.  Also the peroxisome is integral in the development of iNKT cells and as such, these populations should be monitored. . Experiments examining TECS look at a mix of MTEC and CTEC populations. While it is understood that these experiments are required to determine if there is compensation by other scavenger mechanisms, other ROS such as superoxide should also be used for comaprison.

imp_text: This is a complex but well written grant.  The proposal centers around the importance of CXCR4 in B cell development.  While this receptor has been well known to be required for B cell maturation, this proposal presents novel data demonstrating a requirement for CXCR4 on mesenchymal cells for proper B cell maturation.  They then elegantly demonstrate the role for CXCR4 in presenting CLPs to IL-7 producing cells.  Finally, they demonstrate the importance of CXCR4 and IL-7 in autoimmunity.  To test their hypothesis they propose a number of technically demanding yet elegant experiments and will make a number of novel mice. While there are some issues with the cre mice proposed, as well as appropriate controls, this proposal is a strong proposal with overwhelming scientific merit.
sig_text_str: . While CXCR4 has been known as an important receptor in the maturation and development of B cells, no studies to date have shown that CXCR4 is important on mesenchymal cells in the bone marrow. The proposed studies will help bridge a gap in understanding regarding B cell development and the role of the bone marrow stromal niche. .
sig_text_wkn: . There is a lot of emphasis on the novelty of discovering CXCR4 on mesenchymal cells and the importance of CXCR4 in B cell development.  However, it is unclear how this is important in a clinical context.  Basically, if plexifor can be used as an HSC mobilizing agent it is not clear why the cell type it is acting upon is important.  Further, the statement of the research leading to “novel therapeutic discoveries” rings hollow if there are no potential therapies or proposed therapeutics.
inv_text_str: . The investigator has a strong publication record in high level journals and is currently the PI on 3 grants from different funding agencies (both internal and external funding).  All of these center around the bone marrow and B cell development.
inn_text_str: . This proposal is both innovative conceptually and technologically.  It tests the innovative and novel concept that CXCR4 on mesenchmyal cells is important for B cell migration and maturation.  It will use state of the art 2 photon microscopy as well as produce several novel mouse strains (CXCR4 floxed mice crossed to cell specific cre mice as well as triple transgenic Il7 reporter mice to name a few).
inn_text_wkn: . None.
app_text_str: . The proposed experiments are complex yet testable.  The PI will develop a number of unique cre mice to determine the role of CXCR4 on non-HSCs in B cell development. . study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology A Study Section
imp_text: This is a well-written proposal with the ultimate goal to probe one central signaling pathway and the way it determines the outcome of T cell differentiation leading to cellular memory. In particular, the proposal will focus on the understanding a central control mechanism guiding T cell differentiation and function in case of long co-evolved viral diseases such as HIV, Herpes, and Hepatitis C. The PIs propose investigating the role of Foxo transcription factors, Foxo1 and Foxo3, in the progression and clearance of virus infections, and their control over the programming of gene expression in CD4 and CD8 T cells. The project has high significance, novelty and impact, while it also has high feasibility as supported by preliminary results. However, there several concerns regarding the design of the proposed experiments. The main concern is that all Specific Aims are built on one assumption that additive effects of Foxo1 and Foxo3, and the role of IL7Ra are imperative to CD8 T cells activation and differentiation. There are no alternative strategies developed in case, if this hypothesis will be proved to be wrong. How the project and especially Specific Aim 4 with in vivo evaluations will be altered in this case? Furthermore, descriptions of specific methodics of the proposed experiments and endpoints for each Specific Aim are missing. Nevertheless, if successful, the overall impact of the new approaches to induce long-term immunity through vaccination may be significant. The enthusiasm is high.

In particular, the proposal will define how the actin-bundling protein, L-plastin, controls the generation of antibodies; the molecular regulation of B cell motility will be elucidated. The experimental design and alternative approaches are well-developed. The Research plan is backed up by a considerable amount of preliminary data. Overall, this is a significant proposal with a multiple innovative elements. If successful, the proposed studies will have significant impact in the field of humoral immunity, and will identify pathways that are critical to both autoimmunity and immunodeficiency and amenable to therapeutic modulation. The enthusiasm is high.

imp_text: This is a well-written proposal with the ultimate goal to reveal the mechanism of accelerated age-related atrophy, leading to a progressive decline in new (naïve) T lymphocyte production with age. The application addresses an important problem the increased susceptibility of the aging population to emerging viral strains, less responsiveness to vaccination, and lower resistance to many types of infections. The proposed work may potentially have a significant impact in the development of new approaches to reduce or prevent this pathological state. Overall, this is a significant proposal with a multiple innovative elements. However, the order and relationship between the different Specific Aims should need to be revised. In particular, experiments outlined in SA1 would not be necessary, if the hypothesis stated in SA2 would found to be incorrect. Furthermore, the proposed studies have incremental character; the novelty of the project is not high. Nevertheless, the proposed studies have significant translational potential. The enthusiasm is high.
sig_text_str: . The proposal addresses an importance question, the mechanisms for accelerated thymic aging. If successful, the results may lead to the development of new strategies for immune response improvement due to the aging. . With the almost global increase in human longevity, thymic atrophy problem becomes an increasingly important. . The proposal emphasizes on fundamental understanding of unusual sensitivity of thymic stromal cells to metabolic damage, and their deficiency in the red-ox enzyme catalase.
inv_text_str: . PI Dr. Robinson is a Professor in the Department of Cancer Biology at the Scripps Research Institute, Jupiter, FL. He has an extensive expertise in the role of the thymus in shaping T lymphoid differentiation in the steady-state

inn_text_wkn: . Damaging effect from the oxidative by-products of metabolism in the aging and atrophy of most tissues and organisms is well-established and not a particular novel concept.
app_text_str: . A significant amount of preliminary biochemical and genetic data is presented to support the hypothesis that epithelial stromal cells of the thymus are exquisitely sensitive to ROS.
app_text_wkn: . The logic of Specific Aims proposed is not straightforward. The hypothesis stated in SA 2: “test the hypothesis that TEC accumulate more oxidative lesions in vivo than other (control) cells from age/tissue-matched mice” should be tested before the SA1 that aimed at testing “the hypothesis that selective correction of Cat deficiency in thymic stromal cells rescues thymic atrophy.” In fact, if the hypothesis of SA2 does not correct, there is no point to carry our experiments outlined in SA1, as no oxidation stress is involved in thymic atrophy. Specifically, no Cat expression is needed to improve thymic T cell production. . Furthermore, if there is no dependence of ROS, SA3 and SA4 will not be legitimate. Overall, overdependence of all SAs represents a significant thread to the success of the whole project. • The potential pitfalls and alternative strategy section is missing from the application. • Endpoints for each Aim should be more specific.

The approach relies on genetic knockout models – more mechanistic in vitro studies to explain roles of CXCR4 in stromal cell functions need to be addressed. The topic is important and novel, but a more focused scope is needed for successful completion of this project.

imp_text: This R01 application proposes to define the role of LPL, an actin bundling protein, in the differentiation of B cells and the function of activated B cells for the generation of germinal center B cell responses.  The application utilizes the expertise of the PI, who has training in evaluating immunodeficiencies, and basic research related to cell motility and lymphocyte differentiation and function.  The application has many strengths, including a strong integration of studying the functional motifs of the LPL protein in B cells, the signal pathways where LPL is involved, and the cellular immunology related to LPL deficiency.  Overall, successful achievement of the experimental goals would provide important insights into LPLs role in B cells and potential therapeutic targets.  There are some concerns of limitations of either controls used or interpretability of a few experiments (addressed below); however, overall the application is strong and will likely yield a robust research program.
sig_text_str: . LPL deficiencies appear highly relevant to immunodeficiencies where protective antibody responses fail to be generated.  The proposal seeks to understand the significance of LPL and its role in T cell:B cell interactions and in chemotaxis for B cells to function properly during the immune response. . Several aspects of the proposal seek to identify specific domains of LPL that are required for its function, as well as specific signaling molecules that interact with LPL in B cells following activation.  Achieving these goals may to contribute to finding ways to target LPL and its interacting partners in ways that can therapeutically modulate the immune response.  While therapeutics are outside the scope of this proposal, these goals may identify molecules that may be targeted to alter B cell function.

This type of approach may improve teasing apart the phenotype, as the LPL (whole knockout) data already indicate that there is a decrease in GC B cells, suggesting that it will be very hard to study events at the matured GC stage and interactions with Tfh cells. . On a similar note, In C.3.3.C (pg 51-52), the proposal to analyze the products of the GC reaction in Cd19Cre x LPL floxed mice and the affect of affinity for the generation of memory B cells is an interesting one, however, it is unclear that enough GC B cells that would be mem B cell precursors would even be present.  The mixed bone marrow chimeras done in a detailed timecourse after immunization may help to pinpoint when the LPL defect is manifest, but there may be difficulty in interpretation of how reduced cell adhesion affects memory B cell formation (as the goals of Aim 3 implies), and how reduced migration of plasma cells to the bone marrow occur (as the goals of Aim 3 implies), if there are not good GC B cells in the first place. study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: The research program described in this application seeks to define the driving forces behind  the long-standing question of what causes thymic involution.  While this phenomenon has long appeared to be age-dependent and influenced by hormones such as testerosterone, the PI of this application proposes that thymic atrophy is a direct result of a thymic epithethial cell-specific deficiency in the expression of Catalase, resulting in molecular damage (DNA, protein, and lipids) by reactive oxygen species.  In addition, they hypothesize that thymic atrophy caused by ROS-induced damage is compounded by an absence of DNA repair enzyme expression in TECs.  The PI has developed an interesting Catalase expressing mouse that according to strong preliminary data reduces ROS-induced damage and atrophy of thymic epithelial cells.  The aims are well designed and include controls, and the majority of aims have achievable objectives that are interpretable and clear.  Aim 2 which focuses on comparing ROS-induced damage to DNA, proteins, and lipids in TECs (compared to other stromal cell types) is very ambitious and perhaps very difficult, but will provide novel applications to this long-standing question.  In addition, the proposed aims, while separate and distinct, also serve to confirm a compelling and the unifying hypothesis of this application.  The work proposed have the potential to develop a completely new paradigm of thymic involution based on the idea that TECs are unable to repair ROS-induced molecular damage.  Furthermore, if this hypotheses is proven, this research may serve as a basic foundation for the development of therapies that can restore or enhance regeneration of the T cell repertoire in aged or otherwise depleted individuals.
sig_text_str: . Thymic involution is process that has long-reaching physiological effects that result in a progressively limited naïve T cell repertoire with age . Despite the observation that the thymus undergoes extensive atrophy with age, the molecular and cellular mechanisms behind this process remain elusive.  This proposal presents strong preliminary data that supports an intriguing hypothesis that reactive oxygen species results in molecular damage of thymic epithelial cells resulting in thymic atrophy. . This proposal challenges the main dogma in the field that sex hormones are the major driver of thymic atrophy.  While this application does not claim to disprove a contribution in the process by sex hormones, it does provide a compelling alternative (and non-mutually exclusive) hypothesis that if found to be true, provides potential molecular and cellular targets for restoring thymic function in therapeutic settings (such as following lymphoablative therapies).

The PI is very well suited for the science in this application, with expertise in thymocyte differentiation and the processes of selection and gene rearrangement  that occur during T cell development . The PI has an extensive history of publishing impactful papars in journals such as Nature Immunology, Blood, PNAS, Immunity, etc. . The PI has demonstrated as expertise in stromal cell biology and its influence upon T cell development. Contributions include those published in Immunity and Aging Cell. . PI has an extensive history of R01 and other grant funding on diverse topics that regulate T cell development, including grants on the influence of testosterone and Notch signaling . Arrangements have been made to work with Dr. Hannah Rossum (letter of support) for doing analysis of RPS induced molecular damage at the Oxidative Damage and Mitochondrial Function Core at UT Health Science Center San Antonio, to complete this challenging and ambitious analysis. . .

In addition, if this aim does not yield clear results, Aim 3 will at least address the issue of DNA damage using alternative techniques. . Proposal to measure whether TECs are more sensitive than other epithelial cells to ROS damage using comet assays includes strong controls and should yield a clear answer to this question. . Experiments for each aim are distinct and stand alone, but combined, offer a very comprehensive investigation of the central hypothesis that thymic atrophy is a result of TEC-specific Cat and DNA repair enzyme deficiency. .

While the major focus of the study is fixed upon the mechanisms regulating TEC maintenance and atrophy, it would be intriguing to test the protective effects in aged mice in the conditional transgenic mice that maintain Catalase expression following infection, to determine whether these aged mice are protected or have improved correlates of immune protection following immunization compared to WT aged mice.  This would further verify whether preventing thymic atrophy in aged animals is beneficial by actually generating properly selected T cells that are protective to the host (besides just improving of TECs and increasing thymic cellularity). . On a similar note, measuring thymic output may and the phenotype of recent thymic emigrants may be beneficial to the study.  The implication of this intriguing application is that improving TEC function will improve the immune system (particularly in the aged); however, the study would be improved by the addition of at least some measurements of downstream effects including the quantity and quality of thymic output in mice with increased Cat expression in TEC.

imp_text: This application proposes an interesting and ambitious research program to investigate the role of the GPCR chemokine receptor CXCR4 in the trafficking of developing B cells in the bone marrow and the organization of anatomical niches required for B cell development.  There are several important and novel features in this proposal, including the use of 2 photon microscopy to perform in vivo intravital imaging of developing B cells in bone marrow to answer important questions.  These questions include the requirement of CXCR4 on early B cells, CLPs, and thymic stroma, and interactions that occur with IL7 and CXCL12 co-expressing cells.  These outstanding questions have extreme importance to the basic understanding of how developing B cells, stromal cells, and progenitors interact in vivo, and influence the generation of functional and self-tolerant B cells.  Together, these ideas may produce an outstanding long-term research program.  Given the importance of the basic questions outlined in this application, there are however several recommendations to address specific weaknesses in the proposal, that can improve the likelihood of success and improve the depth and quality of analysis.  For example, the application could be improved by the addition of experienced collaborators in fields where the PI does not have a track-record of expertise (eg stromal cells, early progenitors), that are central to the application. Additonal expertise may also help to focus some of the hypotheses and aims to flesh out and clarify the models that are to be tested, and unify the various and diverse themes of the proposal that are centered around B cell development.
sig_text_str: . This application proposes to study the role of CXCR4 on both mesemchymal cells that become bone marrow stromal cells and also on early differentiating B cells . The application could be strengthened by clarifying or providing greater detail, as to how the advances will propel the field forward.

In this regard, their characterization and use of several different Cre Tg lines cross to Cxcr4 flox/flox mice will provide useful insight into which cell types require CXCR4/CXCL12 so that the BM stromal cells are maintained. . Aim 2 is designed to test the hypothesis that CXCR4 is important for proper positioning of CLP to ensure proper early B cell differentiation. . Preliminary data (Fig 3) shows that CLP subsets are closely associated with IL-7+ cells.  Microscopy studies are well designed to look at positioning of CLP subsets and should yield important insights. . Aim 3 proposes to study the migration and localization of self-reactive B cells within the bone marrow.  The preliminary data (figure 4) demonstrate that CXCR4 (by both genetic means and drug inhibition) is important for migration of developing B cells within the bone marrow. . Investigator clearly demonstrates ability to perform two-photon microscopy experiments to visual the behavior of B cells within the bone marrow. . Interesting system has been developed to explore the interactions between IL-7-expressing cells and B cells. . Several interesting aspects of B cell development will be tested in Aim 3, including the combined analysis of cell migration and interaction with stromal cells, and the influence of IL7 on survival, receptor editing, and B cell motility.
app_text_wkn: . One of the stated purposes in Aim 1 is to determine whether CXCR4 and CXCL12 are directly required by the BM stromal cells in the bone marrow; or instead could be utilized by other non-hematopoeitic cells for the support of the bone marrow stroma.  While the Cre transgic mice and even the Cxcl12dsRed/+ mice will be useful for this, it is unclear from the experimental approach how the study will determine whether there is an actual autocrine requirement (page 28) for both CXCR4 and CXCL12 on the stromal cells themselves; particularly because the CD44loVCAM1 stromal cells are absent in the conditional CXCR4 deficient mice, making these cells difficult to study. . The anticipated outcomes for Aim 3 seems confusing in some sense.  The proposal states what these anticipated outcomes are (For example, it is predicted that self-reactive B cells will be clustered around IL7 expressing cells – in which case it would help cells survive and undergo editing) however, it is not mentioned or made very clear how some of these outcomes, would be interpreted, and more importantly, used to verify or disprove the overarching hypothesis for aim 3 (which could also be made more clear).  Thus, while it appears that very interesting observations will be made in Aim3, the Aim could be strengthened by clarifying and restating the hypothesis, and clarying how the expected outcomes will be used to form a working model. . While each independent aim shares similar themes (CXCR4, migration, IL7) and is focused on B cell differentiation in general, at times, the proposed research seems very scattered in the biology that will be studied (stromal cell biology, lymphocyte migration, CLP differentiation, and B cell central tolerance). . Analysis of central tolerance in aim 3 is interesting, but could be enhanced if there were more in-depth analyses proposed that would be used to show whether perturbing IL7 or CXCR4 during B cell development results in the activation of mature self-reactive B cells and/or generation of autoantibodies. .

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology A Study Section
imp_text: The research group will probe the role of Foxo signaling in T-cell biology and development.  This work will test the hypothesis that Foxo TF impact viral clearance and differentiation of T-cell lineages and memory.  The purpose of this investigation is to determine the mechanisms by which Foxo TF regulate T cell development and immune response.
sig_text_str: • A better understanding of immune memory may lead to better and novel vaccines or methods to combat persistent viruses. • It is clear that there is a lot unknown about mechanisms underlying T-cell memory hence studies geared toward this process are important. • Foxo -/- appears to cause T cells to behave in an unusual manner including a sustained presence and a persistant response.  That this may alter the response when exposed to a second challenge is an interesting question.
sig_text_wkn: • Given the complexities of T-cell activation, expansion, memory, etc. it is unclear how impactful the findings of these investigations will be regarding human health.  This is especially true as mouse models will be used and there was little or no discussion about similarities between these processes in murine models and humans. • While the results of Figure 2 clearly indicate that Foxo -/- cells have a greater persistence, the result is relatively mild, especially considering the case of its importance made later in the proposal.
inv_text_str: • This is a submission from a very successful and accomplished scientist with numerous active research grants and a long history of research success.
inn_text_str: • The concept that Foxo may have such a powerful and varied effect on T cells is highly innovative. • The production of mice cited in this proposal will allow for innovative experimental approaches.
inn_text_wkn: • While I agree that production of the mice needed for this work represents an extraordinary amount of effort (and time – 5 yrs), that does not necessarily make this work innovative. • The notion that gene expression may ultimately impact an array of cellular functions (in case, metabolism, differentiation, and immunity) is also not innovative.
app_text_str: •  The PI has done well to establish that techniques are currently working and the initial phenotyping work of Foxo -/- cells during reinfection was helpful. • The proposal addresses very interesting questions regarding the role of Foxo -/- in T cell physiology within the scope of the central themes of the proposal. • Aim 1E is especially well described and will make use of an integrated approach.  The application of metformin is particularly interesting given the wide use of metformin in human populations. • The contingenices in Aim 2 were well considered, logical, and would also provide interesting results.
app_text_wkn: • While a detailed description of all procedures is not needed on the whole the proposal did not include adequate descriptions to allow a clear understanding of proposed experiments. • Much of this work will provide only descriptive results.  Mechanistic details regarding how Foxo TF may be regulating effects is lacking.  What sort of signaling cascades are disrupted as a result of Foxo -/-?  Why?  How?  Are changes in gene expression meaningful?  Some confirmation with protein measures would strengthen this proposal. • Wild type cells express only 2.5-fold more Foxo1 than ko cells.  Given that, it appears there is still a fair bit of Foxo being expressed in Foxo-/- cells.  How effective is the knockout?  A western blot would be helpful.  Clearly, even if this represents a knockdown model it is impacting T cell biology, however, this information would be helpful in better understanding these data. • Throughout there are very few hypotheses stated or indication of expected results.  Likewise, there is little consideration of alternative approaches or plans if hypotheses are not supported (with the notable exception of Aim 2).

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: Summary:  In this proposal the research group will test the hypothesis that the thymus atrophies, at least in part, due to oxidative stress caused by catalase deficiency in stromal cells.  In particular, the hypothesis that this causes DNA damage, coupled with an impaired repair mechanism will be tested.  In the approach stromal cells isolated from mice of various ages will be compared to cells isolated from a mCat mouse line as well as from cells isolated from salivary glands.  This proposal makes use of a combination of animal and cell culture approaches and incorporates a good combination of research questions to address the central hypothesis.
sig_text_str: • Understanding how and why there is a loss of thymus volume and mass with age is important especially considering the clear impact on disease resistance. • The supplementation studies with NAC and vit C as well as the transgenic catalase experiments were convincing that oxidative stress and likely catalase were central features of dysfunction.
sig_text_wkn: • Figure 3 (catalase IHC) is not as clear as the authors would suggest and how this supports the central hypothesis is not evident.
inv_text_str: • This is a submission from an extraordinarily successful and accomplished scientist with numerous active research grants and a long history of research success.
inn_text_str: • The notion that a catalase insufficiency may lead to oxidative stress is highly innovative in regard to thymus loss.
inn_text_wkn: • Given the gene expression studies already published, complementary published data, and the data presented in the submission, results of experiments are predictable. • Many of the approaches used throughout the submission are routine and the aims rather limited in scope.
app_text_str: • The proposal does well to highlight gaps in knowledge that are intuitive but still should be empirically established. • If successful, Aim 2 will be highly informative regarding oxidative stress.  The authors appropriate distinguished between existing oxidative damage (Aim 2) and demonstrating an increase susceptibility to oxidative damage (Aim 3). • Testing how catalase deficiency might also contribute to DNA damage with an impaired capacity for repair is an important consideration (as in Aim 4).  Related, potential follow-up studies noted here are also consistent with the objectives of this proposal.
app_text_wkn: • In Aim 1 it is unclear if catalase will be immediately induced (prevention) or if it will be induced after some thymic loss has already occurred (rescue).  While the former might be an easier test the latter would appear to have greater clinical relevance. • Catalase is not the only H2O2 detoxification mechanism.  What happens to the GPx system and GSH in concert with decreased catalase in the thymus? • The rationale for Aim 4 is entirely dependent on the results of Aim 2 such that if there is not increased DNA damage in Aim 2 Aim 4 is no longer needed. • While it is appreciated that considerable effort will go into gaining sufficient tissues to complete Aim 3, the Aim is very limited in scope.  Might there be additional assays that could be performed that would support increased susceptibility to oxidative stress?

imp_text: Overall Impact This is an interesting proposal submitted by a new and early stage investigator.  Herein, it is proposed that the microenvironment is partially responsible for B cell maturation and lineage determination.  This is a revolutionary concept that may alter our current understanding of this process as it incorporates a previously overlooked aspect of B cell development.  Here, a case is made that CXCR4 is critical to B cell development and that this receptor is fundamental to the interaction of and homing to microenvironments within marrow.

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology A Study Section
imp_text: This is a very well written, sophisticated and important application for understanding the regulation of T cell differentiation and memory post-infection, focusing on FoxO transcription factors (especially FoxO1 and FoxO3), which play central/master roles in numerous cellular processes, such as cell cycle control, metabolism and survival. Aim 1 focus on deciphering the functional roles of Foxo TFs in regulating metabolic changes to accommodate/induce the differentiation of memory CD8 T cells upon infection. Aim 2 explores the gene expression program by Foxo TFs in CD8 T-cells at various activation and differentiation stages, using various transcriptome and ChIP-seq approaches. Aim 3 is focusing on the Foxo TF regulation on CD4 differentiation and memory. Since the underlying mechanisms/signals that govern the transition from activated effector T cells to memory cells upon vaccination are not fully understood, the proposed studies will help to fill these knowledge gaps and significantly advance the field. Aim 4 investigates the contribution of Foxo TFs in immune responses against persistent virus infection, using chronic LCMV C13 strain infection of B6 as a model. The study is highly clinical relevant and there is significant enthusiasm for the investigator to accomplish the study.
sig_text_str: • Dissect the molecular control of T-cell differentiation and memory cell formation upon infection. • Focusing on Foxo TFs to understand the T-cell metabolism in immunity. • The novel concept of fighting virus infection via manipulation of T-cell metabolism.
sig_text_wkn: • While using C13 infection as a model for persistent virus infection model is an interesting idea, it is not clear whether the lessons learned can be translated to human persistent virus infection conditions.
inv_text_str: • The PI is a well-established, senior investigator who has extensive experience in working with T-cell biology, using animal models. The PI is productive and has contributed significantly to the field. He is well suited to undertake this important and complicated project. • Excellent team of experts.  Dr. Moore is an expert in ChIP-seq technology and data analysis. Dr. Goldsmith is an expert in genome wide analysis of immunological data.
inn_text_str: • Over the years, the investigator has developed a battery of genetically modified mice to undertake the study. • Conceptual link of immunity, gene expression, metabolism and differentiation with Foxo TFs.
inn_text_wkn: • None
app_text_str: • Previous work indicates capacity to perform the experiments prescribed throughout the project. • The project is conceptually well conceived. Experiments and methods are well reasoned and logical throughout the application.
app_text_wkn: • It is unclear whether the C13 infection model has already established in the PI’s lab. Also, since the kinetics of immune responses induced by C13 and Arm strains of LCMV infection are different, the contribution of Foxo TFs mediated metabolic changes to T-cell differentiation and memory might be different. Of note, most of the preliminary data were obtained from Arm LCMV infection and Aims 1-3 are largely focused on the acute type of immune responses. Nevertheless, the data generated might be different, but extremely interesting.

imp_text: The objective of the project is to understand the role of LPL in B cell motility and GC formation. The investigator has previously demonstrated that LPL deficiency affects B cell motility both in vitro and in vivo, which leads to diminished splenic maturation of marginal zone B cells. In the proposal, the investigator proposes that LPL is a key mediator of integrin and chemotactic signaling to regulate actin cytoskeleton reorganization, to promote B cell motility. To further understand the role of LPL in humoral response, the investigator will first identify the domain of LPL (especially the serine phosphorylation site at 5’ LPL domain) responsible for actin reorganization and B cell motility, with rescue experiments. The investigator will also study how the integrin signaling and other chemotactic signaling are mediated through LPL (Aim 2). Using the LPL fl/fl mice, the investigator will study the requirement of LPL for GC formation upon virus infection. While the proposed study will forward our understanding of the function of LPL in B cell biology, its enthusiasm is moderate. Aim 3 is more exciting, but the availability of the reagent remains to be demonstrated. Some of the weakness noted include (1) lack of focus: Aim 1 focuses on the functional domain of LPL on B cell motility, Aim 2 switches to the molecular involvement of LPL in Pyk2 phosphorylation, Aim 3 studies the role of LPL in GC formation upon virus infection. The project does not have a clear and coherent theme, and the organization of the Approach section is confusing. (2) It is well established that B cell motility is essential for proper humoral response and factors such as Bcl-6 in B-cell differentiation and motility is very well studied. It is not a surprise that factors affect actin bundling can affect B cell motility and thereby, GC formation. The project lacks novelty. (3) lack of in depth molecular analysis of B-cell motility and GC formation. (4) Some of preliminary data (e.g. Fig 6) are not strong. (5) No data are shown on the LPLfl/fl mice, an essential reagent for Aim 3. (6) Aim 1, Fig 7, only 2.5% of circulating B cells are GFP+. Such low transduction efficiency will make the Aim 1 rescue experiments very challenging. (7) The Aim 2 approach is largely based on “hypothetical educated guess” of interacting factors.

imp_text: This is a very well written application to understand the contribution of ROS in thymic atrophy. The major thesis of the application is to test the hypothesis that accelerated accumulation of genomic lesions caused by metabolic ROS is the major cause of early thymic atrophy. This is based on their previous findings, largely from global gene expression data, that thymic epithelial cells (TECs) are deficient in several key ROS-protection enzymes, particularly Catalase (Cat). Aim 1 is to perform gain-of-function experiments to rescue thymic atrophy by correction of Cat deficiency. Aims 2 and 3 seek to demonstrate that TECs naturally accumulate excessive oxidative lesions in vivo (A2) and are more sensitive to ROS-mediated damage in vitro (A3). Aim 4 is to demonstrate that TECs also possess deficiencies in oxidative damage repair mechanisms.  While there is no clearly path to translate this new knowledge of thymus aging into clinical prevention, identifying deficiencies in ROS enzyme function and repairing mechanisms as key factor is an important step in understanding the underlying mechanisms of early thymus atrophy. A major weakness of the project is its lack of mechanistic study. There is no attempt to study the mechanisms responsible for the deficient Cat and other ROS protective enzyme expression in TECs.  In addition, the survival of TECs requires 1) the 3-dimensional organization of the thymus stromal microenvironment, 2) cross-talk to developing thymocytes. In vitro culture of TECs, even overnight, is challenging – majority of the TECs undergo apoptosis after overnight 2D culture. This will be a major challenge for Aims 3 and 4, in which overnight culture of primary TECs is proposed. No contingency is proposed.  Due to these reasons, the enthusiasm of the project is moderate to high.

imp_text: The proposed studies aim to define the role of the actin binding protein, L-plastin (LPL), in integrating chemotactive and cell adhesion signals in normal B cell motility, germinal center formation, and high affinity T-dependent antibody production. In Aim 1 the domains of LPL required for B cell motility will be determined using in vitro assays and in vivo chimeric mouse studies. In Aim 2, the elements of the integrin-associated Pyk2 signaling cascade that require LPL will be identified and the direct or indirect role of LPL identified.  In Aim 3, the B-cell intrinsic requirements for LPL during T-Cell dependent antibody response will be determined. Strengths of this application include: 1) early stage principle investigator who is well-qualified and productive with a history of research and clinical training in areas directly related to the proposed project; 2) addresses a significant problem (germinal center formation) important in basic immunology with clinical application is immune deficiency, autoimmunity and cancer immunology; 3) strong institutional support that includes a team of established investigators with expertise in cutting edge research techniques that will be used in proposed experiments; 4) a novel LPL floxed model that can be applied to a variety of cell types in basic and translational studies will be developed 5) Aims 2 and 3 have are well designed, with strong potential for defining novel mechanisms that link chemokine receptor signaling and integrin signaling in B cell motility; 6) the highly translational nature of Aim 3 in evaluating the impact of LPL loss on response to West Nile Virus. The proposal is somewhat overambitious but this is mitigated by the expertise of a strong collaborative team that can streamline troubleshooting should the need arise.  Enthusiasm is substantially dampened by the lack of preliminary data to show that LPL-GFP fusion proteins are functional or alternatively a plan to include empty vector GFP controls in Aim 1.

imp_text: The proposed studies aim to test the novel hypothesis that thymic atrophy is caused by an accelerated accumulation of canonical lesions of metabolic damage due to deficiencies in enzymes that protect from reactive oxygen species (ROS) and enzymes that repair oxidative damage in thymic epithelial cells (TEC).  Studies in Aim 1 will use two complementary mouse models to determine whether selective correction of catalase deficiency in TEC can prevent thymic atrophy. Studies in Aim 2 will determine whether TEC accumulate more oxidative lesions (in lipids and DNA) than other age matched tissues. Studies in Aim 3 will determine whether TEC cells are more sensitive to ROS-mediated damage and studies in Aim 4 are focused on determining whether secondary deficiencies in oxidative damage repair exacerbate the effects of catalase deficiency. The strengths of this proposal include: 1) tests a conceptually very novel hypothesis supported by strong, novel, preliminary data; 2) addresses a highly significant problem with implications for basic science and multiple clinical fields 3) PI is productive investigator and establish expert in the field of thymopoiesis with expertise in challenging techniques essential to proposed studies and for testing the proposed hypothesis 4) use of complementary animal models, each addressing weaknesses of the other 5) Overall a well-reasoned, carefully designed and elegant experimental approach. Weakness include 1) overall the grant seems somewhat underdeveloped–studies that evaluate the ability of antioxidants to reverse, not simply prevent thymic atrophy would increase enthusiasm and 2) the feasibility of isolating sufficient numbers of salivary gland epithelia as a control in Aim 2 was not addressed.

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: The proposed studies are focused on determining the role CXCR4 in maintenance of bone marrow stromal cells that support B cell development in the bone marrow and their role in B cell tolerance.  The proposal is based on preliminary data showing that mice lacking CXCR4 in non-hematopoietic cells exhibit a loss of specific BM stromal subsets and an inability to repopulate the B lineage after adoptive transfer. Separate preliminary studies show that CXCR4 on lymphoid progenitors is required for their migration and positioning near IL-7 producing cells. Studies in Aim 1 are proposed to  characterize the role played by CRCR4 in non-hematopoietic BM cells. Studies in Aim 2 will determine the mechanisms controlling common lymphoid progenitor positioning in the BM. Aim 3. In Aim 3 studies will test the hypothesis that reduced CXCR4 function causes autoreactive B cells to move away from IL-7 expressing cells and fail tolerance checkpoints. The strengths of this application include: 1) early stage investigator with expertise in cutting edge techniques that form the basis for many of the studies; 2) addresses an important basic science question with relevance to B-cell mediated autoimmunity and mediation of perturbations of B cell production that occur with aging, infection, and following stem cell transplant. 3) Well-designed experiments using cutting edge techniques that will provide important information on the interplay between CXCR4 and IL-7 in positioning of common lymphoid progenitors and in central tolerance. Weaknesses include 1) the information to be gained from Aim 1B is unclear; 2) the lack of senior author publications by the PI as an independent investigator and 3) an overambitious proposal.
