study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology A Study Section
imp_text: This proposal, which describes experiments designed to gain knowledge of the roles of FoxO1 and FoxO3 in memory CD4+ and CD8+ differentiation, is a good proposal from an outstanding investigator.  The proposal does have strengths, including the PI, an experienced investigator with an established track record in T cell research, and unique mouse models, including conditional deletion alleles of FoxO1, FoxO3, or both, however there are several concerns regarding the approach.  The dedication of four and a half pages to the significance and innovation sections provides excessive background and leaves limited space for the description of the research plan, which is vague.  A large proportion of the proposed experiments are general screening approaches, including gene expression arrays, ChIP seq, and histone methylation screens, with limited proposed hypotheses or descriptions of how the results will be used or interpreted.  Space dedicated to the non-screen experiments proposed is extremely limited, and the research design of these experiments lacks depth and mechanistic design.  These concerns over the approach counterbalance the high quality of the investigators and system.
sig_text_str: . The mechanisms of memory and central memory CD8+ and CD4+ T cell differentiation are incompletely understood, and defining the role of FoxO1 and FoxO3 would be significant.
sig_text_wkn: . The significance section is not clearly written, and the section describing Tfh cells is out of place with the the surrounding sections on memory differentiation.  It is not clear how Tfh cells fit with the rest of the project. . The significance section is excessively long with a great deal of background material.  Although the area of T cell memory differentiation is significant, it is not made clear how the project will advance the field.
inv_text_str: . The PI is a well-established T-cell immunologist, with a strong publication record in the project area. . The PI has established appropriate collaborations to advance the project.
inn_text_str: . The PI’s lab has specialized mouse strains that are well suited to the project and have taken years to develop.
inn_text_wkn: . The PI concedes that the project is not technically innovative, but does not attempt to convey any other aspect of innovation.
app_text_str: . The experiments proposed make good use of FoxO1 and FoxO3 conditional knockout mouse models, which are highly specialized models in the PI’s lab. . Experiments are designed to further recent advances connecting changes in T-cell metabolism to effector versus memory differentiation. . Two different murine models of chronic viral infection are used in Aim 4.
app_text_wkn: . Addition of an IL-7Ra transgene is not the same as blocking down-regulation of physiologic IL-7Ra expression.  No effort is made to ensure that expression of IL-7Ra in the transgenic model is in the physiologic range for the appropriate T-cells. . Experiments in aim 1 are highly phenomenological, with observation of cell phenotype and survivial without any deeper mechanistic experiments proposed.  For example, experiments with rapamycin and metformin include surface phenotype and cell counting with no mechanistic approaches beyond a briefly described PCR array. . Aim 2 appears promising in the first paragraph, with analysis of a micro-array experiment that has already been performed, however the genes selected for description are largely genes that already have an established role in T cell memory, diminishing the novelty of the experiments. . A major set of experiments in Aim 2 are designed to distinguish genes favoring Tcm differentiation from those favoring Tem differentiation, however, it is not clear that these gene expression changes will have occurred by Day 7, as planned.  The Foxo1 deficient T cell model to be used exhibits a persistent effector phenotype.  It is not clear that these cells become either effector or central memory, and therefore, the model may not be the best model in which to evaluate Tcm versus Tem differentiation. . Rather than going forward from the results of the completed micro-array, the experiments proposed in aim 2 describe several general screening approaches, including multiple gene expression arrays, ChIP seq, and histone methylation screens. No clear hypothesis driven, mechanistic, or functional experiments are included. . While the followup of interesting observations regarding FoxO1 and Tfh differentiation are of value, the experiments in Aim 3 on this topic fit very tenuously with the rest of the proposal. . The three sentence description of experiments in aim 3b is insufficient to convey what is actually to be done. . Additional gene expression array and ChIP seq experiments are proposed in Aim 3.  While expected results are described, with specific hits anticipated in Bcl6, Bcl-2 family members, and genes related to metabolism, it is unlikely that gene expression array and ChIP seq general screening approaches are the best way to study these genes/pathways. . Aim 4 describes an experimental system (FoxO1 and/or FoxO3 deficient T cells in two murine models of chronic viral infection) that has strong potential, however the half page description of the research plan contains insufficient detail to convey what is to be done and how the results will be interpreted.

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: In this project, the PI, an early stage investigator, will follow up on the labs recent work showing that LPL is involved in B cell motility and germinal center development. The project is well designed, with aims that test clearly stated hypotheses using direct approaches.  There are some weaknesses in the approach, including dependence on reagents that are not validated, including deletion mutants of LPL and a new mouse model.  Important potential pitfalls regarding the deletion mutants and the use of lentiviruses to express LPL in bone marrow chimeras are not addressed.  An entire aim is based upon a B cell specific deletion of LPL, when there are already observed phenotypes using the germline deletion model.  There is risk that the effort and resources put towards establishing this novel model will not yield significant progress.  There is also some concern that the PI is an early stage investigator without an established investigator as a co-investigator with any dedicated effort.  This concern is somewhat mitigated by the strong training record of the PI.
sig_text_str: . The project will fill substantial gaps in current knowledge of actin dynamics in B cell migration during GC development.
sig_text_wkn: . While clinical syndromes involving actin dynamics and immunodeficiency are identified, it is not clear how enhanced understanding of the molecular biology of actin dynamics will translate to vaccine technology or immunomodulatory development.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an early stage investigator with a strong training record, a reasonable number of high quality publications, and the recipient of a K08 award. . Collaborators have been included to provide technical support where necessary.
inv_text_wkn: . The PI is an early stage investigator, and there is no senior co-investigator in the field with any dedicated effort.
inn_text_str: . Conceptual and technical innovations are clearly identified and listed by the PI.  Establishing connections between actin dynamics, chemokine and integrin signaling, and GC formation is innovative.
inn_text_wkn: . Technical innovations listed, a conditional deletion allele and DNA constructs, use well-established technology.
app_text_str: . The use of deletion mutants of LPL is a very direct way of testing the importance of specific residues/domains. . Hypotheses in all aims are clearly described, and the planned experiments do test the hypotheses. . Incorporation of experiments with West Nile virus in the setting of LPL deficient B cells highlights clinical relevance of the project. . The techniques proposed in the approach are not easy, but are feasible for the investigator and his collaborators.
app_text_wkn: . Reconstitution of LPL by lentiviral transduction raises problems that are not addressed by the PI.  While the potential for low level expression is addressed, the actual expression observed may be excessively high, or may be highly variable from experiment to experiment, depending on the site of integration.   Physiologic regulation of LPL expression will not be present. . There is a small risk that the GFP tag may interfere with the function of LPL.  No preliminary data are included to show a lack of interference. . Structural integrity/stability of LPL deletion mutants may be compromised, leading to phenotypes and experimental results that are incorrectly ascribed to the deleted regions. . In aim 2, it is not clear that isolated primary B cells will yield enough protein extract to allow for several immunoprecipitation experiments with a reasonable number of mice. . The transgenic mouse strain to be used in aim 3 has not yet been derived and validated. . The B-cell specific deletion of LPL in the novel mouse strain may or may not yield significant new insights.

imp_text: Even if the hypothesis is not supported, new information will be generated.  The PI has made it clear how the research results can be used to inform/improve clinical care.  There is a substantial amount of preliminary data for the role of these proteins in other cell types; the role of these proteins in B cells will be novel.  The summary and model (Figure 8) make it easy to see the PI’s future research direction.  The PI has significant support from several of her colleagues at Washington University and the letters of support make it clear that these investigators understand the project and how their expertise will be used.  The PI’s educational background is appropriate for these research studies and the publication record is adequate, although not exceptional.  The number of mice proposed for the studies is reasonable.  In order to conduct the experiments, there are a number of mice that will need to be generated by backcrossing to a different background (CD19-Cre/LPL fl/fl) mice and then these will be bred to CD19 Cre mice.  There is always the potential that breeding will not go as planned and will delay conduct of the experiments in Aim 3.  The investigator has acknowledged this and has proposed to use mixed bone marrow chimeras if breeding is delayed.  Part of Aim 1 is to use lentivirus to infect HSCs to reconstitute expression of LPL in lymphocytes from LPL -/- mice.  The data in Figure 7 are somewhat reassuring, however, no information is provided about whether the percentage of cells expressing GFP is representative of several mice or if instead, their best result is shown.  Given that the PI has the support of Dr. Hong, who has successfully used this strategy in the past, the PI should be able to get guidance if the technique does not work as expected with the additional mutants that are to be generated.  The research proposed here builds nicely upon data that has previously been generated while allowing the PI to bring new techniques into her lab.  There is also a clear plan for how the data (even if they do not support the hypotheses) will allow expansion of the model of the role of actin proteins in lymphocyte motility and lymphocyte activation and maturation.

imp_text: The PI states in the project summary that he intends to use established mouse strains to conduct the research, however, in the vertebrate animal section he states that “most of these strains are not commercially available and must be bred in house”.  Different sections of the grant should not contradict each other.  The overall number of animals that is proposed to conduct these experiments is massive—6000 mice.  The housing and husbandry of the mice will be a significant cost.  The researchers should explore alternatives to obtaining the data using fewer animals.  The PI plans to have one research assistant who will be responsible for maintaining the mice that will be used in the proposed experiments.  It is not clear to me that one full-time person will be sufficient given the amount of work that is required.  The PI has been trained by a well-respected B cell development biologist, Dr. Jason Cyster and has already acquired the necessary training to conduct the proposed experiments.  Although the work proposed here may further increase the understanding of how self-reactive B cells are deleted, it is not readily translated into an understanding of how this process goes wrong in autoimmune disease.  In Aim 1, the researchers propose to identify the key CXCR4+ non-hematopoietic cell subset that is required for B-lineage cell differentiation.  As multiple cell types in the BM express CXCR4, the hypothesis is a bit narrow minded and does not consider that multiple cells types may contribute to B-lineage cell differentiation meaning that knocking out CXCR4 in one cell type may not be sufficient.  Throughout the grant, the procedures are not described in detail.  For example in Aim 3, the PI plans to use intravital microscopy to look at cells in mixed chimeras.  The PI does not say how long after injection of cells, the mice will be visualized and the PI does not address any issues that may be encountered with this procedure.  The PI does not say for example whether or not the mice will be immobilized while intravital microscopy is performed.  The aims are loosely related and it is not clear how valuable the data will be if the data do not support the hypotheses.

imp_text: The central hypothesis of this project suggests that Foxo transcription factor (TFs) play a central role in the formation of memory T cells. While the application describes an elaborate series of experiments using cell culture and knockout/transgenic animal models that will examine the effect of Foxo TF deficiency on memory T cell metabolism, quiescence, recall response, and gene expression, most of the planned studies will identify correlations rather than causality, and thus the work is largely descriptive in nature. Moreover, much of it is also confirmatory, as Foxo TFs have been shown to regulate stem cell quiescence, survival, cell cycle control, and metabolism. Potential outcomes for most of the studies are not addressed, and it is not clear what novel information will be generated from these studies.

imp_text: This new R01 application is from a junior scientist with moderate publication records. No central hypothesis was formulated in the proposal. Three working hypotheses were proposed to study the regulatory role of CXCR4 expressed on non-hematopoietic cells in B-lineage cell development. Preliminary data support these hypotheses. Mouse models and laboratory techniques are available for the proposed studies. Results from these studies will contribute to understanding the mechanism underlying the regulatory role of CXCR4 in B cell development.  CXCR4 has been known to regulate B-lymphopoiesis, and its antagonists has been used to regulate hematopoiesis. The clinical significance of the proposed studies is limited.  Several studies in aim 1 and aim 2 are descriptive without rationales.

imp_text: 2 This is a proposal from a young clinical investigator from the premier medical school (Wash U), who garnered support and advice from senior colleagues, aimed at testing a novel hypothesis postulating that a specific regulatory cytoskeleton protein, LPL, plays an important role in lymphocytes motility and migration, which in turn contributes to development of a strong immune response.  Three aims are to identify involved domains in LPL, define its integrin-associated signaling elements and determine role of LPL in antibody production. Although unlikely that just one protein is the master regulator of so common and vitally important mechanism as actin remodeling and cellular motility, the significance is high because the rigorously planned studies in vivo and in vitro in three independent yet mutually reinforcing aims are likely to yield new important information. Potential problems are carefully discussed and alternatives proposed. However, the amount and diversity of the projected studies seem somewhat overambitious.
sig_text_str: • B-cell motility and migration in the germinal center is important factor in functions of the immune system and advancing our understanding of the molecular regulation of this process is important. • The premise of this study is that specific actin-binding proteins regulate B cell migration in GC, and testing this hypothesis may have a significant impact including identification of new potential therapeutic targets and perhaps design of pharmacological interventions. • The hypothesis is supported by results of pilot studies in vivo (figures 3 and 4).
sig_text_wkn: •   The cellular motility and chemotaxis are vitally important processes for humans and other organisms with immune system. Such functions are usually supported by multiple redundant pathways. How likely is it that B cell motility is controlled by one protein (L-plastin)? • Is L-plastin mediated regulation specific for B-cells? If not, pilot data showing impairment of B-cell migration and GC formation may be the result of alterations in other cell types.
inv_text_str: • Dr. Baker is a new early stage investigator from Wash U, a clinician specializing in pediatrics, infectious disease and immunology, trained in outstanding centers in the US and currently establishing his research lab and direction. His CV features several first-author papers in the JI, Blood and JBC. • Dr. Carter, a seasoned professor in Wash U, brings in additional expertise in regulation of cellular motility by actin-associated proteins. • Dr. Dawson, professor of medicine in Wash U, is an expert in infectious disease and immune system. • Overall, Wash U team looks strong.

inn_text_str: • The hypothesis seems novel and original. • In addition, application of some experimental approaches to this research direction seems novel.
app_text_str: • Research plan is rigorous, and contains three well defined, logical and mutually reinforcing Aims. Aims 2 and 3 are not dependant on success of the previous aims. • Interpretation of results, as well as potential problems and approaches to resolve or circumvent them are well thought through, which is especially commendable for a junior investigator. • Studies of molecular dissection of interactions of LPL with cytoskeleton partners and their functional consequences are well designed and likely to yield important information regardless of the outcome. • Studies on functional role of LPL domain structure are well designed. • Many methodological approaches are the state of the art.

imp_text: 5 This is proposal from a seasoned investigator who collaborates with colleagues providing informal support (no % effort) to test the hypothesis that ROS surplus caused by deficiency of catalase in epithelial cells in thymus leads to the involution of this key organ of immune system. Four aims are proposed to test (briefed by the reviewer): 1) Effect of selective correction of catalase deficiency in the stromal epithelial cells in thymus; 2) Whether these cells are under oxidative stress; 3) Whether they are more sensitive to ROS; and 4) Whether secondary antioxidant deficiencies in these cells are involved. However, the conceptual basis for the hypothesis, and quality of the pilot data seem inadequate to justify the RO1, even a modular one. Either convincing pilot data and scientific rational should be provided, or this project needs to be reformatted into R21 mechanism (given that theoretical aspects of the study are more rigorously addressed).
sig_text_str: • The  scientific premise of this project is to characterize the role of ROS and antioxidant enzyme catalase in thymus. According to the PI, this might be involved in degeneration of the immune system during aging. • Proving the hypothesis that H2O2 surplus is a causative factor of decay of immune system, if feasible, would open a theoretical possibility of therapeutic management using antioxidants.
sig_text_wkn: • The pilot data and projected studies are all about normal animals. If catalase expression level is normally lower in any specific cell type, tissue or organ than in other counterparts in our body, that is the way mother nature designed it to be. If the investigators would provide a link between abnormal level of catalase and any given pathology involving thymus, this would provide a more substantial rationale for the study. • It seems highly unlikely that surplus of this ROS caused by deficiency of catalase is the major factor. Catalase is just one of several enzymes including peroxidases and non-enzymatic antioxidants  that quickly decompose H2O2, which is highly diffusible in contrast with superoxide anion. • No pilot data show elevated level of ROS or oxidized biomolecules that are generally accepted as markers of oxidative stress (isoprostanes, nitro-tyrosine, DNA adducts, even pedestrian MDA). This info, relegated to studies in the Aim 2, must be tested in pilot studies and provided as key supportive pilot data. • Pilot data on catalase deficiency might have limited if any relevance to the enzyme activity in the tissue. • Pilot data in figure 4 are not too convincing and can be explained by effects of NAC and vitamin C on pathways that have nothing to do with thymus except for its enlargement that may be secondary to some systemic or remote effects in the body. • The parameters determined in pilot studies have little if any mechanistic value.

imp_text: In this proposal, Dr. Robinson seeks to evaluate the mechanism of L-plastin activation, the impact of L-plastin on B-cell differentiation and motility, and the effect of L-plastin on germinal centers and T-helper cells.  The PI uses a sophisticated and thorough approach to addressing these Aims by gain/loss of function experiments, and the generation of a mouse model with a conditional deletion of L-plastin.  The potential significance of a better understanding of the role of L-plastin in B-cell motility and function is an enhanced understanding of mechanisms that impact immunity.  However, the impact on of this investigation on clinical diseases is not clearly stated in the proposal.  The investigator is well-educated in immunology, and has created an outstanding network of collaborators to support his goals.  The environment seems exceptional for the completion of this proposal.

A greater understanding of the molecular regulation of B cell motility may enhance the development of immunomodulatory drugs

imp_text: Dr. Murphy’s proposal seeks to determine the effect of ROS accumulation in thymic stromal epithelial cells, as a result of catalase deficiency, on new T-cell generation. The significance of this proposal is clear, as decreased thymic weight and new T-cells, may affect viral clearance and immunity post-vaccination.  The approach is generally solid, but a few additional experiments that evaluate ROS signaling or viral clearance following catalase repletion would strengthen the approach further. The PI is well-established, and has a clear record of success in scientific investigation. The environment and collaborators seem solid. On the whole, an excellent proposal that is innovative and has potential clinical impact.
sig_text_str: . The PI clearly states the importance of this proposal.  Aging thymic stromal epithelial cells are deficient in catalase, which leads to ROS accumulation, thymic atrophy, and decreased new T-cell production . The clinical result of these deficits is increased susceptibility to viral infections, decreased resolution of infection, and impaired responsiveness to vaccination.
sig_text_wkn: . It would be impossible to evaluate thymic epithelial stromal cells in humans. However, decreased numbers of circulating new T-cells in older adults may support the PIs hypothesis. The author does cite some literature that supports a role for age-related thymic atrophy in the Significance portion of the proposal. . The authors could further enhance their clinical significance by demonstrating that viral clearance is improved in those animals in which catalase is over-expressed.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Murphy has an excellent record of academic investigation as evidenced by his academic advancement timeline, his publication record, and his success with grant funding . The proposal is written with clarity and an honest approach to potential pitfalls during the investigation, and how they will be addressed.

The PI states that the role of catalase in thymic atrophy has not been investigated, despite the significant clinical implications in determining the pathogenetic mechanisms at play in this process . Two different expression models for catalase will be used: 1)conditional expression of catalase in mitochondria 2) overexpression of catalase in thymic stromal tissue only.  Further, age-matched other epithelial tissue will be evaluated to determine if it demonstrates sensitivity to ROS similar to TEC in in vitro experiments.

app_text_str: . In Aim 1, mitochondrial catalase will be overexpressed and thymic tissue weighed and cellularity assessed, lymphoid cell phenotype evaluated, anatomic composition and stromal organization assessed.  Additionally, a second mouse model in which catalase is only overexpressed in stromal cells will confirm the initial experiments.  Mice at several different ages will be evaluated. . In Aim 2, primary TEC and control cells will be utilized to evaluate the effects of catalase deficiency on DNA modifications, and lipid peroxidation. Vital fluorescence microscopy will be utilized to assess ROS.  Additionally, in vivo DNA damage will be assessed in situ. . In Aim 3, cultured TEC, Cat-overexpressing TEC and control cells will be subjected to differing concentrations of hydrogen peroxide, and DNA damage assessed using FLARE . In Aim 4, cultured TEC, Cat-overexpressing TEC, and control cells will be evaluated for repair mechanisms to ROS using a global gene expression assay

The evaluation of ROS using fluorescent microscopy is very time and environmentally dependent, and care will have to be taken to evaluate the cells within a short time after exposure occurs . Could thymic preservation in catalase-overexpressors be the result of decreased cellular death (mitochondrial ROS can lead to apoptosis)?  Potential signaling pathways of thymic preservation should be explored.

imp_text: Dr. Baker’s proposal seeks to determine the role of CXCR-4 in mesenchymal stem cell maintenance and differentiation for B-cell development. He intends to investigate this hypothesis through the utilization of conditional-expressors of CXCR-4 and evaluation of IL-7 and lymphoid progenitors.  He intends to examine if IL-7 and CXCR-4 play a role in the recognition of self- and non-self reactive B-cells. He states that a better understanding of these mechanisms may enhance the development of pharmaceutical targets for autoimmune disease, like SLE. Dr. Baker seems like an outstanding early career investigator. He has formal training in immunology during his post-graduate years, and he has published several high-impact papers during that time. He has continued to be productive in his time since he moved to Yale, publishing 2 middle author papers in 3 years. Dr. Baker’s preliminary data and publication record demonstrate that he has the resources and ability to complete the propsed experiments.  However, the proposal does not clearly state that he has scientific or technical guidance from any collaborators (either local or otherwise).  Given the scope and complexity of some of the experiments, it is unclear if they are feasible with the number of personnel Dr. Baker will have available within the time-frame that is indicated. Yale University has adequate core equipment and Dr. Baker’s laboratory has resources to allow for the completion of the experiments. My major concerns revolve around a lack of clarity about what the completion of this proposal contributes to the immunology field as a whole.  The experiments are sophisticated but do not generally seem to evaluate mechanisms in ways that are clinically applicable, i.e. in young/old mice, in control/MRL mice (although Aim 3 does suggest some experiments in an mouse model of SLE).

In Aim1, the proposal will investigate the role of CXCR4 deficiency on HSC differentiation (B-cells and other non-hematopoietic cells), and will determine the mechanism of this effect . In Aim 2, the PI proposes that the effects of CXCR4 are mediated through IL-7, which affects CLP positioning . In Aim 3, the PI suggests that CXCR4 deficiency has been noted in both human and mouse models of SLE, and they will evaluate the relationship between CXCR4, IL-7 and B-cell development in a mouse model of SLE .

imp_text: The PI proposes to test an alternative model for “Host Shut-Off by VSV” based on the data generated in the PI’s and other labs. The PI proposes that the M protein-Rae1 complex inhibits host transcription, and may actually promote transport of a subset of host mRNAs that are associated with host heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) that re-localize to the cytoplasm following VSV infection. The PI stated that “the coupling of transcription, mRNA transport, and translation is a fundamental cell biological process that is likely to be important for host shut-off by many viruses, as well as for other cellular processes that affect host gene expression”, and “Determining the mechanisms of host shut-off by VSV offers a window of opportunity for insight into these questions that are important for both cell biology and viral pathogenesis”. Although whether the understandings of “host shut-off by VSV” can be applied to other viruses needs to be validated in other viruses, research on “host shut-off” by VSV can provide some basic understanding of viral pathogenesis. The Pi has been studying the “host shut-off by VSV” for many years and the possibility of making progress in this is high. imp_text: This R01 application is from joint investigators at the University of Denver and the CDC foundation.  Dr. Kelly is an expert in structural biology with a focus on function; Dr. Berrigan is a virologist with experience in high containment pathogens.  Each investigator brings significant, and required expertise to this grant that explores the viral ovarian tumor domain protease (vOTU) of the L protein of the Nairovirus.  vOTUs target ubitquitin and ISG15 for removal.  Member of Nairoviruses have varying levels of these activities despite having a similarly structure domain; in this grant, the PIs leverage this diversity to explore the functional domain and their mechanism of action.  In addition, the grant describes a reverse genetic system for CCFV which permits exploration of their mutation in the context of infection.  The second aim explores how vOTU activity dicates innate immune response.  The grant also seek to determine if vOTUs govern aspects of species specificity and attempt to produce an improved mouse model for CCHFV.  Overall, this application represents the utility of dual investigator grants.  The combination of structure function with in vitro and in vivo infection are a potent combination.  While there are minor concerns about being both over ambitious, and potentially too risky (especially in regards to animal models), the potential for these studies is great and may lead to improve therapeutics for a broad range of virusea as well as better understanding of how ISGylation and ubiquitination alter immunity to virus infection
sig_text_str: . CCHFV is a potent vector transmitted pathogen that poses a major risk to human populations around the world; related viruses also have potential for economic damage . imp_text: This R01 application is from a new investigator at Penn State.  An expert in enzyme kinetics and NMR, Dr. Walsh applies these techniques to the study of RNA dependent RNA polymerase  (RdRP) activity in poliovirus.  Arguing that structural based studies provide only a snapshot, the grant seeks to use solution state NMR to better define the kinetics and dynamics of RdRP function. Leveraging this information, novel drugs and therapeutics can be developed to treat not only polioviruses, but similar viral RdRps.  The grant builds upon a plethora of resources within the poliovirus field including fidelity mutants (both high and low), vaccine strains with fidelity alterations, as well as novel therapeutics that target HCV RdRps.  This approach takes advantage of cutting edge NMR technology and represents the most dynamic exploration of RdRp function.  Especially important is the evaluation of time frame in addition to positioning; each provides a critical window that likely impact infection.  Overall, this I regard this as an outstanding grant with some minor issues.  These include no examination of an established animal model of polio, lack of development of a few aims as well as concerns about the ability to carry out virology experiments; however, these are primarily minor concerns.

Aim 3 explores mechanism of nucleoside analogues based on NMR shifts in part 1 and their interaction with RdRp mutants in part 2; together, these approaches will be used to test the hypothesis that post-translational conformation changes affect translocations . imp_text: The coronavirus, mouse hepatitis virus (MHV), causes acute hepatitis and seems like an excellent model for understanding virus interaction with liver cells. The MHV protein ns2 is shown to have 2’,5’-phosphodiesterase (PDE) activity and can degrade 2’,5’-oligoadenylate (2-5A), the activator of RNase L synthesized by 2-5A synthetase (OAS). The proposal centers in understanding the role of ns2 and other viral and cellular PDEs in liver macrophages, liver endothelial cells and hepatocytes. The plan to identify identify small molecule inhibitors of viral and cellular 2’,5’-PDEs by high throughput screening is very exciting. The idea to generate chimeric viruses expressing different viral and cellular 2’,5’-PDEs and test their ability to antagonize RNase L and induce hepatitis is really good. Corroborating many of the results obtained in different cell types with mouse studies makes the proposal very strong. The study will certainly be a big step to take the field of therapeutic strategies for human viral hepatitis and other viral diseases forward.
sig_text_str: • Many viral infections induce acute chronic liver pathology with IFN response as the first line of defense. The PIs labs have shown that RNase L is a critical cellular factor for protection against viral infection of the liver. They have also shown that Ns2 is a phosphodiesterase that cleaves 2-5A, an activator of RNase L, and thus prevents RNA degradation. They have also found that viral and host A-kinase anchoring protein 7 homologs of MHV ns2 also cleave 2-5A and potentially have the same function in regulating the OAS-RNase L cycle. The planned study of discovering inhibitors against the viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs may lead to ground breaking antivirals.
inv_text_str: • The team of PIs, collaborators and consultants looks awesome with many many years of experience working together. Combining the complementary expertise in murine coronavirus pathogenesis (Walsh lab) and the IFN induced antiviral OAS-RNase L pathway (Spindler lab) is bound to be very productive. I feel strongly that the project is very well planned and the investigators are leaders in the field.
inn_text_str: • The hypothesis that viral 2H phosphoesterases, including MHV ns2 and its homologs in other viruses, regulate cellular 2-5A levels and hence RNase L activity and its antiviral effects is highly novel. I feel excited about the high throughput assay screening for inhibitors of 2’,5’-PDEs.
app_text_str: Studying the cell type specific activity of the OAS-RNase L pathway in Aim 1 is well planned. The preliminary data supports the hypothesis that the use of inhibitors of viral and cellular 2’,5’-PDEs to enhance RNase L activity selectively in virus-infected cells provides a novel mode of regulation of the antiviral response. Comparing the pathogenicity of ns2 wild type and ns2-H126R mutant in mice is a very good idea. Characterizing viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs and identifying their inhibitors is the best part of the study. Overall the project will shed immense light on cell controls of 2-5A levels during the IFN antiviral response.

imp_text: Understanding the structure-function-dynamics of polio virus encoded RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) and its mutants is paramount to the development of new and next generation antivirals.   Solution-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy is the most suited technique to establish relationships between polymerase function/fidelity and the structural rearrangements that RdRP undergoes. The plan to use 13C-Met, 13C-Ala and 13C-Ile-substituted RdRp to understand the conformational-change steps before, during and after the nucleotide addition that are required for efficient and faithful nucleotidyl transfer and to combine these results with enzyme kinetics and cell-based assays makes the proposal very strong. I feel skeptical if there will be any general trends that can be fathomed by mutating residues in the long range network of hydrogen bonds with Gly64 and His273. I also feel uncertain regarding the general applicability of the results to other RdRPs.

imp_text: This is a grant to understand the “host shut off” mechanism by Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), a prototype for human viruses. Published research has shown that VSV inhibits transcription, nuclear-cytoplasmic transport of mRNA, and translation of proteins in infected cells. The M protein from the virus in association with the nuclear factor Rae1 has been implicated to be a key player in the inhibition of host gene expression. Although nuclear transport has been indicated as the primary target in some studies, conflicting preliminary data from the PIs lab has shown that the transport of a few host mRNA involved in heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (RNP) may be selectively promoted and transcription and translation inhibited. This project proposes understanding VSV viral pathogenesis in two novel ways, one by a study of host RNA-binding proteins inhibiting mRNA transport by UV-crosslinking and RNP immunoprecipitation and second by identifying host RNA-binding proteins inhibiting translation. For the latter, transcripts of key host and viral proteins associated with the cytoplasmic mRNPs are going to be analyzed and RNA silencing of host RNA-binding proteins planned. The answers to both these questions will provide great details and insight into VSV antiviral response. It will compliment the study of the role of the viral M protein being done by the PI. The identification of key host and VSV proteins in promoting selective transcription, transport and translation to cripple further cell biological processes would be a step towards attenuated viruses and vaccine development.

imp_text: The application proposes to derive a more complete characterization of viral factors that inhibit INF Type 1 responses. The long-term goal is to improve our understanding of the role of INF antagonists in viral replication and pathogenesis and, therefore, guide future development efforts of small molecule therapeutics. An MHV model of acute hepatitis will be used. The ns2 protein of MHV blocs the 2-5A synthetase (OAS)-RNase L pathway in macrophages and facilitates the development of hepatitis. Ns2, rotavirus VP3, and mammalian AKAP7 proteins are phosphodiesterases (PDE) that decorate 2-5A, the activator of RNase L. The applicants hypothesize that the OAS-RNAse L pathway in macrophages is critical in protecting the host from developing viral hepatitis. The specific aims are 1. compare MHV replication and activation of OAS-RNase L in liver cells, generate mice with deletions of the RNase I gene and assess the development of hepatitis using WT and ns2-mutated MHV. 2. Study effects of ns2 and host PDEs on 2-5A levels, viral replication, apoptosis, and INF-g induction and identify small molecule inhibitors of PDEs by high throughput screening. 3. generate chimeric viruses expressing different viral and cellular PDE and determine their ability to antagonize RNAse L and induce hepatitis. MHV-infected mice will be treated with inhibitors of PDE to determine effects of controlling 2-5A levels on viral pathogenesis. The application is built upon an observation that the ns2 protien of MHV blocks the OAS-RNAse L pathway and contributes to the development of hepatitis. The majority of the studies are well-planned and appear to have a reasonable chance of reaching a successful or definitive conclusion. The work with MHV replication in liver cells and generating mice with RNAseI deletions increases the enthusiasm for the application. A study of the effects of MHV ns2 and host phosphodiesterases on 2-5A levels and viral pathogenesis using cultured cells also increases enthusiasm as does the generation of chimeric MHV to study the effects of various PDEs on RNase L and hepatitis.  However, the portion of Specific Aim 2 in which small molecule inhibitors of PDEs are identified by HTS detracts from the scientific aims of the project.

imp_text: The applicants propose to study the role of vOTU in inhibiting the innate host immune responses through de-ubiquintinating and deSGlylating. The work is well-designed and the proposal is clearly written. CCHFV is a tick-borne pathogen that can also be spread from human-to-human or in nosocomial settings. As the name implies, the virus is most commonly encountered in the Crimean peninsula, the Congo, sub-Saharan Africa, Southeast Europe and Asia. Estimates of fatality rates in some outbreaks have been in the 5-33% range and, recently in India and Sudan, up to 80%. Thus, the risks to the US population are to travelers to endemic areas and from travelers returning to the US. The virus has been detected in several regions, such as Afghanistan and Iraq where US civilian and military personnel are deployed. Enthusiasm is increased due to the idea that we should be increasing our understandings of potentially serious pathogens before they emerge to become a significant health problem in the US. Enthusiasm is increased further by the applicant’s thorough description of how sequence variations (with introduced mutations or chimeric viruses) will be studies in the context of three-dimensional structural data and enzymatic activity. This is a well-designed plan of work that will likely increase our understanding of how vOTUs help viruses circumvent innate immunity.
sig_text_str: . CCHFV and other Bunyaviruses cause diseases in humans and animals. CCHFV is particularly virulent with death rates ranging from 5-33% and up to 80% in some populations. . Like Ebola, Dengue, Zika, and other viruses, CCHFV has been perceived to be a low level threat to the US population it has not garnered a great deal of attention from the research community. . Because of recent experiences with Ebola and ZIKV, it seems reasonable to dedicate a portion of funding and effort to potentially serious pathogens prior to their emergence in the US population. . Work on vOTU of CCHFV may be applied to other viruses with similar proteases that allow viruses to circumvent the innate immune system.

The vOTU mechanism of virulence may not be the most important area to study for these viruses unless an inhibitor or degrading enzyme can be readily found. It may be more important to expend efforts on vaccines and treatments.

imp_text: Applicants theorize that VSV M protein inhibits cell macromolecule synthesis by interfering with transcription initiation thought an M-Rae1 complex and that M inhibition is separable from virus assembly functions. In Aim 1, they will test the hypothesis that M-Rae1 inhibits mRNA transport by studying the effects of silencing Rae1 expression. In Aim 2, they will study the role of relocalizing hnRNPs in coupling transcription, nuclear transport and translation. Although most virologists are interested to know the exact molecular mechanism by which viruses shut off host translation and interfere with the induction of innate immunity genes, the proposal is unclear on how this information can be used to combat or protect from virus infection, especially in the case of infection by “acute” viruses like VSV, flu, HRV, etc. Thus, enthusiasm is greatly diminished by the academic-like nature of the proposal and failure to spell out in any detail how this will help us improve human health. Scored Review Criteria Reviewers will consider each of the five review criteria below in the determination of scientific and technical merit, and provide a separate score and critique for each.

imp_text: Understanding of mechanisms of host response to viral infections, and interferon (IFN)-mediated regulation/control of viral infections are of great importance, and not only advances our knowledge on the biology of virus and host, but it is instrumental in terms of identification of novel promising antiviral targets and development of innovative antiviral interventions. The proposal is set to examine in detail the mechanism of regulation of IFN-inducible 2’,5’-oligoadenylate (2-5A) synthetase (OAS)-RNAse L-mediated host response  by viral proteins bearing 2',5'-phosphodiesterase (2',5'-PDE) activity.  The proposal is mostly focused on the use of mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) infection in mice as the main experimental system. Aim 1 of the proposal will determine whether OAS-RNAse L signaling pathway in Kupffer cells is the barrier that restricts MHV from entering the liver parenchyma, and thus prevents the induction of hepatitis. Aim 2 is set to evaluate the roles of viral ns2 protein and also other ns2 related viral and host proteins in regulation of OAS-RNAse L pathway, and also plans to identify small molecule inhibitors of viral 2',5'-PDEs (ns2 and VP3 proteins) by means of  high throughput screening. Aim 3 plans to further compare viral and cellular PDEs, and also to further dissect the mechanism that facilitates the protection of MHV from OAS-RNAse L antiviral activities by means of ns2-mediated PDE function. It also will further evaluate in the settings of MHV infection in vivo the potential of the PDE inhibitors indentified in AIm2 in terms of control of virus-induced pathogenesis. The topic of the proposal is of high interest in terms of revealing the mechanistic aspects of the virus-host balance in the context of activated OAS-RNAse L-mediated antiviral response. However, the relevance of the findings regarding virus-host interactions and regulation of the viral infection via OAS-RNAse L pathway that would be obtained in mouse model mostly using MHV to virus infections and related diseases in humans was not well established. In addition, a number of weaknesses have been identified throughout the Research Plan, and especially in Aims 2 and 3 of the proposal. Therefore, the enthusiasm for this proposal is low.

app_text_wkn: • It is not clear whether mouse KC or LSEC can produce IFN in vivo/in vitro. If they can, should the experimental design be modified? (It was mentioned in the application that hepatocytes wouldn't produce IFN beta in response to MHV infection). • Since MHV is able to infect several types of cells, the staining for hepatocyte-specific marker(s) would be very useful for cell type verification (applicant suggested to identify hepatocytes by their parenchymal location). • What if the protein levels of OAS will not change in agreement with the changes of the corresponding mRNA levels? What would be the applicant's model for this situation? Why the levels of RNAse L are expected to change (as a protein)? It seems that applicant suggested that the difference in the outcomes is facilitated by the presence/absence of activation of RNAse L by the levels of 2-5A? • Rationale of creating hepatocyte-specific RNAse L deficient mice is unclear, and is not supported by preliminary data, since no restriction was seen for ns2-H126R MHV (as compared to A59) in terms of infecting hepatocytes. • The experiment with the use of LysMCreRNAseL-/- mice is not explicitly explained in sufficient detail (time line, ablation of RNAse L etc...). • Aim 2 has several weaknesses. • It is not mentioned to what extent the strain A59 represents the properties of a natural wt MHV. • It is not evaluated whether infections induced by the viruses listed in Table 1 were previously linked to RNAse L-mediated antiviral host response. • Expression of suspected PEDs as flag-tagged proteins could be tricky. There are examples that flag versions of proteins do not adequately resemble natural counterparts (even loss of function may occur). No data provided by applicant assuring the functionality of tagged proteins. Thus, Aim 2 could fail. • Aim 2B. What is the evidence that shows that tagged proteins will have subcellular localizations identical to those of non-tagged counterparts? Besides, the only biologically relevant issue here is whether newly demonstrated PDEs exert their PDE activity in context of viral infection, and whether this activity is an important part of regulation of viral infection. In addition, the only biologically relevant subcellular localization is the one that the protein in question assumes during ongoing viral infection. • Aim 2C. Regardless of somewhat promising 4 hits and assays in place, there is no guarantee that Aim 2C will produce efficient inhibitors of viral PDEs. There is no convincing time/effort assessment, and no clear understanding of how many compounds will be actually tested within Aim 2C during a given time frame. Aim 2C could fail. It is a very high risk sub-Aim. Besides, the search for inhibitors is only relevant if newly found PDEs (not ns2) are critical for establishment of productive viral infection/suppression of host response. What is the rationale of searching for inhibitors of host PDEs? Assuming they are found, what would be the use of them? Application states that "HTS will continue until several effective inhibitors, in the nanomolar or low micromolar range when added to cells are identified" - this may not happen within the grant time period. HTS is a very difficult and risky business, and inhibitors that are efficient at low concentration are often not identified during the primary screening (which what the application proposed), and additional involvement of chemist to modify primary hit compounds usually is required, which is also doesn't have any guarantees that the further screening will be successful. If Aim 2C fails, Aim 3C becomes irrelevant. • What would happen if as the applicant suggested the (identified) inhibitor will be used against AKAP7 (assuming that AKAP7 is the major host regulator of OAS-RNAse L pathway): RNAse L will be activated and it may restrict viral infection, but would this also result in excessive tissue damage? This being the case, what would be the applicant suggestion on the regimen of the use of such AKAP7 inhibitor? • Aim 3 also has a number of concerns. • It is unclear why is the introduction of non-MHV PDEs into MHV genome and then assaying if they can replace ns2 function in regard to MHV infection is considered as a valuable approach? How biologically relevant is this strategy to the infections of the viruses from which those PDEs are actually derived? Even if this approach works, the testing of the above mentioned PDEs in the context of the authentic infections of the corresponding viruses still is the must step in order to get biologically relevant data. • What is the significance of finding that non-MHV PDE can functionally replace ns2? What if this non-MHV factor is well active PDE enzyme, but for some reason it cannot functionally replace ns2? What would the applicant's interpretation of such result? Such limitations of the approach are not addressed. • The observed co-localization of PDEs and RTC just would be not inconsistent with the applicant's hypothesis that certain proximity between the site of PDE activity and RTC is necessary in order to promote MHV infection, but it would not prove that there is a requirement for the two above mentioned events (PDE activity and viral replication/transcription) to occur in proximity. Only if no co-localization is observed, it could be concluded that such proximity is not necessary. Thus, based on the proposed approaches, no evidence that proves necessity of the proximity cannot be obtained in principle. • Contrary to applicant's assessment, the grant will not produce the evidence that VP3 is important for controlling rotavirus infection, since the infection experiments with rotavirus will not be conducted. . Future goals are irrelevant, since they would not be attempted in the grant's time frame.

imp_text: The central theme of the application is viral homologues of an ovarian tumor domain protease (vOTUs), especially vOTU of Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV), and their role in evasion of the innate immune response via subverting of IFN-dependent posttranslational ubiquitination and/or ISG15lyation. It is a very interesting topic, and if the proposed research strategy works, important data could be acquired, which would advance the understanding of the mechanisms of virus-mediated down-regulation of the innate immune response that is linked to determining the outcome of virus-induced disease. The obtained new information could be also useful in terms of developing of novel antiviral interventions, which would be of considerable interest, because there are no antivirals or vaccine currently available against such pathogens as CCHFV, and also related nairoviruses (that encode vOTUs), Dugbe virus, Hazara virus, Ganjam virus etc. Aim 1 of the proposal is set to define the relative contribution of nairovirus sequence diversity (including the diversity between the strains of the same virus) on deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities. Aim 2 plans to define relative contribution of nairovirus vOTUs deISGylase activity, deubiquitinase activity, and ISG15 specificity to subvert the innate immune response. Overall, it is an interesting proposal with a number of important experiments, which are expected to produce valuable data. However, the research plan has a number of problems/issues that are analyzed in detail in the criticism of the Approach section. In addition, a number of key details are omitted or not well explained, like, for example, the choice of the virus-producing cells for the CCHFV reverse genetics system. Regardless of the identified problems, there is an enthusiasm for this application.
sig_text_str: . Since (i) vOTUs have been found in all known nairoviruses (family that includes significant human pathogens), and also in other viral families, and (ii) that vOTUs were implicated in the mechanism of virus evasion of IFN-mediated host innate response, the investigation of the role of vOTU's involvement in down-regulation of the host response has considerable significance for understanding of pathogen-regulated immune evasion, and identification of promising targets for novel antivirals, as well as understanding the biology of a number of important virus families (including the aspects of virus-host interactions). . Also interesting is the opportunity to evaluate the species specificity of vOTUs, and test the hypothesis that this specificity is linked to variability of ISG15 in different species. . Application also has a potential to identify a correlation between a particular affinity of a vOTU for Ub, poly-Ub, or ISG15 and severity of disease outcome.

app_text_str: . Applicant's lab has a number of relevant assays/techniques already established. . The bulk of preliminary data supports the proposed course of experiments. . Another plus is the use of the assays like FRET Di-Ub that allow quantitative analysis/comparison of catalytic activity/specificity for poly-Ub substrates. . Important results delineating the mechanisms of actions of vOTUs in terms of cleavage of Ub-modified or ISG15-modified cellular protein substrates are expected to be generated. These results are expected to considerably advance our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of evasion of the innate immune response by OTU-bearing viruses, and at the same time it is anticipated that the data will aid the understanding of the link between the vOTUs properties and the outcome of virus-induced disease. . It will be evaluated how the sequence diversity between different viral OTUs affects their specificity towards the proteins that were modified with Ub or with ISG15. Application will determine whether vOTU of CCHFV (as compared to other vOTUs) represents the only vOTU that possess both kinds of activities, towards ubiquitin and ISG15 substrates, or other vOTU possess dual substrate specificity as well. It will be determined whether the differences between vOTUs are catalytic- or affinity-based. . Reverse genetics system to produce recombinant infectious CCHFV is a considerable plus.
app_text_wkn: . Preliminary data relevant to the proposed research plan needs to be presented as a separate section of the application. . It is not Ub-like IFN-simulated gene 15 (as applicant wrote), but it is UB-like IFN-stimulated gene 15 (ISG15). . What if the suppression of the immune response via activity of vOTU is not the only critical strategy that CCHFV and/or other viruses (expressing vOTUs) use to subvert IFN-mediated immune functions? What is the alternative hypothesis? . It is unclear what information/data supports the suggestion that vOTUs should have the potential to cleave poly-Ub species from almost any type of cellular proteins? What is the applicant's hypothesis of what kinds of cellular proteins can represent the substrates relevant to anti-immune response function of vOTU, and whether there is in vivo certain specificity of vOTU towards particular cellular proteins? It is very important to determine what kind of proteins (conjugated with Ub or UB-like ISG15) are real in vivo substrates of viral OTUs. This knowledge is essential for understanding of the mechanism of virus evasion of host innate immune response. . How exactly the proposal will facilitate development of novel antivirals targeting vOTUs? . What is the significance/importance of studying CCHFV with OTU optimized for mouse ISG15 and examining if it can subvert ISGylation in order to cause disease in mice? The development of small animal model has merits, but the biological relevance to CCHFV infection in humans, as well as limitations of the mouse model should be clearly determined. . Suggestion of developing live attenuated vaccines based on nairoviruses could be a stretch. Feasibility of such vaccine even in case of the success of the grant still will be very much unclear. . Applicant's statement "Additionally, if vOTUs substrate specificity is conserved, therapeutics selectively modulating the affected host pathways could be developed" sounds overly optimistic. The modulation of relevant host pathways could be just not feasible. . Evaluation of the specificity phenotypes of different vOTUs towards Ub/ISG15 substrates is somewhat hampered by the absence of hypothesis of what amino acid residues can actually form the catalytic site and what other amino acid residues can influence the catalytic activity and possibly substrate specificity of vOTUs (could be via long-distance interactions). The research plan should be more sophisticated than just testing the correlations of certain polymorphisms to the results of functional assays. It might be helpful (after initial comparisons of natural viral enzymes are completed) to choose one or two enzymes and begin to introduce single amino acid substitutions analyzing the polymorphisms/residues that differ, and evaluate the impact of each residue separately. This could be more insightful for the understanding of the mechanisms defining the catalytic activity/specificity. These experiments should progress in direction of developing the model of how vOTUs act and differentiate the substrates. Applicant suggested to focus more on the residues that according to the structural data are located in vOTU-Ub interface, but the role/influence of other residues without additional experiments cannot be ruled out. . It is likely that the structures will suggest rather than identify the residues mediating/regulating the enzymatic activity of vOTUs (in Aim 1). The applicant should propose additional evaluation of the structural data in terms of its biological relevance to actual enzymatic activity (i.e., whether the anticipated structures will reflect catalytically active conformation of the enzyme molecule, proximity to substrate etc.). Mutagenesis of the residues likely involved in the catalysis and subsequent functional tests of mutated vOTUs will be the key to further evaluate/test the predictions made by the structure(s). In application, mutagenesis is only proposed for CCHF vOTU. . The result that CCHF vOTU cleavage of K63 and K48 Di-Ub was faster than the cleavage of Ub-AMC may be interpreted not only as additional direct interactions mediated by residues not located in the proximal UIM, but also as regulation by remote residues that might regulate the measured outcome directly or indirectly, and even not via interaction with the substrate. There could exist a functional network of amino acids that are not located in proximity to each other. . It is not clear if (i) most of vOTUs would appear to have dual substrate specificity (for UB-modified and ISG15-modified proteins), and (ii) as stated only ISG15 exerts considerable degree of variability, then what would be the model that will link together the genetic diversity between vOTUs, dual substrate specificity, differences in catalytic and affinity parameters and connection between vOTU activity and outcome of virus-induced disease? . From c2, it is unclear how the mechanism of Poly-Ub specificity of CCHF vOTU will be revealed, while this section is full of technical details. Structural studies would likely not predict all the residues involved in regulation of a particular enzymatic reaction, assuming that the residues outside of actual catalytic site could be involved. Mutagenesis and functional tests would be still necessary to refine the predictions of structural studies. . The potential challenges of proposed approaches are not well evaluated. . The choice of the virus-producing cells for the reverse genetics system was not explained. . Results with the mutant C40A may have an alternative interpretation, as they may suggest that the mutant is defective in virus assembly, etc. Additional experiments are needed in order to reveal whether and why vOTU activity seem to be needed for the assembly and release of infectious CCHFV virions (it looks that double mutant P77D/I13R had very little of OTU activity). The working reverse genetics system could be instrumental in addressing these concerns. In addition, since recombinant infectious CCHFV was produced in IFN-deficient BSRT7 cells, it seems to be somewhat puzzling that C40A mutant virus with inactivated vOTU (activity of which is related to suppression of IFN-mediated immune response) cannot be produced in BSRT7 cells. This may suggest that other than IFN-mediated host response(s) could be involved in regulation of CCHFV infection. . study_section: Virology A Study Section
imp_text: This application is focused on the structure-functional aspects of functioning of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), which is a key type of enzyme for positive strand RNA viruses, and thus can be considered as a valid target for antiviral interventions. The application will use RdRp of poliovirus as experimental subject, and will apply solution state NMR to understand different conformational states of RdRp and transitions between them in order to dissect the mechanism of functioning of the network of amino acid residues involved in the regulation of the catalysis of RNA-directed RNA synthesis. This includes the residues that are located away from the catalytic site, but can exert critical regulatory effect on the fidelity, for example. Preliminary data support the existence of the above mentioned network of amino acids. The approach is expected to be more informative than classic structural studies. Aim1 will be focused on elucidation of the conformational states and their structural transitions required for the RdRp reaction. Aim 2 will address the mechanistic basis for the RdRp derivatives that demonstrate altered fidelity, and Aim 3 will use anti-HCV non-obligatory terminators on the RdRp of poilo in order to address their mechanism of RNA chain termination. Application suffers from a number of problems, which are evaluated in detail in critical analysis of the approach. It remains unclear how the data obtained using RdRp of polio will facilitate the development of novel antivirals against other (than poilo) positive strand RNA viruses, considering that the mechanism of RNA-directed RNA synthesis catalyzed by other RNA polymerases will differ enough from that of poilo, which likely will preclude easy translation of finding made using PV RdRp to RdRp of other viruses. Contrary to the applicant's belief, it is unlikely that application will be able to significantly boost the development of live attenuated vaccines against (other than polio) RNA viruses. It is also noted that other two major weaknesses of the application are insufficient applicant's experience in virology and lack of the involvement of established positive strand RNA virologist. The broad impact of the application is expected to be low, and therefore the enthusiasm for this application is low as well.

Given that certain degree of commonality is expected for the mechanism of RNA-directed RNA synthesis performed by RdRps of different viruses, the results anticipated may be important for improvement of understanding of replication mechanisms of different RNA viruses.
sig_text_wkn: • Significance of the proposal is somewhat overstated. Proposal itself would not produce new antivirals. Understanding of conformational states (assuming applicant would be able to resolve all of them as it was stated in the grant) doesn't guarantee that based on the generated data new drugs will be produced, and development of attenuated live vaccines will be greatly facilitated. The proposal suffers from overstated generalization of the impact of the anticipated results. Even Sabin vaccine is associated with a risk of vaccine-associated poliomyelitis in recipients or close contacts, and this vaccine is considered unsafe in immunodeficient patients. It is unlikely that attenuated live vaccines that supposed to be based on the applicant's results will become universal antiviral strategy against positive-strand RNA viruses. • Suggestion that proposal will facilitate development of live attenuated vaccine strains sounds a bit naive and lacks sophistication, since it is unknown whether the predicted mutation(s) in RdRp will result in viable virus that would be able to induce needed immunity, and at the same time would not be able to mutate to highly pathogenic variant. • Besides, the existent polio vaccine is very successful. In addition, whether the results of the current application will produce any useful information in terms of the understanding how RdRps of other RNA viruses (other than polio) work is unclear. Thus, the choice of RdRp of polio as the subject could be not the best choice, and significance of the anticipated results appears to be somewhat questionable. • The applicant's enthusiasm for development of broad spectrum of antiviral therapies that would be based on his NMR data is premature. There is no assurance that this proposal will generate the data sufficient to predict desired mutants, and it is very likely that the results would not be applicable to other viral RNA polymerases (other than RdRp of poilo), because regardless of the same chemistry of RNA synthesis reaction the RdRps of other viruses will perform the overall catalysis by non-identical mechanisms, which would likely become the major obstacle for applying the data gained for polio RdRp to other viral RdRps. Thus, the applicant's statement "the general principles developed in this proposal can be extended to other viral RdRps and likely beyond to other template-directed nucleic acid polymerases considering the conservation of the overall structural topology, catalytic and kinetic mechanisms among the superfamily of DNA/RNA polymerases" looks overly optimistic.

Although the active site catalytic residues could be conserved, the remote regulator(s) may be not conserved. • Applicant states that he has preliminary data demonstrating that modified nucleoside analogs being tested against HCV can have broad spectrum possibilities to be used against other viral RdRps. • The approach (solution-state NMR) that is proposed to be used in the application apparently would be able to reveal a long range network of the amino acid residues' interactions that is critical for RNA template/nucleotide binding and mechanism of catalysis. The approach should be able to achieve overall better understanding of the sequence of the functional events that take place during the RNA-directed synthesis of new RNA chain, as compared to traditional crystal structure studies. It is expected that the approach will reveal key interactions important for fidelity and thus can be instrumental for prediction of new antiviral targets and may be helpful in structure-functional search for inhibitors of viral RNA genome replication. • Important preliminary work of the applicant (using NMR approach) supports the existence of the network of long distance interactions between amino acid residues that are instrumental for the RdRp catalysis (this includes amino acids located away from the active site).
app_text_wkn: • Application doesn't have a significant virology-related component. • Applicant needs to arrange a collaboration with well-established positive strand RNA virus virologist. • From description of the specific Aims, it is very hard to understand what approaches will be used, how they will work exactly, what would be found. The notion of the network of residues is not sufficient for understanding the strategies of the specific Aims. Therefore, no convincing argument was provided that structural studies proposed will deliver novel information that will predict desired mutants with altered fidelity. • Using inhibitors of HCV RdRp on polio RdRp to elucidate the structural aspects of inhibition mechanism may result in loss of key interactions that only will be present when HCV polymerase is inhibited. We will not learn much about HCV RdRp and its inhibition. Aim 3 will only attempt to dig deeper in terms of mechanistic details, but it is unclear if this Aim will produce anything that can be used for antiviral interventions against other (than polio) RNA viruses, which replication needs to be suppressed. Therefore, low broad impact is anticipated for Aim 3. • Many figures in the application (for example, Figs. A2 and A4) need much extended/detailed figure legends. • The text of the research plan of the application appears repetitious. • The results of the proposal may advance the mechanistic understanding of the functioning of poliovirus RdRp, but their use in terms of virology will be very limited. The understanding of interplay of the amino acid residues within the network of the residues that applicant plans to reveal as important to performing the RNA-directed RNA synthesis will be relevant PV RdRp, but it remains questionable that the newly generated data will facilitate profound understanding on the aspects of functioning of critical amino acids of RdRps of other RNA viruses, regardless of the certain similarities within the motifs of catalytic domains of different RdRps. This could be especially problematic for the residues positioned far away from the catalytic site. The long-distance interactions within the network of the important residues may include amino acids that are not conserved among positive strand RNA viruses, and the mechanism of the influence of the remote residue(s) on the fidelity and overall catalysis could be not conserved among different RNA viruses as well. • In preliminary data, the complexes of RdRp with symmetrical 10-mer template/primer duplexes were used. It is unclear what is the biological relevance of the results using this system to real RNA-directed RNA synthesis. During the RNA synthesis, RdRp usually "sits" on about 18-mer duplex region of the non-symmetrical template/primer complex, to which it supposed to have much higher affinity than the affinity to 10-mer. This supposed to be considered as a factor impacting processivity and fidelity, and may actually result in different RdRp molecule structure/functioning (as compared to complex with symmetrical 10-mer). • It is unclear how exactly the molecular modeling will be done based on the newly generated NMR data. • There is insufficient evaluation of the limitations of the applicant's experimental approach that will impact the applicant's ability to achieve molecular modeling that is expected to reflect biologically relevant aspects of the mechanism of RNA-directed RNA synthesis performed by PV RdRp. • It is unclear what would be the novel end-products of the application that would make a considerable impact (theoretical and practical) on the field of positive strand RNA viruses that encode their own RdRps, especially on understanding the mechanism of RNA-directed RNA synthesis (which these enzymes perform) with the goal of devising novel antiviral interventions (that would be based on the results generated by this application). In other words it is unclear how the anticipated data will significantly facilitate development of "vaccine design strategies and/or the development of novel broad spectrum antiviral drugs" for the viruses other than poliovirus. • The development of live attenuated vaccines (this is what applicant suggested) still could not feasible for many positive strand RNA viruses (even if the mutations that would attenuate these viruses' RdRps will be predicted and confirmed) for reasons that are not related to the mechanism of RdRp functioning. This and other comments suggest that overall impact and significance of the application are somewhat overstated by the applicant. • It is not clear what small molecules/viral RdRp inhibitors will be designed based on the data produced by the application, how exactly this will be accomplished, and what RNA viruses (other than polio) will be thus affected. • Throughout the application, the applicant states several times that no difficulties are expected with a particular approach/experiment/study. Those statements sound as overly optimistic. • Potential problems and pitfalls are not well evaluated. • The description of the experiments often is insufficient in order to picture what exactly will be done, how it will be done, what outcomes/results are expected, what are the limitations of the approach and how exactly the data will be evaluated, and what conclusion(s) will be made based on the obtained result. • It is unclear how exactly the applicant will use biologically-relevant assays on the level of virus infection that would be able to evaluate the validity of the conclusions and predictions produced by NMR experiments. • It is unclear how exactly the extensive evaluation of well known functional mutations (this is proposed in the application) will produce the sophisticated understanding of how RdRp functions and will predict the mutants that can be potentially used for live vaccines against the viruses other than polio. The applicant's statements that "...prediction of fidelity altering mutations in other viral RdRps that may similarly (assuming that similarity goes to PV RdRp) act as a basis of vaccine design for these RNA viruses", "Understanding the effects of the Sabin mutations may uncover a universal mechanism of viral attenuation (i.e. through changing RdRp fidelity)", "A mechanistic understanding of how changes in this strain (Sabin strain of polio) lead to viral attenuation could guide vaccine development for other RNA viruses" and "the results from PV RdRp can be translated to other viral RdRps, considering that similar networks are likely to exist in other polymerases" sound somewhat naive and overly optimistic. No experimental data was provided by the applicant that supported the feasibility of the above mentioned translation of PV RdRp results to RdRps of other viruses. • A number of stated predictions/expectations throughout the application are rather vague and lack specificity. . The description of experiments that will use "cell-based assays", which supposed to be key experiments validating all the data produced by NMR effort is not explicit, incomplete and considerably insufficient.

imp_text: This R01 application is from an outstanding and highly productive established investigator from the University of Pennsylvania.  The major goal of the proposed research is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of how the MHV accessory protein NS2 blocks the actions of 2’,5’-oligadenylate synthetase-ribonuclease L in macrophages.  Mice with cell-type specific deletions of the RNase L gene will be used to assess the development of hepatitis following infection with either wild-type MHV or MHV lacking NS2.  Additional experiments will use a panel of MHV viruses to determine the roles of NS2 and host 2’,5’-phosphodiesterases in antiviral immunity.  Strengths of the application include the excellent and productive PI, strong preliminary data establishing the feasibility of the outlined experimental approach, and the likelihood that the proposed studies will reveal novel information regarding the role of the NS2 protein from MHV in inhibiting the host type I IFN response.  Overall, there is very high enthusiasm for this proposal.

imp_text: This is a new R01 application by a new assistant professor with extensive experience in studying enzyme function and regulation using NMR.  The proposal outlines a series of studies to use NMR to identify all of the conformational states and the transitions between the for the prototypical viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase derived from poliovirus.  The initial studies will use solution-state NMR to monitor and identify the conformational rearrangements in the prototypic viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase derived from poliovirus.  Structural comparisons will be made during correct versus incorrect nucleotide incorporation.  Additional experiments are outlined that will examine the impact of fidelity altering mutations on the structure of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase during the nucleotide additional cycle.  Finally, the proposal will examine the structural states that occur during incorporation of non-obligate chain terminators by the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.  Overall, this is a well written proposal from a new investigator.  Strengths of the application include the important questions being posed that address a current knowledge gap, the novel approach, and the well-crafted scientific approach that is likely to yield novel biological insight into the structure of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases.  There is high enthusiasm for the proposed studies.
