imp_text: This is a new application from an established investigator with an extensive track record in studying the role of VSV-derived proteins in facilitating virus replication.  The preliminary data provided call into question the current notion that the VSV M protein blocks nuclear-cytoplasmic transport by binding to the host RNA-binding protein Rae1 and that subsequent inhibition of host transcription and translation are the result of the inhibition of nuclear-cytoplasmic transport by the M protein.  However, silencing of Rae1 expression in VSV-infected cells inhibits host transcription, calling into question the extent to which the M protein directly inhibits nuclear-cytoplasmic transport.  A straightforward set of experiments are outlined to identify the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of mRNA transport by VSV.  Additional experiments will examine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of translation in VSV infected cells.  Strengths of the application include the strong investigator team, the well written and hypothesis driven proposal and the potential for the results to alter the current paradigm of how the VSV M protein inhibits host cell transcription and translation.  A major weakness of the studies is the incremental nature of the proposed work.

imp_text: This application is aimed at determining the contribution of nairovirus vOTU specificity and activity to immunological suppression and disease outcome. It will also identify the distinct structural features of nairovirus vOTUs and mammalian ISG15s that contribute to the potential differences in the activity and specificity of these proteases. The application contains two interrelated, yet independent aims. This application pools are team of PIs that are highly competent and qualified to perform the diverse studies proposed in the application. Aim 1 of the application proposes to ascertain the effects of nairovirus sequence diversity on their deubiquitinating and delSGylating activities. Aim 2 of the proposal seeks to define the relative contribution of nairovirus vOTU activities to subvert the innate immune response. These studies are well planned and are likely to increase our understanding of nairovirus OTUs as virulence factors. This understanding may also be applicable for other viral families.

imp_text: This application is aimed at establishing the structure-dynamics-function relationships of the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. This is a highly innovative and significant proposal as understanding dynamic contributions to viral protein functions is an understudied area. Dr. Walsh is a new investigator with a significant track record in dissecting dynamic contributions to enzymatic function. In this application, the investigator will use NMR to “watch” the RdRp reaction to elucidate the conformational states governing each step of the nucleotide-addition cycle to discover the mechanistic basis for RdRp activity. The completion of the proposed research will inform future efforts of developing novel antivirals that target the viral RdRp.

imp_text: This application is aimed at determining the mechanism by which VSV suppresses host antiviral responses through global inhibition of host gene expression. Mutant viruses that are deficient in their ability to inhibit host gene expression are dramatically attenuated in their pathogenicity. This attenuation demonstrates the critical role that inhibition of host gene expression plays in the virus’ ability to cause disease. The proposal consists of two interrelated but independent aims. This application lists two PIs as key personnel whose expertise is well suited to these studies and greatly strengthens this proposal.  Overall, this proposal seeks to answer and intriguing question regarding host gene expression during viral infection. The completion of this study will increase our understanding of a critical aspect of the viral life cycle.
sig_text_str: . Understanding control of host gene expression and its impact on viral pathogenesis is critical for establishing how viruses circumvent the innate immune response . Despite being an extremely well-studied virus, this proposal successfully argues that the mechanism by which VSV inhibits host protein synthesis may not be as well understood as currently thought . A thorough understanding of how viruses “deal” with host protein synthesis may have wide ranging impact beyond VSV. . A thorough understand of the mechanism by which viruses shut down host protein synthesis offers an opportunity to develop novel antivirals that target these processes.

imp_text: Overall, the goals of this proposal are to refine the possible mechanisms and kinetics underlying protein aggregation (using Amyloid-beta as a model) using theoretical and computational approaches. Understanding the molecular and regulatory events involved in protein aggregation is extremely important, as a number of diseases (for example) involve some sort of protein aggregation problem. The approaches proposed should provide a roadmap on what is theoretically occurring at the molecular level to regulate peptide aggregation, potentially opening up novel approaches to manipulating aggregation. The group seems well suited to this approach, particularly the first aim, and have employed some of these theoretical approaches to understand how pH may affect aggregation. The first aim seeks to define the roadmap, and identify key rate-limiting areas. The second aim utilizes this information to formulate new simulation protocols to study how peptide chemistry at individual molecules may affect aggregation, a simulation that has not been feasible. The overall approach seems to be a worthwhile endeavor, but there are some issues/problems that temper my belief that the approach proposed is (in contrast to previous work) indeed feasible.
sig_text_str: . Seeks to provide a clearer, more applicable model for protein aggregation that occurs in many diseases that accounts for the long-time scale in which these protein aggregates, which is arguably a large weakness in most protein aggregation studies. . Seeks to find the missing “middle ground” between high-resolution and long time-scale modeling studies. . The logic underlying this modeling approach may have broad applications beyond amyloidogenic molecules.
sig_text_wkn: . Many of the assumptions required for this kind of approach come from other foundational theoretical approaches/models, which ultimately start at a biological observation. These models are continually evolving. How will the models developed as described evolve to incorporate changed assumptions?
inv_text_str: . The PI is a new investigator, and the project seems a natural extension of his previous work. Where he may lack in expertise, he has aligned expert collaborators to assist.
inv_text_wkn: . Success of Aim 2 depends largely on recruiting a suitable post-doc candidate with expertise in modeling molecular dynamics. Having Dr. Cong as a collaborator helps mitigate some concerns about expertise, but someone qualified still has to do the work.
inn_text_str: . The PI proposes a clever approach to trying to solve resolution vs. time problem in trying to understand protein aggregation by uncovering potential key rate-limiting step using a modeling approach (and experimentally vetted), and then incorporating these time components into new simulations of aggregation high-resolution molecular processes that form over very long durations.
inn_text_wkn: . None.
app_text_str: . The overall approach to extend and refine existing models to include additional biologically relevant variables is very logical. . Some of the model refinements/predictions will be tested in a wet-lab setting. . The contrast of AB40 and AB42 (although not emphasized) should provide some basis for assessing how well their models/simulations fit biological observations.

imp_text: This proposal is to support continuance and improvements the BMRB (Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank), a site for curation of both tools and NMR structures that are produced by labs world-wide. Tools like this, akin to PubMed or NCBI, are absolutely essential resources to the biological community. With centralized standards for analysis, and a repository of all data, much larger systems-type questions become much more feasible to approach as computer technologies improve. Moreover, without a centralized and standardized repository for data such as these, individual collections of NMR structures, and the ability to integrate that info with other types of data either simply fade with time, or become impossible. This group has assembled and presided over this service for the past 15+ years, and continue to do an outstanding job. My only reservation is that this service should be supported by NLM or similar sources, more stable than the typical R01 mechanism.

study_section: Biochemistry and Biophysics of Membranes Study Section
imp_text: The primary goal of this proposal is to define and characterize the structure and mechanisms of ligand specificity, of nucleoside transporter proteins. These proteins are involved throughout biology, and are the targets of many drugs and chemotherapeutics; thus identifying the structures of these membrane proteins will undoubtedly aid in drug development. To date, no structures for this family of proteins have been elucidated. The bulk of the proposal revolves around using a CNT from vibrio cholerae (vcCNT) as a model, in large part because of some early success generating crystals (and low-resolution structures) with this protein. The rationale of using vcCNT instead of human CNT could be much more developed. While Aims 2 and 3 do not depend on success in obtaining high-resolution structural information (Aim 1), their impact on biology seems drastically limited (and perhaps in aimed in the wrong direction) because they essentially study the functions of vcCNT instead of focusing on a similar studies using a mammalian counterpart. If Aim1 is successful, though, and this protein has shared key features shared with hCNT (to be tested), then these studies could be a game-changer for nucleoside-transporter targeted therapeutics. If Aim1 is in fact possible, the PI has the experience and training, and is very well positioned to do it.
sig_text_str: • The lack of structural information on nucleoside transporters (NTs) is a significant barrier to rational drug design for ligands/molecules that use these transporters – and there are already several therapeutics that utilize NTs. • The mechanistic details derived from these successful studies should provide the backbone and/or starting point for understanding NT function at an atomic level. • Advances in both areas have the potential to drastically alter how NTs are targeted therapeutically.
sig_text_wkn: • The studies focus on a NT from v. cholerae, an NT with significant, but limited, homology to human NTs. The differences in cellular membranes between (vcCNT) gram-negatives and (hCNT) mammals may (or may not) cause substantial differences in how these proteins function at the molecular level. • While Aim 2 is not fully dependent on success in Aim 1, it’s not clear what is really gained from Aim 2 in the event that Aim 1 does fail. The same applies to most of Aim 3. Success of Aim 1 is critical for the impact of other studies. •
inv_text_str: . The PI is well positioned, and has the relevant expertise, to guide and carry-out these studies to their most successful endpoints. . The PI has had a very productive career as a postdoc, should carry-over in their own lab.
inn_text_str: . The major innovation would be if the investigators can obtain a crystal structure of vcCNT at sufficient detail to resolve bio-molecular events. This would be the first NT ever described at the structural level. Some preliminary data suggesting this goal may be possible.
inn_text_wkn: . There doesn’t seem to be any new approach taken here except using vcCNT as a model for human CNT, and even that may be limited in what it can tell us about mammalian CNTs. . In point 2, aside from the X-ray crystallography, what is innovative? All the other experiments can be done by expressing CNTs in oocytes. All these studies can be performed with other CNTs, if they haven’t’ already.
app_text_str: . Seemingly exhaustive approach to optimize crystallization/obtaining structural details in Aim 1. Aims 2 and 3 are natural extensions – comparing vcCNT to hCNT to validate vcCNT as viable “prototype” model for hCNTs.

The PI cites that vcCNT has “significant sequence homology” (40% identity) with hCNT, but more details on this homology are needed to provide a compelling case that solving the structure of vcCNT will provide useful mechanistic insights into human CNT. Studies in Aim 2 start to approach this, but determining that vcCNT does transports nucleosides (to be determined in Aim2) is a prerequisite to the efforts to crystallize this protein (Aim 1). imp_text: The proposed research will investigate the molecular mechanisms that mediate the role of the CLOCK:BMAL1 heterodimer in mammalian circadian clocks.  The research would combine approaches using NMR, biochemistry, and cell-based studies to determine if and how domain flexibility may mediate activation and repression of clock controlled genes.  The research team will specifically study the C-TAD of BMAL1 and portion of the CLOCK protein coded by exon 19.  These regions have previously been shown to be important for activation and repression of these transcription factors but the exact mechanisms for how these functions change remain less studied.  The author suggest that atomic resolution for these transcription factors will provide  “much-needed” information to advance the understanding of circadian clock function, thus connecting to health.  The authors could do a more convincing job here as the argument seems a bit removed. What evidence is there that polymorphisms in these regions confer effects on the circadian clock?  While a reductionist approach to determine detailed molecular mechanisms is academically interesting, the relevance for any translational insight is limited.

imp_text: This is a sound proposal that seeks to elucidate the structure and function of concentrative nucleoside transporters. While the PI does state that the mechanism of transport by NTs are unclear, the aim of this proposal is to understand the structure and function of the Vibrio Cholera CNTs which may serve as a model for human CNTs. This works on the fundamental assumption that the transport mechanisms are conserved between vcCNTs and hCNTs. The proposal is ambitious and hinges on this crucial hypothesis. However, such an assumption may only be partially true and hence poses a high risk for the success of this proposal. imp_text: This research proposal addresses a theoretical investigation based on computational modeling of amyloid aggregation. While the proposal is of interest, it is unclear how this theoretical and computational based modeling would help further our understanding of the disease progression in Alzheimer’s disease which is characterized by development of amyloid aggregations. The PI proposes that this will allow rational manipulation of aggregation pathways – but provides no proof of concept. Thus, these theoretical models will be just that - “models” and will be unlikely to have any significant impact in Alzheimer’s disease etiology, progression or cure. Had the proposal suggested a theoretical model with structure-activity simulations that could mimic real-time progression of the amyloid aggregates with supportive in vitro studies, this would have been a significant advancement of our knowledge on disease progression and perhaps causation. Of major concern is that the PI has does not have sufficient experience with molecular dynamics components of this project and is relying on a post-doc who is yet to be hired and who will have sufficient experience to take on this task. Despite an innovative approach, lack of preliminary data, despite a previous publication along the lines mentioned in the proposal, and lack of proof of concept dampens enthusiasm for this proposal.

imp_text: The Jamal Jackson group recently solved the crystal structure of the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex to a resolution of 2.28 angstroms, and is proposing to build on this information by performing nmr studies to discern how downstream regions (not shown by the crystal structure) function by controlling the binding to transcriptional coactivators and repressors.  Organization of the grant objective, which is to determine how the C-terminal transactivation domains (C-TADS) regulate CLOCK:BMAL1 activity, include a central hypothesis (C-TADS use intrinsic flexibility to regulate) and a working hypothesis (cis and trans conformers of a X-proline imide bond regulates activator/repressor binding, as a switch; another working hypothesis). This application has only two specific aims: however, Aim 1, which will determine how the switch works to regulate CLOCK:BMAL1 activity, has four discrete subaims; and Aim 2, which will determine how competition for CLOCK Exon 19 binding regulates CLOCK:BMAL1 activity, has three distinct subaims. Importantly, subaim C deals with the determination of how PASD1, which is expressed in human cancer cells and bears sequence similarity with Exon 19, regulates or affects CLOCK:BMAL1 function.  Another working hypothesis associated with Aim 2 is that CLOCK:BMAL1 activator histone methyltransferase MLL1, and CLOCK:BMAL repressor CIPC (Clock-interacting protein, Circadian) are competing for Exon 19 binding. PASD1 is a molecular mimic of Exon 19, and thus is poised as another player in the competitive binding milleau. Support for the objective by the central and working hypotheses is an impressive method of organizing the flow and workplan for this proposal.  Also, integration of the Exon 19 mimic PASD1, which is expressed in human cancers, provides an important connection to human health in this study, which is designed to perform basic research to determine how the heterodimeric CLOCK:BMAL1 complex, in conjunction with appropriate activators and repressors, controls Circadian rhythm. Understanding the important relationship between circadian rhythm and human disease/disorders will likely uncover relationships in addition to cancer and jet lag.

imp_text: This proposal is based on the assumption that protein aggregation is the critical clinical event in diseases such as AD, Huntington’s Disease and prion diseases. The underlying kinetic processes under physiological conditions for the development of these disease states are not understood, and theoretical models that related in vitro experiments that might mimic aggregation under physiological conditions are not developed. Key to the needs of proposed work in this area are that (1) analytic models have lacked the resolution to capture the sensitivity of aggregation processes (taking into account solution conditions and primary sequence); and (2) in silico models do not reach the timescales of in vitro or in vivo aggregation. Aim 1 will develop statistical models of aggregation kinetics.  Objectives are not stated, but many questions are asked, as though much basic information needs to be gathered. The stated result of this aim is that a “kinetic phase diagram” will be produced, that shows how solution conditions can lead to different aggregation pathways and end products. A significant assumption is that these predictions will be testable with measurements made of fibrillization kinetics in a model system of short peptides that will be prepared using peptide synthesizers.  Aim 2 will develop  accelerated computational techniques for protein aggregation.  The rate limiting step in aggregate growth is stated to be the conformational search over H-bonding states, which will be mapped to a one-dimensional “random walk”.  This process is a shortcut to simulate events in a short timeframethat normally occur over a much longer time. Also involved in these calculations will be all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, which will require significant computational resources.The algorithm will seek to distinguish between the kinetic partitioning between fibril pathways and non-fibril pathways.  The non-fibril pathway leads (partially) to the amyloid aggregates. Tasks in this proposal are accompanied by questions, which relate to information that will lead to design of next steps.  For instance, fibril nucleation is an important precursor event in the formation of aggregates.  It is not understood why nucleation occurs, or the mechanism by which it occurs, even though there exist two theories for how it occurs: (1) lateral association of molecules; and (2) intra-molecular extension of beta-structure. Nucleation is termed as “the event with the greatest importance in protein aggregation.)  Thus, there is a lot of basic information to be gathered.  Assumptions are a major part of this proposal.  Models of the chemistry of this disease are also a major part of this proposal. Theories will be used and new theories will be developed. A big investment in computational work and solid-phase synthesis of model peptides will be made.  Complex mathematical equations relating to (1) fibril formation kinetics; (2) probability; and (3) the nucleation rate will be used to develop statistical models. Expected outcomes are stated. Potential problems and alternate strategy sections are included for both aims.  An additional/alternate plan is stated for gathering more data describing oligomer formation rates and stabilities in Aim 1. For Aim 2, rationalization is provided and no alternate plan or strategy is provided. Molecular Dynamics is probably a major component of this proposal, and it probably represents an approach to validation of the theory that oligomers can nucleate using the fibril end as a template. Although this proposal deals specifically with trying to understand the progression of protein aggregation and how this promotes the initiation of Alzheimer’s Disease, there are many assumptions made that may or may not be useful in guiding the studies that are outlined, eg, to produce fundamental knowledge about the molecular basis of the aggregation diseases.

imp_text: This proposal is written to garner support for the Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB), which is the archive for NMR spectroscopic data that derives from biological systems. Funding is being requested by the BMRB through this R01 NIH grant proposal because funding from the National Library of Medicine (NLM) is being discontinued. Funding from the NLM seemed to be appropriate, since the “NLM maintains and makes available a vast print collection and produces electronic information resources on a wide range of topics that are searched billions of times each year by millions of people around the globe.” Also, the NLM “has been a center of information innovation since its founding in 1836.” The stated goal of this proposal is to “sustain BMRB as a powerful resource for the biological NMR and structural biology communities.” There are two stated aims in this proposal, that follow from the stated goal, which are to (1) advance the content, quality and distribution of the BMRB archive; and to (2) actively contribute to the development of the Worldwide Protein Data Bank (wwPDB). Subaims for both of the major aims are focused on validation, quality control and the generation of added content that enriches archive value. The three major functions of the BMRB are (1) content acquisition; (2) validation and annotation; and (3) delivery.  The data model that has been created for these functions is NMR-STAR. The significance and innovation of this proposal are impressive; see bullet points below. The operation of the BMRB is necessary for those engaged in structure-function projects, which includes much of drug discovery.  This proposal is well-written. Funding for the BMRB is of high priority for the advancement of science.
sig_text_str: . BMRB’s data model has the ability to capture, integrate and disseminate the major types of biomolecular NMR data. . Many journals depend on the BMRB to validate and archive NMR data (large quantities) associated with individual publications. . A tremendous number of software systems for calculation, prediction, assignment and validation have been developed using BMRB data.

imp_text: This is an outstanding application from a new investigator, only a year or so into his independent career. Dr. Sullivan has already solved a crystal structure of heterodimeric CLOCK:BMAL1, a major transcription factor regulating circadian transcription. He has now identified a slow prolyl cis/trans isomerization event in this complex and proposes that this conformational event is the molecular switch that regulates binding of activators or repressors to contribute to circadian transcription. He has also identified a cancer-induced protein, PASD1, that represses CLOCK:BMAL1 activity and contributes to unregulated transcription in cancer cells. He proposes to validate and ascertain the molecular events in this repression. The strengths of this proposal are the novelty of the area under study, the strong preliminary data provided, the well thought out, rationally organized and solidly justified research approach, and indeed the investigator himself and the excellent collaborative team he has assembled. Weaknesses are minimal and primarily concern the [necessary] use of protein domain fragments and peptides for the structural studies, rather than the intact proteins. But these are limitations imposed by the NMR approach, which must be used in order to obtain the protein dynamics information to refine the applicant’s model. Quite frankly, this is one of the best applications I have reviewed in quite some time.

study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function D Study Section
imp_text: This R01 is unlike most. The application seeks funding to continue to maintain and expand the Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank (BMRB), a repository for detailed NMR data relating primarily to macromolecular structure. The BMRB has been in existence for well over a decade, and has been supported by the National Library of Medicine. As this funding source is no longer available, the principals are seeking a new funding source. As such, this application/project is not hypothesis driven nor is it a research project per se. The strengths of the application include its significance - the BMRB was established in the late 90’s and has developed into the major repository for NMR derived structural information. Access to this information has allowed other groups to develop and refine new methodological approaches for analysis and refinement of NMR structural information. Another strength is the project leader and his team; the longevity and utility of the BMRB attest to this. Weaknesses include the low degree of innovation. The BMRB is well established, and the proposal seeks funds primarily to maintain and update the database. Another weakness is the rather ambiguous manner in which anticipated new information is expected to accrue. Due to this ambiguity, it is unclear what, if any, new and innovative methodological and analytical tools will actually be developed by the project team, or whether the BMRB will serve primarily as a repository of validated data for use by others outside the group to develop such tools. The application was jargon and acronym-rich, many undefined, making facile detailed assessment somewhat pain-staking.

study_section: Biochemistry and Biophysics of Membranes Study Section
imp_text: This application from a new investigator, Dr. Brett Baker, seeks to obtain high resolution crystal structures of free and substrate-bound forms of a transmembrane concentrative Nucleoside Transporter from Vibrio (vcCNT). The applicant suggests that this particular protein is a good model for human CNTs. Human NT’s are critical in success of chemotherapeutic nucleosides for treatment of cancer and viral diseases. The strength of the application is potential structural information for a class of proteins lacking in such information. Unfortunately, the application has serious weaknesses. First, vcCNT was chosen only on the basis of sequence homology to hCNT3. However, this homology is at best 40%. Furthermore, there are no data to show that vcCNT actually transports nucleosides. Thus, rationale for the protein target under study is weak. The applicant provides only limited preliminary data. High resolution crystal structures of both free and ligand bound forms of the target are essential, yet the applicant has been able to generate only low resolution data for the liganded form, and states that he has been unsuccessful with the apo protein. Finally, the focus on a homolog of hCNT3 is not justified in the context of eventual chemotherapeutic nucleoside drug development, a stated long-term goal. There are several isoforms of hCNT’s, each with different nucleoside specificities and kinetics. Furthermore, the major class of NT’s involved in nucleoside drug uptake is the equilibrative NT’s (ENT’s).  Thus the relevance of the structural data, if it is possible to get it, is unclear.

study_section: Basic Mechanisms of Cancer Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: Prostate cancer is the second leading cause of cancer-related deaths in American men. Understanding the processes involved in prostate cancer progression is critical for the development of better therapies to halt metastasis and to treat patients with metastatic disease.  Based on the previous studies and promising preliminary data on mesotrypsin, this proposal will investigate the role of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer progression, the development of mesotrypsin inhibitors and the efficacy of mesotrypsin inhibitors in vitro and in vivo. This proposal is well written by a junior investigator who has accumulated appropriate experience on biochemistry of mesotrpsin and protease inhibitors. The collaboration is described with involvement in other investigators from different disciplines, and environments are suitable for the experiments.  Literature is appropriately reviewed, the novelty is very high with preliminary data from cultured cells, human samples and mouse model, and experimental designs are laid out in a clear manner.  If successful, results will likely provide a novel therapeutic approach to control prostate cancer. However, there are some concerns. It is unclear about the protein levels of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer specimens, and no preliminary data to support the anticancer effects of BPT1-K15R/R17G inhibitors.  It is highly risky that the success of Aim 3 is dependent on the success of Aim 2.  The PI and the team have limited experience prostate cancer research.
sig_text_str: . Extracellular proteases aberrantly overexpressed in the prostate cancer environments represent a promising category of drug target.  This proposal is to investigate the novel role of mesotrypsin/trypsin IV (encoded by PRSS3 gene) on prostate cancer progression, the molecular mechanisms driving the disease phenotype, and the anticancer efficacy of new mesotrypsin inhibitors.   This proposal presented a set of preliminary data showing elevated PRSS3 in prostate cancer specimens and its promoting role on prostate cancer in vitro and in vivo.  The hypothesis of this proposal is that mesotrypsin represents a key protease in prostate cancer progression, and that potent and selective inhibitors of mesotrypsin could be used to define the specific role of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer models, and could also potentially offer novel therapeutics.  There are 3 aims to test the hypothesis in which the Aim 1 will define the role of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer progression, the Aim 2 will develop potent and selective mesotrypsin inhibitors and the Aim 3 will evaluate mesotrypsin inhibition as a therapeutic strategy.  Overall, this proposal explores the contributions and mechanisms of mesotrypsin to prostate cancer progression as well as the development of potent inhibitors. If successful, results may pave a new therapeutic strategy for prostate cancer control. .

imp_text: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is one of the most commonly diagnosed cancers in the US, but the number of CRC deaths indicates that more effective therapies are still needed.  This proposal is to investigate the molecular mechanisms of alternate pathways of PI3Ksignaling and PDPK1, mutant KRAS for the sensitivity of resistance of CRC, and furthermore to explore the clinical trials of inhibitors of AKT, PI3K, mut-KRAS signaling in patients for CRC therapy.   This proposal presented a set of preliminary data to support the hypothesis that dysregulation of PI3K/AKT and PDPK1/TORC switch in human CRC cells and tumor samples, and targeting both AKT and MEK signaling may provide more effective therapies.  There are 3 aims in this proposal.  Aim 1 will determine the mechanisms of alternate pathways of PI3K signaling for the sensitivity and resistance to targeting therapy of CRC. Aim 2 will investigate the mechanisms of alternate downstream signaling by different amino acid-substituted forms of mutated KRAS for the sensitivity and resistance to targeted therapy for CRC. Aim 3 will conduct clinical trials of inhibitors of AKT, PI3K, and mut-KRAS signaling in patients with advanced CRC using patient tumor biopsy results to confirm observations in the first two aims and identify potential biomarkers for selecting patients with CRC for therapy.  Literature is appropriately reviewed, experimental designs are laid out in a clear manner, and the translational research is highlighted.  Overall, this proposal explores the contributions and mechanisms of PI3K/AKT, and PDPK1/TORC to CRC therapy. If successful, results may pave a new pathway, biomarker, or target for CRC control.  However, there are some concerns. It is unclear how “PDPK1/TORC switch” is activated by AKT inhibition or activation in CRC.  The rationale and the feasibility of the combined inhibition of PI3K and MEK signaling are stated but not convincing at this point, and there is no evidence to indicate this combination will improve the sensitivity of resistant CRC.

imp_text: The applicant proposes to study the role of mesotrypsin, an atypical trypsin isoform, in prostate cancer progression and to design and isolate novel mesotrypsin inhibitors.  The goals of the proposed studies are to define the role of meotrypsin in prostate cancer pathogenesis, design novel mesotrypisin inhibitors with increased specificity, and evaluate the efficacy of mesotyrpisin inhibition in in vivo and in vitro models of prostate cancer.   The concept to be tested is novel and based on studies that demonstrate mesotyrpsin is transcriptionally upregulated in advanced prostate cancer and predictive of prostate cancer recurrence.  One aspect of the work that was down-played was the relevance, if any, of the transcriptional upregulation of mesotrypsin and whether this results in upregulation of protein expression, increased protein action or mislocalization of mesotrypsin.  The correlation observed in figure 1A does not prove causation.  The proposal is innovative to investigate mesotrypsin as a potential novel therapeutic target in prostate cancer, but more mechanistic preliminary data is necessary to demonstrate that mesotrypsin is a causative driver of prostate cancer progression and not just a biomarker associated with progression.  An additional concern is that Aim 3 is dependent upon the successful completion of Aim 2 and identification and production of more specific inhibitors of mesotrypsin than currently exist.  Overall, this is an interesting proposal from an early stage new investigator, but due to the limitations described, enthusiasm is in the moderate range at this point.

imp_text: This is a new proposal that examines the cooperating roles of BRAF activation and PI3’-kinase signaling in melanoma, and how these pathways can be dually inhibited for melanoma therapy. This proposal builds upon years of work from the Murray laboratory investigating melanoma progression and activation of the MAPK pathway via BRAF activation.  TO date, single line therapeutic approaches to inhibiting BRAF signaling have had initial success in patients, however, all patients eventually become resistant to BRAF inhibitors and disease progresses.  Genetic studies have revealed that PI3’K/AKT pathway effectors are often also mutated in melanoma, and might be an effectatious secondary target for inhibitors.  The goal of this project is to design novel melanoma therapies targeting both BRAF and PI3K pathway activation to improve patient outcomes.  This is a well designed proposal balanced with both in vitro and novel in vivo models that recapitulate patient disease.  This studies have potential to lead to significant improvements in melanoma therapeutic strategies.  However, enthusiasm for this proposal is dampened by the extremely ambitious goals and numbers of therapeutic compounds and combinations to be tested.  There are serious reservations as to whether this work can be carried out in the time frame outlined.  Enthusiasm for this proposal is excellent, but dampened by the overly ambitious number of studies proposed.

imp_text: The goal of this well-written application by an experienced investigator is to test the hypotheses that in the context of activation of BRAF oncogene and silencing the tumor suppressor PTEN, PI3 kinase contributes to melanoma development, in AKT-independent manner. Therefore, combined inhibition of BRAF(V600E) and PI3K is a more potent strategy for durable melanoma therapy. To test these hypotheses, the PI employs well-characterized genetic mouse model of melanoma and an extensive collection of pharmacological inhibitors of various kinases along the MAPK and PI3K signaling pathways. The strengths of this application are: 1) the high significance of the proposed research for an ongoing clinical challenge, i. e., treatment of patients with BRAF(V600E) melanoma, 2) a strong collaborative team with wide-ranging expertise. One weakness is the almost fictional nature of the PI’s publication record, i. e., lack of concordance between what is listed in the biosktech as author’s publications with PubMed listings for the many of the title of such publications. Barring this weakness, this is an outstanding application that has high likelihood to advance the field.

This project addresses this problem by proposing to design new melanoma therapies that overcome this challenge. . If the aims of this project are completed, it will advance the knowledge on the role of PI3K-AKT signaling and has the potential to contribute toward durable melanoma therapy.

imp_text: This application addresses an important problem, namely the mechanism underlying prostate cancer metastasis. This application is very nicely and logically written and it has several strengths. For instance it builds upon solid preliminary data generated in the PIs laboratory and for the most part, the experiments proposed are supported by feasibility data. The PI is an experienced and productive investigator, even though her productivity level has not been stellar, and the cadre of collaborators is excellent and coherent. The environment is excellent. The application is supported by mainly cell culture data indicating with gain and loss of function experiments that metatrypsin promotes the migration of prostate cancer cells in 3D assays and in xenografts. The PI proposes three logical aims. Aim 1 proposes to identify the role of metatrypsin in prostate cancer progression by identifying endogenous trypsin inhibitors produced by prostate cancer cells, to determine how metatrypsin regulates the COX-2 promoter and to define the role of metatrypsin in metastasis in a xenograft models. Aim 2 proposes to identify inhibitors of metatrypsin using a candidate gene approach, by using phage display and by solving metotrypsin-substrate crystal structures. Aim 3 proposes to test the effects of metatrypsin inhibitors in vitro and in vivo in xenografts of prostate cancer cells. Anticipated results and pitfalls and alternatives are adequately addressed. Lack of feasibility data in support of Aim 2, and the fact that Aim 3 is dependent on Aim 2 and the unclear nature of the collaboration with Dr. Olinski (to assist with phage display from Poland) are areas of concern.

In vivo experiments in mouse models would increase the confidence that XLF is a bona fide therapeutic target; 4.  The systemic delivery of peptides in vivo, will be a challenge, thus this application will not address whether peptide inhibitors of XLF are bona fide therapeutic agents. imp_text: This application addresses an important problem, namely intrinsic or acquired resistance of colorectal cancer (CRC) to targeted agents. The PI has a track record as a clinical and translational investigator in the field of CRC and has assembled a skilled team of investigators. There has been a tremendous interest in the development of targeted cancer therapies and a great deal of evidence has been provided over the years that mutant KRAs and its downstream signaling pathways play a critical role in the initiation and maintenance or several cancers including CRC. However, the preliminary data provided by the PI in support of this grant are rather weak because are mainly correlative, based on loss of function experiments and there is no or little acknowledgement of the fact that off-target effects elicited small molecule inhibitors or RNAi may confound the interpretation of the data. The experimental approach is similarly based on correlative experiments that are not sufficiently explained.  Several experiments are not supported by preliminary feasibility studies (for instance PDXs). Two clinical trials in CRC are mentioned, but it seems to me that this is not the mechanism to fund personnel involved in the execution of such trials. The effort allocation of the personnel, proposed to perform the described experiments seems insufficient for the tasks proposed. Finally, the grantmanship is poor: large parts of the grant are insufficiently explained, several figures are not legible and a large part of the background section is used to described clinical trials and mechanistic studies, which I feel belong to other sections of the grant. Nevertheless, the topic of the grant is of great potential interest because, if successful, it would change the approach followed to treat CRC.  However, the weaknesses described above significantly decrease the enthusiasm and the score of this application.

imp_text: This is an excellent proposal from an early stage investigator which aims to develop inhibitors of mesotrypsin to treat metastatic prostate cancer. The PI has identified a novel serine protease which is upregulated during prostate cancer progression and which may promote metastatic activity. Strengths of the proposal include the well qualified PI and team of collaborators and the outstanding environment. The significance of this proposal emerges from the new role for mesotrypsin in metastatic disease and the ability of the PI to develop inhibitors of this enzyme which may be effective in metastatic prostate cancer. Innovation was largely restricted to the hypotheses, with most of the technical approaches using standard methods. The overall approach was strong and was supported by strong preliminary data and a well written experimental section. The approach combines drug development and chemical synthesis with cell and animal models to test their efficacy. In particular, the development of an initial inhibitor suggests that additional development will be successful. Some weaknesses were noted, largely relating to the COX2 experiments, with the link between mesotrypsin and COX2 transcription likely to be complex and indirect, so that examining transcription factor binding to COX2 promoters may not reveal the signaling pathway linking mesotrypsin and COX2.
sig_text_str: . Metastatic prostate cancer is a significant problem with inadequate treatment options. Developing new inhibitors for PRSS3 can provide a new approach for treatment. . May provide new insight into how both endogenous protease inhibitors and increased PRSS3 expression may contribute to tissue metastases. . Strong preliminary data supports potential role of PRSS3 in promoting invasion and metastases.

app_text_str: . Well integrated series of experiments exploring role of mesotrypsin/PRSS3 in prostate metastases. Each section is well described, and potential problems and alternate approaches are clearly noted. . Aim 1 is a well described series of experiments to identify potential protease inhibitors which may be substrates for mesotrypsin/PRSS3. A series of predicted targets will be analyzed, as well as provision for searching for new substrates using MS. In addition, the PI will examine the role of mesotrypsin/PRSS3 using a well-defined animal model. . Aim 2 will utilize the PI’s expertise in protein biochemistry to create a new scaffold for drug development and then fine tune this to increase affinity/selectivity. Preliminary data indicates that this should be achievable, and the PI has already created a number of variants which show increased affinity in vitro. The use of phage display to optimize binding affinity is an excellent approach. Further studies aimed at identifying the structural determinants of cleavage (rather than binding) should provide new information on binding versus cleavage and can be used to optimize inhibitor design. . imp_text: This proposal is from an established investigator which will analyze the role of XLF in NHEJ. XLF is a potential drug target for enhancing chemo- or radio-sensitivity, and may therefore provide a new approach to anti-cancer therapy. This project had a number of strengths, including the expertise of the PI and the environment, and experiments designed to sequence and analyze repair defects in XLF negative cells. However, the proposal suffered from multiple weaknesses in both the significance and approach. These included a lack of preliminary data demonstrating that many of the proposed approaches (e.g. photo-affinity labeling; peptide screen) will work, indicating that significant technical development is needed before the aims of the grants can be addressed. Further, testing of the filament hypothesis in aim 1 was limited to a single method which has not yet been validated. In addition, the PI did not provide proof-of-principle experiments demonstrating that disruption of XLF-XRCC4 interaction actually impacts repair. Overall, these problems in the approach limited the overall significance and feasibility of the approach of this project

imp_text: This project will use genetically defined mouse models to examine combination therapy (BRAF/PI3-kinase inhibitors) for melanoma with the aim of increasing response rates and limiting/preventing emergence of drug resistant disease. This project has high significance, since using targeted therapy (BRAF inhibition) frequently leads to initial melanoma regression but is followed by the emergence of resistant disease in a significant fraction of patients. Developing strategies to limit this is therefore key for improving clinical outcomes in BRAF mutated melanoma. This project had many strengths, including the strong clinical relevance of the project, the genetic mouse models of melanoma developed by the PI and the outstanding research team and environment. Innovation was high, including the mouse genetic models and the strong guiding hypotheses which underpin the work. The approach was rigorous with several strengths, including the use of both mouse and cell culture models, clear experiments designed to analyze signaling pathways targeted by BRAF activation and the use of a well defined library of inhibitors, many of which are in clinical use. A few weaknesses were noted, including a lack of detail about how the RPPA data and signal transduction approaches will be analyzed, and limited description of how the data would be used to inform clinical trials. However, the overall approach was considered strong.
sig_text_str: . Understanding how BRAF and PI 3-kinase mutations contribute to melanoma progression, and how resistance to BRAF inhibitors arise, is important for improving therapeutic outcome. . Studying combined BRAF/PI3-kinase inhibition to understand signaling pathways required for melanoma progression has direct clinical implications for use of combination therapy to treat this disease. . Use of defined genetic animal models in combination with well defined inhibitors provides a rigorous approach to dissect the important of BRAF and PI3-kinse pathways in both melanoma progression and to determine if dual inhibitor use is superior.

imp_text: Based on the discovery that mesotrypsin, a minor, atypical isoform of trypsin is upregulated in prostate cancer(PC), the applicant in this proposal will test if this serine protease could serve as a therapeutic target to inhibit prostate cancer metastasis. This well written application lists three aims including unraveling the mechanism of mesotrypsin in cancer progression, screening and characterizing the  mesotrypsin-specific inhibitors  and testing the effect of these inhibitors in preventing tumor cell growth and invasion in 3-D cell culture and  in orthotopic mouse xenografts. The strengths of the application include the applicant’s preliminary data showing consistent high expression of mesotrypsin, enhanced invasion and inhibition of anchorage-independent growth of prostate cancer cells after downregulation of the PRSS3 gene encoding mesotrypsin. The aims of the project, to establish the mechanism of mesotrypsin in PC growth and metastasis , characterization of   specific inhibitors of mesotrypsin which do not  affect other trypsins, and finally evaluate effectiveness of the inhibitors are all reasonable. However, enthusiasm is reduced in view of several concerns about the research strategy. The applicant earlier documented   mesotrypsin’s role in promoting breast cancer associated with the shedding of CD109.In this proposal, the PI will test mesotrypsin’s role in COX2 overexpression leading to PC progression. Thus mesotrypsin’s protease activity may have a pleiotropic role in progression of diverse cancers. The applicant has not demonstrated its exclusive overexpression in PC. Another weakness is in the plan to identify specific inhibitors which will not be substrates for mesotrypsin. This has uncertain prospect for success while the latter part of the proposal is dependent on the identification and characterization such inhibitors.
sig_text_str: . While the role of serine and metalloproteinases in cancer cell invasion and metastasis has been extensively investigated, the discovery that mesotrypsin, a minor member of the trypsin family may have a unique property of not being  inhibited by BTPI and is overexpressed in several cancers including prostate cancer is significant. This provides an opportunity for exploring its usefulness as a therapeutic target. . Preliminary data showing correlation between the mesotrypsin level and cell invasion strongly justify exploration of the  therapeutic benefit of using mesotrypsin inhibitors for treating prostate cancer.
sig_text_wkn: . Although the focus of the proposal is prostate cancer, overexpression of mesotrypsin was observed in several other cancer types. Thus the rationale for testing only prostate cancer is not compelling. . The potential impact of mesotrypsin inhibitors on normal tissues has not been discussed.
inv_text_str: . The PI Dr. Kelly is an early stage investigator and Assistant Professor of  Biochemistry and Molecular Biology at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center in Jacksonville, FL. The PI  was trained as a protein chemist and has extensive experience in serine proteases including mesotrypsin, the central focus of this grant. . His Co-Investigator Dr. Colewin is a mid-career investigator in endocrinology related to urological and thyroid cancers. He has significant publications in cell growth, migration and metastasis of various cancers. He will collaborate with the PI in establishing mouse orthotopic tumor model of prostate cancer. . Another collaborator Dr. Reichle, Assistant Professor and participant in the NCI SPORE in prostate cancer at Mayo Clinic, was trained as a postdoc in Dr. Mina Bissell’s lab at Lab in Berkeley  on Rac signaling and cell migration. He  has been collaborating with the PI and Dr. Colewin for some time as indicated by joint publications.. . The research team’s strength is in the complementary expertise of the investigators.
inv_text_wkn: . The PI does not appear to have significant experience in cancer research although his collaborators have. . None of the investigators has independent grant support from NIH and other national agencies.
inn_text_str: . The plan of targeting mesotrypsin to inhibit prostate cancer growth and metastasis is novel. This is an unusual target for prostate and other cancers  which is not examined by other investigators. . The structural approach to designing mesotrypsin inhibitors which do not act as substrate is innovative. .

The plan to test the impact of PRSS3 downregulation on PC metastases in orthotopic mouse tumor model is also reasonable and would validate  the preliminary in vitro  data. . The plan to identify a novel pseudopeptide inhibitor of mesotrypsin, based on structural parameters of classical trypsin inhibitors, is quite sophisticated which would utilize the applicant’s expertise in chemical biology. . The use of phage display for identifying optimum sequences of Kunitz inhibitors is also a strength. . imp_text: The PI Dr. Washington, is  a mid-career clinician scientist investigating the mechanism of therapeutic resistance in colorectal cancer(CRC). In this R01 application, he will test the hypothesis that acquired resistance to PI3K and AKT inhibitors, commonly used for CRC treatment, arises from aberrant regulation  of PI3K  and mutant KRAS signaling. This application has both basic science focus and translational goal of testing combination of drugs targeting three distinct signaling pathways in a phase II clinical trial. The strengths of the application are (1)recruitment of  co-investigators with the requisite expertise in drug design, pharmacokinetics, biostatistics and pathology and the expertise in clinical trial in a leading cancer research center. The rationale for selection of specific drug targets is justified. However, the project suffers from a major weakness which significantly reduced the enthusiasm. The proposal is far  too ambitious for a single R01 grant. Although the PI has documented experience in clinical trial and has current funding from CPRIT to test effectiveness of an AKT inhibitor in metastatic CRC , multiple signaling pathways and their activation in response to drug treatment would ingenerate additional therapeutic  targets.
sig_text_str: • CRC often develop  resistance to therapy by altering the signaling pathways which serve as the main driver of cancer  growth. A comprehensive picture of various growth promoting signaling pathways and their cross talk may provide an opportunity for personalized approach for treating CRC. • The applicant will exploit precision (personalized) therapy) by selective targeting of CRC based on their signaling mechanism for driving cancer growth and metastasis. • Recent discovery by the PI”s group and others that mutRas (codon12 G->D) may drive advanced stage CRC provides a rationale for initiating a phase II clinical trial  to evaluate response  of  advanced stage CRC to combined use of PI3K, AKT and MEK (downstream of Ras)inhibitors.
sig_text_wkn: . In view of multiple downstream signaling pathways activated by mutant Ras, targeting MEK alone may not be effective in the clinical trial. . The question of systemic toxicity caused by combined  inhibitors of multiple pathways has not been considered.

The research team has complementary expertise in the design of clinical trial.

imp_text: The goal of this R01 grant proposal is to improve therapeutic outcome of metastatic melanoma by targeting the PI3 kinase ->Akt signaling which promotes growth of melanoma driven by V600E  BRAF mutant. The applicant will generate genetically engineered (GEM) mouse mutants in  which melanoma  initiation, progression and metastasis  in mice could be  recapitulated . He will then test the effect of PTEN mutation, observed in some human tumors  on effectiveness of single-  vs. multi-target therapy The project has a strong rationale because,  even though melanoma treatment by targeting BRAF mutant has been initially  effective, the response is short lived for half of the patients. The applicant has laid out a rational designed strategy of identifying the parameters that cause resistance  to therapy. Thus  the strengths of this well written proposal include generation of a sophisticated GEM models, comprehensive approach to identifying signaling pathways that are likely to contribute to drug resistance, and validation of the mouse data in appropriate human melanoma lines; excellent resources  and collaborators for melanoma  studies at UCSF. Finally, the applicant has made significant contribution to the field of melanomagenesis. One weakness of the application is the sole  focus on drugs when immune blockage therapy targeting PD1 and PDL1  could have been included.
sig_text_str: . Melanoma, whose incidence worldwide is increasing, is one of few cancers whose etiologic linkage to specific signaling pathways is broadly understood. Hence the prospect of a strategy to reverse the invariable resistance  occurring in post-treatment tumor cells is highly significant. . The comprehensive approach  of delineating the signaling crosstalk by exploiting the sophisticated  GEM mouse in which the constitutively active PI3K mutant  could be knocked in, is highly significant. .

The PI has recruited collaborators both within UCSF and outside who have the requisite expertise, reagents , cell lines and mouse mutants to address the questions about the mechanisms of melanoma metastasis , response to inhibitors specific for PTEN and PI3K  targets. . The rationale of multiple targets instead of a single (BRAF mutant) target is attractive.

imp_text: This application from a new investigator seeks to investigate a novel protein biomarker for pancreatic cancer metastasis, namely Mesotrypsin (encoded by the PRSS3 gene). The investigators have previously found that mesotrypsin mRNA expression correlates with increased metastasic diseases and reduced disease-free survival. Moreover, PRSS3 silencing reduced the in vitro invasive potential of metastatic pancreatic cancer cell lines. In this application, the investigators proposed to further investigate the mechanism of mesotrypsin, and develop mesotrypsin inhibitors for pancreatic cancer therapy. While the significance is very high, the enthusiasm for this application is tempered by the lack of preliminary data showing feasibility for aim 2 (inhibitor development) and the over-reliance of aim 3 on the successful completion of aim 2.

imp_text: This application seeks to investigate a novel member of the NHEJ machinery, namely XLF. The PI previously showed that XLF is important for ligation of the DNA break. In the current application, it is proposed to further investigate the mechanism of XLF-mediated NHEJ (aim 1), and to develop peptide inhibitors of the XLF-XRCC4 interaction to be used as chemosensitizers (aim 2). Understanding the role of XLF is important, and the investigator team has complementary expertise highly relevant for the proposed studies. However, the enthusiasm for this application is diminished since it is not clear that the proposed approach will uncover novel mechanisms for XLF. Moreover, aim 2 is very premature and the lack of preliminary data makes it hard to assess whether it will be successful in any way.
sig_text_str: . Little is known about XLF; the molecular mechanisms investigated here may result in better understanding of its functions in NHEJ . Targeting XLF may result in novel cancer therapies
sig_text_wkn: . The proposed studies may not directly address the function of XLF. The results obtained from these studies are likely to produce only incremental advances . The absence of preliminary data makes it difficult to judge the feasibility of the approaches proposed . The likelihood of obtaining specific peptide inhibitors of the XLF-XRCC4 interactions usable in cancer treatment is very low. In general, peptide inhibitors have been shown to have a low success rate. In particular, why XLF-XRCC4 interaction is suitable for targeting over other DNA repair interactions, much better studied, is unclear.

imp_text: This is a strong application from an early career physician scientist which seeks to investigate the mechanisms of resistance to AKT inhibitors in colorectal cancer. The strong approach employs both basic science mechanistic studies as well as clinical trials. The approaches are well described, and clear rationales are presented. Aims 1 and 2 will investigate the resistance to AKT signaling in vitro, focusing on alternate PIP3 signaling and on effects of Kras mutations, respectively. Aim 3 is to conduct clinical trials with AKT inhibitors and use patient tumor biopsies to test the hypotheses put forward in the first two aims. The only weakness of this proposal is that it seems too expansive, with many experiments proposed, which may result in unfocused studies. Nevertheless, the enthusiasm for this application remains very high.

imp_text: This is a very ambitious project aimed at characterizing the role of mesotrypsin in metastatic prostate cancer and in the designing and testing of inhibitors. Mesotrypisin is a novel protein that has been associated with prostate cancer progression and metastasis. The PI shows very convincing preliminary data on how Mesotrypsin is related to invasion in cell culture and in mouse models. The project has identified a possible mechanism that connects overexpression of mesotrypsin with tumor microenvironment that may promote invasion. One of Mesotrypsin’s target is the canonical inhibitor APP (protease inhibitor) that contains a Kunitz protease inhibition domain and targets cationic trypsin and Factor Xia. Other targets and possible mechanisms will be identified in the proposal. The PI is proposing a short immersion on the signaling pathway of mesotrypsin. s/he has identified overexpression of COX-2 as a downstream effect. The PI has investigated the structure of the promoter and will analyze the effect of each of its components on the expression of Cox-2 using a luciferase assay. A mouse model will be developed for assessing the spreading of the disease. This model will complement the PI’s current 3D model. Tumor invasion will be followed using luminescence and standard pathology analaysis. Aim 2 focuses on developing mesotrypsin inhibitors. The main obstacle in their approach is that inhibitors may be substrates for mesotrypsin increasing its activity. Two candidates have been analyzed and one of them (BPTI) will be used as a back up in case their proposed experiments fall. The main goal is the development of a backbone that is resistant to mesotrypsin cleavage. Inhibitors will be screend using phage display. Crystal structures will be generated for the best candidates. In Aim 3 the PI will test for the effectiveness of the inhibitors using 3C cell culture and mouse models.
sig_text_str: . Treatment of metastatic prostate cancer is an important problem in the field . Mesotrypsin has been associated with prostate cancer progression . If the project is successful a new set of targets and inhibitors will be identified. The project will investigate a new target, mesotrypsin (the product of gene PRSS3), apparently involved in metastatic prostate cancer .  New signaling pathways (through upregulation of COX-2) will be identified .  New mechanism of action for mesotrypsin has been proposed and will be further investigated . Expands current cell and mouse systems by incorporating new knowledge on mesotrypsin, a newly identified extracellular protease

imp_text: In this project the PI hypothesizes that resistance to treatment in CRC metastatic cancer is partly due to poor stratification of patients. In order to stratify patients the PI proposes to use PI3K/AKT/PDPK1/TORC signaling and of mut-KRAS as classifiers and as guides to identify biomarkers. On one hand mutations in PI3KCA and loss of PTEN activate AKT and PDPK1. Hence AKT inhibition may be surpassed by PDPK1.  Additionally KRAS activate 6 downstream pathways and this aberrant regulation of these pathways is highly dependent on KRAS mutations. The PI will use patient samples from two ongoing clinical trials (TACTICAL & MK-2206). In the first clinical trial inhibitors of MEK, PI3K and AKT are being investigated and it is of adaptative nature. The second MERK trial is an AKT inhibitor for which rare responses have been reported. Using biopsies from the clinical trials the PI will mechanistic studies for signaling regulation (in particular the PDPK1/TORC switch) and for tumor xenographs. A clearly defined model for the PDPK1/TORC switch is presented and, as described, depends on PIP3 levels. If PIP3 is high (PTEN loss and PIK3CA activated) the PDPK1 is membrane bound. If PIP3 is low PDPK1 is active and AKT is not active.  This switch is hypothesized to be associated to CRC and a reason for resistance to AKT inhibition (aim 1). A characterization of proteins associated with the sequestering of proteins to membrane will be performed. Regulation of the KRAS regulated signaling pathways will be studied in cell lines and in tissues (Aim 2) and in particular the PIs will test the “oncogene addiction” hypothesis.   Finally clinical trials will be performed according to the classification of patients. These trials will serve for the identification of biomarkers/predictors of response and their evaluation using xenographs.  Legends in Figure 3 were unreadable

imp_text: The application aims to investigate how HME causing bacteria Whrlichia chafffeensis regulates host gene expression a tandem repeat protein (TRP120). The hypothesis is that TRP120 is a dual function transcription factor, which can use the host PTM (ubiquitinization and SUMO) to gain nuclear access and thus regulate host gene expression. If completed, the proposed study may help develop to develop new strategies or host targets for therapeutic purpose. The study focuses mostly on detailed molecular mechanisms underlying how TRP120 is Ub or SUMO modified and how TRP120 bind to host DNA to regulate gene transcription, as well as identification of potential TRP120 targeted genes. The results will reveal new knowledge about TRP120. However, the study lacks major functional experiments to show that knowledge gained can have important functional benefits in preventing bacterial infection, survival, or host animal health. It is also not very clear if other pathogens use similar mechanisms to change host gene expression. Overall, the proposed study is unlikely to have major impact on the field.

imp_text: This application seeks to determine the structural states of the Shigella type III secretion system (TTSS) component IpaB at various stages of development in the TTSS and in combination with various binding partners.  TTSS play an essential role in the virulence of many important Gram negative pathogens, making this a highly significant topic.  In Aim 1, the applicants will endeavor to use AFM and EM supplemented with biochemical methods to determine if IpaB resides within the needle apparatus.  Although these approaches have not been applied to this type of problem previously, highly qualified collaborators have been recruited to assist with the imaging studies thereby increasing the potential for success. In Aim 2 the applicant proposes to determine crystal structure for the IpaB/IpgC (chaperone) complex, the IpaB/IpaD complex, and for a series of IpaB constructs with the goal of a structure for full length IpaB.  Preliminary crystals for the IpaB/IpgC complex have been obtained.  The IpaB/IpgC structure will be highly valuable as there is controversy about this complex and related Type III-chaperone complexes.  The ability to identify crystallization conditions for other targets is uncertain, however a well-designed workflow is described.  In Aim 3 the applicant seeks to define regions/residues responsible for IpaB’s interactions with IpgC and IpaD.  Experiments using N- and C-terminal fragments of IpaB are proposed for measurement of binding constants of wild type and mutant constructs.  Enthusiasm for this aim is diminished by the apparent inability to utilize full length IpaB.  Overall, these studies address a highly significant problem.  Although enthusiasm is dampened by some aspects of the proposal that are problematic, there is a strong probability that important advances will be made in understanding the structural states of IpaB.
sig_text_str: . Shigella infections are a leading cause of dysentery, both worldwide and in the US . Type III secretion systems play a major role in the virulence of many Gram negative pathogens, including Yersinia, P. aeruginosa, Salmonella, and E. coli. . Information on assembly of the Shigella TTSS and on the structures of the IpaB/IpaD and IpaB/chaperone complexes will be of global interest for other Gram negative TTSS.
inv_text_str: . Drs. Ryan and Pinkert have collaborated for several years on the Shigella TTSS.  They have had previous success in determining the crystal structure of a sub-domain of IpaB. . Dr. Burdell has extensive expertise in EM and image reconstruction, and her participation greatly strengthens the application.
inn_text_str: . The use of AFM and EM to probe the contents of the needle complex at various stages of development is highly innovative.
app_text_str: . Well-established methodology for obtaining large needle complexes for imaging. . Extensive biochemical experience in limited proteolysis of IpaB, with the potential to produce domains that yield good crystals. . Preliminary crystals for the IpaB/IpgC complex have already been obtained.  The structure of this complex alone will be highly valuable in advancing the field.
app_text_wkn: . The ability to crystallize the IpaB/IpaD complex, or to obtain a full-length model for IpaB are both somewhat uncertain. . imp_text: Per authors submission: Shigella flexneri uses its type III secretion system (TTSS) to deliver the effector proteins that promote pathogen entry into human intestinal cells to ultimately cause bacillary dysentery. The type III secretion apparatus (TTSA) consists of a basal body that spans both bacterial membranes and an external needle that is the delivery conduit for translocator and effector proteins. From its position at the tip of the TTSA needle, invasion plasmid antigen D (IpaD) controls the critical first step of type III secretion. We were the first to show that incubation of Shigella with bile salts promotes recruitment of the first translocator protein, IpaB, to the needle tip where it is stably maintained and is able to interact with host cell membrane components. The latter event mobilizes the final translocator protein, IpaC, to the needle tip concomitant with full secretion induction. Although we have uncovered many of the structure-function relationships for the Shigella needle (MxiH) and needle tip (IpaD) proteins, the structure of IpaB has been elusive. However, we have recently solved the structure of a significant core fragment of IpaB and we now propose to build upon this finding to provide a substantial step forward in what is known about the steps governed by IpaB in Shigella type III secretion. The authors hypothesize that IpaB has three distinct structures, depending upon its status in the onset of type III secretion Shigella flexneri is a diarrheal pathogen that is a global public health problem. Its virulence requires a type III secretion system that allows it to invade human intestinal cells. The authors have developed a method for examining the individual steps of type III secretion induction in S. flexneri and they now propose to determine the structure-function basis of the second stsp. This will ultimately allow exploitation of the S. flexneri type III secretion system to prevent disease caused by this pathogen. Per authors: In this study, author propose to uncover important information on: 1) the topographical site of IpaB within the context of the Shigella cytoplasm, TTSA channel and TTSA needle tip complex during the first step(s) of type III secretion activation; 2) the structure of relevant IpaB domains ultimately leading to determination of the IpaB structure with and without its cytoplasmic chaperone; and 3) the molecular mechanisms by which IpaB is able to interact with IpgC, itself, and IpaD as the TTSA becomes activated. This will provide an unprecedented level of detail on the formation of the quiescent TTSA needle tip and the priming event that places IpaB on the bacterial surface where it can sense host cell contact. This will have broader application to other TTSSs, including that of the important foodborne/waterborne Salmonella pathogens and important biodefense agents such as B. pseudomallei. This is an ambitious undertaking with some risks, but with a breadth that is sure to provide important insight into the general process of type III secretion induction.

imp_text: Per authors: Ehrlichia chaffeensis selectively infects mononuclear phagocytes and resides in early-endosome-like compartments, forming membrane-bound microcolonies called morulae. The mechanisms by which E. chaffeensis is internalized, establishes intracellular infection and avoids innate host defenses are not understood, but appear to occur through functionally relevant host-pathogen interactions associated with newly described type 1 secretion (T1S) tandem repeat protein (TRP) effectors. We have determined that TRP120 is translocated into the host cell nucleus, contains a novel TR DNA binding domain, binds a GC-rich DNA motif, and is a substrate of host ubiquitin (Ub) and small ubiquitin-like modifier (SUMO) post translational modification (PTM) pathways, which are known to extensively expand interactive and functional capability of eukaryotic proteins. The goal of this study is to demonstrate that TRP120 is a dual-function transcription factor that has interplay with the Ub/SUMO pathways to mediate nuclear translocation, subnuclear associations and regulate host defense gene expression. Through this investigation we will define the regulatory mechanisms mediating TRP120 trafficking to the nucleus, characterize subnuclear localization and interactions, determine the molecular basis of TRP120-DNA binding, and role of TRP120 and PTMs in modulating host gene expression using state-of-the-art molecular and cellular approaches.

imp_text: The investigators have proposed an important series of experiments to elucidate the conformational and temporal changes occurring in the type III secretion system at Shigella’s invasive site of the epithelial mucosal cells.  As Shigellosis is the second leading cause of death among children under age of five, this research is imperative for future rational drug design to develop agents against this deadly disease.  Overall, the investigators and their collaborators have proposed a well devised research plan with multiple alternative approaches.  Their facilities and the expertise of the investigators will allow for successful completion of the proposed aims in the time frame and budget allotted.  The research is very innovative as this will be the first experimentation to elucidate the structure and potential binding partners of the IpaB and IpaD virulence factors responsible for initial pathogenesis of Shigella infection.
sig_text_str: . Our ability for rational drug design for new agents against Shigella infection, a major cause of diarrheal disease and death in children,  has been hampered by our lack of understanding of the structure of translocator virulence factors and their binding partners in the type III secretion system, responsible as a conduit between Shigella and host intestinal cells.  These studies will provide basis for future studies to prevent disease caused by gram-negative pathogens which use this type of secretion system.
inv_text_str: . Dr. O’Brian has experience leading research in Shigella research and has developed strong collaborations with Dr. Pinkert and Dr. Germundson, which will contribute to the success of the proposed research.  Dr. O’Brian has also developed strong collaborations with the other collaborators who are crucial to the success of the application as well as his laboratory team, which contains multiple competent senior scientists and postdoctoral fellows.  Each investigator has a good publication record in the given research and has demonstrated successful completion of funded projects.
inv_text_wkn: . Although a consortium/contractual agreement is established between Dr. O’Brian and Germundson, it is unclear how research efforts and personnel efforts will be coordinated across the institutions.
inn_text_str: . The proposal aims to determine the full crystal structure of not only the IpaB protein, but also the structure of complexes between IpaB, IpaD but IpaB with IpaC.  The determination of the structure of these complexes will aid tremendously in determining binding regions and potential binding partners critical for Shigella virulence.  In addition, the full structure of the type III secretion needle will be resolved, therefore allowing a 3D model for future drug discovery efforts to determine inhibitors of these interactions.  Finally, the determination of the temporal changes occurring with respect to these proteins and the full formation of the type III secretion needle will be elucidated for the first time.
app_text_str: . The proposed aims have clear cut outline with well-defined technically proficient experimental approaches. The investigators will be using the most advanced equipment to determine crystallographic structures, imaging of temporal location of IpaB within the needle and advanced analysis of the imaging and crystallographic data. Alternative approaches are given for each specific aim along with reasonable anticipated results.
env_text_str: . Dr. O’Brian and Dr. Pinkert’s facilities at Oklahoma State University house state of the art equipment needed to successfully achieve the goals in the specific aims.  In addition their previous collaborations with Dr. Germundson at University of Missouri-Kansas City will provide needed structural computing support.  In addition the investigators will be utilizing the facility at National Center for Macromolecualr Imaging (NCMI) using their advanced JEM microscopes as well as a microscope fitted with a phase plate, needed as an alternative approach for Aim 1 imaging.

However, I have a few concerns: 1) For most of the approaches, there are lacking alternatives. 2) Some of the proposed research methods/approaches are not the best choices.
