The investigators did not differentiate the effects on activation and repression histone methylation markers. Both the activation (H3K4M3) and the repression (H3K9M3) markers significantly decreased. The hypothesis: E. chaffeensis decreases select histone methylation patterns would be hard to support the bacterial effect on regulate gene expression. 4) There is no study proposed would be conducted in animals.

imp_text: The investigator proposes to examine a pathogen that is important to human health by investigating two EPS proteins and the CdrA protein. Some of the proposed aims are likely to provide impactful research, particularly those examining the structure and function of CdrA. Others offer only smaller additional insights over what is already known and the majority of Aim two focuses on the same basic approach which has some caveats.
sig_text_str: . The application focuses on the biofilm matrix produced by P. aeruginosa, a bacterial pathogen that is associated with several diseases and poor health outcomes. A full understanding of the biofilm that protects the bacteria during infection is an important area of research. Determining the structure of the proteins that are discussed in the proposal will be highly informative for future work in trying to target and understand such proteins for therapeutic purposes.
sig_text_wkn: . It is unclear the extent to which much of this proposal will produce novel results. The EPS protein Pel is most likely highly similar to Psl which appears to be reasonably well characterized from the description given in the grant. Investigation into the CdrA protein is a more novel direction. However, the majority of Aim 2 relies on the same experimental strategy of simply deleting these proteins and characterizing the results. This approach doesn’t address potential complications. If these proteins having other important cellular functions then their deletion will simply make the bacteria less healthy which prevents conclusions from being drawn about the importance of their role specifically in the biofilm. This issue dilutes the potential significance of the proposal.
inv_text_str: . The investigator has a record of publications in the field and sufficient resources and collaborators.
inn_text_str: . The structure-function assays proposed here will provide a more in depth understanding of these proteins. While the EPS proteins already have some clear functions, and he work proposed is mainly an extension of what is known, this approach will be particularly informative for CdrA.
inn_text_wkn: . Some of the approaches described here are mainly repeating the same experiments already done for the Psl with Pel or CdrA. Particularly for the case of Pel, this is not very novel. The major hypothesis that will be tested in Aim 2 is that deletion of these proteins will affect bacterial virulence, yet this is almost a given for any particularly important protein required for normal function in this bacterial strain. If the investigators could go further with this aim to better demonstrate the specificity of the role of these proteins and characterization of biofilm specific deficits, that would be preferable.
app_text_str: . Aim 1 employs a range of approaches that have the potential to provide an in depth understanding of the proteins discussed. This diversity of techniques employed to better understand the function of Psl, Pel, and CdrA is a clear strength of the aim.
app_text_wkn: . Aim 2 is almost entirely based on a characterization of 3 deletions, one of which is already well characterized. As such, these assays are all open to the same critique: a deletion could just be effecting some other basic function of the bacteria so changes in virulence or viability, may not be very informative. While it is certainly valuable to study such deletions, ideally they could be paired assays that more specifically examine their function (such as examining the biofilm itself, determining if Pel and Psl can substitute for each other’s functions, examining the effects of mutations or smaller deletions that disrupt the protein’s function in producing the biofilm rather then deting the whole protein, and examining the effects of overexpression).

imp_text: The proposal will test a hypothesis that overexpression of small nucleolar (Sno) RNA, ACA11, in multiple myeloma (MM) with t(4;14) translocation reduces reactive oxygen species (ROS)-induced cell death that in part contributes to MM development and/or progression. The rationale for this hypothesis is based on published and unpublished studies by the PIs that revealed (1) upregulation of a 125 nucleotide long SnoRNA ACA11 from the intronic region of MM t(4/14)-associated candidate oncogene WHSC1 (aka MMSET) in select MM cell lines and primary tumors, (2) ACA11 interacts with a number of small nuclear ribonuclear proteins (snRNPs), and (3) ACA11 expression reduces ROS production in MM cells in part through stress-induced, p53-regulated mechanisms, while ACA11depletion inhibits MM cell growth and enhances efficacy of Doxorubicin in vitro. Three aims are proposed to validate (1) ACA11 interactions with snRNPs to abrogate ROS-induced cell death, (2) ACA11 regulation of splicing of SnoRNAs of RNPs to regulate ROS production, and (3) ACA11 inhibition of ROS production involves p53 signaling. Although the findings that ACA11 is overexpressed in t(4;14) MM cells and tumors and likely functions to suppress ROS through splicing of RNPs and p53 signaling are interesting and potentially novel, the aims 1 and 2 studies are designed to validate interactions of ACA11 with a number of snRNPs and regulation of splicing of a number of snoRNAs by ACA11. These pleiotropic and dynamic interactions are likely responsible for ACA11 regulation of ROS production in MM cells, and thus difficult to judge to the extent a particular interaction or splicing event will be responsible for ROS production. In this regard majority of the outcomes appear open-ended and could interfere with robust interpretation of data to address the stated hypotheses. The involvement of the p53-dependent signaling in regulation of ROS by ACA11, if proven, will be interesting and potentially novel outcome since p53 is generally functional and not mutated in the MM. Here again, the studies designed explore alterations in nucleolar morphology and functions such as pre-mRNA transcription, rRNA processing, rRNA export, polysome formation and protein synthesis by ACA11. Although, apoptosis by p53 has been well documented to drive ROS production in studies conducted almost two decades ago, the studies proposed in aim 3 have somewhat limited focus and depth on regulation of p53 and its signaling by ACA11. Overall although the PIs have the expertise and critical reagents to test the hypothesis, and some studies have potential to elucidate novel mechanisms of nucleolar p53 signaling by a snoRNA, the outcomes of the majority of studies will likely be open-ended and validate the preliminary studies.

imp_text: The proposal is designed to test a hypothesis that miR-30 blocks oncogenic Ras-induced senescence by targeting transcriptional activators of tumor suppressor p16INK4A. In aims 1 and 2, the molecular mechanisms of p16INK4A transcription activation by miR-30 regulated chromatin helicase DNA binding domain (CHD)7 and trinucleotide repeat containing protein 6A (TNRC6A) proteins will be investigated in the presence or absence of oncogenic Ras. In aim 3, the role of miR-30 and its targets CHD7 and TNRC6A in cell transformation and tumorigenesis in vitro, and expression of these markers in human tumors will be investigated. Although a full spectrum of changes associated with cellular transformation and carcinogenesis processes are yet to be understood, bypass of oncogene-induced cellular senescence is known to contribute to oncogene-dependent cellular transformation. A number of tumor suppressors including p16INK4A and p53 have also been well documented to regulate growth inhibitory signaling by senescence as well as apoptosis pathways during embryonic development and adult tissue homeostasis. The current studies will elucidate a novel, molecular function of oncogenic miR-30 to block mutant Ras-induced transcriptional activation of p16INK4A to abrogate senescence signaling in primary, non-immortalized cells. However, the regulation of senescence signaling by miR-30 has already been investigated in various cancer cells. The impact therefore is likely to be moderate since the concepts of oncogene-induced senescence and cell growth inhibitory functions of p16INK4A have been rather well investigated in various in vitro and in vivo studies. The facts that miR-30 is overexpressed in many cancers, its targets CHD7 and TNRC6A are also frequently mutated in colon cancers, and miR-30 signaling regulated senescence signaling in various cancer cell lines, the outcomes of majority of the proposed studies will likely be incremental if not confirmatory.

sig_text_wkn: . Oncomir-30 regulation of senescence signaling has been investigated in various cancer cell lines. . CHD7 is a known co activator of transcription factors that regulate cell proliferation and differentiation. . Activators and/or co-activators of transcription often regulate a diverse array of promoters/genes. The redundancy in their enhancer/co-activation partner(s) and binding to the cis sequences in their target genes often makes their specific targeting to activate tumor suppressors somewhat challenging. In general, with the exception of steroid receptors, therapeutic targeting of transcription factors and their co-activators has thus far had a rather limited success.

The concept overall lacks innovation since the tumor suppressors such as p53 that are known to play key roles in senescence signaling have been previously exploited for therapeutic intervention (for example, p53 stabilizers and/or MDM2 inhibitors). . MiR-30 also targets p53, and loss of p53 and p16INK4A have been demonstrated to co-operate with mutant-RAS, hTERT and SV40 T-antigen-driven transformation of human fibroblasts. Thus, MiR-30 targeting of p16INK4A is a contributory albeit expected mechanism for senescence disruption.
app_text_str: . In general, the published studies and preliminary data support rationales for various studies proposed. These key data include, (1) reporter studies indicate that CHD7 and TNRC6A are targets of miR-30, (2) micro-array analysis show that expression of p16INK4A mRNA is regulated by CHD7, (3) CHD7 enhances transcription through the p16INK4A promoter, and (4) MiR-30 is an Oncomir, and loss of CHD7 and TNRC6A occurs frequently in colon cancers. . The promoter-based analysis of transcriptional regulation studies by CHD7 (aim 1) and the alternative approach to investigate transcriptional regulation of I.B. by CHD7 are well detailed.
app_text_wkn: . In aim 1, the rationale for direct binding of CHD7 to p16INK4A or I.B. promoters is not robust. Although this possibility is recognized, and ChIP-seq studies are proposed, it is likely that CDH7 does not directly bind with respective promoter sequence(s) during senescence signaling and functions more like a co-regulator of transcription factor(s). . Aim 1A4 experiment seems dependent on prior confirmation of direct binding/interaction of CHD7 and p16INK4A promoter. . Aim1A7 studies for TFSEARCH-based transcription factor identification seem open-ended. . Aim1A8 studies to demonstrate binding/interaction of CHD7 with RNA polymerase II are not supported by preliminary data except that another member of the CHD family, CHD8, has been previously found to bind RNA polymerase II and enhance transcription. .  TNRC6 proteins are well-known regulators of various miRNA such as miR-7a and -9. Although miR-30 inhibition of TNRC6A leads to lower levels of miR-7a and -9expression and functions,the molecular mechanisms of miRNA reporter stability and de-adenylation (aim 2) will likely confirm the prior findings showing regulation of miRs 7a and 9 by TNRC6 proteins. .  If the idea is to demonstrate that miR-30 expression or depletion of CHD7/TNRC6A promoted tumorigenesis, then why utilize already transformed, tumorigenic cancer cells such as MCF-7, U2Os, or HCA7. Infact, these cells should be tested for senescence induction following overexpression of CHD7 and/or TNRC6A. . The promotion of tumorigenesis in primary MEFs by miR-30 or knockdown of CHD7/TNRC6A is logical however, if CHD7 promotes senescence by inducing p16INK4A expression, then its depletion together with p53 knockdown has been demonstrated to fully transform human fibroblasts by a combination of hTERT, SV40 and mutant Ras proteins. . In aim 3A2 experiments, the MEFs transduced with miR-30, and mutant Ras together with shRNAs for murine CDH7 or TNRC6A should be first tested in soft agar to determine their transformation since their increased proliferation may not necessarily mean transformation. . The expected outcome in aim 3A3 experiments that CHD7/TNRC6A can substitute for p16INK4a and p53 in transformation of primary fibroblasts is overdrawn.

imp_text: The proposal is designed to test a hypothesis that PI3K-dependent and –independent mechanisms activate Akt signaling in breast cancers. The rationale for this hypothesis is based on studies showing Akt is activated by cyclin A/Cdk2 and ubiquitin ligase Skp2 in a PI3K-independent manner. Aim 1 studies will characterize molecular mechanisms of Akt phosphorylation by CyclinA/Cdk2 and test whether Cdk2 plus Akt inhibitors can suppress mammary tumors that have elevated Akt activation. In aim 2, the molecular mechanisms of Skp2-dependent ubiquitination and stabilization of Akt as well as breast tumorigenesis by E17K mutations in Akt that occur in breast tumors will be investigated. Here a combination of Skp2 and Akt inhibitors will be tested as an alternative to rapalogs or PI3K inhibitors for their potential to inhibit breast cancers with activated Akt. Prior studies (J Cell Sci 2008 121: 979-988) have investigated Akt-Cdk2 in regulation of cell cycle progression and had suggested a rationale for combination targeting of Akt and Cdk2. Although these studies elucidated Cdk2 as a substrate of Akt, the reciprocal activation of Akt by Cdk2/CyclinA albeit interesting is logical and expected for cell cycle regulation and proliferation signaling. Nonetheless, the studies characterizing cyclinA/Cdk2 phosphorylation of Akt at S477 and T479, and their involvement in growth of breast cancer cells and their resistance to DNA-damaging chemotherapy if proven will be novel. With respect to oncogenic mutants (E17K) of Akt that occur in breast cancers and regulation of their activity by cyclinA/Cdk 2, and the fact that E17K mutants of Akt2 and Akt3 lack T479, it is likely that these Akt oncogenic mutants regulate Cdk2 for cell cycle control and abrogation of apoptosis. Similarly, a number of published reports reviewed in Nature Cell Biology 11, 377 - 379 (2009), indicate that Skp2 is a direct phosphorylation target of Akt and Cdk2. Here again, whether Skp2 ubiquitinates and stabilizes Akt to support oncogenic and survival signaling is also logical and expected. Moreover, involvement of K63-linked ubiquitination and stabilization of Akt by Skp2 has also been demonstrated in breast tumorigenesis. Overall although the PIs have the expertise and critical reagents to test the hypothesis, and some studies have potential to elucidate novel mechanisms of PI3K-independent activation of Akt, the outcomes of the majority of studies will likely validate mutually known and expected regulation among the oncogenic players such as Akt, Cdk2, and Skp2 in control of cell cycle and growth and their known potential as targets in combination strategies.

imp_text: One genetic characterization of high-risk MM is t(4:14) chromosomal translocation. Patients with this disease have a shorter survival time and the majority of them quickly move into relapsed or refractory stages of the disease after high doses of chemotherapy. Understanding the pathogenesis of this disease will be helpful for improving the efficacy of current therapeutic drugs and prolonging the patient survival rate. The PIs provide preliminary data showing that the snoRNA ACA11 is associated with the oncogene WHSC1 overexpressed from t(4:14) chromosomal translocation, and overexpression of ACA11 reduces the levels of ROA in response to oxidative stress and prevent MM cells against chemotherapy. The hypothesis of this project is that ACA11 overexpression reduces ROS-induced MM cell death and thereby promoting MM development. The PIs therefore propose three Aims to elucidate the mechanisms by which ACA11 suppresses ROS-induced MM cell death by interacting with RNP’s, modulating splicing of snoRNAs from ribosomal protein transcripts, and regulating ROS production via p53. Preliminary studies are solid and strongly support the hypothesis, and a related paper will be published. The function of ACA11 in MM pathogenesis is new. If the hypothesis is proven, new evidence for prevention of chemotherapy resistance in patients with high-risk MM will be obtained. The design of the proposed studies is clear and logical. However, the current application suffers from a few weaknesses. The proposal does not include preclinical studies using patient samples and mouse models to validate the results obtained from in vitro studies, and this therefore hinders the potential clinical relevance for this project. Additionally, the association of ACA11 overexpression with t(4:14) chromosomal translocation is not clear in non-MM tumors. The study cannot simply extend the conclusion from MM to other tumors. However, overall it is an excellent project to explain the pathogenesis of MM.

imp_text: MiRNA has been shown to regulate cancer development. The miRNA miR-30, which is highly expressed in cancer cells, can disrupt oncogenic ras-induced senescence through a transcriptional co-activator CHD, or through an RNA-binding protein TNRC6A, that can regulate miRNA functionality. Based on these findings, Dr. Ryan proposes to investigate the mechanisms of miR-30 mediated bypass of ras-induced senescence. Aims 1 and 2 will determine the miR-30 mediated CHD7/p16 and TNRC6A/miRNA functionality pathways by using human cancer cell lines and primary murine and human fibroblasts. Aim3 will determine the effects of miR-30 on tumorigenesis and by using colon cancer patient samples and also examine the expression of miR-30, CHD7, and TNRC6A in cancer cells. Dr. Ryan is an established investigator with extensive expertise in the research of oncogene-induced senescence, and the collaborators are experts in the epigenetic research or provide patient samples. The hypothesis has the potential to provide new insights into miRNA-induced bypass of senescence. However, the current application suffers from a few weaknesses. The key component in the pathways such as p16 is known to regulate senescence and TNR6A is known to involve in miRNA functionality. No validation of the mechanisms is proposed using mouse models or patient samples, and thus impairs the clinical relevance for this project. The details of patient samples, which will be used for this study, are also not clear. As such, these concerns limit the overall impact of this application.

Investigation of miRNA effects on ras-induced senescence is important for understanding of the mechanisms of oncogene-induced senescence and cancer development. . Dr. Ryan identified miR-30 as a suppressor of ras-induced senescence with some preliminary data. In this application, a hypothesis that miR-30 regulates ras-induced senescence through the CHD7 and TNR6A pathways will be tested. Determining the role of miR-30 downstream targets in senescence will help develop a new strategy for cancer therapy. . Preliminary results show the potential role of CDH7 and TNR6A in miR-30 and its effect on ras-induced senescence.

imp_text: The PI3K/Akt signaling is one of critical signaling pathways important for cancer development. Several inhibitors targeting this pathway have been developed and currently they have been studied in clinical trials as the therapeutic agents for some cancer types such as breast cancer. In-depth understanding of the mechanism underlying the signaling-mediated tumorigenesis will be a basis for application of the inhibitors in cancer therapy. Dr. O’Brian and the collaborators previously investigated the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway and also provide solid preliminary results that strongly support the proposed studies. In this application, Aim1 will elucidate the mechanism underlying Cdk2/Cyclin A-mediated class I PI3K-dependent Akt phosphorylation and Aim2 will elucidate the class II PI3K-dependent mechanism of Skp2-mediated Akt ubiquitination and Akt2 E17K mutation. Regulation of Akt phosphorylation at the C-terminal by cell cycle components Cdk2/Cyclin A is a new mechanism for Akt activation. Although regulation of Akt ubiquitination by Skp2 E3 ligase and Akt E17K mutation and their effects on tumorigenesis have been demonstrated recently, the mechanistic detail underlying the regulation independently on class I PI3K molecules is still necessary. The PIs designed in vitro breast cancer cell cultures and in vivo tumor (xenograft and transgenic) mouse models and also considered reasonable alternative approaches. There are a few of concerns for this proposal including lack of using patient samples. Additionally, growth factor-mediated non-Akt signaling is not fully considered. Overall, this is an excellent project with new ideas and scientific and potential clinical significance.
sig_text_str: • The underlying mechanisms of the regulation of the PI3K/Akt signaling will be helpful to clinically apply the related inhibitors. • Application of the Akt inhibitors has a side effect not only on cancer cells, but also on normal cells. The proposed study thus wants to investigate the regulation of Akt activation in class I PI3K-dependent (through cell cycle cdk2/cyclin A) or –independent (through Skp2-mediated Akt ubiquitination or Akt E17K mutation) pathways. Completing this study may explain the difference of Akt activity in cancer and normal cells, and therefore improving the application of the inhibitors in cancer therapy. • If the proposed studies are proven, there will be a basis on application of the inhibitor combination treatment (Akt inhibitors plus the inhibitors against Cdk, Skp2, or others) in breast cancer.

imp_text: The PI and author of this proposal try and address an important area of cancer research, which deals with some sort of comprehensive information regarding the role of long non-coding RNAs (LNCs) in cancer. They have chosen B cell lymphoma as the test model, which is also reasonable, especially given the approach the authors want to pursue. If approached in a consolidated and more risk free manner, such a proposal will be informative (like an encyclopedia) simply because the amount of data it can generate. The way the proposal is perceived and presented, there is no doubt in my mind that it will generate plethora of data, because of the techniques involved (RNA Seq and large scale RNAi screens). But again the way the proposal is presented the PI is not able to see through the focused aspects of this research and will be lost between 2nd and 3rd year of research progress. Either he will need to change his approach or he will keep generating data with no effective out come. Add to this fact the proposal and all three aims (especially aim 1 and aim 2) are very risky. When young investigators go for sweeping research and propose projects which attempts to gain knowledge or in a way solve the entire question in a given research field, it generally shows their inability to analyze what might be achievable in a given time period. This proposal is a very good, yet ambitious idea for a consortium of some sort, but not for an individual lab, especially a young one. I am actually sad to mention that limitations of this proposal are very obvious at both conceptual and procedural levels. This is a very exciting field and the Hot air LNC discovery by Gupta et al in Nature is the bright example. There is a big chance that important discoveries may flow out of this field. That is why I feel sad that an opportunity is squandered to present a more focused proposal by the PI. It can not be predicted how many target will emerge from AIM1, on top of that more uncertainty is added by an additional screen in AIM2, thus avoiding any sort of focused research. In an event where 30-50 targets are identified to be important by the time AIM2 is finished, will the PI generate 50 conditional Kos, will that be feasible? I thing that the proposal is too risky and too ambitions is heavily against the research idea of PI. The AIM1 should be approached as a separate R21 application, because it promotes high risk and high reward research proposals. The PI needs to change AIM2 to get out of the stream of another screening and modify to simpler and high through put experiments, such as analysis of proliferation, apoptosis and colony formation ability of genetically manipulated fetal liver cells, using agarose growth cultures or Operon (available at Solan Ketering RNAi facility) or qPCR-based genetic screens for biomarker genes involved in such processes. Adding screen after screen to the proposal presents a picture that the young PI wants to avoid basic mechanistic research, which will eventually lead to discovery in this field. The quality of preliminary data presented in figures is too poor making it difficult to observe data such as Northern blot presented in Fig 3. In addition, the information presented in Fig 3G does not match between what is written in figure legend vs what is mentioned in the text. PI must be more careful. Statistical information which actually lies at the core of this project is very less, eg: how many mice should be involved for such high number of B cell lymphomas (10), with and without involvement of Myc and then proper controls, and then a number which will allow random events to occur where all ShRNAs are allowed to work at least in three cases. It is far too many mice needed, or if not then I can not understand how this will be achieved. I can not understand because PI did not feed this information in a very concise manner in his write up. In any other proposal lack of such and information may be ignored, but because of the strong dependence of this proposal on screening experiments, this procedural and statistical information is central to the execution of this proposal. I also fear that the idea stems and depends a lot from what Lab of Dr. Loew can help contribute. The innovative aspects dealing with genetic engineering of constructs, RNAi and synthesis etc. are his research not the research of this PI, thus I would like to see what innovation this PI wants to bring to the proposal. The fact that LNC are important is not PIs idea, this information is available with scientific community. The PI will need to identify and mechanistically establish his targets in order to claim novelty and innovation in this research field. study_section: Cancer Molecular Pathobiology Study Section
imp_text: This grant proposal supplies an interesting hypothesis and wishes to study how ACA11 affects MM. The authors do note that this will be the first study of this snoRNA, but unfortunately when they go on to describe in their Aims it reads very much like an experimental to do list. This is exemplified by the aims being split into subsections. While some of these do begin with a statement of what they hope to learn by performing the experiment, many do not and just list experiments. It is very clear from the significance section that the investigators are very familiar with studying RNA systems. It is just unclear what the overall goal of this research proposal is as there are too many experiments proposed without a clear purpose. Additionally the investigators mention this could be a diagnostic marker, but fail to clearly state how this goal could be accomplished through their specific studies.
sig_text_str: . Authors have clearly done a lot of work in this area. They have a defined set of MM patients and a significant number of these patients have the described translocation
sig_text_wkn: . Investigators have not published on this topic yet, as their paper is in press. It is also unclear how further understanding this mechanism will help to direct current therapies. As a diagnostic marker it makes more sense.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Ryan who is the PI asking for the most support has a number of publication for which he is corresponding and has a record of obtaining funding and publishing quality papers.
inv_text_wkn: . Dr. Magil, who had just started at WashU as a PI when this grant was submitted does not appear to have a publication for which they are corresponding author, but this is only a minor weakness. When have been a nice piece of data to know who many students or postdocs were in the labs to perform this research.
inn_text_str: . ACA11 is clearly an interesting target and the investigators do highlight how this ncRNA get activated by chromosomal translocation.
inn_text_wkn: . As this is the first study of its kind with this snoRNA, the investigators should have mentioned here a new type of experiment to detect how this translocation is produced and in more detail how it affects MM growth. This is an interesting target but the investigators fail to show how their study can lead to a diagnostic/treatment. It appears they are just proposing to use traditional genome sequencing, although they have previously been successful with this route.
app_text_str: . Investigators plan on using commercially available cell lines, this should provide consistent results
app_text_wkn: . The investigators do mention that they do no plan on utilizing primary patient cells, which is acceptable. However, they do not mention that MM cells are difficult to transfect or apply shRNA techniques as they typically do not survive. The investigators needed to mention how they plan on circumventing this problem. Also the investigators clearly justify why they plan on using commercially available MM cell lines but do not mention in any specific detail what they plan on doing with the cells after they grow them. It is unclear what their approach really is going to be other than growing cells and sequencing them.

env_text_wkn: . Just one co-publication, however not a major weakness

Little is known about how these RNAs affect cancer cell progression, but based on previous literature and the preliminary results from this investigator these non-coding RNAs do affect tumor progression. Aim 1 is straightforward and will generate significant data. It is how the investigators plan to utilize this data in Aims 2 and 3 that make this an interesting study. It is cause for concern that these results may not translate into humans, but these studies will provide the basis for how to explore the precious primary cells acquired from patients. The grant application could have been more impactful by expressing how these studies could lead to new cancer treatments, but this is only a minor issue. The investigators do an good job of expressing how they will use the large amount of data acquired from the genome mining and will engage experts in the field to accomplish those goals.

They want to focus on the subpopulation of lincRNAs but make the arguemtn to study lncRNAs and these are actually involved as the oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Another weakness, that the investigators do point out, is there may be little homology between these murine studies and what actually occurs in humans.

While the investigators have clearly been successful in the past with other cancer targets, it is not clear what has made them pursue this new line of study and how it relates to what they have previously learned with other studies. It is mainly the lack of focus that affect my impact score.

imp_text: The current application addresses the significant gap in our ability to effectively treat multiple myeloma (MM), particularly those 10% of cases containing t(4:14). T(4:14) drives development of MM in these cases, and most current work has focused on the consistently over expressed MMSET histone methyltransferase as the main driver gene. While MMSET over expression is important, based on published literature, it is not sufficient to drive transformation. The PI has discovered that the orphan ACA11 snoRNA is also consistently over expressed in t(4:14) MM cases, and manipulating ACA11 levels influences ROS production and sensitivity to chemotherapy. The work proposed here seeks to test whether ACA11 plays a critical role in MM development. Strengths of the application include the expertise of the PIs, the substantial and reasonably convincing preliminary data, the innovative focus on the under studied ACA11 non coding RNA, and the research environment in which the work is performed. These strengths are offset by a number of important weaknesses. Significance is reduced since the proposed experiments do not rigorously challenge the central hypothesis, rather they characterize molecular mechanisms which may or may not be important for oncogenesis. The application also does not consider whether multiple genes or non-coding RNAs affected by t(4:14) work in combination to drive oncogenesis. The lacks a compelling vision of how ACA11 will advance diagnosis or treatment. Weaknesses in some proposed experiments also dampen overall enthusiasm. Overall, weaknesses and strengths balance leading to a proposed study with expected moderate impact.
sig_text_str: . Understanding how the t(4:14) translocation drives multiple myeloma (MM) in ~10% of patients is necessary before effective therapies can be developed. . MM is largely incurable, so further research in this general area is warranted.
sig_text_wkn: . The rationale for the focus on the ACA11 snoRNA, to the exclusion of MMSET and possibly other genes or non-coding RNAs, is not compelling. None of these individually may be sufficient to drive MM. . It is unclear why the PI believes ACA11 will be a better biomarker than the T(4:14) translocation itself. . The PI does not articulate a vision for how ACA11 would be utilized as a therapeutic target. . Direct links between ACA11 and effects on oxidative stress is unclear and may be quite indirect. . The proposed work does not actually critically challenge the central hypothesis, that “ACA11 plays a critical role in MM cellular transformation.”

imp_text: This study is focused on the role of microRNA miR-30 in suppressing oncogene induced senescence, a key tumor suppressive mechanism relevant to human cancer. In particular, proposed experiments test whether two genes, CHD7 and TNRC6A, are important mediators of miR-30 oncomir activity. Rigorously identifying mechanisms through which microRNAs drive cancer progression is an important and timely goal. A strength of the application is the use of complementary approaches involving animal modeling for rigorous hypothesis testing, molecular biology for mechanistic insight, and human patient specimens for assessing clinical relevance. Additional strengths include the depth and rigor of the mechanistic studies, the highly qualified investigative team, and the excellent research environment. The application does not make clear how the mechanisms uncovered are likely to advance assessment and/or treatment of cancer. The core of the proposed work is an extension of fundamental discoveries already discovered, so innovation is somewhat limited. Mechanisms beyond the two studied here have already been documented in the literature, so at the end of the day the relative importance of these new mechanisms for miR-30 oncomir activity will remain unclear without an integrated and systematic approach. Overall the proposed work represents a solid, rigorous, well designed mechanistic study likely to have modest impact.

imp_text: This application addresses the role of long intergenic non-coding RNAs (lincRNAs) in the pathogenesis of human cancer. Non-coding RNAs have only recently been appreciated for their effects on differentiation, development and disease, but it is unclear how they may influence cancer. Thus the study is timely, and mechanistic insight gained would be significant. The overall multidisciplinary approach is compelling, identification of candidates by analysis of mouse models of B-cell lymphoma then functional validation of those candidates with genetic approaches. The investigative team is well qualified as they have a strong track record of accomplishment in the requisite fields using the proposed approaches. It is unlikely there is a better research environment in which to perform the proposed work. A major weakness of the application, however, is lack of rigorous cross-species analysis. This is complicated by the relative lack of sequence conservation between lincRNAs from mouse and humans. While successful completion of the work will likely yield important new information about the function of lincRNAs, it will be unclear whether these results are relevant to human B cell lymphomas. While use of the mouse Em-myc B cell lymphoma model is well justified, relying exclusively on one model fails to address general relevance, potentially undermining overall significance. There are also potential limitations in the research design which are not addressed by preliminary data. For example, lincRNA expression is manipulated in the same direction as that found in lymphomas, so there is not a formal test whether these changes in lincRNA expression are required for lymphomagenesis. The feasibility of the mouse modeling in aim 3 is also questionable given time constraints. Overall strengths of the functional analysis, the investigative team, and the environment are offset by significant potential weaknesses in general relevance to human lymphoma and experimental design choice.

imp_text: This is a densely written application that seeks to elucidate the molecular mechanism(s) of a small miRNA (miR-30) in facilitating the tumor suppressive process of overcoming/bypassing oncogene-induced senescence.  This work builds on unpublished preliminary data in which miR-30 was discovered in a gain-of-function cell based screen for inhibitors of oncogene-induced senescence and independently found in other studies to be amplified or over-expressed in other human cancers and animal models.  This proposal focuses on additional preliminary data which identify CHD7 and TNRC6A as putative downstream targets of miR-30 and the specific mechanisms by which each may contribute to the inhibitory effects of miR-30.  The preliminary data are extensive and certainly consistent with the applicant’s hypothesis.  However, convincing evidence for their significance in a natural physiologic setting is lacking and experimental focus of Aim 1 is a bit too narrowly oriented on a molecular level and without a strong accompanying phenotypes.  Moreover, alternative outcomes are considered a bit too narrowly without strong experimental justification, raising significant concern over its ultimate impact. In contrast, Aim 2 is weakened by an overly vague hypothesis that is difficult to interpret at a molecular level.

imp_text: This is a well written application that seeks to explore potential causal role(s) and mechanisms of lncRNAs in the pathogenesis of B cell lymphomas (BCL).  The applicant proposes a logical sequence of experiments that begin with: (i) a screen for deregulated lncRNAs in a well-defined myc-driven model of murine BCL by comparison to normal pre-B cells, followed by cross-validation for human orthologs, (ii) a functional loss and gain of function approach to identify tumor suppressive and promoting roles (first in pools, then individually) using cell and animal based screens; and (iii) independent validation of identified lncRNAs for their oncogenic/tumor suppressive potential and normal physiological role in a non-engineeered genetic background (apart from the lncRNA of interest).  Preliminary data provide strong and convincing support for the technical feasibility of at least aims 1 and 2, with appropriate collaborators that makes aim 3 somewhat realistic.  Limitations of this application however include its inherently exploratory/descriptive nature which in and of itself is not necessarily a weakness but is somewhat problematic in this application because of the contingent structure of its aims, raising significant concern over its ultimate impact.

imp_text: This is an outstanding application that seeks to elucidate 2 novel determinants of Akt activation that may contribute to the pathogenesis of breast cancer and ultimately inform the development of novel rational therapies.  This work builds on compelling preliminary data that Akt activation is triggered in normal and tumorogenic settings by the cell cycle specific protein ckd2/cyclin A as well as by ubiquitination via the E3 ligase Skp2.  The specific aims of this application seek to further elucidate the molecular details of these phenotypes and also test their functional significance using inhibitors and in vivo animal models.  The application is greatly strengthened by the recruitment of world-class leaders in the area of PI3K/Akt signaling, E3 ligases and animal models.  Moreover, the impact of this work is likely to be high due to both its broad biological significance in the area of cell signaling and its potential practical application in the development of novel, patient-specific therapies.

imp_text: The proposal aims to characterize the mechanism by which the non-coding RNA (ACA11, a snoRNA) mediates cell death, and the implication for multiple myeloma, which is a recent, novel discovery by the PIs. In the first aim, the authors propose to identify and study the complex in which ACA11 is involved with (to reduce ROS) in live MM cells by CLIP; specific interactions by site-directed mutagenesis of ACA11 with co-localization experiments using identified mutants, and oxidative stress response testing with identified mutants. In the second aim, the authors will identify the substrates in which ACA11 interacts, centered around RPL13a and resident snoRNAs U32a, U33, and U35 which they believe is implicated in the oxidative stress response phenotype. In the third aim, the PIs aim to test the hypothesis ACA11 overexpression interferes with p53-mediated activation of ROS production, and examine the role of ACA11 on nucleolar morphology, function, and nucleolar-stress dependent p53 activation. The proposal is very clearly described, and PI O’Brian has a solid track record for success, and PI Magil is on his path toward independence. It is clear that the proposed will make progress on the biology around the specific molecular players that involve ACA11. Enthusiasm was dampened somewhat from how specifically the proposed insights will lead to improvements in diagnosis/prediction or therapeutic targeting, especially if the mechanism (ROS) is already known. imp_text: This proposal is from a well-established investigator to study the mechanisms underlying the roles of CHD7 and TNRC6A in miR-30-mediated bypass of oncogenic ras-induced senescence, and examine the impact of the miR-30-CHD7/TNRC6A regulatory circuit on cancer development. The objective of the proposal is to obtain mechanistic insights into the novel function of miR-30 in oncogene-induced senescence, with the hope that this will lead to therapeutics targeting cellular senescence. Aim 1 proposes to study the effect of CHD7 overexpression or inhibition on p16INK4A expression and on binding of CHD7 to the p16INK4A promoter. Aim 2 aims to study the role of TNRC6A in global miRNA functionality through dominant negative mutants and P-body integrity and miRNA functionality by two miRNA reporters. The final aim seeks to study tumorigenesis directly by inhibition of miR-30, CHD7, and TNRC6A in cancer cell lines, mouse and primary human tissues. Overall, the proposal comes from a well-established investigator who is a leader in studies of cellular senescence and its relationship to cancer. The proposal aims to investigate a potential novel mechanism (miRNA) for cellular senescence. However, enthusiasm for the application was dampened by the absence of some preliminary data supporting the reagents and concern about some of the assays. In addition, the proposed set of experiments seems extensive given the personnel that are included in the grant (a single researcher to handle the lion’s share of 2 aims), and no additional effort was provided to collaborators for data collection or analysis.
sig_text_str: . miRNAs are an important regulator of a variety of biological processes, and are implicated in cancer biology . cellular senescence is potentially a barrier to tumorigenesis . miRNAs may be implicated in this process of anti-senescence activity, promoting tumorigenesis via miR-17-92. . CHD7 and TNRC6A appear to be actively regulated by miR-30 and may be implicated in ras-induced senescence.
sig_text_wkn: . While the details of the story were laid out, the broad impact was not clearly stated, and was left guessing about senescence as a broader phenomenon and its translational potential. . Furthermore, the potential impact of the study of the two genes of interest – CHD7 and TNRC6A – and how improving the understanding of this circuit will help to understand senescence in general or in the context of cancer was not described. . The authors based their scan from selected the “top 40 targets” predicted by miRbase and Target scan. It remains to be determined how important – and how extensive – this regulatory network in fact is. How does the PI know that these targets are significant factors in this process overall, and that other targets of miR-30 are equally or more important?
inv_text_str: • PI Washington has an extensive and productive track record in p38, ras-induced senescence. • PI Washington has expertise in miRNA studies, as evidenced from a previous publication on the miR-17-92 cluster.
inv_text_wkn: . Note that even though the cover page has marked her as a New Investigator and ESI, PI Washington has Two R01s (and is associate), so assume that this is a typo. . While PI Washington claims to have recently developed mouse model experimental techniques, it was unclear which publications support this claim, a minor weakness.
inn_text_str: . Cellular senescence is a potentially novel mechanism for cancer, and miR-30 may be a novel component of this biological process, with limited studies in primary human cells. Also, mechanisms and targets through which miR-30 regulates senescence are not known. . The idea that a single miRNA could disrupt global miRNA functionality resulting in tumorigenesis is potentially interesting. . Study of TNRC6A could generate new insights on miRNA processing, generally.
inn_text_wkn: . The PI has R01 support to study cellular senescence, specifically. . The rationale underlying the master mIR regulator hypothesis was not detailed. . A weakness was the lack of depth, clarity and the particulars on why study of this pathway, process, specific biology is innovative. This section seemed like a series of claims without warrant. . As an mIR with oncogenic properties, it seems that miR-30 has been studied somewhat, admittedly not as much with respect to cellular senescence. . The novelty of global miRNA functionality is dampened somewhat as other studies have observed that loss of key miRNA components like Dicer or Drosha increase tumorigenesis.
app_text_str: • Aim 1 proposes a number of systematic, complementary experiments to understand how CHD7 operates at the p16INK4A. If CHD7 does not obvious interact at the promoter, alternative approaches to study ras-induced SASP by CHD7 instead, or to perform ChIP-Seq of CHD7. • Aim 2 also several extensive experiments to understand the function of TNRC6A, and is likely involved in miRNA global function. • Aim 3 proposes to study if disruption of miR-30 or CHD7 and TNRC6A promotes tumorigenesis, in a range of model and human cell lines • Aim 3 part B focuses on primary tissues obtained via collaboration.
app_text_wkn: . The focus of experiment in Aim 1 and 2 and aim 3 (in part) are in cell lines; validation or replication in primary tumors or tissues is not a focus, a minor weakness. . Aim 1 proposes numerous experiments; a concern was if each experiment can be reasonably accomplished (in addition to other aims) in the time period of the grant, with a single research associate presumably performing the experiments. . Aim 1 relies heavily on the idea that CHD7 occupies sites at the p16INK4a promoter. If that were not true, or were not obvious, that would substantially complicate several proposed experiments. There is no specific data presented by the authors that there exist CHD7 binding sites that can be investigated, motivating Aim 1 exp #3 - #6, and possibly others. . Aim relies on the use of a CHD7 antibody (ab31824). However, the strength and specificity of this antibody was not described. If the PI knew already that this antibody was a crisp reagent, that would be useful to know (especially for the chip-SEQ as an alternative approach). No alternative approach is described if the Ab turned out not to be reliable. . Aim 2 relies on two reporter assays as a proxy for global reduction of miRNA function. This seems sub-optimal as the relative change for these two genes will give a poor estimate for global change overall. Global functionality seems best assayed by the proposed examination of P-bodies, but that also appears suboptimal as this is an indirect measurement of functionality. . Aim 2 also does not appear to compare the effect of global miRNA for control-type knockdowns that have been shown to promote tumorigenesis. . Aim 3 is interesting, but there is little preliminary data on the data collection steps and that the quality of the tissues (and the manner they are collected) will generate reliable characterization, a minor weakness. . At the end of the approach, it was unclear how the delivery of all the specific aims will overall improve and impact our understanding of cell sencesence, cancer biology, and what the implications and impacts are.

imp_text: This proposal aims to study the role of for lincRNAs in myc-driven B cell lymphoma. In the first aim, they will use RNA-seq to identify lincRNAs that are upregulated or downregulated in Eµ-Myc pre-B cell lymphomas compared to normal pre-B cells (in mice), using synteny to identify human orthogologs. In aim two, candidates from the differential gene expression analysis will be subject to loss-of-function screening using RNAi will be performed to identify lincRNAs whose down-regulation is sufficient to promote cell proliferation, and a gain-of-function screening will be performed to determine whether their ectopic expression can promote cell cycle arrest or apoptosis. In the third aim, high-confidence lincRNAs identified in Aim 2 will be subject to engineering mice to carry conditional or constitutive loss-of-function or inducible gain-of-function alleles, to determine phenotypic and physiological consequences of those targets. PI Ryan is well established in studies of miRNA, and lincRNA represents a new area of investigation. The proposed first and second aims come with some preliminary data that suggests the overall screening efforts have a reasonable chance of success. While lincRNA is an exciting and potentially novel area, enthusiasm for the proposal was dampened by: (i) lack of details enumerating the specific significance and complexity of lincRNA biology relative to previous studies of non-coding RNA, (ii) how the investigators previous efforts in studies of miRNAs enable his work in lincRNA biology, (iii) a lack of enthusiasm on the approach, which involve multiple screening efforts rather than targeted hypothesis testing of specific targets or mechanisms, (iv) dependencies on Aims throughout the proposal.

imp_text: This well-written proposal, with clear aims and hypotheses focusing on defining the role and clinical implications of Sox2 (and its downstream effectors) in prostate cancer survival and growth, has a high likelihood of having sustained, powerful impact in translational prostate cancer research. Specifically, the investigator aims to identify new genes and signaling pathways involved in prostate cancer initiation and progression to identify biomarkers that can have clinical utility for both prediction of prostate cancer disease progression and prognosis, as well as identification of new biomarkers for targeted therapies. Findings from the proposed studies will have the potential to distinguish between prostate cancer patients that are likely or unlikely to metastasize and improve treatment practices for prostate cancer patients. The PI is an accomplished early stage investigator, but one notable weakness is the lack of a collaborative team of equally accomplished co-investigators with complementary expertise. Nonetheless, the PI has the appropriate facilities and resources in place to conduct the proposed aims and has provided a careful description of potential pitfalls and solutions to address them.

study_section: Tumor Progression and Metastasis Study Section
imp_text: This innovative proposal describes a combination of cell-based and in vivo assays to test the hypothesis that acetylation-dependent, dynamic regulation of Net1 localization to focal adhesions and the plasma membrane is required for temporal and spatial regulation of RhoA activation, which underlies breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis. Successful completion of the proposed aims of this study will contribute to the understanding of the Net1 mechanisms involved in motility and invasive potential of breast cancer cells, and could identify novel targets for intervention/therapeutics for metastatic breast cancer. This study’s significance lies in the fact that tumor metastasis is the primary cause of breast cancer death, but the process of breast cancer cell metastasis is not clearly understood and no effective therapies are currently available to prevent the occurrence of metastasis. Preliminary data suggests that aberrant activation of Net1 is an important factor for determining the metastatic potential of breast cancer cells, which this study will examine.
sig_text_str: . The process of breast cancer cell metastasis is not clearly understood and no therapies currently exist to prevent or treat metastasis. This study will address this gap in knowledge by aiming to understand the signaling mechanisms involved in metastasis in order to identify novel targets for breast cancer therapies. RhoA is known to control many processes that are critical to cell motility. This study will examine a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (RhoGEF) that controls the activation of Rho as the hypothesis is that aberrant activation of RhoGEFs may cause increased RhoA activity that occurs in breast cancer. It is unknown which of specific RhoGEFs, but Net1 is the subject of inquiry in this study. This study will also illustrate how Net1 controls FAK, which is an enzyme that plays a crucial role in breast cancer tumorigenesis and progression.
sig_text_wkn: . A minor weakness is that since it is unknown which RhoGEFs contribute to breast tumorigenesis and metastasis in vivo, there is a possibility that this study may yield null results if Net1 is not an important determinant of metastatic potential of breast cancer cells. However, one of the study’s aims is to elucidate the molecular mechanism of acetylation control of Net1, so even if it isn’t the most important RhoGEF, this study will help describes the function of Net1 in breast cancer cell motility and metastasis.

imp_text: This well-written proposal, submitted by a team of highly productive multidisciplinary researchers, aims to understand the interplay between the extracellular matrix (ECM) and hormones (namely prolactin and estrogen) to uncover the mechanisms by which breast tumors become resistant to hormone therapies. The proposed studies will examine a feed-forward mechanism between increased collagen density and altered alignment, which is associated with worse prognosis and altered hormonal signals in ER+, luminal tumors. One major area of significance of this proposal is that there is a dearth of knowledge about the interplay between hormones and stromal density in the development, progression and therapeutic resistance of ER+ tumors, which will be addressed by the proposed in vitro and in vivo studies. imp_text: This outstanding application will explore a novel and intriguing hypothesis that the tyrosine kinase c-Abl, which is oncogenic in hematologic malignancy, can serve as a tumor suppressor, blocking development and metastatic progression of triple negative breast cancer (TNBC), when c-Abl expression and activity is elevated in tumor cells.  The hypothesis stands on a large body of preliminary data, including the two key results: i) constitutive activation of c-Abl converted 4T1 cell derived TNBC tumors to a benign phenotype; ii) The oncogenic influence of TGFß-induced mechanotransduction on TNBC was found to be inversely related to c-Abl expression.  Failing of the c-Abl inhibitor imatinib against advanced breast cancer in clinical trials further strengthens the hypothesis. Merits of the proposal stem from its rational design, comprehensive approach and utilization of 3-dimensional organotypic cultures, in vivo and ex vivo models and clinical specimens of TNBC.  The PI’s strong publications relevant to the proposed research and expertise of the team in specialized techniques such as 3d culture, dual bioluminescent imaging of mice in preclinical studies and real-time intravital imaging of TNBC signaling and microenvironment are the notable strengths of the application. However, broad objectives under each of the four Specific Aims cast uncertainty as to whether all aspects of the planned study can be completed within the requested budget period.  The absence of a timeline for all sub-aims constitutes a weakness.

Dual bioluminescent imaging, affording measurement of tumor growth and TGFß-specific Smad2/3 signaling simultaneously, and intravital imaging of metastatic TNBC cells add novelty to the design. . imp_text: This proposal will delineate how the Rho exchange factor Net1 influences focal adhesion dynamics and regulates cell motility and invasion by altering activity of the focal adhesion kinase FAK.  The applicant hypothesizes that acetylation-dependent aberrant Net1 activation causes its nuclear exit and localization to focal adhesions and plasma membrane, leading to spatial and temporal activation of Rho that culminates in increased breast cancer cell motility, invasion and metastasis.  Novel findings, strong preliminary data and rational experimental design are strengths of the proposal. The merit of the proposal is reduced to some extent based on the following considerations.                 1) Only one cell line, namely the triple negative MDA-MB 231 cells will be examined.  It is important to test the hypothesis in multiple cell lines, especially in ER-expressing breast cancer cells given that metastatic breast cancer in majority of cases is ER-positive.   2) Since constitutive knockdown of Net1 was found to be lethal for MDA-MB 231 cells, xenograft tumors may not develop from cells with Net1 knockdown by doxycycline-inducible shRNAs.  This is due to the possibility that only the cell population expressing sufficiently high levels of Net1 would survive during tumor growth in host mice. In that case, phenotypes between tumors from control cells and Net1 shRNA expressed cells may not be distinguishable.
sig_text_str: • Net1 expression is required for ligand-stimulated breast cancer cell motility and invasion; . Nuclear exit of Net1 is acetylation dependent, and inhibition of HDAC deacetylase by trichostatin A or Sirtuin1/2 by Tenovin-1 stimulated Net1 acetylation and its localization from the nucleus to the plasma membrane; . Nuclear Net1 isoforms interacted with multiple subunits of importin a and importin ß1, indicating that this interaction may normally restrict Net1 isoforms to the nucleus; . Net1 isoform expression was required for FAK and Src activation and phosphorylation of myosin light chain, which promotes actomyosin contraction; . Net1 expression was required for focal adhesion formation during cell spreading on collagen, and integrin ligation stimulated interactions between endogenous Net1 and FAK. . PI’s laboratory generated important tools, such as breast cancer cells which are inducible for Net1 knockdown by shRNAs and mice with Net1 knockout specifically in the mammary epithelium.  These tools will facilitate progress.

app_text_str: . Strong preliminary data support the design of studies under Sp. Aim 1 & Sp. Aim 2 and Sp. Aim 3.2. . Progress will be aided by two very important tools that are already in place–i.e. luciferase-expressing MDA-MB-231 cells that can be induced to delete Net1, as well as Net1 conditional knockout mice. . The design for Aim3.2 is strengthened by including GTRosa26-LacZ reporter strain in the breeding scheme so that the limitation from the stochastic nature of the MMTV promoter activity will be bypassed and Net1 deletion will occur only in LacZ-expressing cells. . Appropriate controls for all experiments are described.
app_text_wkn: . Weakness is in the plan that a single breast cancer cell line (MDA-MB 231, triple negative) will be studied. ER+ cell lines should be assessed for a role of Net1 in the tumorigenicity and metastasis of the cancer cells, since majority of primary breast cancers are ER and/or PR positive, and majority of lymph node and distant metastases retain ER (Cancer Res 66: 9308, 2006, references therein).  Consideration of this issue, at least as a future study, is lacking. . It is possible that during xenograft tumor growth, the pool of Net1-depleted cells will be lost even with a conditional knockdown strategy, since constitutive knockdown of Net1 is lethal.  Thus, only the cell population that expresses sufficient levels of the residual Net1 will survive and produce tumors. In this scenario, even with the doxycycline-induced cells, xenograft tumors that express Net1 sufficiently will develop and tumors with significantly knocked down Net1 will be absent so that no differences in tumor growth and metastasis will be observed between the wild type and knocked down group. . imp_text: Increased mammographic density and mammary tissue exposure to prolactin and estrogen are known risk factors for breast cancer.  The proposed study led by two PIs (Drs. Baler and Keat) will investigate the hypothesis that increased density of the extracellular matrix (ECM) switches prolactin- and estrogen-mediated signaling in ERa-positive breast cancer cells from a pro-differentiation to pro-tumorigenic pathway, thereby promoting disease progression and metastasis.  The hypothesis is built upon preliminary data with ER-positive T47D and MCF7 luminal breast cancer cells to show that increased ECM stiffness from elevated collagen density shifted prolactin-initiated intracellular signaling away from STAT5-mediated anti-estrogen and pro-differentiation effects to ERK1/2 activation and consequent increase in cell survival and invasive response. Strengths are: 1) novel hypothesis; 2) large amount of preliminary data supporting the general tenet of the hypothesis; and 3) novelty of the mouse model that allows breast tumor development in a collagen-enriched environment in response to high prolactin levels in the mammary epithelium. The animal model will be generated by crossing mice overexpressing prolactin in the mammary epithelium with mice expressing non-cleavable collagen1a1, which creates a high-density collagen environment in the stromal tissue.  Also, the proposal benefits from proven track records of the two PIs and the co-investigators, as well as from the information on the receptor status and other clinical descriptors for the 373 breast cancer TMA samples that will be interrogated for collagen alignment by SHG and for various protein biomarkers by multiplexed IHC. However, the research design is incomplete due to the omission of triple negative MDA-MB-231 cells in Sub-Aim 1A, whereas this cell line will be used in Sub-Aims 2C & 3A.  Examination of MDA-MB-231 cells in Sub-Aim 1A, which will examine effects of collagen matrix density on prolactin-initiated signaling cascades and cell behaviors (proliferation, survival, differentiation), would have been appropriate.

imp_text: TNBC has an overall worse prognosis than other subtypes of breast cancer due to the lack of targeted treatment options and increased risk of metastasis.  The PI leads a supportive environment and interacts with a number of collaborators that can significantly enhance this research.  The animal work is well justified and the animal care described in detail.  The translational nature of this work is supported by collaboration with a biostatistician and breast pathologist.  The proposal outlines experiments investigating c-Abl as a potential biomarker for TNBC response to docetaxel therapy, the underlying mechanism of c-Abl interactions with p53 family members, and upstream regulation by TGFb.  Potentially 2 new therapeutic agents could arise from this research (DPH and sercurinine), which would significantly enhance therapeutics for TNBC.
sig_text_str: . TNBC has a higher incidence of metastasis and rapid tumor progression, with limited treatment options than other subtypes of breast cancer. . C-Abl could potentially provide a selective biomarker for TNBC cases with a sensitivity to chemotherapy with docetaxel. . Securinine is an agent used in Eastern medicine for the treatment of cancers.  Understanding the mechanism of its effects as well as efficacy for the treatment of metastatic TNBC could expand therapeutic options for patients with TNBC. . C-Abl has been implicated as an oncogenic target in other types of cancer including leukemia.  If c-Abl acts as a tumor suppressor in TNBC, these findings could alter our understanding of the underlying biology of c-abl signaling.
inv_text_str: . As co-director of breast cancer group and leader of TGF-b focus group, the PI has significant expertise on the experiments detailed in this proposal. . PI has assembled a large team of collaborators with expertise in biostatistics and bioinformatics, breast pathology, contrast MRI and imaging, protein kinase chemistry, as well as skilled members of his laboratory including an experienced research technician, graduate student, and sr. research associate.  In addition, the PI will hire a postdoctoral research associate to execute the experiments detailed in this proposal. . In addition to personnel that collaborate closely with PI, there are also consulting collaborators, including an expert in drug development and biomarker validation, director of the breast cancer program at Case Western, and a fellow faculty member who has expertise with securinine analogues in vivo, which is a focus of aim 4.
inn_text_str: . Strong preliminary data suggesting that c-Abl acts by reversing EMT programs and inhibiting tumor growth in vivo. . Using a novel 3D culture system, PI has demonstrated plasticity of TGFb signaling as a function of tissue compliance. . PI and collaborators have generated novel imaging modalities for TNBC in vivo.  These imaging modalities can be used to examine how treatment alters tumor microenvironment.

imp_text: This proposal addresses a significant gap in the identification of biomarkers for prognosis and treatment of castration resistant prostate cancer.  Sox2 is a novel target pathway, of particular interest given its role in regulation of stem cell activity in embryonic stem cell cultures.  Identification of novel pathways of regulation by Sox2 in prostate cancer cell lines, in vivo, and in patient-derived tissue, could significantly enhance our understanding both of CRPC as well as stem cell biology, which could have impact in multiple fields of research.  The environment for the execution of the experiments outlined in this proposal is strong for prostate cancer biology.  The approach to examine the hypotheses proposed by the PI were also strong, particularly in Aims 1 and 2.  Although the approach in Aim 3 addresses the overarching hypothesis, the genetic combination used to transform the primary prostate cells may not be as clinically relevant.  Although the PI describes consulting a biostatistician regarding sample size for vertebrate animal use, it is not described in the text how the calculations were performed or the group sizes for the experiments performed was not detailed in the animal use section.
sig_text_str: . Castration resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) has few treatment options.  Identification of Sox2 and Sox2 regulated signaling pathways present in CRPC may lead to new targets for therapeutic modalities in this population. . The understanding of Sox2 regulation of genes in adult stem cells would increase the understanding of this biology in a number of fields. . Identification of Sox2 as an early biomarker for CRPC may be important for treatment decisions and prognosis, as there are limited biomarkers that can be used prognostically.
sig_text_wkn: . Transcription factors have been difficult to target therapeutically.  Sox2 itself may be an important biomarker but itself would not be a therapeutic target. . It is not clear that the experimental design in this application could conclusively determine that Sox2 basal cells are the cells of origin for aggressive prostate tumors.
inv_text_str: . PI has a strong publication record in prostate cell xenografts and prostate cancer. . PI has a strong pathology contributor who will oversee tissue collection and processing, which is an important component of Aim 3. . A number of recently accepted manuscripts, including one investigating the role of Sox2 in prostate cancer.
inv_text_wkn: . Biosketches were not included for other key personnel.
inn_text_str: . Sox2 has not been previously explored as a biomarker for CRPC and represents a novel biomarker for this disease. . Identification of how Sox2 functions in CRPC to regulate proliferative effects compared to invasive and metastatic effects will enhance our understanding of Sox2 in adult cells compared with embryonic stem cells.
inn_text_wkn: . It is not clear that targeting Sox2 pathways would directly impact the differentiation state of the cells within the tumor.
app_text_str: . In Aim 1, strong preliminary data is presented in support of the hypothesis that expression of Sox2 in androgen-responsive prostate cancer cell lines may confer resistance to docetaxel and anti-androgen therapy.  Given that FGF5 expression is restricted to fetal development, FGF5 may be a clinically useful therapeutic target. . Aim 2 also has strong preliminary data to support the hypothesis.  The data support the concept of different gene expression profiles between Sox2 in the context of embryonic stem cells and prostate cancer cells. . In Aim 2, the combination of gene expression profiling of laser capture dissected primary tumors with comparative analysis of published gene expression sets promotes the ability to determine prognostic information from their new expression data.
app_text_wkn: . In Aim 2, given the variation of the prostate cancer cell lines, inherent genetic variability in patient-derived samples, and early stage (patient samples) vs late stage (cancer cell lines) comparison, it is not clear that there will be significant overlap with the expression analysis for Sox2. . The combination of oncogenes utilized for transformation of the cultured primary prostate cells in Aim 3 is artificial, in particular Large T antigen.  It is not clear whether this combination of oncogenes in conjunction with forced expression of androgen receptor reflects the biology of CRPC. . imp_text: This is a well written proposal which investigates the role of Net1 in cell mobility and metastasis.  Patients diagnosed with breast cancer metastasis have limited treatment options, and identification of a novel regulator of metastasis, potentially regulated by a clinically relevant inhibitor increases the significance of this proposal.  The PI is in a supportive environment with the necessary resources to perform the experiments outlined in the proposal, as well as collaborators to assist with the mouse model experiments.  The vertebrate animal experiments are well justified, including number and care of the mice.  The experiments outlined in Aims 1 and 2 are well supported with preliminary data and explore clinically relevant mechanisms of Net1 function.  Aim 3 is potentially exciting, however, would be more supported with an initial characterization of the mammary phenotype of the novel Net1 mouse model.
sig_text_str: . Metastasis is a complex disease, and the molecular pathways contributing to cell motility within the tumor have not been well characterized. . Net1 may regulate actin cytoskeletal remodeling which is necessary for cellular mobility and may be critical for the acquisition of metastatic potential. . Net1 may be regulated by acetylation, and HDAC inhibitors, which are already in clinical trials, may be repurposed in targeted therapy for Net1-induced metastasis.  This would be a potential novel therapy for metastatic breast cancer.
inv_text_str: . The PI has a strong background in biochemistry, which is important for the experiments outlined in Aims 1 and 2. . PI and collaborators have successful track records for publication and have previous evidence of collaboration and funding together.
inv_text_wkn: . The PI has not published using in vivo models previously.  This weakness is in part mitigated by collaborators interested in working with the PI with experience in this area. . While both collaborators have experience with transgenic mouse models and xenografts to study cancer, neither has expertise in mammary gland development or tumor pathology which may be particularly useful for Aim 3 of this proposal.
inn_text_str: . RhoA has been implicated as an important regulator of invasion and motility, but the molecular pathways regulating RhoA are not clear.  These studies would contribute to our understanding of one mechanism regulating RhoA activation.  This understanding could be beneficial beyond breast cancer metastasis research. . Inhibitors of histone deacetylases are already in clinical trials.  Understanding how histone deacetylases impact Net1 signaling may expand the utility of these therapeutics, as well as provide for more targeted therapy for metastases. . Net1 has not been implicated in breast cancer metastases, and these studies would provide early evidence for a role in invasion and metastasis in novel xenograft and transgenic mouse models.
app_text_str: . Preliminary data for Aim 1 is strong.  The experiments outlined in the proposal address the underlying question about regulation of Net1 activity through acetylation.  Given the clinical significance of HDAC inhibitors, this investigation into other targets of HDAC inhibitors that might alter metastasis is timely. . Aim 2 examines the relationship between Net1 and RAK in regulation of focal adhesions and cellular motility.  The preliminary data supports their hypothesis, and understanding the role of Net1 in cellular mobility is potentially an important underlying mechanism of metastasis.  The experiments in Aim 2 address their hypothesis.
app_text_wkn: . In Aim 3, the PI states that constitutive knock down of Net1 in MBA MB 231 is lethal, and it is not clear why inducible knock down would also not be lethal to the breast cancer cells in vivo. . The PI has previously shown that Net1 expression is a poor prognostic indicator for ERa+ breast cancer.  It is not clear why the focus is on ERa- MDA-MB-231 cells in Aim 3.1.  It would add strength to their previous results if overexpression of Net1 in relatively low tumorigenic ERa+ cells, such as MCF7 or T47D cells, enhanced tumor growth and induced metastasis. . In Aim 3.2, since PyMT tumor development is very rapid (occurring at or around the end of puberty), if Net1 KO significantly reduces or delays ductal elongation during mammary gland development, it may significantly impact tumor incidence by reducing the number of target cells for tumorigenesis rather than testing its direct significance in cooperation with PyMT as an oncogene.  This subaim would be significantly strengthened by characterizing the effects of Net1 knock down on mammary gland development prior to initiating these tumor studies. . In Aim 3.2, it is not clear why examination of infiltration of macrophages is a part of the primary tumor characterization.
env_text_str: . imp_text: The goal of these proposed studies are to evaluate the role of c-Abl as a tumor suppressor protein in triple negative breast cancer (TNBC). While oncogenic activity of c-Abl in chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and myeloproliferative disorder was well documented, however, contradictory reports exist for its functions in breast cancer. Consistent with its oncogenic activity several studies identified the oncogenic and metastatic functions of c-Abl in breast cancer. However, the PI has evidence to suggest tumor suppressing functions of c-Abl in TNBC.  Lowered expression of c-Abl mRNA in breast cancer agrees with PI’s findings. The proposal has three specific aims that will define molecular functions of c-Abl in TGF-ß oncogenic signaling, its role in p53 tumor suppressor functions and the preclinical rationale for combining c-Abl and p53 agonists as a treatment modality for TNBC. The strengths of this proposal include potentially a novel molecular role for c-Abl in breast cancer, experienced PI and collaborators, and the infrastructure. However enthusiasm for this proposal diminished because of the descriptive and diffused nature of research strategy may result in limited information of the tumor suppressor functions of c-Abl and the suggestion of activation of protooncogene as a targeted therapeutic strategy. In addition, overdrawn conclusions from weak preliminary data and speculative nature of several proposed experiments.

Strengths include the early stage investigator and strong institutional support. Additionally, the project is significant in investigating the role of a transcription factor in androgen resistance in prostate cancer, a major issue in prostate cancer therapy. However, weaknesses were identified in experimental design some of which are descriptive and biased towards well established oncogenes. Additionally some of the proposed specific aims may result in only a marginal increase in the understanding of the role of Sox2 in prostate cancer.
