While Sox2 has been characterized as an oncogene in squamous cell carcinoma of the lung and esophagus through amplification, the preliminary results suggest no amplification of Sox2 in malignant prostate cancer cells. In fact, it was downregulated in early stages of prostate cancer. Considering similar levels of Sox2 expression were observed in normal as well as in ~10% malignant prostate epithelial cells, proposed studies will have only a marginal impact in the field. . Explanation for oncogenic activity of Sox2 is not provided. Based on the absence of Nanog and Oct4 in Sox2 expressing prostate cancer cell lines, it was argued that Sox2 target genes will be different in malignant prostate epithelial cells, the fact that its co-activators were absent in normal prostate epithelial cells (Fig. 2A) suggest that its oncogenic activity may not be a result of its co-activator selection. It may have a complex regulation in cancer vs normal prostate epithelial cells which was not addressed. . Rationale for the oncogenic functions of Sox2 was developed by comparing its co-activators and target genes in embryonic stem cells rather than in normal prostate epithelial cells. . Relative to the presented preliminary results, outcomes of proposed studies of aims 1.1 and 1.2 may result only in a marginal increase in the understanding of the role of Sox2  in prostate cancer. . Specific aim 3 is not fully developed, it is risky, time consuming, and using well known oncogenes such as large T-antigen, which is not prostate cancer specific. A better alternative would be to analyze Sox2 negative and Sox2 positive cancers. . Considering ubiquitous expression Sox2, it may not be a good target for therapeutic development.

imp_text: This application is based on the notion that metastasis remains the most lethal characteristic of breast cancer (BC) and that our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying this process remains incomplete especially for the more deadly triple-negative breast cancers (TNBCs). The proposed studies are designed to study in detail the role of the tumor suppressor c-Abl and how it is mechanistically related to the TGF-beta signaling pathways, the p53 family members and sensitivity to Docetaxel and Securinine in TNBCs. Based on the extensive in vitro and in vivo preliminary findings, the working hypothesis is that measures capable of promoting c-Abl expression and activation will alleviate TNBC development and metastatic progression. Four concisely presented specific aims are proposed to test this hypothesis. The PI will determine the role of oncogenic TGF-beta  signaling and mechanotransduction to inactivate the tumor suppressing functions of c-Abl in TNBCs (aim 1); determine the role of p53 family members in mediating tumor suppression by c-Abl in TNBCs (aim 2); determine the value of c-Abl to predict TNBC response to Docetaxel (aim 3); and determine the therapeutic effectiveness of Securinine to eradicate TNBCs (aim 4). This is a well-structured, visually enhanced and clearly written grant proposal, by a highly competent investigator who has assembled an extraordinary team of collaborators with very specific but complementary expertise. The studies will be carried out in a scientifically conducive environment at Case Western Reserve University. The proposal is hypothesis driven and is strongly supported by extensive (almost exhaustive), mostly published and highly relevant preliminary data. If successfully completed, data from the proposed study will provide credible novel molecular insights into how c-Abl suppresses TNBC tumorigenicity. It may also lead to translational outcomes such as the use of c-Abl as a biomarker for docetaxel response and the use of Securinine and DPH as novel treatment options for TNBCs.  Although a large body of relevant preliminary data convincingly support the proposed hypotheses, the bulk of these data were generated using one cell line that depicts mouse model of breast cancer (murine 4T1 cells). This raises concerns regarding the contribution of c-Abl in the progression of the more complex and heterogeneous human TNBC; Also, the expression/activity of c-Abl does not seem to be restricted to TNBCs (it is expressed in normal cells as well), suggesting that targeting c-Abl may also affect non-cancerous tissues. Given the very compelling supporting data and the above relatively minor short comings, the enthusiasm for this impactful proposed research remains high.

imp_text: As the most common and the second leading cause of cancer related mortalities among American men, the advanced forms of prostate cancers, are treated with androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). Like most cancer therapies, resistance to ADT is very common leading to relapse of highly malignant prostate cancer also referred to as castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC). The growth of CRPC lesions remains a significant clinical problem and requires new strategies to improve patient survival. This application is based on the identification of Sox2 [SRY (sex determining region Y)-box 2] as one of the developmental genes which is highly expressed in adult prostate epithelial cells compared to seminal vesicle epithelial cells. Sox2 is known to be a transcription factor essential for maintaining the survival and pluripotency of undifferentiated embryonic stem cells (ESCs) and an important epigenetic reprogramming factor. The PI and collaborators have shown that Sox2 functions as an oncogene in prostate cancer cells; and that activation of the Androgen Receptor (AR) suppresses Sox2 expression and is sufficient to promote CRPC growth. Sox2 expression in human prostate tissues increases with tumor grade, and most prostate cancer metastases are Sox2-positive. In ESCs, it has been shown that Sox2 requires Oct4 and Nanog as transcriptional co-factors but these co-factors are not expressed in adult prostate epithelial cells. The central hypothesis of this proposal is that Sox2 functions as an oncogene by regulating a novel set of gene targets to promote prostate cancer cell survival and proliferation, and that Sox2 function requires transcriptional co-regulators other than Oct4 or Nanog in adult prostate epithelial cells. To test this hypothesis, three aims are proposed. Overall, a detail investigation of the function of Sox2 in prostate epithelial cells is important and may lead to not only improved understanding of the role of this transcription factor in prostate cancer progression and the development of resistance to ADT but also novel mechanisms that may be exploited to improve the treatment of the recurrent disease. As a transcription factor, Sox2 may influence the transcription of several genes including other transcription factors; identifying the target gene(s) that are druggable and represent the Sox2-modulated, key regulators of castration resistance may be a challenge. Other weaknesses include the lack of details about other key personnel including a biostatistician devoted to the project and descriptions of the scientific environment and available core facilities; insufficient data to support the relationship between the inhibition of microtubules and Sox2 function; the correlative relationship between upregulation of FGF5 and Sox2 overexpression based on one PCa cell line; the unsupported speculation that Sox2 positive cells will lead to metastatic and Sox2-positive tumors; and the uncertainty associated with generating cell lines from primary PrECs. In spite of these weaknesses, the proposed studies have the potential to generate data that may be useful for novel treatment options for castration resistant PCa.

imp_text: This proposal will investigate the hypothesis that altered ECM and collagen organization shift the hormonal response of breast tumor cells towards tumor progression. This hypothesis is supported by preliminary studies demonstrating that increased ECM stiffness shifts prolactin (PRL) signals away from STAT5 and toward ERK1/2, concomitant with increased invasiveness, and reduced estrogen responsiveness, a phenomenon that is commonly seen in advanced ERa+ tumors. These studies will be directed by two PIs with complementary expertise and a strong team comprising amongst others, an expert in imaging techniques, a medical oncologist, a pathologist, and a biostatistician. The study will also be conducted in a scientifically conducive University of Wisconsin Comprehensive Cancer Center. If successfully completed, data from this study may be useful in the discovery of novel therapeutic targets for luminal-like breast tumors which are resistant to anti-estrogen therapies which may significantly improve the outcome of breast cancer patients who fail to respond to these otherwise effective therapies. Such a discovery and the underlying mechanisms may be helpful to prevent more aggressive and metastatic progression of the tumors. This notwithstanding, the most relevant preliminary data are incompletely presented given that these data are not yet published. Only densitometric analyses of blots or quantified IF images are presented. Without some of the raw data, it is hard to make the determination that the purported switch from STAT5 to ERK1/2 activation does occur with matrix stiffness. This underscores the involvement of integrins, FAK and SFK in the PRL-induced signal transduction rather than a potential cross-talk from the PRL receptor. It is possible that other cell survival pathways such as the PI3 kinase/Akt as well as other stress activated kinases could be activated with matrix stiffness. Another major issue lies in the data showing that PRL receptor levels decrease with matrix stiffness, making signaling from this receptor and the effect of PRL, non-essential. Given that the rationale for the proposed studies is based on the hormone-induced switch from STAT5 to ERK1/2 activation, the enthusiasm for the proposed studies greatly diminished with the incompletely presented supporting data.

While the results may be convincing, it is more relevant to show the blots from which the densitometry was performed. The switch from STAT5 to ERK1/2 is the basis for this study. While the changes in STAT5 and ERK1/2 are significant in one luminal-like cell line, T47D cells (Fig. 1-1 and 1-2), the changes are only modest in fibroblasts (Fig.2-4), raising the question as to whether these effects are specific for tumor cells. A modest increase in ERK activation e.g. in the fibroblasts may not substantially account for the major changes in cell behavior. Other cell survival pathways such as the PI3 kinase/Akt as well as other stress activated kinases could be activated by matrix stiffness but are apparently not considered. • PRL acts via its receptor PRLR. The potency of PRL as a ligand to effect changes in cell behavior is to a large extent, dependent on its activation of the receptor. The expression of PRL receptor is shown to paradoxically decrease with matrix stiffness suggesting that the switch from STAT5 to ERK1/2 activation following treatment of cells with PRL does not require PRL receptor and/or PRL. The notion that this is mediated via integrins, SFKs and FAK undermines the logic that PRL signals via its receptor. The proposed experiments may confirm the findings presented in the preliminary data but may not provide a plausible explanation for the change in hormonal action following changes in matrix stiffness. • An explanation for the specific focus on the expression of integrin-alpha6 and MMP2 among other members of these families and at the mRNA rather than the protein level may be helpful to integrate the role of these proteins on the changes in hormonal responses with matrix stiffness.

imp_text: This proposal seeks to conduct an in-depth analysis of Foxo1 and 3 transcription factors in CD4 and CD8 T cell differentiation through regulation of gene expression programs. The PI has published 2 Nat Immunol and 1 Immunity articles demonstrating that the Foxo TFs modulate various properties (expansion, phenotype, functional subset) of T cells, and has generated a host of tools for studying CD8 and CD4 T cell differentiation in response to both acute and chronic infections. Together, these constitute a major strength of the proposal. The PI is also a senior investigator in the field, who has made some key scientific advances. The proposed studies are novel, and have the potential to identify newer means of pharmacologic or immunologic interventions to manipulate T cell immunity. imp_text: The goal of this proposal is to define molecular regulation of B cell motility during germinal center formation vis a vis actin-regulatory protein L-plastin. The proposal is supported by strong preliminary data demonstrating that L-plastin is essential for B cell motility, germinal center formation and class-switched antibodies. Studies aimed at delineating the functional domains and signaling cascades involved in L-plastin mediated B cell motility, and B-cell specific functional significance of L-plastin are proposed. The experiments are well-designed and the proposed studies are novel, with long-ranging impact on our knowledge of antibody production during immunodeficiency, autoimmunity and vaccination. The new PI is well-trained, well-supported and is in an intellectually rich environment with strong collaborators. He has been very productive in his PhD and modestly so during post-doc, but has published a JI paper from his independent lab.

imp_text: This is a R01 proposal by a well-established investigator who seeks to address the role of ROS in thymic atrophy. Based on preliminary evidence that thymic stromal cells are deficient in catalase, a key enzyme involved in protection from oxidative damage) the PI hypothesizes that early thymic atrophy is caused by accelerated oxidative damage of the stroma due to lack of catalase. This is a potentially interesting proposal, that will certainly merit more detailed mechanistic studies in the future. However, at present the reviewer is of the opinion that direct proof that catalase expression specifically by thymic stromal cells can rescue thymic atrophy is needed before embarking on the detailed mechanistic studies. While studies using catalase Tg mice are promising, they may reflect a generalized anti-aging effect of reduced oxidative stress. Moreover, the scope of proposed work is limited. Thus, this proposal better fits the exploratory/developmental R21 funding mechanism.

imp_text: This proposal will investigate the signaling pathways regulated by Sox2 and to use such information to predict cancer progression and to establish Sox2 as a target for treatment of advanced prostate cancer. Understanding the mechanisms and establishing novel therapeutic targets for treating therapy resistant and metastatic prostate cancer is significant. PI is an early stage investigator. The concept that Sox2 expression in the epithelial cells can modulate therapy resistance has some innovation. Hypothesis is sound, rationale justified by preliminary data and research design is appropriate to achieve the goals. The main weakness, in my opinion, is in the magnitude of the study, which encompasses 4 very ambitious aims, which a multitude of approaches, cell lines and mouse models in each one of them. The proposal is also too dense and includes an excessive amount of, not always relevant preliminary data.

The application is very well written and is organized logically to address the main hypothesis. It systematically approaches the problem using both in vitro and in vivo approaches, as well as patient samples. It tackles a highly significant problem in prostate and has the potential to identify new biomarkers and therapeutic targets. This reviewer is highly enthusiastic about the success of this application.

The proposal however, is unfocused, lacks coherence and reads at some points as descriptive and exploratory without a clear direction. It is not clear how the experiments proposed directly address the hypothesis.

imp_text: This is a well-written new R01 application (though it says in the text that it was a resubmission) from an established investigator to study the role of Foxo1 and Foxo3 in T cell memory. Strengths of the proposal include the pertinent preliminary data, availability of elegant conditional knockout mouse models, and several reasonable hypotheses about some roles of Foxo1 and 3 in T cell fate decisions. The investigator seems to be strong (though for a grant reviewed in 2016, this investigator does not list any publications since 2011, and hence got "dinged"). Scientific environment is excellent. The approach was strong but included weaknesses stemming in part from excessive reductionism on the one hand and exploratory data gathering on the other. However, several experiments proposed were quite strong, such as following up on potential roles of Foxo in regulating IL7R and in transmitting the effects of Icos. Aim 4 seemed to be an unnecessary and overcomplicated ad-on.
sig_text_str: . The topic of this proposal is considered to be significant as understanding the transcriptional control of T cell responses is fundamental to our understanding of immune function.
sig_text_wkn: . Many of the studies involve full deletion of a major transcription factor, so the effects are expected to be widespread. Although this is admittedly an important way to start to figure out the role of the factor, the models studied are highly reductionist. One could argue that such models are most useful when they rule out the need for a transcription factor, rather than the reverse. This proved useful in showing that Foxo1 is not needed in Tfh development or function (Aim 3). . The PI seems to suggest strongly the application of this knowledge to vaccination, but the therapeutic manipulation of Foxo transcription factors seems a distant possibility, mainly because this factor is expressed in many cell types in which it has various roles.
inv_text_str: . Todd Baker is a highly experience scientist. He is Professor and Chair of Molecular Biology at UC San Diego. .
inv_text_wkn: . The PI appears to have no publications listed for the last five years.
inn_text_str: . This proposal is moderately innovative. The mouse models are now somewhat standard, but the applicant has assembled an outstanding set of models to investigate Foxo transcription factors in T cells.
inn_text_wkn: . Many of the experiments appear to be modeled on other studies, particularly of Foxo1 in B cells, so they seem to involve rather standard approaches.
app_text_str: . The approach is largely clearly explained and the PI shows that mouse model systems are available to study the role of Foxo1 in T cell subsets and in some cases loss of Foxo1 can be induced after development or T cell activation. . Aim 1 is largely straightforward characterization of the effects of Foxo1 deficiency on T cell responses. Of the subAims, 1c, 1d and 1f seem to be the strongest and best focused. Aim 1e might be premature as it must first be established if T cells survive the absence of both Foxo1 and Foxo3. . Aim 3a is well-focused and likely to lead to clearly interpretable data regarding the role of Foxo1 in transmitting key signals from Icos. . Aim 3b is somewhat cursory but reasonable. .
app_text_wkn: . There are aspects of the approach that are highly reductionistic and also exploratory. . Aim 2 appears to be a basic survey of the transcriptional control by Foxo transcription factors. The experiments are reasonable but broad and exploratory. . Aim 3c involves studies to understand why Foxo1 CD4 T cells die upon activation. Most of the studies investigate oxidative stress or Bcl2 family members. Experiments should be included to investigate modes of T cell killing as well, such as FasL, etc. . Studies in Aim 4 seem forced in that it aims for translational relevance. The experiments combine a highly complicated in vivo infection model with the complex Foxo knockout models. Data is sure to be obtained but the interpretation will be complicated and in the end probably not very useful.

imp_text: This is a good R01 proposal from a promising early career investigator to study the role of LPL on the T cell dependent B cell response. Strengths include the fact that the investigator generated knockout mice and is planning to generate conditional knockouts. The knockout mice have B cell phenotypes consistent with the underlying hypotheses, though LPL may play roles through other cell types as well. The potential significance is that LPL may teach us about highly important processes such as cyclic reentry of B cells to germinal centers. If the key phenotypes are B cell intrinsic, the LPL-fl/fl;CD19cre/+ mice will be a useful model for further study. However, the project is at a very early stage of development and so it is not really clear yet if the correct cell types are being studied. The retroviral reconstitution experiments were also underdeveloped, so it is unclear if the approach outlined will provide useful data. Novelty was modest and technical innovation below average. The research environment is excellent.
sig_text_str: . The proposal is based on a knockout mouse with altered marginal zone B cell numbers, altered in vitro migration, and defective germinal center B cell response associated with a modest reduction in T cell dependent antibody production. The phenotype suggests some biological significance.

inn_text_str: . The applicant has developed a knockout mouse in the LPL gene and identified phenotypes. The proposed use of West Nile virus challenge is unusual, but on balance adds to the proposal.

app_text_str: . This proposal has some solid preliminary data coming from the LPL-/- mouse analysis. . The experimental approach is not unreasonable, but it does not take into account the possibility that findings will fail to confirm the PI's hypothesis. . Migration and transwell studies are important, and should work provided that the level of retroviral expression is comparable to WT. . The straightforward immunization studies will provide readouts for potential defects in the B cell restricted knockouts and the methodology is well worked out. .
app_text_wkn: . Overall, the proposal appears to be a bit underdeveloped, with many open questions that limit enthusiasm at this stage. As a result, many of the proposed experiments are designed to answer basic questions and so appear somewhat pedestrian. . The retroviral transduction approach is reasonable, but until preliminary data is shown that WT control LPL can reconstitute function, the approach is unproven. Also, it was quite unclear what a partial phenotype predicted in the Table would look like. The retroviral technical approach is already being superseded by CRISPR type mutagenesis approaches, hence the overall approach of that experiment seems out of date. . Since only a small subset of B cell migrate, and the KO B cells lack a MZ compartment, it may be that the subset of cells able to migrate well in that assay is simply missing, rather than crippled for migration. This could also explain the relative lack of Pyk in LPL B cells in Fig 1. . While looking in primary B cells is preferred, many biochemical experiments exploring mechanism would be facilitated by use of cell line models. . The PI assumes that in LPL-fl/fl;CD19cre/+ mice the B cell phenotypes will hold. This should first be verified. There should also be a credible plan for what to do if the phenotypes turn out not to be B cell intrinsic. This is especially important because T cells are also apparently affected in the full knockout model. .

Strengths of the application include the experience of the investigator, strong preliminary data, potential scientific and translational significance to bone marrow transplantation, and technical innovation. Some of the significance was tempered by the intensive study already given to CXCR4 and IL7 in the context of bone marrow hematopoiesis. Scientific approaches were relatively strong but the rationale and scope of the studies in Aims 2 and 3 had some flaws. The research environment is strong but the availability of dedicated 2 photon facility was not made clear.
sig_text_str: . Although CXCR4 is a well-known player in hematopoiesis that has been studied intensively, the proposal aims to provide important new information about cell movement and juxtaposition in situ through extensive use of 2-photon microscopy.
sig_text_wkn: . As indicated above, these studies are in part confirmatory of other types of study regarding the roles and significance of CXCR4, IL7, and CXCL12. . Although microenvironment is likely important, B cell hematopoiesis is surprisingly plastic, and can take place in the absence of bone marrow in, for example, osteopetrotic mice. .
inv_text_str: . Dr Jackson appears to be well trained and was highly productive in the postdoctoral phase with Prof. Cyster. . Dr. Jackson appears to have most of the technical expertise required to complete the proposed project.

inn_text_str: . This proposal scores high on technical innovation. The techniques necessary to carry out two photon microscopy in bone marrow are highly specialized and the present proposal provides numerous valuable tools, including well defined mouse models, novel reporter mice, and the availability of specific drug inhibitors. . There was good conceptual innovation in the discussion of the potential role of stromal (non hematopoietic) CXCR4 expression on hematopoiesis. .
inn_text_wkn: . Some of the sections could be improved by further conceptual innovations, particularly Aims 2 and 3.
app_text_str: . Aim 1 was the clear strength of this proposal. The preliminary data were novel and clear, the rationale strong and the experimental approaches appropriate. The studies have scope in that they suggest ways to manipulate engraftment during bone marrow transplantation if autocrine signaling through CXCR4 is important for stromal support of hematopoiesis. . Aim 2 also had clear goals, but the scope for novel discovery seems more limited. It seems likely that the relative placement of CLPs and IL7-producing cells can be determined, but it is less clear what value this information would have. Having a look at the role of IL2 and IL15 in this system was reasonable but speculative. . Studies involving the use of CXCR4 agonist are of great value, though there should be some controls for off-target effects.
app_text_wkn: . . There was limited discussion of pro/preB cell proliferation and its role in altering cell position relative to stromal components. . The relative dependence of cells on the presence of stromal support vs IL7 is well known and known to change with development. The PI appears to be able to identify these cells using surface markers in the static state, but it seems the preB/proB distinction could not be made in 2-photon experiments, which might be limiting. . Aim 3 appeared to be particularly descriptive and the model systems somewhat sketchy. The goals and significance of these studies are somewhat unclear. MD5 B cells are able to edit and the ability to track these cells seems limited. . Taking a look at MRL/lpr mice is interesting in principle, but again speculative and underdeveloped.

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology A Study Section
imp_text: This is a very strong application that addresses the role of Foxo transcription factors in the differentiation and function of multiple T cell subsets. Preliminary data show that CD8 T cells lacking Foxo1 remain elevated and fail to return to a quiescent state after activation. This is explored further in Aims 1 and 2, which address many important aspects of memory T cell differentiation, and will determine the mechanisms responsible. These experiments are very strong and will no doubt contribute significantly to our understanding of pathways regulating CD8 T cell memory. Other preliminary data show increased Tfh and CD4 central memory T cell precursor cells, in addition to decreased Tregs in Foxo1-deficient mice. The mechanism underlying the reason for increased Tfh and Tcm proportions are addressed in Specific Aim 3.  This aim is also very strong, and will decisively address the mechanisms underlying this phenotype, particularly those related to ICOS signaling.  A notable weakness is Specific Aim 4, which does not integrate well with the rest of the proposal.  This is because the models proposed to justify these experiments are overly complex, making them virtually impossible to substantiate. Other weaknesses are mostly minor and relate to technical issues.  In summary, this is an excellent proposal addressing very important biological questions. The proposal is from a very productive investigator, with strong collaborative support, and in an outstanding research environment.
sig_text_str: . Understanding the genesis of T cell memory on a molecular level is critical for improving vaccines and other immune therapies. . This application addresses the role of the Foxo transcription factors in many key T cell types, and will yield critical information regarding their role in T cell differentiation. . The role that Foxo1 plays in T cell metabolism is particularly important, given our knowledge that the metabolic state affects T cell differentiation.
sig_text_wkn: . The connections between the proposed experiments and understanding chronic virus infections are tenuous.  Foxo3 may be important in HIV infection for reasons other than those explored in this application, and there is no evidence presented that indications Foxo1 are involved in T cell exhaustion.
inv_text_str: . Great productivity from previous 2 year ARRA funding. . The PI’s publication record is excellent, both in the last three years and over a long and productive career.
inn_text_str: . The PI has assembled an impressive array of conditionally deficient mouse strains, that represent a unique resource with which to address the research questions. . Several innovative hypotheses are tested.  The hypothesis that ICOS inactivation of Foxo1 is responsible for enhanced Tfh and reduced Tregs is particularly intriguing. . Innovative pathways are presented, which will be tested rigorously in well-designed experiments.
app_text_str: . The experiments presented build on strong preliminary data reporting the presence of a larger population of memory cells following Foxo1 deficiency.  These cells also retain effector molecules such as granzyme B after the acute response. . Specific Aim 1 addresses many important questions relating to the role of Foxo1 and Foxo3 in the memory CD8 T cell response. . CHIP-seq data obtained in Specific Aim 2 will provide very valuable information regarding Foxo1 target genes. . Experiments in Specific Aim 3 will decisively address the hypothesis that ICOS signaling-mediated inactivation of Foxo1 is responsible for Tfh and central memory differentiation. . Specific Aim 3 also very thoroughly addresses the mechanisms underlying the decreased survival of CD4 T cells lacking Foxo1.

While preliminary data support the authors contention that a larger pool of CD4 central memory precursor cells are present in the absence of Foxo1, the data is much less convincing for the larger Tfh population. . Gene expression profiling on Tfh cells will be very challenging given the very small populations shown in the preliminary data.  While the use of in vitro-derived Tfh partly mitigates this concern, it is not clear to what extent they are similar to in vivo-generated Tfh. . study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: This is a highly focused and very well organized, well reasoned proposal that poses clear testable hypotheses.  The premise proposed by the PI is that thymic epithelial cells are more susceptible to oxidative damage due to low expression of catalase, and this leads to thymic involution that is observed in adults. Preliminary data are minimal, but support the hypothesis. This is a significant area because thymic involution leads to reduced thymic output of T cells, restricting the immune repertoire, making elderly patients more susceptible to infections and less responsive to vaccination.  Incisive experiments are proposed to test the hypothesis, and there is a high likelihood of success.  There are some concerns that experiments will compare thymic epithelial cells with only one other epithelial population, salivary gland epithelial cells, whereas epithelial cells from a number of other organs may be more appropriate.  While the focus of the grant is admirable, the work proposed is limited in scope, and do not justify the five year period of funding requested.

Evidence of senior author publications from the PI as an independent investigator would increase the enthusiasm for this proposal. One notable weakness is Specific Aim 3, which seems to use an overly complex series of mouse crosses and bone marrow chimeric mice.  While this is all likely achievable, the possible caveats and limitations of such systems were not adequately addressed. There were also concerns about the interpretation of some of the phenotypes observed in CXCR4 deficiency, as they relate to homing to the bone marrow per se, or specifically homing to IL-7-producing cells.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry B Study Section
imp_text: Dr. Sullivan, an Early Stage Investigator from The School of Pharmacy at Univ. Wisconsin-Madison, proposes a novel approach for identifying new types of secondary metabolites secreted by actinomycetes. These new compounds will be screened for antitumor activity, anti-quorum sensing activity in bacteria and against MRSA (with the help of capable collaborators). The approach relies on metabolomic profiling (via LCMS) of actinomycetes-produced compounds secreted by bacteria grown in various media in a microtiter plate format, which will be followed by the principal component analysis of such compounds (PCA). The compounds with previously undescribed mass/charge ratios are believed to correlate with new types of secondary metabolites. Screening of various media and focusing only on novel compounds is expected to lower the probability of finding already known compounds, which is a major problem in the field. The second novel idea is to co-culture actinomycetes in the presence of other bacteria to induce cryptic secondary metabolite clusters. Marine actinomycete species, which are grossly underexplored as the source of novel natural compounds, will be isolated by the PI during expeditions (from marine sponges living in the waters around Florida Keys and Puerto Rico) as well as from the collection of an actinomycete microbiologist. If successful, the proposal has the potential to establish a new paradigm in more efficient identification of novel natural drug-like compounds.
sig_text_str: • Natural compounds remain to be the major source of novel anti-tumor and anti-microbial drugs. • Re-identification of already known natural compounds is a major problem in the filed. The proposed approach has the potential to solve this problem. • Focusing on marine actinomycetes as a grossly underexplored source of secondary metabolites has significant promise.
sig_text_wkn: • The choice of target processes for secondary metabolites may be suboptimal because neither compounds that activate Notch pathway to inhibit neuroendocrine cancers nor anti-quorum sensing compounds have been proved to be relevant in clinic.

inn_text_str: • Using metabolomic profiling of secreted drug-like compounds is novel.  • Co-culturing as a means of activating cryptic gene clusters is an underexplored way of increasing diversity of produced secondary metabolites.

Are these media sufficiently different to produce the expected diversity of secondary metabolites? • Secondary metabolites are commonly produced at late stages of cultivation, after the exponential growth. Using verified targets would be preferred. • The use of multiple omics approaches to identify gene clusters responsible for novel secondary metabolites seems open-ended. A more focus, candidate approach, that combine the types of compounds with genome analysis, could be more direct and productive.

imp_text: This application proposes detailed mechanistic investigation of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) transport from the inner membrane through the periplasm to the outer membrane of bacteria. The focus is on three components involved in LPS transport, i.e. the innermembrane protein (LptC) that deposits LPS onto LptA, which forms a bridge to the outermembrane protein LptD (or delivers LPS as a shuttle). The proposed methodology involves primarily site-directed mutagenesis to decipher the LPS binding site in LptA, ITC for determining relative protein affinities to LPS in LptA, LptC and LptD, and EPR-based approaches to probe conformational changes occuring in LptA upon binding to LPS or to LptD. Because LPS is essential for most diderms (Gram-negative bacteria), understanding of its transmembrane transport is of fundamental importance in bacteriology. LPS transport also represents an intriguing target for designing new antibiotics. However, it is unclear that experiments proposed here will improve the potential for drug design. Preliminary data and expertise of the PI instill confidence in the feasibility of the proposed studies; however, only modest impact on the field is expected because (i) interactions of the Lpt components have already been characterized in vitro and in vivo, and (ii) resolution of the EPR studies is limited to yield definitive results and it may be subject to interpretation.

imp_text: The majority of the proposal is basic sciences driven and related to Gram-negative bacterial physiology as it relates to LPS transport from the inner membrane to outer membrane along the LPS transport structures. Ultimately, the establishment of these mechanisms underlying LPS transport and the presentation of LPS in the microbes may create new avenues for drug discovery efforts against Gram-negative pathogens.  Although these are not specifics as such studied in this proposal, the amount of potential fundamental new knowledge that could be obtained from this proposed work overshadows the lack of a defined translatable end on the horizon.

The endotoxin LPS is essential for Gram-negative microbe survival as it forms the protective barrier for the microbial cell. . In humans LPS causes septic shock leading to inflammation and death. . The PI claims that an understanding of LPS synthesis and transport will be the foundation on which to develop novel antibiotics.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry B Study Section
imp_text: This application proposes to apply modern drug discovery library approaches to developing better lead-like and diverse screening libraries of natural products.  The applicants intend to apply modern small molecule drug library selection criteria specifically to natural products from marine sources, particularly bacteria that synergistically grow on marine sponges, an area of expertise for the team.  Furthermore, they also propose co-culturing bacteria from these sources arguing that interactions between symbiotic bacteria colonizing marine sponges are conducive to drive production of increased chemical diversity. This proposal comprises an excellent group of established investigators at fine institutions.  Furthermore, the concept of combining modern technologies and higher throughput approaches to the identification of new chemical scaffolds from natural sources is modestly innovative.  Unfortunately, the application has issues with presentation, particularly in the preliminary data relative to what is really new from their purportedly more robust filtering approaches as well as the fact that they allude to new scaffolds but give no information regarding structures and true novelty due to intellectual property issues.  While appropriate protection is oftentimes required by universities prior to disclosure, grant applications are not considered public disclosure; the information presented is not useful in terms of assessing the value of the techniques proposed.  Most of the scaffolds shown appear to be (based on the applicants’ statements) older, known structures – the application is supposed to be demonstrating modern techniques for finding new scaffolds.  Furthermore, several figures in the application are not particularly helpful, one quite garbled (Fig. 2) and others lacking detail and labels on axes.  In general, the application proposes a variety of interesting applications of modern omics discovery to natural product identification and selection, but it is not clear how this whole effort will come together relative to specific numbers expected and clear selection parameters that will produce a good lead-like library of novel natural products.  For example, a broad number of bacteria are projected in total, then combinations/co-cultures and multiple media are selected as well as different possible extraction techniques all leading to what might be a huge number of possible products for assessment.  In what appears to be a totally separate discussion, possible throughputs are discussed, but it is quite difficult to tie the two areas together and really assess what is likely projected and can be done over the period of the proposed program.  It is recommended that the figures should be cleaned up with an eye towards demonstration of the start to finish numbers from strains, cultures and co-cultures, differing media conditions, total extracts and how these will feed through the system and be managed with current and projected throughput.  Possibly a start to finish flowchart from the total numbers of bacteria through the various techniques employed with cutoffs and selection criteria up to the projected number of new chemical entities and how they were selected would clearly demonstrate what this program is doing and will produce.  In that regard, the applicants suggest that they will use modern medicinal chemistry parameters derived from years of pharma experience with synthetic small molecule libraries in order to develop new diverse, drug-like natural products.  A laundry list of parameters is mentioned yet there is little discussion of how these parameters actually relate to natural products and how they will inform selection of more drug-like natural products.  Lipinski, in a seminal article on relating physicochemical properties of small molecules to oral availability, specifically states that natural products appear to be at the fringes if not outside his ‘Rule of Five’ criteria for preselecting orally available drugs.  In fact, that exercise of this application seems somewhat confounding as one should not be preselecting compounds for oral availability as the injectables and encapsulation markets are quite valid.  On the other hand, selections based on solubility and reactivity seem virtually ignored in this application although some of the assessed parameters can correlate with solubility.  In truth, numerous natural product compounds and drugs are metabolically active and chemically reactive leading to toxicity (marine natural products are rife with cytotoxins) and side effects depending on structure and class.  From a clinical perspective, this issue has become much more crucial to drug acceptance and commercial success.  All in all, the application lacks detail and criteria for selecting ideal compounds to plate that will have value in future drug discovery, and it is recommended that a medicinal chemistry consultant with real expertise in selection criteria as well as knowledge of natural products be included in future work Overall, this application is interesting, reasonably significant, and the approaches described have promise for improving and diversifying libraries of natural products.  Unfortunately, issues with presentation, specific details relating to cutoffs and accomplishments and projections for success significantly impacted this review.

The discussion relating to GSK experience with small molecules is somewhat biased relative to conclusions of that article in that target based approaches to new antibiotic discovery was the major failure due to likely permeability issues.  The immediate result was a move to phenotypic primary screens either with pathogenic bacteria or genetically modified strains with specific metabolic readouts allowing some determination of likely targets out of the whole cell screens.  Older chemical libraries were relatively fixed with old privileged scaffolds that show activity (not new or diverse) and newer scaffolds that were either not bioavailable or were metabolically problematic.  There have been numerous computational approaches to improving small molecule library diversity and complexity (e.g. diversity oriented approaches) in order to change this situation.  As correctly pointed out by the applicants, however, new and diverse NPs can certainly contribute. . One of the primary reasons for the decline in approvals is the fact that large pharma is abandoning antibiotic drug discovery due to net present value consideration and cost versus returns, not because they cannot discover new antibiotics.

Application of a diverse set of standard instrumental techniques, experimental methods and analysis tools in combination with an underserved source of natural products, marine sponges and bacteria, including co-culturing of symbiotic bacteria is a strength of this proposed program. . Multiple media choices and growth and isolation conditions are critical to optimizing chemical diversity output. . Two reasonable initial target areas are chosen, a phenotypic screen for bacterial quorum sensing and Notch-1 in cancer under experienced researchers.  The applicants imply that small molecule HTS data will be available for comparison of hit rates and quality, although it is presumed that the synthetic small molecule libraries may have screened in HTS already as per statements in the application.

Figures are a mess and lack clarity – unlabeled axes, presumption that hit rates are exciting without a comparison to a good synthetic library as a control, presumed novelty of output when the scaffolds given appear known already etc.  The really potentially interesting compounds are blinded due to IP issues, and the ones shown (as per the apparent discussion) seem to be known scaffolds for the most part. . All in all a lot of information is presented, yet it is not totally clear how all these techniques come together in a sensible linear fashion to produce higher quality and more diverse libraries.  It might behoove the applicant to reduce examples to the very best example of preliminary screening results that produces really new things and show a clear flowchart of how that strain was selected versus the full proposed strategy in a step-by-step fashion. . A lot of discussion is given to the dogma that NPs are where drug discovery is at and the proposed approach will produce robust numbers of new drug-like chemical diversity, yet, at the same time, apparently many of the reported early hits in the preliminary data do not appear to be novel. . Many of the current NP drugs/library components are broad antimetabolites and cytotoxins (also a feature of marine natural products) – presumably library filtering will apply reactivity filters as such compounds are generally out of favor in the clinic where side effects are profound, but this issue is not discussed. . The applicants constantly allude to using drug-like parameters to winnow libraries but it is not clear how that will be done when NPs oftentimes do not follow Lipinski’s ‘Rule of Five.’ . It is difficult to determine how the applicants picked the total numbers of bacteria that will be found and relate those numbers to what will result and whether the current throughput can handle that level.  A clear diagram covering the program with numbers in feeding through culturing and co-culturing, various media and culturing experiments, through extraction conditions, isolation screening and analysis would help readability.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry A Study Section
imp_text: Understanding the molecular basis of normal physiology and disease has been approached via attempts to control gene function with genomic, spatial, and temporal specificity.  Numerous techniques have been applied toward that goal, but the applicants point out that these methods lack the necessary specificity and temporal control to truly dissect the role of specific genes in normal growth processes and disease.  Hence, it is proposed to use light gated technology to specifically activate novel caged morpholino oligonucleotides (cMOs - single and double lariat forms) that are designed to minimize interactions with binding targets until light activated cleavage.  The applicants also propose that dual (possibly more) cMOs with different wavelength requirements for cleavage might allow interrogation of multiple genes temporally depending on the cleavage/activation sequence. Overall, this is a well-reasoned and written application by an excellent and experienced team at excellent institutions.  The collaboration between the two chemical groups is a plus as the chemistry will require significant effort and diverse views and approaches.  The applicants project bold claims regarding superiority relative to other technologies which remain to be proven especially considering the toxicity and selectivity issues seen with previous forms, although the reasoning for the newer single and double lariat forms appears sound.  Some concerns exist with the single lariat forms in terms of their ability to bind oligonucleotides prior to release as it would appear that they are likely to have longer exposed sequences.  Furthermore, the preliminary data suggest that release may not be 100 % (efficiency of release or selectivity versus wavelength) either in terms of the target wavelength relative to other wavelengths (potential problem in dual systems).  The applicants, however, propose reasonable approaches to looking at these issues and altering outcomes that abrogate these concerns significantly.  As well, toxicity outcomes will just have to be looked at versus the various cage forms and light activated and cleavable linkers, although it is also not clear that what is proposed will advance these systems.  The zebrafish model and the experienced biological collaborator are both strong.  This application is deemed potentially impactful, significant and concerns are minor leading to an excellent evaluation

study_section: Biochemistry and Biophysics of Membranes Study Section
imp_text: The aim of this program is to delineate how the essential endotoxin-transport protein, LptA, transports endotoxin within the cell with projected applications to new drug discovery against pathogenic bacteria.  This is a reasonably well written and modestly innovative application from an experienced and highly qualified team of investigators at quality institutions.  Modest preliminary data are presented or alluded to suggesting that the necessary model systems are in place and that the proposed studies can progress effectively over the proposed five year period.  Enthusiasm was modestly tempered due to concerns regarding the techniques used including protein labeling that might alter properties as well as the study of isolated proteins that might not recapitulate the true biological milieu under which this process occurs.  Furthermore, while the team is strong in the application of biological tools to assess the role of LptA in LPS binding and transport, it appears to lack a person experienced in applying these tools to assay development and drug discovery (active site assessment, druggability etc.) when a stated longer term goal is the application of the tools described to potential drug discovery.  Overall, the work described could have a significant impact on knowledge about LPS transport with potential applications to new antibiotic discovery against new targets. Scored Review Criteria Reviewers will consider each of the five review criteria below in the determination of scientific and technical merit, and provide a separate score and critique for each.

At present the application looks like biologists studying biology just because they have the tools. . Only one publication has accrued from the preliminary work, and no drafts were attached that show synergy and functionality of the team.

imp_text: The investigators propose to develop a template for producing natural product libraries that may reveal novel small molecules with drug-like properties, which may lead to development of new natural drugs or compounds. Although this platform is largely lacking, contrary to the drug development platforms that exist for artificial compounds with therapeutic properties, the proposal in itself is not hypothesis driven. There are hypotheses expressed in Aim 1 and 2, but these could have been more clearly stated throughout the proposal. In addition, a statistics section is missing and there is not enough rationale for clinical applications in the approach. Overall, however, the application is well written and the investigators make a compelling reason for the methodology proposed. study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry A Study Section
imp_text: The purpose of this R01 application is to develop a new class of antisense reagents activated by light, which will be significantly more efficacious than current methods for studies of molecular processes that contribute both to normal physiology and disease in model systems such as the zebra fish. The grant is organized as a primary to Dr. O’Brien with a subcontract to Dr. Anthony Deckers, a collaborator. Because the subcontract is the size of a regular R01, it would be recommended to submit this project as a multi-PI R01 with two separate projects. The inclusion of a multi-PI statement clearly showing what each lab will do would enhance this application. The investigators will use optochemicals paired with novel methods to enhance the temporal resolution of gene antisense experiments. The group has developed several models for silencing genes, and they have shown that they are effective in zebra fish. Optogenetics are still novel and can be used to rapidly silence a gene by light application; a temporal improvement over the commonly used knockout or knockin methods. It is difficult to discern why the investigators have to pay animal overhead, since they appear to maintain their colonies of zebra fish in their own laboratories. It is also difficult to determine who will do what in this two-lab application. If the Deckers lab will perform the methods for combinatorial lariat cMO applications (Aim 3), there is no need for funding of this part of the project until year 3.
sig_text_str: . The proposed studies will lead to a new class of light-activated antisense reagents that will be significantly more efficacious than current reverse-genetic methods. . This lab has developed caged antisense nucleotides, commonly known as morpholinos, to enable light controlled gene silencing with spatiotemporal precision
inv_text_str: . Dr. O’Brien is an Associate Professor at Stanford University. . She received her PhD from Harvard and then did a postdoc at Johns Hopkins, and is well funded from NIH since 2005. . This is a highly accomplished group of investigators that have joined forces in this project.
inv_text_wkn: . A multi-PI statement showing who will do what in the application would have enhanced enthusiasm.
inn_text_str: . Highly innovative project from a leading group in the field.
inn_text_wkn: . If the experiments do not succeed, there is no backup plan.
app_text_str: . The investigators provide ample preliminary data to support their studies. These data are provided in a clear and comprehensible manner.
app_text_wkn: . There are some possible confounds of the study. For example, the investigators mention on page 67 that their previous efforts to generate hairpin cMOs for certain genes were unsuccessful, because the reagents were cytotoxic or “leaky” at doses required for light-activated gene silencing (data not shown). . It is not clear which components of the studies that will be performed by the O’Brien lab, and which will be performed by the Deckers lab. Therefore, it is not clear why one needs to support an R01 equivalent to each of the labs. A better definition of the strengths of each of the groups, and how they will interact (such as in a Multi-PI description) would have enhanced enthusiasm for the proposal. Providing this information at the top of Approach would have made the application more clear. Now, one has to look for the information within the text. . The application is a methods development grant rather than testing specific hypotheses. However, because the development of these novel optogenetic methods and probes can have highly useful application for specific questions in the future, the study still has validity. . The labeling of grant parts is confusing. For example section C.4. represents Specific Aim 3; this is overly complicated and could be simplified. . study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry B Study Section
imp_text: This is a proposal from a young investigator to develop novel approaches to identification of new natural products and selections of these for further screening using metabolomics approaches. A focus on identifying and assaying natural products with more drug-like properties is viewed favorably with the caveat that the well-documented challenges encountered in developing natural products into useful drugs may limit the efficacy of this approach. There is clear innovation in the use of the metabolomics approaches and the use of co-culture. The PI is well-qualified to carry out the proposed studies but has not yet demonstrated development of a robust independent research program. Other investigators add value to the proposal. The approach is generally well thought out but with some significant weaknesses that diminish enthusiasm. .
sig_text_str: . Efforts to more rationally guide the screening of natural products with a focus on chemical diversity and how drug-like compounds are is a worthwhile enterprise.
sig_text_wkn: . While natural products have proven to be excellent discovery tools and have been deployed in the clinic, their development into useful drugs is typically difficult due to their chemical complexity and the need to identify the cellular target of action, so it is not clear that further focus in this area will necessarily have a significant impact on drug development. . A rational case for a focus on natural product discovery approaches being deployed rather than rational approaches based on biological validation of a target, development of appropriate assays, and identification of actives from libraries of drug-like molecules has not been made.
inv_text_str: . The PI clearly has the necessary expertise to carry out the proposed studies. . Dr. Lee and Dr. Corrie add relevant expertise although in their roles as collaborators rather than coPIs the degree of involvement is unclear.
inv_text_wkn: . Listed publications of PI in biosketch are virtually all from time in training, leading to some concern about the development of a robust impactful independent research program. . PI has not secured independent funding since becoming Assistant Professor. . Role of Dr. Chan in proposed studies is unclear.
inn_text_str: . The use of metabolomics approaches to guide library development is innovative. . The use of co-culture approaches to derive novel molecules is also novel.
app_text_str: . Preliminary data is supportive of the feasibility of the proposed approach to identify new active natural products. . The use of co-culture to elicit new natural products is clever and likely to yield new chemical matter. . The mass spec based approach is well suited to identify new products from co-culture experiments.
app_text_wkn: . Assessing chemical diversity solely by mass spec does not provide adequate information to accurately assess the degree of chemical diversity which requires structural information, so the utility of the mass spec based approach to improve on compound selection for screening is not clear. . The use of phenotypic assays for screening comparison of the natural products to traditional HTS library is not viewed favorably. Such screens are subject to modulation via a variety of mechanisms and potentially subject to numerous possible mechanisms for false positives. The use of biochemically based screens would provide a more meaningful comparison of hit efficacy based on chemical properties. . It is not clear how extensively the co-culture approach can be explored as large numbers of co-cultured tests will likely necessary to generate any reasonable number of new chemical hits. .

imp_text: This is a novel and interesting application from a new investigator who is seeking to develop a chemically diverse screening library. The application is founded on the notion that metabolomics can be used to prescreen Actinobacteria so that metabolically similar strains and species can be removed from testing. This would then produce a library derived from organisms with unique chemical signatures. This library, once developed, would be used in a number of screens to derive anticancer and antibacterial therapeutic leads. The final aim of the proposal seeks to deploy metabolomics technologies to co-cultured bacteria to again derive new chemical scaffolds. The application is well written, coming from a strong team, with long experience in natural products development. The use of metabolomics is novel, as is its application to mono- and dual-species culturing. Strong data is presented to support the application, and there is a good chance that leads will be developed for both indications. Weaknesses, however, exist, including key preliminary data not being shown, and a concern that despite the use of metabolomics, compound rediscovery will still be a problem. The bacterial assays in aim 2 are also quite narrowly focused, and aim 3, although quite innovative, is significantly underdeveloped. Ultimately, the methods development take center stage in this application, with the therapeutic development seeming something of an after thought. Collectively, there is strong enthusiasm for the team, the novelty of metabolomics prescreening, and the natural products components of this application, that is dampened by issues with significance and approach.
sig_text_str: . Novel chemistry is urgently required for the development of drugs . Extensive preliminary data is presented suggesting that metabolomics prescreening leads to a diverse screening collection . New anti-cancer and antibacterial therapeutics are urgently needed . Actinobacteria are a rich source of potential drugs . Focusing on marine organisms is a major strength given their predicted diversity, and underexplored nature

app_text_str: . Strong preliminary data is presented to support the application . Aim 1 is likely to generate a novel library of marine actinobacteria that is chemical diverse . Aim 2 will likely produce both antibacterial and anticancer hits . In aim 3 the investigators take a novel approach to coculturing different bacterial species to produce new chemistry
app_text_wkn: . No milestones or inclusion/exclusion criteria are presented. How chemically diverse does a producing organism have to be to make it in to the library? How active does an extract have to be to warrant dereplication? It is suggested 40 strains a year will be developed for fermentation, but this does not sound like enough. . It is suggested that the library will be evaluated alongside commercial chemical collections, but there is no mention of that in aim 2. . No strains or methods are given for the antibacterial testing . It is not clear how much development will occur with dereplicated samples, beyond “pursuing them to the greatest extent through existing collaborations”. This feels rather like an afterthought, and that the library development is more important than drug development. . There is no consideration of toxicity in the application, meaning that even if novel chemistry is identified, it may prove to be toxic. . Aim 3 is perhaps the most novel part of the application, but it is underdeveloped. Strong potential exists that new chemistry will be identified using the metabolomics biasing. However, identify the producing organism and metabolic cluster via genome sequencing, as suggested in the application, is going to be enormously complex. Additionally, the suggestion that transcriptomics and proteomics could be used for similar purposes is likely not true, and experimentally fraught with problems. Collectively, although aim 3 is a really nice idea, it is light on details and specifics. . Potential pitfalls are given only the most cursory of considerations at the end of the application, and are not particularly robust.

imp_text: This is a novel and interesting proposal from a well established and highly productive team, wishing to develop new tools for reverse genetic analysis. In this proposal the investigators seek to generate novel cMOs with single and double lariat forms that can be activated in a delayed manner using light activation. Strengths of the proposal include the team, the novel tools being developed, the strong preliminary data and the environment. Weaknesses exist however, including the value of aim 1 when the tools in aim 2 would appear to be better, and a disjointed and unfocussed aim 3. Given the already strong preliminary data, there is also potential for the proposed studies to be somewhat incremental in the data they generate. Collectively, there is enthusiasm for the team and the technology, that is diminished by problems with significance and approach.

imp_text: This is a new application from a highly experienced investigator to study the final steps in LPS trafficking across the OM of E. coli. The PI has long experience in this field, publishing a wealth of studies and being possessed of a long track record of funding. Three aims are proposed that will determine, in intricate detail, the roles of LptA, LptC and LptD in LPS shuttling, and will likely complete the model on this process. Strengths include the investigative team, the solid approach, the detailed preliminary data, and the mechanistic nature of the application. The primary weakness is one of significance, as this topic has been studied extensively, so the findings have the potential to be incremental, particularly in light of the strong preliminary data already generated. Additionally, the value of LptA as a drug target is not clear, given that it has previously been studied without success. Collectively, this is a very strong grant, that will doubtlessly yield significant information about LPS trafficking in a select number of Gram negative bacteria; it is just not clear that we need the level of detail generated by the proposed studies.

imp_text: Much effort has been placed in generating synthetic drug screening libraries, however historically, natural products have been the single best source of therapeutic leads, especially in the area of antibiotics. Nowadays, discovery of novel small molecules has become increasingly difficult. This proposal aims to use modern approaches, such as genomics and LCMS-based untargeted metabolomics, to evaluate chemical diversity of underexplored marine bacteria, evaluate hit rates in HTS of drug-like natural product libraries compared to commercially available libraries and to evaluate changes in small molecule production between mono-culture and co-cultured bacteria. Select pairs of organisms when cultured together are predicted to produce novel activated cryptic clusters that yield novel natural products. Using these approaches is proposed to generate novel natural reproducible small molecules effective in treatment of cancers and infectious disease.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry B Study Section
imp_text: Current trends in lead discovery are biased towards high-throughput screening (HTS) of synthetic compound collections instead of the testing of natural products (NPs). The complexity of natural product structures are often accompanied by dereplication and synthetic challenges, whereas compound collections of commercial sources or “in-house” origin are easily accessible. Nevertheless, because NPs are known to occupy biologically important chemical space, they continue to be valuable for the discovery of new biologically active compounds. This proposal’s focus on characterization of a library of extracts from marine microbes is significant as secondary metabolites from marine microorganisms are a valuable resource for the discovery of novel pharmaceuticals. LC-MS–based metabolomic profiling that will guide the prioritization of actives is innovative. Preliminary results support the idea that metabolome profiling rather than taxonomic assessment has better relevance to identify bioactive compounds. Although the small data sets may give the impression that it is an effort to provide a nice after-the fact backstory of traditional natural products work. However, the enthusiasm of this proposal is bit mutated because of superficial development of Aim 3. Furthermore, it is confusing why Lipinski’s parameters are given serious consideration for prioritization because NPs are known to violate Lipinski’s rule.

imp_text: KInesin motor proteins move along microtublules using energy derived from ATP hydrolysis to conduct many important cellular functions, including intracellular transport and cell division. Therefore, it is important to elucidate the structural basis of kinesin motor function. Kinesin goes through alternating attachment and detachment of its catalytic head, and it is important to understand the structural changes in kinesin during the Mg-ADP and nucleotide-frees states. To determine the structural changes that lead to movement the proposal proposed to use cryo-EM.The ability of the investigators to obtain structural data of the kinesin-microtubule complex at 5-6Å generates optimism that the elusive high resolution structure of kinesin in the presence or absence of MT can be solved. Experimental plans are appropriately designed, PI has appropriate expertise, and impressive list of collaborators. A minor weakness is that it is not clear which kinesin will be studied, is it KIF5? This is important given that different kinesins are known to exist in different conformations. In summary this is an excellent proposal with minor weaknesses which will likely to exert a powerful influence in the field.

imp_text: This proposal focuses on defining the mechanism involved in translocation of LPS from inner membrane (IM) to outer membrane (OM) through the perisplasmic space. Various models for LPS translocation has been proposes but exact mechanism still remains elusive, which the current application plans to elucidate. Translocation of LPS to OM is a thermodynamically challenging process, which needs energization from the IM. LptA is a key protein of the Lpt translocon that either serves as a chaperone or as a bridge for LPS transport to OM. It is intriguing how the jellyroll structure of LptA can accommodate LPS. Therefore, the specific aims 1 & 2 addressing the molecular basis of LptA and LPS interaction is significant. Aim 3 will address the mechanism of translocation. Experimental plans have been clearly outlined  to accomplish the aims of the project and will be led by a PI who has a solid track record. There is a strong enthusiasm for this project as it is expected that the results from this study will lead to a better understanding of LPS movement to the OM. There is a strong likelihood that the results from this study will exert a powerful influence in the research field.

study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry B Study Section
imp_text: The principal investigator, Brad Sullivan, has proposed to capitalize on metabolomics and various other “omics” methods for developing high throughput screens for novel natural product identification from marine microbiata. This is a very good proposal that has the potential to be successful in isolating novel potential drug scaffolds produced by a largely unexplored source – marine invertebrates. The PI, with his experience in both natural products HTS and marine biology, is well suited to lead this project. While innovative, there are concerns with the approach that call the feasibility of the project into question and reduce enthusiasm overall. Much of the proposal details work that has already been done, and while it appears to have been successful so far, it is not clearly outlined where the project is expected to go. How will the project grow beyond repeatedly identifying lead compounds with antibiotic activity? Additionally, while the notion that co-cultivating strains to produce novel compounds via intercellular signaling is a novel approach inspired by nature, it is questionable whether this will be achieved on the proposed scale. Epigenetic and environmental factors that likely contribute greatly to these processes will be difficult to reproduce in the lab, and this is not addressed.  The flaws in the approach have reduced the overall impact of the proposal.

imp_text: This application proposes a research plan to elucidate the mechanisms underlying ATP-driven kinesin motor movement, which is involved in crucial biological processes such as mitosis. This is an excellent, well-written proposal by an outstanding early-stage investigator. Professor Washington is extremely well-suited to pursue the proposed research, and has already formed several collaborations both within and outside of Yale to further ensure his success. The investigator notes a significant problem in structural biology, which is that asymmetry and heterogeneity inherent in complex biological structures such as the kinesin-microtubule motor complex precludes analysis by traditional crystallization methods. Additionally, previous cryo-EM images have been unable to resolve the structure of active cytoskeletal motors beyond nanometer resolution, making these structures nearly impossible to interpret accurately. Professor Washington addresses these problems by establishing novel methods for collecting and processing cryo-EM data to achieve atomic resolution, vastly improving on existing methods. Preliminary results look promising, and it seems likely that these methods may be successfully applied to capture additional conformations in an active kinesin motor complex as well as with mutated complexes.
sig_text_str: . Microtubule motors underlie many significant biological processes. Unraveling the mechanism of kinesin movement and the structure of the kinesin-microtubule complex is a hugely important endeavor with broad-reaching implications for cancer treatment, public health, and our overall understanding of a fundamental activity within the cell. Successful completion of this project will yield high-impact results and will no doubt be of great interest to the broader community. (major)

This research plan first proposes to work towards a more functional understanding of the protein LptA, a critical protein in the LPS-transfer process. This risky Specific Aim 1 is more exploratory than hypothesis-driven. Aims 2 and 3 purport to probe the interactions and binding behavior between LptA and LPS, as well as with associated proteins in the transport system. imp_text: This grant aims to further develop gene-targeting morpholinos that can be used to control gene expression in a number of biological contexts, particularly in zebrafish in the context of development. Morpholinos have been of critical importance to study essential genes in development, however they have been limited by a lack of temporal control and off target toxicity. The major advancement in this proposal is the development of caged MO’s that can be regulated temporally. The first two aims of this proposal are the development of two classes of lariat cMOs that have different architectures that are designed to be inactive until activated by light. While the development of these tools is important, there is nothing innovative to the proposal and is a continuation of previous work by the investigators. The third aim of the proposal attempts to develop methods for using multiple cMOs in a temporal fashion by use of activating groups that can be cleaved at different wavelengths. What is missing from this proposal is a clear biological example where the utility of the temporal control of the cMOs can be demonstrated.

imp_text: This is an innovative grant that will take advantage of advancements in cryoEM technology, and image analysis (data processing) to ask mechanistic questions about kinesin motors and their interactions with microtubules. The PI has established a strong team of collaborators to address these questions. The general concept of the grant is that higher resolution images will lead to greater mechanistic understanding. There are two broad questions that are proposed – how microtubules stimulate the kinesin motor and how to dimeric kinesin motors communicate. The same approach will be used with each question, utilizing a combination of structures from different nucleotide bound states and structures from mutant structures that are known to have an impact on function. What is not entirely clear in this proposal is exactly how these images and interpretations will be used to further one or more of the models that are proposed for how the kinesin motor works.

study_section: Biochemistry and Biophysics of Membranes Study Section
imp_text: This proposal addresses an important area of microbiology, with the goal towards a greater understanding of the mechanism by which LPS is transported between the inner and outer membrane. This proposal is based on preliminary work by the PI of the proposal and others in the field that have established that the LptA, LptC and LptD/E proteins play an integral role in the process. This proposal aims to use biophysical techniques (EPR spectroscopy), ITC and others to probe the associations of LPS with this proteins and with mutant versions to gain a better understanding of the mechanism by which this occurs. The experiments proposed will be enlightening and the alanine scanning experiment will provide some context towards the regions of LptA that interacts with LPS. There are two models presented for how LptA can act to transport LPS to the outer membrane, however it was not clear how the two models will be differentiated based on the experimental evidence. Furthermore, just because LptA can dimerize or oligemirize in solution, does not mean it will do so in the bacterial cells. Additionally, studies looking at the interaction of LptA and LptC in conjunction with LPS will be slightly artificial as only the soluble portion of LptC will be used. It was pointed out that with only the soluble portion of LptC no energy is needed to transfer LPS to LptA, but previous work has shown that for full length LptC, energy is required. Overall this is a solid grant that is addressing an important question, but some of the experimental set-up may lead to conclusions that are not relevant in vivo.
