imp_text: The application brought forward by Dr. Sullivan addresses the need for novel active compounds that can serve as leads in drug discovery by sampling large numbers of marine bacterial species. Tests rely on computational validation by principal components analysis. The proposal, especially the figure panel representation, lacks of fundamental grantsmanship. Some advice form the senior collaborators mentioned in this application is needed. Too detailed at times with a diluting emphasis on minor components. Overall and in certain paragraphs, the application is not logically structured. More extensive description of figure panels and better labeling of figures will help to understand them fully. A concluding experimental design on how to test potential hits as drugs is missing. Despite the large number of collaborators in research or clinical settings, there does not appear to be an explanation of how the newly identified compounds are being tested. The co-culturing experiments described in aim 3 are intriguing but only described in broad strokes. Potential pitfalls and alternative approaches should be provided for each specific aim.

imp_text: The proposal on studying the LptA-mediated LPS transfer across the periplasm of Gram-negative bacteria has a high potential to identify novel drug targets that will improve the current arsenal of antibiotics. LptA transfers LPS from the inner to the outer bacterial membrane and has to protect the hydrophobic chains of the molecule. However, LPS binding and function in LPS transfer of LptA is currently not understood. The proposal will shed light on these questions using well established methods of the Kelly and Fitch labs. All of the proposed studies depend on the generation of a novel temperature-sensitive LptA mutant strain that would allow for screens of functional LptA mutants. The research environment is well-equipped to conduct the initial strain generation and subsequent screen and downstream experiments. However, there is no guarantee that the team will be successful in generating and appropriately characterizing the LptA mutant strain in a timely fashion.
sig_text_str: . Increase our understanding of the LPS transfer to the outer bacterial membrane will shed light on a mechanism critical for bacterial survival . Binding of LPS to LptA as well as LptA to LptDE will close a knowledge gap of LPS transport from the inner membrane to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane. . There have been preliminary studies with LptA alone, which will now be complemented with LptA-LPS complexes.

imp_text: Proposed research topics in the above mentioned grant proposal should be very relevant in many areas of vascular studies, with this proposal being one of the few to unravel the role of IL-19 in vascular disease. However, there is one major weakness in the Aims of this proposal. In Aim 1, the investigator proposes to determine if IL-19 induces angiogenesis and then builds three more aims on the mechanism by which IL-19 induces angiogenesis. Although there is some evidence in the preliminary data that IL-19 may play a role in angiogenesis, by the author adding the first Aim to solidify this finding makes this proposal questionable. Complete the first two experiments suggested in Aim 1, solidify that IL-19 induces angiogenesis in the preliminary data, and focus the proposed Aims and research plan on the mechanistic studies.
sig_text_str: . IL-19 has been shown to play an important role in wound healing, vascular disease, many immune disorders, and macrophage polarization. However, much of the characterization of IL-19 signaling and activation mechanism has yet to be determined. This study with further our knowledge of the characterization of IL-19, which could be very important in identify future therapeutic targets in multiple vascular diseases.
sig_text_wkn: . Clarification of the role of IL-19 in angiogenesis needs to be completed before activation mechanisms of IL-19 are examined.
inv_text_str: . The author is very proficient in vascular research and one of the first investigators to identify a role for IL-19 in vascular disease. Much of this investigator’s findings are very novel, which is shown in an accomplished publication history.
inn_text_str: . IL-19 is a very under-studied cytokine, especially in vascular disorders, and this proposal has very novel insights and approaches.
inn_text_wkn: . What therapeutic targets could be determined by all of these mechanistic studies? Please add to proposal.

imp_text: The overall goal of this application is to demonstrate that Interleukin-19 (IL-19), an anti-inflammatory, Th2 interleukin, can drive angiogenesis and improve perfusion of ischemic tissue. IL-19 is a newly described Th2, (T regulatory) anti-inflammatory interleukin which until recently, had been ascribed to be inflammatory cell-specific. The PI is currently the only laboratory to investigate a role for this Interleukin in vascular biology, particularly with respect to EC and VSMC pathophysiology. Both inflammatory and anti-inflammatory cytokines participate in wound healing and neo-vascularization, but the role of anti-inflammatory cytokines in angiogenesis and the cross-talk between these processes remain under characterized. In contrast to pervious work indicating that IL-19 suppresses vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMC) migration and proliferation, the PI has recently reported the surprising finding that IL-19 has potent pro-angiogenic effects on human endothelial cells (EC). IL-19 is not detected in normal EC but is expressed in EC in capillaries in human angiogenic tissue. IL-19 is mitogenic and chemotactic for EC, promotes cell spreading, and activates MAPK and Rac1. IL-19 promotes microvessel formation in aortic rings, and PECAM1-positive micro vessels in vivo in mouse matrigel. IL-19 can induce angiogenic gene expression in EC. IL-19 effects are independent of VEGF and bFGF, as neither can induce IL-19 expression, and IL-19 cannot induce expression of either. Neutralization of bFGF and VEGF does not effect IL-19 activity, suggesting a novel, Th2-induced pathway to stimulate EC activation and angiogenesis. IL-19 can polarize human macrophage to the M2, “wound healing” phenotype, and induce angiogenic gene expression in macrophage. These preliminary and published data have driven the hypothesis that IL-19 is a novel vasculogenic cytokine with multiple effector cells. What needs to be determined is if IL-19 can restore blood flow in ischemic tissue, if the major effector cell is endothelial cells or the M2 macrophage, what soluble factors mediate IL-19 effects, and the molecular mechanisms and mediators of IL-19 differential effects in EC and VSMC. The PI will determine if absence of IL-19 attenuates, and if over expression of IL-19 promotes angiogenesis and restores blood flow in ischemic  tissue, if IL-19 regulation of angiogenesis is facilitated by direct effects on vascular cells, or by macrophage M2 polarization, will identify and characterize IL-19 inducible factors necessary for IL-19-driven angiogenesis in vivo, and test the hypothesis that differential expression of IL-20 receptor subunits account for pleiotropic effects of IL-19 in VSMC compared with EC. This application is potentially paradigm-changing as it will implicate a Th2 interleukin as a novel anti-inflammatory, pro-vasculogenic cytokine expressed by inflamed resident vascular cells to promote neovascularization. Overall, this is a well written application that is viewed with strong enthusiasm.

imp_text: The incidence of hypertension increases dramatically with age, is poorly treated in elderly patients, and contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality in our aging society. In rodent models and in humans, vascular aging is characterized by enhanced angiotensin II (AngII) signaling, increased vascular oxidative stress, and increased vascular contraction. The stimuli driving this age-associated vascular phenotype are not well understood and no strategy is known to retard vascular aging in humans. The hormone aldosterone (Aldo) regulates blood pressure (BP) by binding to renal mineralocorticoid receptors (MR) to promote renal sodium retention. The PI previously identified functional MR in human vascular smooth muscle cells (SMC), discovered that SMC MR can be directly activated by AngII, and developed a novel mouse model that allows for inducible, SMC-specific deletion of MR. The PI recently discovered that SMC MR-deficiency prevents the age-dependent rise in BP and many other aspects of vascular aging in mice and theorizes that SMC MR is a global regulator of vascular aging and aging associated hypertension and now propose to explore the mechanisms. New preliminary data contained herein show that AngII activates SMC MR in a PKCd-dependent manner in human SMC and that vessels from aged SMC MR-deficient mice have decreased vascular tone, expression of the LTCC Cav1.2, and contraction to L-type calcium channel (LTCC) agonists and other calcium channel-activating vasoconstrictors. Further analysis of vessels from aged SMC MR-deficient mice reveals decreased expression of the NADPH oxidase subunit Nox2 and lower basal and AngII-induced oxidative stress. Based on these data, the PI proposes the novel hypothesis that in the aging vasculature, SMC MR is directly activated by AngII via PKCd-mediated phosphorylation and regulates Cav1.2 and Nox2 expression and activity, promoting the age-associated increase in vascular oxidative stress and vascular contraction, thereby contributing to increased BP. This will be tested in three specific aims: 1) The mechanism of AngII activation of vascular SMC MR; 2) SMC MR regulation of vascular Cav1.2 expression and channel activity and the resulting impact on vascular tone and contraction; and 3) The mechanism of SMC MR modulation of vascular oxidative stress with aging and the role in vascular tone and BP control. Understanding the direct contribution of SMC MR to BP regulation would fundamentally change the longstanding paradigm that the MR regulates BP exclusively by renal effects on sodium handling, support novel vascular mechanisms for the protective effects of AngII and MR antagonist drugs in human clinical trials, and identify novel mechanisms contributing specifically to hypertension with aging, with important implications for therapy to prevent and treat hypertension and its complications in the growing elderly population.  Overall, this is a well written application, but enthusiasm is limited by the Significance, Innovation, and Approach.

imp_text: The incidence of heart failure (HF) is projected to increase by 25% over the next 20 years with a projected cost of $69.7 billion representing a substantial health and economic burden on the US. In general, HF is characterized by a decrease in contractility and maladaptive ventricular remodeling ultimately leading to impaired cardiac output to the systemic circulation. Immense scientific effort has been focused on unraveling the molecular and cellular mechanisms driving decreased cardiac contractility and while a multitude of changes no doubt contribute, it is generally agreed that much of the contractile deficit is due to a reduction in cytosolic calcium (Ca2+) transients and a decrease in sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) Ca2+ content. Similarly, recent studies have supported the theory that mitoCa2+ content is actually diminished in HF despite elevations in diastolic Ca2+. To examine the role of mitoCa2+ in the development and progression of HF, the PI has developed mutant mouse models of a proposed mitochondrial Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (mitoNCX). The mitoCa2+ microdomain has been under intense investigation due to its significant influence on energy production and cell death and HF in particular, is characterized by both significant metabolic dysfunction and gradual cell dropout. This project is testing the central hypothesis that reducing mitoCa2+ efflux protects against gradual cell dropout and adverse remodeling in heart failure by enhancing cardiomyocyte metabolic and redox capacity. For the first time, utilizing genetic gain and loss of function approaches, the PI will characterize the biophysical properties of this novel exchanger, assess its contribution to cellular physiology and examine it’s role in clinically relevant animal models. The ultimate goal of this research endeavor is to define the role of mitoCa2+ signaling in the development and progression of HF and foster therapeutic application. Overall, this is a well written proposal, but enthusiasm for it is mixed.

imp_text: This application hypothesizes that IL-19, an anti-inflammatory Th2 interleukin, can enhance angiogenesis and improve perfusion of ischemic tissues. They propose to explore this hypothesis is 4 specific aims. 1) Using a total body IL-19 knockout mouse, they will determine if IL-19 regulates angiogenesis in a hind-limb ischemia-reperfusion model. 2) They will determine if IL-19-mediated angiogenesis occurs through a direct effect of IL-19 on endothelial cells (ECs) or is secondary due to macrophage M2 polarization. This aim will use IL-20R knockout mice and bone marrow transplantation techniques. 3) Knockout mice for four soluble factors identified from qPCR array analysis will be used to determine if any of these factors induced by IL-19 actually drive angiogenesis. This aim will also determine if the source of these angiogenic factors are ECs and/or M2 macrophage. 4) Using IL-20R knockout mice, this aim will determine if differential IL-20R subunit expression accounts for the differing effects of IL-19 on vascular smooth muscle cells and ECs. The strengths of this proposal include a targeted and specific approach. Also, this application proposes a novel mechanism of an anti-inflammatory Th2 interleukin with angiogenic properties in inflamed blood vessels. Weaknesses of this application include a heavy reliance on bone marrow transplantation to assess EC vs M2 macrophage contribution to IL-19 mediated angiogenesis. No preliminary data is provided to demonstrate that successfully perform bone marrow transplantation in mice. Thus, while the significance of this work is high, there are major concerns with the proposed approach. Also, numerous grammatical errors throughout the application further dampen enthusiasm.

imp_text: This application hypothesizes that mineralocorticoid receptors (MRs) are present on vascular smooth muscle (SM) cells and these vascular MRs are responsible for aging-induced increases in blood pressure. They propose to test this hypothesis in 3 specific aims. 1) Using siRNA knockdown and targeted mutation techniques, they will determine if angiotensin II (AngII) activates SM MRs via PKCd-mediated phosphorylation of a specific region of the MR. 2) They will use qPCR, immunoblotting, electrophysiology and pressure myography to determine if the MR regulates expression and function of the L-type voltage gated calcium channel, Cav1.2. 3) They will determine if AngII activates the MR to increase Nox2 activity and expression and increase vascular oxidative stress. This aim will also determine if oxidative stress can modulate Cav1.2 function in aged mice. There is also an in vivo component to this aim, designed to determine if a MR antagonist, calcium channel blocker and/or antioxidant can prevent aging associated increases in BP in mice. The strengths of this proposal include a targeted and very specific approach. The investigator has developed an inducible SM-specific MR knockout mouse that will be used in all of the aims. Another strength is that application is exploring a novel mechanism of age-associated increased blood pressure. However, enthusiasm for this application is dampened because in aim 3, the candidate drugs being tested are already clinically used to treat high blood pressure. Also, if the applicant is correct that SM MR signaling ultimately leads to increased oxidative stress that increases Cav1.2 channel function, then calcium channel blockers (CCBs) should be the best line of therapy for high blood pressure, and as mentioned earlier CBBs are already in use clinically. Thus, the significance of this work is low and overall this project is likely to have moderate impact since it focuses on already known blood pressure targets.
sig_text_str: . This project addresses an important problem in the field since most people who have high blood pressure do not have adequate control of their blood pressure, even with access to currently available pharmacotherapies.
sig_text_wkn: . It is not clear how successful completion of the project will change treatment of hypertension. Several classes of drugs, including ACE inhibitors, ARBs, MR antagonists, and CCBs are already used clinically to treat high blood pressure. . Along this same line of thinking, if SM MR signaling ultimately leads to increased oxidative stress that increases Cav1.2 channel function, then shouldn’t calcium channel blockers (CCBs) be the best line of therapy for high blood pressure? CCBs, such as the dihydropyridines, are highly selective for vascular Cav1.2, so it is unclear how the work from this project would be used to develop a more selective and effective target for reducing blood pressure.

imp_text: Overall Impact Score (1-9): This application hypothesizes that the Raf-MEK1 pathway and subsequent activation of yorkie is an important, previously unidentified pathway driving cardiomyopathy in Drosophila. This proposal plans to use Drosophila genetics as a discovery platform to examine new pathways in cardiomyopathy and to translate these findings to humans through 3 specific aims. 1) Using Drosophila genetics, this aim will characterize the role of the Raf-MEK1 pathway in the development of cardiac hypertrophy in the fly. 2) Since YAP1, the mammalian ortholog to fly yorkie, has additional protein motifs compared to yorkie, systematic deletions of combinations of these protein domains will provide new insights into YAP1 function and signaling. This aim will also investigate if temporal activation (before or after development) of YAP1 may explain why mammalian YAP1 induces cardiac hyperplasia and fly yorkie induces cardiac hypertrophy. 3) This aim will determine if YAP1 reduction reduces the severity of cardiac hypertrophy in RafL613V/+ (activated Raf) knock-in mice or in mice after trans-aortic constriction-induced pressure overload.  This proposal is likely to have a sustained, powerful influence on the field of cardiomyopathies because of the targeted and specific approach, and the novelty of the pathway being described. Moreover, the scientific environment is excellent, as is the investigator and the team of collaborators.

imp_text: The studies and investigative team in this proposal demonstrate high potential for advancing the current field of interleukin biology, with specific focus on interleukin 19, which may translate to new therapies for peripheral vascular disease.  Overall, the applicant demonstrates an excellent interpretation of their preliminary results, with a strong hypothesis to be tested and many alternative approaches were considered. The proposal demonstrates an excellent combined use of in-vivo / ex-vivo models with loss of function and gain of function experiments.  However, this proposal is highly ambitious, which dampened my enthusiasm for the proposal.  Moreover, additional human based complementary experiments as shown in Figure 1, would have strengthened the translational aspects of the proposal.  In addition, given the complexity of cytokine signaling the reviewer has some reservations regarding whether these studies will translate to IL-19 based therapies.  But overall, in summary this is an excellent proposal based on the investigative team, preliminary data, interpretation of results and well-designed experiments to test their hypothesis.

imp_text: This proposal investigates the role of IL-19 in angiogenesis. It is based on the premise that IL-19 is proangiogenic in endothelial cells, and induces wound healing M2 phenotype in macrophage. The studies will utilize a variety of genetically modified mice and biochemical assays. The PI has experience in characterizing the effects of anti-inflammatory interleukins in vascular injury. Overall enthusiasm for this application is reduced to moderate range by the lack of attention to important experimental details, inclusion of preliminary data from LDLR-/- mice, and somewhat confusing rationale and experimental approach.
sig_text_str: . Investigation of the effects of IL-19 on angiogenesis is scientifically significant. . Investigation of differential responsiveness of EC, VSMC and macrophages in response to IL-19 and their involvement in the angiogenic process.
sig_text_wkn: . Descriptive and superficial nature of the project.
inv_text_str: . Established investigator with experience in investigation of the role of IL-19 in VSMC and vascular injury . Co-I, Dr Chang, has experience in hind limb ischemia and scanning laser Doppler imaging.

inn_text_str: . Investigation of the role of IL-19 in vascular injury and angiogenesis is innovative. . Published and preliminary data support the overall hypothesis.
inn_text_wkn: . Descriptive nature. . In most parts, the proposed experimental strategy is superficial.
app_text_str: . Preliminary data to show that IL-19 stimulates angiogenesis in vivo in mice and polarizes macrophage to M2 phenotype
app_text_wkn: . Preliminary data are provided that IL-19 accelerates wound healing and decreases expression of M1 macrophage marker ArgII in LDLR-/- mice, suggesting a role for LDLR in IL-19 signaling. These interesting findings were not followed in the experimental approach. . Aim 1 will determine if absence of IL-19 attenuates, and overexpression of IL-19 promotes angiogenesis. However, the experimental approach does not use overexpression strategy, instead treats mice with IL-19. . How the number of angiogenic sprouts will be measured? Metrics indicates CD36+ staining, while experimental strategy uses CD31 positive vessels. How the vascular remodeling will be characterized to compare mature, actively remodeling, and mature vessels? . IL-19 treatment will be started prior to the ischemia or after ischemia? . Aim 1.3 indicates that IL-19-/- will be ligated. It is not clear what will be ligated and how the ligation will be performed? . Aim 2.1 will irradiate mice to eliminate hematopoietic cells. Important experimental details are missing. It is not clear how long the mice will be irradiated, and how the elimination of hematopoietic cells will be tested. . Rationale for Aim 2 is confusing. It is not clearly evident how the experiments of this aim will dissect if IL-19-driven angiogenesis is induced by direct effects of IL-19 on EC or is indirect due to macrophage M2 polarization or both. . Macrophage will also be isolated from the above 4 KO mice. There is no mention of how, and from where (bone marrow, lung or peritoneal cavity) the macrophages will be isolated. This is important because the physiology of macrophages can vary depending on the environment in which they reside and the local stimuli to which they are exposed. . However, these preliminary data are missing from the proposal. . Expected results and alternative approaches section of Aim 4 will perform carotid air-dry injury described in Aim 1. However, studies of Aim 1 do not seem to use the carotid air-dry injury model. . There are few grammatical errors distracting the readability.

imp_text: This proposal uses drosophila genetics and transgenic mouse model of cardiac hypertrophy to examine the role of Raf-MEK1 pathway and activation of Yap1 in cardiac hypertrophy. The strengths of the proposal include the use of invertebrate model to identify genes leading to cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure. A major weakness is the lack of preliminary data to support each specific aim. Identification of signals involved in cardiac myocyte proliferation vs hypertrophy is interesting. However, these processes may be complex due to the involvement of many signaling pathways and cell types. Important technical details are missing lowering the enthusiasm to moderate.
sig_text_str: . Use of drosophila system to understand the signaling mechanism involved in cardiac hypertrophy and heart failure.
sig_text_wkn: . The involvement of some of the components of the proposed signaling pathway in cardiac biology has already been investigated. . Preliminary data (Fig 4) suggest ERK-independent hypertrophy in drosophila. However, transgenic mice studies provide evidence that Raf/MEK-ERK activity is critical for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (JCI 2011; 121:1009-1025; EMBO J 2000; 19:6341-6350). The PI will use the same transgenic mice (Aim 3) to investigate that Raf-MEK signaling directly regulates Yap1 to modulate cardiac hypertrophy and this signaling occurs independent of ERK. No preliminary data are provided to support this hypothesis in mouse heart.

imp_text: This is a well-designed, high impact R01 from an established PI to study a novel signaling network involving in vascular cells outside the renal system and may lead to future studies of specific therapies for patients.  The hypothetical framework to study mineralocorticoid receptor (MR)/angiotensin II crosstalk and the effects in hypertension, a leading cause of morbidity and death throughout the world, is novel and important. The investigators are capable of performing the experiments outlined. The hypothetical framework seeks to understand how angiogensin II can activate MR and lead to biologic events in hypertension by stimulating vascular contraction in smooth muscle cells and ties together events linked to aging and oxidative stress. The PI discusses alternative plans and pitfalls appropriately. The approach is strong but impact would be greater with clearer description of controls for experiments and greater understanding of NADPH oxidase studies. The impact would be stronger with some correlation of events in human cells or tissues. The overall subaims are ambitious but the aims themselves should be able to be addressed adequately even if all experiments are not completed. Overall, this is a high impact proposal.

Also the impact of the proposal was driven by the importance of the disease. The grant is ambitious and it is not clear this investigator and team have the capability of performing everything outlined in the grant based on biosketches and personal statements. The impact would be greater with more detail in the methods, clarity of design and of individual experiments (including controls), expected outcomes, early definition of abbreviations/acronyms. The PI indicates there are other exchangers in the mitochondria. Impact would be higher if outcomes assessed potential compensatory role of these other transporters after experimental perturbations were performed in one (eg, NCX mito). There is some correlation with human disease made but greater association of the pathways proposed for study with human disease would also increase impact of proposal.

imp_text: The central hypothesis of this application is that chronic caloric and lipid excess leads to increased phosphorylation and cytoplasmic localization of lipin 1 in cardiomyocytes, enhancing the nuclear transcriptional regulatory effects of lipin on PGC1-a signal, and by so doing, cardiac oxidative metabolism. There are three aims. In Aim 1, the effects of dietary nutrient manipulation on cardiac myocyte lipin 1 expression, activity, and sub-cellular localization will be studied. In Aim 2, the PI will determine whether loss of lipin 1-mediated PAP activity attenuate the pathogenic response to nutrient overabundance by inhibiting lipin 1-mediated synthesis of diacylglycerol (DAG), triglyceride and other potential lipotoxins. Through a genetic gain-of-function approach, Aim 3 is designed to test whether reactivating nuclear-targeted lipin 1 signal ameliorates cardiac dysfunction in mice fed with high-fat diet (HFD).  The strengths of this application are several. (1) Very little is known about the involvement of lipin 1 in synthetizing potential lipotoxins in presence of excess nutrients, particularly high-fat intake, and on the role of lipin 1 as a regulator of intermediary metabolism in the cardiac tissue. (2). Elegant mouse models of gain-of-function for dissecting cytosolic vs. nuclear lipin 1-based signaling and functions. (3) Highly qualified PI, with an outstanding publication record, pertinent to the proposed science. (4) Research strategy for the in vitro studies (Aim 1 and 2) is well delineated. However, there are also major concerns are as follows. (1) Based on the preliminary data included, it seems that lipin 3 may still play a role; this was not definitely ruled out (2). Exercise training would be a good alternative/additive protocol to perform in mice to establish whether chronic exercise can promote (or preserve) lipin 1 translocation to the nucleus, and dependent oxidative metabolism via PGC1-a in HFD treated mice. (3) Aim 3 that is the most translational one is the least developed one, with unclear endpoints and expected outcomes.
sig_text_str: •Since myocardial lipid accumulation is a hallmark of diabetes and other metabolic disorders eventually affecting cardiac function, finding new mechanisms leading to this buildup may open new avenues to prevent lipotoxic cardiomyopathy; therefore, at least in theory, the present proposal is very significant. • A role for lipin 1 in controlling intermediary metabolism is emerging in several organs/tissues; however, little is known about lipin 1 activity, and factors that modulate if, in the heart. Thus, knowing more about location and function of lipin 1 in the heart is relevant.
sig_text_wkn: • Feeding mice with high-fat diet may produce a mild cardiac dysfunction in mice; therefore, it is not entirely clear how much of the present findings can be translated into human pathology. • The overall significance of the proposal would be enhanced by adding evidence that lipin 1 translocation to the nucleus can be achieved either pharmacologically or through aerobic exercise. • As presented, it is not totally clear whether, and what eventually what pharmacological tool can induce lipin 1 translocation to the nucleus to achieve sizable therapeutically effects, i.e., to mimic the effects eventually produced here by transgenesis. • The significance of the proposal could be strengthened by determining whether altering lipin 1 localization within the cell or manipulating PAP activity alters basal cardiac (isolated myocyte) function.
inv_text_str: • The PI, Dr. Murphy, is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Medicine, Division of Geriatrics and Nutritional Science, at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. He is very-published with contributions in high-profile journals such as Cell Metab., J Clin Invest., PNAS and Cell, all relevant to the present proposal. His lab is very well funded with one R01 as PI, 5 R01s as co-PI, one R42 as PI and other research grants from different agencies. • Drs. Chao and So will be co-investigators; both of them are experts in fatty acid, triglyceride synthesis and metabolism as well as lipid biochemistry. In particular, Dr. So will be in charge of performing (supervising) mass spectrometry for the quantification of lipid species. Overall, the assembled team is very qualified.
inn_text_str: • The idea that, depending upon nutrient availability of the cell, lipin 1 can regulate both anabolic and catabolic pathways in the heart is novel and pathophysiologically relevant. • Increases PAP activity in hearts of mice fed with HFD is another innovative concept of this proposal that may have important implications in the progression of LV dysfunction during metabolic disorders. • The use of cardiac-specific, tetracycline-inducible transgenic mouse that overexpresses PGC1-a in the heart is innovative and likely key to address key points of the proposal.
inn_text_wkn: • Overexpressing lipin 1 (by 2-3 fold) in the heart is an innovative approach, but it is unclear whether any pharmacological interventions can achieve these same levels that supposedly are cardio-protective. • The assessment of mitochondrial and LV function is standard. Likewise, there are no major innovative molecular or biochemical approaches/tests.
app_text_str: • Specific Aim 1 and 2 are well written, the research design is logical, therefore easy to follow. • The PI included a good deal of preliminary data in support of the major contentions of the proposal, particularly when the role (and genetic manipulation) of lipin 1 is concerned. • The assembled team of investigators are in command of the various genetic and molecular approaches proposed, supported by an excellent research environment.
app_text_wkn: •  Preliminary data. The proposal is based on the assumption that lipin 1 is the most represented isoform in the heart; however, gels in Fig.2 show that lipin 3 is also expressed in the heart, and not faintly. Moreover, in fld mice that have constitutive lipin 1 deficiency lipin 3 is also suppressed. This evidence casts some doubts on the specificity of the genetic approach, but, more importantly, raises some issues concerning lipin 3 whose possible influence cannot be rule out here; its role as a potential alternative or additive factor is not considered here. •  Aim 2- It appears that both the fld and cardiac-specific PAP-specific mice are newly generated mouse lines. What is their basal cardiac phenotype? In the Cardiac Functional Analyses and Predicted Results section there is no mention on what LV function is expected in these mice at baseline (in absence of chronic HFD feeding). How echo LV data will be interpreted if either fld or cardiac-specific PAP-specific mice have an altered LV function to begin with? Overall, these mice need a thorough hemodynamic evaluation under basal conditions first. •  Aim 3- The idea of reactivating nuclear cardiac lipin 1 activity in the context of nutrient excess to determine whether this intervention limits the negative impact of HFD on cardiac function is intriguing and novel. The PI proposes two elegant genetic gain of function approaches. However, since exercise is a major modulator of lipin 1 expression, why not testing whether physical training in mice is responsible of lipin 1 nuclear localization? Would exercise be still beneficial in fld mice? These are important questions to ask. •  Aim 3- Is there any pharmacological intervention that may favor lipin 1 localization in mice receiving HFD? If so, this should be tested in addition to genetic attempts to overexpressing lipin 1 in the nucleus; doing so would strengthen the translational potential of these studies. •  Aim 3- The PI proposes studies on mitochondrial and intermediary metabolism in mice receiving HFD, with and without the superimposition of TAC; however, predicted results are not anticipated. It is not clear what exactly we will learn or should expect in terms of changes in mitochondrial function, substrate utilization, etc. •  Overall, the research design lacks alternative hypotheses/approaches, and statistical procedures/power analysis, etc, are not provided.

study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: In this new application, the PI, Dr Baker, aims to define whether amylin buildup in the heart (due to circulating amylin oligomers) accelerates the onset of diabetic heart failure (HF) by altering cardiac structure and function. Three Specific Aims are proposed. Aim 1 is to test whether oligomeric amylin alters cardiac function inducing remodeling in myocytes. Aim 2 is to test whether amylin buildup accelerates diabetic heart failure by impairing cardiac energy substrate metabolism. Finally, in Aim3 the PI will investigate if limiting amylin buildup in the heart (by disrupting the accumulation of oligomeric amylin) will rescue sarcolemmal intergrity in rats that express amyloidogenic human amylin in the heart (HIP rats). The strengths of this application are several. (1) The novel pathogenetic concept that shares similarities with the cardiac deposition of protein aggregates of different etiology/source; (2) the fact that the PI provided ample critical preliminary data to support their hypothesis. (3) The track records of PI and collaborator team that are very strong. (4) The translational potential that is considered high. That said, there are also several major concerns. (1) The current proposal is rather ambitious and the research design is very difficult to follow; 2) pilot data directed to support the central hypothesis that disrupting amylin oligomer accumulation in the heart may lead to improved cardiac function are not included; 3) it is not entirely clear on which mechanistic ground the use of some of these agents is proposed, see, for instance, the use of 14,15-EET.
sig_text_str: • The work proposed will provide a new mechanism whereby obesity and T2D negatively impact on cardiac function, i.e., the presence of large deposits of oligomerized amylin in the heart. • Limiting amylin buildup in the heart, thus its negative functional repercussions could be a novel way to prevent or arrest HF progression in obese and T2D patients. Thus, at least in theory, the proposal is potentially very significant from a practical point of view.
sig_text_wkn: • The overall significance of the proposal could be strengthened by studying the effects produced acute amylin superfusion of human myocytes, in absence and presence of agents capable of reducing the accumulation of amylin oligomers • Specific Aim 3: There no preliminary functional data showing that either plasmin or 14,15-EET effectively improve cardiac function in HIP rats.
inv_text_str: • PI, Dr. Baker, is an Assistant Professor in Residence in the Dept. of Pharmacology at University of California. She has a very good publication record with 53 papers listed in peer reviewed journals such as Circulation Res, Circulation and Biophysical Journal. She pioneered studies on amyloid formation, structure, and pathological mechanisms. • A well-qualified team of co-investigators and collaborators has been assembled and their contribution will significantly aid to the success of the proposed work. In particular, Dr. Stephen Berry at the University of Chicago is an expert in the chemistry of amyloid formation, and his group developed a molecular model of protein oligomerization that explained key features of amyloid formation in vivo. Dr. Berg is a leading authority on cardiac Ca signaling. Dr. Traugott is world-known for studying cardiac metabolism. Their collaboration is a major asset to the proposal.
inn_text_str: • The notion that amylin oligomers are a pathogenic link between pancreatic and cardiac disorders in obesity and T2D and an independent contributor to the HF pathogenesis is somehow novel. • The use of agents capable of disrupting the accumulation of oligomeric amylin in the heart may open new avenues for treating HF due to diabetes. • The generation of rats that express human amylin in pancreatic ß-cells on the insulin II promoter should in theory circumvent the problem that overexpression of rodent (non-amyloidogenic) amylin in mice does not induce amyloid deposition.
inn_text_wkn: • There are many analogies with Alzheimer-like oligomer depositions in the heart, but the PI does explicitly consider whether, and to what respect, the deposition of amylin is different from that due to protein aggregates on different etiology. • Although the use of the agents able of disrupting accumulation of oligomeric amylin could represent a novel therapeutic strategy to reduce or delay the progression of diabetic HF, there no convincing preliminary data in support of this central contention.
app_text_str: • The specific aims are logical. • Most if not all of methods are up and running in the PI’s and co-I/Collaborators’ laboratories. Importantly, the proposed rat models are already available to the PI, although it is not clear why some breeding pairs were provided by Pfizer.
app_text_wkn: • The entire proposal is densely written and verbose (highly repetitive). The experimental design is particularly difficult to follow because of its rather disorganized lay-out. For instance, preliminary data are quite intermingled either with the rationale or specific experimental design, without consistency throughout the proposal. Figure legends are not provided at all, and some figures are barely readable (see Fig.29). • The overall workflow for the three specific aims (Fig.13) is densely packed and it is not clear whether it reflects, in part or in full, the mechanisms/pathways that will be explored in the proposal and how they are connected to each other. • It is totally unclear whether male or female rats will be used. • Of particular overall concern is the lack of alternatives for some subaims and lack of clarity. For SA1, what if the sarcolemmal permeabilization is not the primary defect triggered by amylin oligomers? What alternative hypotheses/analyses will be considered/conducted to explain amylin oligomers cardiac cell toxicity/damage? For SA2A, if cardiac amylin buildup indirectly affects AMPK signal, how this will be tested, and what are the expected ouctomes in pre-diabetic HIP vs. UCD rats? For SA2B, how blocking nitric oxide activity via amylin oligomers would lead to increase production of ROS? While this remains conceptually unclear, it is also not explained at all how this possibility will be addressed. For SA3, the PI mentions MG53 in alternative to P188. How this unspecified drug should works in the heart of pre-diabetic animals?  And what is the expected outcome in terms of cardiac function in HPI and WT rats, in presence or absence of P188 or alternative drug treatment? • In SA2A, the PI states that:” In collaboration with Dr. H. Traugott, we will measure substrate oxidation rates and cardiac power in perfused HIP hearts to assess the amylin oligomer-induced changes in cardiac energy substrate metabolism”. It is unclear what exactly will be measured, and under what conditions. In the Potential Problems/Extensions, the PI discusses possible outcomes in isolated myocytes, but not in isolated whole hearts. Why the latter studies will be performed? The same vagueness involves possible indirect effects of cardiac amylin buildup for which the PI proposes to pursue several pathways without explaining how this will be done and what to expect from these studies (see AMPK). • Experimental design 2B: Notoriously,CH-H2DCFA is not specific for H2O2. A ratiometric detection of intracellular H2O2 level changes can be performed instead, using Hydrogen Peroxide Sensor Hyper. • Specific Aim 3: Would the membrane sealant P188 and EETs be synergistic? Equally important, it is unclear how EETs work in the preventing amylin oligomer formation in the serum. What is the role of fibrinolysis in this context? This should be thoroughly discussed. • Figures 31 and 32 are difficult to interpret and likely incomplete. First, it seems that not in all T2D patients where high amounts of amylin oligomers are present in the serum, elevated amounts of these oligomers are found in the heart. This evidence seems to contradict a bit the main pathophysiological mechanism of the proposal. Second, it is not entirely clear what is depicted in Fig.32 because it seems that amylin oligomers have different molecular weight in Fig. 31 vs. Fig.32. • Overall, the research design is very ambitious, encompassing several in vitro and in vitro techniques; for several of them, it is not clear what the endpoints/expected outcomes and interpretation/alternatives will be. • Statistical analysis is totally missing.

study_section: Hemostasis and Thrombosis Study Section
imp_text: The overarching hypothesis of this application is that apoptosis signal-regulating kinase 1 (ASK1) is a novel regulator of platelet function and thrombosis. To test this new possibility, the PI, Dr. Sullivan, proposes two aims. Aim 1 is to dissect a role for ASK1 in regulating signaling events downstream of platelet agonists (activation) that are involved in the thrombotic process. Aim 2 is designed to test the specific hypothesis that ASK1 functions downstream of GPCRs and exerts its effect through activation of p38 and ERK2 MAP kinase signaling. There are several strong aspects in this proposal. (1) ASK1 may be central to the signaling downstream of a number of platelet agonists, and the physiological relevance of the MAPKs activation in the context of thrombosis remains controversial; therefore, the significance is potentially high. (2) The PI provides a good deal of preliminary data (obtained with cutting-edge approaches) in support of the main contention of the grant. (3) The research team assembled by the PI is very well-qualified to conduct the proposed research. However, there are serious flaws in the present proposal. (1) While Aim 1 I well-designed and easy to follow, it is not clear what we are going to learn from Aim 2 that deals with GPCR/ASK1 signaling, particularly in terms of possible GPCR/ASK1 therapeutic targeting. (2) ASK1 is very sensitive to changes in cell/tissue redox conditions, representing a parallel way of activation with respect to platelet agonist activation of ASK1; however, this possibility is acknowledged but not really pursued as a possible alternative/additive way of ASK1 activation. (3) Based on the enclosed biosketch, it seems that the PI has not been studying platelet function/thrombosis for quite some time.
sig_text_str: • The proposal is highly significant because current agents that are effective in inhibiting platelet activation/thrombosis are mined by severe bleeding complications. • Ascertaining whether ASK1 (and dependent signaling) has a role in platelet physiology/thrombotic could have significant implications in cardiovascular disorders because ASK1 is also a major target for ROS/RNS.
sig_text_wkn: • From the proposal, it is not clear how more information about mechanisms through which ASK1 activation is promoted by platelet agonists could be translated into more effective therapies against pro-thrombotic complications. • The overall significance is somehow diminished by the fact that ASK1 phosphorylation is the only post-translational modification examined here.
inv_text_str: • The PI, Dr. Sullivan is the Director of the Delaware Cardiovascular Research Center. He is well-published. His lab appears to be well-funded with an R01 as PI (that however in during a 1-year no cost extension), a NSF grant as co-PI and an exploratory grant (P20) for which he is Director of a subproject. • The collaboration with Dr. Diana S. Wunder that is an expert of signaling pathways in platelets that may contribute to thrombosis is a major asset to the proposal, along with the contribution of Dr. Lauren V. Parola who has well-documented expertise in studying mechanisms of platelet activation (and their abnormalities) in cardiovascular disorders and sickle cell disease. Both investigators have an excellent publication record, enlisting paper in top-tier journals.
inv_text_wkn: •  During his career, the PI was involved in studying hormone-induced signaling, purification and characterization of a protein called JAM-A as well as in the cloning of the human cDNA that encodes C1B1, a novel integrin-binding protein. This reflects a broad interest in molecular cell biology and signaling. However, setting aside a paper published in 1991 as first-author, his enclosed publication list does not reflect any recent interest/publication in platelet physiology and thrombosis.  It appears that the PI will heavily rely on the expertise of his collaborators for a successful completion of the proposed science.
inn_text_str: • The concept that ASK1 regulates platelet function and thrombosis is novel and may have important practical implications. • The characterization of platelet function and thrombosis in ASK1 deficient mice has never been performed. • The use of laser-induced injury to cremaster arterioles and the use of chimera mice to dissect a role for platelet ASK1 vs. endothelial cell ASK1 are important innovative aspects of the proposal.
inn_text_wkn: • The proposed pharmacological and biochemical approaches are standard.
app_text_str: • The proposal is well-written and easy to follow up to Aim 1. • Aim 1 - The combined use of laser-induced thrombosis and intravital microscopy in mouse chimeras to establish a role for endothelial cell ASK1 is very elegant.
app_text_wkn: •   Although the experimental research design is logical, Aim 2 is totally dependent on Aim 1; no mechanisms alternative to platelet agonists/GPCRs activation of ASK1 are considered in this proposal, including possible redox activation of ASK1. •  Aim 1 – What strategies will be pursued to cement the view that endothelial ASK1 is chiefly involved in defective thrombosis? •  Aim 1- If activation of caspase 3 is affected by the absence of ASK1, what additional functional repercussions on platelets are expected in addition to possible changes in procoagulatory surface? More importantly, should ASK1 be over-expressed under any hematologic or non-hematologic disease conditions, would the PI expect a higher degree of apoptosis in platelets, and if so, through what mechanisms and leading to what functional outcome? In alternative, would changes in caspase 3 activation be used only to index exposure of phosphatidylserine? Either way, the expected outcome/interpretation of this set of experiments in not clear. •  Aim 1- It is not clear how sustained activation of JNK1/2 could contribute to the observed functional defects in ASK1-/- mice, if JNK1/2 has been shown to be required for platelet aggregation and thrombus formation (see Adam F. et al., Blood, 2010). Is JNK1/2 differently activated by low or high doses of platelet agonists? This is not clear. •  How the PI explain preliminary data (Fig.8) showing that high doses of agonists can circumvent defective platelet activation upon agonist stimulation in ASK1-/- KO mice? Mechanisms accounting for this evidence are not provided/discussed. They may circumstantiate/limit the relevance of ASK1 signaling in platelet aggregation/thrombosis. •  Aim 2 – Overall, the aim is very difficult to follow given the apparent complex signaling cascades induced by GPCR leading to the activation of MAP kinase, possibly involving ASK1 activation by platelet agonists. The rather simplistic Fig. 13 does not help grasping what pathways will likely be at play or studied in this aim. It sounds that some of these signaling cascades act in parallel to each other. • Equally important, it is not clear how this voluminous amount of work will help identifying novel therapeutic targets to combat thrombotic disorders. This aim should be restructured, providing the specific questions that will be tested (and how), explaining why defining ASK1-dependent pathways (with respect to more traditional signaling cascades involved in the thrombotic process) is important, particularly in light of paving ese new routes to modulate platelet aggregation/thrombosis. As it is, the translational implications eventually emanating from these studies remain totally unclear. •  Aim 2 – Redox-dependent ASK1 activation may represent an important pathway, parallel or additive to phosphorylation, leading to aberrant platelet activations and thrombosis. ROS-dependent activation of ASK1 is depicted in Fig. 19, but the role of important factors accounting for it such as the redox statues of thioredoxin will not be addressed in the proposal. •  In several places, adequate references are missing (see, for instance, conflicting reports in the Innovation section or in the Rational of Aim 2). •  p values are missing in most of the key (pilot data) figures, and sample size and statistical analysis is not provided.

Aim 1 will characterize lipin 1 in the setting of calorie excess, AIM will phenotype  transgenic mice with defects in lipin 1 and apply shotgun lipid profiling to  these animals and Aim 3 will overexpress lipin 1 (either nuclear or WT)  in mice with lipotoxic cardiomyopathy.  The overall scientific approach to the question is sound and the investigators are experts in metabolic disease and are capable of completing the proposed experiements with a requested funds and available resources.  The question of the role of lipin 1 in metabolic disease is an important one, but I am not clear on the health impact of the suggested study.  While many patients with obesity and diabetes develop heart failure the vast majority of these patients develop and ischemic cardiomyopathy or microvascular dysfunction.  Diastolic heart failure prevalence is increasing, but its relationship to lipid toxicity is unclear and while it maybe related to lipid accumulation in myocytes, this study will not answer this question. Further preliminary data or literature mechanistically linking lipid accumulation to human cardiomyopathies would bolster the clinical significance of the proposed work.

imp_text: The investigators have a novel finding that accumulation of a protein, amylin occurs in diabetic cardiomyopathy.  They hypothesize that this accumulation is a “contributor to the multifactorial pathogenesis of diabetic heart disease and that mitigating amylin accumulation will delay the onset of cardiac dysfunction….” The investigators have experience in studying this protein and have an impressive team of collaborators.  They plan to characterize the effect of amylin accumulation in the heart using a variety of techniques.  There is significant innovation both conceptually and technically in this proposal and the results could yield to potential therapeutic targets in some human cardiomyopathies, but there are some limitations to the study that were not sufficiently addressed in the proposal.  Diabetic mice develop a cardiomyopathy with predominantly diastolic dysfunction and according to the authors rodent amylin does not produce amyloids and thus could not explain the dysfunction apparent in nearly all previous studies of diabetic cardiac disease in rodent models.  Thus while amylin may play a role in diabetic cardiomyopathy in humans, it seems unlikely that amylin deposition is the dominant factor involved.  Amyloid cardiomyopathy is a well described diagnosis and much rarer than diabetes, although  it has been described as the most common cause of death in those >110 years of age Coles LS, Young RD (2012). There are no treatments other than heart transplant and the findings in this study may provide insight in to this and other rare oligomer induced cardiomyoathies.  The authors did not acknowledge this a a barrier to potentially translating this work to clinical applications.

The hypothesis is that this protein is involved in the adaptive angiogenesis.  We currently have little understanding of the mechanisms involved in adaptive angiogenesis and microvascular dysfunction in heart failure.  Further elucidating the molecular mechanisms involved will lead to a better basic understanding of the disease and potentially lead to translational therapeutic targets.  The investigator has abundant preliminary data to support his hypothesis and excellent research environment with multiple collaborators.  Most impressive is the bedside to bench to bedside approach which highlights the likely clinical relevance of the proposal. imp_text: This project is focused around the understanding the role of hyperamylinemia in diabetic heart failure. If the overall hypothesis of this proposal proves correct, then this work will be identify circulating amylin levels as a biomarker for heart disease in diabetic patients, and provide rationale for the development of therapeutic approaches to delay cardiac dysfunction in this patient population. Dr. Murphy is a junior faculty with a track record in the study of amyloid formation and biology. He has received funding from the AHA and the NSF for his work on amyloid aggregate formation in cardiovascular disease. He has recently published a seminal paper in Circulation Research demonstrating that toxic amylin aggregates build up in the heart in humans with obesity and type-2 diabetes, providing rationale for the current study. The team is rounded out by experts in cardiac physiology and diabetes. The environment at Davis is superb for these studies. The project is divided into three aims. The first aim is designed to determine the role of amylin oligomerization in cardiac function. The aim will test the mechanistic hypothesis that amylin oligomerization promotes myocyte remodeling. Both myocyte sarcolemmal integrity and Ca2+-dependent pathways will be studied. The second aim is designed to determine whether amylin buildup accelerates diabetic heart failure. This aim will test the mechanistic hypothesis that amylin oligomerization at the sarcolemma alters the insulin-PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, leading to activation of RAGE, leading to mitochondrial structural changes and ROS elevation. The final aim is designed to determine whether limiting amylin buildup delays heart failure in a model or pre-diabetes. This is a translational aim designed to test the feasibility and develop proof-of-principle data for the reduction of amylin as a therapeutic strategy in diabetic patients.

imp_text: This proposal is designed to study the role of the small GTPase Rnd3 in heart failure. In particular, the mechanisms by which Rnd3 is downregulated will be explored. The rationale for this study is based on the phenotypic observations made in Rnd3 -/- vs +/- knockout mouse models, with the former being embryonically lethal, with the latter presenting with developed dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure in a model of transverse aortic constriction. The end result of this program will not shed light of why Rnd3 was reduced in heart failure patients, rather will describe the phenotype of Rnd3 +/- mice. Still unclear will remain the question of why a heterotypic lowering of Rnd3 levels is observed in some patients. The proposal is divided into three aims. The first aim will study the role of Rnd3 in regulating the Notch transcriptional complex in endothelial cells. The workflow of the Aim is listed rather than providing a rationale for the methods used. The second aim will then look at the role of Rnd3 in HIF-VEGF paracrine signaling in cardiomyocytes. Again, the approach lasts a narrative providing the rationale for the methods used, and rather lists the conditions that will be tested. The final aim will then examine the effects of Rnd3 overexpression and reduction in cardiomyocytes, and will perform rescue experiments to establish the role of Rnd3 in both in vitro and in vivo models. The mouse strains that will be used in Aim 3.3 do not exist yet, and thus represents a potential tragic flaw. Overall, while this work will shed light on the role of Rnd3 in (patho)physiology, the translation of this work to patient care or therapeutic intervention is unclear. Thus, the significance of this work is low.

imp_text: This is a well-written and interesting proposal designed to define the role of Ask1 in platelet biology. The abstract of the proposal rightly points out that a major gap in knowledge in the platelet field is the understanding of what signaling pathways maintain platelets in their quiescent state. However, the aim of this grant is not to fill this knowledge gap, but to now study whether Ask1 plays a role in the downstream mechanisms regulating platelet activation. As the activation of platelets at sites of vascular injury is a requisite for hemostasis, the discovery of Ask1 as a key regulator of platelet activation is mechanistically interesting yet does not provide rationale for the targeted inhibition of Ask1 as a safe and efficacious therapy to prevent thrombosis without effecting hemostasis. Thus, the translation of this study toward clinically utility is low, in contrast to the claims made in the narrative that this study may identify new therapeutic agents. Ask1-deficiency results in a bleeding phenotype – thus, this is not a feasible drug target balancing safety with efficacy. The facilities are sufficient for this study; the team has been working in the field of platelet biology for many years and have an established individual track record in publishing and funding, yet have not established a track record of collaboration.

imp_text: This is a proposal that tests an innovative idea that chronic caloric and lipid excess could lead to increased phosphorylation and cytoplasmic localization of lipin 1, a critical regulator of intermediary metabolism in the cardiac myocytes.   It is also hypothesized that abnormalities in the regulation of cardiac lipin 1 activity can promote glycerolipid synthesis and inhibit its pro-catabolic actions, contributing to the lipotoxic cardiomyopathy that develops during the states of chronic caloric excess.  This approach has the potential to provide new insights into the mechanisms leading to cardiac lipotoxicity and in the future to design new therapeutic strategies aimed at reversing or preventing the functional and metabolic dysregulations leading to heart failure.  As such, the significance is very high and the proposed study promising. The investigator has assembled a strong team with complementary expertise among the individual members of the team. The preliminary data are solid.  Weaknesses include a bit overambitious scope of the experiments, lack of the timelines, respective contributions of the PI and co-Investidators, and grouping/prioritization of the experiments.   Also potential effects of the reactivation of nuclear cardiac lipin 1 on PGC-1a pathway which not only enhances mitochondrial biogenesis and respiration, but may least to increased ROS production and oxidative stress.  Overall, the proposal is of merit and its strengths outweigh its weaknesses.

imp_text: This research project is aimed to investigate the pathological significance of downregulation of Rnd3 in the heart on Notch and HIF1 signaling and associated with this phenomenon molecular mechanisms. The overarching hypothesis of this proposal is that in cardiomyocytes downregulation of Rnd3 results in insufficient angiogenesis by enhancing Notch activity in endothelia and weakening HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling. The PI has made significant progress in this area, and completion of the current project is likely to move this field forward even more.  Weaknesses include large scope of experimental work proposed, where priorities of each task remain somewhat unclear. The difficulties seem to arise from the complexities of the HIF1 and Notch signaling pathways, where multiple protein-protein interactions are involved, and the lack of effective inhibitors of these interactions. Overall, this is an ambitious and complex proposal with many risks, but the potential impact is high.

Clinical and translational significance for the understanding and treatment of the human heart failure.

study_section: Hemostasis and Thrombosis Study Section
imp_text: This grant application seeks to discover the role of ASK1, a novel key signaling molecule implicated in the regulation of platelet function and thrombosis. The main hypothesis of the proposed research is that ASK1 plays a key role in regulating multiple and distinct signaling events to affect the process of thrombosis. The preliminary data suggest that ASK1 functions downstream of GPCRs and exerts its effect through activation of p38 and ERK2 MAP kinases.  The mechanistic information on dynamic regulation of platelet function could help to uncover novel therapeutic targets involved in regulation of multiple events of platelet activation.  Information generated from these studies will potentially lead to novel therapeutic strategies to target activated platelets in such conditions as myocardial infarction and stroke.  Strengths of the application include excellent expertise of the PI and his collaborators, strong preliminary data, powerful and well thought out experimental approaches, high translational potential of the study and potential impact of the mechanistic findings on the entire field.  Weaknesses are an apparent lack of a coherent coordination between the investigators (who are located in 3 separate sites), lack of clear timeline for the project and need for better description of the project workflows and how the data from the first Aim could inform the experimental design in the second Aim.  Based on the enumerated strengths, this proposal is meritorious and has potential for informing a novel design of the inhibitors of platelet function for future translation into the clinic.

study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: While the link between nutrient excess, or high fat diet (HFD), and cardiac lipotoxicity is well known, its detailed mechanism is not completely understood. This project proposes that lipin 1 may be the key player in the cardiac lipotoxicity induced by HFD. This has great significance for elucidating related mechanisms and identifying new therapeutic targets and strategies for preventing or reversing the cardiac dysfunction in lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. The PI proposed that lipin 1 regulates both anabolic (cytoplasmic PAP-mediated lipid synthesis) and catabolic (nuclear transcriptional coactivator function) pathways depending upon the nutrient availability of the cell. The proposed experiments of all three aims are generally good and can be executed by the PI’s team, provided that the hypothesis is correct. The premise of the hypothesis is that cytoplasm lipin 1 promotes the PAP activity function of lipin 1, leading to anabolic effects of lipin 1 to stimulate glycerolipid synthesis and cardiac myocyte lipotoxicity; meanwhile, nuclear lipin 1 promotes/retains its transcriptional coactivator function, leading to catabolic effects of lipin 1 that potentially prevent cardiac dysfunction in lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. This project has novelty by studying lipin 1’s dual functions, their correlation to lipin 1’s cellular localization, and the corresponding mechanisms. However, some key preliminary results are not presented and thus prevent the reviewer from evaluating the project’s feasibility and the hypothesis’s credibility. With large amounts of preliminary data (a total of 12 figures), the PI surprisingly did not include even one cellular localization result of lipin 1 (e.g., under influence by HFD or mTOR-mediated phosphorylation activation, or inhibition of such phosphorylation, etc.), the key data required to support the hypothesis. This can be done easily by either immune(fluorescent) staining the cell with anti-lipin 1 or immunoblot with isolated proteins from cytoplasm and nuclear proteins. It is not known how the project would continue if the cellular localization of lipin 1 remains unchanged after HFD treatment (some preliminary data indirectly suggested this may be the case). There are also several other concerns in the preliminary results and drawbacks in the Approach that collectively diminish the strength of the project. For these reasons, the overall likelihood that this project will have a sustained, powerful influence in the field is low to medium

sig_text_wkn: The link between nutrient excess (or HDF) and cardiac lipotoxicity is well known in the field. The PI proposed a new insight to study this link by associating cellular localization of lipin 1 with its function to the HDF-induced cardiac lipotoxicity. This would provide a novel mechanism of lipin 1 mediated lipid metabolism in the myocardium; however, no preliminary result was presented to show lipin 1 cellular location. This missing and important key evidence would allow reviewers to fairly evaluate the hypothesis. The significance and feasibility of the project is thus seriously diminished without demonstration of lipin 1 cellular localization and its cellular translocation either in cardiac myocyte of mice fed by HDF (in vivo) and/or in cardiomyocyte (NRVM) after mTOR-mediated activation (or inhibition) of lipin 1 phosphorylation (in vitro).
inv_text_str: The PI is an Assistant Professor at Washington University, St. Louis, MO. The PI has training and expertise in lipin, PGC-1 and other relevant fields. The PI has an excellent track record of high-impact publication in the related (lipid and metabolism) field of the project and is well qualified for the proposed study. The PI also has a good funding history: besides being the PI on one R01 grant, the PI has been actively involved in multiple collaborations as Co-I in other’s research grants.

inn_text_str: Study effects of lipid 1 on energy metabolism and glycerolipid homeostasis in the myocardium is relatively new. The PI will use or generate several mouse models that can separate the two molecular functions (PAP activity and transcription regulation) of lipin 1 in vivo. The link of PAP activity of lipin 1 to high fat diet-induced cardiac lipotoxicity is particularly novel, and the study, if successful, would lead to better understanding of the mechanism and factors that contribute to cardiac lipotoxicity in response to lipid overload. The PI hypothesized lipin 1 executes one of its dual functions by its cellular localization – this is novel. Specifically, cytoplasmic lipin 1 localization, induced by HDF and mTOR activation, contributes to the PAP activity function of lipin 1, leading to anabolic effects of lipin 1 to stimulate glycerolipid synthesis and cardiac myocyte lipotoxicity. On the other hand, the PI proposed that nuclear lipin 1 localization promotes/retains its transcriptional coactivator function (to activate PGC-1a target genes) and may potentially prevent cardiac dysfunction in lipotoxic cardiomyopathy in nutrient excess.
inn_text_wkn: The hypothesis is novel and if true, it would provide significant new insight on cardiac lipid metabolism by HDF and nutrient excess in obese patients and identify new therapeutic targets and strategies to prevent and reverse the cardiac dysfunction in lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. However, the proposal fell short and did not provide key preliminary results to convincingly support the project’s feasibility. Specifically, the cellular localization of lipin 1 in the heart cells and its cellular translocation would naturally be key and important feasibility data, and therefore be expected by the reviewers as part of the preliminary results. The lack of this key evidence in the preliminary results makes the proposal’s novelty uncertain. The link with cellular localization of lipin 1 to the HDF induced lipotoxicity would provide a novel mechanism. The feasibility of the project, along with the novelty, is seriously diminished without demonstration of lipin 1 cellular localization and translocation in either mouse cardiac myocytes (influenced by HDF and low fat diet) or NRVMs (influenced by mTOR-mediated lipin 1 phosphorylation).
app_text_str: This is a well-organized and clearly presented proposal with nice background description, logical reasoning and preliminary results to lead to scientifically sound and data-supportive hypothesis. The use of both fld mice, PAP-deficient mice, and other generated mouse models (plus intercross mice with loss of lipin 1 function with PPARa overexpressing mice) are excellent designs that will allow the PI to dissect lipin 1’s dual functions on PAP activity as an enzyme and on transcriptional regulation as an co-activator, separately. The proposed mouse models of lipin 1 “loss-of-function” and “gain-of-function” will help elucidate the role of lipin 1 (and related mechanism of regulation) in cardiac lipid metabolism and cardiac lipotoxicity. The study and separation of lipin 1’s PAP activity and nuclear transcriptional coactivator function are thoughtful designs. The proposed experiments in the three aims are straightforward and the PI’s team should have the capability to perform them and achieve the goals, provided that their hypothesis (lipin 1’s cellular localization decides which one of the dual functions it plays) is correct.
app_text_wkn: As mentioned above, that no lipin 1 cellular location data was presented as part of the preliminary results is a big drawback (it can be easily addressed by an immunostaining of cells or immunoblot of isolated cytoplasm and nuclear proteins for lipin 1 expression). Moreover, the PI did not show the lipin 1 phosphorylation data in cardiac myocyte of mice fed by HFD. As no lipin 1 increase at total protein level was observed after 20-week HFD (Fig. 4C) – for which the PI explained that observation as “increase in PAP activity by HFD is due to post-translational regulation of lipin 1” — the phosphorylation status of lipin 1 (an indicator of lipin 1 being phosphorylated by mTOR and a cytoplasm form of lipin 1 that promotes PAP activity based on the PI’s hypothesis) influenced by HFD and LFD would be interesting and expected by the reviewers to judge. However, again, this important data was not presented in the existing immunoblot (Fig. 4C and Fig. 12). An inclusion of lipin 1 level and lipin 1 phosphorylation status in Fig. 12 would greatly help evaluate the feasibility of this project. For the existing immunoblot in Fig. 12, additional detection of lipin 1 and lipin 1 phosphorylation would directly correlate lipin 1, its phosphorylation by mTOR, and mTOR status to support the cytoplasm lipin 1 mediates HFD-induced lipotoxicity, the base and premise of the hypothesis. In Fig. 3, the transgenic mouse model used to overexpress lipin 1 is PGC-1a transgenic mice. Because PGC-1a is an upstream regulator of lipin 1 gene and a coactivator in lipin 1-mediated transcription regulation, these factors would complicate the endpoint readout. Because PGC-1a transgenic mice affect as well, in addition to lipin 1, other PGC-1a downstream genes such as increase of ERRa and ERRy expression (Fig. 3) and several other target genes (Fig. 6), all these could lead to events that may be related to lipid metabolism, but independent of lipin 1 increase. A specific, exclusive lipin 1 transgenic model would be better to study lipin 1 function and role for this matter. Although the PI did propose in Aim 3 to generate lipin 1 transgenic mice to study directly, the preliminary results derived from PGC-1a transgenic mice that were used to support the hypothesis are not solid. Consequently, the hypothesis based from these results may not well based. The aims of proposed project would still not elucidate how exactly the mechanism of lipid 1 cellular transfer from nucleus to cytoplasm by mTOR phosphorylation.
