study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: The project has merits in significance and novelty. If the hypothesis is confirmed, the project has potential to generate a patient-relevant animal model that mimics human heart failure. The application is well organized and presented, with logical reasoning for most parts of the project. Specifically, the proposed Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis via HIF1a pathway has strong supportive preliminary results, and the designed research plan should be able to achieve the aim. The PI has high-impact factor journal productivity and has the experience to perform the proposed work. However, some important data was missing in the preliminary results that would otherwise greatly assist the evaluation of the project’s potential. For example, level of HIF1a protein expression in human hearts and the comparison of HIF1a protein levels between normal human and failing heart patients were not shown in Fig. 5. Common understanding is that normal human hearts do not express detectable HIF1a (see below for detail), so the clinical potential of Rnd3+/- mouse model, which is based on the premise that normal mouse hearts express high endogenous HIF1a (Fig. 9A and Fig. 13A)—so Rnd3 deficiency (Rnd3+/-) could cause HIF1a decrease, is not clear at this moment without these key preliminary data. Moreover, the proposed Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis involving Notch pathway lacks solid evidence and logical reasoning. Also, there are a number of weaknesses in the approach (research plan), including a lack of assays for assessing whether HIF1a is truly a downstream effector of Rnd3 (more details below). Overall, the likelihood that this project will have a sustained, powerful influence in the field is moderately high.
sig_text_str: The project has potential to generate a more patient-relevant animal model that mimics human heart failure, which is greatly needed for the successful translation of bench studies to clinical therapy and evaluation of a new drug or intervention strategy for cardiac disease in this field.
sig_text_wkn: One important and missing data is the level of HIF1a protein expression in human hearts in Fig. 5. What are the HIF1a protein levels and how do they look in normal human and failing heart patients? It would be nice to see what is the HIF1a protein expression status in Fig. 5A. The correlation of HIF1a and Rnd3 between normal and failing heart patients would truly reveal whether Rnd3 indeed upregulates the HIF1a pathway in Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis in a clinical setting. This information would weigh heavily on the significance of the project in terms of the potential clinical application in human hearts.
inv_text_str: The PI is an Associate Professor at the Institute of Biosciences and Technology, Texas A&M University Health Science Center. The PI has an outstanding track record of productivity with consistent publication at high-impact journals (however, when I searched for one of PI’s PNAS papers related to the Notch pathway, it could not be found by PubMed data search based on PI’s name). The PI has a good funding history and is well qualified for the proposed study.
inn_text_str: The PI’s group, for the first time, proposes and shows that Rnd3 has novel functions as a regulator in the adaptive coronary angiogenesis program. Specifically, Rnd3-promoted HIF1a-VEGF pathway-mediated angiogenesis in cardiomyocytes is novel and have strong supporting preliminary data. If the hypothesis is verified to be true, the project may provide a potentially patient-relevant animal model (Rnd3 +/-) that mimics human heart failure.
inn_text_wkn: The proposed Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis pathway that involves Notch has a lack of evidence and appears somehow superficial. While the first Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis pathway that involves HIF1a is more convincing based on the preliminary results and described logical reasoning, there is still no solid evidence or experiments designed that demonstrated/will demonstrate that Rnd3 directly upregulates HIF1a as part of a downstream pathway in promoting angiogenesis (please see detail below).
app_text_str: This is a well-organized and presented proposal with logical reasoning, supportive preliminary data and related (most part of) research plan for the aims. Particularly, the research theme focusing on Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis via proposed HIF1a-VEGF pathway has merit with strong supportive preliminary results. The Rnd3+/- mouse is a great model to study the hypothesis. The PI has appropriate experience to cover the range of research expertise required, as demonstrated by the preliminary results and PI’s related publications.
app_text_wkn: Normal human heart muscles do not express HIF1a protein but express HIF1a mRNA (http://www.proteinatlas.org/ENSG00000100644-HIF1A/tissue), suggesting the major regulatory mechanism of HIF1a protein presence in human heart is most likely due to HIF1a degradation. It is not clear how under normoxia it would be able to detect HIF1a protein expression unless mouse normal heart or cardiomyocytes express high endogenous HIF1a under normoxia (Fig.  9A, Fig. 13A); if so, the observed discrepancy (difference of mouse and human hearts on their endogenous HIF1a expression under normoxia) and the proposed study in the mouse model may yield different results in human heart cells. Thus the translational or clinical potential of the project (e.g., the Rnd3+/- mouse as human heart failure model) may be compromised. To verify the hypothesis, the PI did not include some important assays that would directly demonstrate whether HIF1a is a true Rnd3 downstream effector for angiogenesis. (1) For example, if the hypothesis is correct, a mutant HIF1a form that is always (constitutively) on would dismiss upstream Rnd3’s influence on angiogenesis – that is, in a situation using cells expressing constitutive-expressed HIF1a (HIF mutant form that has deleted ODD domain so no hydroxylation would occur and the resultant HIF1a protein cannot be degraded (Dev. Biol., 2012: 362:24-41)), would downregulating Rnd3 (e.g., siRNA-Rnd3) still affect the angiogenesis (tubing formation) readout? If Rnd3 downregulation still affects the angiogenesis readout in HIF1a always-on mutant cells, it would suggest Rnd3 might regulate angiogenesis independent of HIF1a pathway. (2) On the other hand, would Rnd3 overexpression (Ad-Rnd3) still be able to promote angiogenesis in HIF1a-KO cells? These assays would help define whether Rnd3 indeed mediates angiogenesis via HIF1a-VEGF signaling pathway. Most proposed binding assays for physical interaction are designed by using enforced tagged expression of the two target proteins (e.g., Aim 1.1-1, etc.), which does not necessarily reflect what occurs in real situation endogenously. There is a lack of evidence that Rnd3 downregulation is the cause (rather an association) for human failing hearts. Specifically, protein expression of HIF1a, the proposed Rnd3-downstream component, was not illustrated in Fig. 5A (an important data point that is missing). The results of Fig. 12 only indicate that Rnd3 overexpression leads to secretion of pro-angiogenic factors. To be specific that it is the VEGF playing a key role for HUVEC tube formation (and thus supportive to the PI’s hypothesis of Rnd3-mediated HIF1a-VEGF pathway), the critical control that contains culture media collected but incubated (or pretreated) with VEGF-neutralized antibody should be included. While the proposed Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis via HIF1a pathway has some supportive preliminary data to back up the logical reasoning, the link of Rnd3 and Notch in mediating Rnd3-mediated angiogenesis in heart is weak and superficial, and lacks supportive data. The PI mentioned that Rnd3 genetic deletion upregulates Notch signaling in brain from their report, but the PI did not provide similar results for heart endothelial cells; and the PI’s claimed publication (Ref. 15) did not include journal volume and page numbers, so the information cannot be accessed or verified. A similar paper by others in the literature showed that Rnd3 deficiency led to a decrease of NICD (an active Notch isoform) degradation in the brain but had no link to angiogenesis. Also, the PI did not provide the background, logic reasoning or data that would link Hes1 transactivation (Notch activity) and VEGF R2/R3 regulation (Fig. 15). Specifically, it is not clear how Rnd3-mediated downregulation of Hes1 transactivation relates to VEGF R2 and R3 (or angiogenesis in general) upregulation. imp_text: The project’s goal is to study the role of ASK1 in platelet function and to seek new therapy for anti-thrombosis and cardiovascular disease. If successful, the project would reveal a novel function of ASK1 and its mechanism of activation in platelets. A majority of the research plan is comprehensive and the team has the competency to complete the project. Some features of the proposed ASK1 activation pathway, however, are predictable due to the fact that it (and MAP kinase cascade) has been well studied. The use of a wide variety of ASK1 activators or platelet agonists in the proposal may result in a vast and complicated endpoint readout due to a number of agonists and their distinct receptors, as well as relevant pathways involved. It is unclear whether the PI’s plan can stratify, consolidate and interpret the data to delineate the mechanism of ASK1 activation and its downstream signaling pathway. The PI has the qualifications to lead the project, but the PI has not published in the last 2-3 years (up to 2011 - the grant submission date). Overall, the likelihood that this project will have a sustained, powerful influence in the field is moderately high.
sig_text_str: The proposed study seeks to find novel anti-thrombotic targets for treatment of thrombotic complication and cardiovascular disease, and therefore it is of significance.
sig_text_wkn: Because ASK1 activation and its signaling pathway are well studied by others in other cells, some of PI’s proposed studies on ASK1 activation (or its downstream signaling pathway) appear to be repetitive of studies already conducted in other cells (such as ASK1 activated MKK3/p38 and MKK4/JNK-pathways) as well as somewhat predictable in platelets; the study may not provide new information for ASK1 signaling pathway in this regard.

app_text_str: Studies take advantage of an existent ASK1-/- mouse model to study the potential roles of ASK1 in regulating platelet function and thrombosis process. Studies have generated a reasonable amount of strong, supportive preliminary results to support its hypothesis. Studies are well designed and contemplate various outcomes and alternative approaches. Studies will use excellent “in vivo” thrombosis assays, including laser-induced thrombus formation in mice. The team proposes to use a chimeric mouse model to dissect ASK1 function from platelets and endothelial cells. The team has appropriate experience to cover the range of research expertise required.
app_text_wkn: A wide range of ASK1 activation agents used in different studies may account for some discrepancy between PI’s preliminary results and literature: for example, ASK1-/- mice abolished both p38 and JNK activations if induced/activated by TNF or H2O2 (Ref. 76, from the group who generated the ASK1-/- KO mice); but, the PI only observed that the same ASK1-/- mice abolished p38 but not JNK activation if induced/activated by thrombin (Fig. 16). These data may suggest that, besides cell type, the chosen inducer/activator (thrombin, collagen, aspirin, TNF, or others) may play a critical role in determining a certain specific ASK1-activation signaling pathway. It is not clear how the PI plan to consolidate or correlate the variety of various inducers/activators or platelet agonists to generalize the mechanism of ASK1 activation in platelets. For example, how will the PI correlate the results of the ASK1 activation pathway from aspirin-washed, collagen-induced wild-type (WT) human platelets to that derived from thrombin-induced platelets from ASK1-/- mice? No experiment was proposed to reconstitute WT ASK1 expression in platelets collected from ASK1-/- mouse to confirm the proposed ASK1 “loss of” function in platelets. Minor issues: 1) The presentation of the experimental plan could be improved - a more focused, concise research plan would assist readers. 2) The legend label “ASK1-/-” should be correctly labeled in Fig. 7.

imp_text: The proposal has the potential to provide useful mechanistic information regarding the functions of lipin1 in the both the nucleus as a transcriptional regulator and as a PAP enzyme at the ER.  These studies will investigate the unique metabolic sensing functions of lipin1 and may provide important mechanistic insight into diabetic cardiomyopathy and cardiac lipotoxicity.  Molecular mechanisms underlying cardiac lipotoxicity are very significant given the clinical relevance and prevalence of these diseases in the Western world.  Mouse models are proposed to study the nuclear functions (transgenic mouse with mutation of 21 mTORC1 phosphorylation sites of lipin1) or PAP functions (hypomorphic allele resulting in N-terminal truncation of lipin1 with reduced PAP activity) of lipin1, which will provide useful in vivo models to assess cardiac function and disease in response to high fat diet and alterations in gene transcription and cardiac lipids.  Thee progress of these studies may be hampered by the inability to fully dissociate the nuclear and PAP enzymatic functions of lipin1.  Thus, it may be difficult to interpret how transcriptional and lipid alterations mechanistically modulate cardiac function and disease in response to lipotoxicity in these in vivo models.
sig_text_str: . Diabetic cardiomyopathy is a substantial public health concern and this proposal will address molecular mechanisms that underlie lipid metabolism and signaling that participates in lipotoxic cardiomyopathy. . Investigation of the effects of mTORC1-mediated phosphorylation of lipin1 on its function will provide novel insight into mechanisms regulating the observed effects of lipin1 on glycerolipid metabolism and downstream signaling and the downstream effectors of mTORC1-dependent signaling.

Elucidating the divergent transcriptional regulatory functions of lipin1 in the nucleus and its role as a phosphatase that generates DAG at the endoplasmic reticulum will provide valuable molecular insight into the mechanisms of caridiac lipotxicity and diabetic cardiomyopathy.  The novel mouse models proposed to investigate these divergent molecular functions of lipin1 in cardiomyocytes will provide useful tools to study lipin1 functions in the heart in response to metabolic stress or diabetic cardiomyopathy. . The investigation of specific lipin1 functions in the nucleus as a transcriptional regulator (PPARa/PGC1a coactivator; SREBP1 repressor) and as a PA phosphatase in the cytoplasm/ER and how this relates to myocardial lipid metabolism and signaling is innovative and the lipin-1 gain- and loss-of-function mouse models provide in vivo tools to study these functions in the heart. . Enhanced cardiac PAP activity in mice fed a high fat diet suggests that lipin1 may be an important metabolic sensor or mediator of lipid signaling involved in cardiac lipotoxicity
inn_text_wkn: . It may not be possible to completely dissociate the nuclear and PAP functions of lipin1.  Although the proposed mouse models may tilt the balance towards respective functions in either cellular compartment, endogenous wildtype lipin1 will still be expressed in the lipin1 21XA transgenic mouse and function in both compartments. Moreover, this transgenic model will elicit artificial levels of overexpression and the hypomorphic allele with deletion of the first 115 amino acids of lipin1 that reduces the PAP activity of lipin1 is odd since the PAP domain remains in tact.  A more elegant strategy would be to generate knock-in mutations in mice that mutate either the PAP domain of lipin1 or mTORC1 phosphorylation sites on lipin1.  This would maintain lipin1 expression at endogenous levels except with the given genetic manipulation that should obliterate PAP activity (and maintain nuclear transcriptional regulator functions) or abrogate mTORC1-mediated regulation (and enhance nuclear transcriptional regulatory functions) of lipin1, respectively.
app_text_str: . In vivo models are generated to enable investigation of the alterations in gene expression, lipids, and cardiac functional response to high fat diet caused by manipulation of lipin1 in the heart.  These will provide mechanistic insight into the function of lipin1 in the heart and diabetic cardiomyopathy and lipotoxicity. . Testing the response to high fat diet and TAC in these mouse models as proposed in Aim 3 are excellent experiments as this may be a good model for the Western diet and hypertensive cardiomyopathy seen in many Americans. . mRNA seq experiments may uncover novel transcriptional pathways regulated by lipin1.

The success of the proposed experiments is contingent upon the proper localization of the given mutants of lipin1 (i.e. mutation of the mTORC1 phosphorylation site results in lipin1 being retained in the nucleus).  Demonstration of the proper localization of lipin1 in vivo with the genetic manipulations proposed by immunolocalization and/or biochemical fractionation would ensure that the proposed mouse models will indeed be able to dissociate the molecular functions of lipin1 in the nucleus (as a transcriptional activator/repressor) and at the ER (as a PAP enzyme). . Generation of a lipin1 transgenic mouse with enhanced nuclear localization that is insensitive to mTORC1-mediated phosophorylation by mutation of 21 Ser/Thr residues may have substantial effects on the functions and/or structure of lipin1 beyond just enhancing nuclear localization.  All these mutations cumulatively could make lipin1 significantly more nonpolar or alter interaction of lipin1 with other proteins. Are all 21 residues phosphorylated by mTORC1? . DAG, which is generated by the PAP activity of lipin1, serves as an important second messenger signaling molecular that initiates critical signaling cascades in cardiomyocytes such as PKC. imp_text: The proposal will investigate the roles of Rnd3 in both cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells in the heart in response to pressure overload.  Rnd3 heterozygous mice exhibit defects in angiogenesis and more fulminant cardiac disease in response to pressure overload suggesting an important role for Rnd3 in adaptive cardiac angiogenesis.  Investigation of the critical functions of Rnd3 is innovative and the authors propose to investigate how Rnd3 may mechanistically regulate Notch signaling in endothelial cells and HIF1a-VEGF signaling in cardiomyocytes to mediate its effects on cardiac angiogenesis.  The proposal is exclusively focused on the effects of Rnd3 on Notch signaling in endothelial cells and HIF1a in cardiomyocytes.  Although this may indeed provide mechanistic insight into the adaptive cardiac fucntions of Rnd3, the proposal lacks the tools to precisely tease apart the effects of Rnd3 in endothelial cell versus cardiomyocyte signaling and function such as conditional Rnd3 knockout mice that would allow for deletion or haploinsufficiency of Rnd3 specifically in endothelial cells or cardiomyocytes.  This type of strategy would greatly improve the proposal and allow for much clearer delineation of the functions of Rnd3 in the various cardiac cell types and where Rnd3 functions to mediate the adaptive angiogenic program.  Instead, the proposal relies mostly on studies in the Rnd3 heterozygous mouse, which may be hampered by systemic effects of Rnd3 haploinsufficiency and may make it difficult to determine the cell types Rnd3 is functioning in.  Investigation of Rnd3 gain-of-function in in vivo and its subcellular localization in cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells would also help elucidate its molecular functions.
sig_text_str: . Investigation of molecular mechanisms that mediate adaptive angiogenesis in response to cardiac stress has promise for aiding in the identification of new therapeutic strategies to treat heart disease. . Reactivation of angiogenesis may be a novel therapy for cardiac disease and therefore, determination of the molecular mechanisms that underlie this process will provide valuable insight and inform future studies. . Rnd3 is downregulated in human heart failure, suggesting it may have important functions in cardiac disease pathogenesis.  Therefore, investigation of Rnd3 function in the setting of cardiac disease is significant.
sig_text_wkn: . Clinical trials for proangiogenic factors have not recapitulated the success of studies in animal models, suggesting that it may be difficult to efficaciously target angiogenesis in the treatment of cardiac disease.

inn_text_str: . Rnd3 function in the heart has not been previously investigated.  Rnd3+/- mice exhibit defects in cardiac angiogenesis and studies investigating the underlying mechanisms will provide novel insight into mechanisms underlying angiogenesis in response to cardiac stress. . Determination of novel molecular pathways that regulate responses to cardiac stress, specifically the roles of Rnd3, a small GTPase with unknown roles in the heart, is innovative and novel.
inn_text_wkn: . The applicant will utilize a previously established heterozygous knockout for Rnd3 (haploinsufficiency) to test the functions of Rnd3 in cardiomoyctes and endothelial cells in the heart in response to pressure overload rather than a more elegant strategy such as lineage-specific deletion of Rnd3 in endothelial cells or cardiomyocytes.  Generation of a conditional null allele for Rnd3 to delete Rnd3 with Cre-medieated recombination specifically in endothelial cells (i.e. Tie2-Cre) or cardiomyocytes (i.e. a-MHC Cre) would perhaps be a better alternate strategy that would circumvent systemic effects of Rnd3 happloinsufficiency, allow for much clearer determination of the functions of Rnd3 in endothelial cells vs. cardiomyocytes, and provide a novel mouse model to investigate Rnd3 function in a tissue and temporal-specific manner. . The applicant will investigate Notch signaling in endocardial cells and HIF1alpha signaling in cardiomyocytes, which have been extensively studied. . The proposal will exclusively investigate how Rnd3 may modulate previously established mechanisms and molecules regulating HIF1a in cardiomyocytes (i.e. PHD-mediated hydroxylation) and NICD in endothelial cells and does not propose to study novel mechanisms whereby Rnd3 may regulate these pathways or other pathways with critical roles in angiogenesis, which may be independent of these previously established mechanisms

Rnd3 heterozygous mice provide an in vivo model to investigate the effects of reduced Rnd3 expression on cardiac signaling and angiogenesis in response to pressure overload, which will provide mechanistic insight into the functions of Rnd3 in the heart. . Transgenic mice to overexpress Rnd3 in cardiomoyctes (a-MHC) or endothelial cells (Tie2) will provide extremely valuable animal models to elucidated the functions of Rnd3 in the given cell types in the heart and how this contributes to the proangiogenic function of Rnd3. . Investigation of the molecular mechanisms underlying protection in Rnd3 heterozygous mice provides a model that is relevant to human disease, mimics cardiac disease in the setting of chronic hypertension (a common occurrence in Americans), and to investigate adaptive cardiac angiogenesis, which may have implications in treatment of human disease.
app_text_wkn: . Lineage-specific deletion of Rnd3 would be the ideal approach to identify the endothelial cell vs. cardiomyocyte functions of Rnd3 and to test the paracrine hypothesis that Rnd3 acts in cardiomyocytes to enhance HIF1a signaling and VEGF secretion.  Results from studies in the Rnd3 heterozygous mouse are confounded by systemic haploinsufficiency of Rnd3 and make it difficult to determine whether the protective/proangiogenic functions of Rnd3 originate from its roles in cardiomoyctes or endothelial cells.  Rescue experiments with a Notch inhibitor or CoCl2 (Aim 3.2) will be difficult to compare to each other and generally difficult to interpret since these pharmacological treatments may be protective and/or ameliorate angiogenesis independent of functioning directly downstream of Rnd3. . Transgenic mice overexpressing Rnd3 specifically in the heart or endothelial cells (Aim 3.3) will be very useful mouse models to study the effects of Rnd3 gain-of-function in vivo.  The generation of these mice is hardly described in the proposal and the rescue experiments proposed (cross to Rnd3+/-) will likely be difficult to interpret on the background of Rnd3 haploinsuffiicency.  However, these will be very useful models to investigate the function of Rnd3 in endothelial cells vs. cardiomyocytes and the associated molecular signaling (and consequent effects on angiogenesis).  Does the applicant expect that Rnd3 overexpression in cardiomyocytes or endothelial cells would enhance angiogenesis and protect from pressure overload? . Endothelial cell/cardiomyocyte co-culture experiments will be technically challenging and results may be difficult to interpret (Aim 3.1). . The molecular mechanisms of the angiogenic and protective functions of Rnd3 are contingent upon its expression and subcellular localization in cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells.  The applicant does not show preliminary data or propose experiments to look at the relative abundance or subcellular localization of Rnd3 in these cell types.  Immunoblotting for Rnd3 in cardiac endothelial cells versus cardiomyocytes and immunostaining for Rnd3 along with endothelial cell and cardiomyocyte markers in mouse hearts (with and without pressure overload) and isolated cells would be very informative as to the potential molecular functions of Rnd3, where Rnd3 is downregulated in cardiac disease, and whether Rnd3 is dynamically localized during disease.  Indeed, many of the hypotheses tested in the proposal rely on the specific subcellular localization of Rnd3 and these experiments could potentially rule out a number of the hypotheses to be tested (i.e. Rnd3 regulates HIF1a stability in the cytosol or regulates its transcriptional complex formation in the nucleus of cardiomyocytes).  All the hypotheses tested in Aim1 require nuclear localization of Rnd3 in endothelial cells to regulate Notch signaling.  Rnd3 is even overexpressed with a myc-tagged construct in Fig13C where its overexpression enhances the nuclear localization of HIF1a yet the applicant fails to show coimmunostaining for Rnd3, which would greatly inform the potential mechanisms of its regulation of HIF1a. . There is no alternative approach to investigate the protective functions of Rnd3 if effects on Notch and HIF1a signaling do not rescue the phenotype in Rnd3 heterozygous mice. . Studies in HUVECs in Fig12 do not include a control with media from wildtypecardiomyocytes expressing endogenous levels of Rnd3. . Some proposed studies lack experimental details (i.e. How will NICD ubiquitination be detected in Aim1.1?  Will NICD be immunoprecipitated and blotted for ubiquitin?  If so, does the applicant have an NICD antibody that works for IP?  Or we they need to overexpress a tagged form of NICD?)_

imp_text: The proposed studies will investigate the role of Ask1 in platelet function and thrombosis.  This will provide useful information on the molecular mechanisms involved in thrombosis, which has a significant impact on potential treatments for human disease.  The research strategy outlined is composed largely of various assays that will provide descriptive information about platelet function in the presence or absence of Ask1 but ultimately may not lead to a complete understanding of how Ask1 mechanistically regulates platelet function or why Ask1 null mice have a severe bleeding phenotype.  While the preliminary data certainly indicate an important role for Ask1 in thrombosis and in platelets, the proposed experiments predominantly employ diverse models of thrombosis and a diverse set of biochemical and molecular assays, in many cases with varying doses of agonists or pharmacological agents, and some of which may pose technical challenges.  Thus, there is concern that there may be difficulty interpreting the data from this diverse panel of experiments.  These studies would be perhaps benefited by some additional genetic strategies to test the role of specific signals upstream or downstream of Ask1 to clearly determine components of a signaling cascade that Ask1 is involved in that contributes to its role in platelet function.  A more refined experimental setup with comparable strategies targeting the upstream and downstream effectors of Ask1 in platelets would more clearly delineate the signaling circuitry whereby Ask1 mediates its prothrombotic functions.  Also, some sort of Ask1 gain-of-function approach will go a long way in testing the applicant’s hypotheses about Ask1 in platelets, including several of the assays for platelet function proposed in Aim 1.  Functional and molecular studies using platelets from the kinase-dead and constitutively active knock-in Ask1 mutant mice proposed to be generated in Aim 2 would probably be the best way to evaluate the role of Ask1 in platelet function and thrombosis.

This proposal seeks to elucidate molecular mechanisms that underlie platelet activation, which will inform future therapeutic strategies to treat cardiovascular diseases associated with clot formation, including stroke. . The aims outlined could elucidate the roles of Ask1 in platelet function and MAPK signaling that plays critical roles in thrombosis, which is clinically relevant.

inn_text_str: . The roles of Ask1 in platelet function have never been investigated and Ask1 knockout mice demonstrate a requirement for Ask1 in thrombosis.  Therefore, this proposal will provide novel information regarding platelet functions of Ask1 and may provide insight into MAPK signaling pathways that are important specifically in platelets and/or for thrombosis.
inn_text_wkn: . Roles for MAPK signaling in platelet function have been previously proposed, although there is novelty in the investigation of Ask1 specifically.
app_text_str: . Proposed studies will provide informative descriptive information about the effects of Ask1 deletion on various aspects of platelet function and the potential contribution of upstream GPCR or GTPase signaling in activating Ask1 in platelets. . Constitutively active and kinase-dead mutant knock-in mouse models proposed in Aim2 will provide excellent in vivo gain- and loss-of-function models, respectively, to study the function of Ask1.  Performing many of the platelet functional assays described in Aim 1 and analysis of signaling upstream and downstream of Ask1 in platelets from these mouse models will provide sound functional and mechanistic insight into the role of Ask1 in thrombosis.
app_text_wkn: . There are a number of grammatical errors and typos in the proposal. . Aim 2 utilizes a host of pharmacological or genetic strategies to try to dissect the role of various upstream signals (GPCR signaling, Rho signaling, etc) in activating Ask1 in platelets.  However, the proposed experiments use various and divergent approaches to target each upstream pathway (i.e. pharmacological inhibition of PLCß downstream of Gq versus small peptide inhibition of G13) to assess their relative contribution to Ask1 activation, and this does not allow for an accurate comparison. . Aim2 is somewhat of a fishing expedition for all GPCRs and GEFs upstream of Ask1 and MAPKs and MAPK targets downstream of Ask1, which may yield promising results but also may yield results that are difficult to interpret or inconclusive. . There is no real description of how the constitutively active or kinase-dead Ask1 knock-in mice will be generated in the proposal or how they will be used experimentally. . It is unclear how the authors will address the cooperative thrombotic functions of Ask1 in platelets and endothelial cells if studies proposed in Aim 1.1 indicate an endothelial function for Ask1 in thrombosis. . Some of the preliminary data/experimentation is not sufficiently described.  Figure 8 is uninterpretable to the reader.  There is no explanation of how these aggregation assays work or what the readout is, which traces are WT or Ask1 KO platelets are not indicated, and axis values and labels are illegible. . Fibrinogen binding assays in Fig 10 lack a control without treatment with the integrin aIIb ß3 activting peptide.  Does Ask1 deletion reduce fibrinogen binding to platelets at baseline?

imp_text: This proposal suggests a novel hypothesis regarding lipin 1 role in metabolic function and dysfunction in the myocardium linked to heart disease in obese and diabetic patients.  The Investigator has generated and will continue to generate novel mouse models that separate the proposed functions of lipin 1 to allow for independent assessment on heart function and disease progression.  This work could lead to a new understanding of the molecular mechanisms giving rise to lipotoxicity and heart failure in obese and diabetic patients as well as further the understanding of lipin 1 function.  These results could yield new targets for the prevention and treatment of heart disease in a rapidly growing portion of the world population.  These results would provide a focal point for investigating heart failure that may result in many new studies of lipins in heart failure.

study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: The PI is using two versions of Lipin 1 that separate its phosphatase activity from its transcriptional regulatory activity. The PI posits that when Lipin 1 is phosphorylated by mTOR it is cytoplasmically localized and utilizes a phosphatase activity to increase triglyceride synthesis. This occurs during lipid overload. In contrast when lipid is not present in excess, Lipin 1 become relatively hypo-phosphorylated and is retained in the nucleus where it activates fatty acid oxidation genes and suppresses fatty acid synthesis genes. The two tools the PI utilizes are 21XA Lipin 1 in which mTOR phosphorylation sites are mutated to alanine. The other mutant that the PI utilizes is a delta 115 Lipin 1 which has diminished phosphatase activity but retains its transcriptional activity, and thus can still activate fatty acid oxidation genes. The hypothesis is strong and novel indicating bi-functional roles for Lipin 1. Moreover, the hypothesis is significant because the switch in Lipin 1 activity could be the basis of the accumulation of triglyceride in the heart, and thus the basis for cardiac lipotoxicity. The problem with the grant is that while the constructs apparently perform as hypothesized, the PI has not shown that they have the appropriated change in phosphorylation. Moreover it is unclear how diminished expression of Lipin 1 affects its subcellular localization and the relationship to altered phosphorylation. Direct data showing the predicted changes in phosphorylation would be very useful to support the PIs hypothesis.

imp_text: The PI has observed that the levels of the small GTPase Rnb3 are reduced in human heart failure. Moreover, the PI has generated an Rnd3 +/- mouse that developed severe heart failure in a mouse model of transvers aortic constriction. The PI has generated preliminary data showing that there is an angiogenesis defect in these mice and that Notch signaling is enhanced whereas Hif 1 alpha signaling is diminished. The PI proposes a complex series of experiments to show that Rnd3 negatively regulates Notch 1 signaling in endothelial cells by regulating proteolytic degradation of intermediates leading to increased VEGF receptor expression. Whereas in cardiomyocytes Rnd3 inhibits Hif 1 alpha degradation resulting in the promotion of Hif 1 transcriptional activity and increased VEGF expression. Finally in Aim 3, the PI will put in Notch 1 antagonists and Hif 1 agonists to determine if they will overcome the effects of Rnd3 haplo-insufficiency on cardiac function. The strengths of the proposal includes some preliminary data that Rnd3 plays a protective role in promoting angiogenesis and preventing cardiac failure. However, there are several significant weaknesses including the lack of experimental details concerning the complex biochemical and biophysical experiments to be performed to determine degradation and binding of signaling intermediates. The most significant weakness is in the sequence of the specific aims in which failure of Aim 3 will obviate any positive outcomes of Aims 1 and 2.

study_section: Myocardial Ischemia and Metabolism Study Section
imp_text: This is an interesting study by an early investigator seeking to understand the mechanisms underlying a potentially unique obesity linked Type II Diabetes (T2D) that results in heart failure.  The primary assumption is that circulating levels of amylin forms toxic oligomers, leading to accumulation of amylin oligomers, fibrils and plaques that are only present in those who experience heart failure, and that similar deposits are not present in those without heart failure or in those who are lean and non-diabetic.  The aims of the proposed study seek to confirm the proposed link between amylin build up and heart failure and then longitudinal manipulate the pathways to change the trajectory of buildup and subsequent impact. There is significant translation merit to this proposal, which represents a synthesis of preliminary studies. Confirmatory findings would provide evidence for pursuing follow up human studies of circulating amylin and relating them to risk for heart failure. Downstream is the possibility of impacting therapeutic strategies, particularly for those with T2D.  While there were some details in the approach that could have benefitted from further clarification, overall this application seems a worthwhile endeavor by a promising young investigator who has also assembled a strong team of complementary skills/knowledge to ensure successful execution and appropriate interpretation of study findings.
sig_text_str: . Type II diabetes (TD2) and heart disease are leading chronic diseases attributable to premature death as well as high healthcare costs to monitor and treat.  They are also often co-morbid conditions.  This application seeks to identify the pre-disease pathways that lead to TD2 related heart failure. Presumably doing so will provide testable treatment models that eventually be applied to humans

imp_text: This application by Dr. Murphy aims to investigate the general hypothesis that hyperamylinemia contributes to cardiac dysfunction in type 2 diabetic rats. To that purpose, a combined in vitro/in vivo approach will be used. It will be investigated in cardiomyocytes whether amylin oligomers disrupt sarcolemmal integrity and activate Ca2+-dependent pathways for remodeling and hypertrophic signaling. It will also be tested whether amylin buildup impairs cardiac energy substrate metabolism. In vivo experiments will compare disease progression between HIP rats, which overexpress amyloidogenic human amylin in the pancreas and UCD rats, which express non-amyloidogenic rat amylin. It will be investigated whether repair of sarcolemmal integrity improves cardiac function in HIP rats. It will also be tested whether proteolytic enzymes such as plasmin block amylin oligomerization and enhance their solubility. The investigator was at the forefront of discovering a role for hyperamylinemia in cardiac dysfunction in diabetes. Yet, the proposed research approach is novel and significant. The proposed research plan is well developed and the preliminary data are supportive of the general hypothesis.  The PI has assembled a talented team of complimentary investigators, which can assure a successful completion of the research plan. Enthusiasm is slightly reduced by the lack of considering alternative explanations, by the lack of describing the rat models and their limitations and by not taking into account inflammatory parameters.

The PI will use a relevant rodent model, i.e., the HIP rat model, in which human amylin is being generated. Human amylin seems to accumulate in the rat cardiac tissue.

imp_text: In this application, Dr. Sullivan aims to identify novel pro-angiogenic factors promoting the adaptive myocardial angiogenesis in response to pressure overload, in view of the failure of VEGF and HIF1a-based clinical trials. The PI will investigate the contribution of the small GTPase Rnd3 in the conversion from a healthy to a failing heart. The rationale for this study comes from the observation in microarrays that Rnd3 mRNA expression is significantly reduced in failing human myocardium. This motivated the generation of global Rnd3-/- mice. Since these mice are embryonically lethal, haploinsufficient Rnd3+/- mice and Rnd3 overexpressing mice were generated. Cardiomyopathy in these mice will then be tested in cardiac stress models, including transverse aortic constriction. Preliminary data demonstrate that Rnd3+/- mice are hypersensitive to cardiac stress, with 47% fewer capillaries, reduced levels of pro-angiogenic HIF-1alpha and VEGFA, and dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure after 3 weeks of pressure overload, as compared to wild type animals. The PI wants to test the main hypothesis that downregulation of Rnd3 impairs angiogenesis, by enhancing Notch activity in endothelial cells and by weakening HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling in cardiomyocytes. In the first two aims, the PI will investigate whether Rnd3 interferes with the Notch transcriptional complex in endothelial cells and with the HIF1a-VEGF paracrine signaling axis in cardiomyocytes. In the third aim, he will investigate the feedback loop mechanism between paracrine HIF1a-VEGF and Notch signaling and he will assess whether a Notch inhibitor, a HIF1a-VEGF agonist, and genetic reintroduction of Rnd3 into endothelial cells and cardiomyocytes can correct the angiogenic defect. Although the rationale for the study is based on observations in human hearts, the significance of the approach remains questionable, in view of the fact that the PI proposes improved VEGF-R and HIF1a signaling as mechanism of action of Rnd3 and since agonists of these pathways have failed in clinical trials. The research plan is well written, but there are some flaws in the research design. As such, human VEGFA induces more efficient signaling by activating differentially the VEGF receptor subtypes in human cells than mouse VEGFA, indicating species differences. This may complicate data interpretation from the experiments in which HUVEC were treated with supernatants of mouse cardiomyocytes.  There is also a complete lack of considering effects of Rnd3 on other signaling pathways, apart from HIF1a-VEGF, like Rho GTPase family members. HUVEC are not a good model for angiogenesis, rather coronary microvascular endothelial cells should be used, preferentially of mouse origin. The mouse studies lack detail throughout and the number of mice needed is nowhere indicated, which is unacceptable. All of these points limit my enthusiasm for this otherwise interesting application.

imp_text: In this application Dr. Jackson aims to characterize the role of the enzyme Ask1, which is an upstream regulator of p38 MAP kinase and JNK found to be expressed in platelets, in thrombotic pathology. Since platelet activation is regulated by both positive and negative regulators, dysregulation of these endogenous regulators may promote thrombotic complications seen in various diseases. As such, the identification and functional elucidation of novel regulators may foster the identification and generation of therapeutic agents towards thrombotic disorders. Currently available pharmacological inhibitors either cause severe bleeding or induce tolerance. The PI proposes that Ask1 may represent a novel therapeutic target for controlling platelet activation in thrombotic disease. He proposes a combined in vitro/in vivo approach using several mouse models. In vivo models include FeCl3-induced carotid artery injury, laser-induced injury to cremaster arterioles and collagen/epinephrine-induced pulmonary thromboembolism. In aim 1 the PI proposes to evaluate the role of Ask1 in platelet function and thrombosis, including the characterization of the thrombotic phenotype of Ask1-/- mice. A lot of the experiments in this aim have already been performed, as shown in the preliminary data section, apart from the laser-induced injury model. As such, this aim lacks novelty. In aim 2, the PI will try to elucidate the mechanism through which Ask1 is activated by platelet agonists and he will investigate the involvement of GPCR and the p38 and ERK2 signaling pathways in this. It is unclear why only in sub-aim 2.2 also human platelets are being used, whereas mouse platelets are used in all other sub-aims. Although the search for novel regulators of platelet activation is significant, I am not convinced that inhibitors of Ask1 can represent good therapeutic candidates. The reason for this is that Ask1-/- mice have a severe bleeding phenotype, which indicates that inhibitors of Ask1 will have this side effect. Moreover, as partially addressed by the PI, Ask1 is also very important in the cellular compartment interacting with platelets, especially the endothelium, where it regulates barrier function, apoptosis and inflammation. Overall, my enthusiasm is significantly dampened by these concerns.

sig_text_wkn: . The significance and the critical barriers to progress in this area are not well discussed in the aims page. . Since Ask1 also plays an important role in other cells, like endothelial cells, which interact with platelets, it is difficult to envisage how data generated in global Ask-/- mice can give platelet-specific information and how this application will move therapy forward, as indicated by the PI. As such, significance is questionable.

In view of the important role of Ask1 in both endothelial barrier function and apoptosis, it will be very difficult to distinguish the contribution of the enzyme to platelet-mediated versus endothelial-mediated pathology in the different models. This is a major criticism. . The proposed p38 pathway is also involved in endothelial apoptosis, barrier function and inflammation. Pharmacological inhibitors of the signaling pathways under investigation can lack specificity, as pointed out by the PI. imp_text: Changes in lipid metabolism that occur in the lipotoxic myocardium are intricate and require further investigations into the regulatory mechanisms that link these alterations to cardiac dysfunction.  The current proposal identifies lipin 1 as a novel mediator that regulates both fatty acid oxidation and glycerolipids synthesis, dependent upon nutrient availability, through the molecular target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1).  The role of lipin 1 in the development and progression of cardiac lipotoxicity will be tested using innovative loss-of-function and gain-of-function mouse models.  The PI has a strong track record of investigating the roles of transcriptional factors in the regulation of cardiac lipid metabolism and has a high probability of successfully completing the proposed aims of the project.  Furthermore, the results obtained from the project have a high likelihood of further advancing the knowledge of the pathogenesis of lipid metabolism in the obese and diabetic heart as well as have clinical significance for the treatment of cardiac dysfunction in human patients.
sig_text_str: . Lipotoxic cardiac dysfunction is a significant health concern requiring more novel approaches to understanding the etiology of the disease.  Examining the role in lipin 1 may reveal a new therapeutic target. . imp_text: Obese and diabetic patients have elevated risk of developing cardiovascular disease.  Although the pathology of the disease is likely multifactorial, uncovering mechanisms responsible for the development of cardiac dysfunction are of high priority.  The current proposal details a novel mechanism by which amylin, a compound release by the pancreatic beta-cells, accumulates in the myocardium and induces cardiotoxicity resulting in pathogenic remodeling and altered cardiac metabolism.  In addition, a novel therapeutic strategy using a “membrane sealant” protects damaged cell membranes and rescues cellular dysfunction.  To test the hypothesis, a transgenic rodent mouse that expresses and releases human amylin from the beta-cells was developed.  This novel model has strong clinical implications and relevance for amyloid-mediated cardiac dysfunction in the type 2-diabetic population.  The PI’s publications indicate significant expertise in diabetes, beta-cell dysfunction, and amyloid biochemistry.  The relatively limited track record of cardiac research is a concern specifically for experiments proposed in Aim 2.  However, the inclusion of senior faculty as collaborators and consultants aids in this regard.  The rescue experiments proposed in Aim 3 are quite novel and the potential exciting findings have strong translational implications.

imp_text: Heart failure remains a critical health issue for millions of Americans.  Despite the tremendous efforts of basic scientists, findings of from animal models have not translated to clinical treatment.  Angiogenesis is a critical component of the myocardial stress response to both pathological and physiological stimuli.  In heart failure, impaired angiogenesis has been identified as a potential factor in disease progression.  The current project seeks to elucidate the angiogenic role of Rnd3, a Rho GTPase protein, in the heart failure.  The interesting preliminary data shows a significant downregulation of Rnd3 in end-stage human heart failure, stimulating the generation of a haplosufficient mouse model to study the mechanistic role of Rnd3.  The proposal suggests that Rnd3 orchestrates a complex interaction between HIF1alpha and VEGF signaling pathways in both the cardiomyocyte and endothelial cells that regulate angiogenesis.  The PI has a track record of studying these pathways in the heart and is likely to achieve the proposed aims.  Results of the study have a high probability of both basic and clinical significance.

study_section: Atherosclerosis and Inflammation of the Cardiovascular System Study Section
imp_text: The myocardium is anatomically non-redundant and thus there are multiple mechanisms that suppress inflammatory processes. Preliminary work has determined that cardiac inflammation is regulated in part by PD-1 and PD-L1. Newly developed mouse lines with lineage-specific deficiencies of PD-1 and PD-L1 will be utilized to determine PD-1/PD-L1 intracellular pathways in response to cardiac inflammation. Previous studies have shown that statin plus rapamycin upregulate PD-L1 expression and thereby promote tolerance to inflammation. The results of these studies could elicit therapeutic strategies to thwart myocardial inflammation and its sequelae and provide future treatments for patients with inflammation of the heart.

imp_text: Arterial walls are predominantly composed of smooth muscle cells (SMC).  Their contraction and relaxation determine blood flow and pressure. study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: Humoral immunity plays a critical role in defense against extracellular pathogens, microbial toxins and intracellular pathogens (during extracellular existence). Understanding mechanisms governing the production of highly effective antibodies is of crucial importance in the development of vaccines. In this proposal, Pi will investigate the role of an actin-bundling protein L-plastin (LPL) in regulating the maturation of B cells, B cell motility and germinal center formation during humoral immune responses. The central hypothesis is that L-plastin links integrin and chemotactic signaling to the actin cytoskeleton and that L-plastin is required after integrin engagement to enable cellular motility-and is thus essential for GC formation. The strengths of this proposal include: (1) significance of the work towards understanding the mechanisms that regulate antibody responses; (2) strong preliminary data that forms the basis for the experiments; (3) excellent investigator and collaborators; (4) mostly feasible experimental plan. Weaknesses include (1) Concerns about the feasibility of aim 1; (2) aim 2 is a little diffuse and significance is unclear; (3) lack of attention to the possible altered lymphoid architecture to the immune response in aim 3. Overall this is a strong grant with moderate weaknesses that tempers the overall scientific impact.

Proposed work has the potential to provide new insights into the role of l-plastin in integrating extracellular cues into a coordinated B cell response in terms of motility, germinal center formation and antibody responses.

app_text_str: . Provides excellent preliminary data that global LPL deficiency reduces the number of B cells especially the mature follicular and marginal zone B cells (Fig. 1). Further, preliminary data shows that LPL-deficient display impaired responses to CXCL12/13 and integrin ligation. Interestingly, CXCL12 or antigen receptor signaling-induced phosphorylation of Pyk2 (Proline-rich tyrosine kinase 2) is reduced in LPL KO B cells. . In Fig. 2, PI shows that LPL deficiency reduces the differentiation of germinal center B cells (following injection with SRBCs), number and size of GCs in spleen. Further, the levels of antibodies are reduced in LPL KO mice. . To assess the B cell-intrinsic requirement for LPL, PI adoptively transferred B cells from WT or LPL KO mice into congenic CD45.1 mice, which were subsequently injected with SRBCs. The total number of donor GC B cells are reduced in the recipient mice. This suggested a B cell-intrinsic requirement for LPL in the development of GC B cells. . Aim 1 will identify the critical domains of LPL, such as N-terminal serine phosphorylation site and actin-binding domains, required for B cell motility. The experimental approach entails the generation of lentiviral vectors that express the wild type and mutant versions of LPLs. These viruses will be used to transduce HSCs from LPLKO mice, and the virally transduced HSCs (GFP+ve) are adoptively transferred into irradiated LPLKO mice. These mice will be assessed for marginal zone B cell development. Further, the motility of transduced B cells will be assessed by transwell assays and intranodal two-photon microscopy. . Aim 2 will define the elements of the integrin-associated PyK2 signaling cascade that require LPL. Building on the observation that PyK2 phosphorylation is reduced in LPL KO B cells, PI will define the signaling components upstream of PyK2 phosphorylation in LPL KO B cells. Specifically, PI will test a model in which LPL is required to maintain a molecular complex that links sites of integrin adhesion with the actin skeleton. Co-localization of paxillin, vinculin, talin, PyK2, F-actin or LPL will be examined by confocal microscopy. . Aim 3 entails the development of B cell conditional LPL KO mice. These mice will be examined for B cell activation, differentiation, proliferation, apoptosis, motility etc.  Additionally, T-cell dependent antibody responses, generation of memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells will be assessed. Lastly, control of WNV infection will be tested in these mice.

B cell-specific deficiency for LPL might alter the motility of B cells, which in turn might lead to disruption of cellular distribution (topologically) and lymphoid architecture. This might underlie problems in GC development, antibody responses etc. This potentially confounding problem has to be taken into account. . study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: ): One of the prominent features of aging is the age-associated thymic atrophy, decline in thymic output and contraction of the naïve T cell repertoire. Consequently, aging is associated with diminished responses to vaccines and increased susceptibility to infections. This proposal is focused on understanding the mechanisms underlying thymic atrophy, with special emphasis on thymic stromal cells. There is precedence that alteration in thymic stroma contributes to atrophy and exciting preliminary data implicating a role for catalase deficiency serves as the premise for this proposal. PI posits that thymic stromal cells are deficient in key enzymes (especially catalase) involved in protection from damage caused by reactive oxygen species (ROS), as well as several enzymes that repair such damage. The central hypothesis is that epithelial stromal cells of the thymus are exquisitely sensitive to ROS by virtue of these deficiencies, and that thymic atrophy is a consequence of accelerated accumulation of metabolic damage. Aim 1 will test the hypothesis that selective correction of catalase (cat) deficiency in thymic stromal cells rescues thymic atrophy. Aim 2 will test the hypothesis that TEC accumulate more oxidative lesions in vivo than other cells from age/tissue-matched mice. Aim 3 will test the hypothesis that TEC are more sensitive to ROS than epithelial cells from other age-matched tissues. Aim 4 will test the hypothesis that secondary deficiencies (e.g. DNA repair) in oxidative damage repair mechanisms exacerbate the stromal effects of Cat deficiency. This is an outstanding proposal with several strengths including: (1) strong preliminary that supporting the hypothesis; (2) expertise of the PI and the investigative team; (3) clearly articulated proposal; (4) feasible experiments. Weaknesses include: (1) narrow focus of the proposal; (2) lack of studies to characterize T-cell maturation, thymic output and effects on the peripheral T-cell repertoire. The proposed work is expected to provide new mechanistic insights into age-associated thymic atrophy and might have sustained impact in the field from the standpoint of development of therapies to enhance thymic output in the elderly.

The experiments in this proposal will examine the role of thymic stromal cells in mediating age-associated thymic atrophy. New insights from the proposed work might lead to development of therapies to mitigate age-associated loss of thymic function in the elderly.

PI provides solid preliminary data linking catalase deficiency in thymic stroma to atrophy of thymus: (1) thymic stromal cells express low levels of catalase using microarray (Fig. 1) and immunocytochemistry (Fig. 3); (2) Dietery supplementation with N-acetyl cysteine and Vitamin C ameliorates thymic atrophy in mice (Fig. 4); (3) transgenic expression of catalase enhances thymic cellularity. . Aim 1 will test the hypothesis that selective correction of catalase (Cat) deficiency in thymic stromal cells rescues thymic atrophy. Here, in the first approach, PI will conditionally overexpress catalase in TECs using Foxn1-Cre mice. In the second approach, mice expressing the ubiquitous Cat gene will be crossed to the IL-7R-/- background. These mice will receive bone marrow cells from WT mice. The first approach is feasible. . Aim 2 will test the hypothesis that TEC accumulate more oxidative lesions in vivo than other cells from age/tissue-matched mice. PI will use HPLC to analyze for ROS-induced oxidative damage to DNA and GC/MS to characterize lipid peroxidation. These assays will be done in the lab of van Rossum (UT-San Antonio). . Aim 3 will test the hypothesis that TEC are more sensitive to ROS than epithelial cells from other age-matched tissues. Cultured primary TECs, Cat-Tg TEC or EC from salivary gland will be exposed to hydrogen peroxide and assessed for DNA damage using the Comet assay. Comet assay seems to be functional in the PI’s lab (Fig. 5). .  Aim 4 will test the hypothesis that secondary deficiencies (e.g. DNA repair) in oxidative damage repair mechanisms exacerbate the stromal effects of Cat deficiency. Here, PI will test the ability of TECs from WT and Cat-tg mice to repair ROS-induced damage in a modified version of the Comet assay.

imp_text: This application is focused on understanding the role of interactions between bone marrow stromal cells and hematopoietic stem cells/B cells in the B-cell development and tolerance. The premise of this application is the finding that CXCR4 expression on radiation-resistant cells is required for the B cell lineage supportive stromal cell niches. Aim 1 will assess the effects of stromal cell-specific CXCR4 deficiency on the maintenance and development of wild type hematopoietic stem cells. Aim 2 will determine the mechanisms controlling lymphoid progenitor cell (CLP) positioning in the BM relative to CXCR4/IL-7/CXCL12- expressing cells. Aim 3 will characterize the mechanisms and dynamics of B cell negative selection in BM. The proposed work is highly significant because it will provide new insights into the mechanisms underlying B-cell development and tolerance from the context of interactions between BM stromal cells and developing B cells. The proposal is innovative both conceptually and technically. Additional strengths of this applications include: (1) strong preliminary data; (2) well-written proposal; (3) carefully thought-out experimental plan; (4) masterful use of different mouse strains; (5) excellent outline of pitfalls and caveats. A minor weakness is that some experiments are descriptive and are not expected to directly test a hypothesis. In summary, reviewer has high enthusiasm for this outstanding proposal.

app_text_str: . The first guiding hypothesis is that cell-intrinsic CXCR4 is required for mesenchymal stem cell maintenance and/or differentiation into stromal cells that express factors (IL-7, CXCR4 ligand CXCL12) essential for B cell development. PI will test this hypothesis by: (1) deleting CXCR4 in radiation-resistant cells: (2) identifying the requirement for CXCR4 in subsets of non-hematopoietic stromal cells in B cell differentiation; (3) determining how CXCR4 in non-hematopoietic cells enables B-cell lineage differentiation. . Second hypothesis is that B lymphocyte development requires CXCR4-guided movement of lymphoid precursors towards IL-7-producing cells. Specifically, PI provides excellent preliminary data that CXCR4 expression in hematopoietic precursors is required for development of B cells, T cells, NK cells and granulocytes. Such a phenotype resembles that of IL-7 deficiency. PI hypothesizes that CXCR4-deficient lymphoid progenitors are unable to receive sufficient IL-7R signaling because they cannot position themselves appropriately with IL-7-expressing mesenchymal/stromal cells. Here, PI will assess the positioning of CXCR4-deficient CLP subsets relative to IL-7+ve cells by IF histology of lethally irradiated IL-7-reporter mice reconstituted with CXCR4fl/fl FLT3-Cre+ or control BM. Additionally, PI will also assess the positioning of CXCL12/IL-7-expressing cells (reporter mice) with CLPs. Further analyses include quantification of B cell-specific TFs and B cell lineage differentiation potential of CXCR4-deficient and sufficient CLPs in vitro. . Central B cell tolerance entails clonal deletion or receptor editing. The third hypothesis is that CXCR4 controls the positioning of autoreactive immature B cells in IL-7-expressing BM niches and that IL-7 promotes lymphocyte survival such that cells can undergo receptor editing. imp_text: This new application by the PI aims to address mechanisms functionally linking calcium and redox signaling in arterial smooth muscle. Aim 1 first tests the hypothesis that NADPH oxidase and L-type calcium channels colocalize in caveolae. Secondly to see if a subpopulation of peripheral mitochondrial play in role in functional coupling of redox and calcium microdomains, and lastly assess if this functional coupling contributes to arterial dysfunction in obesity. The PI is trained in muscle physiology approaches and has sufficient infrastructure to complete the experiments. The PI is also collaborating with other investigators within her institution for the necessary expertise needed to complete the project. There is a logical body of preliminary work documenting why the PI would like to investigate redox and calcium microdomains to arterial function and the development of dysfunction in obesity. The data generated supports that the approaches that will be used will work, and the pitfalls are very well laid out. However it is unclear how the PI will proceed If specific aim 1 is unsuccessful , as aims 2 and 3 rely on the success of aim 1.The PI states that she is investigating redox signaling but in fact it is just ROS generation coupled to calcium response. And ROS is just a part of redox signaling. Although Aim 3 is interesting, my enthusiasm was moderated by the fact that it was the least developed aim with no information on how many mice the PI plans to use per experiment to ensure the validity of the results. Some of the outcomes stated by the PI do not appear to be directly being tested in the experimental approaches, eg reduced NAPDH oxidase activity due to impaired Rac1 translocation, depletion of cellular cholesterol etc. Therefore while this appears to be an interesting hypothesis to explore, there were several limitations majoring upon the outcomes and the success of each aim.

Aim 2 serves to assess EC-specific anti-atherogenic mechanisms and identify novel endothelial cell Kalirin-associated proteins with a proteomic approach. Lastly Aim3 determines molecular mechanisms by which macrophage Kalirin reduces atherosclerosis by assessing Kalirin’s Rac- and Rho-GEF activity in macrophages. The proposal is extensive but builds logically on preliminary data provided. It is likely that the proposal will shed light on the mechanisms of how Kalirin provides this anti-atherogenic property in endothelial cells and macrophages.

imp_text: This proposal builds up on previous work by this group and others showing that the PD 1/PD L1 pathway appears to be a central negative regulatory checkpoint in controlling immune responses in the heart. Although, the project is driven by an intriguing and innovative observation and hypothesis, cutting-edge of genetically modified mouse lines and mouse models, strong collaborators, and exceptional expertise of the PIs within the project area.  However, a major weakness of this proposal is that it is not focused, diffused and over ambitious for five years RO1 proposal. The proposed aims can easily be 4 RO1s in a program multi-PI grant. Because of the complexities of the cellular expression of PD-1 and PD-L1, it is still unclear how the pathway is actually engaged to suppress myocardial inflammation and finding out which cells (endothelial, myocyte, and dendritic cell PD-L1, and by myeloid PD-1) are more dominant in regulation cardiac inflammation as suggested in aim1 is essential for the following aims. Although, the strength of the proposal is the selective lineage specific PD-1 and PD-L1 conditional knockout mice, and several mice models of adaptive and innate immune myocarditis to be used.  However, this approach will require very extensive breeding and characterization of mice lines, BM transplant, which makes the proposed studies not feasible in the time frame of 5 years. In addition, aim 3 is premature and not promising, since systemic inhibition of the PD-1/PD-L1 pathways by immunotherapy is under clinical trials for several types of cancer and suggests that inhibition of this pathway if not targeted to the heart it might exert side effects on other organs or tissues. In summary, the project is quite ambitious and diffused, including mouse, human, and in vitro studies, and could be improved by a better focus. In particular, this reviewer suggests focusing on studies proposed in aim1 for this proposal, then the mechanistic and translational questions proposed in aim2 and aim3 would be better justified for future applications.
sig_text_str: The tight regulation of innate and adaptive immune responses in the heart serves to prevent maladaptive inflammation, and when they fail, inflammatory responses contribute to the pathogenesis of myocardial diseases including viral and autoimmune myocarditis, cardiac allograft rejection, acute ischemic injury, and chronic remodeling and heart failure. This proposal will focus on the PD-L1/PD-1 pathway that has been shown to play a role in modulating myocardial inflammation and because of recent attention in the clinical research arena on targeting this pathway. There is a significant gap in our knowledge about the inflammatory cellular interactions that are regulated by PD-1/PD-L1. A better understanding of those mechanisms is key to the design of potential therapeutic strategies to limit inflammatory damage in the setting of several cardiac diseases.
sig_text_wkn: This proposal extends previous studies by this group and others showing that PD-L1/PD-1 pathway play a role in modulating myocardial inflammation and in T-cell mediated adaptive immune response. While upregulation of this pathway is beneficial in the setting heart inflammation, it might exert unwanted effects in the setting of cancer therapy.

imp_text: This application seeks to understand the role of kalirin a protein whose gene variants has been recently identified to associate with human atherosclerosis, in atherosclerosis. This is a relatively novel and unexplored area of research, as kalirin typically has been associated with the CNS and neurons biology and not vascular biology. The PI hypothesized based on solid preliminary data a that Kalirin is an atheroprotective protein. In this proposal, kalirin cellular pattern of expression, and several potential mechanisms of action that mediate its anti-thermogenic effects will be explored, using both in vitro and in vivo animal models and cell or tissue restricted expression manipulation “conditional cre” mice to identify which cells are more dominant or responsible for those effects of kalirin. The hypothesis that Kalirin protects against atherosclerosis, through its RhoGEF1 domain, its inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS)-association domain, or other protein-protein interaction domains is interesting. Aim 1 will determine whether Kalirin reduces atherosclerosis through activity of its RhoGEF1 domain, its iNOS-interacting domain, or both domains. Aim 2 will determine molecular mechanisms by which EC Kalirin reduces atherosclerosis, by investigating flow-induced EC signaling as a function of Kalirin expression, by identifying novel EC Kalirin-associating proteins with a proteomics approach, and by comparing atherosclerosis between Apoe(-/-) mice with tamoxifen-inducible heterozygous Kalirin deficiency. Aim 3 will determine molecular mechanisms by which macrophage Kalirin reduces atherosclerosis, by defining Kalirin’s Rac- and Rho-GEF activity in macrophages, by determining whether macrophage Kalirin augments macrophage secretion of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10, and whether Apoe(-/-) mice with macrophage-specific Kalirin haploinsufficiency develop more atherosclerosis. Together, these focused proposed studies will elucidate specific cellular and molecular pathways by which Kalirin protects against atherosclerosis in mice. Additional strength includes the collaborating team and the environment of University of Duke. imp_text: This is an outstanding, focused and well written proposal; the project is driven by an intriguing and innovative observation and novel hypothesis, which is supported by strong preliminary data using state of the art toolsets and evidence that support a novel model/hypothesis related to platelets a -granules structure and function. This project is a basic science in nature that addresses a central question in platelet biology, namely, how the a-granule, the major secretory organelle of the platelet is organized functionally to support agonist-diverse secretory responses. Those questions will be addressed by three well-designed interrelated but independent aims. The major strength includes the use of cutting-edge intracellular imaging technology, strong collaborators, and exceptional expertise of the PI within the project area. State of the art high-resolution imaging technologies, to study human platelets as well as platelets from relevant genetically modified mice needed to definitively answering the Specific Aims and solving the hypothesis-driven questions posed. The outcome of the proposed studies whether in support of the hypothesis of a single class of a-granule in which proteins are packaged zonally and then selectively secrete cargo proteins via specialized subdomains/extensions of the granule that are enriched in fusion/docking machinery “spigot hypothesis” or not, it will have a high impact on the field of platelets physiology which is central to thrombosis/hemostasis, platelet dependent diseases. Potentially, this project might even improve our understanding of the biology of other granules containing cells, like leukocytes, endothelial cells among others. There are no major weaknesses. Overall the studies are based on carefully planned experiments with relevant human and mouse platelets that will be utilized in the study and the study is expected to have a high and sustained high impact in this field.

imp_text: This is a mechanistically driven proposal aiming to understand how replication progression complexes are targeted to the replication fork, in particular how the leading and lagging strands are differentially regulated. The studies address in human cells findings previously described in yeast. The investigators have appropriate experience to conduct the studies and the preliminary data is clean and support feasibility. The application could be strengthened by additional consideration of how yeast studies might further power the investigation. Greater general attention to detail would be helpful, including documenting the working relationships of the research group, detailing resources such as funding, facilities, and equipment that will facilitate the research, and more fully revealing interpretive aspects of the approach, such as exemplified in the preliminary data.
sig_text_str: . Despite years of study, there is a limited understanding of how DNA polymerases are targeted to replication forks, and this project proposes to clarify the role of the CMG and GINS in forming a replication progression complex, or RPC, in human cells, as it has been suggested in budding yeast. .
sig_text_wkn: . imp_text: The importance of germinal center development has been well established; however the molecular mechanisms required for lymphocyte trafficking following signaling to the actin cytoskeleton remain unclear.  The PI has recently demonstrated a critical role for L-plastin in B cell motility.  Thus, the goal of the current application is to determine whether L-plastin (LPL) is essential for germinal center formation by (1) determining which LPL domains are important for B cell motility; (2) assessing Pyk2 signaling in LPL deficient cells; (3) generate mice lacking LPL in B cells and assess GC formation during a T cell-dependent antibody response.  The PI has developed a strong team of collaborators to test a novel set of hypotheses using a unique mouse model.  Thus, the successful completion of the proposed studies has the potential to have a significant impact on the fields of autoimmunity, vaccine development, and immunodeficiency.

imp_text: While it has been established that the thymus is critical for T cell development and maintenance of the T cell repertoire; the mechanisms that regulate thymic involution remain elusive.  Thymic stromal cells are thought to play an important role in thymic atrophy and the PI has recently shown that thymic stromal cells are deficient in key enzymes involved in protection caused by reactive oxygen species.  Thus, in the current proposal the PI seeks to test the hypothesis that thymic atrophy is due to metabolic damage, primarily due to the loss of a specific enzyme, catalyse.  To test this hypothesis, four specific aims are proposed, in which the PI will restore the catalyse deficiency in stromal cells and determine if it rescues thymic atrophy.  In addition, he will determine whether the loss of catalyse renders thymic epithelial stromal cells more sensitive to oxidative damage, compared to other epithelial cells.  This is a well-written application by an established investigator. The proposal is innovative in concept and follows a logical progression, based on strong preliminary data, and its successful completion has the potential to significantly contribute to the field.  The collaborations further strengthen the application. A minor weakness in the proposal is that the PI does not propose any experiments to assess the TCR repertoire or potential changes in the immunodominant T cell response following the reconstitution of catalyse.  Thus, these studies may highlight the important of catalyse in thymic architecture and structural integrity, but will not provide information on potential alterations in T cell differentiation or effector functions.
sig_text_str: . There are many factors that contribute to thymus involution (aging, infection, radiation) . However, it is unclear how to restore thymic function.  This application proposes a novel mechanism by which to rescue thymic stromal cell function. . If successful, these proposed studies could have significant impact on the field by shedding light on how to restore the numbers of naïve T cells.
sig_text_wkn: . Thymic atrophy can be due to at least two different mechanisms:  (1) Apoptosis of double positive thymocytes and (2) alterations in thymic epithelial cells.  This application addresses alterations in thymic epithelial cells, with the implication that restoring thymic structural integrity will lead to a concomitant rescue of the thymocyte population (lack of apoptosis).

In aim 2, the PI will assess the mechanism by which the loss of catalyse leads to the loss of stromal cell function in the thymus by measuring damage (in DNA and lipids) in TEC compared to other epithelial cells. . Studies in Aim 3, are based on the hypothesis that TEC are more sensitive to ROS by treating with hydrogen perioxide  and conducting the Comet assay. . Lastly, the goal of Aim 4 is to test the hypothesis that other deficiencies in oxidative repair mechanisms contribute to the effects of catalyse deficiency in stromal cells.  Thus, they will look at recovery times following DNA damage in the presence and absence of catalyse restoration to see if there is an additional factor/enzyme that is playing a major role.
