study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: This is a strong application from a junior investigator.  The PI is focused on investigating mechanisms regulating B cell migration and positioning throughout development and activation.  In this application, the PI seeks to test the hypothesis that the chemokine receptor CXCR4 is critical in BM stromal cells for the development of B-lineage supportive stromal cell niches.  To address this hypothesis the PI proposes to generate novel mouse models using available transgenic and knockout models in combination with intravital 2-photon microscopy.  Specifically, the PI plans to characterize the impact of CXCR4-deficiency on the maintenance and differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells, as well as assess the mechanisms by which CXCR4 signaling instructs stromal niches to support B cell development in the bone marrow.  This is a technically challenging proposal that has the potential to shed light in an underdeveloped area.  While this is a high-risk, high-reward proposal the productivity and the potential impact of the proposed work increase enthusiasm for this application.
sig_text_str: . This study provides the opportunity to examine the mechanisms by which immature B cells exit the bone marrow. . It has been reported that CXCR4 and its ligand CXCL12 can counteract the egress-promoting cues in lymphocytes; however the mechanisms by which CXCR4 signaling antagonizes egress is unknown and this proposal seeks to address this important question.

In Aim 2, the PI proposes to test the hypothesis that intrinsic CXCR4 expression in CLPs is required for their positioning in contact with IL-7-producing cells. To test this hypothesis, the PI plans to treat IL-7 reporter mice with the CXCR4 antagonist AMD3100, and measure the distance between CLPs and IL-7+ cells by immunofluorescence histology. . The goal of Aim 3 is to assess whether autoreactive B cells are dependent on IL-7 for survival in BM and require CXCR4-mediated migration for their positioning within IL-7+ BM niches. In Aim1, the authors base the gatekeeper theory wherein the Kupffer cells control viral access to the rest of the liver based on differential expression of OAS genes in bone marrow derived macrophages (BMMs) as compared to hepatocytes. BMMs are a pretty specialized subset of macrophages and have been shown to have differential gene expression compared to tissue-resident macrophages or peritoneal macs. It would be helpful to see OAS gene expression in primary kupffer cells or bone marrow derived DCs to rule out specificity of BMMs as a cell type. imp_text: This proposal aims to expand our understanding of function of RNA dependent RNA Polymerases (RdRp) by using NMR spectroscopy to investigate the conformational changes of known fidelity mutants including mutants derived from the Sabin strain and determine the mechanism behind the chain termination induced by nucleoside analogs targeting RdRps. These experiments will expand our basic understanding of RdRps, an essential enzyme and drug and vaccine target strongly conserved across RNA viruses. The applicant is well placed to answer these questions as he has a strong background in NMR chemistry, the support of the chemistry department and an impressive history of productivity despite being early in his career. The proposal includes sufficient preliminary data indicating that the applicant can feasibly accomplish the proposed experiments in the outlined timeline.
sig_text_str: . The experiments proposed here would result in a much more thorough understanding of functionality of RdRps - an essential enzyme conserved across RNA viruses - by analyzing all possible conformational state using solution-state NMR. . Analysis of conformational changes in known fidelity mutants including all the mutants in the Sabine vaccine will result in a more mechanistic approach to viral vaccine design. . Nucleoside analogs are a class of antiviral drugs that function by incorporating into the RNA strand but resulting in chain termination through as yet poorly understood mechanisms. In Aim3, the applicant hypothesizes that these compounds induce chain termination by interfering with RNA translocation, which if confirmed, could help predict drug resistance sites.
inv_text_str: . The applicant has significant expertise in NMR chemistry and experience working with poliovirus RdRp. The applicant is also strongly supported by his department and collaborators with complementary expertise in RNA polymerase enzymatic assays and cellular infections. . The applicant’s productivity is impressive with 3 publications (1 in press) within three years of his faculty appointment despite a year’s stoppage on his tenure clock.
inn_text_str: . Mutations far outside the active site have been shown to affect enzymatic fidelity despite not causing any structural changes. The applicant proposes that a long-range network of neighbouring amino acid interactions could affect the conformational stability of the enzyme resulting in altered enzymatic fidelity and lower viral pathogenicity. This theory, if confirmed, will increase the potential to find enzymatic site-mutants by scanning a much larger area and thereby increase chances of identifying an attenuated virus vaccine strain. . The applicant proposes that the RNA polymerase mutations in live attenuated polio vaccine strain contribute to the viral attenuation that makes it an effective vaccine. If confirmed, this would provide a mechanistic approach to the proposal to use RdRp fidelity mutants as vaccine candidates in multiple RNA viruses.

These in-vivo experiments would be useful to mechanistically understand the contribution of various site mutants to fidelity and subsequently viral virulence.

imp_text: This proposal will change the current understanding of VSV-mediated host cell shut off which is predicated on vsv-mediated blockage of nuclear-cytoplasmic transport. The investigator has presented convincing preliminary data that transport of nuclear ribonuclear proteins (nRNP) into the cytoplasm does occur in vsv-infected cells and offers a new model wherein these ribonuclear proteins preferentially associate with new viral mRNAs as opposed to host mRNA. The experiments outlined in this proposal would answer some fundamental questions about transcriptional and translational control by investigating the role of nuclear ribonuclear proteins (nRNP) in VSV-mediated host cell shut off.  The investigator has been highly productive and has a lot of experience in working with VSV and has a consultant who is experienced in RNP biology. The experiments outlined are feasible within the time frame and the preliminary data is quite convincing. The experiments proposed in this study will help settle on a definitive model of VSV-mediated host shut off and highlight a novel role for nuclear ribonuclearproteins in the cytoplasm during VSV infection.
sig_text_str: . The experiments proposed in this study will confirm a different model of VSV-mediated host cell shut down than the current one, which if true, will move the field in a substantially different direction. . The study highlights a new level of feed forward loops between nuclear RNA binding proteins transport to cytoplasm, host cell transcription and translation.
inv_text_str: . Investigator has years of experience working with VSV and specifically the matrix protein. Additionally, the investigator has a letter of support from an expert in RNA binding nuclear proteins which should help address the second aim.
inn_text_str: . VSV M protein mediated host cell shut down is comprehensive and using this system, the investigator can analyze the differences between transcription of newly synthesized mRNA (in this case viral mRNA) and pre-existing mRNA. Besides shedding new light on mechanisms that viruses use to subvert host cell transcription, this study will also allow us new insight into the cellular mechanisms of rapid transcriptional responses in a clearly defined system. . Challenges the prevailing view of VSV-mediated inhibition of nuclear transport. The investigators have clear data showing that some nuclear RNA binding proteins are clearly exported to the cytoplasm via a mechanism that requires M-Rae1 interaction.

imp_text: The overall goal of this proposed research is to determine how the VSV M protein (only 26kD) has such a profound effect upon host gene expression. Two principle Aims to test the novel hypothesis that M protein effects transcription rather than nuclear-cytoplasmic transport are to determine roles of host RNA-binding proteins in (1) mRNA transport inhibition and (2) (host) translation inhibition. imp_text: This new and very well written multi-PI R01 submission is proposing to study the role of the RNase L pathway in regulating acute hepatitis during mouse coronavirus infection. It is of great importance to understand how viruses evade or antagonize the host innate immune response and how this ability contributes to virus-induced pathogenicity. Once those molecular mechanisms are better defined, targets for antiviral treatment can be identified and appropriate countermeasures developed. The investigators of this application have discovered that mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) ns2 protein can antagonize the interferon response in liver macrophages by blocking the OAS-RNase L pathway and ultimately induce hepatitis. These preliminary data led to the development of the overall hypothesis that in liver macrophages the OAS-RNase L pathway is critical in protecting the host from developing acute hepatitis. Further, inhibitors of viral and cellular 2’, 5’-PDEs enhance RNase L activity and provide a new target for development of antiviral strategies. Three specific aims are proposed to address their hypothesis; aim 1 will evaluate the role of RNase L signaling in primary Kupffer cells in blocking MHV from inducing hepatitis. Aim2 will determine the role of ns2 related viral and host 2’, 5’-PDEs in antiviral immunity. And lastly, aim 3 will investigate the role of cellular and viral PDEs on pathogenicity in vivo. The investigators have extensive and complementary expertise in murine coronavirus pathogenesis and innate immunology. Of particular strength of the application are the preliminary findings contributing to a sound scientific premise for the study, the thoughtful integration of characterizing the cellular responses in primary cells rather than cell lines, the availability of RNase L KO mice, the availability of a reverse genetics system to generate chimeric MHVs, and the availability of a high-throughput system to screen for 2’, 5’-PDE inhibitors. Potential concerns are that MHV is a strict mouse pathogen and that the role of OAS-RNase L pathway needs to be demonstrated for human-specific hepatic viruses. Overall, this reviewer has high enthusiasm for this proposal and this application has high promise to identify a novel target in the host-virus interaction as therapeutic target.

imp_text: In this application, a new investigator who has been an assistant professor since 2008, proposes to study the relationship between structure, dynamics, and function of the poliovirus RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (PV RdRp). The active site and mechanism of nucleotidyl transfer are conserved in viruses and therefore make it an important target for development of broad-spectrum antivirals. To fully understand the molecular mechanisms of how RdRp functions, one needs to determine and characterize accessible structural states governing each step of its catalytic cycle. This information is of great importance if one wants to predict fidelity-altering mutations that can affect the enzymatic activity of the RdRp, and support development of small molecules interfering with the structural transition or use this information for vaccine development. The investigator proposes to combine solution-state, multidimensional NMR spectroscopy with molecular dynamics simulation and enzyme kinetic studies to characterize and describe the conformational states of poliovirus RdRp. Preliminary data demonstrate that the applicant has all necessary expertise and protocols established to apply NMR spectroscopy to study interacting amino acids networks in the function ad fidelity of PV RdRP. The first aim will determine the conformational states of PV RdRp throughout its nucleotide addition cycle. The second aim will delineate structural and dynamic changes induced by fidelity-altering mutations. Lastly, aim 3 will identify the structural states that can be captured by incorporation of chain termination nucleoside analogues. Particular strengths of this application are a compelling set of preliminary data contributing to a well-outlined experimental plan that addresses an important topic. The third aim broadens the basic studies to a translational application by using structural data to test compounds for their antiviral activity. While this reviewer acknowledges that experiments evaluating the development of potential escape mutants, as well as in vitro infection studies with PV RdRp mutants are included, their description is very short and not detailed enough. Furthermore, this reviewer would have liked to see that a small in vivo study would have been included to demonstrate proof-of-concept to evaluate antiviral activity of chain termination nucleoside analogues. Overall, this application has high promise to yield novel insight into the molecular mechanisms of viral RdRp and enthusiasm for this application is high.
sig_text_str: • Defining the molecular mechanisms of viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp) is of importance for establishing the relationships between polymerase function and fidelity, as well as potentially revealing novel targets for antiviral therapeutics. • Sorting out the accessible individual structural states of the catalytic cycle and defining the transitions at the molecular level between these states is key to a complete understanding of how virus RdRp function. • Previous studies by the investigator have established the protocols to apply solution-state, multidimensional NMR spectroscopy to study the conformational states of poliovirus RdRp during its kinetic process.

imp_text: This is a new R01 application from an established investigator who has been working on the aspects of Vesicular Stomatitis Virus (VSV) matrix protein interference with host cellular responses for a long time. VSV has been utilized as a model virus for many non-segmented RNA viruses to characterize the influence of individual viral proteins on cellular responses. Furthermore, VSV appears to be an excellent candidate for the development of vaccine candidates. While the VSV matrix protein is a fairly small protein, it is able to effectively inhibit host gene expression (resulting in inhibition of transcription, nuclear-cytoplasmic transport of host mRNA, and translation of host cellular proteins). Based on a large body of preliminary data, the applicant proposes an alternative model of how VSV matrix protein inhibits host gene expression. The primary objective of the proposal is to demonstrate that the complex of VSV matrix protein with the host RNA-binding protein Rae1 inhibits transcription. Furthermore, hnRNPs re-localize to the cytoplasm and appear to be involved in translational control of VSV. The strengths of this proposal are the applicants experience with VSV matrix protein biology, the presented preliminary data, and the application of novel techniques (RIP-Chip and PAR-CLIP) to study regulation of gene expression by RNA-binding proteins. Those aspects give this proposal the potential to provide significant mechanistic insight into important aspects of VSV lifecycle and pathogenesis. The weaknesses include that it is not clear from the proposal how new findings could be translated to other RNA viruses or how this information would contribute to the development of novel vaccine candidates. Furthermore, the superficial description of some of the planned experiments and the style of describing preliminary data and experimental approaches make if difficult to follow, where data or experimental designs are described. Overall this is an excellent application with potential to generate important information about VSV matrix protein interaction with host cellular responses.

imp_text: This investigator has identified a gap in the knowledge surrounding the molecular mechanism of NTs due to the lack of atomic structures of the transporters. This is a proposal on an important topic from an early career investigator with nice potential. There is enthusiasm for the project and the importance of advancing our understanding of the mechanism of nucleoside and nucleoside drug transport by prokaryotic and eukaryotic CNTs as this will potentially facilitate the development of new therapeutic reagents. The author proposes to determine the structure of the concentrative nucleoside transporter from Vibrio cholerae using X-ray crystallography and to characterize the function of the transporter using various biophysical techniques including isothermal titration calorimetry and a radioactive flux assay using the transporter reconstituted in vesicles. The proposal has three aims: 1) structure determination of vcCNT, 2) functional characterization and comparison of vcCNT and hCNT, and 3) investigation of the molecular basis of specificity for nucleoside drugs as well as nucleosides by vcCNT and comparison with hCNT. As resistance to nucleoside anticancer drugs is a major clinical barrier to successful treatment this research has the potential to facilitate drug design and improve drug delivery. imp_text: This is a well written application by an early stage investigator with a strong, hypothesis driven approach that is supported by strong preliminary data. The PI suggests that the serine protease, mesotrypsin, is both a novel biomarker and a therapeutic target for metastatic prostate cancer. The PI proposes to develop novel inhibitors of mesotrysin and to evaluate the effects of mesotrypsin knockdown and mesotrypsin inhibitors using a combination of 3D cell culture in vitro approaches and in vivo using prostate xenografts. The approach of using existing protease scaffolds and identifying orthogonal modifications to increase both stability against mesotrypsin degradation and affinity for mesotrysin is innovative and likely to yield some interesting results. The strength of the application lies in pursuing research in these areas. However, as structured, Aim 3, which involves determining the efficacy of mesotrypsin inhibitors which have not yet been developed, is entirely dependent upon success in Aim 2. Furthermore, while the PI presents interesting data regarding potential effects of mesotrypsin on COX-2 expression, this interaction is likely indirect and the proposed experiments deviate from the central hypothesis, which is that mesotrypsin acts to promote prostate cancer aggression by degrading various canonical serine protease inhibitors. It seems that the PI should remain focused on the latter aspect of mesotrypsin’s activity. Lastly, it appears that mesotrypsin is important for initial extravasation from the primary tumor site and seeding of the secondary site, but is not necessary for tumor growth. Would mesotrypsin inhibitors be used as prophylaxis against distant metastasis? More investigation on mesotrypsin localization and temporal expression in clinical samples would be of benefit.

While high levels of mesotrysin detected in excised primary tumors appear predictive of future metastasis, removal of the primary suggests that the metastatic cells had already spread prior to the surgery. Therefore, it is not clear how an inhibitor of mesotrysin would be used as a therapeutic strategy.

study_section: Developmental Therapeutics Study Section
imp_text: This is an ambitious undertaking with a high potential for impact. The selection of appropriate patients for treatment with current and developing molecular therapeutics is a key question, which is central to this proposal. The main objective is to determine mechanisms of resistance to PI3K and AKT inhibitors, and having defined these mechanisms, to initiate clinical trials to address this issue. The central premise, that use of xenografts derived from patients will enable examination of patient responses in parallel to actual clinical tests, is of utmost importance as this will potentially enable more rapid decision making while minimizing patient risk. The ability to perform the animal research in parallel to the human studies is of particular significance. The major concern regards activation of the clinical trial in Aim 3, for which clear biomarkers must be successfully identified in Aims 1 and 2. There are a number of technical concerns with the presentation of the grant itself. Some elements of the grant were loaded out of order and needed to be rearranged before reviewing. The “Protection of Human Subjects” section contains an annotation to clarify criteria #6 in reporting adverse events. The clinical trial protocol is provided as an appendix in Draft form. It appears that information contained in the Vertebrate Animals regarding specifics of experimental design section should have been included in the main grant body.

The central hypothesis of this proposal is that key Pseudomonas aeruginosa exopolysaccharides (Psi and Pel) and an associated protein (CdrA) influence formation of a biofilm matrix prior to conversion to a highly mucoid population. Insights into this early stage of biofilm formation could facilitate approaches to block Pseudomonas infections early, thereby prolonging life of infected patients, although such approaches have not been particularly effective thus far. imp_text: This is a very focused grant aimed at understanding the role of Type 1 Secretion (T1S) of the tandem repeat protein effector TRP120 in host response to Ehrlichia infection. That said, it is not clear that this is a major obstacle in preventing development of effect therapeutics for Ehrlichia and other obligately intracellular bacteria. In fact, there was limited comparison with other obligately intracellular bacteria in this proposal. Tandem repeat proteins play important roles in a variety of pathogens, and studying these proteins will provide valuable insights into how different pathogens manipulate the host during infection. However, this proposal was very poorly written – the grant did not provide a perspective on the scope of this disease, there are numerous misspellings and run-on sentences, undefined abbreviations, figures that are too small to read, and other grantsmanship issues that made this proposal difficult to digest. Many of the proposed experiments would be better described in a table, rather than dense paragraphs (e.g. sites proposed for genetic modification in Study 1.1). The proposal also intermingles background and experimental design. In addition, the crux of the scientific method is based upon the concept of “testing” an idea with the expectation that the results could either disprove a hypothesis or support a hypothesis, but not “prove” a hypothesis. However, the use of “To demonstrate” as done in the specific aims implies that the PI has already decided on the conclusion of the study. Given the public attention to problems with unrepeatable experiments and sloppy science, a poorly written proposal does not instill confidence that the experimental work will be any better. If you are going to “challenge the current dogma and establish a new paradigm” you need both convincing experimental evidence and compelling arguments.

imp_text: This innovative, well-written proposal by an early-stage investigator is focused on a novel virulence trait of an important human pathogen, Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Preliminary data demonstrates that P. aeruginosa can degrade the potent immune signaling molecule sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) and its precursor sphingosine. The goal of this proposal is to dissect the bacterial physiology of S1P degradation, and the impact on host response to P. aeruginosa infection. The role of S1P on P. aeruginosa infections may lead to alternative therapeutics that will offset the failure of antibiotic treatment due to resistance.
sig_text_str: . Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important human pathogen, particularly in patients with Cystic fibrosis or a variety of other conditions. Treatment of these infections is often unsuccessful due to the lack of effective antimicrobials. . Although there are many groups studying biofilms in Pseudomonas (and a large number of other bacteria), the role of S1P degradation in influencing bacterial growth and host immune response is a unique angle to understanding persistence and virulence. . The fact that this pathway seems to be shared with a number of other important lung pathogens makes an understanding of this pathway potentially broadly applicable. . Sphingosine-1-phosphate is a bioactive lipid mediator that regulates the vascular and immune system as well as multiple other important physiological functions in mammals, and therapeutics that target S1P have been developed for applications in human medicine.

This early stage investigator had excellent training and experience with a broad array of experimental approaches in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, from genetics to biochemistry to structural biology. . The PI has a good publication record for this stage in his career. . The Co-investigator, Dr. Judy Heyn, has expertise in analytical chemistry that will be valuable for the proposed studies.

The importance of S1P in host signaling is well known, so the manipulation of this substrate by bacteria to modulate virulence is not surprising but poorly understood. . Mycobacterium tuberculosis has been shown to decrease sphingosine kinase to increase its intracellular survival.

imp_text: This solid proposal offers to study the structure of the tip of the Shigella Type III secretion system, with a primary focus on the needle tip protein, IpaB.  Studies have suggested that this protein is essential for the proper assembly of the needle tip, based on a chaperoning activity, as well as potentially serving an important role in contacting host cells for recognition purposes.  While some structures of IpaB exist, they are of small fragments.  This proposal offers the opportunity to study the structure a larger fragment of IpaB, and in the context of its binding partners, IpgB and IpaD.  Investigators will use a variety of biophysical techniques (crystallography, atomic force microscopy, and EM) to probe the location and structure of IpaB, and to assay the role that IpaB plays in the assembly of the TTSA.  While the molecular analysis of IpaB and its partners will be probed, there is no proposed work to link any of these discoveries to the physiology of Shigella on the whole. Based on the presence of significant preliminary data from these groups, it is likely that this proposal will be successful on most, if not all, Aims.

imp_text: This proposal to study the structure of the Psl EPS layer of Pseudomonas provided a number of tantalizing clues that Psl (or Pel) is required by the “primary inhabitants” of the Pseudomonas population of the CF lung.  Unfortunately, there is no hard evidence that Psl is required for persistence of these strains, nor evidence for the requirement of Psl for eventual conversion to the disease-causing mucoidy strains.  These investigators, while at the top of this field, propose to study the protective qualities of the Psl EPS layer in the context of neutrophil-mediated killing.  It is already well known that EPS layers protect bacteria from both external stressors and host immune systems, so the proposed “in vitro” experiments provide little gain in our understanding of Psl function.  Finally, the overall writing in many sections is poor and confusing, and does not clearly lay out experimental design or hypothesized outcomes.

imp_text: This well-written proposal links sphingosine-1-phosphate metabolism in Pseudomonas to lung infections in mouse model systems; deletions in the sphingosine-responsive sphR gene cause virulence and competition defects in vivo.  While the data suggests that the ability of Psudomonas to metabolize host S1P is crucial for its ability to colonize and persist in the host, the direct link between actual sphingosine metabolism and infection has not yet been made. Therefore, the proposed in-depth studies of solely the sph operon, while interesting for basic research, may not provide essential information towards the pathogenesis of Pseudomonas.  With additional data showing that Pseudomonas strains with only deletions in sphD and sphC are actually defective in pathogenesis (proposed in Aim 3), this proposal would be greatly strengthened, and would justify the further study of sphingosine metabolite analysis proposed in Aim 2.  Interestingly, this proposal DOES identify a requirement of the SphR regulator for pathogenesis, which clearly shows that Pseudomonas is responding to host sphingosine.  Because WT bacteria cannot complement .sphR bacteria during infection, however, it is unlikely due to the modulation of the host immune system, as this proposal suggested a few times.

This proposal focuses on the importance of Pseudomonas’ ability to alter host membrane sphingosine (and derivatives) during infections, without making a clear distinction that either are truly important for Pseudomonas infection. In co-infections of wild type and .sphR strains, wild-type bacteria should be able to metabolize host S1P, thereby allowing .sphR strains to grow.  Since sphingosine metabolism cannot be complemented in trans during infection (Fig. 6B), it is unlikely that simple host sphingosine metabolism by Pseudomonas is critical for infection. . Only data for .sphR shows defects in pathogenesis, cannot yet link other sph genes to function in pathogenesis, suggesting a new (and potentially long) search for SphR-responsive genes that function in colonization/persistence.

imp_text: The PI proposes to dissect the roles of IpaB in the Shigella type III secretion. The hypothesis is that IpaB has distinct structures and contexts depending upon its position during the early stages of type three-secretion apparatus (TTSA) needle tip assembly. The PI will use a structural biology approach to test the hypothesis, which may produce information for both developing TTSA as drug targets and understanding the mechanisms by which gram negative bacteria use TTSA to promote colonization in response to environmental cue. This is a very exciting proposal.
sig_text_str: Shigella flexneri causes global public health problems. The TTSA enables Shigella flexneri to invade human intestinal cells. Thus, determining the structure-function of TTSA may produce information for exploiting the S. flexneri type III secretion system to prevent disease caused by this pathogen.
inv_text_str: . Strong bacterial pathogenesis experts plus structural experts
inn_text_str: Bile-induced TTSA activation mechanism will be investigated by revealing the multi-facet structural changes of IpaB. Novel information is expected.
app_text_str: Aim 1 will determine the location of IpaB within quiescent and active needles by microscopically examining the needles at various stages of activation from different mutants and sheared needles from wild type and engineered strains. These are a series of straightforward experiments since there are no concerns on either the bacterial mutants or the detection method; Aim 2 will solve the crystal structure of IpaB in various forms, including cytoplasmic, free, and TTSA needle tip-associated forms and Aim 3 will identify IpaB sites for IpgC binding and for interaction with IpaD respectively. imp_text: The central hypothesis is that Ehrlichia chaffeensis TRP120 trafficks to host cell nuclei to regulate host gene expression for promoting the bacterial survival in the phagocyte endosomal compartment. Three aims will be used to test the hypothesis: Aim 1 is to determine the role of eukaroytic post translational modification in TRP120 nuclear localization and define subnuclear localization and molecular interactions; Aim 2 is to characterize TRP120 as transcriptional factor, including TRP120-DNA interactions, transcription factor function, and role of TRP120 PTMs; Aim 3 is to examine the capacity of TRP120 to modulate host target gene expression and epigenetic patterns in a cellular context. This is a very well defined molecular pathogenesis study focusing on a single potential virulence factor TRP120. The narrowly defined study model may impose two concerns: TRP120 may not be crucial for the bacterial survival in the phagocytes and identifying specific host targets or substrates of TRP120 may be risky using the proposed approaches.

imp_text: This is a clearly presented, generalized investigation of the importance of a class of non coding RNAs on myc driven lymphoma by an accomplished younger investigator.  It is currently not known whether these generally low abundance, long, non-coding,  intersperse RNAs act as tumor suppressors or oncogenes but there are examples of both in other contexts.  The scope of this proposal would identify modulators of myc driven cancer.  The approaches are feasible with the expertise of the PI and her collaborators.  However enthusiasm is dampened because of the general low abundance of these RNAs and the unknown frequency of pertinent targets. Greater clarity of how to prioritize the candidate target list would have been welcomed particularly given the relatively low conservation of the sequence between species.  Given the past experience of the PI in investigating as many as two targeted gene each year for four years, a realistic restriction on the number of RNAs that could reasonably be investigated in vivo would have been welcomed. The strong approach utilizes a combination of loss of function, using shRNA inhibition and targeted mutations and gain of function, that are proven feasible for coding RNAs.  However as noted by the PI, over expression methods have greater challenges for noncoding RNAs. Further, the potential of LncRNA to only reflect regulatory processes rather than being functional themselves, presents a major challenge because many of the experimental approaches are based on the paradigm of coding transcripts. Never the less, this proposal, while very ambitious, has great potential for significant impact.

imp_text: Understanding the practical aspects of drug resistance is an important goal in galvanizing greater patient response to existing chemotherapeutics. The PI and her associates have proposed that certain RNA protein interactions might regulate reactive oxygen species release in multiple myeloma model systems perhaps leading to a drug resistant phenotype. The approaches planned are logical and progressive and should permit accurate assessment of the veracity of the model. Since the nucleolus can initiate response to a diversity of external stimuli (including ROS), and that stress response is frequently allied to drug resistance, the fact that the over-expression of ACA11 is associated with the nucleolus imbues further relevance. There are some issues associated with the approaches used to search for interacting proteins (the results may be quantitatively overwhelming) and those nucleotide sequences within ACA11 and also for the somewhat superficial (or linear) definition of, and mechanisms used for, ROS detection.

As a consequence, understanding how resistance occurs is a critical component of improving therapies. . Multiple myeloma is exquisitely influenced by oxidative conditions. imp_text: MiRNA’s have been determined to have a variety of important regulatory functions in cells. Pathologies exemplified by cancer have irregularities in miRNA expression patterns that imply considerable functional significance. As a consequence, the general goals of this application have the potential to provide information that may advance our understanding of transcriptional regulation and a wide range of cellular processes that imbue oncogenic potential in cancer cells. Perhaps the specific approaches suffer a little in terms of innovation. There already exists a good deal of published material detailing the importance of miR-30 in cancer and growth regulatory pathways, and most of the present aims will confirm and extend such observations. As a translational component, measurements of miR-30, CHD7 and TNRC6A in a battery of human tumor samples will be enacted, further dissecting the relevance of the former on expression patterns of the latter products. If completed, these goals will proscribe a greater understanding of how miRNA’s might act as global regulators of oncogenic processes. imp_text: This is a well written and highly detailed application with extreme focus on signaling pathways that are know to have critical importance to cancer cell growth. There is significant existing interest in developing drugs that selectively target signaling pathways downstream from the Akt axis. The PI’s laboratory has been instrumental in defining important components of these kinase-based pathways and thereby advancing many of the facets of these efforts. The present application serves to continue such endeavors and extend them into dissection of how mutations in Akt might serve to differentially activate growth pathways in breast cancer cells. The premise that an E to K transition at position 17 in Akt might influence activation of PI 3 K and other downstream events linked to growth has merit and may prove to be predictive of response to drug treatments in patients harboring this mutation. In effect this could be part of an individualized medicine approach. Moreover, inhibitors of Cdk2/cyclins are showing significant early promise in the clinic. Greater understanding of their mechanistic importance as drug targets may be forthcoming from the experiments designed herein.

imp_text: The grant has many important concepts related to TNBC progression, however the proposal is packed with loosely related ideas and was difficult to follow. The compelling concept the constitutively active cAbl can block TNBC progression is worth pursuing, however the proposal has so many ideas jammed together that each aim might be developed into its own grant. For example, Aim1 is to determine the role of TGF-b signaling and mechanotransduction (ie changes in ECM stiffness) to inactivate cAbl in TNBC.  The concept of mechanotransduction is of interested it is not fully developed in this aim. While this might be a stimulus for cAbl, changes in ECM composition or amount should then be evaluated in the TMA (Aim1C) to help establish a clear link between mechanotransduction – cAbl – and TNBC.  The second aim seeks to determine downstream signaling from cAbl via p53 family members but then goes on to look at a potential activator or cAbl and the role of cAbl in non-TNBC progression. Aim 3 clearly evaluates the role of cAbl in TNBC and non-TNBC responsiveness to docetaxel.  Lastly, Securinine is an interesting therapy and has some relation to the p53 family member, p73, however it is otherwise not related to the first three aims and seems like a random addition to the proposal. Overall, good concept and important area of breast cancer but it was very hard to follow.

imp_text: Clearly written hypothesis with well controlled experimental design set to test the role of Sox2 as an oncogene in castration-resistant prostate cancer. imp_text: The investigation into the regulation and function of Net1, a RhoA specific GEF, will advance the field to better understand the complex role of RhoA GTPase in breast cancer cell motility. imp_text: This well-written grant proposes innovative new methods to isolate novel chemical compounds from marine bacteria that could prove therapeutically useful. The proposal made a convincing argument for why such novel sources of bioactive compounds are badly needed in the field and for a novel means to analyze complex metabolite mixtures. The PI proposes to use novel PCA analysis of MS data to uncover novel compounds at much higher efficiency than previously used methods. The preliminary data appears using this method appears very promising, as the group has already uncovered a novel bioactive compound that activates the Notch1 receptor. Further, the proposal seeks to advance the co-culture methods of bacterial species that may reveal novel compounds not present in monocultures. Preliminary data for this methodology also appears strong, with the isolation of a potentially very important novel antibiotic against MRSA. Overall this proposal appears innovative, with the potential to add new methodology and make great gains in the field of drug discovery.

imp_text: Underexplored sources, such as marine bacteria, have become an increasingly productive resource of novel small molecules with therapeutic potential. The goal of project is to evaluate secondary metabolomics as a broadly useful tool to reinvigorate natural products discovery from bacterial fermentations. The proposal aims to develop new approaches to natural products discovery with an exciting focus on improving the novelty of hits and increasing drug-like or lead-like structures within the library of novel secondary metabolites. The PI focuses on high-throughput screening, primarily in the therapeutic areas of oncology and infectious disease. In this proposal, the PI, L. Jackson, proposes to apply an LCMS-based untargeted metabolomics approach to guide the selection of the least redundant chemistry synthesized by the bacterial strains studied. The hypothesis put forward that secondary metabolomics guided library selection will increase the novelty of hits, and drug-like natural product libraries will yield increased hit rates compared to commercially available libraries. The secondary metabolomics approach is a novel tool to maximize chemical diversity and minimize chemical redundancy when constructing screening libraries of drug-like molecules for drug discovery. L. Jackson also proposes to use metabolomics, genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics to investigate interspecies interactions. Understanding the systems biology governing interspecies interactions and secondary metabolite production will uncover new mechanisms to activate cryptic clusters.

Validate metabolomics through an LCMS-principal component analysis approach will be a useful tool for designing natural product libraries containing drug-like and lead-like molecules for HTS . If successful, The outcomes of this proposal will be: (i) a template for producing natural product libraries enriched in new/novel small molecules with drug-like properties; and (ii) a platform for rapidly determining organisms where interspecies interactions change secondary metabolite production . A new approach to enable lead-molecule discovery from rich sources of natural products that could effectively reduce the redundancy of isolating know natural product would be a great significance and impact to the field.

app_text_str: • The strategy proposed herein offers an attractive approach to improve the detection of inter-species interactions that activate “cryptic” biosynthetic clusters which could be later used to understand interspecies signaling using genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics. The preliminary data supports the hypothesis that LCMS-PCA is a viable technology. From 47 strains from ascidians, 12 new structures were identified based on the score plot (e.g. peptidolipins B-F, WMMB-224, WMMB-247 and WMMB-215) and the LCMS-PCA method enable the segregation of strains based on the chemistry produced. They also performed PCA on a set of strains and subsequently generated a heat map to visually inspect chemical diversity which revealed little overlap and mostly complementary chemical space based on retention time and MW. Also the quantification method has been crafted to analyze highly diluted solutions of bacterial cultured with flow rate on the LCMS corresponding to ~10ng/mL. The work on mono-culture (vs co-cultured bacterium) appears well advanced and will be most likely successful, but the PI should envision that the hit rates will not be tremendously higher than by more conventional methods. Indeed the approach maybe well suited to select chemical diversity from numerous strains of bacteria in a HTS fashion, but the structural information which is pivotal in the discovery of novel and bioactive scaffold comes very late in the screening process. With a late-stage structural determination, the risk of structural redundancy might still be important. Overall the approach is well defined and exciting in terms of novel natural products that could be discovered by implementing the technology.

imp_text: This proposal from Todd Kelly (Yale University) entails a detailed study of the role of microtubule interactions in the function of kinesin to better understand the fundamental aspects (atomic and structural) and steps involved in the motility of dimeric kinesin. The Pi proposes to determine the atomic basis of microtubule-stimulated function by kinesin motor domain as well as the structural basis of communication between the kinesin and the microtubule during translocation: Kinesin motor walk along the microtubule To this aim, the PI proposes to use cryo-EM to enable a high resolution structure determination of the kinesin-microtubule complex and other techniques (saturation transfer EPR and AFM) to resolve structural modification happening during the dynamic process.  Kelly proposes to combine the cryo-EM methods with the use of saturation transfer EPR (ST-EPR) to quantify orientational disorder in the binding modes of kinesin to microtubules (unique sensitivity of this method to microsecond rotational dynamics within complex assemblies). The fundamental discoveries that such research could afford are significant, but the direct implications of such very fundamental findings to the development of kinesin motor inhibition by small molecules or other means are unclear. This project appears to be oriented towards the fundamental understanding of the phenomenon itself (kinesin walk) without interrogating the possible applications of the structural interactions to other classes of microtubule interacting proteins. The fundamental nature of this project would appeared more attractive to other funding agencies such as the NSF.
sig_text_str: . The understanding of the kinesin motor protein walk along the microtubule at the atomic/structural level would be of great significance to better understand the dynamic process. . Studying how kinesins use ATP to move along filaments inside of cells could potentially clarify the means by which inhibitors may interfere with kinesin function, and how certain mutations can lead to failure of motor motility. Such finding would be also very significant. . The cryo-EM method and the algorithm to treat the data and obtain high-resolution imaging are significant tools to enhance the current image processing methodology and ability to resolve kinesin-microtubule complexes at subnanometer resolution. . These techniques have enabled the first direct visualization of the microtubule seam at high resolution (Kelly and Downing, 2007).

imp_text: This is an interesting proposal, investigating the mechanism by which IL-19 can affect angiogenesis in response to ischemic insult. The proposal contains novel and thorough approaches to investigate this mechanism, and is supported by strong preliminary data. The lack of a disease model diminishes the impact slightly, as it would be very interesting to know if this mechanism was altered in diseases where wound healing/angiogenic responses are impaired; this would lend much credence to the importance of IL-19 in vascular health. The presentation of the aims is complex and at times confusing, making it difficult to understand the rationale. Nonetheless, the scientific merit of this proposal is high, as is the innovation and impact.

This work could also have broad-ranging applications to post-MI cardiac recovery. . Connects local effects of IL-19 in ECs with systemic effects of macrophage activation.

imp_text: This proposal investigates a novel pathway involved in the development of cardiac hypertrophy, to understand the progression to heart failure. The PI utilizes the flexibility and malleability of the drosophila genome to test for genetic determinants of cardiac hypertrophy, and then translates the mutations to key elements of these conserved pathways into mice. The approach, novelty, and innovation of this proposal are extremely high. This is an inventive way to rapidly investigate a new pathway that could take years if using only mice. The overall hypothesis is that IL-19 is a novel angiogenic, anti-inflammatory cytokine with multiple effector cells. The aims are to 1) test the hypothesis that IL-19 expression regulates angiogenesis. Determine if absence of IL-19 attenuates, and if over expression of IL-19 promotes angiogenesis, 2) determine if IL-19 regulation of angiogenesis is by primarily facilitated by direct effects on vascular cells, or by macrophage M2 polarization, 3) identify and characterize IL-19 inducible factors necessary for IL-19-driven angiogenesis in vivo. Identify if these factors are primarily secreted by IL-19-stimulated EC or by IL-19-stimulated M2 macrophage, and 4) test the hypothesis that differential expression of IL-20 receptor subunits account for pleiotropic effects of IL-19 in VSMC compared with EC. The Applicant presented convinced preliminary data to continue pursuing the main hypothesis: that Interleukin-19 (IL-19), an anti-inflammatory, Th2 interleukin, can enhance angiogenesis and improve perfusion of ischemic tissue. However, the application may benfit from joining aims 1 and 2, and adds a new preclinical aim studying the fects of IL-19 in animal models of vascular injury. One of the main strengths of the project will be to know if IL-19 is a new angeogenic factor and may lead to the development of new therapeutics for balloon angioplasty, stem replacement, and allograft vasculopathy. Second, the hypothesis the differential expression of IL-20 receptors subunits account for pleiotropic effect of IL-19 in VSMC compared to EC, here this effects may be modulated by a bias ligand effects of IL-19 in VSCM compared to a more general effect in EC. It will be interesting to investigate if differential expression of the IL-20 receptor leads to bias effects by IL-19 in different cells and physiological conditions. This additional approach could give new directions to the development of therapies modulating effects of IL-19 in VSMC or EC.

imp_text: Overall Impact The hypotheses propose in this project is that interaction between the Raf and Hippo pathways affect post developmental alterations in YAP1 activity to regulate the development of cardiac hypertrophy. The aims to test the hypothesis are: 1) Determine whether Raf-MEK1-mediated cardiac hypertrophy occurs via regulation of the Hippo-yorkie pathway in flies and identify signaling pathways that function downstream of yorkie., 2) Identify the specific modular domains in mammalian YAP1 that drive cardiomyocyte hypertrophy or proliferation, 3) Determine whether a reduction in YAP-1 modifies the severity of cardiac hypertrophy or heart failure in RafL613V/+ knock-in mice or wild-type mice after TAC-induced pressure overload. This proposal long-term goal is to understand the molecular signals that modulate the development and progression of cardiac hypertrophy and dilated cardiomyopathy using Drosophila genetics as a discovery platform and translate the findings to humans. To achieve this goal, the overall objective of this application is to examine the Raf-MEK1 pathway and the activation of yorkie in cardiac hypertrophy. My central hypothesis is that crosstalk between the Raf-MEK1 and Hippo-YAP1 pathways drives cardiomyocyte decisions towards hypertrophy or hyperplasia. The Applicant has experience in the field and presented sufficient preliminary data to continue persuing the main hypothesis. It is important to establish that this is a combination of fly genetics models combines with mouse mammalian model of disease. The application is divided in three aims one use fly as a genetic model to decipher mechanism of cardiac hypertrophy, followed by a second aim using cardiomyocytes in culture to corroborate findings (interdependent aims), and a third aim using mouse models to validate the initial findings. The application has limited flaws. Aim a and 2 should be combine into one aim and develop another aim using mammalian models of disease (mouse), and in this new aim screen for possible manipulators of the Raf-MEK1 and Hippo-YAP1 pathways as possible new therapeutics for cardiac disease.

imp_text: The application proposes to investigate the role of kalirin in atherosclerosis.  Polymorphisms in the kalirin gene has been associated with increased atherosclerosis but the relationship has not get been previously explored.  The experiments proposed will carefully investigate the role of karilin in endothelial cells and macrophages as wells a investigate the multiple function of the proteins in terms of RhoGEF activity, its effects on eNOS and iNOS, and its protein scaffolding capability.  Strengths of the propose are that it looks at both tissue level disease as well as specific molecular functions and has 2 investigators with the capabilities to perform these experiments.  A more careful exploration of the isoforms in human tissues/disease and the specific polymorphisms would increase the translation appeal of the grant but overall it will investigate a novel and potentially important protein in atherosclerosis.

SNPs for karlin have been shown to be associated with atherosclerosis which makes the haploinsufficiency model used here relevant since patients likely also have a decreased amount of functional genes rather than complete knockout.

imp_text: This application is designed using mouse models to determine whether PD-L1/PD interaction is a critical checkpoint for myocardial inflammation mediated damage and whether altering this interaction can prevent T cell sensitization.  Aim 1 uses tissue selective inducible KO mice to determine if PD-L1 KO in endothelium, dendritic cells, or myocardium modulate T-cell mediated inflammation. Aim 2 looks at PD-1 deletion in the myeloid line and its effect on myocardial inflammation.  Aim 3 looks at dendritic cell tolerance and the role of PD-L1 and KLF2 in this process. Affirmative findings would reveal tissue specificity of PD-L1 expression importance in myocardial inflammation, PD-1’s role in this process in myeloid cells, and how dendritic cell tolerance may affect T-cell inflammatory activity.   The strengths of the application include highly innovative new conditional KO animal models to discern tissue-specific contributions of this pathway to myocarditis, the potential therapeutic translation for the pathway as a myocarditis treatment, and strong, highly experienced PIs.  These strengths are mitigated by a lack of clarity of as to which PI is in charge of what portions of the application, 1 PI with insufficient effort toward the application to be PI, and incremental significance/innovation relative to the prior work already reported by the PIs (see significance/innovation weaknesses below).  Pathways besides PD-1/PD-L1 should be considered as to how they may interact with this pathway. The environmental section also appears to be in part from a prior application with multiple apparently erroneous references as delineated below.  There is also a human subjects section that appears out of place.  These concerns make the likely impact of this work to be moderate.

imp_text: Write a paragraph summarizing the factors that informed your Overall Impact score The PI proposes a novel model where plasmalemmal caveolae containing NADPH oxidase and L-type Ca2+ channels closely appose peripheral mitochondria to form a permissive subcellular environment suitable for the functional convergence of Ca2+ and redox microdomains.  The PI will test in Aim 1 if NADPH Oxidase is colocalized with L-type Ca channels in the caveole.  Aim 2 tests if peripheral mitochondria play a role in coupling NADPH Oxidase and these calcium channels.  Aim 3 will test if this superstructure is active in obesity related arterial dysfunction.  Strengths of the proposal include a well-trained promising new investigator in an excellent environment with a proposal applying several innovative new techniques.  Enthusiasm is mitigated by reduced significance in light of the likely modest effect these findings are likely to have on treatment of blood pressure, a paucity of relevant and applicable preliminary data, and a couple key critical flaws in the study design and preliminary data (apocyanin is not a specific NADPH Oxidase inhibitor calling into ? the premise of the proposal and lack of detailing of how overlap quantification will be done which is critical to study interpretation).  Taken together, the overall impact of this proposal is likely to be at best moderate in its current form but could be considerably better with addressing the challenges to the proposal delineate in this summary.

imp_text: This proposal, using mouse models of Kalrn (-/+) is designed to determine the mechanism by which Kalirin (one of 2 mammalian proteins with 2 guanin nucleotide exchange factors for Rho family G proteins) modulates risk for atherosclerosis.  They propose to test whether kalirin has an atheroprotective effect through its RhoGEF1 binding domain/iNOS interacting domain or both, determine how flow-induced signaling in endothelial cells is affected by kalirin expression and which proteins may be involved in interactions with kalirin to alter atherosclerotic signaling using proteomic methods and a tamoxifen-inducible heterozygous kalirin KO model, and investigate kalirin’s role in macrophages as it relates to atherosclerosis.  Key strengths of this application include a strong environment, excellent investigator, and targeting of a potentially important under-explored regulator of atherosclerosis.  Innovation is also strong with the inclusion of tissue specific KO models.   Methods are described in exquisite detail.  Enthusiasm is dampened by the overall somewhat unfocused overall application with exploration of common signaling pathways in a setting novel questions as to how kalirin has apparently opposing roles in different tissues and how that is regulated would seem to be the more interesting and potentially clinically relevant questions.  There are some important issues in portions other approach to be addressed as well.   Overall this is application is likely to have moderate impact based on the above concerns.

imp_text: This is a multiple PI-based collaborative study to elucidate the functions of viral PDEs in antagonizing IFN-induced RNase L to cause hepatitis. The science here is exciting because 1) the novel activity of MHV ns2 as well as its homolog proteins to repress IFN response will be defined. 2) studying cell type-specific regulation of RNase L activity by viruses could find the link between IFN antagonism and viral pathogenesis leading to hepatitis. 3) Inhibitors, if found, could be valuable for discovering the function of viral or cellular PDEs as well as for developing novel anti-viral therapeutics. The two PIs are experts in the field of MHV pathogenesis and RNase L pathways and prepared for all the required resources for conducting the proposed study in excellent environments. Minor weaknesses include insufficient justification for using cellular PDEs and generation of recombinant viruses in the proposed study and possible drawbacks for the use of the inhibitors. Nevertheless, there is overwhelming enthusiasm toward this virology research, which could yield interesting and important scientific findings.
sig_text_str: • OAS-RNase L pathway is an important cellular defense mechanism. Determining the activity of viral and host 2-5-PDEs (downregulating levels of 2-5A) is of high significance. • Studying the role of macrophages in restricting virus from entering the liver could enhance our understanding about viral pathogenesis. • Inhibitors to be screened may have high potential for therapeutics and other purposes.
inv_text_str: • Two PIs are experts in the fields of the proposed study. • Having multiple consultants increase the feasibility of the project.
inn_text_str: • The new function of RNaseL antagonists is to be investigated. • Discovering and testing the inhibitors blocking viral 2-5-PDE provide innovative facets. •
app_text_str: • Cell type (macrophage) specific function of MHV ns2 impairing RNaseL system will be investigated by using genetically modified animal system. • Ns2 mutant-expressing MHV is available. • In the aim 2, the function of diverse viral and cellular 2-5-PDEs will be evaluated regarding the activity, virus growth, cellular apoptosis, and IFN response. • The inhibitor, if found, blocking the activity of viral or cellular PDEs could be useful for determining the role of these proteins in multiple cellular processes as well as designing new anti-viral drugs. •

Is there any as yet unknown function of these PDEs that may affect virus replication other than antagonizing RNase L? • The inhibitors are not well characterized yet. imp_text: The purpose of this excellent study is to determine novel mechanisms of how vOTUs (viral homologue of the ovarian tumor protease) of nairoviruses regulate deubiquitination and deISGylation. The proposed study will utilize in vitro assays determining the substrate specificity and structural analysis as well as the experiments with recombinant CCHFVs in vitro and in vivo. The PI has established all the assays and resources needed for the project and is fully qualified to conduct the proposed study. The immune evasive activity of nairoviruses is novel and important for understanding the viral pathogenicity and virus-host interaction. The proposed experiments could produce interesting data and test the hypothesis. However, no plan is found to identify the direct cellular target proteins of the vOTUs that are critical for virus replication. Also, the effect of vOTU on the cellular ubiquitination/ISGylation system and other cellular processes is not well discussed. Despite the presence of these minor flaws, this is a highly interesting study that could have a high impact on the virology research.
sig_text_str: • CCHFV (Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus) belongs to Nairovirus of the Bunyaviridae family and is classified as a category C priority pathogen. • vOTU evades innate immune response (type I IFN) by cleaving ubiquitin and ISG15. Investigating the activity of vOTUs could unravel important mechanisms for nairovirus pathogenesis and virus-host interaction.
sig_text_wkn: • The ubiquitination and ISGylation can affect numerous cellular proteins’ functions. However, the impact of the vOTUs on the cellular physiology is not fully considered.

study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: The project proposes to study the mechanism by which VSV shuts off host gene expression by regulating transcription, mRNA transport, and translation processes. Aim 1 will investigates if hnRNPs regulate the transport/transcription of cellular mRNAs upon infection and aim 2 will identify host or viral proteins associated with mRNPs that control translation. The strength of this proposal is the quality of the PI who has long studied this mechanism as well as strong environment to perform this proposed study. Also, the observation that several hnRNPs that were accumulated in the cytoplasm upon VSV infection is interesting. However, it is unclear whether hnRNPs are crucial for the shut-off process or not. imp_text: This interesting proposal of a productive new investigator addresses the cellular machinery in meiosis. If successful, the study will reveal critical mechanistic aspects of this process, which remain poorly understood. Specifically, it will provide a better understanding of aneuploidies (errors in chromosome segregation) which is a leading genetic cause of miscarriage and Down syndrome. Many protein components in chromosome segregation are known but their molecular functions and interactions remain mysterious. The PI established an outstanding team of collaborators and a focused research plan to study three major components in “meiosis I” (the first stage of meiosis): the monopolin complex, the Hop1 protein, and Zip 1 (in the synaptonemal complex). The project stems from seminal studies on the monopolin complex, which the PI purified for the first time as a postdoc. Additional preliminary data support each aim. The successful completion of the proposed studies is likely to exert a sustained impact on the field of meiosis. Parts in each Aim rely on the expectation that new recombinant proteins will be soluble and crystallized successfully. The proposal is densely written and often too focused on structure solving (and its technical aspects) failing to develop clear hypothesis-guided experiments. Expected outcomes and alternative approaches are underdeveloped. A timeline is missing. Some grantsmanship issues that dampened enthusiasm can be easily corrected by the PI.
sig_text_str: • (major) The potential to understand the molecular basis of chromosome segregation defects is highly relevant to human health including Down syndrome and Turner’s syndrome. • (major) A unique combination of studies on protein structure and interactions address a critical information gap in the field. The studies lay the groundwork to define function and mechanism of factors in chromosome recombination and segregation.
sig_text_wkn: • (moderate) Are the proposed studies in yeast likely to improve the understanding of meiosis I in vertebrates? This significance-related issue should be discussed in the proposal.
inv_text_str: • (major) The PI performed the first reconstitution and structural study of the yeast monopolin complex during his postdoctoral research. The proposal stems from this major achievement. • (major) A strong team of collaborators (with support letters) providing expertise in meiosis in vivo assays, yeast genetics, microscopy, NMR and proteomics. Some of these labs are neighbors to the PI’s lab.
inn_text_str: • (major) A powerful combination of structural and biochemical approaches to dissect function and mechanism of relevant proteins in meiosis I (i.e., homolog chromosomes crosslinks and segregation). •
inn_text_wkn: • (major) Working hypotheses are missing or underdeveloped in some places. For example, the PI will determine whether or not Mam1 directly regulates Hrr25’s kinase activit, and also its substrate specificity. Also, the PI expects to generate a detailed picture of a protein’s mechanism in meiotic regulation. What are the driving model(s), specific hypotheses, expected and alternative outcomes (and drawbacks) in the experiments?
app_text_str: • (major) A focused approach to study a limited set of relevant proteins in different aspects of meiosis I. • (major) Substantial preliminary data, including a major achievement in the PI’s postdoctoral research. Namely, the reconstitution and structural studies of the yeast monopolin complex. • (major) A balanced combination of biochemical and genetic studies: mutation impact on protein structure and interactions (in vitro assays) and on function in vivo (yeast genetics assays). • (major) Aim 1 is a logic continuation of the PI’s work as a postdoc working with Stephen Harrison.
app_text_wkn: • (moderate) Several studies require crystallized proteins and complexes (e.g., Hrr25 kinase, Csm1 in Aim 1, Hop2 in Aim 2, Zip1 in Aim 3) but successful crystals of proteins alone or in complex are not available yet. However, preliminary crystals of Hrr25 are promising. Also, some protein constructs have been expressed in bacteria. • (minor) A support letter from Dr. Harrison is missing. Confirmation that this lab is no longer working on the monopolin complex (i.e., Mam1 and Hrr25 subunits) in Aim 1 would be ideal.

imp_text: This is a strong new proposal from Dr. Darnell Jackson who discovered the minor form of spliceosomal splicing (U12-dependent introns) that occurs in a few mRNAs. The focus is on the U4atac snRNA in the minor spliceosome. Several natural mutations in the U4atac snRNA gene cause severe developmental disorder microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type I (MOPD I). If successful, the PI will define the functional consequences of these mutations on splicing, and thus the molecular basis of U12-associated disorder. The approach is innovative and relevant to genomic medicine. It addresses molecular mechanism of known MOPD I-causing mutations, and examines several SNPs that the PI identified in all four snRNAs from the minor spliceosome. Of particular significance is the preliminary data suggesting that some SNPs are new recessive MOPD I alleles. The PI and his collaborators rely on well-developed biochemical assays of splicing, use an vivo snRNA functional assay that is quantitative, and a novel transcriptome analysis of MOPD I patients. Only a few reservations regarding some assays with recombinant proteins and synthetic RNAs, presence of endogenous snRNAs and snRNA constructs in the same cells are noted. In brief, the team of investigators is ideally suited to perform these studies.

So, these studies are relevant to other splicing related pathologies.

imp_text: This in an exciting competitive proposal by a senior investigator who has made substantial contributions to the current understanding of ribosome biogenesis. The studies test an innovative model. If successful it will help better define the function of critical protein and RNA factors that control the biogenesis of the 40S SSU in yeast. A hypothesis-based approach combines strong synergy in yeast genetics (Murray lab, PI) and in vitro biochemistry with purified components (Cobbett lab, Co-I). Strong preliminary data led to four logic aims with the focus to understanding the role of the helicase Ecm16 and its cofactors in SSU biogeneis. The studied protein (Ecm16, Bud23, Rps2) and RNA (U3 snoRNA) components have counterparts in higher eukaryotes. So, understanding the molecular basis of translation control (e.g., common up-regualtion in cancers) and identification of drug targets and therapies is relevant to human health. Enthusiasm for this proposal was dampened by the use of tecniques that may provide limited information (e.g., chemical probing). It remains unclear if the central Ecm16 is a bona fide helicase with unwinding activity. The proposal would benefit from incorporating complementary techiques to identify RNA-protein contacts. The incorporation of clips technologies would be ideal. Dr. Cobbett will perfom experiments in several critical subaims (biosketch and letter of support are included) but it is unclear if funding support is allocated for this lab.
sig_text_str: • (major) The potential to understand how a critical helicase in ribosome biogenesis is controlled. This is important because the function and control mechanism of most eukaryotic helicases remain to be defined. • (major) The potential in translational research potential with the identification of possible drug targets and therapies in diseases involving translation defects or upregulation (e.g., in most cancers).

imp_text: This proposal aims to elucidate the structures and physical protein-protein interactions of a small set of proteins important for different aspects of meiotic chromosome structure, recombination, and segregation.  The PI plans to carefully dissect those machineries to isolate relevant well-behaved assemblies for 3D structural analysis, and provide information on mutations that may disrupt individual aspects of a protein’s structure or protein-protein interactions.  This proposal comes from a highly qualified new investigator who has determined the core structure of the monopolin complex during her postdoctoral studies. The PI proposed to continue study the mechanism of sister kinetochore cross-linking by the S. cerevisiae monopolin complex, investigate the different conformations and protein-protein interaction of Hop1 and the self-assembly properties and protein-protein interactions of Zip1.  However, lack of solid preliminary data that demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed structural studies, even in aim 1 which is the continuation of her postdoctoral studies, is the major weakness of this proposal.
sig_text_str: . The system proposed is an important system and yet poorly understood. . Understanding the mechanism of this system has been partially hindered by difficulties in isolating meiotic chromosome-associated proteins to study in vitro, and the PI has demonstrated some success in isolating some of the proteins in their soluble form.
inv_text_str: . The PI is a highly qualified researcher coming from a well-known lab.  She has the expertise in structural characterization of multidomain proteins. . The PI has assembled a group of expertise for collaboration.

imp_text: U12-dependent spliceosome is a low abundance spliceosome that is responsible for splicing introns in approximately 800 human genes.  It differs from the U2-dependent spliceosome in the small nuclear RNAs required for their function.  A rare autosomal recessive disease called MOPD I was shown to be caused by any of several point mutations in the U4ata snRNA gene. These mutations drastically reduced the in vivo function of U4atac snRNA assayed in a heterologous system and reduced the level of splicing of several U12-dependent introns in patient-derived cell lines.  The proposal aims to first analyze the biochemical function of mutants in U4atac snRNAs to reveal what step(s) during spliceosome maturation/assembly is/are disrupted by the various mutations; secondly to determine the transcriptome changes associated with the 51G>A U4atac snRNA MOPD I mutation to reveal what genes are most affected by the mutations; and lastly to determine the function effects of minor snRNA gene polymorphisoms. Both aim1 and aim2 are well developed, and the results will provide insights into how those mutant U4atac snRNA may affect the assembly of a functional spliceosome.  However, in aim 3 the bioinformatics studies of snRNA polymorphisms missed most of the MOPD I mutations, that raises the question on how this method may provide a coverage/prediction on potential disease-causing mutation in the major and minor snRNAs.
sig_text_str: . The U12-dependent introns are distributed in a small set of human genes (~800).  Many of these genes are essential for cell viability growth and development. . Mutation in the spliceosome components can cause diseases, and several naturally occurring mutations in U4atac snRNA are responsible for MOPD I.
inv_text_str: . The PI has a strong track record and expertise in the field of mRNA-splicing. . The co-PIs are experts in bioinformatics and are highly capable of carrying out the sequencing and analysis of snRNA genes in Aim3.
inv_text_wkn: . Since RNA-seq studies are performed in Christain Buben’s lab in MIT, Dr. Buben should be a co-PI.
inn_text_str: . Since the minor spliceosome (U12-dependent) affects a relatively small number of introns (~800), it provides a tractable model system for studying the effect of its mutations on the downstream target genes. This is somewhat innovative.
app_text_str: . Aim1 is nicely developed with preliminary data clearly supporting the hypothesis. . Aim2 is also cohesively developed.  The PI and the collaborator group sequenced the RNAs in MOPD I patient cells and demonstrated that many genes are affected. So they proposed to further identify those mostly affected genes. . In aim3, the PI and the co-PIs proposed to use bioinformatics to investigate the snRNA gene polymorphisms.  They have revealed other gene variations in U4atac and demonstrated that some of those mutants can significantly disrupt the activity.
app_text_wkn: . Minor: In aim1, the PI proposed to test other mutants in competition experiments, however there is no details on the potential disruption of Sm binding to the 111G>A mutant. . Major: In aim2, the PI reported that 434 genes are significantly affected in MOPD I patient cells, however, connections are missing between the 45 most affected U12-dependent introns and those genes.  In addition, do all the 434 genes contain U12-dependent introns? . Major: In aim3, 1000 Genomes data plus 452 individuals in Central Ohio did not cover the dominant mutants detected in MOPD I patients.  This raises the question whether the sampling size is still not large enough, or this method can not fully predict all potential diseasing causing mutants.

imp_text: During DNA replication, DNA polymerases (pols) are recruited to the replication forks through protein-protein interactions.  Eukaryotic replication fork consists of Cdc45-Mcm2-7-GINS (CMG) complexes and other proteins.  The PI proposed to examine the interactions between those proteins: first to reveal the preference of pol-epsilon and pol-delta on leading and lagging strand synthesis; second to examine interactions between replication proteins and hCMG complex; lastly to examine the influence of mutations in psf1 on replication. This is a very important system, and the PI has accumulated a large amount of preliminary data.  However my enthusiasm diminished due to lack of critical experimental details and potential pitfalls.
sig_text_str: . This proposed study is on an important system, if successful, the result can help to understand how proteins are recruited to the DNA replication fork. . This system is from human.  The proposed studies may help to provide molecular insight into how mutants of the DNA replication proteins make affect DNA replication.
