imp_text: This application proposes to study a highly significant biomedical problem, how a virus subverts the cellular immune response, and will address the underexplored yet highly important area of what happens early in a viral infection. The basic hypothesis, virus-mediated destruction of 2-5A and preventing activation of RNase L , is highly innovative. The studies are generally very hypothesis driven with clearly defined goals and endpoints. Studying the problem at the level of individual enzymes, whole cells and in animals will give a global picture of the role of the 2-5A destroying phosphodiesterase in enhancing viral infectivity. Expanding the studies to other viruses and their likely encoded 2-5A phosphodiesterases is a great idea and the proposed studies are very strong. Balanced against this, however, are the HTS approaches to develop inhibitors. These are woefully underdeveloped and the applicant appears unaware of the difficulties with this approach. The applicant and collaborators are well trained for the proposed work and the environment is great.
sig_text_str: . Novel targets for antiviral treatments are extremely important medically. The applicant proposes to develop just such a target, namely by inhibiting a viruses ability to decrease the cellular levels of 2-5A. This target appears applicable to multiple viruses. (Major) . These studies address an important issue biologically, the early interactions between the virus and the cellular immunity responses. They will fill in important gap in our knowledge of this area. (Major) . Expanding these studies to proteins in other viruses that may degrade 2-5A is very significant in that it would expand the generality of this activity as a potential drug target. (Major)

imp_text: Poliovirus polymerase, the subject of this application, is an extremely important enzyme medically and can provide a paradigm for polymerases from other RNA viruses. The results of this work will be very significant in that they will provide a much more detailed understanding of this enzyme, and may provide ways to think about the mechanism of many other enzymes. The combination of enzyme kinetics, dynamics and structure is particularly innovative. The approaches used are generally appropriate and should provide the needed data. The attenuated virus enzyme studies and the inhibitor studies are very interesting. Slightly offsetting these significant strengths are the off-putting statements regarding drug development and some moderate weaknesses in the approach. The applicant plus collaborators and environment are both excellent.
sig_text_str: . Poliovirus is clearly a very important virus, and other RNA viruses that encode an RNA dependent RNA polymerase are likewise important. (Major) . Understanding how mutations distal from an active site can affect the active site is a major biochemical question. (Major) . The potential role of dynamics in regulating catalysis is intriguing and worthy of study. (Moderate)
sig_text_wkn: . The PI posits that the data obtained will inform drug design for RNA dependent RNA polymerases is really quite naïve. It is remarkably easy to develop good small molecule inhibitors of virtually any enzyme. Especially for nucleotide analogue inhibitors, but also for all small molecule inhibitors, the key factor determining success is not so much the target but how the inhibitor interacts with other enzymes/proteins within the cell. (Major)
inv_text_str: . The applicant and collaborators are adequately trained for the proposed work, and together provide an outstanding team that should be able to bring the proposed studies to fruition (Major).
inn_text_str: . The combined use of kinetics (steady- and pre-steady-state), dynamical measurements (NMR), structure (NMR) and molecular dynamics is highly innovative. (Major) . The idea that the attenuated strains of poliovirus have a polymerase with altered fidelity is very interesting. (Major) . imp_text: This is a new application from a new investigator who proposes to biochemically and structurally characterize proteins required for chromosome pairing and recombination during meiosis I. The process of meiosis is fairly well-defined at the level of genetics and cell biology, but we still know very little about the process at the biochemical and molecular levels and this proposal aims to address these gaps in our knowledge. In addition to increasing our understanding of this fundamental biological process, this proposal is also directly relevant to human health. Improper chromosome segregation during meiosis I leads to aneuploidy which usually results in miscarriage, but can also result in genetic disorders such as Downs syndrome. As such, this proposal investigates important questions at a level that have not yet been answered. This project, and in particular Aim 1, build on the PI’s postdoctoral work, and thus, the PI has the necessary experience to complete the aims. However, one concern is that the project seems overly ambitious. A large number of experiments examining different aspects of chromosome segregation and meiotic recombination are proposed, and there are likely to be many technical hurdles to overcome. Part of the reason these proteins have not been well-defined at the molecular level is that they are part of large complexes, difficult to purify, and not particularly well-behaved in solution. The PI uses a combination of truncation and co-expression of the proteins to overcome some of the solubility problems, but there still may be significant challenges in obtaining enough material for structural and biochemical studies. Finally, while the topic of the proposal is highly significant, the research plan tends to describe a list of experiments without explaining how the results from the experiments will answer key questions about meiosis I. These two issues dampen enthusiasm for an otherwise exciting project. imp_text: Write a paragraph summarizingthe factors that informed your Overall Impact score: The topic of this proposal is outside of my area of expertise. This is a new proposal from an established investigator to study the mechanism of the U12 spliceosome to understand how mutations in the snRNA component, U4atac, manifest in a rare autosomal recessive disease, microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism (MOPD1). Specifically, this proposal seeks to determine what functions of U4atac are affected by the mutations, and what genes/cell types are most affected by the mutations. In addition this proposal will evaluate effects of SNPs in snRNAs on the function of the U12 splicing system. In addition to providing structure-function information to understanding the mechanism of the spliceosome, these SNP studies will create a database that will be useful in making clinical correlations between snRNA mutations and other disease states. The proposal is generally well-written and strong preliminary data is presented to support each of the aims. The mechanistic studies in Aim 1 are well-developed and likely to define defects in splicing caused by MOPD1 mutations (and SNPs in Aim 3). Transcriptome analyses in Aim II will reveal defects in gene expression due to splicing, but it is not clear whether the approach will be sufficient to identify the genes associated with the pathology of MOPD1. Another weakness in the proposal is that alternative possibilities were not discussed, nor were potential problems anticipated and addressed. These issues dampen enthusiasm for a proposal that has potential to increase our understanding of the relationship between splicing defects and disease.

inn_text_str: Mutations in spliceosomal components give rise to a number of diseases but the mechanistic basis is not understood. The MOPD1 mutations provide a good model system for beginning to understand how splicing defects manifest in disease because a relatively small population of introns is affected, those spliced by the U12 system. . Propose to use a novel quantitative in vivo snRNA functional assay to assess the effects of MOPD1 mutations.
inn_text_wkn: . Much of the proposal is based on analysis of “big data sets” to catalog effects of mutations to snRNAs.
app_text_str: Aim I addresses the mechanistic defects in U4atac function caused by MOPD1 mutations. The majority of MOPD1 mutations cluster the base-paired region of a stemloop structure suggesting the mutations disrupt this structure which is important for protein binding. The hypothesis to be tested is that these mutation reduce binding of one or more proteins to the spliceosome and strong preliminary data support this hypothesis. . Because patient samples are limited, modified snRNAs were developed that would allow for the formation of splicing complexes from exogeneous snRNAs only, and “orthologous spliceosome”. When transfected into cells, these modified snRNAs will not form complexes with endogenous snRNAs so the effects of the mutations on complex formation can be examined in a wild-type background. . Aim I will analyze steps in the splicing reaction that are affected by MOPD1 mutations utilizing an in vitro assay to measure splicing of introns that have been found to be affected in vivo. Thus, the PI will be able to identify the step in the splicing reaction that is affected, and possibly why some introns are affected to a greater degree than others. . Aim II presents a solid approach to analyzing the transcriptome to determine how MOPD1 mutations alter splicing and affect the transcriptome. This will do two things: 1) correlate splice site sequences with splicing efficiency and 2) identify genes and pathways that are adversely affected by MOPD1 mutations and that may contribute to the pathologies of the disease. . Aim III diverges from the MOPD1 theme and will analyze the effects of SNPs in the snRNAs of the U12 splicing system on function. This will create a structure-function database that can be used to make clinical correlations with other disease states, and can be used to predict the effects of mutations to the snRNAs identified in other studies.
app_text_wkn: Alternative possibilities and potential problems in the approach are not discussed. . It is not clear in Aim I how measurements of rates of splicing U2-and U12-dependent introns will be used to learn about the mechanism of MOPD1 mutations. . The approach to the harder question in Aim II is to determine what defects in the transcriptome give rise to the pathology associated in MOPD1. The PI proposes to examine splicing of U12-dependent introns in two genes that may be associated with growth defects ORC3 and NOP2. But a broader approach to identify novel factors was not discussed. It is not clear if this aim will successfully identify genes affected by splicing defects that give rise to the pathologies of MOPD1.

imp_text: This is a new proposal from a distinguished investigator. The goal of this project is to dissect the molecular architecture of the human replication complex. Two main lines of investigation are proposed. The first is to determine how the appropriated DNA polymerases are targeted to the fork, and the second is to determine how Ctf4, Mcm10, claspin, Tim-tippen, FACT, and Psf1 affect helicase and polymerase activity at the fork. The overarching hypothesis is that the CMG helicase forms the core of the replisome and targets appropriate polymerases to the fork. Accessory proteins then modulate the activity of the DNA polymerase and helicase. In addition to defining mechanisms and interactions required for this fundamental biological pathway, the effects of mutations in Psf1, a component of GINS and the CMG, on replication and replisome function will be investigated. These mutations are directly relevant to human health because they were identified in a small cohort of patients that presented with growth retardation, immune deficiencies and a predisposition for osteosarcoma. Overall, the proposed studies are highly significant. The one shortcoming of the proposal is that the proposal focused primarily on preliminary work that had been done, and did not develop the experiments that would be done as part of the funded work. This concern is reduced to some degree by the strong track record of the PI, and thus, the impact of this work is likely to be high. imp_text: This application aims to study the function of several proteins in the 90S to pre-40S transition, a process in ribosome biogenesis. The proposal focuses on four proteins, the RNA helicase Ecm16 (Aim 1), the methyltransferase Bud23 (Aim 2), and RNA binding protein Imp4 (Aim 3), and the ribosomal protein Rps2 (Aim 4). The proposal uses a combination of biochemical and genetic approaches with the aim to define specific substrates, enzymatic activities, and interactions between the proteins. The proposed experiments are likely to provide insight into the function of the factors and into their interaction. Such findings, while descriptive, are likely to advance our understanding of the studies steps of the ribosome biogenesis. However, the application fails to combine insight from the experiments in the individual aims to systematically advance the understanding of ribosome biogenesis. There is no attempt to devise predictive models and to integrate insight gained in the individual aims. The aims are somewhat disjointed and it remains unclear to which extent the proposal will accomplish more than incremental progress.

imp_text: This is a beautifully written proposal from a well-established investigator to address the role of Foxo transcription factors (TFs) in T cell differentiation and function. This proposal is based on the PI’s recently published work and preliminary data, suggesting the critical role of Foxo TFs in regulating memory T cell fate decision and long-term maintainance. Here, he extends this study to further dissect the temporal effects of Foxo on memory T cell formation, function as well as the maintainance of quiescence.The PI also aims to elucidate how Foxo TFs regulate cellular metabolism and chromatin remodeling, which is innovative, and would provide new mechanistic insights into our fundmental understanding of T cell differentiation and function. Futhermore, the PI broadens his research of Foxo TFs into T follicular helper cells to investgate the connection between ICOS signaling and Foxo-mediated transcriptional regulation. Lastly, the PI proposes that inactivation of Foxo TFs may lead to better viral control in persistent viral infection models. This idea is derived from the strong connection between Foxo3 inactivation and HIV elite controllers, which makes this aim intriguing and significant. This proposal seems overambitious at the first glance, but it all together centers on Foxo-regulated gene expression programs that govern T cell differentiation and energy metabolism. With such a focus and well-qualified PI, I have no doubt that the proposed aims can be sucessfuly carried out. Strengths of this proposal include: strong preliminary data, significant hypotheses, robust genetic mouse models, well-experienced PI and research team, and rigorous approaches. I have high enthusiasm and very few criticisms.

imp_text: This is a clearly written proposal from a new investigator. The PI plans to define the role of actin-bundling protein L-plastin (LPL) in B cell motility, germinal center (GC) development and T cell-dependent antibody generation. The prelimary work has provided strong evidence to show that LPL-deficient B lymphocytes exhibit reduced motility, GC formation as well as antibody production.  An important central concept is that LPL links integrin and chemotactic signaling to the actin cytoskeleton, which is critical to transmit “outside-in” signaling through a Pyk2 signaling cascade. This is novel. Complex in vivo experiments with lentiviral vector directed mutagenesis, chimerisms and two-photon imagining will facilitate the dissection of the model, and there are clear-cut predictions which is a strength. Aim 3 is particularly strong since it uses a genetic model of B cell conditional deletion of LPL to test its role in T cell-dependent antibody production during immunization and West Nile virus infection. Overall, this is an excellent application that will make an important contribution to the field of immunology. Although there are some technical caveats, they are easily addressable. I thus have high enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: • The proposed work addresses a key regulator of germinal center formation, which is critical to generate long-lasting humoral immunity. A better understanding of how B cells integrate adhesive cues and chemotactic signaling to gain proper motility and interaction with T cells will provide insight into potential therapeutics aimed at treating autoimmune diseases and immunodeficiency. This is therefore a highly significant proposal.

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: This is an R01 application from a well-established investigator that examines how catalase in thymic epithelial stromal cells (TEC) affects aging-related atrophy of thymus. The PI presents the hypothesis that catalase as a key enzyme protects TEC from ROS induced damage and in turn prevents thymic atrophy. This proposal was based on an unexpected finding from the PI’s previous publication, which reveals the surprising expression pattern of catalase in thymic stromal cells. This observation leads to the hypothesis that the decreased expression of catalase in TEC with age might be the main cause of thymic atrophy. More intriguingly, the PI provides strong genetic evidence that the correction of catalase deficiency in a transgentic mouse model can sucessfuly rescue thymic atrophy. This proposal has many strengths, including excellent record of PI’s productivity, the significance of hypotheses, the strong preliminary data that firmly support the proposed work, the rigor of most of the approaches, and a highly collaborative environment. The generation of conditional expression of Cat in TEC with Foxn1-Cre in a novel approach and a key reagent to test the overall hypothesis. The caveat is that this mouse model may take a long time to make and could even fail, which poses a risk to the subsequent studies in almost all the Aims. Despite this minor technical problem, the overall strengths substantially overweigh the weaknesses, resulting in a high level of enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: • This study will deepen our understanding of how thymic atropy is being regulated through a previously unidentified pathway. Given the importance of thymus function in aging related immune responses to infection and vaccination, a better understanding of the root cause of acclerated thymic atrophy is highly significant.

imp_text: This application emanates from a senior and productive investigator in the regulation of T cell activation and dynamics during and post antigenic challenge. The premise of this project is to delineate the role of FOXO1 and 3 transcription factors in the differentiation and function of CD8 T cells, CD4 TCM, TFH and their relative regulation during immunizations and viral challenges, focusing on the bioenergetics program of T cells. The approach is made feasible by the generation of congenic murine strains allowing for deletion of FOXO1 and/or 3 at specific times post antigenic challenge in select cell lineages. The proposal will address the role of these TF systematically during various phases of T cell activation, expansion and transition to memory as well as restimulation and finally during chronic viremic and latent infection. These studies are complex, smabitious but expected to further our understanding of the relative control effected by FOXO TFs in various T cell subsets and transition phases in relation to some key pathways that intersect with these TFs.
sig_text_str: • The role of FOXO1 and 3 TF in T cell differentiation, and the regulation of critical receptor regulating expansion and contraction of T cells has been shown, but this approach expands the investigation to understanding the role of FOXO1 and 3 in acute expansion/differentiation such as during acute infection, the long term memory reliance on these factors. • Understanding the interection of various key pathway of T cell differentiation and the regulation exerted by TF is relevant for potential future treatment and enhancement of vaccines (e.g. generation of TFH).
inv_text_str: • Dr. Baker has pioneered many of the T cell regulatory pathways and produced salient advances in the field of immunology.
inn_text_str: • Delineation of the precise contribution of FOXO1 and 3 in the expansion and differentiation of T cell subsets, while not a novel approach will be done with an unprecedented deteail, thanks to the patient generation of several congenic murine strains. • Delineation of transcription pathways linked to select T cell phenotypes during infections, persistent infections, cancer or immunization may pave the way for novel therapeutic approaches and enhanced immunizations. • The determination of the role of FOXO TF relative to mTOR is relevant as well as the ICOS/FOXO1 interplay in the differentiation of TFHs.

The studies should provide advances to the field and are onducted in an outstanding environment.

imp_text: This application proposes a focused and detailed investigation of the role of CXCR4/CXCL12 interactions in the regulation of B cell ontongeny in the bone marrow, their production and selection.  The project proposes a detailed evalautation of the non hemoatopoietic bone marrow cell lineages that play a deterministic role in the CXCR4 meediated differentiation and traffic of B cell prescursors in the bone marrow. Next the role of this chemokine in the negative selstion of B cells will be evaluated, The studies are targeted, supported by preliminary data and the availability of many KO and transgenic murine strains and the expertise of the PI in in vivo imaging. Concerns in general are mostly minor: The PI is still relatively early in his career, and while he has been quite productive, the addition of a senior hematologist might have been welcome. A better diagrammatic presentation of the various expeiments and their interpretation would have facilitated the comprehension of this ambitious approach. Nevertheless, the project is expected to provide relevant data for this specific differentiation in an important compartment.

imp_text: The investigators present a thorough – but often difficult to read - discussion of research into the role of 2’-5’ PDEs (e.g., the ns2 protein) in viral infection. The goal of the proposed research is to determine which cells are initially infected in an MHV model, search for inhibitors of the 2’-5’ PDE enzyme, and study the roles of viral and host 2’-5’ PDEs. However, the proposal provides little argument that the results would have a major impact on the field. Determining the cell type that is first infected by MHV and the roles of host vs viral 2’-5’ PDE are somewhat interesting, but the real question for this reviewer is “How important is this work for developing anti-viral therapies?”. The investigators plan to screen for 2’-5’ PDE inhibitors, but one needs to first determine that an inhibitor would have any anti-viral utility. Are inhibitors of this enzyme already available? If so, do known inhibitors have any effect on viral infectivity? If they do, is a new inhibitor needed at all? How much morbidity and mortality is caused by viruses that contain ns-2 type enzymes? Aim 2B (determine the role of 2’-5’ PDEs in viral replication) is undertaken to answer a part of these questions, but transfection with plasmids to that may over-express the enzymes may not necessarily give accurate or relevant results. The proposed work may lead to some interesting results, but the premise that novel 2’-5’ PDE inhibitors are important for human health is not supported.
sig_text_str: . This work would illuminate the role of cellular and viral 2’-5’ PDEs in MHV infection.
sig_text_wkn: . This work appears to seek only incremental advances in understanding the clinical importance of 2’-5’ PDEs. . The proposal does not explain the need for this research or predict the long-term benefits to be reaped from it. . Preliminary work is needed to assess whether there is any practical utility for discovering a novel inhibitor, which is a major goal of the proposed research. . The proposal does not give the possible implications of many of the desired results: Why do we need to know the cell type that is initially infected? What will we do differently if we determine the relative roles of cellular vs viral 2’-5’ PDEs? Most importantly, how will this work lead to anti-viral therapies? . What is the human and economic impact of viruses that express 2’-5’ PDEs?

imp_text: The proposed research will focus on the vOTU enzyme of the virus CCHFV, a potent human pathogen with the potential to spread to populated parts of the world. Members of this family have very high species specificity, which may be attributed to vOTU. This proposal presents a sound plan to characterize the X-ray structure, enzymatic activity, and cellular target of vOTU. It would show which of enzyme’s two activities leads to viral infectivity, and which portions of the enzyme are likely drug targets. It would confirm suspicions about the identity of the cellular target of the enzyme (i.e. ISG15), and whether differences in this target among species is responsible for the striking differences in CCHFV mortality. The PI proposes to incorporate mutations into the virus to directly confirm their effects upon virulence in vivo. Finally, he proposes to create the first usable animal model to study the human virus.
sig_text_str: . CCHFV is an emerging pathogen with a potentially-high, very species-specific mortality rate. The viral OTU enzyme may play a dominant role in its lethality and thus is an important target for study. . The proposed work may confirm the suggestion that ISG15 is the major determinant of specificity and lethality. . There is no known treatment or vaccine for CCHFV infection. Identifying the target of vOTFs may inform development of therapeutics and vaccines.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Walsh is well experienced in studies based on protein biochemistry, nucleic acid biology, and X-ray crystallography. He has a respectable track record of success in research on CCHFV and OTU. The Co-Investigator has worked for several years on CCHFV, and his expertise is validated by his access to a BSL4 facility.
inv_text_wkn: . Most of the work will be carried out by grad students and post-docs. However, these students have demonstrated their competence in producing the preliminary results, and a plan is available to replace the post-docs when they move on.
inn_text_str: . This is the first attempt to characterize the enzymatic activities and structure of vOTU. . Engineering the virus to express altered vOTF circumvents potential artifacts from overexpression of such enzymes. . Engineering virus with altered vOTU activity will provide valuable information on the targets of this enzyme.

Creation of mouse lines that are susceptible to human virus will enable development of vaccines and therapies.

imp_text: The proposed research aims to elucidate a very basic and critical process in the function of RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRp’s). This class of enzymes are essential to viral replication, and the results may be applicable to other polymerase or even non-related enzymes. If successful, this work could lead to major advances and far-reaching insights into the function of polymerases, with vast potential importance for studying normal and pathological states. The solution state NMR methods of analysis are novel, but they have been verified. The model enzyme being studied, Polio virus RdRp, is well characterized and represents a very important biological target. The work may provide insight into the mechanism of action of drugs that are currently used, but not understood. Understanding this mechanism is essential for developing additional therapies.
sig_text_str: . RdRp’s are provide a powerful target for anti-viral therapies. This proposal seeks to observe a viral RdRp in action, elucidate the basic mechanism of how it acts, and understand how it is inhibited by anti-viral drugs. . The understanding provided by this research would significantly advance the body of knowledge surrounding RdRp’s. . Better understanding of these basic mechanisms can directly lead to searches for better mechanisms of inhibiting common, serious viral infections (e.g, Hepatitis C virus). This work will also directly study the mechanism of action of a class of anti-viral drugs.

Dr. Yu has good experience in the Kelly lab, and has produced much of the preliminary results presented.

The work proposes to show how mutations in distant parts of a protein molecule affect the active site through a network of interactions, a notion that is quite unexpected. . The results are expected to show for the first time the mechanism of action of one class of potent anti-viral drugs.

imp_text: In this proposal the investigators will study the importance of mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) ns2 protein and other viral (e.g. rotavirus VP3) and cellular (e.g. AKAP7) proteins that have 2’-5’ phosphodiesterase (PDE) activity. Especially, they will investigate the inhibitory activity of PDE on antiviral 2’-5’-oligoadenylate (2-5A) synthetase (OAS)-RNase L antiviral pathway using primary cells (liver macrophages [Kupffer cells; KC], liver endothelial cells and hepatocytes) and RNase L knockout mice, as well as wild type and ns2 mutant MHVs (Aim 1).  Subsequently, the investigators propose to identify small molecule-inhibitors of viral (e.g. MHV, HCoV OC43, HCoV HEC4408, BCV and human and animal rotaviruses) and host 2’-5’ PDEs using an in vitro cell culture model (Aim 2).  Finally, they will focus on the mechanism of MHV nsp2 and cellular AKAP7 on the protection of MHV and test the anti-viral activity of small molecules using MHV chimeric viruses and mouse model.  Overall, this proposal is very difficult to follow, and there is repetition of information throughout the proposal. The central hypothesis stated under the section on significance (innovation) is not novel and innovative as suggested by the investigators. However, there are several other sub-hypothesizes that appear to be novel and innovative. The justification for using MHV as a model to study the pathogenesis of human viral hepatitis (e.g. hepatitis, A, B and C) and selecting antivirals targeting PDE is not clearly stated; particularly in light of the incidence of human hepatitis cases have dropped significantly due to vaccination and use of antivirals.  The antivirals studied in this proposal may be important against MERSCoV and other animal and human coronaviruses, but they do not emphasize that aspect in this proposal.  The investigators should identify the impact of this study on other zoonotic coronaviruses.  There is a disconnection between Aim 1 and the other two Aims.  It would be better to focus on Aims 2 and 3 of this proposal. Above shortcomings reduce the enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: . Proposal is focused on mechanisms of viral pathogenesis (host-virus interaction) and development and screening of antivirals (translational). . Identification of small molecules to be used as antivirals against coronaviruses is very important. . Study focuses on identifying novel molecular mechanism(s) of subversion of RNase L pathway by MHV ns2 and other viral and cellular PDEs. . In summary, the proposed study will further expand the knowledge on the role of  RNase L and innate immunity (IFN) against viral infections. The mechanism of MHV to circumvent the innate response may provide insight into the mechanism used by other viruses.  This study may also lead to discovery of novel antiviral targets and antiviral drugs.
sig_text_wkn: . The investigators do not address the importance of findings from this study to the understanding of other important human and animal coronaviruses or other viruses causing hepatitis in humans. . In this proposal, RNase L pathway has been extensively studied. This may not be the only host factor associated with the virus-induced pathology, and there may be other host factors which may play a critical role in immune evasion and pathogenesis of MHV.
inv_text_str: . This is a collaborative research project between two well-experienced senior investigators, Drs. Walsh and Spindler. They have produced some of the preliminary data described in this proposal. Dr. Walsh has over 30 years experience working with the MHV.  Research has been focused on identified virus and host determinants associated with cellular tropism and virulence.   . Dr. Spindler is an expert on innate immunity and devoted over 32 years to study the interferon-regulated OAS-RNAase L pathway in the suppression of viral infections and cancer. . In addition, they have six collaborators/contributors (multi-institutional) with necessary expertise to complete the project.
inn_text_str: . The development and screening of antivirals based on small molecules targeting the viral and host PDEs is novel and important. . The proposed study is innovative, and it may identify common mechanisms used by different viruses (coronaviruses, toroviruses, rotaviruses) to evade innate immune response.  This would allow for development of antivirals that are effective against multiple viruses. . In vivo experimental studies will utilize genetically engineered mice.
inn_text_wkn: . The PDE activity of MHV ns2 and rotavirus VP3 has been previously reported and as indicated above, this reviewer is less enthusiastic about Aim 1. The in vitro studies may identify the differences between the cell types but as indicated in the pitfalls section, in vivo proposed comparative studies using different primary cells (Aim 1) may not advance the knowledge on MHV pathogenesis or other viruses causing hepatitis, as well as other coronaviruses.
app_text_str: . The investigators combine multiple cell culture systems, viral reverse genetics and contemporary gene knockout techniques to study host virus interactions. . The proposed studies will clearly provide insight into RNase L pathway, PDEs and inhibitors that may be used as potential antivirals.
app_text_wkn: Aim 1. . The experiments proposed on primary cultures of Kupffer cells, endothelial cells and hepatocytes do not seem to completely address this aim (Kupffer cells restricting viral entry into liver parenchyma). Preliminary studies shown (Fig 2) were performed in BMM rather than Kupffer cells obtained from the liver (which would be the target for this study). imp_text: The primary objective of this study is to elucidate all of the conformational states and the transitions between them for poliovirus RNA dependent RNA polymerase (PV RdRp) using a novel technique known as the solution state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR).  This technique allows for study of the structural states and delineates the transitions between these states as RdRp progress through catalytic cycle.  The investigator proposes a detailed experimental plan to study PV RdRP that could be extended to study the RdRps of other RNA viruses. Hypotheses are stated and the three aims are clearly laid out and include; (Aim 1). Elucidate conformational states and their structural transitions required for the RdRp; (Aim 2). Elucidate the mechanistic basis for RdRp derivatives exhibiting altered fidelity reaction using mutants; and (Aim 3). Elucidate the mechanistic basis for chain termination by anti-HCV nucleoside analogues.  The investigator also provides a significant amount of preliminary data and detailed description about the approach. The low fidelity of RdRp enzyme of RNA viruses and lack of proofreading capability leads to emergence of viral quasispecies, which is the key mechanism of RNA viral evolution leading to emergence of viral variants with different neutralization, drug resistance and virulence phenotypes.  The investigator envisions that findings from this study would benefit both human and animal health by identifying the basis for the differences in polymerase fidelity as mutations occur in the viral RdRp.  Specifically, the findings would allow for the development of safe modified live virus vaccines and antiviral drugs against RNA viruses.  The proposal involves basic and applied research and the overall impact of this study is high.

imp_text: This is an interesting project to study the host cell shut-off mechanisms by the vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) in mammalian cells.  The investigator justify this study by pointing out the existence of some discrepancies in the literature and envision that this proposed study will identify new mechanism(s) of host shut-off by VSV. The investigator proposes to test a novel hypothesis using contemporary laboratory techniques.  Overall, the proposal is well written, and the investigator provides a significant amount of preliminary data.  The experimental approach is appropriate.  The major weakness is that the investigator does not provide how the findings from this study could benefit human health.
sig_text_str: . This is an interesting basic research project to test a new research hypothesis using contemporary innovative technology. . The investigator is thinking outside of the box and has come up with a new testable hypothesis to better understand the mechanism(s) of host-cell shutoff following VSV infection in mammalian cells.
sig_text_wkn: . The investigator indicates that findings from this study would resolve the existing discrepancies.  However, she does not explain the overall impact of findings from this study.  How it would benefit human health, particularly in the area treatment of cancer and infectious diseases is not discussed.
inv_text_str: . The investigator has extensive experience studying the inhibition of host gene expression by the matrix (M) protein of VSV. . The proposed work is based on previous work in his laboratory.  Preliminary data for this study was generated from a one-year pilot R56 grant proposal. . Dr. Kelly has established a research collaboration with Dr. Karne at Duke University, who has over 35 years experience in RNA protein interaction. . It is clear that synergy between these two laboratories would facilitate the proposed work.
inn_text_str: . This is an innovative basic science research project. . The concepts are innovative, and the investigators propose a new hypothesis for host-cell shut off. . They hypothesize that M protein forms a complex with Rae1 which inhibits host gene expression (platform hypothesis) at the transcription, transport and translational levels as opposed to M protein directly interacting with other cellular targets to shut off the host protein synthesis. . The investigators provide significant preliminary data to support the basis of their new hypothesis. . They propose to use two new innovative techniques to study the control of mRNA expression by RNA-binding proteins (figure 6). . The proposed study uses innovative techniques (eg. RIP-ChIP and PAR-CLIP, proteomics and siRNA) and investigates the role of hnRNPs in VSV host shut-off. .

It would be better to target more than one housekeeping gene to prove their point. . The investigator will use a qPCR approach to quantify cellular mRNAs as it is more specific that in situ hybridization. It is not clear which specific mRNAs will be targeted  e.g. those associated to stress, antiviral response or others. study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: The ability of viruses to evade or antagonize the host type I IFN response plays an important role in viral tropism and disease pathogenesis. However, the precise cellular and molecular mechanisms by which viruses impede tissue specific host defenses leading to virus-induced pathology remain elusive. The coronavirus, mouse hepatitis virus (MHV), causes acute hepatitis in its natural host and provides a useful model for understanding virus interaction with liver cells. The MHV protein ns2 blocks the IFN-inducible and potent antiviral 2’,5’-oligoadenylate (2-5A) synthetase (OAS)-RNase L pathway in macrophages and facilitates the development of hepatitis. The ns2 protein and related viral (rotavirus VP3) and mammalian (AKAP7) proteins are 2H phosphoesterases with 2’,5’-phosphodiesterase (PDE) activities that degrade 2-5A, the activator of RNase L. Our overall hypothesis herein is that the OAS-RNase L pathway in macrophages is critical in protecting the host from developing viral hepatitis. The investigators will evaluate this hypothesis by completing 3 specific Aims: Aim 1. To test the hypothesis that RNase L signaling in liver sinusoidal macrophages (Kupffer cells) restricts virus from entering the liver parenchyma and inducing hepatitis. Aim 2. To determine the roles of ns2 related viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs in antiviral innate immunity Aim 3. To determine and compare the “proviral” and RNase L “antagonist” activities of cellular and viral 2’,5’-PDEs, Overall, the proposal is addressing a significant issue, as it seeks to better define the role of viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs in antiviral innate immunity and its effect on viral pathogenesis. This could significantly expand the current base of knowledge pertaining to modulation of IFN responses by viruses. While the significance of the proposal was strong, the innovation is quite limited. Conceptually, the proposal has some innovative features, but the technical innovation is limited. The research team is strong and complementary and the research environment is adequate to complete the proposed studies. The major concerns with this proposal is associated with the Experimental Approach. There is little to no preliminary data shown to support the Aims. The investigators cite Appendix material in multiple places that is not provided and should not be considered in the evaluation of the application. Many studies lack proper controls and there are significant shortcomings in considering pitfalls and alternative approaches. While the ideas and concepts presented are interesting, some of the issues and concerns noted could be associated with misunderstanding due to poor grantsmanship. This is not a global issue, but many parts of the grant could benefit from careful proof-reading and a more user-friendly presentation of the material prior to re-submission.

study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a ssRNA (-) nairovirus that produces fever, prostration, and severe hemorrhages in humans. Recent reports have identified a viral homologue of the ovarian tumor protease (vOTU) located within the nairovirus genome and implicated its possible involvement in down-regulation of the Interferon type 1 immune response through cleavage of post-translational modifying proteins ubiquitin (Ub) and Ub-like interferon-simulated gene 15 (ISG15). As a result, it has been suggested to be a virulence factor. This proposal will determine whether dual deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities are conserved functions of this subclass of proteases in vitro and in vivo. Additionally, these experiments will gain insight into their mechanism of recognition for Ub and ISG15 allowing greater predictability of currently unknown vOTUs. The proposal will also seek to evaluate a potential correlation between the in vitro activity/substrate specificity of these nairovirus vOTUs and overall virulence of the nairoviruses in question. While the technical innovation associated with this proposal is relatively limited, the conceptual innovation is strong and contributes positively to the overall novelty of the proposal. Overall, this proposal is well assembled and addresses a significant public health concern. The hypotheses are well laid out, easy to follow, and if successful, will result in highly mechanistic insight associated with nairovirus vOTUs. The experimental approach has very few identified weaknesses. The resulting information will also provide critical insight into the role that other vOTUs play in viruses that may ultimately have practicality in the development of prophylactics targeting vOTUs. The PI has assembled a highly complementary team of investigators that will significantly contribute to the success of the proposal and the Environment at the University of Denver is acceptable to complete the described studies.
sig_text_str: . CCHFV is a tick-borne virus that causes severe hemorrhage in humans. In general, this virus is a minimal risk in the US. But is a greater threat to individuals in countries where the virus is distributed. No FDA approved vaccines or therapeutics are available and CCHFV is considered a dangerous emerging human pathogen. . CCHFV is not the only nairovirus that causes human disease and the findings of this proposal could yield insight associated with the related nairoviruses. . If the proposal is successful, then the findings should reveal mechanistic insight associated with vOTUs beyond nairovirus. . The proposal will shed insight into broader mechanisms associated with host-virus interactions and virus evasion mechanisms.

app_text_str: . Specific Aim 1 will ascertain the effects of nairovirus sequence diversity, including that which exists between strains, on their deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities. The investigators propose studies that will reveal the full effects of sequence diversity on the ability of vOTUs from CCHFV strains and other nairoviruses to recognize mono-Ub and ISG15. Additional studies will resolve the origin of nairovirus vOTUs selectivity for cleaving certain poly-Ub linkages to predict activity of unknown vOTUs. Finally, the investigators will determine the influence of ISG15 species diversity on the delSGylating activity of nairovirus OTUs. . The preliminary data supports the proposed hypotheses and are well presented. . The experiments are well laid out and should yield significant mechanistic insight. . Specific Aim 2 will define the relative contribution of nairovirus vOTUs deISGylase activity, deubiquitinase activity, and ISG15 specificity to subvert the innate immune response. Here, the investigators will engineer CCHFVs that possess vOTUs with inactive vOTUs, or vOTUs with shifted specificity for Ub, poly-Ub, or human or mouse ISG15. They will use these recombinant CCHFVs to determine which deubiquitinating and/or deISGylating activities predominately influences suppression of IFN and other inflammatory cytokines activity. Finally, the investigators will determine whether CCHFV with a vOTU optimized for mouse ISG15 can efficiently subvert mouse ISGylation to cause disease in mice.

study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: Many viruses suppress host antiviral responses through the global inhibition of host gene expression, often referred to as “host shut-off”. Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), the prototype rhabdovirus, is a well-established example of a virus that suppresses antiviral responses through the global inhibition of host gene expression. The host shut-off in VSV-infected cells is particularly extensive, resulting in the inhibition of host transcription, nuclear-cytoplasmic transport of host mRNA, and translation of host proteins. The prevailing view in the literature is that M protein blocks nuclear-cytoplasmic transport by binding the host nuclear factor Rae1 and that the inhibition of host transcription and translation are downstream effects of the inhibition of nuclear-cytoplasmic transport. However, more recent data from our laboratory and others are inconsistent with this view. Based on these recent results, we propose an alternative model. Rather than a primary effect on transport, we propose that the M protein-Rae1 complex inhibits host transcription, and may actually promote transport of a subset of host mRNAs that are associated with host heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) that re-localize to the cytoplasm following VSV infection. In addition, host hnRNPs that relocalize to the cytoplasm appear to be involved in translational control in VSV-infected cells. Thus the alterations in transport and translation of cellular mRNAs may be downstream effects of the coupling of host transcription with subsequent steps in host gene expression, which are mediated by host RNA-binding proteins. This coupling of transcription, mRNA transport, and translation is a fundamental cell biological process that is likely to be important for host shut-off by many viruses, as well as for other cellular processes that affect host gene expression. Determining the mechanisms of host shut-off by VSV offers a window of opportunity for insight into these questions that are important for both cell biology and viral pathogenesis. These questions will be addressed in this project. Aim 1 is to determine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of mRNA transport by VSV. A combination of new UV-crosslinking and RNP immunoprecipitation approaches will address this question. Aim 2 is to determine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of translation in VSV-infected cells. The role of both host and viral proteins associated with mRNPs in controlling translation will be determined by analysis of transcripts associated with key proteins associated with cytoplasmic mRNPs and by RNA silencing of host RNA-binding proteins. Overall, this proposal is based on a significant amount of speculation and the significance and innovation of the work is not well presented. The investigators are proposing a mechanism that is counter to the current paradigm without providing sufficient preliminary data to support their hypotheses. The Aims are based on weak rationale and are not well formulated. The studies lack sufficient detail to convey confidence that the investigators can complete the described studies, which appear to be very broad and lack the resolution to effectively evaluate the hypotheses.

imp_text: This project is focused on understanding mechanisms of innate immune response, in particular, OAS-RNase L pathway and its interactions with accessory protein NS2  of MHV. In particular, the aims will establish (1) whether RNAase L signaling (and its varying levels of activity) mediates MHV infection, and thus through NS2 driven depletion leads to acute infection; (2) determine the roles of NS2 and host protein with 2’,5’-phosphodiesterase (2’,5’-PDE) activity in antiviral innate immunity and to identify potential inhibitors; (3) to compare various activities of viral 2’,5’-PDE and to establish their role in viral pathogenesis. This project is based on findings from recent collaboration about the NS2 and PDEs and addresses a unique aspect of host-pathogen interaction in hepatitis. Overall, while the proposal is on an important topic and would enable the coPIs to glean insights into some fundamentally important mechanisms (with potentially broader implications outside of MHV model), the writing is rife with jargon and too many inconsequential details, detracting from the main idea of the project and hampering my enthusiasm for the proposal. On the other hand, the section on potential PDEs (Aim 2) should’ve included at least a schematic sequence alignment of homologs that highlights 2H motifs.

imp_text: This is a well-written proposal from a new investigator. The project is focused on elucidating the conformational states and structural transitions involved in function of poliovirus RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), including delineating changes associated with altered fidelity and the mechanics of termination through the nucleoside analogues. The PI is leading one of only two labs in the world that studies RdRp through NMR, and is uniquely qualified to perform this work. Overall, the proposal is well laid-out, and my only reservation comes from having a 3rd aim, which – while being in line with the overall investigation trajectory - appears a bit ambitious to occur in parallel with the other two large aims.
sig_text_str: . The proposal will investigate the structural changes on PV RpRp throughout its catalytic cycle in the attempts to delineate specific amino acid residues responsible for changes that disrupt the enzyme function. . Because of the relatively conserved  nature of RdRps in viruses, these insights will likely apply to other viruses with such polymerases and would be helpful for development of novel anti-polymerase treatments. . Likewise, due to conservation, some of the structural insights may even be applicable to DNA polymerases, thus, enhancing the potential impact of this work.
inv_text_str: . The PI Dr. Robinson is a new/early stage investigator with a solid track record and established expertise in structural chemistry and NMR. . Dr. Robinson leads one of two labs worldwide who use NMR to understand RdRps. . A group of experts with close interests is available at Penn State, and is collaborating with the PI
inn_text_str: . Because of major challenges in crystallizing RdRps, as well as dynamic function of these enzymes, NMR approach allows the PI to study conformational changes at different stages of the catalytic cycle .  Instead of thinking of changes in individual residues, the project attempts to infer conformational fluctuations that stem from such changes, thus, shifting the focus from deleterious mutations to changes underlying protein dynamics (hence, function) shifts. Thus, leading to better understanding of functional consequences of mutation(s).

imp_text: This application proposes to determine whether dual deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities of the ovarian tumor protease (vOTU) of nairoviruses directly subvert the Interferon type 1 immune response and act as a virulence factor. Successful completion of the project would have a significant impact by providing the foundation to develop selective and broad spectrum based anti-viral treatments. The application is novel and innovative. Overall, the PI is well qualified to complete the structure based experimental approaches, while the Co-PI has expertise in nairoviruses (CCHFV), virus-host interactions and a reverse genetic system to elucidate in cellulo and in vivo effects.
sig_text_str: • There is no vaccine or prophylactic available for treatment of CCHF virus or any other nairovirus related diseases, so the need is great. • Multiple nairoviruses have the ovarian tumor protease (vOTU) which may subvert (down-regulate) the Interferon type 1 immune response and act as a virulence factor, therefore characterizing the direct role of vOTU deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities may have broad applicability across virus families. • Delineation of the role of vOTUs play in viruses may be used to advance the development of selective and broad-based prophylactics targeting vOTUs. • The use of a reverse genetics system capable of producing replication-competent CCHF virus, or other nairoviruses provides the ability to identify essential amino acids that are critical for defense against viruses.
sig_text_wkn: . No weaknesses were noted
inv_text_str: • The PI, Dr. Kelly, is an investigator with expertise in enzymology and X-ray crystallography and drug discovery through structure-based discovery. • Dr. Kelly’s lab has elucidated the first reported structure of vOTU/human ubiquitin complex and has expertise in enzymatic and structural characterization of nairovirus vOTUs. • There are strong letters of support from key personnel; Dr. Ebert, John Evans Professor and previous Vice Provost for Research at DU and Dr. Christon, Professor of Pharmacology, Director of the UCD-AMC Macromolecular X-ray Crystallography Center, Co-Director of the UCCC Structural Biology Core Facility and Director, Program in Structural Biology and Biochemistry in support of administrative matters and X-ray crystallographic studies. • The Co-PI: Dr. Berrigan, is a Senior Research Specialist, Special Pathogens Branch, CDC, Atlanta, GA. with access to BSL4 facilities. • Dr. Berrigan has established a collaboration with Dr. Kelly to identify molecular probes for CCHF vOTU. • The Co-PI led a team to develop the first reverse genetic system for CCHF virus and Arenaviruses from cloned cDNA to generate recombinant CCHFV. • Dr. Berrigan has a background and expertise in nairoviruses (CCHFV), virus-host interactions and a reverse genetic system to elucidate in cellulo and in vivo affects of various DNA constructs of nairovirus vOTU’s.
inn_text_str: • Protein crystallography combined with NMR to determine the enzymatic activities of vOTUs from multiple nairoviruses is an innovative approach. • The use of a reverse genetics system capable of producing replication-competent CCHF virus, or other nairoviruses provides the ability to identify essential amino acids for deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities that are critical for defense against viruses. • These experiments may generate key information to determine whether these virus-specific mitigating strategies can be effectively used to treat CCHFV and other respiratory pathogens such as severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS) coronavirus.
inn_text_wkn: • No weaknesses were noted
app_text_str: • Substantial preliminary data to support their hypothesis that vOTU deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities affect virulence (Fig. 6E) • Excellent descriptions and discussions of alternative approaches including: 1) replacement of CCHF vOTU with the vOTU from DUGV, ERRV regarding poly-Ub specificity, 2) generation of a suicide substrate to assess the ability of mCCHF vOTU to recognize mISG15 and determine the kd of mCCHF using ITC and 3) siRNA knockdown of ISG15 and E1-like ubiquitin-activating enzyme ISGylation machinery to see if species specificity can be reversed.
app_text_wkn: • A minor weakness is the number of mice to be tested per group for statistical significance for the CCHFV mouse model (specific aim 2iib) to determine if a CCHFV with a vOTU, optimized for mouse ISG15, can cause disease.

imp_text: This PI proposes using solution state NMR to “watch” the conformational rearrangements in polio virus RdRp to in order to establish the structure-dynamics function relationships, to discover how RdRp fidelity in each state is affected by polymerase mutations and to determine mechanism of HCV antiviral nucleosides. Elucidating RdRp fidelity as an antiviral target may have broad effects across many families. Successful completion of the project would have a significant impact by 1) demonstrating that changes to internal protein fluctuations impact RdRp fidelity and thus, could be used toward the development of attenuated vaccine strains, 2) validating that the RdRp is a novel target for development of broad-spectrum, antiviral therapeutics, and 3) providing mechanism of action of a novel class of small molecule nucleoside inhibitors that are efficacious against HCV. Overall, the PI has proposed a well-thought-out approach. Last, the established collaborations with investigators for molecular dynamic (MD) simulations, kinetic analysis and cell-based assays is a significant strength.
sig_text_str: • Positive-strand RNA viruses are significant human pathogens that cause a number of acute and chronic diseases. • There are a variety of steps in the replication cycle of RNA viruses that can be targeted for antiviral development, however, the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase from positive strand RNA viruses is of significant interest as inhibitors may work prophylactically and/or post-infection and there is evidence that live attenuated vaccine (based on RdRp altered fidelity) protect mice in a lethal challenge model. • The molecular mechanisms of RdRp may be delineated by characterizing the structure and dynamics of polio virus and thus, may be translatable to other RNA viruses. • Identifying the functional and fidelity mechanisms of RdRp may lead to anti-viral strategies.

imp_text: This PI proposes to test how the matrix (M) protein from vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) inhibits host gene expression by 1) UV-crosslinking and RNP immunoprecipitation approaches to determine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of mRNA transport by VSV, and 2) analyzing transcripts associated with key proteins associated with cytoplasmic mRNPs and RNA silencing of host RNA-binding proteins. If successful, the short term impact would change the paradigm and suggest that the M protein-Rae1 complex primarily inhibits host transcription leading to transport of host mRNAs that relocalize to the cytoplasm. The long term outcome would be elucidation of the mechanism of “host shut-off” for VSV that could be applied to other viruses to develop novel viruses for use as vaccines and treatment of cancer. Overall, the application is well written, uses state-of the-art approaches to analyze host and VSV gene expression and provides preliminary data to support their hypotheses.
sig_text_str: • Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) is an established example of a virus that suppresses antiviral responses through the global inhibition of host gene expression. Determining the mechanisms of host shut-off by VSV may provide fundamental information to address how viruses like VSV cause disease. • Many viruses suppress host antiviral responses through global inhibition of host gene expression. Determining the mechanism of action of M protein and the function of Rae1 (an RNA –binding protein) in regulating host transcription in VSV “host shut-off” may be translatable to other viruses.

imp_text: In this application the PIs seek to develop a better understanding of how coronaviruses evade or antagonize the host type I IFN response.  They will focus on a murine model system where MHV strain A59 infects mice.  The synthesis of the accessory protein ns2 leads to the inactivation of 2’,5’ oligoadenylate and the failure to activate RNase L, which is thought to degrade newly replicated viral RNAs.  The preliminary is quite convincing and clearly indicates that further analysis of this potential mechanism of immune suppression warrants further study.  Furthermore, the PIs have combined expertise on both the murine model system and RNase L.  The experiments designed to test the signaling hypothesis are straightforward and should lead to useful new information, although the assay that is presented for examining RNase L activity relies on the degradation of host rRNA rather than looking at viral RNA.  It would seem that by the time that the cellular rRNA is being degraded that the cell is going to be apoptatic. Enthusiasm for the grant is also diminished by the experiments designed identify and characterize ns2 like proteins from other coronaviruses.  It seems certain that the PIs will find some, but having additional ns2 like proteins is not going to necessarily address how the function in vivo.

To achieve this goal the PI will employ a combination of high resolution NMR analysis and kinetic analyses of both wild type and mutant PV RdRp enzymes.  Additional information will be gotten from the analysis of anti-HCV nucleoside analogs that lead to chain termination.  This combination of approaches has the potential of yielding a much more accurate understanding of the various stages of the polymerization reaction, including how mutations outside of the enzyme active site lead to inactivation.  Although there is some concern that the NMR resolution on this rather large protein will not be as good as the PI thinks, overall this project offers the potential of producing very important new insights into the function of PV RdRp enzymes.  As such there is high enthusiasm for this project.

imp_text: Overall Impact Score (1-9): This application proposes a series of experiments to examine how a model virus (VSV) leads to the inhibition of host gene synthesis after it infects mammalian cells.  The PI points out the there are two conflicts models for how host inhibition occurs.  The prevailing model states that the virus inhibits blocks nuclear-cytoplasmic transport.  The PI has data to suggest that the actual mechanism relates to the inhibition of host gene transcription.  The experiments described in the application address two issues that relate to VSV function: 1. To determine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of mRNA transport by VSV and to determine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of translation.  Considering that the PI believes that inhibition of transcription is a primary result of VSV infection, it is somewhat surprising that there are not experiments proposed to more definitively address this question.  The experiments described will provide a great deal of new data, but they are not going to answer the most important question, namely how does the VSV encoded M protein lead to a cascade of events that effectively shut down host gene expression.
sig_text_str: . This application seeks to address important questions regarding how viral infections of mammalian cells shut off host gene expression using the VSV virus as a model system. . imp_text: This is an exceptional proposal leveraging compelling preliminary data that the MHV A59 ns2 virulence factor has phosphoesterase (PDE) activity targeting 2-5A for degradation leading to reduced RNAse-L activity in virus infected cells and that this PDE activity is required for MHV A59-associated hepatitis in a murine model. The three well thought out specific Aims will address the role of the ns2 protein and similar proteins from other viruses in counteracting 2-5A levels and activation of RNAse L and the role this plays in viral pathogenesis and infection. Aim 1 will compare the roles of RNAse L activation in Kuppfer cells, sinusoidal endothelial cells and hepatocytes in regulating MHV infection and will test the hypothesis that the OAS-RNAse-L pathway in Kupffer cells is important in restricting viral access to the liver parenchyma. Aim 2 will identify and characterize 2-5’ PDEs from the host and different viruses and their roles in viral replication and cellular innate responses. In addition the PIs will screen small molecules for their capacity to inhibit viral and/or host 2-5’ PDEs. The identification of 2-5’ PDE inhibitors is exciting as it promises a possible new class of anti-viral drugs. In Aim 3, the PIs will examine the role of nsp2, cellular 2-5’PDEs and other viral PDEs in promoting viral replication and antagonizing RNAse L activity using chimeric MHVs to express them and test their capacity to rescue MHV ns2 mutants. The authors also hope to test 2-5’ PDE inhibitors they identify for in vivo toxicity in mice and for their capacity to inhibit MHV infection. This is an exciting prospect.
sig_text_str: . The RNAse-L pathway is an important host antiviral defense mechanism. However our understanding of how viruses overcome this defense is as yet rudimentary. This proposal is expected to substantially inform on mechanisms by which viruses that encode PDEs targeting 2-5A overcome host innate defenses and cause disease. . Identification of small molecule inhibitors of viral and/or host PDEs may lead to development of novel antiviral compounds. . The concept of different cellular and tissue-specific levels of 2-5A and how this regulates susceptibility or resistance to viral infection is important. Equally, the negative regulation of these levels by host PDEs suggests that susceptibility to viral infection of some tissues might be modulated or druggable by PDE inhibitors. . Knowledge of the nsp2 PDE activity in MHV A59 should spur investigation of similar activities in MERS and SARS coronaviruses.
sig_text_wkn: . Minor weakness. It’s unclear what role viral or cellular PDE activity will have in control of human hepatic viral infections. The viral PDEs being studied are all derived from viruses that either do not infect humans or do not cause hepatitis in humans.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Kelly is an experienced and productive coronavirus researcher and brings expertise in virology and the manipulation of the MHV genome. . Dr. Spindler brings complementary expertise in the type I IFN system and assays to assess the levels of 2-5A and RNAse L . Drs Kelly and Spindler are established investigators with strong track records of success. . The multi-PI plan is well thought out and provides evidence that the investigators are already collaborating effectively.
inn_text_str: . Novel hypotheses will be tested that will expand our knowledge of the interaction between the innate host defense system and viral countermeasures . Development of kuppfer-cell specific RNAse-L knockout mice . The proposal will screen for novel inhibitors of host and viral PDEs that may have broad applicability as antiviral agents.

imp_text: This is an interesting proposal with an intriguing hypothesis that differences in substrate specificities for certain ubiquitin linkages and ISG15 linkages of nairovirus encoded Ovarian tumor domain proteases (vOTUs) within the L-protein determine nairovirus’ virulence. The corollary of this hypothesis that the authors propose is that cleavage of ISG15 and/or particular Ub linkages during viral infection allows these viruses to perturb type I interferon response and evade innate responses. Overall, the proposal was hard to follow because of sloppiness in the writing – I had to re-read some paragraphs several times to get the gist. Nevertheless, the proposal has merit, as understanding the molecular basis for the vOTU virulence is important. My enthusiasm overall was also lessened by doubt about some of the preliminary findings and by a lack of rationale for some of the experiments. I didn’t find a clear line of reasoning behind some of the proposed experiments or an explanation of how the results of these experiments would advance the field. An additional concern was that no mention was made of the possibility that the RdRP domain of the L protein might influence vOTU function and specificity; the PI mentioned the effect of the RdRP portion on localization within cells during viral infection.
sig_text_str: . It seems likely that in the context of viral infection, the vOTU domain of the L-protein of nairoviruses acts to suppress the type 1 IFN response . Addressing the mechanism by which vOTUs mediate IFN suppression is important . Lack of therapeutics and vaccine strategies makes studying mechanisms by which these viruses cause disease an important goal.

And is there a correlation between activity and/or specificity of vOTUs and virulence? . It’s a good idea to try to obtain a modified recombinant CCHFV that has a vOTU specific for murine ISG15.

Similarly, the investigators are largely relying on their ability to recover viable mutant recombinant CCHFV for the ‘in cellulo’ and mouse experiments that they propose in Aim2. . Concern that mutations that ablate the function of vOTU in vitro will prevent recovery of viable recombinant virus. Initially, the PI found that replication in the context of a minigenome was not affected by a catalytically dead (C40A mutant) vOTU domain; however, they now find that this same mutant when introduced into the genome cannot be recovered as a recombinant virus in a system where IFN is not an issue. This raises doubts as to the validity of the hypothesis that vOTU is not required for replication and raises the possibility that vOTU domains play an additional role during the viral replication cycle that is unrelated to de-ubiquitylation/de-ISGylation activity. . Some of the preliminary data is weak. Fig. 3A shows data in duplicate, yet shows relative activities with error bars. Sample size is too small to make any firm conclusions. Also unclear if this is two independent experiments or simply duplicates of one experiment. . imp_text: This is an interesting proposal to investigate a new model of how VSV inhibits host transcription, Nucleocytoplasmic transport, and translation. VSV induces host shut-off and Dr. Walsh proposes a new paradigm for how this occurs during infection. The PI proposes that the viral M protein by interacting with the host RNA-binding protein Rae1 forms a complex that interacts with other host factors leading to primary inhibition of host transcription with a selective inhibition of host mRNA export from the nucleus such that host hnRNPs are exported to the cytosol where they inhibit translation of host mRNAs, but not viral or newly synthesized host mRNAs. Four alternative models are proposed and the PI proposes experiments to distinguish these models. The ideas are novel. However, the proposal is weakened by being poorly organized, having preliminary data that are not wholly convincing, and a complex approach that would appear to have many confounding variables that may not be controllable. Overall, I felt that the PI ran out of steam in Aim 2, which was hard to follow and had insufficient rationale and attention paid to possible problems. I was also concerned that much of the proposal relies on discovery-based approaches (proteomics, RIP-Chip, PAR-CLIP), where specific hypotheses would not be tested/ formulated until after this data had been analyzed. In addition, there was no discussion of the problems and technical challenges associated with collection and analysis of data using these discovery approaches.
sig_text_str: . VSV is an important model system for understanding the mechanisms of virus-induced host shut-off. . Host shut-off following VSV infection is well characterized and the viral matrix protein is known to be primarily, though likely not wholly responsible. . Rae1 has been identified as being an important host factor in VSV-mediated host shut-off
sig_text_wkn: . Not clear from the data presented that the VSV mechanism of host shut-off is more generalizable to other viruses.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Walsh is highly productive and has a well-established track record in this field. He has made seminal advances in this area in the past. . A collaboration with Dr. Kerne, and expert in ribonomics is appropriate and strengthens the proposal.
inn_text_str: . Innovative new model(s) of the mechanisms by which VSV induces host shut-off that challenge the existing paradigms.
inn_text_wkn: . The ‘Ribonomics’ approaches are not particularly novel. The PAR-clip and UV-crosslinking approaches have been around for several years now so are not particularly innovative. . Use of microarrays instead of RNA-seq is an older technology that lacks the coverage available with RNA-seq. I guess this may have been an innovative grant when first submitted??
app_text_str: . Aim 1 will re-address the important question of whether or not the VSV M protein inhibits Nucleocytoplasmic transport in infected cells and the effect of silencing Rae1. . Models of how M protein may be mediating host shut-off are interesting and worth investigating
app_text_wkn: . Examining Nucleocytoplasmic transport by subcellular fractionation and real time RT-PCR requires selection of a handful of mRNAs. Findings with these mRNAs may or may not provide data supporting the PIs hypothesis. Even if they do, the question will remain unanswered for many other mRNAs. What about pre-mRNAs and splicing? It would seem that a better approach might be to use RNA-seq. . Won’t Experiments with recombinant mutant virus with the M51R version of M have a confounding effect in that the resultant host expression of host ISGs might suppress replication and also affect host translation and transcription? . The finding that hnRNPs are in the cytosol of VSV infected cells is an interesting correlative observation; however, there are many other host RNA-binding proteins. Focusing on hnRNPs and the mRNAs they interact with in AIM 1 seems likely to provide a biased view of the possible mechanisms of translational suppression. . The reactive Biotin-thiol chemistry chosen for biotinylating 4SU-labeled mRNA is very important for efficient recovery – this was not discussed. Lack of technical details here is a concern. . Details regarding the PAR-CLIP data analysis pipeline was not mentioned or discussed. . The preliminary data (Fig. 8) showing the protein composition of ribosome-associated mRNPs from VSV-infected cells was not particularly convincing. Fraction 5 is supposed to be different from mock and infected cells in the presence of puromycin – well maybe… is the best I could say. . AIM 2 refers to Figure 9B – which isn’t present. Overall Aim 2 seemed to be rushed and didn’t really make sense. It also referred to Aim 3 (also not present). . Is Rae1 the only host protein that M interacts with?

imp_text: Research proposed in this early -investigator initiated new R01 application is to establish the involvement of mesotrypsin (PRSS3) in prostate cancer invasion and metastasis.  The PI has identified PRSS3 as an upregulated gene in metastatic prostate cancer with prognostic significance.  Based on the mechanistic action of PRSS3 in cleaving its protease inhibitor substrates, the PI has proposed to develop selective PRSs3 inhibitor that will be tested in vitro and in vivo.  Major strengths include the research approach to define the underlying mechanism by which PRSS3 promotes prostate cancer progression and research designed to identify a selective PRSS3 inhibitor. Other strengths include Dr. Walsh’s expertise in serine protease/inhibitor analysis complemented by her collaborators with expertise in 3D culture, orthotopic mouse model of prostate cancer and the techniques of phage display selection, protein engineering generally well-planned and carefully-crafted experiments, and the excellent environment to carry out the proposed studies. However, there are some weaknesses that limit the potential impact of the proposed research.  They include the lack of inclusion of primary human samples in the proposed studies, and being a new investigator the number of experiments proposed seemed to be over ambitious in nature. Also, all of the data on PRSS3 expression is solely based on q-PCR.  No data was presented on PRSS3 protein expression which is a concern. Therefore, although the proposed studies are potentially interesting and the experiments are well designed, due lack of studies of primary human samples and diagnostic and therapeutic impact of the proposed studies on the prostate cancer field is rather unclear and limits the impact of this study significantly. Therefore, expected impact of the proposed research is moderate. In conclusion, despite several strengths, the potential impact of this project on improving clinical management of patients with prostate cancer is uncertain. It is not very evident that PRSS3 is even expressed in the primary tumors at the protein level. Although limited in #s, protein expression by immunohistochemistry in the protein atlas data base shows complete absence of expression of PRSS3 protein expression in all the 20 samples analyzed. imp_text: Aberrant regulation of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and RAS signaling pathways play major roles in resistance to many new molecularly targeted therapies in CRC development.  The overall objective of this proposal to mechanistically define the molecular switch between PI3K/AKT and PDPK1/TORC that could lead to resistance to PI3K and AKT inhibitors and specific aminoacid substitutions of mutant KRAS that activate different downstream signaling pathways that underlie the resistance to these inhibitors.
