imp_text: The well-established, capable team assembled here appears to have the skills necessary to complete the proposed work in what appears to be a good research environment. The approaches to be taken here would lead to a thorough understanding of the biology of mesotrypsin and the inhibitors to be discovered here. However, the inhibitors proposed to be discovered here may have only limited therapeutic relevance given their short half-lives. While PEGylation approaches may improve inhibitor properties, it is not clear that these inhibitors would be readily translatable, although they may immediately lead to valuable tools for understanding the biology of mesotrypsin. The team says little or nothing about investigating off-target inhibitor effects in vitro prior to moving into cell culture and animal models, and this may result in a large increase in cost and expense compared to what would be incurred for biochemical approaches to investigating inhibitor specificity. While the inhibitors would be some of the first against mesotrypsin, their novelty would not be that high, especially given the existence of a moderately potent lead identified already by the team.

imp_text: A well-resourced investigator proposes mouse studies that he suggests could impact the development of clinical treatments for melanoma. For the most part, the application is technically sound, but it is difficult to assess the ultimate impact of the work. The relevance of the mouse models in question to human presentations of melanoma are unclear. If it can be shown that these models and their responses to treatment are highly predictive of the behavior of human melanoma, this work would be highly impactful. Another important consideration for how impactful the work may be are the properties of the inhibitors used here, which are still under development and in some cases are known to inhibit several kinases, potentially confounding analysis of observations in studies. Finally, the number of melanoma patients that may ultimately benefit from this work may be small, as the patients would need to exhibit the genetic features evaluated here in order to be eligible for treatment.
sig_text_str: . Combination of excellent mouse models and numerous small molecules capable of interfering with several portions of the signaling pathways implicated in melanoma progression.
sig_text_wkn: . It is difficult to predict the potential significance of the work, especially since the letter of collaboration most directly related to the translational aspect of the work (Dr. Dube’s letter) is missing. If the mouse models accurately represent the disease in humans, then the significance could be high, but this is not fully apparent. . The application suggests that the microenvironment may influence disease progression, but does not adequately justify why treatments targeting the microenvironment such as checkpoint blockade antibodies will not be considered here. . The success of this work depends heavily on the quality of the inhibitors to be used here, and the broad specificity of several inhibitors to be used may confound analysis of the data. . The number of melanoma patients that may ultimately benefit from this work is limited, at most, to those patients identified as having the genetic features of interest that may them suitable for treatment.

Chronic bacterial colonization of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an opportunistic bacterial pathogen, accounts for the majority of CF infection-associated clinical problems. Biofilms are structured communities of microbes encased within a matrix and exhibit resistance to antimicrobials and host defenses. It is likely that biofilm is the major contributor to the chronic colonization of P. aeruginosa in CF but the mechanisms remain unclear. This application proposed a nicely laid out research plan to investigate the contribution of biofilm formation by two extracellular polysaccharides (EPS) and a protein, CdrA, which are critical components of the P. aeruginosa biofilm matrix. imp_text: Dr. O’Brian proposes to characterize the mechanism of action of the intracellular pathogen Ehrlichia chaffeensis protein TRP120. This protein is transferred by type 1 secretion into host cells, where it is translocated to the nucleus. The mechanism of nuclear localization and its effects on host transcription are the focus of the proposal. In particular, TRP120 does not contain a nuclear localization sequence and the mechanism of nuclear localization is thus unknown. Dr. O’Brian proposes a novel mechanism that requires ubiquitination for translocation and involves SUMO modification for target activity. This will be tested using in vitro assays including site-directed mutagenesis of TRP120 and EMSA, transcriptional activation in live cells, and transcriptome and genome-wide characterization. The overall approach is ambitious and represents an encompassing study on TRP120 function. Dr. O’Brian’s track record on Ehrlichia chaffeensis and resources are excellent. However, the proposal lacked depth in its description of experimental details, did not present clear alternative approaches, and did not describe specific controls to evaluate the outcomes. In particular, if the predicted outcomes are not observed, it is not obvious what will be done next and how the unexpected outcomes will affect the interpretation of the model.

imp_text: This application addresses an important microbiological problem with direct public health relevance: the assembly of the Shigella TTSS, which is a key virulence determinant. A major aspect of the proposal is the role of the IpaB protein, which represents a protective antigen and is implicated in TTSS activation. The application draws together experts in Shigella pathogenesis, protein biochemistry, EM, and X-ray crystallography to investigate interactions between components known to be involved in major steps in the assembly and activation of the TTSA needle. The aims focus on (1) characterization of the needle itself; (2) determination of crystal structures of various components alone and in complex; and (3) binding studies to investigate regulatory interactions between those components. Strengths of the application include a compelling public health issue, exciting preliminary data, including the structure of the IpaB N-terminal core, possible co-crystals, and some early binding data. These complement a wide array of constructs and functional data available to the team. The experimental approaches are well chosen to address the questions raised. However, the descriptions are in several places superficial, reflecting the relatively early stage of many of the studies. Aims 2 and 3, in particular, seem underdeveloped. Numerous crystal structures and binding interactions are proposed, but in many cases the reagents are not yet in hand or have proven problematic, and no 'breakthrough' data suggest there is now a unique opportunity to move ahead. Multiple pitfalls are not addressed. Overall, while the team and environment are strong, these issues substantially reduce enthusiasm for this particular application.

imp_text: This application explores the biochemistry of major components of the matrix formed by non-mucoid P. aeruginosa biofilms. The central hypothesis is that non-mucoid EPS components protect Pa from antimicrobials and immune attack during a proposed "therapeutic window." The aims are: (1) to define the biochemistry of EPS and CdrA interactions in non-mucoid biofilm matrix; and (2) to explore the impact of deletion or overexpression of Psl, Pel, and CdrA on immune responses to Pa. The team and environment are excellent and have generated a substantial set of published and preliminary data. Additional strengths include a wide variety of established approaches that suggest feasibility of many experiments. It is well-established that biofilm formation serves as a barrier to clearance of Pa infections, which are a major source of mortality particularly in the context of immune compromise. As a result, uncovering new therapeutic targets could have a large impact. However, the linkage between the proposed experiments and any potential therapeutic application is not outlined in any detail. The experimental techniques and the overall animating hypothesis are relatively straightforward. Furthermore, the aims are somewhat unfocused and include experiments that appear tangentially related to testing of the central hypothesis. Indeed, aim 1, while likely to expand our knowledge of the biochemistry of non-mucoid biofilms, does not strongly test the central hypothesis. In aim 2, potentially divergent effects from opsonized vs. non-opsonized bacteria may complicate analyses, and no clear framework is presented for deconvoluting the effects. These factors lead to an overall moderate level of enthusiasm.

imp_text: This is a very well-organized and scientifically rigorous application that proposes to explore a novel mechanism of action for a T1SS-dependent virulence factor secreted by the tick-borne pathogen E. chaffeensis. Published and preliminary data support the hypothesis that TRP120 acts not only as an attachment factor, but also as a regulator of host gene expression. The three aims focus on (1) how host post-translation modifications are hijacked to mediate nuclear translocation; (2) how TRP120 mediates sequence-specific transcriptional activation and repression; and (3) how TRP120 acts globally to perturb host-cell gene expression programs, e.g., through epigenetic changes. Strengths of the application include the exploration of new forms of pathogenic hijacking of host-cell gene expression, a strong array of tools well-suited to tackling the questions at hand, and the likelihood that new data will emerge on the exploitation of ubiquitination and/or sumoylation pathways to direct intracellular trafficking. The experimental logic is clear and tackles a series of key questions that will collectively provide a comprehensive investigation of the phenomenon at multiple levels. The investigator and the environment provide high confidence in the success of the program. There are a few minor weaknesses. In terms of significance, it remains unclear what role TRP120's gene-expression effects play in HME pathogenesis, and the experimental effort in that direction is limited (end of aim 3). In terms of approach, it is not entirely clear how the applicants will deconvolute effects of PTMs on protein abundance/degradation vs. trafficking, nor how they will disentangle overlapping effects of TF, DNA modification, and subnuclear localization on gene expression. Nevetheless, overall enthusiasm is high.

imp_text: Effectors delivered into host cells by bacterial pathogens are essential for virulence, detailed study of effectors can lead to our understanding of not only pathogenesis but also host signaling mechanisms as many host processes are not detectable under physiological conditions. By focusing on TRP120, an effector of Ehrlichia chaffeensis, this application is posed to reveal some exciting insights of this obligate pathogen. The proposal is very clearly written and most of the proposed experiments are well-thought, particularly those in Aims 1 and 2. The potential to uncover the role of ubiquitination and sumoylation in the nuclear shuffling and activity of TRP120. The mechanisms of TRP120-DNA interaction and its role in gene expression in Aim 2 were also warranted and will likely lead to novel information of the function of TRP120. Aim 3 is a major weakness of the proposal as the proposed experiments mostly are descriptive, which will not likely add more from the experiments in Aims 1 and 2. Another major weakness is the lack of biochemical study of TRP120. In addition to DNA binding, does this effector confer any biochemical activity to its cellular targets?  How are the proposed TRP120-induced epigenetic modifications achieved? The lack of detailed biochemical study makes many of the observed phenomena unresolved, these issues dampened the overall enthusiasm of the otherwise exciting proposal.

imp_text: Efficient degradation of molecules involved in immune signaling is an important strategy for many bacterial pathogens. Based on solid preliminary results, the applicant proposed to study the mechanism and role of sphingosine -1-phosphate metabolism in the pathogenesis of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The strength of the proposal includes quite comprehensive preliminary results, the inclusion of a collaborator with highly complementary expertise and a highly workable model. The major weaknesses include the omission of some important controls in critical experiments and the not-so-thoughtful alternative approaches. For example, the applicant showed that SAP phosphatase can remove the phosphate from S1P, which would predict that overexpression of bacterial phosphatases in the screening which a major component in Aim 2 will lead to many false positive clones. It is not clear how the applicant will distinguish those from the one that is physiologically important. Given these reasons, the enthusiasm of this proposal is not high.

Preliminary results suggest that sphingosine directly activates SphR, these genetic results should be validated by the EMSA assay, i.e., does sphingosine require for the DNA binding activity of SphR? . The recombinant protein of SphR shown in Fig. 8 is of low quality. Further purification with size exclusion or ion exchange column is necessary. . imp_text: In this grant, the applicants propose to look at the role of S1P/sphingosine in PA virulence/infection.   Whilst the grant is solidly written and the significance is high, I have several concerns that lead to the lower score.  There is little preliminary data and what there is for the in vivo study suggests that S1P metabolism may not be so important (eg less than 1 log reduction in infection after S1P inhibition).  More data would help firm this up perhaps. Furthermore, there is no mention of which PA strains will be used.   Also, the statistics seem poorly thought out – I would recommend a consultation with a statistician before resubmission.  Finally, in the pitfalls/alternate approaches section, I came away with the impression that “everything is up and running in the lab and will work”.  In my experience, this rarely happens and my thought should be given to alternate approaches in cases things do  not work out exactly as intended.

app_text_str: . Aim 1 proposes to characterize S1P/sphingosine metabolism and its control at the genetic level.  This seems to be mostly confirmatory to what is already known and unlikely to bring significantly new findings to the table. . Aim 2 and its more biochemical/mechanistic approach seems solid.
app_text_wkn: . Give this reviewer’s experience with murine models, with inflammation studies and flexivent, an n=5/group for the mice is woefully underpowered.  The applicants said that they did power calculations, but the power is likely to be different for flexivent vs bacterial numbers etc . The preliminary data for the mouse experiments appears to show less than a log fold change in infection which is quite small, suggesting that inhibition of S1P/sphingosine metabolism may have only small effects on infectinos in vivo. . It is not clear which strains of PA they are using.  Are they using a common lab strain such a PA01?  If so, they should also use common clinical isolates of PA which are freely  available from the CF Foundation. . Beyond the in vivo expts, I have other concerns with the stats. For example, for the the in vitro expts, they are proposing to do [paramertric] t-tests on n=3s.  However, t-tests assuming a normal distribution and this assumption cannot be met with an n=3. . Only male mice are being tested – no justification is made for this.  Given that there are gender differences in both CF and COPD, and that the NIH has directed that gender be factored in both genders should be tested.

imp_text: The proposed study offers an improvement on a genetic tool that has the potential to further expand the reach of photochemical gene regulation and developmental biology. More efficacious cMOs can applied to other fields where they can be used to better understand antimicrobial resistance and/or production through inhibition of bacterial genes. It might serve as selective anticancer chemotherapy through site-specific irradiation. The study is well throughout, where various aspects of the synthetic routes will be explored to select the most effective synthetic reagent.  Though the study is well-thought out, the improvement on current cMOs technology will not lead to complete elimination of the current pitfalls. While the proposed cMOs have reduced cytotoxicity, this is already in place with cyclic cMOs. Basal activity is still expected though reduced from the current MOs.  Successful completion of the aims will expand light-gated technologies, there are tools currently available/being explored that allow for selective gene regulation (such as siRNA), and therefore, this new tools are not necessary to expand the field of developmental biology.

imp_text: This application by a new investigator aims to use “bacterial metabolomics” to generate libraries of novel and diverse natural products, generally a worthwhile undertaking.  Strengths: The application has some novel and interesting aspects, such as characterization and separation of strains by their metabolite profiles, and an attempt to increase diversity by bacterial co-culture.   The PI presents preliminary data that it is feasible to characterize biosynthetic activity of bacterial strains by LC-MS. Weaknesses: The application is unfocused; a difficult read with many moving parts and seemingly unconnected sections.  Different biologies are mixed with different questions of how to improve diversity, each one essentially constituting a research direction by itself.  The significance section states ambitious goals: validation of metabolomics,  improving hit rates and novelty of leads, improve detection of interspecies interactions to activate cryptic biosynthetic clusters, and unravel interspecies signaling using variety of ‘Omics.  These are laudable goals, but the proposed studies are far too superficial to generate any of this knowledge in detail.  While preliminary results support an ability to separate strains by chemistry, it does not become clear from the document how studies based on this result will  result in a deeper understanding of how bacteria communicate with each other in the context of modifying metabolism.  It is not clear what exactly the outcomes will be for each aim and what would actually constitute success. These issues substantially detract from an intriguing idea with potential to generate novel compound libraries.  As presented, the impact of these studies is hard to judge but likely low.

study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function C Study Section
imp_text: This application by a new investigator aims to elucidate molecular mechanisms of kinesin movement along microtubules (MTs).  MTs have been the subject of intense study for many decades, but the repertoire of analytical methods to analyze MT-associated protein complexes at near atomic resolution is limited due to the helical structure of MTs and the fact that MT-protein complexes are highly heterogeneous.  This leaves cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) as the method of choice, resulting in limited resolution. The applicants have made significant improvements in cryo-EM imaging methodology that resulted in the reconstruction of a MT-kinesin complex at 5-6A.  The research plan is ambitious but appears feasible, and strong collaborators in excellent environments will contribute to success.  Most studies exploit the strengths of the PI as an expert in cryo-EM, but AFM to confirm presence of doubly attached dimers on MTs, and saturation transfer EPR to quantify stationary vs. mobile heads will be employed also.  Importance, gaps in knowledge, and technical capabilities are very well explained.  Weaknesses if any are minor and involve a lack of alternative approaches and an uncertainty about how the studies will advance the field towards therapeutics.  These minor weaknesses do not, however, diminish enthusiasm for a technically challenging, outstanding proposal from an experienced investigator who has developed methods and collaborations to tackle an important unresolved problem in kinesin function.  Given the continued interest in MTs as therapeutic targets and a broad scientific interest in fundamentals of molecular motors , impact is likely to be high.  It is hard to imagine that no new and useful information will be generated through these studies.
sig_text_str: Kinesins are important for transport of molecular “cargo “ along microtubules (MTs).  They are implicated in numerous diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases and possibly cancer. While kinesins and their basic functions have been known for a long time,  efforts to target kinesins for therapeutic  value have been limited by an incomplete understanding of the molecular and structural basis of kinesin function. .
inv_text_str: . The Pi is an experienced expert in the field of molecular motors and cryo-EM .  He made seminal contributions to the field and authored a recent PNAS paper . The proposed studies leverage an existing ACS starter grant to the PI. . The PI has assembled a capable team of experts in their respective fields with complementary expertise. . Dr. Sauter at the University of Gottingen is a renowned expert in Atomic Force Microscopy. . Dr. Taylor is the Director of the U Minnesota Biophysical Spectroscopy Center
inn_text_str: The structural elucidation of MTs bound to associated proteins is a formidable challenge.  Cryo EM is the only method that has been successfully applied to MTs and associated proteins, but its resolution is limited compared with X-ray crystallography. Existing methods have not captured the structure of actively “stepping” kinesin dimers, when bound to MTs, and there here is even controversy about which structural features are essential for function. The applicants have developed the first algorithm that extracts 3D resolutions from imperfectly decorated, heterogeneous assemblies of kinesin with MTs. Their studies have partially confirmed prior predictions but also generated novel results that form the basis for new hypotheses, which will be tested in the experimental plan. Their improved methodology is platform technology and will be used in a series of well-designed experiments, including kinesin mutants. The cryo-EM studies will be supplemented by atomic force microscopy and saturation electron spin resonance studies .
app_text_str: The applicants propose to  develop improved analytical cryo-EM capabilities to achieve sub-nanometer resolution of kinesins bound to and moving along MTs.  Methods and many reagents are in hand. The team has made prior contributions to the field, as in a recent PNAS paper. Aim 1 is to determine atomic basis of MT-stimulated by the kinesin motor domain.  This will apply their newly improved cryo-em methods to known mutants of kinesin. Aim 2 is to solve the structural basis of how the two “heads” of kinesin interact during translocation on the MT.  This is important because the two heads need to “communicate” with each other during movement in order to synchronize their catalytic cycles. They have already solved a first 3D reconstruction of an isolated kinesin dimer. Now They propose solving sub-nanometer reconstructions of moving kinesins on the MT to test the effects of kinesin mutations predicted to affect the strength of the dimer interaction. With their expertise and methodology this elusive and challenging task seems feasible. The newly developed method will be platform technology to analyze other, previously untractable, MT-associated factors. The cryo-EM studies will be supplemented by AFM to confirm presence of doubly attached dimers on MTs, and saturation transfer EPR to qiantify stationary vs mobile heads. .

study_section: Biochemistry and Biophysics of Membranes Study Section
imp_text: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS) is essential for bacterial survival and an important defense factor. To be displayed on the outside of the bacterial membrane, LPS is transported through the periplasmic space by a series of transport proteins termed LptA-G.  Deletion of LptA is lethal to bacteria, suggesting that interfering with LPS transport is a viable strategy to discover new antibiotics.  While LPS transport has been functionally validated in many studies, the precise details and molecular mechanisms of transport are unknown. Here the applicants propose to elucidate the details of LptA mediated LPS transport through a series of well-designed structural studies.  The thoughtful, detailed research plan aims to elucidate functionally essential residues in LptA, characterize the binding of LPS to LptA, and extend studies to upstream and downstream members of the Lpt family.  The plan reflects the deep experience of the PI with biophysical evaluation of conformational dynamics of bacterial membrane proteins. Techniques are in place.  Many reagents are in hand and where they are not, efforts are underway to create them. A capable team of collaborators has been assembled and the environment is excellent.  Given the paucity of novel antibiotics in the face of increasing bacterial resistance, the studies might well reveal novel points of interference with bacterial survival, which would have a major impact on the field of antibiotic therapy.
sig_text_str: . There is a dire need for novel antibiotics, especially for gram negative bacteria. . Discovery of novel antibiotics has been slow and challenging . The LPS transport system could be a novel point of attack to selectively affect bacterial survival.
sig_text_wkn: A discussion of what effects inhibition of bacterial LPS transport would have in the context of human disease is missing.
inv_text_str: The PP is a highly experienced biophysicist uniquely qualified to direct the proposed studies. He is a continuously funded, collaborative investigator who has extensively worked on protein/ligand binding. The co-I Dr. Fitch is a seasoned microbiologist with an active research program in bacterial pathogenesis who will generate the novel temperature sensitive reporter strain.
inn_text_str: . The molecular details of how LPS is transported by Lpt proteins are not completely understood . There appears to be no in vivo assay for LptA-mediated bacterial survival.  A novel mutant LPTA strain that cannot sustain growth at 42C but is complemented by wt LPTA provides a system to test functional importance of LPTA mutations. . X-ray structures have been obtained for LptA but lacked electron densities for LPS. imp_text: The focus of this application is to synthesize caged morpholino oligonucleotides (MOs) that can adopt single- or double-lariat conformations. A light-cleavable tether can achieve terminus-to-backbone or terminus-to-base linkage. Linker photolysis will release the MOs for efficient MO/RNA hybridization and gene regulation. Gene regulatory studies will be conducted with zebrafish models. Successful completion of this application has the potential to develop new technologies and tools for gene regulatory studies.
sig_text_str: . Morpholino oligonucleotides (MOs) are excellent tools for gene regulation. . Caging of MOs and light activated initiation of their functionality are advances in the application of MOs in gene regulation in in vivo models. . Zebrafish is a useful model to test the application of caged MOs. . Currently available caged MO technology has several limitations and the present application is aimed at developing technologies to overcome these limitations. . This is a powerful technology and will have applications as a gene regulatory tool in several other model systems.

study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function C Study Section
imp_text: This application aims at establishing the mechanism of kinesin motor protein function using cryo-electron microscopic (EM) methods, in conjunction with other structural and functional techniques, including atomic force microscopy (AFM) and saturation-transfer electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy. The applicant’s research has made progress in solving a new 3D reconstruction of the kinesin-microtubule complex at ~5-6 Å resolution. This application will define structure/function studies of site-directed mutants in the kinesin catalytic domain and test the mechanistic aspects of microtubule binding of kinesin. The resuts of these studies may have applications in kinesin targeted drug development and in advancing studies on filament-binding proteins.
sig_text_str: . Kinesin plays an important role in the function of microtubules, including cell division, flagellar motility and neuronal vesicle transport. . The fine structure of microtubule-kinesin complex is not known at present. . Cryo-EM is a viable method for high-resolution structural elucidation of kinesin complexes. . There is a controversy over the mechanism of the kinesin motor region.

study_section: Biochemistry and Biophysics of Membranes Study Section
imp_text: This project addresses an important problem of understanding the proteins and mechanisms involved in the synthesis and transport of lipopolysaccharide (LPS) or endotoxin, the outer membrane protein of Gram-negative bacteria. Specifically, this project will use state-of-the-art biophysical techniques, such as laser light scattering, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy and isothermal calorimetry, to characterize the interaction between the transporting protein, LptA and LPS. The data generated from this study might expand our understanding of LPS transport, and enable rational antibiotic drug design to block essential steps in bacterial growth and survival.
sig_text_str: . LPS is an outer membrane glycoprotein that protects the cytoplasm of pathogenic bacteria and acts as a highly selective permeability barrier. . LPS is a toxin to mammals, including humans, and can cause various inflammatory diseases and death. Therefore, an understanding of the mechanism of the synthesis and transport of LPS is important to develop new antibiotics for Gram-negative bacteria. . LptA is a periplasmic protein that plays an important role in LPS transport. . Proposed studies in this application to quantify the binding of LptA with LPS are significant to understand LPS transport mechanisms and to develop new antibiotics.

study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: This is an interesting approach to determining how coronavirus and other viruses that produce a similar ns2 protein with homology to known phosphodiesterase (PDE) enzymes may control the RNase L based response to IFN after viral infection. The PI’s proposal to first determine the ability of the ns2-related proteins to regulate 2’5’ A levels in cells, and how this relates to cellular immunity is positive. Specific inhibitors of these enzymes could indeed be the basis for novel antivirals. However, this reviewer was not convinced about the significance of the work, given the the lack of clarity and careless writing in the research plan, and the problem that the small molecules could target both viral and cellular PDEs. Scored Review Criteria Reviewers will consider each of the five review criteria below in the determination of scientific and technical merit, and provide a separate score and critique for each.
sig_text_str: . The team has already shown that ns2 mutation prevents viral hepatitis in their animal model. Thus it is important to explore the role of this protein in preventing a proper IFN/RNase L response . They have good cell and animal models for testing eventual inhibitors arising from the HTS screening
sig_text_wkn: . SARS CoV does not produce this protein and is still lethal, so there must be other factors involved beside ns2 inhibitionof the IFN response in coronavirus lethality. Ns2 is not required for viral growth except in interfering with the immune response. . Their planned inhibitors may also target cellular enzymes. It is not clear that they can identify an inhibitor that will regulate the viral proteins specifically, since human proteins can have similar 2’5’-A degrading activity. The PIs do not seem to think this is a problem, however. . Although 4 logs of decrease in viral growth is impressive, it suggests that this is the limit of usefulness for any inhibitor of PDE activity. Thus the inhibitors must be used with other antivirals. Further, the circle of viruses the inhibitors can be used against is small and will not extend even to SARS. It is not even clear how much relevance this will have to human hepatitis viruses. . The authors discuss identifying structure/function cursorily, but the PIs’ specialties do not lie in understanding structure-function relationships for advanced inhibitors.

The multi-PI plan is detailed, with clear roles for researchers experienced in immune assays, liver cell specialists, the IFN response, high throughput screening (HTS), and the animal experiments.

It is not clear how much time this person will dedicate to the project, as there will certainly be other projects on the docket for this center. study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: This is a very interesting work, with a high potential to explain immune suppression by highly pathogenic viruses. The combination of structural work with assays and testing in an animal model promises to yield very significant results for the role of the viral OTU-like proteases in immune suppression. Reservations on the overall impact are mostly due to the sparse description of the plan for identifying inhibitors of the proteins, and how specific these will be for the viral proteins. A more clear description of the assays for interpreting the effects of the mutations on the viral activity would have helped here. Scored Review Criteria Reviewers will consider each of the five review criteria below in the determination of scientific and technical merit, and provide a separate score and critique for each.
sig_text_str: The researchers are studying highly pathogenic nairoviruses and have the necessary background and biosafety labs to combine structural work with cell based and in vivo studies.
sig_text_wkn: . There may be other factors contributing to the extreme pathogenicity of CCHFV besides the target specificity of its proteases.
inv_text_str: . Experience in this area and with determining the structure of the viral OTUs. . Excellent combination of researchers who also have access to the necessary BSL for the work . The PI is experienced and the group has already determined the structures of CCHFV DUGV OTUs
inn_text_str: . Excellent plan to give a different perspective on the role of the OTUs that cannot be gained simply by overexpression of the protein
inn_text_wkn: . There seems to be quite a bit of work done already in this area. . May be a bit too centered on the viral proteins without regard to studies on related proteins. The proposal for example never clarifies how closely the human OTU resembles the viral ones, except that the former are larger. This is an important point for avoiding drug interactions.
app_text_str: . Very good preliminary work for this, and the PI has the experience in high throughput screening that could help to bring this work into the future as a drug design target . The plan to distinguish the cleavage specificity of the different OTUs is straight forward and may reveal the mechanistic basis for why certain nairoviruses are more lethal. The detailed plan to test the role of the ISG sequence in this specificity is also appropriate. . The combination of skills will allow the work to proceed quickly
app_text_wkn: . The NMR side of the work is not well developed in the proposal and is obviously preliminary. The question is whether they can indeed use this methodology to study protein-protein interactions with enough sequence specificity to reach a model for the chemistry involved. They do however show a reasonably well resolved spectrum (Fig. 4) of one of the proteins. . The work is very ambitious. The time line may need to be extended. The HTS work does not indicate how they can skew their selection for inhibitors that are specific for the vOTUs. . The proposal begins strong, but later sections degrade into alphabet soup. This may be a function of the complex nature of the subject matter, but the experimental description gets more dense and harder to understand in the later aims, especially for the proposed animal studies, the interaction of the OTUs/ISG types and (especially) the specific characteristics of the various cell lines. The investigators should have included a glossary or summary of their abbreviations and more figures that illuminate the different cell lines and animal models. study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function C Study Section
imp_text: The proposal’s goal is to understand from a structural level how kinesin motors function. Kinesins are molecular motors that travel on microtubules and serve as agents to deliver “cargo” throughout the cell. In addition, they are required for cell division and for motility of cilia/flagella. How kinesins move on the microtubule and the structural basis for their function has not been fully established. Using Cryo-EM technology and image processing that they have developed the goal is to solve a 3D structure of the kinesin bond to microtubule. In combination with mutagenesis studies it will be possible to define the critical features of how kinesin functions. These studies will illuminate how other filament binding proteins such as dyneins and myosins function as well as providing new tools to study molecular motor complexes. This application drives towards near atomic resolution of kinesin bound to microtubules. Overall this is an outstanding application from a junior PI that started her lab in 2011. She has integrated herself with several collaborators and also with sites that have instrumentation at the Scripps institute and expertise in kinetic measurements. imp_text: This proposal will determine the function of a series of proteins involved in the transport of Lipopolysaccharide to the outer membrane of bacteria. These proteins LptA-G reside within the Inner and Outer membrane and through previous genetic studies shown to be important. However, a biochemical study of their function and the exact mechanism of how LPS are transported from the IM to the OM, i.e. the cell surface of bacteria. The main focus is on LptA and the critical amino acids for its function. Aim 2 will measure the interaction of LPS and LptA using a variety of approaches including EPR and isothermal titration calorimetry. Aim 3 will address how LptA transfers the LPS to other Lpt proteins such as LptC and LptDE. In this aim LptA mutants will be used to measure its interactions with LptC and LptDE. Overall this a solid application that has great significance in understanding the process of protein transport through the Lpt proteins. The PI is well trained in this area of research. The approaches are standard, but will provide a mechanism of how the Lpt proteins interface in the bacteria cell wall. However, the scope seems to be mainly focused on LptA interactions with LPS and other Lpt proteins. These biochemical interactions are not studied with respect to function so there may not be a strong correlation with interaction and function in vivo.

imp_text: This proposal, by an established Investigator, is directed towards a molecular dissection of LPS transport and focuses primarily upon the interaction of LPS with LptA, a periplasmic “LPS chaperone.” While the role of LPS in bacterial viability is evident, and the problem of how this molecule is conveyed to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane is quite interesting, the proposal has some significant flaws that sharply diminished Reviewer enthusiasm. While a clever genetic screen is proposed, the interpretation of its results will not be clear; also, integration of this approach with the known crystal structure is scant (Aim 1). The use of EPR to determine the LPS/LptA binding interface is highly problematic (Aim 3).
sig_text_str: . LPS is a significant component of the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, many of which cause diseases of significant public health concern . The mechanism by which a hydrophobic molecule, such as LPS, gets transported through hydrophobic and hydrophilic environments is an interesting biophysical problem
sig_text_wkn: . While the LPS transport system is essential for bacterial viability, the “druggability” of the proteins in this system is not convincingly presented.

imp_text: The PI, an early stage investigator, proposes to develop new approaches to natural products discovery.  He will utilize his expertise and training in both the areas of marine biology and natural product screening techniques to develop libraries that are enriched in small molecules with drug-like properties, and will identify new small molecules from screens of interbacterial interactions which yield secondary metabolites and also investigate their production.  Strengths of the application are the novelty of the natural product screen of molecules specifically generated during interbacterial communication/interactions (Aim 3), and the source of the natural products (marine sponges and bacteria) to yield novel diversity in the library. Weaknesses of the proposal are substantial, including the lack of detailed or methodical approaches in each of the Aims (e.g. how MS analysis of samples will be performed, what types of assays will be used to identify leads), as well as the expectation of investigating regulation of native biogenesis of novel compounds in these uncharacterized species (Aim 3B) seems overreaching for the scope of this PI and this study. In addition, biohazard management is not sufficiently discussed.

Utliizing the virtually untapped resource of marine organisms for NP discovery is a significant horizon in the field. . The PI cites current issues regarding the limited pipeline currently being used for NP –based discovery and wants to ameliorate this situation by opening this avenue of research into generating marine-based NP libraries.

imp_text: This is a new proposal by a new (but not early stage) investigator describing studies characterizing the motility functions ascribed to dimeric kinesin motor proteins.  The basis of the proposal is that there is a fundamental lack of information regarding the structural basis of kinesin’s stepwise movement and the utility of having a dimeric form for kinesin function.  The long term goal is to impact therapeutic developments for cancer and other disease, as structural understanding of this process could inform better target specificity. The overall aims are to use cryoEM and 3D reconstruction to investigate the microtubule/kinesin complexes in states of ATP/ADP cycling and binding/release. The strength of the approach in Aim I draws from strong preliminary 3D reconstruction data and a comparison of wildtype and mutant kinesin which will be followed up in the proposed work. A distant relative of this kinesin family, kar3, will also be investigated to determine whether there is actually a structural distinct mechanism for this family member, as was perhaps erroneously proposed in the literature. The approach is expected to address this conundrum. Aim 2, which investigates the structural relationship between the two heads of dimeric kinesin and microtubules by using overlap mapping of images at two different resolutions, is particularly interesting and innovative. There is much enthusiasm with regards to the use of the proposed approaches to more accurately define and characterize kinesin/microtubule interactions.  There are some weaknesses identified in the Investigators section, as to the contributions of various collaborators to the project. The environment at Yale is exceptional for this type of work in the areas of structure/function and biophysical measurements.

imp_text: The project aims to elucidate the mechanism of cardiac protection by the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway against myocardial inflammation. This is particularly significant at present because of the emerging popularity of immunotherapies targeting the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway for the treatment of cancer and viral infection. The two PIs are very strong, with well established history of collaboration and records on studying PD-1/PD-L1 function in immune cells and heart. Innovations are noted in concept and technical approaches. The experiments are well designed with detailed studies that help elucidate the contributions of different cardiac and immune cell types in cardiac protection against inflammation. Additionally, an aim is included to explore the therapeutic potential of enhancing PD-L1 expression in dendritic cells for T cell tolerance to myocardial antigens. A concern is that the budge and time requested may not be enough for the number of transgenic lines needed and the amount of work required to accomplish the project.
sig_text_str: . The project focuses on molecular mechanisms underlying myocardial inflammation, which has a high clinical relevance in chronic myocardial injury, fibrosis, and heart failure. . The PD-1/PD-1L pathway is currently targeted in immunotherapies against cancer and viral infection. However, the risks to inflammatory heart disease should be carefully assessed.
inv_text_str: . Both PIs, Drs. Jackson and Schaffer, are well established in the field of immunology, especially in the studies of PD-1/PD-L1 pathway. Long-established collaborations are evident between the two PIs, as well as with the other key person, Dr. Frazier, who will provide well-characterized antibodies. . The publication records of the two PIs are impressive.

Using drugs to promote tolerance to cardiac antigens through upregulation of PD-L1 expression in dendritic cells and dendritic cell transfer represent an innovative idea for clinical therapies in cardiac protection.

imp_text: This is an excellent application from a junior investigator who has established his independent lab for about three years. The project focuses on an interesting question that addresses the interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and Ca2+ signaling in arterial smooth muscle cells, where deregulation can lead to hypertension and stroke and is commonly associated with obesity. The PI was well trained in smooth muscle physiology and Ca2+ signaling and has made progress in independent publication and grant funding. The proposal has conceptual and technical innovations. Experimental approaches are well explained and reasonable. It is expected that important knowledge will be gained from these studies. Some concerns are found in certain experimental plan and lack of discussion on potential conflicting outcomes that may result from using multiple drugs to target similar mitochondrial pathways.

Both calcium ions (Ca2+) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) are important signaling messengers. Their interplay is an interesting question that has not been studied very well.

imp_text: The proposed project aims to address how different proteins are selectively released from a-granules of platelets under conditions that either promote or inhibit angiogenesis. This is an important question that will impact our understanding and clinical therapies for vascular health. The PI is a leading expert in using electron tomography to resolve structural organization of organelles with established experiences in platelet biology. The idea that proteins in the a-granules are organized in distinct zones and released in a kiss-and-run fashion in response to specific stimuli is innovative and the combined use of electron microscopy and super resolution fluorescence microscopy to construct 3D models is technically sounding. The experimental approaches are clearly explained, but preliminary data demonstrating the feasibility of many of the designed approaches and the likely outcomes are rather scarce. More importantly, the current high resolution technology may still not be adequate for the questions asked. The restricted use of mainly two proteins, with one of them from exogenous source, also limited the enthusiasm for the proposed work. imp_text: This is a highly innovative proposal that addresses important aspects of the inflammatory response in myocarditis.  The PI has proposed that PD-1 and PD-L1 are central to maintaining an anti-inflammatory environment in cardiac tissue.  The authors provide compelling preliminary data that define the focus of the proposal and provide a strong experimental plan to test their hypotheses.  The PI has provided excellent thought on how these studies interact with the whole biological system and currently apply to immunotherapies used for other diseases.  Overall these data form these studies should provide significant new data that may well identify therapeutic targets and approaches for treating or preventing myocarditis.
sig_text_str: . The proposed experiments are highly significant to advancing our understanding of the biological role of PD-1 and PD-L1 in maintaining an anti-inflammatory environment in cardiac tissue.  The PI demonstrates a broad thought process of the potential role and effect of the PD-1 and PD-L1 on the entire biological system, as well as the effect that many current immunotherapies may be playing on the expression of these proteins and how the changes in expression may affect the therapy or the biological state of the patient.  The experiment design is very strong for all 3 aims, although very ambitious.  The investigators are highly qualified to conduct the proposed studies.
sig_text_wkn: . The experiments proposed are extensive and ambitious.  The use of 3 different models of myocarditis may be excessive and prevent the PI from achieving an in depth understanding of the function of PD-1 and PD-L1 in any one of these models.  A focus on just one, maybe 2, of these models would have been sufficient.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Murray, Professor of Pathology, Harvard University, is an accomplished, productive investigator and is highly qualified to perform the proposed work. . Dr. Schaffer, Harvard University, is also an accomplished, productive investigator with a background in T cell costimulation and immune function.  She will provide significant additional expertise to these proposed studies.

Use of the genetically modified animals in the myocarditis models greatly strengthens the experimental design of this proposal. . The models of myocarditis the PI proposes to use are well developed. . Inclusion of translational therapeutic approaches.
inn_text_wkn: . The only concern for the innovation of this proposal is its overall ambitious nature.  It is  unclear whether or not all of the proposed experiments can be performed in the proposed time frame.
app_text_str: . Aim 1 is a comprehensive analysis of the role of PD-L1 expression on hematopoietic cells, cardiomyocytes, and dendritic cells in two different model of myocarditis, CD4+ T cell and CD8+ T cell mediated.  The experiments are conceptually well designed, and use excellent mouse models to test the proposed hypotheses.  Proposed experiments will use the investigators’ well-designed models of myocarditis, and should yield significant results regarding the role of PD-L1 in protecting the cardiomyocytes from inflammation. . In Aim 2, the PI will investigate the PD-1-PD-L1 pathway in myeloid cells and the overall effect on inflammation in the heart.  These are again well designed, complex experiments that in some part appear to replicate the studies in Aim 1, but using a ischemia model of myocarditis.  Given the resources available and experimental design, these experiment should provide new information or at least confirm data from Aim 1. . Aim 3 is focused on developing methods using dendritic cells and expression of PD-1 and PD-L1 to induce tolerance in T cells and prevent inflammation in myocarditis.  The PI demonstrates that statin plus rapamycin induces PD-L1 on DC cells and will investigate if these DC inhibit CD4+ and CD8+ T cell mediated myocarditis.  This aim has a stronger mechanistic component, and like the other aims is well designed and should produce data that will test the proposed hypotheses.
app_text_wkn: . The proposal is very ambitious for Aim 1 and Aim 2.  While the experiments in Aim 1 are focused on PD-L1, both CD4+ and CD8+ models of myocarditis will be investigated in a total of 7 sub-sub aims, as well as sub aims for human cardiomyocyte studies, cytokine therapy studies, and a mechanistic aim that is dependent on results in an earlier sub aim.  Aim 2 has similar issues and introduces yet a 3rd model to test the role of PD-1 and PD-L1.  Additionally, many of these experiments involve complicated mouse breeding or generation of BM chimeras that could prove to be difficult to attain due to the multiple genetic alterations being introduced into a single mouse. . The repetitive testing of the role of PD-1 and PD-L1 in multiple cell types using 3 different models of myocarditis makes the primary focus of this proposal to be somewhat descriptive than mechanistic.  Some mechanistic experiments are proposed but most are based on deletion of PD-1 or PD-L1 and asking if disease susceptible has changed or not. . This reduces confidence in the KO model. . It is not clear which of the models of myocarditis will be used for Aim C2A or C1A.

imp_text: This proposal is focused on identifying the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which kalirin reduces the incidence of atherosclerosis.  Kalirin is a candidate athero protein that has been identified in epidemiological gene studies, and structurally contains numerous domains that mediate protein-protein interactions.  The proposal is well written and is based on an interesting hypothesis and strong experimental design for assessing the role of diet, kalirin expression levels, and the mechanisms by which it prevents the development of atherosclerosis. The primary model to be investigated is the Apoe-/- mouse that is susceptible to athero, and crossing it with KALRN +/- hetero-KO mice to investigate its role in athero generation.  The investigators involved have been productive, and have the expertise necessary to successfully complete these studies.  The potential impact of these studies on future treatment of atherosclerosis, especially for those with a genetic predisposition, is very high.
sig_text_str: . The focal area of this proposal, atherosclerosis, is an important area of clinical concern.  Understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms of atheroma development has significant potential for new directions in clinical therapy.

app_text_str: . In Aim 1, the investigators will investigate the role of iNOS and determine the role of the kalirin RhoGEF1 domain in its ability to inhibit athero development. iNOS inihbition will be accomplished using a pump to constantly dose the animals with a selective iNOS inhibitor, and the mice will be placed on a low fat diet or a Western diet.  This is a complex analyses of the role of kalirin, diet, and iNOS on athero development, but the investigators will do a comprehensive analysis of the pathology in the mice that should generate considerable amount of data allowing them to decipher how these 3 variables are interacting and influencing athero development.  In the 2nd part of this aim, the PI will investigate the role of the RHOGEF1 domain of kalirin in its anti-athero function by using an inhibitor of that domains function, ITX3.  In this approach, athero will be mechanically induced in vivo and the injury immediately exposed to ITX3 or control. While there are some potential limitations to this approach depending on outcome, these experiments could provide important information regarding the function of kalirin in athero. . Aim 2 is focused on identifying endothelial cell (EC) specific mechanisms of kalirin activity in preventing athero.  PI proposes to determine if kalirin promotes eNOS activity, perform proteomics on EC cells to identify proteins that bind to kalirin, and determine the in vivo function of EC produce kalirin using conditional knockouts and the same experimental analyses in Aim 1.1.  Collectively, this is a very large number of experiments to complete this aim. The PI proposes using kalirin deficient and knocked down EC for the eNOS studies, and will use Adeno encoding kalirin to enhanced kalirin expression in these cells to show WT phenotype when kalirin expression is restored.  The pathway analyses selected in combination with eNOS measurements should provide a clear understanding of whether or not the eNOS pathways is involved.  The EC conditional knockout mice are a strong addition to these studies, although it would have been supportive of the PI to include data demonstrating the quality of the knockout.  Finally, given the multitude of protein binidng domains in kalirin, the PI may be under estimating the number of proteins that will be identified in the proteomics approach. . The experiments in Aim 3 are focused on the role of kalirin produced by macrophages in atherosclerosis.  These experiments are similar to Aims 2.1 and 2.3, with the exception that a somewhat different pathway is investigated for macrophages, and a kalirin conditional knockout that targets macrophages and granulocytes will be used.  In addition, the potential of kalirin to promote IL-10 production, an immunosuppressive cytokine, will be investigated.  As for Aim 2, these experiments should provide interesting new data regarding pathways used by different cell types in their response to kalirin, and help to identify the molecular and cellular mechanisms involves in the physiological response to kalirin.

Supporting data demonstrating the efficacy and quality of the conditional knockouts would have strengthened those aims.

imp_text: The proposed studies are focused on identifying structural characteristics of the alpha granules in platelets that may be involved in content specific release upon platelet activation.  While the investigators and the instrumentation available to conduct the proposed studies are both considered outstanding, the significance of the findings as they apply to our understanding of platelet function is not well developed.  The importance of the structural studies is clear, but the lack of mechanistic studies combined with a biological component to link the structural findings to the function of the platelet is a weakness.  The study of platelets from the knockout mice is a strong addition to these studies, but some data indicating that the mouse platelets are structurally and functionally similar to the human platelets upon which the preliminary data is based would strengthen their inclusion into the proposal. Strengths • Investigators track records, and the instrumentation available to conduct the proposed studies. • Focus of the proposal on expanding our understanding of platelet function. Weaknesses • Proposal would be strengthened by the inclusion of data indicating that there is content specific release of proteins from platelet and/or platelet granules after activation. • Lack of functional data and proposed biological functional studies to complement the structural studies.

study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is an emerging threat that causes severe disease in humans and is fatal in 5-80% of cases despite modern medical facilities.  CCHFV has spread in Europe, Asia, and Africa and is an increasing threat to the US.  No treatments or vaccines for CCHFV are approved.  This proposal seeks to further characterize a recently proposed virulence factor of CCHFV, the viral homologue of the ovarian tumor protease (vOTU), which appears to impair host interferon response through its deubiquitinating and/or deISGylating activities.  The PI, Dr. Kelly is a new investigator that has formed a significant collaboration with co-investigator, Dr. Berrigan at the CDC who can perform proposed studies using CCHFV in a BSL4 environment.  Drs. Kelly and Berrigan separately accomplished the key preliminary work that has inspired this proposal and made it possible - namely solving crystal structures of vOTUs from CCHFV and another nairovirus (Dugbe) bound to ubiquitin as well as establishing a reverse genetics system to study CCHFV.  Therefore, they have the skills and expertise needed to succeed in accomplishing the multidisiplinary aims in this proposal.  If successful, this effort will significantly characterize vOTUs as virulence factors and illuminate the mechanism by which they evade host immunity.  Such insights could lead to identification of theraputic or prophylactic measures against CCHFV.
sig_text_str: • The experiments will test the hypotheses that variable vOTU substrate specificity for UB and ISG15 affect disease severity.  More fully establishing this link would be a major advance as it would solidify vOTUs as virulence factors and provide a target for drug and/or vaccine candidates. • Aim 1 is carefully designed to explore nariovirus vOTU sequence diversity on deubiqitinating  and deISGylating activities. • Aim 2 seeks to define the relative contribution of these activities in subverting host innate immunity.

study_section: Virology A Study Section
imp_text: This is a new R01 application by a new investigator to establish the structure, dynamics, and funciton of polio virus (PV) RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) by using NMR to “watch” conformational rearrangements in solution.  The PI published postdoctoral work focused on using NMR to study conformational dynamics of a different enzyme (dihydrofolate reductase), and he has already published findings on “Long-range interaction networks in the function and fidelity of poliovirus RNA-dependent RNA polymerase studied by nuclear magnetic resonance.”  The PI’s successes in this area to date provide confidence that his group will be able to accomplish the aims of this proposal.  Since structure and dynamics are highly conserved among RdRps, the concepts learned from the proposed studies will be genarally applicable to RNA viruses.  RdRp conservation also makes it an attractive broad-spectrum antiviral target for vaccines and therapeutics.  Factors influencing RdRp fidelity will be explored with the goal of being able to predict attenuating mutations for the rational design of vaccine strains.  Additionally, the basis for chain termination by nucleoside analog drug candidates currently in development for HCV, but that have broad-spectrum potential, will be explored to aid further development of these antiviral compounds.
sig_text_str: • This ambitious proposal is to elucidate all conformational states, including transitions for PV RdRp using NMR coupled with enzyme kinetics. • The wealth of information on a critical enzyme highly-conserved among all RNA viruses will be of high utility for vaccine and drug design. • Targeting RdRp is a potential universal antiviral strategy.

study_section: Virology B Study Section
imp_text: The PI has a long-standing interest in how many viruses suppress host antiviral responses, and has pioneered work showing the VSV M protein is the major inhibitor of gene expression in VSV infected cells.  This excellent proposal combines the best new ideas generated from multiple past NIH awards that funded similar work and were used to generate extensive initial data.  These data have been described in a manuscript in revision for publication in PLoS Pathogens.  This proposal will explore the mechanism of how VSV M protein couples transcription, mRNA transport, and translation to effect “host shut-off.”  As noted, these are fundamental cell biological processes that are likely important for other viruses and cellular processes that affect gene expression. As such, the proposed work has significant potential to influence several fields.  Furthermore, specific novel models will be tested that challenge and seek to shift current thinking on the mechanisms of host shut off for VSV as well as the function of several host RNA-binding proteins.  Minor weakness with the application include a lack of specific future directions and a timeline.  While the two described Aims are detailed and extensive, significant progress toward accomplishing these aims has already been made.  For a 5 year application, it would have been helpful to get a timeline and more of a glimpse of the PI’s vision for where this project will ultimately lead.
sig_text_str: • As noted by the applicant, descrepancies exist in the literature as to the extent to which VSV blocks nuclear-cytoplasmic transport.  If successful, the experiments proposed in Aim 1 will considerably resolve these discrepancies. • Aim 1 will also clarify the role of Rae1 as well as how hnRNPs respond to VSV infection, which may be applicable to other viruses and forms of cellular stress. • The M-Rae1 complex models suggested by the applicant’s data will be tested and has the potential to significantly influence thinking in the field. • Advanced methods such as RIP-Chip/RIP-Seq and PAR-CLIP will be used along with proteomics approaches to generate large amounts of data on multiple proteins and transcripts involved. • Aim 2 will test the “relocalization of hnRNPs hypothesis” as a mechanism of coupling the steps influencing protein expression in VSV infected cells.  The effects of both host and viral proteins will be explored

study_section: Atherosclerosis and Inflammation of the Cardiovascular System Study Section
imp_text: This application from three experienced and highly accomplished investigators proposes to use a combination of genetically altered mice and in vitro assays to investigate the cellular and biochemical mechanisms behind PD-1/PD-L1 immunoregulation of myocardial inflammation.  The PIs are leaders in this field, have numerous prior publications and collaborations and are likely to continue this success.  Strengths of this proposal include the unique mouse models that will be developed and the basic need for further understanding of inflammatory pathways contributing various pathologies of the heart.  The experiments are very well planned and take full advantage of collaborative resources between the investigators.  But there are several weaknesses to this proposal.  Many of the PIs’ conclusions will rely too heavily on genetically modified mouse models, which may not bear clinical relevancy.  There is a lack of innovation in the approach, and new methodologies exist that could enhance the proposed work.  Furthermore, the PI already has significant NIH funding for a project investigating PD-L1-expressing cells in myocardial inflammation. Although funds may be better spent on PI’s with different and more innovative approaches to this research, it is highly likely that this experienced team will produce impactful results.  Overall, this is an exceptional team for the proposed work in an excellent research environment, and although the team could benefit from more innovative approaches or a younger collaborator, this work is likely to have a high impact on the understanding of myocardial inflammation and may result in novel therapeutic strategies.
sig_text_str: . The PD-1/PD-L1 pathway is indeed very understudied in terms of myocardial inflammation . The expression of PD-1 by macrophages and monocytes remains an unanswered question . A variety of pathologies could benefit from a better understanding of the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway . Enhanced Treg generation via PD-1/PD-L1 based therapies could be beneficial for a variety of other inflammatory disorders in addition to myocardial inflammation, including diabetes, atherosclerosis, multiple sclerosis etc. . The investigators have an extensive expertise and history of achievement in the area of PD-1/PD-L1 immunoregulation
sig_text_wkn: . There are several other investigators currently working in this area . It is likely that the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway will have to be combined with other therapeutic targets to achieve clinical efficacy

PI’s Washington, Schaffer and Frazier all have an extensive history of publishing together and their labs are likely very accustomed to their collaboration . The individual expertise and mouse models of each PI are nicely complementary for this proposal

inn_text_str: . The PI’s will develop unique knockout mouse models to carry out the proposed work . The idea of modulating cytokines to ameliorate myocardial inflammation is relatively novel concept that has not been proposed by many others

Very little detail was written in this section of the proposal . Other than mouse models, no novel methodologies or technologies will be developed for this work that could benefit other investigators . Regulation of cardiac inflammation via PD-L1 is not innovative, and has been the focus of work by other groups for several years prior
app_text_str: . Investigators will build upon their previous work using methods that have been successful for them in the past . Experiments are very thorough and well planned to investigate specific cell populations . Key collaborators have been carefully selected to probe specific questions . Excellent combinations of in vitro and in vivo work to probe mechanisms
app_text_wkn: . Too heavily reliant on new mouse models, which can be time consuming to optimize and may not work as planned.  Furthermore, the majority of the proposed mouse models have not been previously developed . It is not always clear how quantitative data will be obtained from in vivo experiments, for example, when comparing multiple doses of T cells to assess myocardial inflammation.  How they will assess the extent of myocardial inflammation for comparison and determine statistical significance is not described, and these experiments can be subjective . Many experiments are “hit or miss”, as in very little will be learned if experiments do not go as planned or if the proposed hypothesis is not observed . Experiments could benefit from newer strategies.  For example, three separate molecules for cytokine therapy are proposed. A highthrougput in vitro screen of these molecules in different combinations and concentrations coupled with RNAseq would allow more extensive characterization of cell modulation as well as direct the selection of dosages for in vivo testing.

imp_text: This application from a junior investigator aims to improve the mechanistic understanding of the crosstalk between Ca2+ and oxidative stress and how this influences global arterial function and dysfunction. They are specifically probing the mutual connections of these signaling pathways to mitochondrial ROS and plasmalemmal cavaeolae, which is based upon a unique model that they have developed over several years that is in need of validation.  A combination of TIRF imaging and the administration of therapeutically relevant small molecule activators that influence arterial function is employed to test this model.  The PI presents a combination of novel in vitro techniques with well-designed in vivo rat models that will likely generate useful data regardless of whether the proposed models or hypotheses are supported.  The use of multiple independent approaches of both low and medium risk, suggests that the proposed work is highly likely to generate useful data with a possibility of having medium to high impact on the field.  The environment is excellent for the outlined experiments, and the junior PI has enlisted the expertise of multiple local co-investigators for assistance when necessary.  This proposal may have significant impact on the understanding of arterial dysfunction in several important diseases, may lead to a better mechanistic understanding of as well new applications for commonly used therapeutics (mainly statins), and may produce new TIRF-based methods of imaging and assessing Ca2+/ROS signaling.  A weakness of the proposal is that while the data may lead to a better understanding of the Ca2+/ROS pathway, the relevance of this model to pathophysiological processes will be difficult to confirm and may be inconclusive.  Extrapolating results from single cell in vitro experiments to whole tissue function will neglect contributions from a wide range of cell populations and signaling pathways. imp_text: This proposal and subaward intend to address central questions concerning the specificity of the bioresponsive mechanisms of platelets.  In particular the basic question of whether platelets randomly release cargo from their alpha-granules or have context-appropriate responses has yet to be answered. Platelets are a critical yet understudied component of blood capable of releasing hundreds of different proteins, and improved understanding of their mechanisms of function may lead to novel therapeutic targets and strategies.  The PI and co-investigator are senior researchers, and they will comprise a team with extensive experience and expertise in intracellular vesicle trafficking/fusion as well as the diverse imaging techniques that are proposed to investigate platelet alpha-granules.  A combination of electron tomography, immunogold labeling, and super-resolution light microscopy will be employed along with several strategic knockout models.  Investigators provide complimentary expertise and their locations in separate institutes and mutual expenses justify the use of a subaward.  The environment is excellent for this work, in particular since the PI has extensive access to cutting-edge microscopy that was recently funded by his own large NSF award.  The co-investigator is an expert and pioneer in understanding vesicle fusion events, with genetically modified mouse models that nicely complements the PI’s expertise in microscopy and imaging.   Since such a large and vital component of blood remains poorly understood, and the investigators have previously demonstrated their expertise with the proposed methods, it is likely that this proposal will be low risk within a medium to high impact on the field. Very basic unanswered questions necessary for therapeutic modulation of platelet function will be addressed . Preliminary data suggests a similarity in alpha-granule organization and protein zoning between platelets with organelles (Weibel-Palade bodies) in other well-studied cell types. This is an important problem as these factors and their dysfunction contributes to aneuploidy and human disease.  The proposal is highly innovative in that it takes an integrated approach using a combination of biochemical, biophysical, and genetic techniques to characterize components of the monopolin and synaptonemal complexes participating in meiosis I. The proposal is from a young investigator with a strong track record and a high probability for success as an independent investigator who is well versed in the methodologies needed to make major impacts on the field.  The environment at the Ludwig Cancer Institute at the University of San Diego is ideal for this integrated approach to a complex biological problem.

imp_text: The long-term goal of the proposal is to understand the role of the minor U12-dependent spliceosome in the disease microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type I (MOPD 1).  This work is important not only for the rare disease MOPD 1 but also for the growing links between mutations in spliceosomal components and human leukemias.  The studies will analyze mutations identified in MOPD 1 patients for their effects on splicing as well as downstream processes affected by any changes in the spliceosomal machinery.  The last aim will investigate single nucleotides polymorphisms in snRNAs identified in population studies for their effects on U12-dependent splicing.  The studies are innovative in the sense that more information will be gained on the role of U12-dependent splicing in human disease. The most innovative aspect of these studies is in using transcriptome analysis to identify downstream processes affected by mutations in components of the U12-dependent spliceosome to better equate underlying genetic changes with disease phenotype.  The major concern with this proposal lies in aim 3 where the significance of studies on SNPs found in the general population is largely unknown.  The PI is a senior investigator who made major contributions to the splicing field early in her career and still publishes regularly in high profile journals.

imp_text: The goal of the proposed study is to examine early steps in the biogenesis of the yeast 40S ribosomal subunit focusing on factors involved in mediating the interactions of U3 snoRNA with 90S pre-ribosomal particles.  These are fundamental studies on the molecular processes involving some of the myriad of factors that transiently associate with pre-ribosomal particles during ribosome biogenesis.  At present, these studies have little impact on human health though the PI states that these studies will set the stage for investigators carrying out translational research, thus somewhat diminishing the significance of the work.  While the proposed studies will provide a detailed characterization of the roles of several factors involved in early steps in 40S subunit biogenesis, the proposal has relatively limited innovation.  The PI is a senior investigator with a strong publication record in high profile journals.

imp_text: The overall focus of this project is on the regulation of T cells.  Strengths of the project include the importance of this area, the long term productivity of the PI, and the sound design of many of the experiments.  The weaknesses include the lack of important preliminary data (which is simply referred to as “data not shown”), the lack of important details on bioinformatics in one key study, and the overly ambitious approach with inclusion of Aim 4, which extends beyond the focus of the overall goals of this proposal.

sig_text_wkn: . The lack of key preliminary data makes it difficult in some cases to determine if the plans are ideal for this proposed studies.
