inn_text_str: . The PI states that the innovation is not technical, but rather in the integration of several concepts to contribute to T cell activation, survival, and memory.  This is a valid statement to some extent.
inn_text_wkn: . Integrating transcription, metabolism, differentiation, and immunity is a sound approach, but not exclusive to this proposal.
app_text_str: . The PI makes a strong case for most aspects of this project, assuming that the “data now shown” is indeed as stated. . The overall concept of integrating gene expression, metabolomics, differentiation, and immunity studies is a strength of this project. . Many of the studies are well-developed. . Discussions of possible outcomes are well-reasoned.
app_text_wkn: . Aims 1, 2, and 3 are integrated and focused on the overall objectives of this proposal.  The addition of Aim 4 is more peripheral to the objectives of this project and creates an overly ambitious project for a 5 year plan.  Aims 1, 2, and 3 have 11 components and Aim 4 adds an additional 3 components.  It is difficult to determine how all of this can be accomplished in the absence of a timeline, which is lacking in this proposal. . The other major weakness of this proposal is the lack of providing key preliminary data in support of the chosen directions.  While it is a fact that space is limited in these applications, the writing style is overly verbose and the inclusion of a recitation of vaccines in human history totally unnecessary.  A more concise and focus application will leave room for supplying needed preliminary data to provide support for the planned study designs. . The plans to monitor the success of adaptive transfers are not provided.  This is important since, as the PI states, small numbers of T cells can work effectively. . In Aim 2a, no plans for bioinformatics is presented.  There will be a massive amount of data generated and whether anything meaningful will be forthcoming requires a careful and considered systematic approach for prioritization and processing. . The PI states that Cd4-Cre and Foxo1 are genetically linked with an expected recombination rate of just 2%.  This makes the success of this study unlikely without a massive breeding plan, requiring enormous amounts of funding, which does not seem to be a component of this modular budget, given the scope of the rest of this proposal.  It would be more effective to generate a new Cre model on a different chromosome. . Little consideration is given to potential obstacles/problems and how they will be addressed.

imp_text: The goal of this project is to determine the role of loss of catalase in thymic stromal tissue on age-related atrophy.  The central hypothesis is that epithelial stromal cells of the thymus are sensitive to Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) damage because of exzynme deficiencies related to preventing and repairing ROS damage including catalase and Super Oxide Dismutases (SODs) and that thymic atrophy is a consequence of accelerated accumulation of metabolic damage.  Four aims are proposed.  Aim 1 will test the hypothesis that selection correction of catalase deficiency in thymic epithelial stromal cells rescues thymic atrophy.  Aim 2 tests the hypothesis that these epithelial cells accumulate more oxidative lesions in vivo than other tissues.  Aim 3 will examine the in vitro responses to ROS of thymic and other tissue epithelial tissues.  Aim 4 expands to examine the impacts of other gene changes related to repair of ROS protections.  Strengths of the application include the significance of the research problem and innovative hypothesis for the cause of thymic atrophy.  The inclusion of strong published and preliminary data supporting reduced catalase expression and the consequences of forced expression of catalase on thymic atrophy are additional strengths.  The PI and research environment for this project are also outstanding.  Many of the planned experiments are strong and will test the proposed hypotheses.  Weaknesses include the overly ambitious scope in Aim 4 with the limited planned personnel, some lack of experimental plans or insufficient development of some plans, confusion with some of the preliminary data, and the lack of a true test of the overarching hypothesis.  These weaknesses are sufficient to greatly reduce enthusiasm for this project as proposed in spite of the potential importance of these studies.

imp_text: Immune metabolism is an emerging area or interest.  This is proposal that weaves together several threads related to the role of FoxO proteins in immune metabolism and in CD8 memory development: first, the proposal aims to examine the role of FoxO and metabolism in the development of CD8 T-cell memory.  Second, understanding the development of CD8 T-cell memory at a systems level in FoxO-intact and FoxO-KO mouse. Third, to determine the role of FoxO1 and FoxO3 in the development of Tfh and central memory T-cells.  Finally, the PI proposes to examine the memory response to persistent infection (LCMV-clone 13 and mHV-68) in the context of WT and FoxO mutant mice.  The strengths of the proposal are that the proposed aims are focused on the role of FoxO. The questions are relevant and experimental approach addresses the stated goals of the proposal and are logically presented.  There are three main weaknesses: first, the studies are large in scope and broad.  It’s not clear if this laboratory can complete the proposed studies in the time and funds allotted. For instance, the ChIP-seq experiments will require more time to complete and interpret than anticipated (a time line would have helped). Aim 4 is also an example where the complexities of the experiments are overly simplified.  Second, the proposal lacks any anticipated results, what the outcomes of the proposed experiments are and how each of the outcomes may be interpreted.  Additionally, while in some case contingency plans are provided, pitfalls and alternative approaches are not consistently given.  Finally, many of the experiments proposed have been already published at the time this proposal was submitted, so real novelty is lacking, or differentiation between published and proposed experiments is not well documented.

imp_text: This proposal examines the role of catalase (Cat) in thymic atrophy.  Four hypotheses/aims are proposed focused around the mechanisms that lead to atrophy. First, the PI hypothesizes that that thymic epithelial cells (TEC) are deficient in Cat; the PI will overexpress Cat in the TEC to assess if these mice are protected from thymic atrophy. Second, Cat deficiency leads to more ROS and damage; this will be tested using biophysical methods and microscopy.  Third, that TEC are more sensitive to ROS-induced damage. The PI will use Comet assay with titration of H2O2.  Finally, the PI proposes that in the absence of repair enzymes Cat deficiency is exacerbated. To this end, they will measure the ability of TEC (or control cells not deficient in CAT) to repair damage caused by peroxide.  Overall, the studies are well controlled; the presentation of experiments is clear and logical.  Collaborations are documented for assays not currently in the PI’s lab.  Extensive preliminary data for the hypothesis is provided.  The only minor weakness is that Aim 4 is dependent on Aim 3 and therefore these should be a single aim.  A second minor weakness is that the PI raises the question of why thymic atrophy occurs post-puberty in the significance section, but this aspect is not addressed to any extent in the proposal (cf. Chekov’s gun).  While understanding of the mechanisms that lead to thymic atrophy is interesting, both humans (and other mammals) survive for a significant part of their life without their thymi and no evolutionary pressure apparently exists to maintain the thymi past puberty. A translational perspective and increasing the novel/innovative aspect to the proposal would increase enthusiasm.

imp_text: This application aims to understand how Foxo family of transcription factors affects the program of T lymphocyte differentiation and memory – a fundamental question with high significance in immunology and immune diseases. The strengths include the conceptual integration of gene transcription, metabolism, differentiation and immunity, as well as the technical rigor using several mouse genetic and disease models. The approach is comprehensive in such way that the Foxo transcription factors are studied in the context of other important signaling networks, transcriptional programs, and metabolic landscape. The PI and collaborators have extensive expertise in T cell biology and Foxo family. The environment at UCSD is outstanding. Moderate/minor weaknesses include: the proposal is somewhat diffused and unfocused, with several important questions asked, and many mouse models involved; the experimental tools and methods are also standard; preliminary data are supportive but not exceptionally strong.

imp_text: Elucidation of the regulatory mechanisms that govern germinal center formation and antibody production is essential to understanding clinical immunodeficiencies and autoimmune disorders. This application proposes to define the role of the actin-bundling protein L-plastin in integrating the chemotactic and adhesive cues essential for B cell motility and germinal center formation. The PI is an early stage investigator but has established several collaborators with expertise in various aspects to ensure the success of the proposed studies. The three aims laid out comprehensive sets of experiments with complementary approaches to assess the mechanisms of LPL actions in B-cells: structural functional relationship, interaction with integrin-signaling complex, and roles in B-cell activation, survival and activity. Wash U is an excellent environment with strong support for immunology research. Minor to moderate weaknesses: 1) LPL-specific disease relevance and translational strategy are not well discussed; 2) inadequate personnel effort because only two research technicians were listed to complete the studies in addition to the PI himself; 3) a minor weakness in innovation since the essential role of LPL in T and B cell motility upon chemokine stimulation has already been described and published; 4) several concerns in Approach are noted: In Aim 1, the bone marrow chimeras experiment only adopts a small percentage (2.5%) of viral injected cells, which will make phenotype characterization and interpretation difficult. At least for the functionally important mutations, knock-in mice will be more desired strategies. LPL mutants have not been characterized in vitro. In Aim 2, confocal microscopy and co-IP will only test whether LPL is in the same integrin-signaling complex, but not test whether there is direct interaction, and which protein is the direct interacting partner. Mutagenesis or pull-down experiments with recombinant proteins would be needed.
sig_text_str: • Elucidation of the regulatory mechanisms that govern germinal center (GC) formation and antibody production is essential to understanding clinical immunodeficiencies and autoimmune disorders. • Identifying key regulators of GC formation is essential for the correct diagnosis and treatment of patients presenting with recurrent infections. • Effective vaccine development requires a more detailed understanding of mechanisms leading to long-lived production of high affinity, neutralizing antibodies.
sig_text_wkn: . From translation point of view, since LPL plays important roles in several immune cell types such as T cell and neutrophils, it is unclear how LPL can be specifically targeted pharmacologically. . It is also not thoroughly discussed how LPL links to immunological diseases.

inn_text_str: • This application will dissect a unique model of dysregulation of actin dynamics that impairs GC B cell development and T-dependent antibody production. • This proposal will identify a new mechanistic link between chemokine receptor and integrin signaling critical for B lymphocyte motility. • This work will generate new mouse genetic models including LPL flox mice and B-cell specific LPL knockout mice. . This study will also establish new lentiviral constructs for in vivo mutational analysis of LPL using chimeric mice.
inn_text_wkn: . The essential role of LPL in T and B cell motility upon chemokine stimulation has already been described and published, thus conceptually less novel. This proposal will further dissect the mechanisms for how LPL functions in B cells and GC formation.

Two-photon microscopy will be used to measure in vivo B cell motility, including intranodal velocity, motility coefficient, and meandering index. . In Aim 2, a series of approaches will be employed to characterize whether LPL affects signaling upstream of Pyk2 phosphorylation, modulates formation of integrin-associated signaling complexes, and interacts directly or indirectly with integrin-associated signaling complex. These approaches are comprehensive and complementary. . In Aim 3, a series of experiments will be performed to determine whether B cell LPL KO mice are defective in B cell activation and maturation, generation of mammery B cell and long-lived plasma B cells, and clearance of west nile virus. These experiments extend previous published work to further define the functions of LPL in B cell regulation.

imp_text: It is important to understand the dynamic interactions and molecular mechanisms underlying hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) differentiation in bone marrow (BM), and how BM stromal cells impact hematopoietic precursors and shape lineage specification. This proposal will test the hypothesis that 1) CXCR4 is required for mesenchymal stem cell maintenance and/or differentiation into bone marrow stromal cells that express IL-7 and CXCL12 and critically support B cell development; 2) CXCR4 in lymphoid progenitors is also required for B cell development by guiding their position and movement towards IL-7 producing stromal cells; 3) CXCR4 also modulates B cell negative selection in BM by controlling the positioning of autoreactive immature B cells in BM niches so that IL-7 promotes lymphocyte survival and receptor editing. imp_text: The proposed project examines an important developmental niche and seeks to elucidate cellular communication between bone marrow stromal cells and developing B cells that ultimately control immune responses and/or lead to autoimmunity. The strengths of the proposal lie in the significance and potential impact to the field, innovative methodology, and strong New/Early Stage principal investigator. The proposal, at times, uses the PI’s expertise to develop creative methods to examine specific questions. Weaknesses include a number of descriptive subaims and an apparent divergence from the type of detailed experimental design praised above as a strength, with Aim 3D serving as an example of both. Some of the aims, while highly descriptive, would nonetheless be informative and beneficial to researchers in the field. Overall, this proposal is highly coherent as a comprehensive set of hypotheses and experiments, involves an investigator with this the background and expertise to succeed in the completion of the Aims, and could significantly impact the field.

CXCR4 is the target of an existing clinical agent (AMD3100) and so extended knowledge of the full role of CXCR4 in the BM is attractive.

imp_text: Based on the preliminary results showing that Foxo transcription factors (TFs) control the expansion, activation phenotype and localization of CD4 and CD8 T cells, the applicant hypothesizes that Foxo TFs play a central role in the formation of memory T cells. The applicant will study the role of Foxo TFs in the control of bioenergetics and CD8 memory (Aim 1), profile genes regulated by Foxo TFs in CD8 T cells (Aim 2); study follicular helper T cells (Tfh) and CD4 central memory precursors (Aim 3) and the role of Foxo TFs in the progression of viral disease models (Aim 4). Strengths of the application include the expertise of the investigator, the environment and the research topic. However, this proposal has several major weaknesses, which include the poor articulation of the rationale of the studies, the lack of hypothesis-driven experiments, the poor narrative and the lack of focus. Therefore, the enthusiasm for this proposal is low.

study_section: Cellular and Molecular Immunology B Study Section
imp_text: Preliminary observations from the PI’s lab show that thymic epithelial stromal cells (TEC) are deficient in several key enzymes that protect cells from damage by metabolic by-products, including catalase. Genetic replacement of catalase for example prevents or delays thymic atrophy. The PI hypothesizes that early thymic atrophy is caused by an accelerated accumulation of the canonical lesions of metabolic damage, due to innate deficiency in catalase. He will test the hypotheses that selective correction of catalase deficiency in thymic stromal cells rescues thymic atrophy (Aim 1), TEC accumulate more oxidative lesions in vivo than other (control) cells from age/tissue-matched mice (Aim 2), TEC are more sensitive to ROS-mediated damage than epithelial cells from other age-matched tissues (Aim 3), and secondary deficiencies in oxidative damage repair mechanisms exacerbate the stromal effects of catalase deficiency (Aim 4). Strengths of the application include the excellent narrative, the expertise of the PI in the area of the proposed studies, the quality of the preliminary data and the excellence of the research environment. If successful, these studies will advance the knowledge on the mechanisms of thymic atrophy, thus highlighting the significance of this proposal. Weaknesses include the modest innovation and the use of standard experimental approaches. However, these weaknesses are minor, and do not dampen the high enthusiasm for this project.

imp_text: Preliminary data from this early stage new investigator indicate that CXCR4 is expressed by non-hematopoietic bone marrow cells in mouse. The PI therefore hypothesizes that CXCR4 is required for mesenchymal stem cell maintenance and/or differentiation into stromal cells that support B cell development. The PI also hypothesizes that CXCR4 in lymphoid progenitors is important for the development of B lymphocyte precursors towards IL-7 producing cells, and B cell receptor editing. Thus, the applicant will characterize the role played by CXCR4 in non-hematopoietic bone marrow cells (Aim 1), determine the mechanisms controlling common lymphoid progenitor positioning in bone marrow (Aim 2), and characterize the mechanisms and dynamics of B cell negative selection in bone marrow (Aim 3). Strengths of the proposal include the expertise of the investigator, the significance of the research, the experimental approaches and the innovation. Additional strengths include the preliminary data that support the feasibility of the project. However, there are concerns that the proposal is too ambitious and may not yield substantial advances. The organization and narrative of the proposal are also areas of concerns. These are minor weaknesses, which are outweighed by the strengths.  Thus, the enthusiasm for this research is high.

imp_text: This proposal is aimed at determining the role of actin-bundling protein L-Plastin (LPL) on B cell mobility. Such information is valuable for the understanding of germinal center development during humoral immunity. Mentorship and research environment are strong. Equipment and facilities are adequate. However, the proposed study has some redundancy with the previous work or preliminary results of the PI, and the purpose of the study is less focused and based on multiple fragmented hypothesis. The general impression about the proposal is exploratory in nature without a clear, specific hypothesis. It is overly ambitious to attempt to “clearly define the role of LPL in B cell motility, GC development and T-dependent antibody generation.” Furthermore, it is not quite clear whether Dr. Sullivan is able to complete the whole project independently given her publication record and personnel composition.

imp_text: This is a well written proposal addressing an important issue of immune system development, thymus atrophy and subsequent compromised immune responses. It is novel to propose stromal tissue mechanism as potential therapy to amend this condition without directly targeting the immune cells. Dr. Murphy has been studying thymus immunobiology for 20 years with sufficient experience and strong publication record. The research environment of Scripps is superb and adequate enough to take on the project. There is some moderate concerns about the tissue extraction techniques for TEC isolation and the workload of the single postdoc to be named to complete the proposed research since they are unique and technically sensitive (Particularly Aim 2).

imp_text: The proposed project is aimed at determining role of CXCR4 on B cell development and selection in bone marrow (BM). It is an important field in hematopoietic cell differentiation particularly with respect to the development of central tolerance as well as auto-immunity. The study has solid background support and techniques applied merit certain novelty. It is a natural continuation of the work done by PI and colleagues. However, the multiple central hypotheses and overly ambitious designs make the proposal less focused and confusing about what is the overall goal of the project. The main work proposed is narrowed to flow cytometry and imaging analysis of stromal and immune cell numbers from large number of transgenic lines and lack of real mechanistic investigation of cellular and molecular features and interactions between CXCR4 and IL-7 in BM that are the driving force for B cell mobility and differentiation. Some proposed experiments are also duplicative of previously documented results from the PI and colleagues.
sig_text_str: . The proposal discuss a significant question related to hematopoietic cell differentiation in BM testing how CXCR4 shapes the stromal niche and provide IL-7 to facilitate B cell development. The results obtained can be critical in providing a basis for understanding how guidance cues shape the BM stromal cell compartment and influence cell lineage decisions.
sig_text_wkn: . Too many hypotheses are proposed and tend to lose the focus of the goal. It is not clear whether the PI is investigating B cell immunity (as indicated by title) or the bone marrow biology as a whole. . While not focusing on a B cell-specific goal, the proposed research may lead to contradicting results with respect to the role of CXCR4. . The study is widely diffused and overly ambitious by examining non-hematopoietic cells, hematopoietic pro-genitor cells and B cells in separate Aims, involving 15 transgenic lines.

For example, Fig.4 showed that the CXCR4 controls B-lineage cell migration in BM, which is the essential goal for Aim2A. • Aim 1A, a great number of subsets (HSCs, LMPPs, CLPs, CMPs, GMPs, MEPs) are counted by flow cytometry as an indication of stromal defect in CXCR4-deficient mice. Also, myeloid cell subsets (neutrophils, dendritic cells, and inflammatory and patrolling monocyte subsets), B and T lymphocytes, NK cells, developing erythrocyte progenitors in BM and peripheral lymphoid organs (blood, spleen, peripheral and mesenteric lymph nodes, peritoneal cavity and peyer's patch) will be counted. It is concerned that whether isolation of all these tissue and cells are manageable and whether the amount of tissue isolated is adequate to analyze so many cells. • Aim 1B, according to the proposal, the PI will analyze “mice 6-8 weeks after reconstitution by flow cytometry in order to enumerate B-lineage cells, T-lineage cells, myeloid cell populations (predominantly dendritic cells, neutrophils and monocyte subsets) in primary and secondary lymphoid organs, and developing erythrocyte subsets (nucleated CD71+ Ter119+ cells) in BM”. Substantial amount of animals will be involved in this experiment and no details regarding isolation and number of cells that will be reconstituted and whether sufficient amount of cells for each of these subsets can be obtained. • Aim 2A, analysis of common lymphoid progenitors (CLP) in this subaim cannot represent the effect of IL-7 on B cells. Therefore it is not clear what’s the relevance of this subaim to development of B cells. • Aim 2B, the genes selected (E2A, EBF, FOXO1, and PAX5) are not B cell specific and participate other cellular developments such as T cells. It is not stringent enough to predict B cell fate by the measurement of mRNA expression of these genes in purified Ly6D- and Ly6D+ CLPs. • Aim 3 mostly involves use of microscopic imaging to determine the dynamics of B cell negative selection in BM but claiming its goal as finding mechanism of how central tolerance is regulated is an overstatement. Too many hypotheses are raised in this Aim. • Details about how imaging results can be quantitatively analyzed and statistical analysis performed are missing. • Justification of animals is not adequate. With an average of 1500 mice per year, 15 transgenic lines, and the concern of the stability of two graduate students as the main driving force of the project, it is not clear whether all the aims can be completed in the proposed time frame.

imp_text: This R01 application is a new submission from Drs. Jamal Washington and Reagan Spindler to investigate the regulation of the IFN antiviral response by viral and host proteins. Their groups have found that the ns2 protein from the murine coronavirus (mouse hepatitis virus, MHV) facilitates the development of hepatitis by blocking the 2’,5’-oligoadenylate (2-5A) synthetase (OAS)-RNase L pathway in macrophages. ns2 has 2’,5’-phosphodiesterase(2’,5’-PDE) activity that down-regulates intracellular levels of 2-5A. High levels of 2-5A trigger RNase L activity and the antiviral response. In this application, these groups will attempt to further define the role of ns2, cellular 2’,5’-PDEs and RNase L in this pathway in turn forwarding our understanding of viral mechanisms of pathogenesis and host defense. This proposal is broken down into three aims that look at this pathway from both the perspective of primary tissue culture and their previously developed mouse models. In Aim 1, the investigators will compare the activation of RNase L in liver sinusoidal and parenchymal cells by wild-type and ns2 defective MHV. The results will be compared with the pathogenesis observed in the mice with specific ablations of IFNAR or RNase L. In Aim 2, new viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs will be identified and their role in supporting viral replication will be assessed. A subset of this aim is to identify potential 2’,5’-PDE inhibitors via high-throughput screens based on the investigators previously developed L protein activity assay (and further assessed in vivo in Aim 3). Aim 3 will assess subcellular localization and the mechanism of action of ns2 2’,5’-PDE activity. Additionally, the pro-viral/RNase antagonist activity of 2’,5’-PDEs of cellular or viral origin will be determined with the use of chimeric coronaviruses. The application is based on strong preliminary data from two PIs with a combined six decades of experience on these topics. The proposed research has a potential to have significant impact on our understanding of the 2-5A-OAS-RNase L pathway and it’s place in viral pathogenesis and the antiviral cellular cascade. For this reason there is enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: . Mouse hepatitis virus infection of mice serves as a model system for the study of virus-induced hepatitis. . Virus-host interactions that determine whether an infection is established are critical to our development of new antiviral strategies. . Viral (MHV ns2 or rotavirus VP3) and host (AKAP7) proteins that share 2’,5’­phosphodiesterase activity could be targets of inhibitors geared toward accumulation of 2­5A in the cell, a situation that leads to activation of the RNase L and subsequent activation of the host antiviral pathway. . Such inhibitors could form the basis for new anti-viral therapeutics and/or diagnostic tools.

imp_text: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is a bunyavirus in the nairovirus genus and is the causative agent of serious human disease (causing fever and hemorrhages) and having a fatality rate range from 5-80% depending on quality of care. Other nairovirus, including Nairobi sheep disease virus (NSDV), as well as Hazara (HAZV), Dugbe (DUGV), and Erve (ERVV) viruses, have less severe outcomes in humans, however result in economic impact in the livestock industry (ex. NSDV). Each of these virus carry an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, called the L protein. The N-terminal region of L from these viruses harbors a viral homologue of the ovarian tumor protease (vOTU). This protease has been implicated in possible down-regulation of the Interferon type 1 immune response through cleavage of post-translational modifying proteins ubiquitin (Ub) and Ub-like interferon-simulated gene 15 (ISG15). For this reason, vOTU has been suggested to be a virulence factor. This application is a new submission by Dr. Brett Walsh, a new investigator with experience as a structural and molecular virology of nairoviruses. This proposal looks at the deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities among nairoviruses vOTU protease domains in vitro and in vivo. Conservation is matched with previous and proposed structural studies (x-ray crystallography and NMR) to yield a better picture of the detailed interaction between vOTU and conjugated mono-and poly-Ub species. These studies will inform mutagenesis studies that will potentially allow tailoring of CCHFV viral pathogenesis to other organisms (ie. human to mouse). All experiments are paralleled by in vitro assays, viral growth kinetics and in some cases mouse studies (with reverse engineered viruses). The proposed experiments spring forward from the previous work of Dr. Walsh and colleagues and the applications provides a nice preliminary data. The results here will have impact on design of new models for monitoring viral pathogenesis and generating systems for inhibitor evaluation in vivo. There is much enthusiasm for this application on a pathogen in a family with new emerging threats.

imp_text: RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RdRPs) are unique, integral proteins to RNA viruses and thus are established targets for antiviral therapeutic design. To this end, newly developed nucleoside analogues have proven to be effective inhibitors in recent studies against HCV. Many structural studies have been performed on RdRPs from positive strand RNA viruses (including poliovirus, PV), however there are limitations to the static structures derived from these x-ray crystallographic studies. Dr. Jay Kelly, a new investigator, provides a new R01 submission with plans to expand on the current database of RdRp structural snapshots by using solution state nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy and molecular dynamics to observe conformational rearrangements of the PV RdRP throughout the nucleotide addition cycle. Whereas the studies could be performed on any RNA virus having an RdRP with a three-dimensional structure, the merit on using PV as their model system is in the wealth of kinetic data that has been compiled by previous investigations. An underlying theme in this proposal is the identification of amino acid residues in the polymerase that generate long range interactions and how these residues are related to modulation of polymerase fidelity. The proposed studies will use differentially-labeled protein in NMR experiments to observe dynamic movements of wild-type and mutant (that are known to increase and decrease RdRP fidelity) RdRP. Structural studies will be complimented with kinetic and cellular inhibition assays. These experiments will be rounded out with an analysis of molecular mechanism of chain termination of recently developed anti-HCV nucleoside analogue. This proposal provides a wealth of preliminary prediction on the expected outcomes of the experiments giving it the appeal of being simply crafted but expected to succeed. The results should extend beyond PV or positive strand viruses, in general, as a roadmap to develop mutant RdRPs for attenuating viruses, as a long-term goal for vaccine design. There is much enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: . Many positive strand RNA viruses are serious human pathogens with no available or poorly profiled therapeutics. RdRPs are active targets for new therapeutic design. . In lieu of good drugs, RdRPs with mutations that affect fidelity could be the basis for designing new vaccine virus strains. . The mechanism of action leading to chain termination by nucleoside analogues (with substitutions beyond the 3’-OH site) in the nucleotide addition reaction is not understood. The studies proposed here could shed light on this, in turn leading to better strategies for designing better more specific inhibitors in the future.

imp_text: The dual goal of this proposal is to continue the development of the BMRB public database by advancing its content, quality and distribution to keep pace with the increased complexity and volume of NMR data being generated by the research community, and to contribute to development of the pdb. Both goals are extremely important as this is a public service that the BMRB has been offering to the research community for decades. This proposal outlines both the impact of the BMRB on the research community and the new developments that will propel the BMRB to play even a wider role. The methods proposed are cutting edge and will keep in pace with the advancements in structural biology. The proposal thus is significant, extremely timely, innovative in proposing novel ways of data usage, validation, retrieval and high throughput submission, and in fills a major gap and plays a unique role in the community as there are no other such databases.

The BMRB as a depository of studies of individual biological systems is a great resource for developing improved forcefields, predictive technologies, and methods for automated data collection and analysis.

They propose biochemical and structural experiments to assay vOTU’s function as deubiquitinating or deISGylating protease. They do present a good amount of preliminary data with the biochemical experiments so there is confidence that they will be successful with these experiments. He also proposed to develop a virus that can infect mice so that they can develop a model in mouse to test therapeutics. The genetic experiments are very nice, but they didn’t do a great job justifying the value of the mouse model. Physiology of mice is very different from humans. imp_text: This proposal focuses on RNA-dependent RNA polymerases (RDRPs) that are key for RNA viruses to replicate. Dr. Walsh proposes to use NMR to study the dynamic conformational changes that occur during nucleotide addition. He plans to use polio virus RDRP as a model and compare it to avirulent strains, like the Sabin strain. They hypothesize that virulence is tied to the polymerase fidelity and that studies of RDRP kinetics will allow them to predict amino acid changes that can serve as the basis for novel vaccine strains. They will also use nucleoside analogs (used against hepatitis virus) to determine how they affect the RDRP function. The strengths include that RDRPs are key for RNA viruses that cause many diseases and characterization of how the nucleoside analogs inhibit RDRP function is pretty interesting. The main weakness from the proposal is the sell on how this will be important for identifying attenuated strains for vaccines and promoting rational design for drugs. It’s not clear that knowing exactly how the RDRP works will actually be more effective in identifying attenuated viruses or if designing drugs based on knowledge of the enzyme function will be more effective than randomly screening small molecules.

imp_text: The PI establishes that the field lacks structural information on CNTs, which limits the knowledge about nucleotide specificity and basic functions. A caveat is that the CNT that will be studied structurally is from V. cholera due to expression and purification challenges with the human form. The molecular mechanisms of both the human and the homolog will be explored to determine how CNTs both recognize and transport their nucleotides and therapeutic analogs. Several issues significantly dampen enthusiasm for the proposal. First, all three aims depend heavily on obtaining a crystal structure, and this has clearly proven enormously challenging so far. It is not clear how the subsequent mutagenesis and models will be guided in the absence of these structures. Second, there is not enough compelling evidence that the vcCNT is a good model for hCNT. Since all aims rely so heavily on structural information from the vcCNT, this is a significant concern. The investigator is a young PI who has been quite productive in her postdoc and has already obtained funding from several foundations. The proposal is clearly written. imp_text: The proposed research has some highly innovative approaches combining a combination of NMR studies with functional cell-based assays to determine structurally-based mechanistic details around the regulation of CLOCK:BMAL1 in both normal cellular and disease processes.  The approach is very sound and the PI and associated team appears highly qualified to perform the research. There is potential for long-term impact from the proposed research.
sig_text_str: . The proposed research should reveal structurally-based mechanistic insights of CLOCK:BMAL1 conformational changes that regulate its transcription factor functions. . The determination of specific protein-protein interactions of CLOCK:BMAL1 with PASM1 and other proteins involved in the regulation of CLOCK:BMAL1 would provide significant interaction information that may be atomically resolved.
sig_text_wkn: . Unclear how the proposed research will directly allow/facilitate the generation of novel therapeutic strategies that reinforce normal circadian rhythm. Future directions that go beyond the scope of the proposal discusses the possibility of developing high-throughput screens for small molecules. . The premise that the slow protein conformational change of CLOCK:BMAL1 is energetically costly is not well-founded.  Most conformational changes are not that energetically costly in contrast to utilizing protein-turnover for regulation. . The premise that PSAD1 is a negative regulator of CLOCK:BMAL1 in not well-cited.  Missing definitive reference: http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1097276515002221 which was not published by the PI or his group, even though it was put forth as preliminary data from his group.
inv_text_str: . While not uniquely qualified for the proposed work, the principal investigator appears highly qualified to apply solution NMR to studying the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex, especially given previous NMR research on the heterodimeric bHLH-PAS transcription factor.
inv_text_wkn: . While the PI has established key and critical collaborations for the proposed research, none of these collaborators are co-Investigators on this proposal.  Also, there is no indication that these are on-going collaborations established prior to this proposal. . A central piece of preliminary data stated in the spec aims (i.e. crystal structure of CLOCK:BMAL1) is really a product of the PI’s postdoctoral mentor’s lab, of which he played a part in the work, but he does not appear to be the central generator of the preliminary data, which is crystallography-based and not NMR-based.
inn_text_str: . There is some innovation in using NMR to study key protein-protein interactions of CLOCK:BMAL1 with normal and disease-causing regulators of its function, given that parts of CLOCK:BMAL1 are unstructured and have resisted previous attempts at crystallization. . The combined peptide and mutation analysis to characterize interactions between CLOCK:BMAL1 and CRY1 and p300 via chemical shift perturbation analysis has some real innovation. . The combination of functional assays with the P625A mutants is innovative in trying to demonstrate the importance of the cis/trans conformational changes in CLOCK:BMAL1 circadian functions.
inn_text_wkn: . The simple description of combining functional assays with NMR structural studies in the “Innovation” section does not demonstrate an innovative synergy.  Luckily, innovation shines through later in the proposal. . NMR is not the best nor easy method for determining thermodynamics of proteins.  Luckily, the proposal later indicates the use of isothermal titration calorimetry will be used. .
app_text_str: . Preliminary NMR data strongly supports the slow exchange model around the P625 that is proposed and the spectra demonstrate feasibility of the proposed NMR studies in Aim 1. The chemical shift perturbation method to identify interacting protein-peptides and to identify the protein/peptide binding interface is very efficient and reasonable in Aim1B.  Have reasonable alternative plan. . Aims 1C and 1D represents a well-thought-out combination of NMR experiments and functional assays to verify the importance of the cis/trans conformational change around P625 and determine the key peptidyl propyl isomerase(s) needed for conformational exchange that enables proper CLOCK:BMAL1 function.  Cited cis/trans antibody paper to support antibody approach. . study_section: Bacterial Pathogenesis Study Section
imp_text: This proposal takes a structural biology approach to understanding the maturation processes that lead to formation of a functional type III secretion system (TSST) in Shigella. The overall focus is on IpaB, with the underlying hypothesis being that this protein, in response to the presence of bile salts, plays a critical intermediary role between tip assembly via IpaD and induction of secretion into host cells via IpaC. The other key component of this process is IpgC, which serves as a chaperone for IpaB and thereby prevents its interaction with itself in a manner that promotes its interaction with IpaD at the needle tip. It is hypothesized that this step-wise progression is likely to be representative of other TSST systems, albeit in response to signals other than bile salts. Thus, Aim 1 uses genetic and biochemical methods to track IpaB as it progresses from the cytoplasm to the needle tip. Aim 2 then examines the crystal structures of IpaB at various stages of its interactions with IpgC and ultimately IpaD. Aim 3 is an extension of Aim 2 in which the investigators will dig deeper to gain a better understanding of specific interactions between all of these components.  Overall, the studies are based on compelling preliminary data, well described, comprehensive, and well within the expertise of the collective investigative team. Based on this, my enthusiasm for this proposal is very high. Having said that, this enthusiasm is dampened somewhat by the fact that all of the proposed experiments are limited to structural biology studies without any attempt to confirm the significance of these studies based on biological correlates. Put another way, the investigators propose extensive studies to define the molecular interactions between all of the “players” in the Shigella TSST system, but they do not describe any experiments to assess the impact of disrupting these interactions on biology (i.e. translocation of effector proteins and invasion of host cells) beyond generic statements such as “phenotype analyses will be used to help in understanding the biochemical findings”.

imp_text: This proposal focuses on Ehrlichia chaffeensis, an obligate intracellular tick-borne pathogen. The authors propose to build on their recent observation that E. chaffeensis utilizes type 1 secretion “nanomachines” to export tandem repeat protein (TRP) effectors that alter multiple host cell processes via both changes in gene expression and epigenetic changes and that these changes ultimately promote the intracellular lifestyle of the bacterium. The have also demonstrated that one of these (TRP120) has very interesting biological properties that include potentially important transport into the nucleus following appropriate modification (ubiquitination and/or sumolyation) and the ability to bind GC-rich host cell DNA sites associated with genes that have a broad impact on host cell transcription. They propose that this is a means of “hijacking host cellular functions to infect, replicate, and evade the host immune response”. The stated hypothesis is that “TRP120 is a dual-function Sp1-like transcription factor that binds regulatory GC-rich motifs and utilizes host Ub and SUMO pathways to obtain PTMs [post-translational modifications] that mediate nuclear localization and gene expression regulatory functions”. Thus, they propose three aims that, generally speaking, focus on 1) defining the mechanism by which TRP120 is translocated into the nucleus in the absence of an identifiable nuclear localization sequence, 2) define the TRP120 amino acids that define its interaction with host cell DNA and the manner and extent to which it acts as a transcription factor impacting host genes, and 3) define the overall extent to which these events impact the phenotype of host cells. Based on the underlying hypothesis, all of these aims are entirely logical, although the proposal is very dense and would have benefited greatly from the inclusion of a model outlining the hypothesized steps in this pathway and how each aim relates to each of these steps. However, this does not detract from the fact that an abundance of preliminary data is presented that supports the individual components of this hypothesis, and thereby the basis for the proposed experiments, or that certain elements of the proposed hypothesis appear to be highly novel. That said, enthusiasm is dampened by the fact that no direct evidence is presented to indicate that any of these events, or for that matter TRP120 itself, does in fact play a role in ehrlichiosis.

imp_text: This is an excellent proposal that addresses the important clinical problem of P. aeruginosa biofilm-associated infections and does so in a comprehensive manner that is well-supported by preliminary data. Importantly, this includes data demonstrating that the system under study, which focuses on the hypothesis that P. aeruginosa can detect and degrade specific host signaling molecules (sphingosine-1-phosphate and its precursor sphingosine) as a means of modulating the host immune response in its favor, does in fact have a significant impact on the ability of P. aeruginosa to cause infection in a murine lung model. In investigate the mechanistic basis for this, the PI proposes to 1) elucidate the manner by which SphR controls sphA and sphBCD induction at the level of DNA binding, substrate specificity, and the downstream effects of sphA and sphBCD induction; 2) identify components of the S1P degradation pathway including identification of the relevant phosphatase(s) that convert S1P to sphingosine and evaluating the hypothesis that SphC and SphD are responsible for sphingosine degradation; and 3) examine the impact of sphingosine degradation on P. aeruginosa infection. Further enthusiasm is generated by the fact that this signaling system has not been well characterized but appears to be conserved among diverse microbial pathogens including M. tuberculosis. The experiments themselves are well thought out, well described, and comprehensive, and appropriate alternatives are discussed.

The strengths of the proposal include its significance, the PI and his team, the availability of specific mutants to examine the mechanism and of purified proteins with which to work.  However, these strengths are outweighed by weaknesses, including the reliance on the structure of peptide fragments of the full protein for binding and structural assays, when the investigators themselves argue that this may not provide a full picture of the complete protein’s structure. Furthermore, many of the proposed experiments in aim #3 are dependent on the results from aims #1 and #2.  These concerns reduce enthusiasm for this proposal.

imp_text: This is a proposal by an established team of investigators to explore the structure function relationships of 3 products produced by P. aeruginosa, 1 protein and 2 extracellular polysaccharides, that are linked to biofilm formation.  The strengths of the work include its significance, and the PI and his team.  However, there are weaknesses that reduce enthusiasm for the proposal. The major of these is that the rationale for the choice of the proteins to study is weak.  There is no evidence to support the idea that these proteins are critical for biofilm formation in vivo by P. aeruginosa.  Furthermore, while some of the proposed experiments in aim #2 examining complement interaction have some merit, they are overshadowed by the lack of overall rationale for the choice of proteins.  Furthermore, aim #1 seems premature given the lack of support for a role for these proteins in biofilm formation in vivo. These concerns reduce enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: . The prominent role that P. aeruginosa plays in the pathology of Cystic Fibrosis give this proposal high significance. . The mechanism by which biofilms are formed and interact with the immune system, and with antibiotic sensitivity is unclear.
inv_text_str: . This is a strong investigative team with the necessary expertise to complete the proposed work. .
inn_text_str: . Standard approaches are utilized.
app_text_str: . The investigators have a collection of clinical isolates what could be useful. . Some of the experiments proposed in aim #2 examining the interaction with complement are good ones. . The use of strains carrying inducible plasmids for cdrA, Psl and Pel will allow for nuanced investigations of the role of these molecules in interacting with neutrophils (aim #2). .  The availability of purified Psl, Pel and cdrA are pluses for the interaction experiments. .
app_text_wkn: . The rationale for the choice of study of these 2 polysaccharides and protein is not well articulated.  It is not clear whether these 3 molecules are important for biofilm formation in vivo.  Stronger evidence needs to be provided prior to embarking on most of the proposed experiments. . The investigators do not address some significant caveats to the use of some of the P. aeruginosa mutant strains that may affect the ability to interpret the results.  This includes strains that over produce c-di-GMP, or other components that may alter the stoichiometry of any interactions. In addition, other potential issues that such mutant strains may have that affect their growth (e.g.) are not discussed. . There are strains proposed (e.g. in fig. 6) that clearly no not express much of either of the polysaccharides under study, reducing the significance of looking at these molecules. . There are a number of significant variables in the experiments proposed in aim 1.1 that may make it difficult to fully interpret the data generated. . Some data examining the role of Psl and Pel in the clinical isolates would provide some reassurance that these two molecules are important and provide a stronger rationale for aim #1, e.g. do they all form biofilms, particularly in vivo. . In some of the experiments in aim 2, the investigators propose to test biofilms of strains carrying deletions in cldA, Pel or Pelf for effects on complement resistance. However, if these molecules are important for biofilm formation, then those states will not be possible or less likely and so it’s not clear how such experiments will be interpreted. . .

imp_text: This is a proposal by an early stage investigator to explore the ability of P. aeruginosa to detect sphingosine and Sphingosine 1 phosphate (S1P) to manipulate the host immune system during infections. The strengths of the work include its significance and the novelty of the idea of bacterial detection and use of these products for virulence/growth, the PI and her team, the preliminary data and some of the proposed experiments.  This is somewhat tempered by some of the proposed experiments, including a lack of consideration of the function of S1P in manipulating parts of the immune response, the lack of consideration of interactions between bacteria and host cells that may provide a more mechanistic understanding of the process, and a fairly crude analysis of bacteria host interaction. However, there is high enthusiasm for this proposal.
sig_text_str: . The prominent role that P. aeruginosa plays in the pathology of Cystic Fibrosis makes this work highly significant. . The mechanism by which P. aeruginosa is able to manipulate the immune system is poorly understood. . This is a potentially novel pathway or mechanism of bacterial virulence. .
inv_text_str: . The PI and her team are well qualified to perform the proposed work. .
inn_text_str: . This is a novel potential pathway that may be used by P. aeruginosa to grow in vivo or manipulate the immune system. . State of the art but standard approaches are proposed.
app_text_str: . Good evidence for in vivo and in vitro relevance of this potential pathway. . A good screen in place to detect and identify component of the Sphingosine and S1P pathways. . Bacterial mutants and other approaches are in place for the performance of the work. .
app_text_wkn: . The function of S1P in immune system is barely discussed and warrants more consideration as it relates to Pseudomonas being able to manipulate the immune system by this pathway. . It is unclear whether local depletion of these products will have enough of an effect on the immune system for the virulence of the bacteria. . While the PI will examine bacterial metabolism as a role for the presence of this pathways, the focus seems more on the role of this pathways in manipulating the immune system. It is possible that the bacteria use sphingosine and S1P as a carbon source, given the abundance in the lung where the bacteria reside, rather than to manipulate the immune system. . Aim 3 is a crude analysis of bacterial host interactions and more nuanced experiments may be needed to tease out any effects of the mutants. . Experiments that can distinguish reduced bacterial colonization vs reduced virulence are not well delineated. Reduced numbers of bacteria could also reduce inflammation driven by the mutants. . Experiments to directly examine bacterial/host interactions effects in vitro would have been good to determine the role of the pathway in manipulating the immune systems or bacterial growth vs virulence. . It is also not clear how the PI will distinguish non-specific phosphatases from specific phosphatase in their proposed experiments. . Experiments attempting to find a S1P phosphatase should include the transport studies to determine whether this is also taken up by the bacteria since that is a formal possibility. It is also possible that the bacteria can detect S1P directly. . .

imp_text: Over millennia of viral human evolution, viruses have evolved mechanisms to thwart mammalian host type I IFN responses. The mechanisms for this are not well understood. The investigators propose to investigate mechanism of viral virulence in the coronavirus, mouse hepatitis virus (MHV). They hypothesize that the OAS-RNAse L pathway in macrophages plays a critical role in protecting the host from viral hepatitis. RNAse L is activated by 2-5A and when active, cleaves both viral and host RNAs in order to prevent the infection from spreading. They hypothesize that certain MHV protiens such as ns2 degrade 2-5a via their phosphodiesterase activity and in effect, shut down RNAse L mediated anti-viral defense mechanisms. The relative strengths of this hypothesis driven, well written applications include outstanding Co-Investigators, excellent academic institutions, novel hypothesis and elegantly designed experiments. Additionally, they have a neat mouse model which they can use to ask in vitro, in vivo and biochemical questions. Relative weaknesses include some limitations in approach. They do not have the LysMCre RNAse L KO mouse, aim 2c is essentially a fishing expedition and the large numbers of mice which is indicative of a somewhat diffuse approach in scope of experimental design.

imp_text: The proposed application seeks to better understand the pathophysiological basis of Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) and how it causes infections with exceedingly high mortality in humans but not animals. The investigators propose to test the hypothesis that vOTU (ovarian tumor domain protease) are the relevant virulence factors which function to disarm the type I IFN mediated antiviral defense systems by undoing two key posttranscriptional modifications which operate the IFN response, namely, ubiquitination and ISGylation activities. The overall strengths of this application include the very well trained PI, strong team of investigators, good preliminary data, somewhat novel hypothesis which can elucidate key steps in viral pathogenesis. Relative weaknesses include few details on how animal models will be used and correlation between biochemistry of cells and innate immunity. Since CCHFV only causes disease in humans but not animals, anything discovered in animal models, though necessary to use to study innate immunity, may have limited application to viral pathogenesis.

imp_text: Viral mechanisms whereby virus inhibit cellular translation, also known as “host shut-off” are not well understood but an active area of research. The rhabdovirus, vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) appears to mediate host shut-off via VSV matrix (M) protein. However, the mechanism of this process is unclear. The investigators propose a novel hypothesis that VSV protein M forms complex with host nuclear factor Rae1 and together form a “platform” whose primary function is to completely shut down host transcription. As a result of this, certain RNA binding proteins (RBPs) complexes are transported into the cytoplasm and the end results is that newly transcribed mRNAs are given preferential treatment by the polysomes in translation, whereas the existing mRNAs are shuttled off to “less-productive” ribosomes and have decreased translation. The strengths of this application include well written, hypothesis driven application, strong team of investigators, which is highly innovative and uses newly developed state of the art techniques (PAR-CLIP) to test the hypothesis. Additionally, the techniques are do-able. Relative weaknesses include a non-existent alternative approaches section, if any of the techniques were not to work as advertised this may represent problems. There are some questions of downstream applications of using HeLa cells and lack of animal models which would have strengthened the significance of the proposed experiments.

imp_text: The goal of this proposal is to use a drosophila model to identify evolutionarily conserved pathways that modulate cardiac hypertrophic signaling. Specifically, the central hypothesis is that crosstalk between the Raf-MEK1 and Hippo-YAP1 pathways mediates cardiac hypertrophy. A key piece of preliminary data indicates that Raf mediated hypertrophy in the fly is independent of ERK, and is potentially mediated by yorkie/Hippo signaling. The experiments in Aim 1 are designed to (1) determine if MEK plays a role in fly hypertrophy and its ability to interact with Hippo, (2) determine the hypertrophic activation of yorkie, (3) determine if deletion of yorkie prevents hypertrophy in the fly model, (4) characterize yorkie-dependent gene expression. Aim 2 will determine the role of mammalian YAP1 on myocyte growth and proliferation. Aim 3 will then determine the role of YAP1 KO on the development of cardiac hypertrophy. Overall, this proposal is interesting and proposes to study innovative pathways in the development of cardiac hypertrophy. However, the use of a fly model to identify key signaling and gene mediators of this pathway is questionable in its ability to translate. In addition, much of the information gained from Aim 1 and 2 will not be employed in the “translational” aim 3 using mouse models of cardiac hypertrophy. Aims 2 and 3 appear to be outside of the PIs expertise and are very under-developed.
sig_text_str: . Utilization of new models to study Raf-MEK1 and Hippo-yorkie signaling in the hypertrophic myocardium.
sig_text_wkn: . The utility/translational potential of these results are unclear since it will be done in a fly model. How well will these results translate to mammals/humans. Specifically, it’s not clear how much functional conservation there is from yorkie to YAP1. The PI states that mammalian YAP1 has additional protein domains and conveys a different functional phenotype from yorkie (proliferation vs. hypertrophy).
inv_text_str: . Applicant has an ongoing K08 grant. . Junior faculty member with strong training background and potential for success. Has a strong publication record including 2 senior authored papers.
inn_text_wkn: . The use of the fly model is an interesting approach, but there doesn’t appear to be much innovation in the experimental approach.
app_text_wkn: . In Aim 1.2, it’s unclear whether overexpressed GFP-tagged yorkie will accurately recapitulate activity (nuclear-cytosolic shuttling) of wild-type yorkie. Subsequent to this, the rescue effect of yorkie deletion will be determined along with identification of yorkie-dependent gene expression in the hypertrophic fly heart. The experiments in Aim 1 all appear to co-dependent on the fact that activated yorkie drives hypertrophic gene expression in the fly heart. How valuable will the gene expression data really be if this is not the case? . In Aim 2, the endpoints for assessment of NRVM hypertrophy and proliferation are scant. Why not include gene markers for hypertrophy and proliferation in addition to just cell size and BRDU? How will enrichment and purity of myocyte culture be ensured? (Contamination by other cell types such as fibroblasts will surely give confounding results, especially related to proliferation). Also, there is little discussion of experimental endpoints that will be employed in adult myocytes – will these be isolated myocytes? Can the PI truly measure hypertrophy or proliferation in adult myocytes? What advantage to the adult cells have over using just NRVMs? . Aim 3 is viewed as extremely ambitious and risky while not giving much detail on experimental endpoints to assess cardiac function and rescue effects following TAC. There are too many mouse models considered without enough rationale given (e.g. why will inducible MerCreMer mice be needed? What benefit do these animals provide over constitutive alphaMHC-Cre? This model can be tricky to employ if the PI has no experience with tamoxifen inducible deletion models). Aim 3 is also the most costly, in depth, and time-consuming aim, and is not supported by in vivo preliminary data using mouse models.

imp_text: In this highly focused proposal, the PI aims to assess the localized functional interactions between redox signaling (NADPH oxidase activity) and Calcium channels in arterial smooth muscle cells. The hypothesis to be tested is that communication between redox activity and Calcium signaling occurs in highly localized microdomains where caveolae and peripheral mitochondria are in close apposition, and that such interactions between mitochondria and caveolae are important for normal SM function and hyperactivation of SM activity in obesity. The strengths of the proposal are 1) the fundamental importance of the question being addressed, 2) the well thought out, logical experimental design, 3) the expertise of the PI and his colleagues, 4) the preliminary data which strongly support the hypotheses proposed, and 5) the highly innovative approaches proposed.
sig_text_str: . Metabolic diseases such as obesity are very prevalent and cause significant morbidity and mortality especially via cardiovascular effects. In the studies proposed, the PI will assess the molecular mechanisms that cause smooth muscle cells to contract and how these are affected in health and disease using obesity as the disease model.
inv_text_str: . The PI was one of the people to first identify t L-type calcium channel, and he/she has been highly productive since starting his own laboratory at Colorado State University. Concurrent funding does not appear to overlap with the studies proposed. For example, he has an AHA grant on Calcium sparklets in hypertension, which presumable has led to the strong preliminary data in this proposal. . The PI has put together a strong team of investigators from Colorado State (e.g. Stuart Evans, Micha Tumas) who will provide expertise in bioengineering and voltage gated ion channels.
inn_text_str: . There is a high degree of innovation here starting with the proposed hypothesis to identify a new functional interaction between caveolae and mitochondria. . Innovative approaches are proposed including high resolution TIRF microscopy, use of novel genetically encoded fluorescence reporters for localized ROS levels, the development of an approach to simultaneously visually assess ROS and Calcium channel activity in individual cells, and others. The PI clearly states that some of these proposed novel approached may not work. But, that if this is the case, the data can still be obtained using less elegant, but still effective, approaches.
app_text_str: . The studies proposed are highly logical and progress from assessments of whether caveolae and/or caveolin is necessary for functional coupling of NADPH oxidase and Ca channel activity, to assessment of localization of caveolae vs. mitochondria within the cells, so testing the potential role of this interaction in mediating the response of arterial smooth muscle cells to angiotensin II (and other agonists) using whole vessel physiology and imaging. Expected results and interpretations are discussed as are alternative approaches. . Aim 2 is focused on a potential specific role of peripheral mitochondria in the NADPH oxidase/Calcium channel interaction. This is an intriguing hypothesis, and worth testing.  However, the preliminary data supporting this aim are not as strong and additional discussion of potential pitfalls is needed. . Aim 3 is to test the hypothesis that the functional interaction between NADPH oxidase and L-type Calcium channel activity plays a role in arterial dysfunction in obesity.  This is an important goal that will tie in the fundamental findings from Aims 1 and 2 with a disease process.  However, the metabolic changes that can occur in obesity are so complicated and multifactorial, that it is not likely that fully conclusive evidence will be revealed by the studies proposed.  However, the investigators have proposed to use multiple complementary models of obesity as well as to test the effects of an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor, and the data obtained will point the way to future more definitive studies that can focus on specific aspects of a high fat diet perhaps with a focus on specific fats themselves.
app_text_wkn: . It is not clear how specific the drugs that they propose use are for mitochondria. For example, is it possible that rotenone, CCCP, diazoxide, etc. will affect NADPH activity in caveolae independent from their effects on mitochondria? Also, if these drugs affect mitochondrial function, the cells make be dysfunctional such that the effects observed are not due specifically to a loss of localized interactions between caveolae and mitochondria. . The potential feed-forward ROS signaling between NADPH oxidase in caveolae and the electron transport chain of mitochondria is an interesting hypothesis, but it is not clear to what extent this will be tested using the proposed approaches. . Some of the important experimental design concerns are dealt with in too vague of a manner.  For example, “when possible we will use knockout mice (e.g. the caveolin-1 knockout) … . The aims are interdependent such that if Aim 1.1 fails to show that caveolae are necessary for the coupling being studied, it is unclear whether Aims 1.2. and 1.3 would be performed as proposed. This would be a more serious concern except that the preliminary data are quite strong.

imp_text: The focus of this proposal is to test the potential protective role of Kalirin against atherosclerosis. Genome wide association studies have indicated a statistically significant association between the Kalirin gene (KLRN) and the risk of atherosclerosis. The PI’s lab has published (manuscript in appendix, but appendix not available) that Kalirin expression in isolated smooth muscle cells has effects that would increase the risk or severity of atherosclerosis. However, based on additional preliminary data, the PI proposes that Kalirin plays an overall protective role based on its effects on macrophages and/or endothelial cells. The strengths of the proposal are the 1) highly clinically important need to better understand the molecular mechanisms of atherosclerosis, 2) the focus on a single gene to assess its role, 3) the expertise of the PI and co-investigators, 4) the availability of animal models of Kalirin knockdown and inducible cell-type specific knock-out, 5) the strong preliminary data showing that Kalirin acts as a GEF for downstream G proteins and has differential effects on iNOS vs. eNOS, and 6) balanced in vitro and in vivo approaches proposed. The major weaknesses are the somewhat confusing presentation of background findings and preliminary data (although the model shown in Figure 2, which puts the preliminary data together, is very helpful), and that the true test of whether Kalirin expression in endothelial cells has a protective effect against atherosclerosis is not tested upfront directly. There are more strengths than weaknesses, and important findings could result from the proposed research.

Genomic loci have been identified that correlated with rick of atherosclerosis, and each of these loci needs to be assessed for its potential molecular role in promoting or preventing atherosclerosis

app_text_str: . The preliminary data in Figure 3 strongly support the contention that Kalirin protects against atherosclerosis in an Apoe-/- mouse model on a Western diet with thickening of the neointima and a higher percentage of the aortic area being taken up by atherosclerosis. . Despite confusing data in Figure 4, the subsequent data support the contention of the PI that Kalirin expression in macrophages leads to decreased nitrite production, and that knockdown of Kalirin decreases eNOS activation and p-PAK phosphorylation, all of which support the studies proposed to determine whether Kalirin’s protective effects as shown in Figure 3 are due to decreased iNOS activity and/or promotion of eNOS activity. . Mouse models are available and VE-Cad-Cre-ER studies will be able to definitively show whether Kalirin knockdown in endothelial cells promotes or inhibits development of atherosclerotic lesions using multiple models of atherosclerosis. . imp_text: This is a well written and clear proposal to test the hypothesis that the underlying cause of differential granule content release from platelets under different conditions is nonrandom distribution of granule contents within individual granules. There is a second hypothesis as well – that granule secretion is caused by docking of granules with the DMS through granule extensions that are rich in fibrinogen. The proposed studies are designed to provide definitive support or refutation of the proposed hypotheses.  The strengths of the proposal are the 1) innovation, 2) expertise of the investigator in the complementary microscopy approaches proposed, 3) superb team of investigators, 4) intriguing preliminary data, and 5) the care with which the PI makes sure to clarify what he is proposing. The main weakness is that I don’t see how the findings will actually address the mechanism for differential platelet granule secretion under different conditions. If the protein contents of alpha granules are not uniformly distributed throughout the individual granules, how does this address the differential secretion? It will be important to definitively prove that there are not consistent specific subtypes of alpha granules with different cargo because this hypothesis is appealing and needs to be definitively supported or, in the case of the preliminary data shown here, refuted. But, the alternative explanation does not make sense as the mechansims for differential release.

imp_text: This application  unites state of the art imaging of nanoregions of the  arterial smooth muscle cell to the understanding of the regulation of Ca transport into and the contraction of these cells and the control of blood pressure. The grant tests the hypothesis that the ROS produced by NADPH or by electron transport in peripheral mitochondria stimulates the L type Ca channel. These elements are thought to be  organized by their close apposition to the  caveolae. The first two specific aims exploring the role of caveolae and the peripheral mitochondria in attempting to  validate the importance of the co-localization of these elements in the regulation of this network, are excellent. The third specific aim, in which the applicant attempts to apply knowledge gained in the first two aims, to the understanding of the production of hypertension in rat genetic or dietary models of obesity, is less strong. This is due to the complexity of the system and the need for additional preliminary data.

These experiments will result in a disruption in the co-localization and of the fuctional coupling. Most of these approaches are eminently reasonable and feasible. In discussing the expected outcomes the applicant is appropriately cautious for the most part. • The rationale for the choice of rats is well articulated. • In aim 2 a very similar approach is proposed the role of peripheral mitochondria in regulating the ROS cross talk.  A test of the very interesting hypothesis that such mitochondria are closely apposed to caveolae is proposed.. The electron transport of these mitochondria  could generate ROS that reciprocally talks to NADPH oxidase and consequent activation of the L type Ca channels. • In aim 3 The applicant proposes to explore the relationship between obesity, coupled NADPH oxidase and L type Ca channel activity  and hyperension. The choice of models: Zucker fatty and lean  ratsl and obesity prone and obesity resistant rats is excellent. Also to be explored is the effect of weight loss induced by sleeve gastrectomy is also a strength.
app_text_wkn: • Aim 1 •   The proposal is heavily focused on imaging, the specialty of the applicant, so a little more biochemical reasoning might have been appropriate.specific .The Ca sparklets and ROS signals are claimed to be less than I micron apart. Do they or can they physically interact, or is the cross talk largely attributable to the   proximity of the ROS to the articipating molecules, i.e. is this co-localization required to enable ROS to act on the channels before they are reduced? •  As caveolae and their disruption plays such an important role in the application, it would have been useful to count the number and size of caveolae in regions of plasma membrane of SMCs, after the major interventions. •   In the model shown in figure 1 of the application NADPH is shown as being present in the caveolae. Yet this is not the impression given on page 43 under expected results. Clarity on this issue would have been helpful. •   With the use of HMGcoA reductase inhibitors, it is expected that their effects are msinly on the prenylation of Rac, but as the applicant suggests he will  explore effects on the cholesterol content of caveolae. This should have been more explicitly described, namely the cholesterol content of isolated caveolae—easy to do. • The applicant emphasizes the importance of examining multiple vascular beds. Most of his SMCs will be derived from cerebral arteries. It would have been helpful to have some preliminary data on another bed. • Aim 2. • The close apposition of peripheral mitochondria to caveolae is how close. In any event to the extent that their role depends  on their proximity  probably by the proximate release of ROS. ROS is generated by the electron transport of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which has to traverse the outer membrane to get to communicate with the NADPH oin the caveolae or the l Type Ca channels. Thus it seems that ROS is the signal connecting these two organelles, with no direct molecular contact. • The applicant should comment on  the hypothetical basis for the peripheral localization of these mitochondria in proximity to the caveolae? Is there something special about these mitochondria? • Aim 3. •   This is the weakest of the three aims, partly because of the complexity of the obesity models. Hypertension is not always present in obesity.  With the Zucker fatty rats there is an increase in NADPH in young rats and the Ca sparklets in the SMCs of these rats, still normotensive,  is as numerous as  was seen with AngII stimulation—cf figure 7 and figure 12. Thus there appears to be coupled signaling without hypertension. Hypertension only appears in older rats. The applicant speculates that the coupling increases with age. What about the  possibility that there is a further enabling promoter of  the hypertension of obesity.? •   In the obesity prone rats an increase in caveolae is noted but not in the resistant rats. Is there any mapping data that suggests a role for genes controlling caveolar functioning in these rats?

imp_text: This is a timely investigation of the role of kalirin in endothelial cells and macrophages in protecting against the development of atherosclerosis using selective hapolinsufficiency in each of these cells. The applicant has employed these variants and pharmacologic approaches to target iNOS inhibition and eNOS in endothelial cells and IL-10 in macrophages. Despite the runting seen in global homozygous deficiency, selective homozygous deficiency in each of the target cells  could well b much more useful, without runting. This would facilitate more definitive rescue experiments and by using domain mutants a very helpful mechanistic analysis, especially to complement shotgun proteomics.

imp_text: Overall Impact  This is a strong and well focused application from an accomplished investigator along with a valuable collaborative team. The application is concerned with the micro-anatomy of the platelet granule, in which the applicant hypothesizes that platelets contain a single population of alpha granules, containing subdomains that will be defined by state of the art imaging and immunochemical procedures. These subdomains are thought to be the basis for differential secretion in response to different agonists. The intelligent use of mouse and human mutants is a strong feature. Some minor weaknesses are identified. The cell biology of the platelet to come out of this study should be valuable. However, the possible therapeutic implications of the anticipated outcomes could have been laid out in more detail. SCORE 2.
