imp_text: This application relies on the use of high-resolution imaging technologies to study the structure and mode of secretion  of platelet a-granules   The model proposed for platelet secretion is innovative The investigators are well qualified to implement the proposed project and the imaging facilities of the PI and his collaborators are state of the art . New knowledge that will emerges from this project will be relevant to atherosclerosis thrombosis and cardiovascular disease
sig_text_str: The PI will  use high-resolution imaging technologies (electron tomography and super-resolution light microscopy ) to study the structure and function of platelet a-granules  ,the way the protein cargo is organized within the granules and the mechanisms by which this cargo is released. Success of the project will  increase our understanding of the mechanisms that contribute to atherosclerosis thrombosis and cardiovascular disease

imp_text: Microcephalic Osteodysplastic Primordial Dwarfism type I (MOPD I) is a a rare autosomal recessive disease. Recent MOPD I studies implicated mutations in the snRNA gene encoding U4atac, a component of the U12-dependent spliceosome that mediates the removal of a subset of introns in a small numer of human genes. The main PI has extensive experience in studying spliceosomal assembly and function. The consortium co-PI is an MD/PhD with experience studying genetic variation in the context of disease. The two PIs collaborated previously in the discovery of the U4atac mutations in MOPD I. Here, they propose to analyze biochemically the defects caused by the mutations in U4atac, to determine the changes in the transcriptome of cultured fibroblasts carrying the MOPD I-linked mutations, and characterize the effects of a surprising amount of genetic diversity discovered within the genes encoding the snRNAs of the U12-dependent spliceosome. The first aim fits squarely in the wheelhouse of Prof. Scott and will likely be informative. The second and third aims are much more speculative and I am not convinced that, as proposed, they will yield the kind of information that is suggested. This project is expected to have only a moderate impact on the field.
sig_text_str: . Splicing is an essential process and the roles of U12-dependent splicing are unclear and need to be better understood. . The existence of a human disease linked to mutations in a component of the U12-dependent spliceosome fuels the interest in this subject.
sig_text_wkn: . It is stated that “Mutations in these sequence elements are estimated to account for up to a third of all genetic diseases (10)”, referring to the sequence elements affecting splice site choices. I do not find support for this statement in the paper cited. I think this is a major overstatement of the significance of cis-acting sequences affecting splicing. . I do not follow the applicants’ logic regarding the potential importance of the apparently high frequency of SNPs in U12-dependent spliceosomal snRNA genes. “Negative D values indicate an excess of rare variation, consistent with population growth or purifying selection. Negative selection (purifying selection) is likely to be preventing the fixation of harmful mutations in these genes.” I understand this to mean that the variants that are observed are not harmful, i.e., not deleterious to function. The idea seems to be that individuals with two variant alleles may have phenotypes qualitatively similar to MOPD I. Yet these individuals are considered normal. Were there among this group individuals who were homozygous or compound heterozygous for variants? This information seems like crucial support for the hypothesis that should be readily available.
inv_text_str: . Both PIs and the teams they have assembled clearly have the requisite expertise to carry out the proposed studies.
inn_text_str: . The role of U12-dependent spliceosome defects in MOPD I is not at all understood, and study of the mutations linked to MOPD I will reveal new insights on normal splicing function. . The unusual frequency of SNPs in minor snRNA genes is intriguing.
inn_text_wkn: . Biochemical and sequencing approaches are fairly standard.
app_text_str: . The biochemical analysis in Aim 1 has already generated informative results and no doubt further study will be fruitful.
app_text_wkn: . Aim 2: “A possible consequence of this would be to skip splice from the N-1 intron to the N+1 intron removing the two exons flanking the U12-dependent intron. We will specifically search for these events in the RNA-Seq data.” Why has this analysis not already been done? This would be a particularly important piece of evidence, and only requires analysis of data already in hand. . “It is important to determine if the transcriptome differences that we have detected are actually due to the U4atac snRNA mutation or to other differences between the cell lines examined.” Yes, this is a critical piece of information and without it it is impossible to know if the provided data are meaningful. Crucially, the cells examined were fibroblasts derived from umbilical cords. It is stated that MOPD I is characterized by “slow growth both pre- and postnatally, very sparse or absent hair, microcephaly with several characteristic brain defects including the lack of the corpus callosum, as well as defects in limb bone, facial structure and joint formation.” Apart from the absence of appropriate controls for the current data, I am not convinced that analysis of the genes expressed in cultured fibroblasts will provide useful information about genes expressed in the various cell types that are affected in MOPD I. . I do not understand the importance of the SNPs in Aim 3 and I do not see how the various SNPs to be tested will be prioritized so that a huge amount of effort is not expended towards sequence changes that may not be important. . This application requests an enormous amount of money to carry out experiments that, to me, do not seem particularly expensive.

imp_text: The applicant is a senior investigator who has been working on this subject for decades and has a proven track record of obtaining NIH funding and producing high-impact research. His lab has developed several new techniques to address mechanisms of eukaryotic DNA replication. This proposal examines a number of protein complexes already known to function in this process, focusing on the CMG complex. For the most part, the preliminary data and past successes indicate that the proposed experiments are likely to be successful. I have a few concerns with some of the chosen approaches. However, I find the overall direction of the project to be unfocused and it feels like these aims will merely fill in a few missing details in a big picture that is already quite well fleshed out. These studies are likey to have only a moderate impact on the field.
sig_text_str: . DNA replication is a fundamental biological process and a complete understanding of this process is essential for understanding human disease.
sig_text_wkn: . The experiments address what appear to be relatively minor issues in the field and the focus is diluted across a number of distinct factors (DNA polymerases, Ctf4, FACT, Tim-Tipin, Psf1), rather than focusing on a specific, unanswered molecular question and addressing it from multiple angles. I worry that the picture that would emerge from these studies would be, “These various factors also interact with the CMG complex and alter its function in various ways,” rather than, “This specific factor does exactly X to CMG function”.

imp_text: The PI is a Professor with a background in biochemistry who has made a career in exploiting molecular genetics to tease apart mechanistic details regarding ribosome assembly. The co-investigator is an Associate Professor who has begun a collaboration with the PI that complements the genetic expertise with biochemical and structural expertise. (The title page indicates that this grant has New Investigator status, but I don’t understand why, as both investigators have a history of NIH funding.) This combination of expertises is quite compelling. The project addresses a very specific and very compelling hypothesis, that the conserved methyltransferase Bud23 serves as a quality control sensor during ribisome biogenesis by recognizing a specific structural feature of an intermediate assembly step. This model is well supported by preliminary evidence. The approach combines elegant genetics with sensitive RNA and protein biochemistry to elucidate particular aspects of various steps in the production of the precursor of the small ribosomal subunit. Each experiment is carefully crafted and the possible results and their interpretation are clearly presented. There are some potentially risky experiments that rely on the acquisition of certain kinds of mutants, but the preliminary data presented and the track record of the PI suggest that these are likely to be successful. Overall, I believe that this project will have a high impact on the field.

imp_text: This is a multi-PI application from two highly accomplished investigators who propose to study the molecular and cellular mechanisms of viral antagonisms against host IFN-mediated restriction. Specifically, the PIs will use a murine coronavirus, mouse hepatitis virus (MHV) which causes acute hepatitis, to interrogate how the viral ns2 protein functions as 2’,5’-phosphodiesterase(2’,5’-PDE) to down-regulate the intracellular levels of IFN-induced 2-5A, thereby preventing the activation of RNase L, which degrades viral and cellular RNA. Studies from the PI’s groups have also shown that host AKAP7 and some other viral proteins are 2H phosphoesterases related to ns2 and cleave 2-5A thus preventing activation of RNase L. In this application, the PIs propose three specific aims. In Aim1, they will investigate the cell type specific activity of the OAS-RNase L pathway, with a particular focus on live-specific macrophages Kupffer cells (KCs). Their overall hypothesis is that RNase L signaling in liver KCs restrict MHV from entering the liver parenchyma and inducing hepatitis. They will test this hypothesis by comparing MHV replication and activation of the OAS-RNase L pathway in primary cultures of KCs, liver sinusoidal endothelial cells and hepatocytes.  The requirement of ns2-mediated PDE activity to antagonize RNase L for virus spread to the liver parenchyma and induction of hepatitis will also be studied. In Aim2, the PI will determine the roles of ns2 related viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs in antiviral innate immunity by investigating viral and cellular PDE enzymes in regulating 2-5A levels and RNase L activation. They will also use some libraries to screen for inhibitors of MHV ns2, rotavirus VP3 and cellular AKAP7 and assess their effects on viral replication. In Aim3, the PIs will use the available MHV animal model and chimeric MHVs expressing foreign PDEs to investigate the ability of cellular and viral PDEs to regulate the OAS-RNase L pathway and viral pathogenesis in vivo. They will also use these inhibitors to study the effects of 2’,5’-PDEs on viral pathogenesis during ongoing infections in the MHV mouse model. Overall, this is a strong application based on some promising preliminary data, with three specific aims and potential pitfalls clearly outlined. Results from the proposed experiments shall help understand the impact of viral and cellular 2’,5’-PDEs on the regulation of the OAS-RNase L antiviral pathway and should aid in the development of therapeutic strategies against viral hepatitis and potentially other viral diseases. The application has some minor weaknesses related to data interpretation and experimental design. For example, it is unclear how viral infection itself might modulate cellular PDEs, which regulates viral infection and pathogenesis. Given the structural and functional similarities between viral and cellular PDEs, it is unknown if each or both have been undergoing positive selection as well as their evolutionary relationships.
sig_text_str: . The finding that the MHV accessory protein, ns2, antagonizes the type I IFN response in macrophages and promotes the induction of hepatitis is significant. . The data showing that ns2 is a phosphodiesterase that cleaves IFN-induced 2’,5’-oligoadenylates(2-5A) and thus prevents RNA degradation by RNase L is an impressive finding. . imp_text: This R01 application is from a new and early stage investigator, who proposes to determine the contributions of nairovirus ovarian tumor domain protease (vOTU) to host immunological suppression and disease outcomes. vOTUs are present within the L-proteins of Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) as well as other known nairoviruses yet do not have apparent RdRp activity. Rather, these proteins have the ability to reverse post-translational modifications of host proteins by ubiquitin (Ub) and Ub-like interferon-simulated gene product 15 (ISG15), the latter of which are known to play a critical role in regulating antiviral proteins of the interferon (IFN) type 1 response. Currently, vOTUs are considered a potential nairovirus virulence factors. In this application, the PI proposes two specific aims to dissect the role of vOTUs in modulating the deubiquitination and deISGylation of ISG15. In Aim 1, the PI will examine the effects of nairovirus OTU sequence diversity on their deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities. They will also resolve the origin of nairovirus vOTU selectivity and determine the influence of ISG15 species diversity on the deISGylating activity of nairovirus OTUs.  In Aim 2, the PI will determine the contributions of nairovirus vOTUs deISGylase activity, deubiquitinase activity, and ISG15 specificity to subvert the innate immune response. These will accomplish these by engineering CCHFVs to have inactive vOTUs or vOTUs with shifted specificity for Ub, poly-Ub, or human or mouse ISG15. They will use these recombinant CCHFVs to determine the effect of vOTUs in deubiquitinating and/or deISGylating ISG15 and subsequent suppression of IFNa/ß and other inflammatory cytokines activity and viral pathogenesis. Overall, this is a good application based on some promising preliminary data, yet with some weakness in experimental design and data interpretation.
sig_text_str: . Crimean Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) causes severe hemorrhages in humans and has mortality rates as high as 80%, with currently no FDA-approved vaccines or therapeutics. Study of CCHFV is therefore important. . The viral homologue of an ovarian tumor domain protease (OTU) is present in many nairoviruses as well as some RNA+ viruses, and can reverse post-translational modifications of host proteins by ubiquitin (Ub) and Ub-like interferon-simulated gene product 15 (ISG15). Investigation of the underlying mechanisms involved should provide new insight into how OTUs function as virulent factors through evading host immunity. . The diverse spectra of diseases caused by CCHFV and other nairoviruses in different species are intriguing, which highlights the likely crucial role of intrinsic host innate immunity in viral infection and pathogenesis.

imp_text: This R01 application is from an established investigator, who proposes to understand how VSV M protein suppresses cellular gene expressions. Two specific aims are proposed. In Aim 1, the PI will determine the effects of silencing Rae1 on the nuclear-cytoplasmic transport of newly synthesized mRNAs induced by VSV infection by testing the hypothesis that the M protein-Rae1 complex inhibits transport of most newly synthesized cellular mRNAs and that relocalization of hnRNPs reflects the preferential transport of a subset of host mRNAs. The PI will also test an alternative hypothesis that hnRNPs may be transported without their associated cargo mRNAs and but associated with cytoplasmic mRNAs. In Aim 2, the PI will determine the role of Rae1, hnRNPs, and cytoplasmic RNA-binding proteins in the control of translation in VSV-infected cells; in particular, the PI will test the hypothesis that translation of pre-existing cellular mRNAs is inhibited whereas translation of newly appearing viral mRNAs is enhanced. The strength of this proposal includes well-accomplished PI, interesting and promising preliminary data, and innovative hypotheses and/or techniques. Overall, this is a strong application, and completion of it will provide new insights into the inhibition of host gene expression by VSV and other viruses.
sig_text_str: . The ability of VSV matrix (M) protein to inhibit host gene expression, which is genetically separable from its function in virus assembly, is an important topic. . Emerging evidence from the PI’s lab and others have indicated that, rather than a primary effect on transport, the M protein-Rae1 complex inhibits host transcription, and likely promotes transport of a subset of host mRNAs that are associated with host heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs), which re-localize to the cytoplasm following VSV infection. This is an important new direction in the field. . Determining the mechanisms by which VSV M protein functions to shut off host gene and suppress antiviral response could offer new insight into virus-host interaction.
sig_text_wkn: . VSV is not an important human pathogen. The direct impact on other pathogenic human viruses remains unclear.

imp_text: This is a multiple PI proposal. The proposal is based on the PI’s recent finding that the MHV protein ns2 blocks the IFN-inducible and potent antiviral 2’,5’-oligoadenylate (2-5A) synthetase (OAS)-RNase L pathway in macrophages. The hypothesis was also supported by the fact that the ns2 protein and related viral (rotavirus VP3) and mammalian (AKAP7) proteins are 2H phosphoesterases with 2’,5’-phosphodiesterase (PDE) activities that degrade 2-5A, the activator of RNase L. The PIs aim to probe the role of viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs in antiviral innate immunity and its effect on viral pathogenesis. Hypothesis is that the OAS-RNase L pathway in macrophages is critical in protecting the host from developing viral hepatitis. Three Specific Aims are: (1) To determine if RNase L signaling in liver macrophages (Kupffer cells, KC) restricts virus from entering the liver parenchyma and inducing hepatitis. (2) To determine the roles of ns2 related viral and host 2’,5’-PDEs. (3) To determine and compare the “proviral” and RNase L “antagonist” activities of cellular and viral 2’,5’-PDEs. Novelties and Significances: The proposed studies will investigate a novel mode of regulation of the IFN antiviral response with broad implications for the control of viral infections that extend beyond hepatitis to virus mediated pathologies in other organ systems. Expected results include defining the role of KC as “gatekeeper” that prevents viruses from entering into the liver parenchyma and defining proviral and RNase L antagonist roles of diverse viral and cellular 2’,5’-PDEs. It is anticipated that further understanding of the competition between virus and type I IFN signaling, particularly the OAS-RNase L pathway, will aid in the development or refinement of therapeutic strategies for human viral hepatitis and other viral diseases. Overall, this is an excellent proposal with high significance and novelties. The PIs are both established investigators. The approaches are well organized and feasible.

imp_text: The proposal is based on experimental results that 1) vOTU was identified within the L-protein of CCHFV and 33 other known nairoviruses; 2) the initial X-ray crystallographic structure of vOTUs from CCHFV and DUGV revealed its interaction with human Ub; 3) vOTUs are able to reverse post-translational modifications of host proteins by ubiquitin (Ub) and Ub-like interferon-simulated gene product 15 (ISG15); and 4) Ub- or ISG-modification of host protein is an antiviral defense, so the vOTU may be related to viral virulence. Given the viral evasion is critical for viral pathogenesis, the proposal was to address an important question of whether vOTU “deubiquitinating and deISGylating activities among nairovirus vOTUs correspond to the ability of these viruses to evade the host immune system and cause disease”. Overall, the PI proposed a very interesting study focusing on the function of vOTU. Although most of work has been reported from many laboratories regarding the vOTU effects on the ubiquitination and/or ISGylation, it is novel to investigate whether vOTU is included as viral virulence via in vivo studies. imp_text: This application proposed to solve an argument of how VSV infection shuts off the host cell gene expression program. The PI proposed a different model from the prevailing views. Previously, it was thought that VSV M protein interacted with Rae1 to inhibit the nuclear-cytoplasmic transport of mRNA because it was thought that Rae1 primarily functioned in nuclear-cytoplasmic transport. The PI recently found that silence of Rae1 directly suppress host gene transcription, therefore, the PI hypothesized that there is a new model for M protein to shut off host cell. The new model is that M protein primarily inhibit cell gene transcription and the effects on transport or translation is the downstream effects of the coupling of host transcription with subsequent steps in host gene expression, which are mediated by host RNA-binding proteins. Two aims were proposed: 1. Determine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of mRNA transport by VSV. 2. Determine the role of host RNA-binding proteins in the inhibition of translation in VSV-infected cells. Overall, the proposed studies are significant because it aimed to solve a problem that is important for us to understand how the virus block the host gene expression. The new model challenged the prevailing view of “the effect of host shut-off is presumably to set the virus at an advantage by reducing competition between viral and host products for limited cellular machinery”, so the proposal is creative and novel. In addition to that it argues with a previously existent model, the PI proposed an alternative model, namely, a “platform” model; the studies were focused; and the approaches were sufficient. This reviewer has only one minor concern as this is for NIH funding, the clinical implication is unclear.

imp_text: The proposal aims to perform NMR structure and dynamic measurements on poliovirus RdRp to reveal the mechanism of fidelity control. The proposal will use a variety of NMR measurements including advanced relaxation-dispersion measurements to characterize interconversion time scales in wt and variety of mutant RdRps with altered functions.  This is strong proposal from a well prepared new investigator. The environment at Penn State is excellent and there are collaborators there that have a mutual interest in RdRP. Enthusiasm for the proposal is tempered by a few factors. The limited labeling strategy is practical, but I am afraid the structural information gained will not be sufficient to inform antiviral design as the PI states as the ultimate goal. While there is an MD collaboration, which could potentially provide a high resolution picture of the various conformational states, there is limited information about this collaboration. I feel this proposal, especially given the limited labelling strategy, could greatly benefit for a more comprehensive and more tightly integrated modeling component. My other concern is more general and relates to whole idea of perturbing fidelity of this enzyme. I don’t feel this proposal will resolve why both higher and lower fidelity mutations are effective at inhibiting viral pathogenesis. Of course resolving this is beyond the scope of structural biology, but nonetheless it is an intriguing aspect. Furthermore I am concerned that created low fidelity RdRps could have unforeseen consequences by generating more virulent strains.

imp_text: This is a new R01 application from an Early Stage Investigator focusing on the structural analysis of multiple proteins involved in chromosome recombination and segregation during meiosis. The PI proposes to study the structure of monopolin in the kinetochore, of Hop1 in meiotic recombination and of Zip1 during recombination and crossover in budding yeast. The experiments are well described and the preliminary data is strong, but it is unclear what the premise of the proposal is, why these particular proteins were chosen apart from being accessible for structural analysis and how they relate to each other functionally. Each of the Specific Aims is very ambitious and spans from structural analysis to functional studies, which is both a strength and a weakness: a strength because the structural detail obtained can be used to introduce specific mutations to study protein function in vivo, a weakness because the proposal is very diffuse and it is unclear how a new investigator will accomplish all the proposed work. The PI is a well-trained and productive scientist and the study of meiotic control is certainly important and impactful. Some of the techniques proposed are highly innovative and will provide deep mechanistic insight into protein function and regulation of meiosis. However, some doubt remains on the feasibility of the work. In summary this is a very good proposal from a talented young investigator, but the breadth in the scope and uncertainties regarding feasibility dampen enthusiasm.
sig_text_str: . Meiotic control is critical for sexual reproduction and understanding how chromosomes are sorted and recombined during meiosis has strong relevance to both basic biology and human health
sig_text_wkn: . It is unclear why the investigator selected the proposed proteins and how they functionally related to each other. The proposal almost reads like three separate applications all focusing on meiosis.
inv_text_str: . Strong early stage investigator with excellent training and productive high-impact publication record . Expertise is demonstrated in the proposed techniques and the group of collaborators and consultants is strong to support the proposed work
inn_text_str: . While some of the proposed approaches in structural biology are standard, the PI proposes innovative combinations of techniques to link structure and in vivo function. . The in vivo analysis approach looking at centromere orientation in Specific Aim 1d is very powerful. . The combination of x-ray crystallography and cryo-EM will provide detailed structural insight.
app_text_str: . Each aim focuses on a different molecular mechanism controlling different aspects of chromosome recombination during meiosis. The approach starts with structural biology and careful mutation analysis to explore specific molecular interactions. Each aim concludes with structure-function studies which would provide insight into the regulation of meiosis. . If even a portion of this work is completed as described, the proposal will be highly impactful.
app_text_wkn: . The PI indicates in the Approach that his postdoctoral mentor, Dr. Harrison, has agreed to let him take the project, reagents and techniques to his own laboratory, but there is no letter from Dr. Harrison to support that this is the case. . In Specific aim 1c, 2a and 3a the PI indicates that crystallization is still being optimized for the desired proteins. It is unclear whether crystals will be obtained to resolve structure at the appropriate resolution. This would be particularly problematic for Hop1 which exists in multiple conformations. . While the Specific Aims are independent, which is a good thing, each Aim comprises of a large number of experiments and it is unclear whether they will all be feasible in a new laboratory.

imp_text: NOTE: This application was tricky because they used approaches that were state of the art in 2012, but are not any more. I put myself back as if it was 2012 because this is an excellent application and beautifully written. I will point out where the reviews will be different in 2017 in the Approach section. This is an excellent new R01 application from a leader in the field of splicing regulation focusing on the role of spliceosome disruption in a severe human condition Microcephalic Osteodysplastic Primordial Dwarfism type I (MOPDI). The PI and others found that mutations in the small nuclear RNA RNU4ATAC cause MOPDI. The proposed work carefully studies how the disease mutations disrupt RNU4ATAC function, uses patient cells to determine how spliceosomal dysfunction affects the transcriptome and extends into exploring how mutations in other snRNAs could also alter splicing and RNA expression. This proposal is logical and beautifully written and combines the mechanistic analysis of disease mutations with more basic studies which will expand our knowledge of splicing regulation in general. The premise of the proposal is very strong and the experiments are clearly outlined and feasible. If successful this project would be highly significant as it would contribute to our understanding of 1) MOPDI and other disorders where splicing is affected and of 2) the role of little studied snRNAs in splicing regulation. Overall, this is an outstanding proposal from an excellent investigator and there are only very minor weaknesses which will be outlined in the Approach.
sig_text_str: . MOPDI is a severe rare disorder affecting the development of multiple organs and belongs to a larger class of dwarfisms affecting cell proliferation and differentiation . Regulation of RNA splicing is a fundamental biological process which is critical for all aspects of cell differentiation and function and the role of regulatory RNAs is still poorly understood. This proposal would make significant advances in both basic and disease biology. . It is not clear how some snRNAs contribute to splicing regulation. This proposal will not only define the role of U4ATAC in MOPDI, but also explore the role of this and other snRNAs in the spliceosome and RNA expression

Specific Aim 3 will test the hypothesis that the frequently observed SNVs in snRNA genes may have a role in differentially regulating splicing in different individuals and may also contribute to disease. This is a more speculative hypothesis, but it is potentially really impactful because this work would increase our understanding of the role of snRNAs in splicing regulation.

Comparison of multiple lines and controls may be needed. . IF THIS HAD BEEN REVIEWED IN 2017: . imp_text: This is a new R01 application from an established investigator exploring the regulators of assembly of the small subunit (SSU)/S40 of ribosomes. The PI which is a leader in the study of ribosome assembly had identified the methyltransferase Bud23 as a critical checkpoint in SSU assembly in budding yeast, which as a model for eukaryotic biology. The proposal will test the hypothesis that Bud23 monitors assembly status of the SSU until the central pseudoknot (CPK), a site binding of all four ribosomal subunits and a critical structural element of the ribosome, is properly formed. For this to happen the PI proposes that multiple steps are triggered by Bud23 via the RNA helicase Ecm16. The proposed research will show that Ecm16 mediates dissociation of U3 snoRNA to trigger formation of the CPK (Aim1), that Bud23 activated Ecm16 helicase activity (Aim2), that then Imp4 stabilizes the RNA complex (Aim 3) and finally that Rps2 is the final cofactor for CPK stabilization (Aim 4). The experimental design is logical and clear testing a well-defined mechanistic hypothesis. Extensive preliminary data and through alternative approaches indicate that the project is feasible. This work is likely to have high impact on our understanding of ribosome assembly, which is critical for all aspects of cellular function and survival. This is an excellent proposal from an outstanding team of investigators outlining a clear experimental plan to unravel the regulators of ribosome assembly.
sig_text_str: . Understanding the molecular mechanisms regulating ribosome assembly is important not only as a biological problem, but has also translational potential as transcription is altered in multiple disorders and cancers.
sig_text_wkn: . None noted
inv_text_str: . The PI, Dr. Murray and co-PI Dr. Cobbet are both experts in the field of ribosome assembly and constitute an excellent team to pursue the proposed studies. . They have also enlisted Dr. Mantello to supply expertise on mass spectrometry
inn_text_str: . The proposal is highly conceptually innovative because it will clearly define the steps that are critical for assembly of the small ribosome subunit S40.
app_text_str: . The proposal articulates in four specific aims, each focusing on a step on the assembly of the CPK and on a specific regulator. . Specific Aim 1 focuses on the RNA helicase Ecm16 to determine how it functions in cleavage of specific CPK precursors. If successful, the studies using cold-sensitive mutants to identify intermediate complexes are particularly interesting and will provide mechanistic insight in how the helicase functions. . Specific aims 2 to 4 are designed to define how the complex formation is orchestrated between Bud23, Ecm16, Imp4 and Rps2. By genetic analysis and EMSA the PIs will define the timing of interaction of these proteins with the CPK and its precursor RNAs to define exactly how the SSU is assembled. . Most reagents are already available in the labs and preliminary data is very strong. As some of the experiments are risky (e.g. the cold-chase to identify Ecm16 intermediates listed above) acceptable alternatives are proposed.

imp_text: The contribution of mesotrypsin to prostate cancer as an aberrantly expressed protease that cleaves protease inhibitors is novel and has the potential of providing both insight into the biology of prostate cancer and presenting a novel therapeutic target. In the context of the mesotrypsin activity in prostate cancer, the research team is well suited to investigate this molecule. However, the research scope is very narrow and its impact on the disease itself is based on generalized assumptions for cancer with limited considerations for properties unique to prostate cancer. The impact of the project is limited by lack of considerations for androgen dependent vs. castrate resistant and androgen independent disease. This is critical as most clinically relevant disease is currently managed within the context of its response to androgen. In addition, prostate cancer in humans metastasizes primarily to bone. The absence of a skeletal metastasis model is scientifically limiting since organ-specific metastasis often is associated with organ-specific mechanisms. Discovering mesotrypsin contributions to lung metastasis is therefore not necessarily (or even likely) to reveal the contribution of mesotrypsin to skeletal metastasis.
sig_text_str: . The project addresses a novel protease that may contribute to the progression of prostate cancer. . The unique nature of this protease may offer therapeutic approaches that are independent of existing treatments and can therefore be additive or even synergistic to existing clinical intervention.
sig_text_wkn: . The absence of consideration for existing androgen-based strategies and the evolution of androgen resistant/independent therapies greatly diminishes the likelihood that the project, as proposed, can make meaningful contributions to the treatment of prostate cancer.
inv_text_str: . The PI is clearly a leader in Mesotrypsin research and has the knowledge to investigate this molecule . The other team members are well integrated and established expertise in the fields of animal models and MMP biology.

Considerations of downstream signaling mechanisms is focused on changes in gene expression that maybe entirely correlative with little causative links with mesotrypsin, or with only indirect relationships.

The animal models, while appreciated for their orthotopic approach, do not address two key components of prostate cancer: a) the role of androgen and evolution of androgen resistant/independent disease and b) the lack of a model that addresses skeletal metastasis. . The analysis of “signal mechanism” by investigation its regulation of Cox-2 seems bases on correlative evidence at best. There are significant morphological changes in cells expressing the catalytically dead mesotrypsin and these changes are likely to cause a myriad of changes in gene expression. There no evidence that Cox-2 changes are causative, only that Cox-2 is required for an in vitro phenotype associated with mesotrypsin. . Aim 3 is entirely dependent upon aim 2. Without viable candidates, a different approach should have been taken to investigate the contribution of mesotrypsin to prostate cancer.

imp_text: Considering that cytotoxic, DNA-damaging agents continue to be key clinical strategies, the proposed work could significantly impact our ability to treat cancer by developing inhibitors of XLF which might act as sensitizers to radiotherapy and chemotherapy. The proposed strategy of aim#2 is a high-risk, high-reward challenge that could be transformative not only in improving treatment but also providing evidence of successfully sensitizing patients to cytotoxic therapies that emphasize the tumor without disrupting other biological functions. The parallel analysis of XLF activity on the DNA could provide structural and functional understanding that complements the therapeutic potential.

imp_text: Melanoma initiated with a BRAF driver mutation are common but melanoma-initiating mutations in BRAF are invariably accompanied by cooperative silencing of tumor suppressors. The proposed studies target PI3K pathway inhibitors as a mechanism to achieve long-lasting efficacy in the treatment of melanoma. Identifying a means to disrupt the PI3K pathway that is enabled by loss of PTEN could synergize with BRAF inhibitors and delay or prevent evolution of resistance under treatment with BRAF inhibitors. There is some concern that the exclusive focus on PI3K dependent signaling does not address the possibility that other mechanisms of resistance might evolve quickly. The studies are well designed and will provide both mechanistic insight and therapeutic strategies but there is little emphasis on the identification of possible mechanisms of resistance outside of PI3K pathways or melanoma that does not rely on cooperative silencing of PTEN.
sig_text_str: . The evolution of resistance to pharmacological inhibition of BRAF (vemurafenib) emphasizes the importance of cooperative disruption of additional signaling pathways. The proposed studies emphasize the role of PI3K pathway that is targeted with the loss of PTEN. . Combination treatment (BRAF and PI3K pathways) could offer significant and lasting improvement in the treatment of patients with BRAF driver mutations. . The proposed studies will reveal not only therapeutic benefits but provide also define mechanistic underpinning of the synergy in signaling between BRAF and PI3K.
sig_text_wkn: . Alternative paths to resistance to pharmacological inhibition of BRAF most certainly exist. While the proposal is not expected to account for them or to address them, there is little reflection on the chances that resistance to combination therapy to BRAF and PI3K pathways will develop or exist de novo.

imp_text: This new RO1 proposal aims to address mechanistically how mutations in small nuclear RNAs, important components of the splicing machinery, impact cellular transcriptome and contribute to specific pathologies. Mutations in U4atac snRNA gene, one of the 4 low abundance snRNAs specific for U12 dependent spliceosome, are causally linked with Microcephallic Osteodysplastic Primordial Dwarfism type I (MOPDI). However, the effects of the mutations on the splicing of target genes and how that leads to disease is not understood. Based on their published work and preliminary data, the PI proposes to analyze 1) biochemical consequences of the known MOPD1 mutations on U4atac snRNA functions; 2) gene expression changes affected by these mutations using iPS cell lines derived from the fibroblasts of two MOPD1 patients carrying a particular U4atac mutation; and 3) functional consequences of SNPs in U4atac snRNA. Well written and carefully devised research plan, key collaborators, and preliminary data are major strengths of this application. Successful completion is likely to have significant impact on understanding molecular basis of MOPDI as well as identifying novel disease mutations.

imp_text: Semiconservative DNA replication requires that a helicase unwind the DNA double strand template.  The so called replicative helicase “Cdc45-Mcm2-7-GINS (CMG) complex” unwinds DNA duplex with the 3'–5' polarity suggesting that CMG is placed on the leading strand of a replication fork.  Based on the central hypothesis that the CMG complex constitutes the core replication fork structure, this new RO1 proposal aims to investigate how other human replication proteins interact with this complex and influence DNA replication.  In Aim 1, they propose to develop and utilize in vitro assays that couple the hCMG helicase with replicating Polymerases to demonstrate that Pol e and Pold have strand specific roles in the synthesis of leading and lagging DNA strand, respectively.  Aim 2 will examine physical and functional protein interactions of hCMG in replication; and Aim 3 will focus on the impact of mutations in Psf1 (a component of the GINS complex) on activities associated with the CMG helicase and DNA replication in human cells.  Results of these experiments will establish specific roles for each polymerase at the replication fork, and provide molecular details of other factors at the fork during DNA synthesis.  Although the proposal is only moderately innovative conceptually, PI’s outstanding expertise in the replication field, well established assays, strong preliminary data are strength of this application. This project is likely to have significant impact in advancing the basic understanding of proteins at the replication forks and how they interact with the replicative helicase complex during DNA synthesis.
sig_text_str: . DNA replication is the most basic and fundamental process, and identifying what molecular factors contribute to faithful duplication of genome is essential to understand cell growth and proliferation during normal and pathological conditions. . This proposal utilizes elegant biochemical approach to address how human replicative helicase complex hCMG interacts with DNA polymerases and other replication proteins to execute DNA replication, and investigates the impact of mutation in one of the factors on the functions of hCMG complex.

imp_text: Using Saccharomyces cerevisiae as model organism, this new RO1 proposal aims to investigate molecular mechanisms involved in the transition from the pre-ribosome particle (90S) to the cleaved pre-40S ribosome. Their data suggests that a methyltransferase Bud23 protein is required for 40S biogenesis, and mutations in the RNA chaperone Imp4 and RNA helicase Ecm16 can suppress Bud23 loss. Based on their preliminary genetic and biochemical data, they propose a model that integrates the functions of these factors and the conserved U3 snoRNA in mediating critical transition from 90S to pre-40S ribosome. They propose that Bud23 recognition of its binding site in the small subunit ribosome marks the assembly of small subunit and triggers Ecm16 activation. This promotes the release of U3 snoRNA and associated proteins such as Imp4. Subsequently, binding and folding of pre-40S particle by Rps2 stabilizes the formation of central pseudoknot (CPK) structure and facilitate processing. Aim 1 will examine Ecm16 functions in vivo, identify Ecm16-mediated changes in cofactor composition and the RNA structure of the pre-40S particle, and use genetic approach to identify Ecm16 substrates. Aim 2 will test whether Bud23 activates Ecm16 helicase. Aim 3 will test whether Imp4 stabilizes RNA duplex that is a target of Ecm16 helicase, and Aim 4 will test the ability of Rps2 as a folding cofactor to stabilize the CPK. imp_text: An understanding of the molecular mechanisms that govern recombination and chromosome segregation in meiosis are important for devising means to prevent human aneuplodiies, which constitute both significant economic and human health concerns.  This proposal focusses on characterizing protein interactions between known components of several essential meiotic structures, namely the monopolin complex involved in sister kinetochore cohesion and orientation, the Hop1 complex involved in regulating homolog versus sister recombination, and the synaptonemal complex.  The work is hypothesis-driven, and controls and possible outcomes and interpretations are clearly laid out for each aim.  There is an impressive amount of preliminary data, and in particular, biochemical data that support the feasibility of the proposed work. The investigator is proposing to use cutting edge methodologies, and has established collaborations with experienced colleagues when appropriate. The combined use of biochemical, structural and in vivo genetic approaches to assess  protein interactions and test the consequences of alterations is a major strength of the proposal. This is potentially very high impact work, as understanding the function, assembly and regulation of these structures has been central to the field for quite some time.
sig_text_str: • This proposal addresses a collection of highly significant problems relevant to meiotic chromosome segregation, and thus to the underlying mechanisms involved in generating human aneuploidy, a health issue of major social and economic importance. • Our current understanding of how chromosomes physically interact to accomplish the necessary steps of centromere orientation and regulation of synaptonemal complex assembly is limited by a paucity of detailed, structural information about interactions between the involved proteins.  Success of the proposed studies will provide critical insight into how the monopolin complex assembles to ensure monoorientation of sister chromatids at meiosis I, and perhaps resolve a current debate in the field of the role of condensins in this process. • These studies will reveal interactions between that protein complexes ( Hop1, Zip1)  that regulate and establish assembly of the synaptonemal complex, a essential structure for ensuring homolog associations and recombination. This structure is a central focus of the field, and the work proposed here will provide critical insight into its assembly. Its study has been hindered in part by the refractory nature of some of the components to biochemical studies, a problem that appears to have been at least partly solved by the various biochemical approaches employed here.

imp_text: Our understanding of the relationship between of RNA splicing and human phenotypes (including disease) is in its nascent stages.  Diseases such as MPOD I suggests that snRNAs play an important role in splicing decisions that can have biologically important consequences.  By characterizing how disease-associated mutations alter spliceosome assembly and splicing outcome, these studies may have a significant impact on our understanding of how such mutations alter phenotype.   Identifying target RNAs in which introns are retained in MPOD I mutants could potentially identify therapeutic targets for intervention in this disease. Determining the consequences of naturally occurring SNPs in snRNAs may further our understanding of which residues are critical for function, and how alterations in snRNAs may lead to changes in sRNA splicing profiles.

imp_text: This proposal aims Nairoviruses represent an emerging class of infectious agents that, given globalization, has and may likely lead to future human epidemics. Therefore, a proposal such as this, which aims to characterize a fundamental viral process, is of significant health value. Specifically, this proposal seeks to investigate viral proteases (vOTUs) involved in the deubiquitinylation and deISGylation (removal of ISG15) of the nairovirus CCHFV through a series of enzymological and structural approaches, coupled with cellular and whole organism (murine) functional studies. The strength of this proposal lies in the established expertise of the investigator towards the biophysical study of viral enzymes important for pathogenesis. The straightforward approaches in aim 1 plays directly into the strengths of the laboratory and is anticipated to yield valuable information towards understanding species and substrate selectivity with respect to the catalytic differences of vOTUs. Aim 2 uses a novel reverse genetics approach for CCHFVs, which this investigator established. This is an exciting development of a system that is sure to be of significant value to the field. However, the proposed approach for Aim 2, while conceptually in the correct direction, somewhat oversimplifies the likely challenges associated with the generation of mutant viruses – and dampens my enthusiasm for the proposal.

study_section: Virology A Study Section
imp_text: This proposal seeks to examine the reaction dynamics of poliovirus RdRp using a combination of enzymology and NMR spectroscopy. The purpose of this endeavor is to provide unprecedented atomic-level reaction kinetics of this enzyme, which is an important prototypical viral RdRp; a successful outcome of this proposal will significantly advance our understanding of how polio RdRp utilizes NTPs (natural and synthetic) for nucleic acid incorporation and how it maintains fidelity. The extension of the work might then serve as the basis for other viral RdRps, which typically has a high degree of conservation. The experimental approaches proposed play to the strengths of the investigator and his team; they have a proven and growing track record on characterizing a number of important viral enzymes including polio RdRp. The significance of the work is dependent on how extensible much of the information gleaned from polio RdRp can be translated to understanding the RdRps of current and emerging viruses – which is somewhat at odds with the scope of the program since there is no mention of comparing their results to (recombinant) enzymes from other viruses.
sig_text_str: . Viral RdRps remain an attractive target of antiviral therapeutics. Proposals that aim to understand the conformational changes of RdRp would represent a significant progress in our understanding of this class of virulence factor.
sig_text_wkn: . Poliovirus, while remaining endemic in a handful of countries, has largely been eradicated. Proposals that attempt to translate/validate the molecular information gleaned from work on polio RdRp to the RdRps of viruses that are of current global concern, would increase my enthusiasm for its ‘significance’ and transformative value.
inv_text_str: . The work proposed capitalizes on the strengths of the investigator towards the biophysical study of polio RdRp. He possesses a growing track record of publications that directly characterize a number of enzymes, including polio RdRp, which would suggest that he has the background and training to lead this investigation.
inn_text_str: . RdRp has long been a target for the development of therapeutic interventions, with some small molecule inhibitors (or siRNA therapies) in various clinical trials and/or applications. Using NMR as a means to provide more dynamic information is very innovative and can serve as a foundation for the development of novel therapeutic strategies targeting RdRp.

imp_text: This proposal attempts to investigate the role of the matrix protein, encoded by the VSV virus, in co-opting host cellular gene expression. The molecular interactions between virus and host, especially at the post-transcriptional level, remain poorly understood and therefore this study represents a significant need. The use of new data-intense approaches such as RIP-Seq and PAR-CLIP are appropriate for the questions asked; to determine what cellular RNAs are differentially localized by mislocalized hnRNPs during viral infection. However, it is this same innovative approach that leads to some concern given this group’s relative inexperience with such high-throughput technologies. While it is recognized that Dr. Kerne is in close geographic proximity and is willing to assist in such approaches, less clear are how the computational analyses will be performed and interpreted. As this is a central aspect of one of the aims, the enthusiasm for this grant is dampened.
sig_text_str: . This proposal aims to examine how cellular gene expression is altered by Matrix (M) protein, which is a virally encoded protein of the VSV virus. The interactions between host and pathogen molecules remains poorly understood – particularly at the post-transcriptional regulatory level, and this proposal seeks to investigate one such circuit. . The work proposed, in using VSV model, is well-positioned to reveal fundamental principles of gene expression that can be usurped during pathogenesis.

imp_text: Mesotrypsin as a serine protease that is upregulated in advanced prostate cancer and is predictive of prostate cancer recurrence. Mesotrypsin actively promotes the malignancy and that potent and selective inhibitors of mesotrypsin could be used as novel therapeutics. The goals of this proposal are to define how mesotrypsin promotes prostate cancer progression, to develop mesotrypsin inhibitors with improved selectivity and stability toward mesotrypsin, and to evaluate mesotrypsin inhibitors for therapeutic efficacy in models of prostate cancer progression. Investigations on the role of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer, which is also upregulated in several other cancers, play a similar role in cancer progression and metastasis. Why mesotrypsin is preferred over other targets for new therapeutics is not discussed clearly. Further, translational significance of mesotrypsin inhibition is not explored in the current proposal. Are there clinical trials already in progress? Whether mesotrypsin inhibitors used alone or as a combination therapy? Project mostly explores the basic biology of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer and aiming to synthesize new compounds. Why investigators have picked Cox-2 as a downstream target over hundreds of other targets identified in gene array experiments (data not shown) is not clearly understood. Overall, designing and developing new selective mesotrypsin inhibitors will be useful.
sig_text_str: The proposal will investigate 1. role of mesotrypsin in prostate cancer progression; 2. develop potent and selective mesotrypsin inhibitors; 3. evaluate mesotrypsin inhibition as a therapeutic strategy. Consequently, the long-term, overarching goal of this research is to study role of mesotrypsin in cancer metastasis via cox-2 induction and design new mesotrypsin inhibitors for prostate cancer therapies.

imp_text: • BRAFV600E is essential for melanoma progression, however, its expression is insufficient for conversion of normal melanocytes to malignant melanoma cells. BRAF are invariably accompanied by cooperative silencing of tumor suppressors such as PTEN or CDKN2A. Around 50% of patients achieved response in the Phase 3 trial with pharmacological inhibition of mutationally activated BRAF with vemurafenib. Further, responses were generally short-lived due to acquired drug resistance. Furthermore, many patients developed non-melanoma skin tumors, due to “paradoxical” pro-tumorigenic effects of vemurafenib on dormant tumor-initiating cells expressing mutated HRAS. Long term goal of this project is to design new melanoma therapies that: 1. Augment the overall response rate and the extent of each patient's primary anti-tumor response; 2. Inhibit the onset of lethal drug resistant disease and; 3. Diminish the pro-tumorigenic side effects of BRAF inhibitors. Project is clinically relevant and translational applicability is strong. PI is also collaborating with clinical investigators who are involved with phase 3 trial of BRAF inhibitors. It is also possible that study may not be successful if combined BRAFV600E/PI3’K inhibition is not superior to single agent inhibition of BRAFV600E or PI3’K alone. Also none of the specific aims are designed to analyze tumors from patients enrolled in phase 3 trial to assess significance of pathways proposed.
sig_text_str: • The proposal will investigate how best to employ BRAF inhibitors for melanoma therapy to: 1. Maximize therapeutic benefit; 2. Minimize emergence of lethal drug resistant disease; and; 3. Mitigate potentially harmful side effects (pro-tumorigenic effects). Consequently, the long-term, overarching goal of this research is to design BRAF inhibitor-based combination therapies. • State-of-the-art genetically GEM models, human melanoma cell lines and a range of clinically relevant pathway-targeted inhibitors are employed to elucidate the molecular mechanisms of BRAFV600E/PI3’-kinase pathway cooperation and the consequence of combined pathway-targeted blockade in a pre-clinical setting. • Project overall is very translational in nature. • New targets/drug combinations could be identified for treatment of melanoma. • Study is testing vemurafenib that is being used in phase 3 trial. • Study, in future, could also be utilized with other cancer models having similar mutational status and drug resistance.

imp_text: Shigella flexneri uses its type III secretion system (TTSS) to introduce proteins that facilitate entry of the pathogen into human intestinal cells, leading to bacillary dysentery. The investigators discovered that incubation of Shigella with bile salts promotes recruitment of the first translocator protein, IpaB, to the needle tip where it is stably maintained and is able to interact with host cell membrane components. They recently solved the structure of a significant core fragment of IpaB and propose to expand this work to decipher the steps governed by IpaB in Shigella type III secretion They hypothesize that IpaB has three distinct structures, depending upon its status in the onset of type III secretion: a) it interacts its chaperone in the cytoplasm to prevent the premature formation of protein-protein and/or protein-lipid complexes; b) it interacts with IpaD within the nascent TTSA to control secretion; and c) it interacts with itself and IpaD at the needle tip where it is poised to sense host cell contact. Here they propose to 1) Determine the location of IpaB within quiescent (nascent) and active needles; 2) Solve the crystal structure of IpaB with and without IpgC to determine the structural differences that exist for the cytoplasmic, free and TTSA associated forms of IpaB; and 3) Target key sites and regions proposed to be involved in the protein-protein interactions of IpaB to determine the roles of these interactions in type III secretion induction. This is a well crafted proposal from experts in the field who knows and have the necessary expertise to lead this study to success. However, because the major aims depends on IpaB structure, it is better to have the crystal structure of IpaB in hand to justify feasibility. It is not clear from the proposal that how the knowledge gained here will help to treat infections? imp_text: Pseudomonas biofilms and immunity Biofilms are microbial communities enveloped within a matrix. They exhibit resistance to antimicrobials and host defenses. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common pathogen forming biofilms and causes lung infection in CF and immunodeficient patients. The focus of this application is on studying two extracellular polysaccharides (EPS) and a protein, CdrA, which are critical components of the P. aeruginosa biofilm matrix. Aim 1 will focus investigating structure-function relationships necessary for P. aeruginosa biofilm matrix integrity. Aim 2 will define the roles of biofilm matrix components in modulating interactions of P.aeruginosa with antimicrobials, complement, and human phagocytic cells. Their rational is that because biofilm matrix provides a shielding role, studies aimed at understanding the structure and functions of EPS and CdrA will provide knowledge to develop novel therapeutic strategies. This is a highly relevant study proposed by a group of scientists with appropriate expertise. The discovery that Psl, Pel, and CdrA contribute to biofilm formation in nonmucoid strains, which are believed to be the first to colonize CF patients, is important because it suggest that biofilm formation and EPS synthesis likely precede the switch to mucoidy. This is highly innovative as it represents a new paradigm for P. aeruginosa pathogenesis and exposes a critical window of opportunity for immunological or chemotherapeutic intervention, because once mucoid P. aeruginosa emerges prognosis of CF patients worsens. Interventions aimed at targeting EPS and CdrA will improve management of both acute and chronic P. aeruginosa infections. imp_text: P. aeruginosa secretes enzymes that can degrade the potent immune signaling molecule sphingosine1phosphate (S1P) and its precursor sphingosine. This alters the host immune response, which allows progression of P. aeruginosa infection and the pathogenesis of disease. This is an application from a new investigator, with sufficient expertise in the subject. They propose to understand the role of P. aeruginosa S1P and sphingosine metabolism during the course of lung infection. Toward this goal their plans are to characterize the recognition and degradation system used by P. aeruginosa to respond to S1P and determine the impact of S1P degradation on P. aeruginosa virulence in the lung. They also have a central hypothesis that P. aeruginosa detection of S1P induces genes necessary for S1P degradation, which promotes virulence. Specifically they will characterize S1P and sphingosine dependent transcription in P. aeruginosa, identify the components of the S1P degradation pathway; and examine the impact of S1P degradation on P. aeruginosa infection. This work is highly significant because it will reveal metabolic links between bacterial pathogens and the host, and potentially lead to novel antimicrobial or antivirulence therapies. imp_text: This is a multi-PI application to determine the functional role of ACA11, a snoRNA, which is an orphan H/ACA class non-coding RNA overexpressed in Multiple Myeloma (MM) with t(4;14) chromosomal translocation. It is designed to focus on elucidating the mechanism by which ACA11 exerts its inhibitory effects on ROS-induced cell cycle arrest and cell death in t(4;14) MM cell lines. Strengths of the proposal include: 1) Focused study on the biological role of a specific ncRNA, snoRNA ACA11 in MM with t(4;14) chromosomal translocation. This particular subtype of MM has a shorter survival rate in an already incurable disease. 2) The PI’s recent publication and preliminary data strongly support the working hypothesis. 3) Investigation on the molecular mechanisms through which ACA11 exerts its inhibitory effects on stress stimuli-mediated ROS production and ROS-induced cell death. 4) Data obtained from the proposal have translational value. They will not only facilitate the development of novel therapeutic strategies for the MM patients with t(4:14) chromosomal translocation, but also may identify ACA11 as a potential biomarker for MM diagnosis. A few weaknesses have been identified. 1) The functional studies of cancer biology do not sufficiently match with the proposal’ title and main hypothesis. There is little consideration to test whether overexpression of ACA11 may lead to multi-drug resistance and tumor cell invasion/metastasis in MM. 2) All proposed experiments will be performed using MM cell lines. At least partial laboratory data should be confirmed with clinical analysis of MM patient samples. 3) Study design including in vivo animal models, such as the development of transgenic mouse models with wild-type ACA11 or ACA11 mutants may significantly improve the proposal. In summary, the proposed studies will further our understanding of the biological function of ACA11 in the development and/or progression of MM with t(4;14) chromosomal translocation. imp_text: This is a new application to determine the novel function of miR-30 in disruption of oncogene-induced senescence and promotion of tumorigenesis. It focuses on studying how miR-30 exhibits its biological function through directly targeting CHD7, a transcriptional co-activator, and TNRC6A, an RNA-binding protein essential for miRNA functionality. Several strengths have been identified in the proposal: the concept to examine the impact of the miR-30-CHD7/TNRC6A regulatory circuit on cancer development; in-depth understanding of the roles of CHD7 and TNRC6A in miR-30-mediated bypass of oncogenic ras-induced senescence; the clinical studies aiming to establish that miR-30 contributes to human cancer development by suppressing its direct targets CHD7 and TNRC6A; the PI’s experience in the research area. The score driving weaknesses are: 1) Although Aim 3B is designed to determine the expression levels of miR-30, CHD7 and TNRC6A in human colon cancer samples, for the majority of the proposed studies, it is not clear which cancer types/subtypes this proposal intends to target. 2) Primary BJ and/or WI-38 human fibroblasts are the only host cell lines for almost all of the experiments designed in aims 1 & 2. 3) The rationale to use BJ and WI-38 cells as well as MCF7, U2OS, and HCA7 cells (aim 3) is not clear. It lacks detailed information about their basal expression levels of miR-30, CHD7, TNRC6A and their oncogenic ras status. 4) The mechanism study in aims 1 & 2 appears to be dependent upon the success of aim 3, which is to establish CHD7 and TNRC6A as miR-30 targets in human cancer. Overall, this application is likely to have a modest impact on our understanding of the miR-30-CHD7/TNRC6A regulatory circuit on human cancer development.

study_section: Molecular Oncogenesis Study Section
imp_text: This multi-PI application is to elucidate the molecular mechanisms that control Akt activation in breast cancer. It is hypothesized that aberrant activation of Cdk2/Cyclin A, Skp2 and Akt somatic mutations contribute to the hyperactivation of Akt signaling pathway in breast cancers. The proposed studies intend to define a unique molecular signaling signature that will guide the development of novel inhibitors and/or combination therapies in treating breast cancer. Strengths of the proposal include: 1) Akt hyperactivation frequently observed in breast cancer leads to therapeutic resistance and a poor prognosis, thus is a significant clinic problem in the treatment of breast cancer. 2) Proposed studies focus on the novel mechanisms of Akt activation in breast cancer – one is cell cycle dependent, cdk2/cyclin A-mediated direct phosphorylation of Akt; another is Akt ubiquitination by Skp2, as well as E17K oncogenic mutations in Akt1 and Akt2 leading to activation of Akt in a PI 3-K-independent manner. 3) Data obtained may provide a rationale for the exclusion of PI 3-K inhibitors for treating certain subtypes of breast cancers. Instead, they will inform the use of Cdk2, Skp2 and Akt inhibitors for targeted therapy to achieve optimal treatment efficacy in the clinic. 4) Excellent collaboration between two outstanding investigators in Drs. O'Brian and Wan, whose distinct expertise compensates with each other very well. A few weaknesses are noted. 1) It lacks consideration using drug-resistant breast cancer cell lines and clinical samples of breast cancer to demonstrate the relationship between Akt activation (phosphorylation) and Cyclin A/Skp2 in the real situation. 2) While preliminary studies showed that Skp2 expression was specifically increased in TNBC, no study design was proposed to further verify this observation in the clinical samples of TNBC. 3) Akt reactivation upon inhibition of PI-3K in breast cancer cells may be due to increased expression of erbB3 and/or other receptor tyrosine kinases without aberrant activation of Skp2 and/or Akt somatic mutations. Thus, the hypothesis in Aim 2 should be modified accordingly. In conclusion, the current proposal will significantly improve our understanding of the molecular mechanism of Akt hyperactivation in breast cancers. However, the clinical relevance-related studies need be enhanced. The overall impact of this project will be modest to high.

imp_text: The goal of this proposal is to investigate the role of PD-1 and PD-L1 in inflammation in the heart. In particular they are keen to know which cells express and respond to this protein and associated ligand. To this end they will test cardiac cell behavior with and without these proteins. Then they will test myeloid involvement and finally develop method to therapeutically induce T cell tolerance to myocardial antigens in the context of CTL-induced myocarditis (autoimmune). The concept is new and could lead to therapeutic strategies to quell aberrant immune responses. The concept seems somewhat naïve from these experienced investigators as it does not seem to appreciate the fact that some inflammation is of course beneficial.  In addition, they fail to consider the variation in inflammation with different forms of heart failure and instead seem to lump them all together.  The approach is good by and large, however despite the extensive animal studies they fail to appropriately address sex as a biological variable. In addition, the proposal would be strengthened by evidence that augmentation of PD-1/PD-L1 signaling can positively alter inflammatory responses. However, the investigators are quite good and the environment is appropriate for the work.
sig_text_str: . The proposal is significant as it seeks to identify mechanisms why which PD-1/PD-1L regulate inflammation in the context of cardiovascular disease. . The premise is supported by preliminary data showing an increase in inflammation and a decrease in survival in mice lacking PD-L1 and PD-L2 in response to CTL-mediated myocarditis.
sig_text_wkn: . The premise is somewhat marred by the many cell types of both the immune system and the heart that express PD-1L, such that the primary effects are difficult to discern. . In addition, and contrarily, PD-L1 is highly expressed in human heart following infarction.  Given the fact that most individuals suffer poor remodeling and long term failure following an infarction it seems counter-intuitive that enhanced PD-L1 expression would be beneficial (as it is already there).

The second is that inflammation might be tempered by cytokine and cytokine blocking reagents with DC transfer.

The second primary weakness is little evidence that aberrant inflammation can be positively regulated by alterations in PD-1L (or PD-1). . Other more minor weaknesses include the following. First, the preliminary data with human tissue is weak in that only one histologic section is shown, at high mag and with no attempt at repeated measures or quantification calling into question scientific rigor. . Second, there is confusion associated with the cytokine induction studies. It would seem IL-17 induced expression of PD-1L, but with the tolerance induction protocol, the expression of IL-17 goes down? Consideration of sex as a biological variable is not well addressed; there is mention of using female lymphocytes in equal numbers of male and female recipients but without motivation.

imp_text: The goal of this proposal is to link ROS with calcium signaling and further to localize mitochondrion that specifically participate in this association. Having shown that the in vivo function of U4atac snRNA was reduced and U12 dependent introns are retained in patient-derived cell lines, the author proposes to dissect the molecular defects associated with these mutations. imp_text: The proposed research describes the characterization of proteins at the replication fork and the role they play in replication. The author argues that different DNA polymerases are responsible for different aspects of replication (leading vs lagging strand), a distinction they assay through their use of biotin labeled dUTP in a unique in vitro assay (Aim #1). The author also proposes to investigate the roles of other proteins found at the fork, namely the interaction between Ctf4 and CMG, since CTF4 promotes the helicase activity of CMG in vitro (Aim #2). The work proposed will provide useful information about the regulation of replication but portions of the proposal appear to be more of a laundry list of experiments, making it difficult to understand the rationale for some of the experiments and how they will further our understanding of how replication is regulated. Indeed, the specific questions that the author wishes to answer, particularly in Aim #2, are unclear. These major weaknesses detract from this proposal.

This processing and assembly reaction involves multiple factors including the helicase Ecm16, Bud23, Imp3, Imp4 and Rps2. imp_text: This project is based on the applicant’s previous findings that vOTUs, a domain present in L protein encoded by nairovirus, contain proteolytic activity that cleaves off ubiquitin or ISG15 from their modified proteins. Since modification of cellular proteins by both ubiquitin and ISG15 is known to be important for INF-mediated signaling, the author proposes the project to study the structure-function relationship of vOUTs in inhibiting this innate antiviral response. While some of the studies proposed in the project are interesting, the enthusiasm of the proposal is significantly hampered by several major weaknesses: 1) The proteolytic activity of various vOTUs toward ubiquitin and ISG15 is determined in vitro and its physiological relevance is unclear; 2) There is no effort in identifying the exact cellular/viral proteins whose modification by ubiquitin/ISG15 is affected by expression of vOUTs; and 3) The controversy whether vOUTs are directly involved in viral replication as a component of the L protein is not resolved.

The applicant criticizes that previous characterization of the proteolytic activity of vOUTs is not physiologically relevant, yet their proposed experiments measuring the activity are not any better, as all of them are in vitro assays using purified proteins. imp_text: This project is raised to determine the mechanism through which the virus-encoded M protein inhibits host protein translation. M protein is known to bind a host protein called Rae1. In contrast to the currently-held view that M protein induces host shut off by blocking nucleus to cytosol transport of host mRNA though inactivation of Rae1, the applicant raises a new idea that the complex formed by M protein and Rae1 inhibits host cell transcription, and the observed block in mRNA transport and translation is simply a downstream effect of the inhibition of mRNA synthesis. While this new idea is generally supported by the preliminary data present in the proposal, focusing on such a narrow point as the major goal of the project reduces the significance of the project. Instead of studying M protein-induced inhibition of global transcription, which is the novel discovery made by the applicant, the two aims raised in the proposal instead dig into details of the well-reported downstream effects of RNA transport and translation, which also reduces innovation of the proposal. Moreover, most experiments analyzing mRNAs bound to hnRNPs or affected by manipulations of these proteins do not support the hypothesis raised in the project even if the expected results are obtained.

The applicant has observed that unlike normal cells in which hnRNPs are mainly located in nucleus, some of these proteins are exported out to cytosol in virus-infected cells as a result of M protein-induced global inhibition in gene transcription. Based on these observations, in Aim 1 the applicant proposes to use mRNAs known to bind these shRNPs during translation to determine whether they are preferentially transported out of nucleus during viral infection. This approach will only work if hnRNPs bind to the same mRNAs during translation and transportation, and the mRNAs can only be transported out of the cells through these hnRNPs. Neither of these two assumptions has been proved to be the case. . The accumulation of hnRNPs in translation complex of virus-infected cells may not be specific to the infection but rather a consequence of inhibition of gene transcription, as other approaches inhibiting global mRNA synthesis also caused accumulation of these proteins in cytosol. . In Aim 2, it will be impossible to determine whether the detected mRNAs bind to hnRNPs during translation, transportation or other events. The proposed pulse labeling experiments also cannot determine whether the observed difference is caused by the effect of hnRNPs on protein translation or mRNA transport.

Aim 1 is about refining crystal production in order to obtain a high resolution structure of vcCNT.  Aim 2 focus on showing that the prokaryotic transporter shares a common mechanisms of transport to the human version.  Aim 3 focus on drug binding and transport. imp_text: Dr. O’Brian previously demonstrated that Ehrlichia chaffeensis secretes a protein, TRP120, into it’s host cell’s cytoplasm, where it is ubiquitinated, translocated to the nucleus, and modifies host cell transcription. The current proposal aims to delve deeper into the mechanisms of those phenomena. A major weakness of the proposal is that the majority of studies use artificial systems that probably do not replicate natural occurrences. For example, during E. chaffeensis infection, TRP120 becomes ubiquitinated and translocates to the nucleus. However, when host cells are transfected so that they produce TRP120, it is necessary to cotransfect with a mutant ubiquitin in order to get translocation. This implies that Ehrlichia produces another protein(s) and/or manipulates host cell post-translational modification machinery to cause TRP120 translocation – the application does not address that point. It is also unknown whether TRP120 modified with mutant ubiquitin behaves in the same manner as naturally-modified TRP120. These and other flaws severely reduce enthusiasm for this proposal.
