Throughout the proposal, Dr O’Brian writes with utmost confidence that the hypotheses are correct, e.g. constantly describing studies that will “demonstrate” that something happens, rather than test whether or not it happens. . When produced by E. chaffeensis during infection, TRP120 translocates to the host cell. Ectopically produced TRP120 (produced following transfection) does not translocate. The implied use of other bacterial and/or host factors would be useful to investigate. In order to obtain translocation of ectopically-produced TRP120, Dr O’Brian must co-transfect with a mutant ubiquitin (which does not multimerize). There are no studies to determine whether TRP120 bound by that mutant ubiquitin is comparable to TRP120 bound by normal ubiquitin. . Some proposed studies, such as 2.2, will transfect host cells to produce ectopic TRP120 to determine its effects on host transcription, but will not co-transfect with the mutant ubiquitin. Dr O’Brian’s data indicate that ectopically-produced TRP120 does not go to the nucleus, making the proposed study impossible to interpret. . DNA-binding assays do not use full-length TRP120, but instead use a small protein fragment. Justification is not provided. Neither is it shown that the fragment binds DNA in the same manner as does full-length TRP120. All results using the polypeptide fragment are of questionable value. . DNA-binding studies do not address binding specificity (i.e. use of specific and nonspecific competitors). Related to this, the applicant proposes that TRP120 affects DNA-binding by host Sp1, but actual competition studies are not proposed. . The figures and legends are extremely tiny, and several figures are illegible (e.g. Figs 5 and 9). These figures are valuable for interpreting the proposal, but the reviewer is left in confusion because they cannot be read.

imp_text: Dr Murphy reports that sphingosine is a major component of lung surfactant, and that Pseudomonas aeruginosa that are unable to catabolize sphingosine are at a competitive disadvantage compared to wild-type bacteria. He has identified an apparent DNA-binding protein named SphR (a member of the AraC family) and two adjacent operons that are involve with sphingosine catabolism. He hypothesizes that P. aeruginosa detect a precursor of sphingosine (sphingosine-1-phosphate, S1P) to degrade S1P, which promotes virulence, and that this alters host S1P and sphingosine signaling pathways. This is an intriguing hypothesis, but Dr Murphy does not propose any studies that would specifically test those hypotheses, which a very significant weakness.
sig_text_str: . Mutants of sphR, which encodes a probable regulatory protein, were 10-fold less able to infect mouse lungs (as ascertained by competitive co-infection studies with wild-type vs. sphR mutant bacteria) . Wild-type P. aeruginosa can grow with sphingosine as the sole nitrogen source, whereas sphR mutants cannot survive on sphingosine. This suggests that bacteria able to utilize sphingosine have a competitive edge over mutants.
sig_text_wkn: . Dr Murphy will test his hypotheses in vivo only with an acute model of mouse lung infection (inhalation, then assess results after 24 hours only). The major lung-associated human health problem with P. aeruginosa is related to persistent colonization as a result of chronic diseases such as cystic fibrosis. The short-term assays will not provide any insight on that major human health threat. . Dr Murphy hypothesizes that degradation of lung sphingosine by P. aeruginosa represents a way for the bacterium to alter host S1P and sphingosine signaling pathways (bold type in the “significance” section). No studies are proposed to test that hypothesis. . The “innovation” section similarly states that “detection of S1P represents a new way to eavesdrop on host immune signaling”. No studies are proposed to test that hypothesis. . The “innovation” section further states that “detection of S1P and sphingosine is a novel strategy to regulate virulence”. The preliminary data indicate that bacteria able to degrade sphingosine are better at acute colonization of mouse lungs. This could be due simply to the wild-type bacteria being able to use sphingosine as a nutrient. Furthermore, there are no studies planned that will specifically test the hypothesis that P. aeruginosa detect S1P or sphingosine to regulate virulence properties.

The overall impact is medium-to-high given the technical expertise of the investigator and the significance of the question. The overall impact is high given the importance of LPS in human disease and as a method for controlling bacterial infection. study_section: Synthetic and Biological Chemistry A Study Section
imp_text: The aim of this project is to develop caged morpholino antisense oligonucleotides (cMOs) either with terminus-to-backbone or terminus-to-base linkages to target gene expression, as well as to use a combinatorial approach that will take advantage of chromophores with different cleavage wavelengths to induce wavelength-selective inactivation of multiple genes. The proposed research is significant in that it will improve many of the limitations of the existing MOs, in particular the multiple-target RNA hybridization, due to their curvature and in the case of the ones with terminus-to-base linkages due to the disruption of Watson-Crick base pairing. The preliminary results are strong, many of the steps described under the approach being already proven and the team of investigators has extensive expertise in this field leading to confidence on the proposal’s success.
sig_text_str: • MOs have been extensively used to target RNA, disrupting translation, splice junctions, etc. Caged MOs (cMOs) have the advantage that their hybridization to     the target RNA can be optically controlled. The PIs have developed several generations of these cMOs and applied them study gene function in zebrafish embryos. The new generation that they propose to develop reduces the ability of the cMOs to hybridize with RNA prior to photoactivation, they do not require accessory oligonucleotides or multiple caging groups. • The developed cMOs have multiple applications, beyond the context of the proposed research.
sig_text_wkn: • None noted
inv_text_str: . Both investigators have extensive experience in this area, both the Kelly ad Deckers labs pioneered the development of first generation cMOs. Strong letter of support from Dr. Shen Lee with whom one of the PIs collaborated in the past. The synergy between the investigators is excellent.
inn_text_str: . The development of this new generation cMOs is innovative in that it will allow combinatorial gene knockdowns. Additionally, these new cMOs are superior to existing cMOs by having higher efficacy, reduced toxicity and applicability during later developmental stages.
inn_text_wkn: . None noted
app_text_str: . The preliminary data is strong for each specific aim. Initially cMOs with various linker sizes that targeted ntla, spt, and ptf1a transcripts were used as a proof-of-concept system. Additionally a piperazinylphosphorodiamidate MO dimer was prepared, as well as an NPOM-caged thymidine that was used to produce a nucleobase-caged MO that successfully targeted the chd gene in zebrafish. Moreover, preliminary data to support the development of cMOs with multiple chromophores was presented. . The rationale for the choice of chromophores and type and length of linkers is well described. . The proposed experiments are well developed and follow a logical progression. Most of the proposed in vivo experiments have been performed with other cMOs as shown in preliminary studies. . Potential pitfalls are briefly discussed for each specific aim, although the investigators are confident on the outcome of most experiments considering that several steps have already been tested in preliminary results.
app_text_wkn: . Lariat cMOs with differing macrocycle sizes and configurations will be prepared and in vitro experiments will be used to test their efficacy and select the most effective ones for which in vivo experiments will be pursued. The proposed in vitro experiments that will indirectly test the cMOs binding to their targets are quite elaborate involving in vitro transcription and translation systems. It is surprising that there are no proposed experiments that will test the direct binding of the cMOs to their RNA targets. In addition to providing information about the molecular interactions between the cMOs and their RNA targets, such experiments should include control experiments addressing the off target binding of the cMOs.

study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function C Study Section
imp_text: This project seeks to use high resolution cryo-EM, X-ray crystallography, saturation transfer EPR and kinetic analysis to test a model that describes how the microtubules stimulates the steps of the kinesin catalytic cycle. Additionally it will try to characterize the molecular basis for communication between the two heads of a fully functional dimeric kinesin as it translocates on microtubules. The scope of the project seems to be very narrow and the PI did not do a great job at describing the significance and innovation of the work. The proposal was very dense, too detailed for the non cryo-EM expert, making it very hard to follow the actual hypothesis that was tested at each point. While there are sufficient preliminary results for the cryo-EM work, I have some concerns regarding the success of the  site-directed mutagenesis and subsequent saturation-transfer EPR experiments.
sig_text_str: . The discussion of the current limitations of the cryo-EM methods for characterizing  the interactions  between the two heads of dimeric kinesin
sig_text_wkn: . The work proposed was not put into context, with the exception of the broad statement that “kinesin is implicated in numerous ailments, including Parkinson’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders”, no strong arguments were made why understanding the structural and functional mechanism of this motor is relevant. . There should have been a clear discussion on how the knowledge derived from this work might be applicable beyond the kinesin context.
inv_text_str: . Dr. Sullivan has a proven track record in the field of cryo-EM, especially applied to studies of kinesin. He has assembled a team of collaborators who will help him accomplish different aspects of the proposal, experiments that will not be possible in his own lab. Strong letters of support.
inv_text_wkn: . Grantsmanship. The proposal was very hard to read, it felt disconnected and it did not seem to follow a clear progression. In many places the reviewer had to connect the dots, both the Significance and Innovation sections could be greatly improved. There were also some typos present.
inn_text_str: . The discussion of the novelty of the first method they developed for solving 3D reconstructions of actively stepping kinesin dimers.
inn_text_wkn: . With a few exceptions, the innovation section was simply a list of the methods that will be used in the proposal to address specific questions. Many of these points should have been made in the Significance section.
app_text_str: . The proposed experiments will test new models that functionally link the kinesin’s ATPase cycle to microtubule attachment by solving near-atomic resolution cryo-EM structures of the kinesin-microtubule complex in the no-nucleotide and ATP bound states. . Strong preliminary data on some parts of the proposal, especially the cryo-EM experiments.
app_text_wkn: . Overall the Approach section was very detailed and hard to follow at times, full of technicalities that did not necessarily enhance the understanding of the goals of a particular experiment. . Under aim 1.2 for the elucidation of the structure of the kinesin’s ADP-Pi state a BKinM construct which fuses conventional kinesin motor domain to a specialized N-terminal extension found in the BimC kinesin isotype will be used. It is unclear how the data obtained for this construct can be directly extrapolated to the wild type kinesin, since this construct has a higher affinity for microtubules than the wild type kinesin. . Point-mutations of essential residues proposed to be implicated in the microtubule attachment and subsequent functional studies are proposed. There are no control  experiments proposed to test the structural integrity of the point mutants. . For the saturation transfer EPR experiments bifunctionally labeled kinesin constructs will be generated by introducing surface cysteine at specific points. What is the confidence in the success of the production of these mutants? Similarly as discussed above, what control experiments will be performed to test the structural integrity of these mutants? . imp_text: The BMRB is very clearly a critical resource in the portfolio of public resources available to structural biologists today. Given that access to structural information often informs and heightens the impact of other types of “wet lab” and modelling investigations there is no doubt this resource greatly accelerates the speed of important medical discoveries. Continued support of this resource will have enormous impact on a very wide range of fields. The support and enabling of 3,500 publications makes this quite clear. There are very few enabling resources that can make a similar claim. Without such a resource, there is not much point in continuing to collect NMR data. And without it, all of the tools developed to view and interact with NMR data becomes pointless. Given this very broad impact on productivity. I view this as a must fund proposal. That said, I must comment that much of the proposed new tool development seems peripheral to the main mission of the BMRB. I feel the budget is quite inflated, and that the staffing to support the development of new tools is work that should be competed separately on a case by case basis.

imp_text: The PI outlines new theoretical models to study the formation and evolution of amyloid aggregation. The primary focus is on developing new methodology that permits both high-resolution information and long time scales.  Current approaches either limit resolution to extend time scales, or offer high resolution but short duration simulations. The PI posits that their approach will afford deep knowledge on the actual physiology of amyloid formation and disease progression. Although the approach seems solid and is an area of need in the amyloid field, the proposal suffers on several fronts that limit its impact. First, the proposal as constructed is difficult to read, is ill-formulated and would greatly benefit from peer editing.  Second, the PI indicates that high-resolution models are needed, because the information garnered from crystallography is unreliable due to it only isolating one of many substructures possible. The PI then uses the crystal structure as the basis for justifying the use of their methodology.  The two elements seem contradictory and weaken the proposal substantially. Third, there are several large assumptions that are made to simplify and justify their approach. In the proposals current form there is little justification for these assumptions and if any of them are incorrect any information garnered from this approach is nullified. An example is the simplification of the system to focus only on the residue identity of a specific location to determine the kinetics and energetics of H-bond formation. It is most likely that neighboring residues and possibly residues 2 or more positions away from the central residue will impact these values. The authors briefly comment on this limitation at the end of the proposal but not in a suitable manner to overcome my concerns. Page 1 of 3

sig_text_wkn: . It is unclear if the assumptions being made to validate their approach are reasonable. As such, the significance of any outcomes are only as reliable as their assumptions. The PI would benefit from further preliminary data showing more reliable predictions.

study_section: Biochemistry and Biophysics of Membranes Study Section
imp_text: The submitted proposal outlines methodology employing Vibrio choleae concentrative nucleoside transporter (VcCNT) as a model for human CNT proteins. The general approach is to use x-ray crystallography to decipher the molecular mechanism employed by hCNT to transport nucelosides and nucleoside based drugs for the ultimate generation of new therapeutic reagents. The approach centers around the hypothesis that the fundamental mechanisms of nucleoside transport is conserved between prokaryotic and mammalian CNTs. The PI is very well qualified to tackle the proposed research and has ample background in the use of crystallography, ITC, fluorescence and patch clamp methods to interrogate membrane bound transports. Based on his background, the detailed preliminary data and detailed well thought out proposal, there is a high probablility for success that can impact the broader community.  Two main factors limit assignment of a higher overall impact score. First, although the central hypothesis is likely fairly safe, the authors propose experiments in aim 2 and 3 that can readily validate this central hypothesis. Namely the use of known hCNT mutations that disrupt nucleoside recruitment and transport (E308 , E322 and E498; aim 2c). The grant would have been much stronger if this was a primary focus as any failure of these mutations to disrupt signaling would nullify their central hypothesis. The second major factor limiting the proposal is related to the first.  The authors identify in aims 2 and 3 numerous known residues imperative for selection, recruitment and transport of nucleosides and nucleoside based drugs via hCNTs. In light of this, it makes one wonder how much the structures in aim 1 (and central goal of the proposal) will advance the field as it seems more than likely the structures will just confirm and explain known residues involved in CNT function. As a result of the two points above, my excitement of an otherwise very well conceived grant is dampened. Page 1 of 3

imp_text: The PI has obtained key preliminary results suggesting that the circadian transcription factor CLOCK:BMAL1 activity that regulates expression of ~4000 genes is mediated by a key region, exon 19, and a prolyl cis-trans isomerization switch.  Further the PI has identified a cancer-induced protein, PASD1, that shares sequence analogy with exon 19 and may mediate repression of CLOCK:BMAL1 in cancer cells.  Major strengths of the proposed approach are the focus on structural/ molecular basis of control of protein expression in generation and maintenance of circadian rhythm and aberrance thereof in cancer cells.  The approach is intended to sort out inhibitory and stimulatory interactions of regulatory players, CRY and CBP/p300, respectively, with the regulatory region.  Clarifying the role of PASD1 in modulating and regulating CLOCK:BMAL1 activity may unveil how PASD1 interaction with clock-interacting protein circadian (CIPC (inhib)) and histone methyltransferase (MLL1 (active)) disrupts clock function.

imp_text: What is proposed is an expansion of the developed one-dimensional random walk model of peptide aggregation to an application that can address mechanisms of and key factors in assembly of peptide aggregates in disease states such as Alzheimers.  A central focus is that while such toxic aggregates develop over extremely long time scales in vivo, current computational approaches are not able to adequately encompass this time frame.  Two aims are elaborated.  The first is to exam the variables affecting nucleation and fibrillogenesis and to identify important rate limiting steps in the process utilizing a random walk approach of association.   The second is to combine the first with molecular dynamics analysis that will permit extrapolation to dramatically longer timescales than currently accessible with ultimate application the AB40 and AB42 peptides of Alzheimer’s placques. imp_text: This is a proposal to provide funding for the maintenance and evolution of the Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank.  This was previously supported by the NLM but funding was significantly reduced due to altered NLM perspectives.  The Biological Magnetic Resonance Data Bank is an important resource for structural biology and endeavors to provide a two-way capability by which relevant stored information can be queried, downloaded and manipulated.  As indicated in the proposal, much of the requested funding is in the form of maintenance, though this in itself is an ever-evolving process with significant demands for flexibility and alteration.  This is understandable and worthy of support.  More speculative is the nature of the actual advances that will be made from the proposed aims and it is difficult to judge what can be accomplished given the absence of metrics respecting this.

study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function B Study Section
imp_text: Circadian rhythms represent one of the most fundamental aspects of animal behavior.  The PI proposes to investigate structural and functional aspects regulating the molecular machinery underlying circadian rhythms.  He further links his study to dysfunctional/pathological disruptions of circadian rhythms that occur in cancerous tissues.  While not completely cohesive in his overall goal to unravel the function of intrinsically disordered regions of CLOCK- BMAL1, this reviewer feels that the potential outcomes of this research are likely to provide both important fundamental and biomedically relevant insights.
sig_text_str: The PI promises to investigate two specific aspects of the molecular machinery regulating circadian rhythms.  Specifically, the PI wants to tie the conformational flexibility/disorder of the BMAL1 c-terminal binding region to its function as circadian chemical oscillator.  The PI further proposes to investigate the role of binding to CLOCK Exon 19 contributes to the function of the CLOCK-BMAL1 complex.  In particular the PI proposes to explore the role of PASD1 in mimicking CLOCK Exon 19 and disrupting circadian rhythms, as observed in certain cancer cells.
inv_text_str: Dr. Jay Sullivan has a solid publication record and scientific background in the specific research he proposes.  He utilizes a wide range of both in vitro and in vivo characterization techniques, many of which he has extensive experience with.    These are all positive indicators that he will be able to perform the experiments proposed here. .
inv_text_wkn: . The PI states that his main goal is to unravel the structural basis for the regulation of the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex in the disordered regions.  The second specific aims does not seem to be well integrated with this stated overall goal.
inn_text_str: The innovation provided by this proposal is the integration of mechanistic structural and functional assays in unraveling the workings of circadian rhythms.  Equally important is the potential for gaining new insights into the regulation of circadian rhythms.  Towards this end, the PI has put together a well thought-out complement of experimental approaches. .
inn_text_wkn: The PI states that his main goal is to unravel the structural basis for the regulation of the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex in the disordered regions.  The second specific aims does not seem to be well integrated with this stated overall goal. .
app_text_str: The first specific aim of the PI is to investigate the role of a cis-trans transition in the disordered C-TAD region of BMAL1 as critical time-dependent switch regulating the binding and unbinding of CRY and CBP/p300 to this region.  The PI has generated preliminary data that cyclosporin A, an inhibitor of the peptidyl proline isomerase, can retard and completely abolish CLOCK:BMAL1 activity in a dose-dependent manner.  In Aim 1 the PI then proposes to use solution NMR to (a) determine the cis/trans conformation by locking in either one of these two states. For aim 2, the PI focuses on the role of the antagonism between MLL1 and CIPC in regulating CLOCK, and how a cancer-related protein PASD1 in disrupting circadian rhythms via interactions with CLOCK that the same Exon 19 binding site.  The proposed biochemical binding assays certain could provide some important insights into the cyclic regulation of CLOCK function.  The cell assay for characterizing PASD1 function, in particular, seems a nice way to quantitate the role of PASD1 in dysregulating CLOCK function.
app_text_wkn: It is not a priori clear how easy it will be generate the  “lock in” states of the two distinct cis/trans states of the C-TAD region of BMAL1. However, this is a critical part of both the in vitro and in vivo experiments proposed for all the experiments in specific aim 1.  The PI either needs to clarify why this is simple “state of the art” or should provide some preliminary result indicating that he can generate at least one of these two conformation, either in vivo or in vitro.

imp_text: While shared resources such as the BMRB are valuable and important facilities in support of basic research, it is this reviewer’s understanding that the R01 funding mechanisms is reserved for hypothesis-driven basic research. This application, instead, asks for facilities support without any clear and independent research agenda.  The specific aims of the applications are overly broad and it is completely unclear whether the support requested is used to investigate the quality and predictive capacity of specific algorithms, who would perform such research, and what specific problems/questions will be addressed.  Instead this seems to be essentially a request for basic infrastructure support.  As such it should probably be submitted as a P40 application.  This fundamental short-coming of the application seems to make any further review redundant. This overall evaluation does not imply that the BMRB doesn’t serve a very valuable function. In fact, such shared resources do deserve funding support.  It only expresses the reviewer’s opinion that an R01 application is not the appropriate funding mechanism for such infrastructure support.

sig_text_str: The structure and detailed molecular understanding of various transporters function remains a basic challenge in cell and molecular biology.  The PI proposes to investigate the structure/function relationship of concentrative nucleoside transporters (CNTs) with their three different isoforms expressed in different tissues.  CNTs are also involved in transmembrane transport of nucleoside-derived drugs, including the anticancer drug gemcitabine and several anti-viral drugs.  A better understanding of the structure of various transmembrane channels and how their structure informs function is certainly an important basic research goal.
sig_text_wkn: The PI’s argument that understanding the structure of CNTs might improve targeting of anticancer/antiviral drugs seems a bit farfetched since the PI himself notes that it seems to be the expression levels of CNTs that appear to induce drug resistance. There are also residual concerns about the degree to which the prokaryotic vibrio cholerae CNT (vcCNT) replicates the structure and function of human homologs. .
inv_text_str: Dr. Brett Baker has a solid background in the area of protein crystallization and the characterization of ion channel using electrophysiology.   This provides a solid foundation for his proposed work on crystallization and characterization of the bacterial nucleoside transporter.
inv_text_wkn: A concern is his lack of recent publications since assuming his new position as associate professor at Duke – despite significant support from several funding agencies.
inn_text_str: The PI has identified crystallization conditions for the cvCNT channel and has collected preliminary structural data.  This structure suggests some unusual and intriguing structural organization.
inn_text_wkn: Equilibrium binding studies and measurements of transport rates, while certainly important, are not exactly at the forefront of scientific innovation .
app_text_str: The PI has already expressed, purified and crystallized the bacterial homolog of the human CNT.  In addition, he has collected preliminary structural information from these crystals.  This bodes well for the PI’s ability to obtain high-resolution crystal structures for vcCNT in the presence and absence of bound nucleosides The functional characterization of the vcCNT and hCNT proposed by the PI seems reasonably straight forward.  The proposed mutations of the vcCNT in the regions of high sequence alignment between vcCNT and hCNT (Fig. 5) are a nice way to look at preserved structure/function elements.
app_text_wkn: There are residual concerns whether the PI will be able to resolve the phasing problem in order to obtain high-resolution structures.  However, the PI does propose a variety of alternative approaches to solve this issue.

imp_text: This is an excellent proposal by a broadly trained and very competent young investigator. The specific aims are hypothesis driven and address the fundamental molecular mechanism for gene activation by the CLOCK:BMAL1 transcription factor, a central player in establishing and maintaining circadian in mammals including humans. The PI has assembled an impressive team of collaborators, has a well-equipped laboratory and strong institutional support to carry out this fundamental research with promise for important translational applications.
sig_text_str: . Maintenance of normal circadian rhythms are crucial to life forms of all types. In mammals, it is crucial to time the peak activity of integrated biochemical processes with the solar day. . In humans, loss of this internal 24-hour circadian clock leads to diabetes, metabolic syndrome, cancer, and premature aging by disrupting the temporal coordination of physiology with our behavior and the external environment. . A strength of the proposal is the PI’s focus on establishing the molecular mechanism for one of the key components of the molecular circadian oscillator, the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex, a transcription factor that activates a very large number of genes. . The significance of the proposal is that the new mechanistic knowledge is expected to advance both basic and applied knowledge in circadian control of human physiology.

He has trained with leading scientists in NMR spectroscopy and in Circadian Rhythm biology. He is proficient in carrying out in vivo studies using cell culture to study circadian rhythms in synchronized cells in vivo. This is a powerful tool and he has assembled the necessary genetic constructs for doing so. He is also proficient in NMR spectroscopy to monitor conformational changes in peptides (i.e. cis/trans isomerizations of prolines) and association of proteins. . The PI has assembled a very impressive set of collaborators that bring complementary expertise to help to achieve the goals of the proposal. Each collaboration is carefully documented in the research plan and with appropriate letters.

The innovation of this proposal stems from the inter-disciplinary training of the PI and his facility using techniques from cell biology to solution NMR spectroscopy, which enable him to formulate and test molecular, atomic-level hypotheses regarding function that are biomedically relevant. . The two specific aims test novel, specific hypotheses revolving around the concept that CLOCK and BMAL1 transcriptional activation domains use intrinsic flexibility to regulate binding of activators and repressors to contribute to 24-hour timing of the molecular clock.

app_text_str: . The PI will address two specific aims: 1) how a dynamic conformational switch based on cis-trans isomerization of a specific Proline in the BMAL1 activation domain regulates CLOCK:BMAL1 activity and 2) how competition for binding to the CLOCK activation domain regulates CLOCK:BMAL1 in normal clock function and in human cancer. . The main tool for obtaining atomic-level mechanistic information is nuclear magnetic resonance NMR spectroscopy. The biological relevance of the NMR observations will be confirmed with quantitative in vitro biochemical work and with cell-based studies using a cultured cells transformed with a reporter gene that contains a promoter responsive to CLOCK:BMAL1, which drives a luciferase gene, yielding a luminescence readout that can be monitored as a function of time. In this way subtle changes in the period and amplitude of the circadian rhythm can be monitored. . The PI plans to use mutated peptide substrates that are locked in the cis or in the trans conformation and which can be introduced into cultured cells to determine which conformation binds activators and which binds inhibitors. . A strength of the proposal is the specificity of the hypotheses to be tested and the clearly designed experiments to determine conformations in vitro and test the effects in vivo

imp_text: This proposed research is significant because concentrative nucleoside transporters (CNTs) are an important family of transmembrane proteins, responsible for active transport of nucleosides across cell membranes as well as nucleoside-like drugs, which have proven very useful in cancer and anti-viral therapy. The proposal addresses an important gap in our knowledge: the lack of atomic-resolution structures of members of this protein family and detailed knowledge of their mechanism of action and the features of specific family members that confer specificity for particular nucleosides and drugs. In view of the difficulties of crystallizing human CNTs, the PI has developed a bacterial model system and has accumulated promising preliminary results that indicate likely success in determining the 3D structure of the bacterial protein, from which a 3D homology models of human CNTs can be built an analyzed. Appropriate functional studies on the bacterial and human proteins are planned. The main concern of this reviewer is that the possibility of directly solving a human CNT structure using cryo-EM, which does not require growing diffraction quality crystals, is not considered or even mentioned by the PI.

The proposal concerns a physiologically significant family of integral membrane proteins, human concentrative nucleoside transporters (hCNTs), that use active transport to import nucleosides into cells for biosynthesis. CNTs also function to import nucleoside-derived drugs across cell membranes, including important anti-cancer and anti-viral drugs. . There is a lack of atomic-resolution 3D structures for these proteins. This proposal addresses the need for 3D structures to advance detailed mechanistic understanding of these important molecules. . The mechanism of active transport (i.e. nature of the ion that is co-transported) is not known and will be investigated. . Successful completion of the aims of the proposal will fill these gaps in our knowledge that could inform the design of new drugs that can enter target cells more easily through these transporters and improve bioavailability.

imp_text: The proposal seeks to address a major, unresolved challenge in the study of protein aggregation diseases such as Alzheimer’s: that the timescale for in vivo aggregation can span years to decades. This challenge has been partially addressed by experimental approaches by altering the experimental conditions for in vitro studies so as to accelerate the process, which necessarily leads to questions about the transferability of the resulting conclusions to the actual in vivo processes. The situation is also difficult for computational approaches, where analytic theories that can address such long timescales lack microscopic basis, while atomically-detailed simulations fall many orders of magnitude short of the timescales of the present inadequate experimental approaches. The PI therefore seeks to combine results of atomically-detailed simulations with analytic theory. A key obstacle to the success of the approach is the PI’s lack of previous experience with atomically-detailed simulations. Relevant methodological details and preliminary data are also lacking in the proposal. Since this portion of the proposed work is critical to the development of the desired combined model, it is raises questions about the likelihood of successful accomplishment of the project goals.
sig_text_str: . Successful completion of the project has the potential to substantially expand understanding of the molecular details that govern protein aggregation and determine the propensity of particular peptides and not others to form aggregates that cause diseases such as Alzheimer’s
inv_text_str: . The PI has had extensive training and a history of successful publication to support the analytic component of model development. Collaborating scientists have strong publication records in their respective areas (experimental studies of peptides, and molecular dynamics simulations).
inv_text_wkn: . The PI lacks expertise to carry out or direct the atomically-detailed molecular dynamics simulations that are a critical component of the proposal. Furthermore, no training plan is presented to help the PI gain the appropriate necessary expertise.
inn_text_str: . The combination of a developed analytical model with new data from atomically-detailed molecular dynamics simulations is an important innovative approach and can establish a new class of models to study these aggregating systems.
app_text_str: . The PI has already made major strides forward in the analytic component of the model. The PI’s training has laid a strong foundation for this achievement, as demonstrated by previous publications and the data included in the present proposal. Colleagues with complementary strengths (experimental studies of peptide aggregation; atomically-detailed molecular dynamics simulations) have been identified and each has a strong history of publications and funding in their areas of expertise.
app_text_wkn: . Atomically-detailed molecular dynamics simulations will be a critical component of the success of the proposal. imp_text: This is new exciting proposal by an early stage investigator describes studies aimed at adding much needed understanding for the biochemical and molecular basis of chromosomal recombination and segregation during meiosis in yeast. The PI chose to focus on a small set of proteins that are important players in the process. The detailed biochemical, structural and biophysical characterization of these factors proposed are nicely planned out and described. They also play well to the investigator’s strengths. Most importantly, the proposed studies utilize well-defined reconstituted approaches that are likely to provide a high-resolution view of the meiosis machinery. The PI also appears to have recruited collaborators to tackle some of the studies. The in vitro studies are nicely complemented by the in vivo studies. As a postdoctoral fellow with Stephen Harrison, the investigator used these approaches to successfully study the monopolin complex. In aim 1, the PI plans to expand on these studies by exploring the hypothesis that the complex mediates co-orientation of sister kinetochore through interactions with its head. The aim combines a carefully designed set of experiments that combine X-ray crystallography, functional, protein engineering and in vivo studies to look at the architecture of the complex and its interaction with protein partners and how changes affect its function in the cell during meiosis. Aim 2 focuses on the biochemical characterization of the factor Hop1 and its role in mediating recombination. Again this aim, combines in vitro and in vivo studies; here to examine the structure of Hop1 and its conformational flexibility, its binding partners and how changing these properties affect meiotic recombination in yeast. In aim 3, the investigator plans to study the synaptonemal complex and in particular how potential oligomerization of zip 1, a component of the complex, and its interaction with SUMO affect the assembly of the complex. Overall, the proposal was nicely written and addresses a topic of high importance and interest. The PI has had productive graduate and postdoctoral training and confidence is high that he is capable of carrying out the proposed studies. Findings from this proposal are likely to lay a foundation for future work on homologous recombination and chromosome segregation during meiosis.

This proposal focuses on exploring the detailed molecular mechanism of some of the factors involved during the events of meiosis I and how they affect chromosome recombination and segregation. . Defects in meiosis I could lead to aneuploidies, which in some instances lead to human disorders. Investigating the role of the different factors could result in a better understanding of the origin of these disorders.

imp_text: This is a new exciting submission from an established investigator. The proposal addresses the fundamental biological process of replication initiation in humans. In particular, the proposed studies are focused on the biochemical characterization of replicative proteins known to associate with the large helicase complex of CMG. The proposal outlines a careful analysis of the interactions between these protein factors and the replication fork complex and how these interactions mediate the helicase and replication activities of the complex. The proposal builds on strong preliminary data for all aims. The recent discovery by the PI that biotin-dUMP is efficiently incorporated by hPold and hPola but not by hPole is potentially tremendously useful for the in vitro characterization of leading and lagging strand synthesis. This in principle could paint a more focused picture of the replication fork. Findings from these experiments are likely to provide key information about how different factors contribute to the synthesis of each strand and whether their contribution is strand specific. In aim 1, the PI plans to establish the activities of hPold and hPole. using biotin-dUTP as a substrate in leading and lagging strand synthesis in vitro using purified components. Once these activities are established, the studies will focus on exploring whether replication factors have strand-specific activities during replication. This aim plays to the PI’s strength in biochemical reconstitutions of complex biological machines. Recent studies in yeast have identified a set of replicative factors that interact with the replication complex. Aim 2 expands on these studies by characterizing their human homologues. The proposed studies address the interaction between these factors and the CMG complex and how intermolecular and intramolecular interaction affect the activity of the complex in vitro. These interactions will also be validated in vivo using a PLA assay. Again, the preliminary data for this aim is quite extensive and showcases the feasibility of the proposed studies. Finally in aim 3, the PI proposes to study how mutations in Psf1 (a subunit of GINS complex), which has been associated with developmental and immunological defects, affect complex formation, its helicase and replication activities. In general, the proposal studies are carefully planned and well described. The topic is significant as it addresses a fundamental biological problem. The PI’s is group is one of the few that has been doing these sort of studies using reconstituted human factors. Findings from the proposed studies are more than likely to shed key insights into the replication process and how different factors affect the activity of the replication fork.

Understanding the role of different factors in the assembly and function of the replicative complexes is important. The proposal uses a reductive approach to study this process in vitro, which is likely to provide a high resolution view of the contribution of the different factors to replication. . Many of the studies in the DNA replication field use model organisms like yeast. The studies proposed here focus on the controlled characterization of the human proteins, which, although homologous to the ones in yeast, appear to fulfill slightly different functions. These in vitro studies are likely to reveal some important clues of how different factors interact with the replication machinery and modulate its activity. The studies are also nicely complemented by in vivo experiments aimed at validating these interactions. . Studies in aim 3 are also novel as they address how mutations in Psf1 seen in patients affect the activity of the CMG complex. They include careful biochemical characterization that are likely to provide some hints on the pathology of some of these diseases that have been associated with Psf1.

imp_text: This is a new exciting submission from an established investigator who has made significant contributions to the field of ribosome biogenesis. Recent studies by the PI’s group have identified a set of conserved protein factors that are involved in the early events of small ribosomal subunit biogenesis. In this proposal, the PI proposes to extend these studies by adding mechanistic insights into the order of events that must take place to go from the pre-ribosome particle to the pre-40S particle using yeast as a model organism. In particular, the PI proposes to explore the model that 1) the protein factors Imp4 and Imp3 bind the U3 snoRNA to unwind it so it can anneal to pre-RNA 2) Bud23, a methyl transferase, binds the complex and activates the RNA helicase Ecm16, 3) Ecm16 dissociates the U3 snoRNA, which opens the site for Rps2 binding, 4) the pre-40S particle is released post cleavage at A2 and Bud23 dissociates. In aim 1, the PI proposes to explore the role of the essential DEAH-box ATP-dependent RNA helicase in removing the U3 snoRNA from pre-ribosome particle. The proposal takes advantage of a number of biochemical approaches to purify intermediates at different stages of the process using different Ecm16 variants followed by proteomic and RNA analysis. Changes in complex compositions will be also accompanied by structural probing of the pre rRNA to gain an understanding of the structural changes induced by Ecm16. Aim2 expands on these studies through in vitro characterization of Ecm16 ATPase and helicase function using model RNAs. The goal of these studies is to test the hypothesis that Bud23 activates Ecm16. Preliminary data from the PI and his collaborator has found that many of the mutations that suppress the bud23. phenotype to map to the RNA chaperone Imp4, which is known to interact with U3 snoRNA. In the third aim, the PI plans to test whether these mutations in Imp4 reduce its binding to the snoRNA. By engineering mutations into U3 snoRNA, the PI also wishes to test the hypothesis that reducing the affinity of Bud23 to U3 suppresses the bud23. phenotype. Finally the PI plans to carry out a genetic screen to identify rps2 mutants that interact with bud32 in an effort to delineate a functional role for the interaction between rps2 and the central pseudoknot in the pre-40S particle. Overall, the proposal builds on strong preliminary data and is likely to add some insight into the mechanism of ribosome biogenesis in eukaryotes. The PI has made significant contributions to the field and has recruited a key collaborator to tackle the U3 snoRNA interaction. The enthusiasm was a little tempered by the significance of some of the proposed studies. On one hand, the first aim addresses important questions regarding the pathway of pre-40S ribosome assembly and is more than likely to shed some light onto the composition of the different intermediates and the associated conformational changes. On the other hand, the studies proposed in the fourth aim are incremental as they tackle the detailed interactions between the different protein and RNA partners.
sig_text_str: . Ribosome biogenesis is a fundamental process in all-living organisms. The proposal addresses a key early step, during which the pre ribosome particle is processed into pre 40S particle. . The proposal seeks to establish the biochemical role for a number of factors in mediating the processing of pre rRNA using a variety of approaches. Although the investigator has previously identified a number of these factors as playing a role in ribosome biogenesis, their precise contribution to the process is lacking. The proposed studies address these important questions head by utilizing a variety of biochemical and genetics approaches. These studies are poised to add much needed understanding to the order of events that have to take place during early steps of ribosome biogenesis. . Ribosome synthesis is a highly regulated process and certain cancers exploit some of these regulatory steps to increase ribosome production. The proposed studies have the potential to provide some key information about how the process is regulated and whether it is relevant in certain cancers. .
sig_text_wkn: . Some of the proposed studies, especially in aim 2 and 3, appear to be incremental and are not likely to add much to our understanding of ribosome biogenesis. The experiments that could potentially contribute to the field appear to have been carried out and the bulk of the experiments are aimed at getting the finer details of the interactions between the factors. . It is unclear from the proposal what sort of larger impact the studies are likely to have to the field of ribosome biogenesis.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an established investigator at the university of Texas, where he has been for more than two decades. His group continues to contribute to the field of ribosome biogenesis. They have recently ordered the events of cytoplasmic maturation of the 40S subunit and identified a translocation-like cycle that monitors the functional status of the ribosome. Relevant to the proposal here is the group’s recent discovery of Bud32 being genetically and biochemically linked to the export of the small subunit. . The co-PI is appropriate for the collaboration proposed for the work on the U3 snoRNA.
inn_text_str: . Studies in aim 1 focused on the characterization of the composition and structural changes to the pre-ribosome and pre-40S particles are clever. By using different Ecm16 variants, the authors plan to trap complexes at different states and analyze the composition using mass spec and footprinting to probe the RNA structure. These experiments will yield snap shots of the assembly and biogenesis pathway of the ribosome and provide a catalogue of assembly factors and ribosomal proteins that are recruited to the ribosome during different stages of ribosome biogenesis. . Ribosome dysfunction has been associated with a number of diseases. Indeed, increased production of ribosomes is a hallmark of many types of cancers. The proposed studies take advantage of the easy to manipulate model organism yeast to look at ribosome assembly and its quality control. The findings are likely to be transformative and tell us something about how the process might be sped up, for example in cancers.
inn_text_wkn: . Some of the proposed studies are arguably low resolution. Some of these experiments are more amenable to cryoEM approaches. As a result, the proposal could have benefited from having a structural biologist as a collaborator. . While some of the proposed genetic screens are likely to identify new factors in the assembly pathways, it is unclear how much mechanistic insight will be gained by these approaches.

study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function B Study Section
imp_text: The PI proposes to elucidate CLOCK:BMAL1 activity and its interactions with activators and repressors to develop a mechanism for CLOCK:BMAL1 involvement in circadian rhythm.  Pursuit of this project is worthwhile, considering CLOCK:BMAL1’s involvement in homeostasis and cancer activity. The PI has the necessary expertise to carry out this project and has sought collaborators with proven track records.  Of some concern is potential overlap of the PI’s proposed work and that of his former postdoctoral mentor.  While not particularly innovative in terms of the approach, it does make a strong effort to combine in vitro and in vivo studies.  The approach is the strength of the proposal with two specific aims, each focusing on the different proteins in the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex.  The proposed investigations follow a logical path to study activation/repression of the two proteins in CLOCK:BMAL1.  Potential pitfalls are outlined and discussed.  If the work is concluded in both specific aims, a clear picture of CLOCK:BMAL1 activity will be developed.  While the data will not have a direct impact on clinical or therapeutic studies, the scientific knowledge generated in this work will provide a sound foundation for such investigations.  The institutional commitment at UC Santa Cruz is strong.
sig_text_str: The work described in this proposal would address the lack of understanding of CLOCK:BMAL1 complex activity.  The ultimate goal of the PI and collaborators is an understanding of CLOCK:BMAL1’s role in circadian rhythms and homeostasis.  The work described is necessary to develop a mechanistic understanding of CLOCK:BMAL1 and will provide a thorough understanding of CLOCK:BMAL1 activity.
sig_text_wkn: The data would ultimately be used in clinical research or the design of therapeutic strategies to activate or repress CLOCK:BMAL1.  While it is clear how scientific knowledge will be improved, the impact on biomedical practice is not in the immediate future.
inv_text_str: • The PI is well prepared for this work.  The PI is an expert in NMR spectroscopy and its use to determine biopolymer structure after his postdoctoral positions.  The PI’s publication record reflects this. • Collaborators bring necessary skills to provide required materials (proteins, etc.) and support.
inv_text_wkn: • The PI does not have a significant amount of prior grant activity.  This is probably to be expected for a young investigator. • Of more concern is potential research conflict and overlap with the PI’s postdoctoral mentor (Takahashi).  Takahashi is a CLOCK:BMAL1 expert.  While the PI feels no conflict will arise, the proposal seems geared to fully explore the dynamics of CLOCK:BMAL1.  It is hard to imagine the PI will not be competing in some form with his postdoctoral mentor. • Additionally, there is no conflict resolution in the leadership plan mentioned between PI and collaborators. • Also, there is some worry that the PI (3 calendar months effort), one graduate student (~50% effort over 12 calendar months on Aim 2), a newly hired postdoc (100% effort on Aim 1 for 12 calendar months), and one technician (12 calendar months) will be able to accomplish all goals of the proposal.
inn_text_str: The proposal describes a worthwhile investigation of CLOCK:BMAL1 using standard biochemical techniques and instrumentation including NMR spectroscopy, isothermal titration calorimetry, and fluorescence microscopy.  Biophysical measurements are merged with in vivo studies in cells.
inn_text_wkn: The approach is not necessarily innovative.  It combines standard biophysical and molecular biology techniques to investigate a worthwhile problem.
app_text_str: • The proposal outlines a well-designed approach with two specific aims.  Specific aim one focuses on conformational changes in BMAL1 and investigates the roles of activators (p300/CBP) and repressors (CRY 1/2) on BMAL1 conformational switching.  Specific aim two investigates CLOCK Exon 19 binding activity and how it regulates CLOCK:BMAL1 activity. • The specific aims are independent on one another and only merge together when both specific aims are completed to generate a picture of activator/repressor-induced conformational changes in CLOCK:BMAL1 and how that influences CLOCK:BMAL1 activity. • Also notable is the use of both in vitro and in vivo studies to relate biophysical measurements with CLOCK:BMAL1 activity in cells. Potential pitfalls are outlined and discussed.
app_text_wkn: • The work seems feasible, but the limited number of researchers is worrisome (see Investigators). • Also concerning is the acknowledgement that the ability of PASD1 to repress CLOCK:BMAL1 activity could arise independent of MLL1 association.  Wouldn’t genome-wide screens be useful whether the hypothesis is correct or not?
env_text_str: The PI has access to necessary instrumentation as well as lab space.  Institutional commitment to the project is strong (NMR spectrometers housed as UC Santa Cruz, etc.).
env_text_wkn: • While PI has preferential access to NMR spectrometers, it is not clear user demand on the instruments and any wait times for experiments when spectrometers are in use. • Also, it is not clear how wait times on instrumentation shared with other investigators at UC Santa Cruz could impact the PI’s progress.

study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function D Study Section
imp_text: The PI proposes to conduct both theoretical and computational studies of protein aggregation.  This project is worthwhile, considering protein aggregation involved in Parkinson’s diseases, Huntington’s disease, and prion-induced diseases.  Both the PI and main collaborator have the necessary expertise to see this project forward.  However, there is no leadership or conflict resolution plan.  The theoretical and computational studies in the proposal will help explore the long timescale of protein aggregation and unify many in vitro experiments of protein aggregation.  Two specific aims are proposed.  The first seeks to develop a protein aggregation phase diagram which could be of immense use to protein researchers.  Unfortunately, the theoretical basis does not seem very specific.  How will different denaturants (or stabilizers not considered by the PI) affect hydrogen bonding on-off rates?  How will the values of parameters in the theory be set?  Specific aim two seeks to develop a model of protein aggregation using novel molecular dynamics simulations, but it is not clear how this data would be used by the scientific community or biomedical researchers.  KSU has provided the necessary environment for successful pursuit of this proposal.
sig_text_str: . Since the timescale for protein aggregation in diseases such as Alzheimer’s, Huntington’s, and prion diseases is on the order of decades in vivo, direct study of aggregate formation in vitro is untenable.  Therefore, in silico methods provide an alternative to study nucleation and growth of protein aggregates under physiological conditions. . The work described will provide the theoretical framework necessary to understand nucleation and aggregate growth pathways in vitro and extend these observations to in vivo processes under physiological conditions. . Theories developed in this work could impact therapeutic protocols and describe initiation of such diseases as Alzheimer’s, Huntington’s, and prion diseases.
sig_text_wkn: . In the first specific aim, it is clear that a protein aggregation phase diagram could be of immense use to therapeutic or clinical researchers.  However, it is not clear how data from the second specific aim would be used.  It would certainly advance scientific knowledge in this field, but it use seems limited.

There is no mention of the number of months per year the two postdoctoral research associates and two graduate students to be hired for this project will dedicate to the project. . app_text_str: . Dr. Sullivan has preliminary theoretical results on fibril growth rates that are directly applicable to this project.  These results lay the ground work for this project. . study_section: Macromolecular Structure and Function D Study Section
imp_text: The proposal seeks funding for BMRB, a noteworthy and extremely valuable resource for the NMR and structural biology communities.  The archival of protein and nucleic acid NMR data in BMRB will help facilitate investigations into structure-function relationships, clinical research, and therapeutic design at other institutions.  A large portion of the budget is dedicated to BMRB staff, although the staff has been together for many years and has a proven track record of success.  BMRB projects indicated in the proposal are sound and necessary for the continued growth of BMRB.  However, the research plan is not fully developed, only hinting at potential projects in some areas.  Additionally, no timeline is indicated to prioritize projects as well as set time expectations for some of the more nebulous ideas in the proposal.  The University of Wisconsin-Madison has dedicated space to the project for many years and will continue to do so.
sig_text_str: • The proposal outlines the significant role BMRB (Biological Magnetic Resonance data Bank) plays in archiving NMR spectroscopic-determined structures and constants of proteins and nucleic acids along with the retrieval and visualization of this data to the scientific public. • As a public data archive, BMRB contains quantitative NMR data on proteins and nucleic acids that are needed by researchers at other institutions to develop forcefields for computer simulations, structure prediction algorithms, and data collection and analysis protocols. • Many journals now require deposition of investigator NMR data into BMRB as part of the publication process. • If the aims of this proposal are met, NMR data deposition and acquisition will be streamlined, protocols to mine the archive will be enhanced, and integration of NMR data with the wwPDB will continue.
sig_text_wkn: The project will have no immediate impact clinical or biomedical practice.  Instead, the greatest impact in this area will come from other investigators that use the BMRB for structure-function relationships.
inv_text_str: • It is not clear why PI Baker is listed as a New, Early Stage Investigator when he has been awarded numerous NIH grants in the past. • PI Baker has more than enough capability to carry out this project.  PI Baker has been head of the BMRB since 1988. • Prof. Losev is director of the CHTC which will provide infrastructure for the BMRB. • Elmer Ursler has been Director of BMRB since 1994 and is well qualified to continue to direct the BMRB. • Collaborator Yehor Ioannou, now at the University of Athens, has been involved in BMRB and will continue to develop search and query systems for the NMR data. • Sufficient support staff are also listed. • To summarize, the BMRB has the necessary leadership and intellectual capital to continue.
inv_text_wkn: No clear leadership plan is presented, as well as conflict resolution.  However, given the time the main investigators and collaborators have worked together, it is probably not necessary.
inn_text_str: • It is difficult to decouple BMRB innovation from the innovation of outside investigators that use the archive to generate tools to study and predict biopolymer structure.  Without the BMRB, much of this outside innovation could not germinate. • The BMRB’s NMR-STAR ontology and data format adopted by the NMR community indicates BMRB plays a leadership role among NMR spectroscopists.  The advancement of this data format will integrate structural, dynamic, and chemical information.  This information is valuable to current structural biologists and will help train the next generation of NMR spectroscopists. • BMRB and PDBe software to annotate and validate NMR structure depositions will be very useful to the NMR community.
inn_text_wkn: Much of the innovation that arises from BMRB comes from investigators outside the BMRB that use the NMR data archive to develop tools for structure prediction and peak assignments.
app_text_str: • The proposal has two specific aims.  The first seeks to improve the deposition and extraction of NMR data, adopt NMR validation tools for peak shifts, and develop a query system to mine the archive.  The second specific aim focuses on integration of NMR data of proteins and nucleic acids in the wwPDB archive. • The two specific aims are independent of one another, so both may be pursued simultaneously. • Both specific aims are also synergistic and are designed to make NMR spectroscopy data on proteins and nucleic acids more readily available to the scientific community.
app_text_wkn: • If the BMRB existed solely as a data archive, it would serve as a great resource for structural biologists.  However, its expansion and development in this proposal is not well defined. • For instance, in Section 1.d.3, the PI mentions that methods will be pursued for checking reasonableness of NMR data, but specific  methods or models are not provided. • In Section 1.d.4.1, the PI mentions that implementation of data visualization tools “may require” significant updates to the DEVise engine.  If there are significant updates, no timeline is provided to predict when these updates may be completed.  It is also not clear how diverting resources to these updates may impact other BMRB projects. • The second specific aim does not follow the same formatting as the first specific aim that had a fourth “Research” section.  Instead, much of the research is found in the “Approach” section in the second specific aim.  Section 2.c.2.3.2 contains phrases that “useful statistical parameters” and “theoretically sound methods must be found” for the evaluation of structural models against NMR chemical shift data, but no specifics are given as to what parameters or methods are to b used.  Additionally, the PI mentions “Research into these questions” regarding dynamics information in validation and structure determination could be productive, but is not clear what that that research would entail. • There are no pitfalls discussed or fallback options if the certain approaches do not work (see bullet points above).  There is no timetable for the projects mentioned in the proposal.

Will the CHTC continue to maintain the clusters for the BMRB?

imp_text: The circadian clock controls the rhythmic gene expression and cellular function, disturbance of which may lead to cancer and other diseases. The proposed work is thus highly significant as it will determine the structural and biochemical basis for regulation of CLOCK:BMAL1 complex that is a master transcription factor regulating rhythmic expression of 15% of genome. The PI is an Early Stage Investigator who has excellent training and publication record and thereby is capable to lead the project with helps from the experienced collaborators. All the required major equipment is available to the PI’s lab that already has a graduate student and technician dedicated to the project. The strength of the research design comes from the multidiscipline approaches ranged from structural determination to functional characterization in vitro as well as in cells. The weakness is lack of alternative models for potential regulatory interactions and drawbacks associated with overexpression of the target proteins. Overall this is a strong proposal from a new investigator with outcomes expected to impact the circadian field not only in terms of molecular mechanisms but also implications to cancer.
sig_text_str: . The circadian clock regulates cellular activities with 24-hour rhythms that coincide with the solar day. CLOCK:BMAL1 is a circadian transcription factor that directs the rhythmic transcription of 15% of the genome. The proposed research will advance our mechanistic understanding of this key molecular oscillator by investigating the structural and biochemical basis for its alternating interaction with transcriptional coactivators and repressors. . The circadian clock may be deregulated to increase cancer cell proliferation. The proposal will use a newly identified protein PASD1 that is upregulated in colon and perhaps breast cancers and represses the CLOCK:BMAL1 activity to address this possibility by studying PASD1 interaction with this transcription factor and competition for a coactivator, and impact on rhythmic gene expression in colon and breast cancer cells.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an Early Stage Investigator who has been trained as a NMR spectroscopist, and published seven high impact papers including the most recent first-author Science paper for the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex. The PI has started a lab two years ago and now has a graduate student and a technician who have been trained to conduct the proposed experiments. In addition a postdoc will be recruited to do the other experiments including using NMR to solve protein structures. . Three collaborators will help the PI to complete the project by providing reagents that are required for the PI’s experiments and conducting experiments that cannot be done by the PI. A contributor will work with the PI to train the graduate student and postdoc to do the NMR experiments. They all promised 0.5 calendar month effort to the project.
inv_text_wkn: . It is unclear how the proposed NMR experiments for aim 1 will be divided between the PI and the postdoc.
inn_text_str: . The project will test a novel hypothesis that a cis/trans isomerization of a conserved X-Pro imide bond regulates the binding of an activator or a repressor to the C-terminal transactivation domain of BMAL1. NMR will be used to solve the structures of the cis and trans C-TAD conformers. The binding interface between the conformers and the activator/repressor will be mapped and the binding affinity measured. The cis/trans conformation equilibrium will be perturbed by mutations and peptidyl prolyl isomerases to assess the effect on the transcriptional activity. . Similar to the C-TAD of BMAL1, the Exon 19 domain of CLOCK binds both activator and repressor. Interestingly the PI discovered that PASD1 protein that shares sequence similarity with the Exon 19 is upregulated in colon cancer, and represses the CLOCK:BMAL1 activity in human embryonic kidney cell line and associates with CLOCK:BMAL1 in a CC1, the Exon 19-like domain, dependent manner. This leads to novel hypotheses that the Exon 19 domain can sample multiple conformations but is locked into a specific one when bound to the activator or repressor, and that PASD1 competes with the activator for binding to CLOCK:BMAL1 to repress its activity. To test this hypothesis they will study the interactions of purified Exon 19 domain with its binding partners including peptides from the activator and repressor as well as PASD1 protein or CC1 domain. In addition, the effect of PASD1 expression on the CLOCK:BMAL1 activity will be studied in colon and breast cancer cell lines.
inn_text_wkn: . The biophysical, biochemical and cellular techniques are all well-established. No new techniques will be developed.
app_text_str: . High quality NMR data have already been obtained for the C-TAD of BMAL1; thus, solving the structures of the cis and trans conformers is feasible. In particular, the conformer with the C-terminal seven residues looped back to contact the predicted IxxLL helix may be more stable for the structure determination. The mutagenesis experiments will follow to break this potential intramolecular contact, and more importantly to generate all trans or mostly cis conformer that will be verified by NMR. . The cell based systems proposed in Aim 1c are complimentary. While the endogenous BMAL1 in 293T cells may complicate the interpretation of the activity data from  the BMAL1 C-TAD all trans-mutant, the bmal1-/- clock reporter cell line that will be constructed should reduce the background activity. . Aim 2a will use similar methodology to identify the minimal domains of MLL1 and CIPC that bind the Exon 19 domain, and characterize the bindings by NMR, ITC and co-IP. These experiments are feasible.
app_text_wkn: . In vivo CLOCK and BMAL1 form a complex that binds either activator or inhibitor. Most of the proposed binding experiments will use either protein in the absence of the other one. How the results can be extrapolated to the CLOCK:BMAL1 dimer is not known. In particular can the dimer binds to two coactivators, two repressors, or one each simultaneously? . In Aim 1B, CRY1 and p300 minimal fragments that can bind BMAL1 C-TAD and the full-length CRY1 and p300 proteins were use interchangeably, which makes assessment of the experimental design difficult. However, the approaches, pull-down, ITC and NMR to quantify the binding and map the binding site are standard, and should work if the binding affinity is sufficient. But the concentration ranges of the proteins required for these binding assays to get meaningful results were not discussed. Moreover, for the co-IP experiment to confirm the physiological relevance of the in vitro observed interactions, the concentrations of the binding proteins must be at the physiological range, which may not be reached by the proposed transient transfection. Also, how does one know the transiently expressed BMAL1 is in complex with the endogenous CLOCK while it binds to CRY or p300? . Generation of the cis and trans conformer specific polyclonal antibodies in Aim 1D seems risky. Using them to determine the temporal kinetics of this X-Pro isomerization switch is possible, but western blot analysis to determine the cis/trans conformer ratio is semi-quantitative to the best, and manipulation prior to the analysis such as cell lysis may artificially impact the results. . The Aim 2A seems falling short by not investigating the functional significance of the identified antagonistic interaction of MLL1 and CIPC with CLOCK. . The preliminary data in Fig 5b shows that PASD1 binds the CLOCK:BMAL1 heterodimer, but not the monomers. Therefore the binding site for PASD1 must only be present in the heterodimer. The PI hypothesizes that the C-terminal region of CLOCK and/or BMAL1 is the binding site for PASD1, and proposed to use the C-terminal truncation mutants to test the hypothesis. However, the mutant will be co-expressed with its full-length binding partner (e.g., CLOCK deltaC mutant with full-length BMAL1). Then if PASD1 can bind the C-terminal of either CLOCK or BMAL1 in the heterodimer, the results from these binding assays will be all positive, but the conclusion that both C-terminal domains are not required for PASD1 binding cannot be drawn. . PASD1 contain a CC1 domain that is similar to the Exon 19 domain of CLOCK which may bind to MLL1 and CIPC, the coactivator and repressor. Is it possible that PASD1 uses the CC1 domain to bind MLL1 or CIPC to affect the activity of CLOCK:BMAL1?

Other biophysical instruments such as ITC and CD are also available. Intellectual environment at UCSC is rich to facilitate the project and the development of the PI and trainees.

imp_text: Protein aggregation is a major cause of aging diseases such as Alzheimer’s. The physical mechanisms of protein aggregation revealed in vitro currently cannot be extrapolated to in vivo conditions without appropriate theoretical models that have sufficient resolution and molecular dynamics simulations at longer time scale. The proposal will develop both, and test the resulting models and algorithms by experiments in a model system. The PI has been well trained for most of the proposed work and collaborators have been recruited to cover the other required expertise.  The approaches were reasonable and feasible with the available computational tools. The enthusiasm was, however, dampened by lack of details for the proposed bench experiments that would specifically test the predictions from the models and simulations and thereby validate and refine the theories.
sig_text_str: . Alzheimer’s and other diseases are caused by the formation of intracellular protein aggregates in a timescale of decades, which prevents direst studies of the aggregation process in vivo. While aggregation kinetics has been investigated in vitro under non-physiological conditions that accelerate the process, it is not known how to extrapolate the results to the in vivo process. Detailed theoretical models and computer simulations could provide solutions to this problem, which is the objective of the proposed work
sig_text_wkn: . It was claimed that the theories of protein aggregation will find other applications such as dynamics of intrinsically disordered proteins and stability of therapeutic proteins, which is a bit of exaggeration without knowing what the theories are and their generalizability.
inv_text_str: . The PI is an Early Stage Investigator who had extensively trainings in theoretical biophysics of biopolymerization including amyloid peptide. He has published eight first-author papers in prestigious journals like PNAS, JACS and JCP. . Dr. Tanney is an expert in peptide aggregation filed, and will supervise a graduate student from the PI’s lab to perform the bench work to test the theories. . Dr. Cong has the expertise to train a postdoc from the PI’s lab to run the MD simulations.
inv_text_wkn: . No calendar month effort was mentioned for key collaborators Drs. Tanney and Cong. . All the postdocs and graduates students for the project are TBD, which raised the question whether the proposed work can be accomplished on time.
inn_text_str: . Theories of protein aggregation have struggled with a tradeoff between resolution and accessible timescales. The proposal will first use high resolution microscopic models to identify the rate limiting steps of aggregation process, and then develop computational methods to access long timescales using targeted simulations on the rate limiting steps.
inn_text_wkn: . This approach has been accomplished in protein folding field; thereby, it is not entirely new.
app_text_str: . In Aim 1, statistical models will be developed to explore how protein sequence, concentration and solution conditions will impact the aggregation kinetics. The end product is a “kinetic phase diagram” that predicts how aggregate formation rates and shapes would depend on experimental conditions, and that is said to be a prerequisite to extrapolate in vitro experimental results toward physiological conditions and pathological timescales. . In Aim 2, a new algorithm will be developed to simulate amyloid formation that involves large number of molecules and very long timescales, and the simulation results will be tested using a small peptide model system.
app_text_wkn: . The theoretical models will be tested and refined against experiments of a model peptide system. But what predictions from the models will be verified by what experiments was not described. Numerous biochemical and physical measurements will be used to monitor the rate and size of the peptide aggregates. However, the experimental details were not provided. . Without a kinetic phase diagram, it is difficult to imaging this end product and how it would link the in vitro data to in vivo process. . Different words were used to describe protein aggregates such as fibril and oligomer, and their interactions such as nucleation and lateral association. To a non-expert, what do these words mean? Cartoon representations like Figure 3 would help. . From the short description, it seems that only the elongation rates will be measured in the model system with different peptides. But there will be many other outcomes from the new algorithm and simulations. How these predictions will be verified was not mentioned.
